setup: You're Nadine Alvarado, emailing the daycare owner after a near-miss pickup mistake involving Mia and asking what happened and what changes are being made.

a.text:
Hi Nadine,

I’m writing back because I understand your concern, and I take it seriously.

Yesterday, a substitute helper didn’t recognize the person trying to pick up Mia. She stopped and called you to confirm before releasing her, which is why nothing happened–but I agree she shouldn’t have gotten that far. That’s a failure in our process, and it’s on me.

Going forward, anyone picking up a child who isn’t immediately recognizable must show ID at the door before any call home. I’m retraining that substitute and she won’t work here again until she’s demonstrated she knows the updated procedure.

I know this is unsettling, and I appreciate you bringing it to my attention. Please let me know if you’d like to discuss.

Best,  
Daycare Owner

b.text:
Nadine,

I’m glad you emailed, and I’m sorry you had that call. You’re right to be upset—it’s a terrifying thing to get a call like that about your child.

Here’s what happened yesterday: our substitute helper was at the door when someone came for Mia. She didn’t recognize the person, so she stopped and called you to confirm before Mia was released. That’s why you got the call and why Mia stayed here. But you’re absolutely right that it shouldn’t have gotten that far. The person should never have been brought to Mia or put in a position where we were calling you to verify someone at the door. No child goes with anyone who isn’t on the approved pickup list, and an unfamiliar person has to be checked against that list before we even get the child. The sub skipped that step because she didn’t know the routine well enough.

Since yesterday I’ve added an ID check at the door: anyone picking up has to show ID, and we check it against the approved list before the child is brought out. No exceptions, even for people we know. I’m also retraining the substitute on the pickup policy, and she won’t be working pickup again until I’m confident she has it. I’m going over the same procedure with my regular helper so everyone is doing it the same way.

I’m not going to minimize this. It shook me too. If you want to sit down and go over Mia’s approved pickup list with me, or just talk through it in person, I’m here.

Thank you for coming to me directly.

[Your name]

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer After 8 Months of Market Sourdough

I bought the Corlane SM6 last March because my old mixer started dying on 1,200-gram batches of stiff bagel dough. I bake almost every day for the Saturday market: two or three loads of sourdough, plus bagels twice a week. The SM6 has been on the counter the entire time.

The motor is the reason to consider this machine. A double batch of 65% hydration bagel dough (about 1.8 kg of very stiff stuff) never made it hesitate. No stalling, no overheating, no that-smell-of-hot-plastic. It just chewed through it on speed 2 for eight minutes. KitchenAid’s equivalent 5-quart bowl-lift would have been screaming by minute four. That extra torque is real.

Two problems showed up fast. The bowl-lift lever started squeaking after six weeks. I hit it with WD-40 once a month and it stays quiet for three weeks, then starts again. Annoying, not fatal. Worse: the stock dough hook is too short for the deep bowl. On a 900-gram loaf it barely reaches the bottom third of the dough. I ordered a third-party spiral hook ($28) and that fixed it. Corlane should have shipped the right length in the first place.

Price: $429. That’s $80 more than the KitchenAid Professional 5 Plus that most people would compare it to. You’re paying for the extra power and the bigger bowl. If you mostly mix cookie dough and cake batter, that extra money is wasted. Those jobs don’t need this motor.

If you knead heavy dough every week—sourdough, bagels, pizza, pretzels—buy it. The motor earns the extra $80. If that’s not you, skip it and get the KitchenAid. I wouldn’t own anything else at this point.

b.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: 8 Months of Nearly Daily Use

**Quick take:** The motor is worth the money. The accessories aren't. Full verdict at the bottom.

---

I've been running the Corlane SM6 for eight months now, and it gets used almost every day. I bake sourdough for a weekend farmers market stall, so this isn't a "unboxed it and made two batches of banana bread" review — this machine has mixed hundreds of batches of dough since it landed on my counter. Here's what eight months of hard use looks like.

## The motor is the whole reason to buy this mixer

The test that kills most home stand mixers is stiff, low-hydration dough — and I run the SM6 through that test constantly. A double batch of bagel dough, stiff enough that plenty of consumer mixers would stall out or walk themselves across the counter, runs through this machine without hesitation. No stalling, no straining, no standing there with my hand on the bowl waiting for it to recover. I can walk away and weigh out the next ingredient while it kneads.

If you've ever heard a mixer bog down in the middle of a bread dough, you know how quickly that becomes a dealbreaker. In eight months of near-daily bread work, the motor has never done that to me once. That is the entire case for this mixer.

## Two real problems

**The bowl lift lever squeaks.** Not a catastrophic issue, but it's a monthly maintenance item — I hit it with WD-40 about once every four weeks or it gets genuinely annoying. For a machine at this price, it shouldn't squeak out of the box, and it shouldn't squeak eight months later either.

**The included dough hook is too short for the bowl.** This is my biggest complaint. The SM6's bowl is deep, and the stock hook doesn't reach far enough down — dough at the bottom of the bowl just sits there, not getting worked in. I ended up buying a third-party hook, which solved the problem completely, but it means the hook that ships with the mixer is effectively useless for exactly the kind of dough this machine is built for. Factor that into the price.

## Speaking of price

The SM6 is $429. The comparable KitchenAid is $349. So the real math is: an $80 premium over KitchenAid, plus the cost of a replacement dough hook on top.

## Verdict

**If you're kneading heavy dough every week — bread, bagels, low-hydration anything, double batches — buy it.** The $80 premium buys you a motor that genuinely doesn't stall where other mixers in this class will, and after eight months I trust it with my market bread. Deal with the hook swap, keep a can of WD-40 under the sink, and it earns its spot on the counter.

**If your mixer mostly sees cookie dough and cake batter, skip it.** You'd be paying an $80 premium, plus a new dough hook, for a motor you'll never stress. Buy the KitchenAid and put the savings toward something else.

That's not a hedge — there's exactly one question that determines the answer, and it's whether stiff dough is a weekly event in your kitchen. For me it is, and I'd buy the SM6 again tomorrow.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
Every Saturday since tenth grade, I showed up at my family’s restaurant before the lunch rush. My hands were already familiar with the routine: wipe the counters, stock the napkins, clock in. My parents were already in the kitchen, my grandma somewhere behind the line, moving fast.

One Saturday the POS system just died. Screen went black mid-order. Customers waited. I didn’t panic. I grabbed a pen and a stack of yellow tickets, wrote out each order by hand—drinks, pho bowls, the works. A new hire watched me, confused. I just handed them a pen and said, “Copy what I write. Start with the name, then the bowl.” We ran the whole lunch rush that way. No system glitches, just orders and hands moving.

Later, I taught that same hire my grandma’s spring roll fold. Grandma never wrote it down; she just showed once, years ago, and I’ve been copying it ever since. The rice paper, the water temperature, the amount of shrimp, the roll and the tuck. I walked the new hire through it slow, showing the crease, the dip. She got it after a couple tries. I didn’t say it was about tradition or skill. I just said, “Watch the fold, then do it.” She did.

On breaks, I’d slip into the walk-in cooler. It was cold, smelling of garlic and vinegar. I’d pull out my calc textbook and try to find where I left off. Derivatives, limits, whatever was due Monday. The cooler hummed. Some nights the math felt easier than the dinner rush. Other nights I just sat there, pencil in hand, waiting for the timer on my phone so I could go back out.

I’ve worked every weekend for two years now. Some days it’s just showing up, doing the same things, over and over. I don’t have a grand conclusion about how it built my character. I just know the rhythm of the line, the feel of the pen on ticket paper, the way the numbers in my book look different after a shift. I’m tired a lot. But I’m also steady.

b.text:
The register went black around two on a Saturday. The dining room was full enough that the floor had become a maze of chairs and trays. My father pressed buttons that should not have been pressed. My mother looked at the line by the door and said, “Write it down.”

I took order slips. I knew which ones were for dine-in and which ones were for pickup, because I have done this since sophomore year. I started writing. Pho no beef. Bun cha, grilled pork, less carrot pickle. Spring rolls, six, no peanut sauce. Two plates of broken rice with egg.

setup: You're everyone at the startup. Yesterday's 40-minute outage was caused by a bad database migration during deploy.

a.text:
Hi all,

**Status first: everything is back to normal.** The outage yesterday lasted about 40 minutes (roughly 2:00–2:40pm), and we've fully fixed it. No data was lost, and there's nothing customers need to do on their end.

**What happened:** During a routine software update, one step in the process needed to make a change to our database. That change ended up locking up a piece of the system far longer than expected, which is what took us offline. Once we identified it, we reversed the change and service came right back.

**What we're changing:** These particular database changes are the risky ones. Going forward, we'll only run them during a scheduled maintenance window rather than as part of a normal update. That keeps the risk contained to a planned, low-traffic time instead of the middle of the workday.

**For anyone who fielded customer complaints:** thank you for holding the line during a frustrating stretch. If any customers are still following up, feel free to let them know the issue was a brief, resolved technical problem on our side and that everything is running normally again. Send anything you're unsure how to answer my way.

Happy to walk through more detail with anyone who's curious. Thanks for your patience yesterday.

[Your name]

b.text:
Yesterday around 2:00 PM, we had a roughly 40-minute outage. The service is fully restored, and we’ve confirmed the underlying issue is resolved.

The outage was caused by a database change included in an otherwise routine deployment. That change temporarily blocked access to a key part of the application for much longer than expected, which prevented customers from using the product normally.

We rolled back the change to restore service, then verified that everything was operating normally again. We know some of you received customer complaints during that window—thank you for handling those conversations while we worked on the fix.

To prevent this from happening again, database changes of this type will no longer run as part of normal deployments. We’ll schedule them in dedicated maintenance windows, where we can manage the risk and impact more carefully.

We’re also reviewing our deployment checks and rollback process to make sure we catch this kind of issue earlier.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
## The Market Isn’t Crashing. Sellers Are Just Still Pricing for Last Year.

If you’re watching homes sit longer this spring and wondering whether the local market has suddenly fallen apart, my answer is no.

What we are seeing is not a crash. It’s a correction in expectations.

In our ZIP code, the median days on market has gone from eight days last spring to 34 days this spring. That is a meaningful change, and sellers should take it seriously. At the same time, list prices are still up 6% year over year—even though showings per listing have dropped by about half.

Those numbers tell a very clear story: sellers are still asking more, while buyers are showing up less often. That gap is why inventory is lingering.

The problem is not that there are no buyers. There are buyers. Well-priced homes are still selling, often in under two weeks. The difference is that today’s buyers are more selective, more payment-conscious, and far less willing to chase a home that feels overpriced from the moment it hits the market.

I am seeing this firsthand. I currently have three sellers whose homes have been on the market for more than 60 days, and none of them wants to reduce the price. In each case, the resistance is understandable. They remember last spring, when homes could receive multiple offers almost immediately. They have neighbors who sold at peak enthusiasm. They see headlines about prices still being higher than last year.

But last year’s strategy does not automatically work in this year’s market.

A home can be worth more than it was a year ago and still be priced too high for today’s buyer. Those are not contradictory statements. Sellers need to stop treating last year’s sale prices as a guarantee and start treating current buyer behavior as the real market signal.

The first two weeks matter more than ever. That is when a listing gets the most attention, the most online traffic, and the strongest pool of active buyers. If a home enters the market at an aspirational price and receives limited showings, no offers, or repeated feedback about price, waiting rarely fixes the problem. It just gives buyers more reason to wonder what is wrong with it.

A listing that has been sitting for 60 days does not become more attractive because the seller holds firm. It becomes stale. And stale listings often sell for less than they would have if they had been positioned correctly from day one.

This is the market we have now: not a bargain-basement market, not a panic market, and not the frantic market of a year ago. It is a market that rewards accuracy.

Sellers who price based on what they hope to get may wait. Sellers who price based on what buyers are willing to pay are still moving. The homes selling quickly are not necessarily the cheapest homes. They are the homes that make sense for their location, condition, competition, and monthly payment.

The good news for sellers is that prices have not collapsed. Demand has not disappeared. A properly priced, well-presented home can still command serious attention. But the era of testing the market with an inflated price and expecting buyers to negotiate upward is over—for now.

The market is sending sellers a message. The smart ones are listening.

b.text:
The market has changed. A lot.

If you’ve been watching headlines and waiting for a dramatic crash, this is not that. What we’re seeing in our part of the Midwest is something much more ordinary, and honestly, more fixable: sellers are still pricing to last spring, while buyers are moving at this spring’s speed.

Here’s what the numbers are telling us in plain English. In my zip code, the median days on market has jumped from 8 days last spring to 34 days this spring. That’s a big shift. At the same time, list prices are still up 6% year over year. On paper, that sounds like a strong market. In practice, showings per listing have dropped by half.

That mismatch is the story.

A home can be beautifully updated, in a great neighborhood, and still sit if it’s priced like we’re in the frenzy of 2021 or early 2024. Buyers are not chasing the market the way they were. They’re selective. They’re comparing more homes. They’re taking their time. And they are absolutely willing to move quickly for the right house — but only when the price makes sense.

I have three sellers right now who have been on the market more than 60 days and still don’t want to adjust. I get it. Nobody likes hearing that the number they hoped for isn’t the number the market is supporting. But the market does not negotiate with our feelings. It responds to value, condition, and price. If a home is sitting, the market is telling you something. Ignoring that signal doesn’t make the message go away.

What’s frustrating is that some sellers are treating a slower sale as a sign that buyers are “broken” or that the market is weak. That’s not what this is. The buyers are there. They’re just no longer willing to overpay for homes that are priced ahead of the curve.

And that’s the part sellers need to catch up to.

The homes that are priced right are still moving. In fact, the well-priced homes are still selling in under two weeks. That’s the real market right now. Not the stale listing that sits for two months. Not the overpriced home that gets a handful of showings and no offers. The homes that are aligned with today’s pace are selling, because buyers recognize value when they see it.

So if you’re thinking about selling, here’s my blunt advice: don’t ask what your neighbor got at the peak of last spring. Ask what buyers are actually paying now. If you want a quick sale, price it to win attention immediately. If you want to test the market, be prepared for silence. There isn’t much middle ground anymore.

This isn’t a crash. It’s a reset. And the sellers who understand that are the ones who are going to come out ahead.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
## I Used to Talk Couples Out of Winter Weddings. Now I Try to Talk Them Into It.

For the first four years I did this, if a couple emailed me about a January date, I'd gently steer them toward May. Nothing dramatic — just a "have you considered late spring?" tacked onto the end of my reply. I thought I was doing them a favor.

I've shot eleven winter weddings in the last two years. I've changed my mind completely, and not for sentimental reasons. Here's the actual case.

### The light in November is better. Not different — better.

This is the part that surprised me most, and it's the part I'd want to explain to you if we were sitting across a table.

A June wedding at three in the afternoon, overcast, is flat. It's clean and it's usable and I can absolutely work with it, but there's no direction to it. Faces get lit evenly from a giant gray dome and there's nothing to model against — no falloff, no shape. I end up hunting for a doorway or a tree line or something, anything, to give the light somewhere to come *from*.

In November at three in the afternoon, the sun is already low, and the trees are bare. That combination does something I cannot replicate with equipment. The light comes through the branches instead of getting caught in a canopy, so it's directional and warm, and it breaks into these long soft shafts that fall across a face at an angle. Bare branches also make an incredible background — graphic, dark, uncluttered — where the same trees in June are a wall of green mush behind your head.

Golden hour in June starts around 8:15pm, which is usually the middle of dinner or the middle of dancing, and I'm asking you to leave your own party. In November, golden hour lands somewhere around 3pm to 4pm — which is very often *already* your portrait window. The best light of the day arrives exactly when you scheduled portraits, instead of ninety minutes after your last guest has committed to the dance floor.

### The venue is mine.

In June I'm sharing a parking lot with three or four other vendors. That's not a complaint about other vendors — most of them are people I like and would happily grab a beer with. But it means the good spot behind the barn already has a videographer set up in it. It means the bridal suite has hair, makeup, a planner, a florist, and a second shooter all trying to occupy the same eight feet of window light. It means I'm waiting my turn.

In February I pull in and there are two cars. Venue staff have time to answer questions and unlock doors. Nobody's rushing your ceremony because there's a second event loading in at six. I have the whole staircase. I have the whole field. I'm not negotiating for thirty seconds in the best corner of the room — I can actually *use* it, try three things, and pick the one that worked.

That difference shows up in the gallery. It's more time, less friction, and more of my attention on you instead of on logistics.

### It costs you meaningfully less.

Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for couples across the board — not just my rate, but venues, florals, rentals, blocks of hotel rooms. Venues that are booked eighteen months out for a Saturday in September will have three open dates in January and a real incentive to fill them.

I'll be straightforward about the trade-off, because I'd rather you hear it from me: you get less daylight. If you want a 6pm ceremony outside with a sunset behind you, winter isn't going to give you that. Winter weddings need a timeline built around a shorter day — ceremony earlier, portraits earlier, and a genuine willingness to be outside for fifteen minutes when it's cold. Every couple I've shot in winter has done it in a coat, laughed about it, and gone back inside to a room that felt warmer by comparison. Candlelight and warm interiors photograph beautifully, and there is nothing like the way a lit-up venue looks against a 4:45pm blue-dark sky.

### If you're deciding right now

I'm not going to tell you weddings are lovely in every season and you should just pick whatever feels right. That's true and it's also useless to you.

What I'll tell you is this: if your date is flexible, and you care about how your portraits look, and you'd rather spend the difference on food or a longer honeymoon than on a peak-season Saturday in June — look at November through February. I'll show you galleries from all eleven of them and you can decide for yourself.

Reach out and we'll talk through dates. I'll tell you honestly which ones give me the best shot at making something good for you.

b.text:
For the first four years I shot weddings around here, December through February was basically my hibernation period. I used it to catch up on taxes, clean my lenses, and wait for the spring rush. 

Then, over the last two years, I ended up shooting 11 winter weddings. And honestly? I think I prefer them to the June madness now. 

If you are currently looking at venue calendars and trying to decide if an off-season date is worth the gamble, here is the actual truth about winter weddings from the person holding the camera.

**The 3:00 PM November light beats June almost every time.**
Everyone worries that winter weddings look bleak because the leaves are gone. In reality, the light through bare trees around 3:00 PM in late November and December is incredible for portraits. Because the sun stays lower in the sky all day, we get this warm, directional glow that lasts for hours. Compare that to a standard June afternoon, where I’m either fighting harsh overhead sun that gives everyone raccoon eyes, or dealing with heavy, flat overcast skies that wash out the background. Give me bare branches and low winter sun any day. 

**You save about 30%, and it shows up in the breathing room.**
Most couples start looking at winter dates for the math: between venue drops and off-peak minimums, a winter wedding in our metro area generally runs about 30% cheaper for the couple than the exact same Saturday in September. 

That financial perk is great for you, but the side effect of booking in the off-season is what makes the day actually *feel* better. In June, popular venues and city portrait spots are a complete logjam. I’m routinely sharing the loading zone with three or four other wedding crews, waiting in line with another bride to use the one good staircase, or trying to angle my camera so a stranger’s catering van isn’t in the background of your first look. 

In January, we have the run of the place. Your vendors aren't exhausted from working a triple-header weekend. The venue staff isn't rushing to flip the room for a Sunday brunch wedding. The whole day just moves at a human pace.

**The logistics aren't that scary.**
Yes, it’s cold, and yes, it gets dark at 4:30 PM. We just build the timeline differently. You do a first look at 1:30 PM, we knock out your outdoor portraits in twenty-minute bursts with someone holding your heavy coats just out of frame, and by the time the sun drops, you’re already inside with a drink in your hand. Candlelit ceremonies actually look like candlelit ceremonies, instead of competing with the 8:00 PM summer daylight.

If you have your heart set on an outdoor tent reception, obviously, wait for summer. But if you’re on the fence—and especially if you like the idea of keeping an extra 30% of your budget while getting better portrait light and zero crowds—don't sleep on the winter dates.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
**Coming Home**

The airport was the first thing. My wife had the car keys and our daughter had a sign she'd made with glitter glue that said WELCOME HOME DAD, and she was holding it up with both hands. Then she saw me come through the gate and she turned around and hid behind her mom's leg.

She was six. The last time she'd seen me she was five, and I'd been gone a little over a year. I had the same face and the same duffel bag. I stood there with my hands out, not sure if I was supposed to step closer or wait. My wife said, "Hey, look who it is," in the voice you use with a dog that's scared of the vacuum. After a while our daughter peeked out one eye, then the other. Then she came out and handed me the sign without looking at me and went back behind her mom.

I didn't take it personally. I'd spent a lot of that year thinking about what I'd say when I got home, and none of it was about this, so I just kept holding the sign.

The grocery store was two days later. My wife had asked me to pick up cereal because she was too tired to go, and she figured it was an easy job. I walked in and stopped at the end of the cereal aisle. It was not the same aisle. There were forty kinds, maybe more, on shelves that went up past my head. Some were the same brands I remembered but in new colors. Some I'd never heard of. There was a whole section that was just granola and something called "clusters."

I stood there for twenty minutes. I counted the boxes on one shelf, then I started over. A woman with a cart asked if I needed help reaching something, and I said no, thanks, I was just looking, which was true. Eventually I grabbed the box I'd bought every week before I left, the plain one with the bear on it, and I felt stupid about how relieved I was. I put it in the cart and went home. My wife asked where the other stuff was, and I said I got what we always get, and she looked at me for a second and didn't push.

For the first few weeks I slept facing the door. I had done it for so long I didn't know I was doing it. You get used to sleeping with one eye half open, and to sleeping with your back to a wall or a corner where you can see the whole room. At home our bedroom door had a cheap brass knob and I'd always been able to see it from the bed. Now the door was on my left and I had to turn my whole body to see it. I'd wake up at three and my heart would be going and I'd be sure somebody was in the hall.

My wife had bought one of those little door stops shaped like a frog, and some nights she'd wedge it under the door so it stayed open, and some nights I'd get up and close it again without thinking, and she'd notice in the morning. Neither of us said much about it.

Our daughter asked once why my door was always open now. I said I liked hearing the house. She said that was a weird reason, and I said yeah, probably, and she went back to her cereal. It was the bear one. She'd picked it out herself.

b.text:
# Coming Home

The cereal aisle stopped me cold. I stood there for twenty minutes looking at forty different boxes. Frosted Flakes, Honey Nut Cheerios, some kind of granola I'd never heard of, store brand versions of everything. A woman reached around me to grab a box of Cinnamon Toast Crunch. I didn't move fast enough. I apologized. She said it was fine.

I couldn't remember what I used to eat for breakfast. I tried to picture the box, the colors on it, something that would make the choice easy. Nothing came. I picked Cheerios because it was simple. Plain. I knew what I was getting.

My daughter was six when I left. She was almost seven when I came back.

She didn't know me at the airport. I watched her standing next to my wife, both of them looking for me in the crowd. When I walked up, my daughter stepped back and hid behind my wife's leg. Just her face showing, watching me. My wife had prepared her. She knew her dad was coming home. But knowing something and recognizing someone are different things.

I crouched down. "Hey, sweetheart," I said.

She didn't move. My wife put her hand on her shoulder and said my daughter's name. Soft. Like she was reminding her of something she'd heard about but never seen for real.

It took her a few minutes. Then she came out from behind her mother's leg and let me pick her up. She felt heavier than I remembered. Or maybe I was just out of practice holding things that mattered.

The first week home, I slept with the bedroom door open. First night, I couldn't do it. I got up and pushed the door until it was just barely cracked, enough to see the hallway. My wife asked about it in the morning. I didn't have a good answer. She said we should try leaving it open. That it would be better. Normal.

So I tried. Second night, third night. I'd wake up in the dark and the open door looked wrong. Like a gap. Like something missing. I'd lie there for an hour before I could fall back asleep. My wife said to give it time.

By the second week, the door being open didn't wake me up as much. By the third week, I stopped noticing it. Sometimes now I don't think about it at all.

a.text:
1/7 Last Saturday night, 220 people showed up for Hendricks County Food Bridge's annual gala. I cried in the kitchen at 7:45 pm. Not sad tears. You'll understand in a sec. Thread on the evening, the disaster, and the $38,000 you all said yes to. 🧵

2/7 Context for folks new here: this gala funds roughly a third of our year. Pints of milk, canned goods, fresh produce, the delivery van that runs 4 counties. Without it, the shelves go bare by September. So yeah. High stakes for a tiny nonprofit.

3/7 Two days before the event, our caterer called. "I'm in. I'm out. Can't make it work." 220 plates. 48 hours. I sat at my kitchen table in my work clothes and thought, well. We're serving cheese cubes and crackers at the Holiday Inn ballroom.

4/7 I called everyone I knew. Then I called Maggiore's. Full honest ask: "We are desperate. Can you feed 220 people Saturday?" They said yes. Full dinner. Baked chicken parmesan, the works. Delivered, plated, on time. Maggiore's, you saved our whole year. Thank you. Truly.

5/7 So. Saturday night. 220 neighbors in a room. The auction got loud. Someone's grandma won the fishing trip. A volunteer I've known for nine years grabbed my hand mid-speech and said "you good?" and I was. The room felt like a family reunion where everyone brought a plate.

6/7 Final number: $38,000 raised against a $30,000 goal. That's roughly 12,000 meals. That's the September problem not being a problem. Every dollar here is someone choosing to be in the room with us, which honestly matters more than the total.

7/7 So thank you. To everyone who bought a ticket, volunteered at the door, donated an auction item, or just shared the flyer. And Maggiore's specifically: you had no obligation, and you showed up like it was your own family's kitchen. That's the county we live in. Grateful beyond words. 🤍

b.text:
1/ We set a $30,000 goal for Saturday's gala.

We finished the night at $38,412.

Here's what that means, and the story of how the dinner almost didn't happen at all.

2/ Thursday morning, two days out, our caterer called to cancel. Staffing issue on their end. No dinner for 180 guests.

I will not pretend I handled that call gracefully.

3/ By noon I'd called eleven places. Everyone was booked or couldn't scale. Then I called Maggiore's on Main.

Tony Maggiore listened to the whole thing, asked how many people, and said "we'll figure it out."

4/ They closed their dining room Saturday night. Their entire kitchen crew worked our event. They brought their own linens when they realized we were short.

And they refused to invoice us. Not a discount. No invoice.

5/ So: thank you to Tony and Gina Maggiore, and to Marcus, Delia, Sam, and the whole Maggiore's team. You saved this event and you did it without making us feel like a burden.

Go eat there. Seriously.

6/ Thank you also to our presenting sponsors, Whitlock Insurance and Bower & Reed Dental, to our 31 volunteers, and to everyone who raised a paddle when we asked.

7/ What $38,412 does: roughly 96,000 meals through our pantry network, and it funds the refrigerated van repairs we've been deferring since March. That van is how we get fresh produce to Coatesville and Amo.

8/ Twelve years running this gala and I've never had a week like the last one. Grateful is not a big enough word.

More soon on what's next. For now, thank you, Hendricks County.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
**Stop Calling It a Crash: The Real Story Behind Our Local Housing Shift**

I’ve been selling homes in this suburb for ten years. I’ve seen the wild frenzies, the steady climbs, and the occasional dips. Lately, I’ve been hearing a lot of nervous chatter from both buyers and sellers about the current state of our local real estate market. People are throwing around the word "crash." 

Let’s cut through the noise. The market isn't a complex puzzle right now, and it doesn't depend on a dozen shifting macroeconomic factors. The reality is incredibly simple: this isn't a crash. It’s a seller reality check.

Let’s look at the actual numbers in our zip code. Last spring, the median days on market was eight. This spring, it’s 34. Furthermore, showings per listing have dropped by half. If you only look at those data points, you’d think the bottom was falling out. But here is the crucial stat the doom-scrollers are ignoring: list prices are still up 6% year over year. 

Prices aren't plummeting. What has changed is the pace, and the vast majority of sellers simply haven't caught up to it. We are dealing with a massive disconnect between what sellers think their home is worth and the actual behavior of today's buyers. 

Right now, I personally have three sellers whose homes have been sitting on the market for over 60 days. All three are flat-out refusing to drop their price. They are clinging to the "list it high and wait for a bidding war" mentality of two years ago. They aren't victims of a bad market; they are victims of their own stubbornness. They want 2021 prices in a 2024 market, and they are willing to let their listings grow stale to get it. 

Those stubborn sellers are exactly why our median days on market has jumped to 34. The average is being heavily skewed by overpriced inventory that is just sitting and rotting. 

Here is the unvarnished truth: if you price your home correctly for today's reality, it is still selling in under two weeks. The buyers are absolutely still out there, and they are still buying. They just aren't tolerating overpriced ego-trips anymore. They are doing their research, they know what the comps are, and they are only making moves on homes that are priced accurately from day one.

The local housing market hasn't broken. The buyers are behaving perfectly rationally. It’s the sellers who need to wake up and catch up.

b.text:
The Local Market Isn’t Crashing. It’s Just Resetting.

For the past few weeks, my inbox has been full of the same question: Is the local market crashing? Based on the data I’m seeing every day, the answer is no. What we are experiencing isn’t a collapse—it’s a correction.

Here are the facts. This spring, the median days on market in our zip code jumped from 8 to 34. Showings per listing have dropped by half. Yet, list prices remain up 6% year over year. A crash would mean prices plummeting and homes becoming unsellable. Instead, we’re seeing a shift in momentum.

The bottleneck isn’t demand; it’s pricing. I currently have three listings that have been on the market for over 60 days. My sellers are refusing to adjust their prices despite the lack of offers. They are holding out for last year’s pace, but the market has moved on.

Here is the reality: I have listings that are priced correctly, and they are still selling in under two weeks. When you align with current reality, buyers are still out there. This isn’t a disaster for homeowners. It’s a wake-up call. The market isn’t broken; it’s just slower than it was a year ago. If you want to sell, you need to meet it where it is, not where you wish it to be.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

Outdoor spigots can freeze and burst when Minneapolis temperatures drop below zero. The good news: winterizing them usually takes less than 10 minutes per spigot.

The most important thing is to disconnect every garden hose. Leaving a hose connected is one of the biggest causes of frozen outdoor faucet and burst-pipe calls we get in January.

## 1. Disconnect Every Hose, Sprayer, and Timer

Remove garden hoses, splitters, spray nozzles, timers, and anything else attached to the outdoor faucet.

Even if the faucet is turned off, water can stay trapped inside a connected hose. When that water freezes, it expands backward into the spigot and the pipe inside your wall.

After disconnecting the hose:

- Drain it completely
- Coil it up
- Store it in a garage, shed, or basement if possible

Don’t leave a “short hose” or sprinkler attachment connected either. It only takes a small amount of trapped water to create a problem.

## 2. Find and Shut Off the Interior Water Valve

Many Minneapolis homes have an indoor shutoff valve for each outdoor spigot. It may be located:

- In the basement ceiling near the exterior wall
- Near your water meter or utility room
- Under a sink in an older addition
- In a crawlspace or mechanical room

Turn the valve clockwise to shut off water going to the outdoor faucet.

Not every house has separate shutoffs, especially in older homes. If you cannot find one, don’t force random valves. You do not want to accidentally shut off water to part of the house.

## 3. Drain the Outdoor Spigot

Once the interior shutoff valve is off, go outside and open the spigot fully.

Let it run until the water stops. This drains the water left in the pipe between the interior shutoff and the outdoor faucet.

Leave the outside spigot open for the winter after it has drained. That gives any remaining moisture room to expand instead of building pressure inside the pipe.

Some interior shutoff valves have a small drain cap or bleeder screw near the valve. If yours does, place a small cup or towel underneath it and open it briefly to drain any water on the house side of the valve. Close it again when it stops dripping.

## 4. Install a Foam Spigot Cover

A basic foam faucet cover costs around $3 to $5 at most hardware stores. It is inexpensive extra protection, especially on older homes or exposed walls.

To install it:

1. Make sure the spigot is drained and left open.
2. Place the foam cover over the faucet.
3. Tighten the strap or drawstring so it fits snugly against the siding.

A foam cover is not a substitute for shutting off and draining the line. It helps, but it cannot protect a faucet with water trapped inside it during a Minneapolis cold snap.

## What If You Have a Frost-Free Spigot?

Many newer homes have frost-free outdoor faucets. These have a longer valve stem that shuts the water off farther inside the heated part of the house.

They are more freeze-resistant, but hoses still need to be disconnected. A frost-free spigot can still freeze if a hose is left attached because water cannot drain out properly.

If you are not sure whether your home has frost-free faucets, winterize them the same way: remove hoses, shut off the indoor valve if one is available, and drain the outdoor faucet.

## Signs an Outdoor Pipe May Have Frozen or Burst

Check your outdoor faucets in spring before using them regularly. Call a plumber if you notice:

- Little or no water coming from the spigot
- Water leaking inside the basement or wall when the outdoor faucet is turned on
- Damp drywall, stains, or a musty smell near an exterior wall
- A cracked spigot or visible damage around the faucet

A frozen outdoor pipe often does not start leaking until temperatures warm up and the water is turned back on.

## Don’t Have an Interior Shutoff Valve?

If your outdoor spigot does not have an interior shutoff, it is worth having one installed. A dedicated shutoff makes winterizing easier and gives you better protection during Minneapolis winters.

Our family plumbing company can help locate your outdoor water lines, install shutoff valves, replace aging spigots, and repair frozen or burst pipes.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Outdoor Spigots in Minneapolis

To winterize your outdoor spigots, shut off the water inside, disconnect your hoses, drain the faucets, and add a foam cover. Do this before the first hard freeze—not after the faucet has already iced up.

## 1. Shut off the interior valve

Find the shutoff valve for each outdoor faucet. In many Minneapolis homes, it’s in the basement near where the pipe runs through the exterior wall.

Turn a round handle clockwise until snug, or turn a lever handle a quarter-turn so it sits perpendicular to the pipe. Don’t force a stuck valve.

**Can’t find an interior shutoff—or don’t have one? Call us.** We can check your setup and recommend the right way to protect it. Some frost-free faucets don’t have a separate shutoff, but they still need proper winter preparation.

## 2. Disconnect every hose

Remove garden hoses, splitters, timers, and other attachments from each spigot. Drain the hoses and store them for winter.

**Leaving a hose connected is the big mistake. It’s behind most of our January burst-pipe calls.** A connected hose can trap water in the faucet and keep it from draining—even if the faucet is labeled “frost-free.”

That trapped water can freeze and split the pipe inside the wall. You may not discover the damage until you turn the faucet on again.

## 3. Open the outdoor spigot and let it drain

With the interior supply shut off and the hose removed, open the outdoor faucet. Let the remaining water drain out, and leave the faucet open for winter.

If the interior shutoff has a small drain or bleeder cap, place a bucket underneath and carefully open it to release trapped water. Close the cap afterward. If you’re unsure which part to open, give us a call rather than loosening fittings.

## 4. Add a foam faucet cover

A basic foam cover costs around $3 and adds insulation around the outdoor faucet. Secure it snugly against the siding.

A cover is extra protection—not a substitute for disconnecting the hose and draining the line. During a Minneapolis cold snap, a foam cover alone won’t reliably protect a water-filled pipe.

## No Shutoff, a Stuck Valve, or a Faucet That Won’t Stop Running?

Call our plumbing team before freezing weather arrives. We can inspect your outdoor faucet, address shutoff problems, and help protect the piping inside your home.

If you only do one thing on this list, make it this one. Leaving a hose attached is the single biggest mistake we see, and it accounts for the majority of our burst-pipe calls in January. Even if you have a modern "frost-free" faucet, leaving a hose connected traps water inside the pipe right inside your exterior wall. When that trapped water freezes, it expands and splits the copper pipe inside your house. You usually won't even know it happened until you turn the water back on in the spring and flood your basement.

### 2. Shut Off the Interior Valve
Head down to your basement or crawlspace and find the water line that leads to your outside faucet. Follow the pipe back from the exterior wall until you find the shutoff valve. 

Turn this valve off completely:
* **If it’s a lever handle (ball valve):** Turn it 90 degrees so the handle is perpendicular to the pipe.
* **If it’s a round wheel (gate valve):** Turn it clockwise until it stops. 

If you have two outdoor spigots—say, one in the front yard and one in the back—make sure you find and shut off both interior valves. 

### 3. Drain the Spigot
Go back outside and turn the outdoor faucet all the way on. Let any remaining water trickle out. 

Once it stops dripping, **leave the outdoor faucet in the open position** for the winter. If any water is still sitting in the line, leaving the valve open gives that water room to expand if it freezes, rather than bursting the pipe. 

*(Note: Go back inside and check the shutoff valve in your basement. Many shutoff valves have a tiny "bleeder cap" on the side. Put a bucket under the valve, unscrew that little cap to let the last few drops of water out of the line, and screw the cap back on tight.)*

### 4. Put on a $3 Foam Cover
Head to the local hardware store and buy a cheap foam faucet cover for a few bucks. Loop the string over the faucet handle, push the foam dome tight against the siding of your house, and lock the clip in place. It’s cheap insurance that blocks the wind and keeps a little bit of heat from your house trapped around the fixture.

***

### Don't Have an Interior Shutoff Valve?
A lot of older homes in Minneapolis and St. Paul don’t have separate shutoff valves for the outdoor plumbing, or they have old gate valves that have rusted open and won’t budge. 

If you go down to your basement and can't find a shutoff valve—or if you have an older brass faucet outside and no way to isolate it from the inside—give our shop a call. Don't force a stuck valve, or you might snap the stem and have a much bigger problem on your hands. We can come out, install a new quarter-turn ball valve inside, or upgrade your setup to a frost-free sillcock before the deep freeze hits.

b.text:
How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

If you have an outside spigot, here's exactly how to winterize it before it freezes:

**1. Disconnect your hoses.**
This is the big one. Leaving a hose connected is the cause of most of our January burst-pipe calls. A connected hose traps water in the pipe, it freezes, expands, and the pipe bursts inside your wall. Disconnect every hose, splitter, and timer from every outside spigot.

**2. Shut the interior valve.**
Go inside your basement or utility room and find the shut-off valve for your outside spigots. It's usually on the pipe leading to the outside wall. Turn it clockwise until it's fully closed.

**3. Drain the spigot.**
Go back outside and open the spigot all the way. Let any remaining water drain out. Leave it open for a few minutes to make sure it's empty, then close it again. **4. Add a $3 foam cover.**
Pick up an insulated foam faucet cover from any hardware store and put it over the outside spigot. It's cheap insurance against our Minneapolis cold snaps.

That's it.

A lot of older Minneapolis homes don't. If you can't find an interior valve for your outside spigot, don't just leave it — that's when pipes freeze and flood basements. Give us a call and we can help you figure out your setup or install a proper shut-off and frost-free sillcock.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
The modern high school day is often structured like a marathon with poorly timed stops. For juniors and seniors, the midday meal period rarely functions as intended. Instead of a restorative break, lunch frequently becomes a logistical bottleneck that forces older students into cramped spaces and rushed schedules. Restricting campus access to underclassmen while treating upperclassmen as younger siblings overlooks the reality that students in grades eleven and twelve possess the maturity and planning skills to make responsible midday choices. Our district should implement an open campus lunch policy for juniors and seniors. Doing so would resolve severe cafeteria overcrowding, align with regional precedents that prove punctuality can be maintained, and provide the focused mental break that students consistently report needing.

The most immediate problem with the current lunch structure is spatial. Our cafeteria was designed to accommodate roughly 220 students per wave, yet we currently seat 340 juniors and seniors during the same period. That leaves over a hundred students without adequate seating, pushing them into hallways, empty classrooms, or out the door entirely just to secure a place to eat. Forcing everyone to remain on campus under these conditions breeds congestion, increases noise levels, and wastes valuable minutes between periods. Opening the campus to older students would instantly reduce the headcount during peak lunch hours, allowing the remaining population to sit comfortably, finish meals without rushing, and transition back to afternoon classes with less friction. Administrative control does not require sacrificing basic comfort, and alleviating a documented overcrowding crisis is a straightforward reason to adjust the policy.

Beyond logistics, concerns about open campus lunch often hinge on the assumption that older students will abuse the privilege and cause chronic tardiness. Historical data from comparable districts directly contradicts this worry. Three neighboring school systems—Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—already allow open campus lunches for upperclassmen, and each has publicly reported attendance figures showing no measurable increase in tardiness. These districts share similar geographic layouts and demographic profiles, which means physical access to nearby businesses is equally feasible here. When schools establish clear check-out expectations and monitor arrival times, students generally return promptly. Trusting juniors and seniors to manage their own time yields consistent results, whereas blanket restrictions only reinforce an outdated, paternalistic approach to scheduling.

Student perspectives further strengthen the case for this shift. In a survey of eighty students across both grade levels, seventy-one responded positively to the proposal. Respondents consistently noted that after two consecutive hours of morning instruction, staying in a crowded, loud cafeteria drains attention rather than restoring it. Many pointed to quieter off-campus locations as opportunities to decompress, complete light assignments, or simply step outside between periods. A predictable midday reset improves concentration for afternoon coursework, particularly in subjects that demand sustained focus. Ignoring nearly nine out of ten surveyed students in favor of maintaining a congested status quo undermines the very purpose of a healthy school environment.

Critics will inevitably raise safety and truancy concerns, arguing that releasing older students off campus creates liability risks or opens doors to missed periods. While these worries warrant thoughtful management, they do not justify preserving an inefficient system. Proper implementation requires standard administrative protocols: digital sign-out logs, verified emergency contacts, and clear academic consequences for unexcused absences. Districts that have adopted similar frameworks report minimal incidents because accountability measures pair effectively with student responsibility. Removing a restriction based on hypothetical worst-case scenarios prevents all students from benefiting, including those who follow the rules consistently.

The current lunch arrangement treats a routine daily transition as a containment exercise rather than an opportunity to build independence. Implementing open campus lunch for juniors and seniors would immediately relieve cafeteria overcrowding, follow a tested regional model that maintains punctuality, and honor student feedback regarding mental fatigue and focus. High schools should prepare students for adult decision-making, not restrict movement solely to simplify supervision. By adopting a more flexible lunch policy, our district can demonstrate confidence in its older students, streamline daily operations, and ultimately foster a calmer, more productive academic atmosphere.

b.text:
Let Juniors and Seniors Leave for Lunch

Every day at 11:42, our lunch wave turns into a scramble for chairs. People end up sitting on the floor in the hallway or standing around trash cans trying to eat because there is nowhere else to go. Our school should allow open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. It would fix a real space problem, it has already worked in schools near us, and students are clearly ready for it.

The most immediate reason is space. Our cafeteria only seats 220 people, but there are 340 students assigned to that lunch wave. That math does not work. When more than a hundred students do not have a seat, lunch is not really a break. It is loud, crowded, and stressful, and custodians and lunch supervisors have to deal with the overflow. Letting juniors and seniors who want to leave go off campus would take pressure off the cafeteria for everyone, including freshmen and sophomores who would stay.

The other thing is that we know this policy can work because nearby schools are already doing it. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow open campus lunch for upperclassmen. According to their published attendance stats, none of them have seen a rise in tardiness since they started it. That matters because the biggest worry adults have about open lunch is that students will not get back in time for fifth period. In these three districts, they do get back. There is no reason to assume our school would be different.

Some teachers and parents might still argue that only some juniors and seniors are responsible enough to handle leaving campus. But at this point most of us are driving to school, holding part-time jobs, and applying to college. Going out for lunch and getting back on time is a pretty basic level of responsibility. I surveyed 80 students at our school and 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch. That shows students actually want this privilege and understand what comes with it.

Open campus for juniors and seniors is not about getting out of school. It is about trusting upperclassmen with a normal choice and solving an overcrowding problem at the same time. The cafeteria cannot fit us, other schools have proven it does not cause tardiness issues, and students support it. It is time for our school to make the change.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/ I made a pricing mistake.

I raised prices 40% on everyone overnight.

In a week, we lost 30 of our 140 customers.

2/ What I got wrong:

Existing customers didn't sign up at that price. I changed the deal without warning, without explanation, and without giving them a choice.

It wasn't the new price that broke trust. It was the surprise.

3/ What I changed:

I reversed the overnight increase for existing customers and put them back on the price they signed up for.

New pricing now only applies to new customers going forward.

4/ I also owned it publicly with the customers we lost instead of quietly hoping no one noticed.

A pricing change is a communication problem first, a numbers problem second.

5/ Lesson I'm taking from this:

Never surprise the people already paying you. If the price needs to change, explain why, give people time, and respect the deal they originally signed up for.

Building in public means sharing this part too.

b.text:
1/
Last week I made the worst pricing decision since starting Tallyup.

Tallyup is a small subscription tool that helps gym owners track member retention.

We had 140 customers.

I raised prices 40% on everyone overnight.

30 of them canceled in a week.

Here’s what happened and what I changed.

2/
The change was blunt:

I updated our pricing, and every active customer’s next charge was 40% higher.

No warning email.
No grandfathering.
No explanation.
Just a bigger charge.

3/
Then the cancellations hit.

30 of our 140 customers canceled in 7 days.

These were gym owners already using Tallyup to track retention. They weren’t asking for a price increase—I just handed them one.

4/
The mistake wasn’t raising prices.

The mistake was doing it:
• overnight
• on existing customers
• without notice
• without explaining the value

Price is a promise. I broke it.

5/
What I changed:

First, I rolled the increase back for every customer who was active before the change.

They’re back on the old price. No surprise 40% renewal.

6/
Second, the higher price now applies only to new customers.

If I ever change pricing for existing customers again, they’ll get advance notice and the option to keep their current rate.

7/
Third, I emailed the 30 customers who canceled.

I apologized, took responsibility, and offered their old price back.

I’m not going to guess how many will return. Some conversations are still open.

8/
Fourth, I now write the pricing-change email before I change pricing.

If I can’t explain the increase honestly in one short email, I’m not ready to ship it.

9/
After those cancellations, 110 of the original 140 remained.

I traded short-term revenue for trust, and that’s the right trade.

If you’re building indie SaaS: don’t surprise the people who already said yes.

10/
That’s the update.

Back to building Tallyup—this time without breaking trust.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
# Why I Like Photographing Winter Weddings Now

For a long time, I thought of winter weddings as the exception to the wedding season. After six years photographing weddings around this metro area—and 11 winter weddings in the last two years—I’ve changed my mind. I genuinely look forward to them.

The light is a big reason. Around 3 p.m. in November, sunlight comes through the bare trees at an angle that gives portraits shape and warmth. I’ll take that over flat, overcast June light more often than you might expect. We do have to plan for an earlier sunset, but when we build portraits into the timeline before it gets dark, that short window can be excellent.

Winter also feels less crowded. In June, I’m often sharing a venue parking lot with three or four other vendors arriving, unloading, and trying to work in the same spaces at once. In winter, there’s usually more room to move and a little less of that peak-season rush. It doesn’t change what matters about your day, but it can make the experience calmer.

And there’s a practical difference: my winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for couples. If you’re flexible on your date, that’s worth considering alongside the photos you want.

I wouldn’t tell you to book a winter wedding if you’re dreaming of a long outdoor cocktail hour. You’ll want a plan for the cold and a timeline that respects the early sunset. But if you like the idea of quieter venues, beautiful afternoon light, and a little more room in your budget, winter deserves a serious look.

b.text:
# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings

*Or: a confession from a photographer who spent years dreading them.*

For my first few years shooting weddings in this city, winter inquiries felt like a calendar problem. I said yes because January needed filling, not because I wanted the job. Somewhere along the way, that flipped. I've shot eleven winter weddings in the last two years, and they're now the bookings I look forward to most. Since a lot of couples asking me "when should we book?" are really asking "when is the best wedding," let me make the case for the season nobody plans for.

## The light. I'm serious about this one.

In November, around 3 p.m., the sun is already low. It comes in sideways through the bare branches, and those leafless trees break it into shafts and patterns that no lighting kit I own can replicate. There's direction to it. It gives a face shape.

Here's the part that might get me in trouble: that light is better for portraits than what we often get in June. Flat overcast June light is like a giant ceiling fixture — even, forgiving, and forgettable. Everyone is lit identically from every angle, which sounds kind and is actually the problem. Portraits need light with an angle and an opinion, and bare-tree light at 3 p.m. in November has both.

And because the sun sets early, your best-light portraits happen mid-afternoon — when your makeup is fresh and you've still got energy — instead of at 7:30 p.m., after you've been on your feet for eight hours and the schedule has already slipped twice.

## Nobody is fighting over your Saturday.

In June, I pull into a venue lot and there are regularly three or four other vendors there — another photographer's van, a videographer, a florist's delivery, all of us on overlapping timelines.

You feel that even if you never see the parking lot. It's why the getting-ready suite has a stranger's garment bag in it. It's why the coordinator is impossible to find, why the room flip starts while your grandmother is still sitting in it, why everyone is rushing. In January, the venue is yours. My timeline holds. The staff isn't stretched thin, so they're not rushing you either.

I know "the parking lot was roomy" sounds like a photographer convenience. It isn't. Calm is the thing I need most on a wedding day, and winter days have it.

## The part you already guessed: it's cheaper.

Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for couples than peak-season dates. That's not a gimmick — it's how the industry prices the slow months, and it adds up fast. That difference is your videographer, or a real chunk of your venue, or the honeymoon.

But I want to be honest about the other side of it, because I've had couples seem almost apologetic about booking a discounted date: I'm not shooting eleven of these a year out of charity. The discount exists because demand is lower. I keep saying yes anyway because these have become my favorite weddings to shoot — the calm, the light, the day that actually runs on schedule. You're not getting a lesser wedding at a lower price. You're getting the same wedding at the time of year fewer people want it.

## Yes, it's cold. Plan for it, don't fear it.

I won't pretend otherwise. We plan around it: portraits in twenty-minute bursts with a warm room to retreat to, and a timeline that puts the outdoor portraits in that good light instead of after dark. And coat shots are not a compromise — a great coat is a better portrait prop than a shawl pretending it isn't freezing. The short day is a constraint, but it's the kind that makes the timeline better, not worse.

## If you're flexible on your date

Ask me about winter. After six years shooting in this area, I know exactly which spots near you hold that low November light at 3 p.m. — and my winter calendar has room in it.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
# Open Campus Lunch: A Practical Solution for Juniors and Seniors

Every lunch period at our school feels like controlled chaos. Our cafeteria seats 220 students, but 340 juniors and seniors eat during the same lunch wave. The result is an overcrowded space where students struggle to find seats, eat standing up, or skip lunch entirely. Our school should implement open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. This policy would alleviate overcrowding, trust students with more independence as they prepare for college, and has already succeeded in similar nearby districts without the negative consequences some might fear.

The most obvious reason to allow open campus lunch is that it solves a genuine space problem. Our cafeteria is operating at 155% capacity during the lunch period. This overcrowding creates an uncomfortable environment that makes it difficult for students to actually eat and socialize. By allowing roughly half our junior and senior class to leave campus, we'd reduce the lunch crowd to manageable levels while still having food available for those who stay. This isn't about preference—it's about basic logistics.

Some people worry that open campus lunch would lead to increased tardiness when students return from off-campus lunch. However, three nearby districts already allow this policy. Fairmont High School, West Linn High School, and Cascade High School all permit open campus lunch for upperclassmen, and their published attendance data shows no significant rise in tardiness rates. These districts have successfully managed the policy without sacrificing academic punctuality, suggesting that our students can be trusted to return on time as well.

A survey I conducted of 80 students at our school revealed that 71 would support an open campus lunch policy for juniors and seniors. This 89% approval rate shows genuine student interest and suggests that most upperclassmen would approach this responsibility seriously rather than abuse it.

Open campus lunch also acknowledges that juniors and seniors are nearly adults preparing for life after high school. College students manage their own time during lunch breaks without supervision. Allowing older students limited off-campus freedom during lunch treats them as more mature and gives them practice making independent decisions. This builds confidence and responsibility at an important developmental stage.

Our school should implement open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. We have a clear overcrowding problem, evidence that this policy works in similar schools, and strong student support. It's time to give our oldest students the freedom and respect they've earned.

b.text:
# A Reasonable Case for Open-Campus Lunch

At our school, 340 students are assigned to a lunch wave in a cafeteria that seats only 220. That leaves 120 more students than available seats. Before discussing whether students should be allowed to leave campus for lunch, we should recognize that the current system already has a problem. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch would help relieve overcrowding while giving older students a reasonable amount of independence. With clear expectations for returning on time, open-campus lunch would be a practical policy rather than an unnecessary risk.

The strongest reason to consider open-campus lunch is the lack of cafeteria space. Students should not have to compete for a seat during the part of the school day meant for eating and taking a break. Letting juniors and seniors leave would reduce the number of students trying to use the cafeteria at once. It would not guarantee an open seat for everyone, since we do not yet know how many students would leave each day. However, it could ease the pressure without requiring the school to expand the cafeteria. Students who prefer to stay on campus could continue eating there, with less crowding.

A common objection is that students who leave campus will return late. That concern deserves attention because lunch should not interfere with instructional time. However, nearby districts offer evidence that open-campus lunch does not necessarily cause more tardiness. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade already allow it, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. Their experience does not prove that our school would have identical results, but it does challenge the assumption that allowing students to leave would automatically create an attendance problem. Instead of rejecting the policy based on what might happen, our school should consider what has happened in comparable districts.

Students at our school also strongly support the change. In a survey I conducted, 71 of 80 students favored open-campus lunch—nearly 89 percent of those surveyed. This survey does not represent every student, and popularity alone does not make a policy effective. Still, it shows substantial interest among the students who responded. A policy that addresses an existing space problem and has strong student support deserves serious consideration.

The school could introduce open-campus lunch through a trial period for juniors and seniors. Students would remain responsible for returning before their next class, and repeated tardiness could result in losing the privilege. The school could then review attendance records and cafeteria crowding before deciding whether to continue the policy. This approach would give administrators evidence from our own campus while keeping consequences clear.

Open-campus lunch would not solve every problem in the school day, but it could improve a lunch system that currently asks 340 students to share 220 seats. Nearby districts have shown that allowing students to leave does not have to increase tardiness, and many students here want the option. A carefully monitored policy would give juniors and seniors more responsibility while addressing a problem the school already faces. That is a reasonable change worth trying.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
6-Month Review: The Jarvik L2 Standing Desk

I've been working remote as a software engineer for 3 years, and I've had the Jarvik L2 for exactly 6 months. 8+ hours a day, 5 days a week, with two monitors, a standing mat, and a lot of typing. I paid for it myself. No sponsors, no affiliate links.

Here's the honest breakdown for anyone actually researching this desk:

**Setup & Build:**
Assembly took me about 45 minutes solo. Instructions are clear, hardware is labeled. The frame is heavy steel and feels solid. The laminate top on mine (60x30") has held up with no scratches or sagging, even with my dual monitor arm clamped on the back.

**The Good: The Motor**
The dual motor is the best part of this desk. It's fast — goes from my sitting height (71cm) to standing (107cm) in about 7 seconds — and it's genuinely quiet. I can adjust it mid-Zoom call without anyone hearing it. No grinding, no whine. For that alone, it beats every desk in this price range I've tried.

**The Bad: Stability & Presets**
Two real problems have shown up with daily use.

1.  **Wobble at full height.** I'm 5'9" and use it at 107cm. If I'm just browsing, it's rock solid. But when I'm typing hard — like really hammering out code for an hour — there's a noticeable side-to-side wobble. My monitors shake slightly. It's not going to collapse, but it's distracting. If you're over 6' and need to go higher than me, it will be worse.

2.  **Memory presets drift.** This is annoying. I saved my sitting and standing heights to the keypad. About once every two weeks, both presets are off by about a centimeter low. I have to hold the button to re-adjust and then re-save. Jarvik support said it's "normal calibration drift." It is not normal. A preset should be a preset.

**The Ugly: The Cable Tray**
The included cable tray is garbage. It's a flimsy, thin metal basket with sharp edges that is way too small. It barely fits a power strip, and once you add 4-5 cables, it sags in the middle. I replaced it after week two with a $25 under-desk tray from Amazon. Factor that into your cost.

**Verdict: Price Matters**

At **$549** (the sale price I paid), the Jarvik L2 is worth it. You are getting a fast, quiet dual-motor frame that works, despite the wobble and preset issues. It's a great value at that price.

At **$749** (its full retail price), do not buy it. There are more stable options with better quality control at that price point like the FlexiSpot E7 or Uplift V2 when they're on sale. The drifting presets and useless cable tray are unacceptable for $750.

**Bottom Line:** Catch it on sale. If you do, it's a 7.5/10 workhorse. At full price, it's a 5/10 pass.

b.text:
Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6 Months Later

I bought the Jarvik L2 six months ago for $549. I'm a remote software engineer, so this thing gets 9-10 hours of use a day, five days a week, switching between sitting and standing 3-4 times daily. No sponsorship, no affiliate links, just my own money and my own back pain.

**The motor is actually good.**

This is the best part of the L2. Dual motor, goes from my sit height of 73cm to my stand height of 109cm in about 12 seconds. It's quiet enough that I've moved it mid-Zoom call and no one noticed. Just a low hum, no grinding, no jerk at the start/stop. After six months of daily moves, it hasn't slowed down or gotten louder. Jarvik got this right.

**It wobbles at full height.**

I'm 5'6" and stand at 109cm. If I'm typing normally, it's fine. If I'm typing hard — like actually hammering out code in a hurry — there's noticeable side-to-side wobble. My 27" monitor on a single arm visibly shakes. It's not going to tip, but it's distracting. Below 100cm it's rock solid. Above 105cm, don't expect to do any precision work without some shake. For a desk that advertises a 125cm max height, that's weak.

**The memory presets don't hold.**

It has 4 presets, which I liked. I set 1 to 73cm and 2 to 109cm. After a week or two, 2 was stopping at 108cm. Recalibrated. A month later, it was at 107.8cm. It's drifted about a cm every time. Not the end of the world, but annoying when you paid for presets so you don't have to look at the display. I now just hold the up button and watch the numbers. The controller is basically dumb up/down after six months.

**The cable tray is garbage.**

Thin, sharp-edged metal basket that mounts under the back. My power strip doesn't fit in it flat. My dock barely fits. After two weeks, cables were sagging out the back anyway because there are no real retention clips and the included velcro straps are a joke. I replaced it with a $25 aftermarket tray from Amazon and haven't thought about it since. Factor that into your cost. Jarvik should just not include theirs.

**Verdict**

At $549 on sale, keep it. The frame and motor performance for the price is solid if you work under 110cm and can live with resetting your presets and trashing the cable tray.

At $749 full price, absolutely not. The wobble and preset drift at that price are unacceptable when you're in Uplift / FlexiSpot E7 territory. Wait for the sale or buy something else.
