setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The couples who let go of the shot list often end up with the photos that feel most like *them*.

The Barrera wedding is a perfect example. The rain changed the plan, and we moved everything under the pecan tree.

There was no point trying to force the day back into the original schedule. We adapted—and made room for the moments that happened there.

A shot list can be helpful for family portraits and must-have details. But it can’t predict the weather, and it doesn’t need to choreograph every moment.

Sometimes the best thing you can do is trust your photographer, stay present, and let the day unfold.

b.text:
The Barreras had a shot list. Eleven pages, color-coded, shared with me three weeks before the wedding. Then it rained on the day.

We had planned golden hour photos at the overlook. Instead, we moved everything under the big pecan tree behind the barn, and the light coming through the wet leaves was soft and even. The family portraits took longer than planned because we kept finding new spots. Somewhere in there, the couple stopped posing and started laughing at something their nephew did, and that's the photo they framed.

I've been doing this for 8 years, and I've noticed a pattern. The couples who hold their shot lists loosely tend to end up with the photos they talk about most. Lists are useful for making sure the important people get photographed. But the images that stop you when you scroll back through a gallery are usually the unplanned ones: a grandmother fixing a boutonniere, a look between two people that nobody staged.

If you're planning your wedding, here's what I'd suggest:
- Keep a short list of must-have shots, not a full script.
- Tell your photographer what matters to you emotionally, not just what looks good on paper.
- Give yourselves permission to change plans when the weather or the venue has other ideas.

Rain or not, the best part of the day usually happens between the scheduled moments. A good photographer's job is to notice it and be ready.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
# Matting: Why It Happens and How to Get Ahead of It Between Visits

The dogs I see most often for de-matting are almost never neglected dogs. They're the ones whose owners did everything right at the bathtub — and then bathed.

That's the part that surprises people. You're not supposed to bathe your way out of a mat. You're supposed to brush your way out of a mat, *before* the tub. Water is what turns a small tangle into a felt pad. The fibers swell, the mat compresses, and when it dries it sets like a piece of wool fabric. A coat that felted tight while wet is ten times harder to take out than a dry mat, and a lot of the time it comes out in chunks instead of coming out at all.

So the order matters: **brush first, bath later.** When you do finally bathe, rinse thoroughly and dry completely — damp spots under the collar or behind the ears are exactly where a new mat starts forming.

## Brush the coat, not just the surface

Most people brush the top few layers of hair and call it done. That's where mats begin, but it's not where they live. Take your slicker brush and work it down to the skin, section by section, using short line strokes. Pull the brush down the coat in one direction, a couple of inches at a time, then lift and reset. Don't swirl it in circles — circling snags the undercoat and tangles the hair tips into knots, which is basically how you build a mat on purpose. Short, straight strokes lift the loose hair out. Circles make it.

Be patient with double-coated breeds especially. Husky, malamute, chow, golden retriever, shepherd, any doodle — that dense undercoat has to move for air and water to get to the skin, and it's the undercoat that mats first. Work down to the skin and the loose stuff comes with you.

Curly and wavy coats need a slightly different approach. For tight curls — poodle, cockapoo, bichon, shih tzu, labradoodle — a slicker on its own can tighten a curl into a rope. Use a metal pin brush or a curly-coat brush to open the curls up first, then follow with a slicker to lift out the shedding undercoat. For looser wavy coats, a wide-tooth comb does most of the work.

## Start where the mats actually start

If you only have fifteen minutes, spend it in the right places. Every mat I've ever worked on began behind the ears, under the front legs, or in the armpits. Start behind the ears, then under the front legs, then the armpits and chest, then the belly and the tail base. Work in small sections so you're not missing anything and you're not tangling what you just detangled.

Go over your dog at least every couple of days for curly breeds, and twice a week for double-coated dogs. Ten focused minutes with a slicker beats an hour on Saturday, every time.

## When you spot a mat forming

Don't reach for the brush or the comb. That's how small mats get bigger.

Put a little conditioner or detangling spray directly on the mat and work it in with your fingers, gently separating the fibers. Use your fingertips to tease the mat apart in small pieces, from the outside in, while the conditioner does its work. Give it a few minutes to soak in. Then take your slicker or comb and pick through the loosened mat in short strokes, pulling out a little at a time. You'll get it. It takes longer than a brush-out, but it takes less time than a groomer untangling a coat that welded itself into one solid piece while it was wet.

## The one thing I wish every dog owner knew

Don't bathe a matted dog. Don't even bathe a dog with a mat *forming* unless you've been working on it at home and it's gone. Come in and let me handle the matting first, then we can do a bath and blow-out. Wet matting is what puts dogs on my table under sedation, and it's completely avoidable.

And please — no scissors. I know it's tempting to cut a mat out like you would a burr. But mats pull tight against the skin, and the skin underneath moves and folds, and one snip is all it takes to open a cut. Bring your dog in and I'll do it safely.

Mats aren't a sign of a bad owner. They're usually a sign that somebody bathed a dog who needed brushing. Book a brush-out between your full grooms — it's cheaper, faster, and far kinder on the coat than trying to rescue a mat after the fact. Give me a call and we'll set up a schedule that fits your dog's coat and keeps your wallet happy.

b.text:
I see this constantly and it breaks my heart a little every time. Someone brings their doodle or golden or Aussie in after a few weeks at home, the coat looks okay until I get my hands in it, and then I find those tight little mats starting behind the ears and under the front legs. Nine times out of ten they tell me they just gave the dog a bath thinking the water and shampoo would loosen everything up. It does the opposite. Wet matted fur just turns into a felt pad. Once that happens you’re not brushing it out anymore, you’re cutting it out.

Brush first. Always. Before the bath, never after. Get a decent slicker and work in short, straight line strokes, not big circles. Circles just roll the hair over itself and make the problem worse. Start behind the ears and right under the armpits because that’s where the friction happens first, then move through the rest of the body in sections so you actually finish an area instead of hopping around. If you already feel a mat starting to form, stop. Don’t grab the brush yet. Work a little conditioner into it with your fingers and let it sit for a minute so the hair can slide instead of snap. Then you can try the slicker. If it still won’t give, leave it for us. That’s what we’re here for.

A few minutes a couple times a week like this keeps most double coats and curly coats from turning into a project between visits. Your dog will thank you and so will I.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
**The Spring Market Reality Check We Can’t Ignore**

Ten years in this job teaches you that real estate has seasons—not just weather seasons, but mood seasons. And right now? The mood has shifted, but the data tells a more interesting story than the headlines might suggest.

Let’s start with the numbers from my own zip code. Last spring, the median days on market was a blistering 8 days. This spring, it’s 34. That’s a quadrupling of time on market, and it’s real. Showings per listing have been cut in half. You’d think that would send prices tumbling, right? But here’s the thing: list prices are still up 6% year over year. That’s not a typo. Buyers are more selective, and sellers aren’t budging—at least not yet.

I’m living this tension right now. I have three sellers who’ve been on the market for over 60 days, and none of them will drop their price. They’re anchored to comps from a year ago when bidding wars were the norm and “sight unseen” offers landed in my inbox. That market is gone. But here’s the twist: homes that are priced accurately from day one are still selling in under two weeks.

So what’s really happening? This isn’t a crash. I’ve seen crashes—foreclosures stacking up, prices in freefall, panic. This is something different. This is a seller pool that hasn’t caught up to the new pace. Sellers are flying blind on old expectations, thinking a “For Sale” sign is a magic wand. It’s not. Buyers have more options now, and they’re using them. They’ll look at three more houses before pulling the trigger, and they’ll notice when your price feels like a relic from last year’s frenzy.

The 6% year-over-year price growth is proof that the market is still fundamentally sound. Values are holding because demand isn’t gone—it’s just being smarter. The sellers who get that, who price for today’s buyers instead of yesterday’s bidding wars, are the ones cleaning out their garages and moving on. The ones who don’t? They’re the reason the median days on market shot up to 34.

If you’re thinking of listing, don’t let the slower pace scare you. Let it focus you. Price aggressively for the market we’re in, not the one we wish we had. That doesn’t mean giving your house away—it means respecting the buyer’s reality. Because the market hasn’t stopped; it’s just stopped waiting for you.

b.text:
If you’ve been watching the "For Sale" signs in our neighborhoods linger a little longer this spring, you’ve probably heard the rumors: the market is stalling, buyers are vanishing, the sky is falling.

Let’s skip the panic. The sky isn’t falling. But we do have a reality check overdue, and it’s time to talk about it plainly.

Here is the math in our zip code right now: Last spring, the median days on market was eight. Eight days. You planted a sign on a Thursday, held an open house on Saturday, and sorted through five offers by Sunday night. 

This spring? The median days on market is 34. 

At the same time, showings per listing have dropped by half. There are simply fewer people walking through front doors on any given weekend. 

Now, if you only looked at those two numbers, you’d assume prices are plummeting. But they aren’t. List prices are actually up 6% year over year. 

So what’s actually happening? 

It’s not a crash. It’s seller denial.

Right now, I have three listings where the sellers are firmly refusing to adjust their prices. All three have crossed the 60-day mark. We aren’t lacking marketing. We have professional photography, floor plans, digital ads, the works. What we lack is a time machine to take us back to the spring of 2022, when buyers would waive inspections and pay $30,000 over asking just to secure four walls and a roof.

Those days are over. Buyers today are contending with higher borrowing costs, and they’ve become fiercely discerning. They aren't boycotting real estate—they’re boycotting fantasy pricing. 

The most frustrating part of my week is watching this standoff happen when the proof is right in front of us. In our exact same neighborhoods, the homes that hit the market priced accurately for *today’s* rate environment—not last year’s wish list—are going under contract in under two weeks. The buyers are out there, pre-approved, motivated, and writing checks. They just refuse to overpay for a house that needs a new roof and hasn't updated its mechanicals since 2004.

When your house sits past the 30-day mark, it doesn’t become more valuable. It gets stale. Buyers don’t look at an aging listing and think, *“What a rare gem.”* They think, *“What’s wrong with it, and how much lower can I bid?”*

This isn't a mysterious, unpredictable market. It’s actually very simple: the frantic pace is gone, and the fundamentals are back. If you want to sell your home this spring, you can’t test the market with an aspirational number and hope a desperate buyer bites. 

Price it right from day one, and you’ll hand over the keys in two weeks. Price it for three years ago, and I’ll see you at day 60.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
Roadstar DC4 Review – 14 Months / 140k Miles

Been running the DC4 for 14 months and about 140,000 miles, so it's had plenty of windshield time.

Biggest pro: it already paid for itself. Got caught in a lane-change accident last fall, sent in the footage, and insurance approved my claim in 9 days. Normally that's a 6-week fight. It was clear enough they didn't argue it.

Cons: The rear cam at night gets grainy past about 30 feet. You can tell it's a vehicle, but don't count on reading a plate back there after dark.

Suction mount is junk in the heat, too. Fell off twice last summer. Switched to the adhesive mount and it hasn't moved since — just use that from the start.

Also forget the app. It needs WiFi to pull footage, which is useless at most truck stops. I just pop the SD card out and use my laptop.

Overall, worth it for the front cam alone.

b.text:
**RoadStar DC4 Dash Cam – 14 Months & 140K Miles In**

Been running the RoadStar DC4 for over a year now, and it’s mostly held up to the abuse. The front cam is solid—day or night, footage is clear enough to make out license plates at highway speeds. The rear cam? Not so much. Night footage gets grainy past 30 feet, but it’s still better than nothing.

Biggest win? Caught a four-wheeler sideswiping me during a lane change. Insurance had the claim approved in nine days instead of the usual six weeks. Worth every penny for that alone.

The suction mount is garbage in summer heat—fell off twice before I swapped it for the adhesive mount. Stick with the adhesive; it hasn’t budged since.

The app’s a joke. Needs Wi-Fi to pull footage, which is useless at most truck stops. I just pop the SD card and transfer files to my phone. Not ideal, but it works.

Battery life’s decent—no issues even in extreme temps. Build quality’s solid, no random shutdowns or overheating.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: 8 Months of Nearly Daily Use

**Quick take:** The motor is worth the money. The accessories aren't. Full verdict at the bottom.

---

I've been running the Corlane SM6 for eight months now, and it gets used almost every day. I bake sourdough for a weekend farmers market stall, so this isn't a "unboxed it and made two batches of banana bread" review — this machine has mixed hundreds of batches of dough since it landed on my counter. Here's what eight months of hard use looks like.

## The motor is the whole reason to buy this mixer

The test that kills most home stand mixers is stiff, low-hydration dough — and I run the SM6 through that test constantly. A double batch of bagel dough, stiff enough that plenty of consumer mixers would stall out or walk themselves across the counter, runs through this machine without hesitation. No stalling, no straining, no standing there with my hand on the bowl waiting for it to recover. I can walk away and weigh out the next ingredient while it kneads.

If you've ever heard a mixer bog down in the middle of a bread dough, you know how quickly that becomes a dealbreaker. In eight months of near-daily bread work, the motor has never done that to me once. That is the entire case for this mixer.

## Two real problems

**The bowl lift lever squeaks.** Not a catastrophic issue, but it's a monthly maintenance item — I hit it with WD-40 about once every four weeks or it gets genuinely annoying. For a machine at this price, it shouldn't squeak out of the box, and it shouldn't squeak eight months later either.

**The included dough hook is too short for the bowl.** This is my biggest complaint. The SM6's bowl is deep, and the stock hook doesn't reach far enough down — dough at the bottom of the bowl just sits there, not getting worked in. I ended up buying a third-party hook, which solved the problem completely, but it means the hook that ships with the mixer is effectively useless for exactly the kind of dough this machine is built for. Factor that into the price.

## Speaking of price

The SM6 is $429. The comparable KitchenAid is $349. So the real math is: an $80 premium over KitchenAid, plus the cost of a replacement dough hook on top.

## Verdict

**If you're kneading heavy dough every week — bread, bagels, low-hydration anything, double batches — buy it.** The $80 premium buys you a motor that genuinely doesn't stall where other mixers in this class will, and after eight months I trust it with my market bread. Deal with the hook swap, keep a can of WD-40 under the sink, and it earns its spot on the counter.

**If your mixer mostly sees cookie dough and cake batter, skip it.** You'd be paying an $80 premium, plus a new dough hook, for a motor you'll never stress. Buy the KitchenAid and put the savings toward something else.

That's not a hedge — there's exactly one question that determines the answer, and it's whether stiff dough is a weekly event in your kitchen. For me it is, and I'd buy the SM6 again tomorrow.

b.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer - 8 Month Review**

I've had the Corlane SM6 on my counter for 8 months now. It runs almost every day. I bake sourdough for the Saturday farmers market, so this thing has mixed a lot of dough.

Here’s what actually happened after 8 months of real use:

**It does not stall on heavy dough.**

That’s why I bought it. I do a double batch of bagel dough every Thursday night - 65% hydration, super stiff - and my old mixer would overheat and start to smell. The SM6 goes through it without stalling or walking across the counter. For my regular market sourdough, two loaves at a time, it barely sounds like it’s working. If you knead low-hydration dough, the motor is legit.

**Two annoying things I didn’t expect.**

First, the bowl lift lever squeaks. Loudly. About three weeks in it started. I have to hit it with WD-40 once a month or it screams every time I raise the bowl.

Second, the dough hook that comes with it is too short for the deep bowl. At a single batch, the dough just sits under it and it spins in the air. I ended up buying a third-party spiral hook for $35 and now it actually kneads like it should. That should have come in the box.

It’s $429. The equivalent bowl-lift KitchenAid is $349 right now, so you’re paying $80 more.

**Verdict:**

Worth it if you knead heavy dough every week. That motor will save you if you’re doing sourdough, bagels, or brioche on repeat like I am.

Skip it if you’re mostly doing cookies and cake batter. You don’t need to pay extra and deal with the short hook and the squeaky lever for that.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
When I first started shooting weddings in this area six years ago, I’ll admit I was a May-to-October purist. Like most people in the industry, I looked at winter as the off-season—a time to back up hard drives, update my website, and wait for the spring thaw. 

But over the last two years, something shifted. I ended up booking and shooting 11 winter weddings, and those 11 days completely changed how I look at the calendar. 

If you are currently staring at a venue's availability calendar trying to decide on a date, let me make a case for the colder months. Here is the honest, unfiltered truth about why I’ve grown to love winter weddings—and why they might actually be the best choice for your photos, your budget, and your sanity.

### 1. The Light is Superior (Seriously)
Everyone thinks summer is the prime time for portraits, but June light can be incredibly harsh and flat. If it’s overcast, the sky looks like a giant, boring softbox. If it’s sunny, we’re dodging squint-inducing glare and heavy shadows at noon. 

Winter light is different. Because the sun sits lower in the sky all day, the light has a softer, more dramatic quality. Specifically, the light through bare trees around 3:00 PM in November is unmatched. It creates this warm, directional glow that filters perfectly through the branches. It gives your portraits a rich, cinematic texture that you simply cannot replicate during a high-noon shoot in mid-July. 

### 2. We Aren't Fighting for Parking
During the summer peak, venues are turning over events like factory assembly lines. If you get married on a Saturday in June, chances are I’m arriving at your venue only to fight for a spot in the loading dock with three or four other vendors who are either rushing to pack up the afternoon event or scrambling to set up yours. The energy can feel frantic.

In November, January, or February? The vibe is entirely different. The venue staff is relaxed, I’m not sharing the parking lot with a fleet of delivery vans, and we actually have the breathing room to create without feeling like we’re on a stopwatch. That calmness trickles down into your entire day.

### 3. You Save Roughly 30%
Let’s talk about the math. Planning a wedding is expensive, and winter is the ultimate budget hack. On average, winter bookings run about 30% cheaper than peak-season dates. 

That 30% discount isn't just on the venue rental, either. Many caterers, florists, and, yes, photographers are more flexible with their pricing or packages during the winter months. Saving that chunk of your budget means you can invest more into the things you actually care about—like upgrading your menu, booking your dream band, or extending your honeymoon.

***

There is a quiet, cozy elegance to a winter wedding that gets lost in the summer rush. If you’re willing to embrace a chill in the air and a slightly earlier sunset, the payoff is a stress-free day, a healthier budget, and portraits with the kind of light most couples wait all year for. 

My calendar for the upcoming winter is starting to fill up, but I still have a few dates open. Let’s bundle up and chase that 3:00 PM golden hour together.

b.text:
# Why I Like Photographing Winter Weddings Now

For a long time, I thought of winter weddings as the exception to the wedding season. After six years photographing weddings around this metro area—and 11 winter weddings in the last two years—I’ve changed my mind. I genuinely look forward to them.

The light is a big reason. Around 3 p.m. in November, sunlight comes through the bare trees at an angle that gives portraits shape and warmth. I’ll take that over flat, overcast June light more often than you might expect. We do have to plan for an earlier sunset, but when we build portraits into the timeline before it gets dark, that short window can be excellent.

Winter also feels less crowded. In June, I’m often sharing a venue parking lot with three or four other vendors arriving, unloading, and trying to work in the same spaces at once. In winter, there’s usually more room to move and a little less of that peak-season rush. It doesn’t change what matters about your day, but it can make the experience calmer.

And there’s a practical difference: my winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for couples. If you’re flexible on your date, that’s worth considering alongside the photos you want.

I wouldn’t tell you to book a winter wedding if you’re dreaming of a long outdoor cocktail hour. You’ll want a plan for the cold and a timeline that respects the early sunset. But if you like the idea of quieter venues, beautiful afternoon light, and a little more room in your budget, winter deserves a serious look.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/  
I made a pricing mistake with Tallyup.

I raised prices by 40% for everyone overnight.

Within a week, 30 of our 140 customers had left.

Here’s what happened—and what I changed.

2/  
The mistake wasn’t raising prices.

Tallyup had changed since many customers first subscribed. The old pricing no longer reflected the value we were providing.

The mistake was treating a pricing change like a switch:

Old price → new price  
No transition. No context. No room for customers to adjust.

3/  
I underestimated how the change would feel to customers.

A 40% increase might be reasonable on paper.

But to a gym owner receiving an unexpected bill, it’s still a 40% increase overnight.

The math made sense to me. The rollout didn’t.

4/  
The churn was immediate:

30 of 140 customers left in one week.

That’s roughly 21% of the customer base.

It was painful, but it made the problem impossible to ignore.

5/  
The biggest lesson:

Pricing isn’t just a number.

It’s also timing, communication, trust, and whether customers understand the value they’re paying for.

I focused too much on the first part.

6/  
What I changed:

I stopped thinking about pricing as a one-time decision.

It needs to be treated as an ongoing product decision—something to revisit carefully, communicate clearly, and roll out deliberately.

7/  
I also became much more cautious about making a broad pricing change all at once.

When you’re a small SaaS, it’s easy to make a decision in a spreadsheet and forget that every row represents a real customer relationship.

8/  
I’m still glad I looked at pricing.

Tallyup needs to be a sustainable business, and pricing has to reflect the value the product creates.

But sustainable pricing shouldn’t come at the cost of surprising the people who helped build the business.

9/  
The uncomfortable version of the lesson:

A pricing increase can be “correct” and still be handled badly.

The 40% increase wasn’t the only issue.

The overnight rollout was.

10/  
For other indie founders:

Don’t only ask, “What should we charge?”

Also ask:

- How will customers experience this?
- How much notice do they need?
- How can we explain the value?
- What would make the transition feel fair?

11/  
I lost 30 customers in a week because I optimized for the new price instead of the long-term relationship.

That’s a mistake I don’t plan to repeat.

Pricing is part of the product. Treat it that way.

b.text:
I raised my prices by 40% overnight. In one week, 30 of our 140 customers canceled. As a solo founder building Tallyup (a subscription tool that helps gym owners track member retention), this was a harsh pricing lesson. Here’s what went wrong and exactly what I changed. 🧵

The decision seemed logical on paper. I’m an indie SaaS builder and needed to align pricing with reality. So I updated the billing page for every single user at once. No warning. No segmentation. Just a hard 40% jump.

The fallout was immediate. 30 customers left in seven days. Most weren’t mad about the platform—they were reacting to the execution. Churn spiked. Trust cracked. I realized quickly that in lean SaaS, reliability and communication are part of the product.

What I changed:
• Stopped the blanket increase for existing users. They stay on their original rate.
• Rolled out the new pricing exclusively for new signups.
• Sent transparent emails explaining the shift, tying it directly to the features that protect gym retention.
• Offered a direct reply channel for anyone who needed to discuss options.

The result? Panic stopped. Retention stabilized. New sign-ups converted better because the messaging finally focused on outcomes, not a sudden invoice bump. Pricing isn’t a lever you yank. It’s a relationship you manage.

Takeaway for indie hackers & founders: If you raise prices, give people a bridge, not a cliff. Transparency beats speed every time when you’re building alone.

Have you ever run a sudden pricing test? What did it teach you? 👇

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
To the Editor:

Every weekday morning in my house starts the same way: a chorus of alarms, heavy sighs, and me trying to coax two exhausted middle schoolers out of bed. If your household is anything like mine, you know the struggle is real. Our kids are chronically sleep-deprived, which is why I’m writing to urge our community—and our school board—to support the proposed 8:45 a.m. start time.

This isn't just about making our mornings a little less chaotic. It’s a matter of basic health. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. Science tells us that during puberty, children’s sleep cycles naturally shift later. They aren't just being lazy; their brains physically resist falling asleep early. Expecting them to absorb pre-algebra at 7:45 a.m. is fighting a losing battle against biology. 

We already have proof right here in Millbrook that a later start works. Just look at the results from the pilot program at Lincoln Middle. When Lincoln pushed its start time back, the school saw a noticeable rise in attendance, and first-period grades went up. When we give kids just a little more sleep, they show up, and they actually learn. 

I know some parents are worried about how this change will affect transportation. Change is hard, and logistics are always a puzzle. But if you read the school board’s proposal closely, you’ll see they have already addressed this. The plan includes a smart re-tiering of our bus routes. By shifting the windows for elementary, middle, and high schools, the district can handle the new schedule using the fleet we already have, without costing taxpayers extra money. It’s a practical, well-thought-out solution.

Our school board votes on this proposal next month. As parents, we want to give our kids every tool possible to succeed. Let’s support a policy that prioritizes their mental health, safety, and academic success. Please join me in contacting the school board to voice your support for the 8:45 a.m. start time. It’s time to let our kids get the sleep they need.

b.text:
**Please Give Our Kids the Sleep They're Not Getting**

*To the Millbrook Gazette and Members of the School Board:*

I'm not a policy person. I'm a parent of two middle-schoolers in Millbrook, and every school morning I'm negotiating with a teenager who is too tired to get out of bed.

With a 7:30 a.m. first period, that means a 6:15 wake-up call. Do the math backward, and a 13- or 14-year-old is going to bed around 10:15 p.m. — and then doing homework after that. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends 8 to 10 hours of sleep for teens, and in 2015 formally urged middle schools to start no later than 8:00 a.m. and high schools no later than 8:30 a.m. The AAP didn't write that recommendation because it sounded nice. It wrote it because the evidence links adequate sleep to attendance, behavior, grades, and even fewer adolescent driving crashes.

Then I read the results from our own pilot at Lincoln Middle, and the case stopped being theoretical. Attendance went up. First-period grades went up. [Insert the specific figures from the pilot.] In our building, on our watch, the students who got a later start showed up more often and did better in the classes that used to be hardest to face. That's not a national study being imported from somewhere else. That's our district's own data.

The objection I'm hearing most often at board meetings is the buses. It's a fair question, and I had the same one. But the proposal already re-tiers the routes: the early runs are remapped around the elementary and high-school start times, and the middle-school runs are rebuilt around an 8:45 bell. No rider is dropped and no bus driver is left with a route that doesn't work. Re-tiering is the whole point of the plan — the schedule change and the transportation change were designed together, not one after the other.

I'll also say plainly what I'd be losing: an earlier start is more convenient for working parents. If the 8:45 start means some mornings are harder for my family, I say so. But convenience for adults shouldn't be weighed against the documented well-being of the children on those buses and in those first-period classrooms.

There's one more thing worth saying. The kids are not the problem. They are 12 and 14 years old, and they are doing exactly what their bodies tell them to do. We're the adults making the schedule.

The board votes next month. Please approve the 8:45 start. Our kids' sleep — and our own pilot results — are asking you to.

*— [Your Name], parent of two middle-schoolers, Millbrook*

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
1. **Shut off the boiler and circulator.** Let the baseboards cool before you work. Water at a bleeder valve can be hot enough to burn you.

2. **Find the bleeder valve** at the end of the first baseboard unit closest to the boiler. Place a cup or small container underneath it.

3. **Open the valve slowly** with a radiator key or flathead screwdriver, whichever fits. You may hear air hissing out. Keep the cup in place until water comes out in a steady stream with no hissing.

4. **Close the valve snugly.** Don’t overtighten it—you can crack the valve seat. Wipe it dry so you can tell if it drips afterward.

5. **Move from unit to unit, working outward from the boiler.** Bleed each baseboard, including the basement loop. A mistake we see on cold-baseboard calls is bleeding only the upstairs units and skipping the basement loop, where the trapped air often is.

When you’re done, turn the boiler and circulator back on and check that each unit heats up. If a valve keeps dripping, no water comes out, or a baseboard stays cold, don’t loosen any pipe fittings to try to fix it. Give us a call so we can check the system pressure and the affected loop.

b.text:
1. Shut off the circulator pump and boiler at the control switch or breaker. Bleeding a pressurized, running system forces fresh air back in, wastes time, and can damage the pump seals.

2. Find the bleeder valve on each baseboard unit. It’s a small brass fitting, usually half an inch across, located on the end cap where the supply and return pipes meet. Every unit in the loop gets one.

3. Cup a small container directly underneath the valve. Keep a shop rag folded over the rim to catch drips. You’re only going to release a few ounces per unit.

4. Open the valve slowly using a dedicated bleeder key or a flathead screwdriver. Turn counter-clockwise just enough to break the seal. You’ll hear air hiss out, followed by sputtering water. Keep it cracked until the stream runs completely steady and silent—that means the air pocket is gone.

5. Close the valve by turning clockwise until it stops, then tighten it firmly with one additional quarter-turn. Snug is all it takes. Overtightening shears the rubber washer or cracks the valve seat, which turns a three-minute maintenance task into a leaky fixture replacement.

6. Work your way through every unit in the loop, always starting with the baseboard closest to the boiler and moving outward to the farthest room. Water carries air as it circulates, so purging from the source pushes trapped pockets cleanly out through each valve.

The single biggest reason I show up to houses for cold radiator calls is that homeowners only bleed the upstairs units and completely ignore the basement loop. Air rises with the heat and migrates with the water flow, which means it consistently settles in the lowest part of the system—the basement circuit. Skip that loop and the rest of your house will stay cold regardless of what you do upstairs. Purge the basement first or treat it equally, and your zones will balance fast.

Once you’ve run through every unit, verify the system pressure on the gauge. It should read 12 to 15 psi when the boiler is cold. Top off with a filling loop or garden hose adapter if needed, restart the boiler, and let each zone pull hot. 

If you complete this entire process and still get lukewarm floors or major temperature swings, the culprit is usually a worn circulator, partially closed zone valves, or sediment buildup in the piping. Call us out, and we’ll diagnose it properly before the first hard freeze.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
Keeping your pup’s coat smooth and tangle-free between grooming visits isn’t as tricky as it seems—once you know the right moves. The biggest game-changer? Always brush *before* the bath, never after. Wet matted fur turns into a stubborn felt pad, and once that happens, the only fix is a close shave. Trust me, I’ve seen it too many times.

Start with a slicker brush and use short, straight strokes—no circles. Work in small sections, beginning behind the ears and under the front legs, because that’s where mats love to sneak in first. If you spot a mat forming, don’t reach for the brush right away. Instead, work a little conditioner into it with your fingers to loosen things up. Only then should you gently comb it out.

And here’s the mistake I see all the time: people bathe their dog first, thinking the water will loosen the mats. Spoiler—it does the opposite. Water tightens those tangles right up, making them nearly impossible to brush out. Save yourself (and your pup) the hassle by brushing first, then bathing. A little effort now means fewer mats later, and that’s a win for everyone.

b.text:
I hear the same thing at almost every appointment: "I don't know how she got so matted, I just bathed her last week." And that's usually the problem — not in spite of the bath, but because of it.

The mistake I see constantly, and I mean constantly, is bathing a matted dog because it seems like the water and shampoo will soften everything up and make brushing easier afterward. It feels like it should work. It does the exact opposite. Wet fur that's starting to mat doesn't loosen in the tub — it tightens. The water compresses the tangles, and as everything dries, it shrinks and felts together into something closer to a rug than a coat. A mat that would've brushed out in five minutes on dry hair can turn into a solid pad after a wash and dry. So here's the rule, write it on the fridge if you have to: brush before the bath, never after. Brush the whole dog out first, then bathe. The bath is a reward, not a repair job.

When you brush, use a slicker — the one with the fine bent pins — and work in short line strokes, like you're plowing little rows. Not circles. Circling just swirls the hair around and pushes mats tighter into themselves, and it's easy to lose track of where those pins are, which is how skin gets scraped. Line strokes let you see what you're catching and get all the way down to the skin instead of just smoothing the top layer. That top layer is the trap, by the way. setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
**A 22% Prevented Planting Premium Hike and a Cap That Punishes Family Farms**

USDA raised the prevented planting base rate in our region by 22% this year. On my corn and soybean farm, that increase adds about $46,000 to the cost of coverage at the exact same time I needed it most. Because of the rain this spring, I only got 60% of my acres planted by the late-May deadline.

That means 40% of my intended acres were left out of the ground. Prevented planting coverage is supposed to help manage that kind of loss. But the premium hike is only part of the problem. The other part is how the acreage caps work.

Under the current cap structure, there is a limit on how many prevented planting acres are recognized. In a wet year like this one, that cap does not just trim a few edge acres—it can leave a meaningful share of the actual loss unsupported. For a family operation like mine, that matters. We do not have endless ground to spread across or the same ability to absorb policy gaps as larger operations nearby. When the cap excludes acres, the financial hit is proportionally bigger on our operation than it is on the bigger farms around us.

That is what makes this so frustrating. The premium just went up 22%, but the protection still does not fully reflect the acres family farmers are trying to plant. We are paying more for a safety net that is less responsive to the way our operations actually work.

SB 214 would fix the acreage cap. It would not eliminate bad weather, and it would not make crop insurance cheap. But it would make prevented planting coverage work more fairly by recognizing the acres farmers truly intended to plant, rather than forcing a cap that hits mid-size family operations harder than it should.

I am a fourth-generation farmer. I am not asking for a handout. I am asking for the rules to match the reality we face when the fields stay too wet and the planting window closes.

If you support keeping family farms competitive, contact our state legislators and ask them to support SB 214. For operations like mine, this is not an abstract policy debate. It is a real cost, in a bad year, made worse by a cap that no longer makes sense.

b.text:
**A 22% Hike, 60% of My Acres, and a Bill Worth Your Phone Call**

This year USDA raised the base rate on prevented planting coverage in our region by 22 percent. On my operation that works out to roughly $46,000 more than I paid last year for the same protection.

I'd have paid it grudgingly in a normal spring. This wasn't a normal spring. The rain started the second week of April and did not quit in any meaningful way until it was too late to matter. By the late May final planting date I had 60 percent of my acres in the ground. The other 40 percent sat there with standing water in the low spots and mud you couldn't drive a four-wheeler across, let alone a planter. Anybody farming west of the river knows exactly what I'm describing because you were looking at the same thing out your own kitchen window.

So the year I actually needed prevented planting coverage is the year the premium jumped by nearly a quarter. That's the first thing I want people to sit with.

Here's the second thing, and it's the reason I'm writing.

The rate hike doesn't land evenly. The way the acreage caps are structured, the full increase applies across every acre on an operation my size. Once an operation crosses the cap threshold, the effective cost per acre starts coming down. The result is that the two large operations that farm on either side of me, both good neighbors, both running several times my acreage, are seeing a smaller percentage increase in their total premium cost than I am. Same county. Same rain. Same deadline. Same 40 percent left unplanted. Different bill.

I ran the numbers with my crop insurance agent, who I trust and who didn't argue with me. On a per-acre basis I'm paying meaningfully more for the same coverage than the operations next door. Not because I'm a worse risk. Because I'm smaller.

I don't begrudge the bigger outfits. They didn't write the rules. But a program that's supposed to help farmers stay in business through a bad spring shouldn't be quietly structured so that the fourth-generation operation on 1,200 acres carries a heavier share than the one on 6,000. That's backward, and I don't think it's what anybody intended when the caps were drawn up.

SB 214 would fix the acreage cap. It adjusts how the threshold applies so the premium increase falls proportionally instead of piling onto the operations least able to absorb it. It doesn't take anything away from the larger farms. It doesn't touch the coverage itself. It just corrects the math so that a 22 percent hike is a 22 percent hike for everybody, not 22 for some and less for others.

The bill has been sitting in committee since February. I'm told it's stalled less from opposition than from nobody making much noise about it. That part we can do something about.

If you farm in this county and you had ground you couldn't plant this spring, you already know what I'm talking about. If you didn't have that problem this year, you will eventually, and the cap will be waiting for you when you do.

Call your state senator. Call your representative. Their numbers are on the back page of this newsletter. Tell them you farm here, tell them how many acres you got planted by the deadline, and tell them you want SB 214 out of committee and onto the floor. You don't need to be eloquent. You need to be one more voice they can't ignore.

I'll be at the county meeting on the 14th. If you want to compare premium statements, bring yours. I'll have mine.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
**Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now**

I used to think winter weddings were the off-season compromise. After six years in this metro area and 11 winter weddings in the last two years, I’ve changed my mind for reasons that are more specific than “every season is beautiful.”

The first reason is money, and I’ll be blunt: winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for you. That’s not because the photos are worse or vendors are phoning it in. It’s because demand drops. Venues have open Saturdays, caterers have openings, and photographers like me have calendar gaps we’d rather fill with a wedding than leave empty. You can often get the higher package, the second shooter, or the venue you actually wanted for the same budget that would have bought you a peak-season baseline. I’ve watched couples do exactly that.

But I didn’t come around just because it’s cheaper. I came around because the images can be better.

The light through bare trees around 3 p.m. in November is honestly better for portraits than flat overcast June light. I know that sounds like a hot take, but I’ve shot both. In June, I’m often dealing with a flat white sky or harsh overhead sun that makes people squint and turns every tree into the same green background. In November, the sun sits lower. It comes through bare branches at an angle, and it gives you warm, directional light that’s much easier to work with for portraits. The trees themselves become part of the composition—branches instead of a green wall. Some of my favorite portraits from the last two years were taken in the middle of a mostly empty park at 3:15 p.m., no sweating, no squinting, no waiting for another group to clear the frame.

That brings me to the part nobody puts in a brochure: in winter, I am not sharing the parking lot with three or four other vendors like I am in June. That matters more than it should. In peak season, popular venues get stacked with multiple events. You’re waiting for the loading zone, waiting for the elevator, waiting for the staircase while another photographer works the same shot. It eats into your timeline and adds background noise to what should be a calm day. In winter, it’s usually just us, the venue staff, and your people. The day moves differently. I can actually take my time with details instead of looking over my shoulder for the next vendor’s arrival.

Yes, winter has a shorter light window, and yes, it can be cold. We plan for that. We do portraits in a 20-minute block when the light is right, keep coats nearby, and have an indoor backup. After 11 winter weddings, I’ve found that constraint usually makes the day feel more intentional, not less.

If you’re trying to stretch your budget or you just want a wedding day that doesn’t feel like a crowded peak-season Saturday, ask me about winter dates. I have the availability, I have the experience, and now I actually have a preference.

b.text:
When I first started shooting weddings in this area six years ago, I’ll admit I was a May-to-October purist. Like most people in the industry, I looked at winter as the off-season—a time to back up hard drives, update my website, and wait for the spring thaw. 

But over the last two years, something shifted. I ended up booking and shooting 11 winter weddings, and those 11 days completely changed how I look at the calendar. 

If you are currently staring at a venue's availability calendar trying to decide on a date, let me make a case for the colder months. Here is the honest, unfiltered truth about why I’ve grown to love winter weddings—and why they might actually be the best choice for your photos, your budget, and your sanity.

### 1. The Light is Superior (Seriously)
Everyone thinks summer is the prime time for portraits, but June light can be incredibly harsh and flat. If it’s overcast, the sky looks like a giant, boring softbox. If it’s sunny, we’re dodging squint-inducing glare and heavy shadows at noon. 

Winter light is different. Because the sun sits lower in the sky all day, the light has a softer, more dramatic quality. Specifically, the light through bare trees around 3:00 PM in November is unmatched. It creates this warm, directional glow that filters perfectly through the branches. It gives your portraits a rich, cinematic texture that you simply cannot replicate during a high-noon shoot in mid-July. 

### 2. We Aren't Fighting for Parking
During the summer peak, venues are turning over events like factory assembly lines. If you get married on a Saturday in June, chances are I’m arriving at your venue only to fight for a spot in the loading dock with three or four other vendors who are either rushing to pack up the afternoon event or scrambling to set up yours. The energy can feel frantic.

In November, January, or February? The vibe is entirely different. The venue staff is relaxed, I’m not sharing the parking lot with a fleet of delivery vans, and we actually have the breathing room to create without feeling like we’re on a stopwatch. That calmness trickles down into your entire day.

### 3. You Save Roughly 30%
Let’s talk about the math. Planning a wedding is expensive, and winter is the ultimate budget hack. On average, winter bookings run about 30% cheaper than peak-season dates. 

That 30% discount isn't just on the venue rental, either. Many caterers, florists, and, yes, photographers are more flexible with their pricing or packages during the winter months. Saving that chunk of your budget means you can invest more into the things you actually care about—like upgrading your menu, booking your dream band, or extending your honeymoon.

***

There is a quiet, cozy elegance to a winter wedding that gets lost in the summer rush. If you’re willing to embrace a chill in the air and a slightly earlier sunset, the payoff is a stress-free day, a healthier budget, and portraits with the kind of light most couples wait all year for. 

My calendar for the upcoming winter is starting to fill up, but I still have a few dates open. Let’s bundle up and chase that 3:00 PM golden hour together.

a.text:
After eight years shooting roughly 35 weddings a year in the Texas Hill Country, I’ve seen the same pattern repeat: the couples who ditch the shot list always end up with the best photos.

The Barrera wedding is my favorite proof. We had a plan—locations, timelines, a detailed shot list. Then it rained. Hard. We moved everything under the pecan tree. No staged portraits in the field, no formal group shots in the barn. Just family huddled together laughing about the weather, the bride holding her bouquet under the branches, the groom shielding her with his jacket.

Those are the frames that tell the story. Not the checklist.

If you’re planning a wedding: build the timeline, but don’t treat the photo list like a contract. Leave space for the moment. The best images usually happen when the plan breaks.

To vendors: encourage your couples to let go a little. The magic isn’t in the checklist—it’s in the reaction.

Ready for a Hill Country photographer who actually plans for the rain? Let’s talk.

b.text:

The Barrera wedding is a perfect example. The rain changed the plan, so we moved everything under a pecan tree. It wasn’t the setup anyone had pictured—but it gave the day room to unfold naturally.

That’s when the best photographs happen: not because every moment was planned, but because the couple could be present in the moment they were actually having.

Of course, a list of must-have family groupings is helpful. But you don’t need to script every image. Leave space for the unexpected, too. Sometimes the weather has other plans—and they can turn into your favorite photographs.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
On my first day in the ER, I worried I would get in the way. I was a first-year nursing student, and I knew there was a lot I had only practiced in a classroom. By the end of the week, I had learned that I could be useful, even while I was still learning.

One patient needed a wound cleaned, and his wife was stuck in traffic. He kept looking toward the door. I couldn’t make the cleaning hurt less or get his wife there sooner, so I asked if he wanted me to stay. He took my hand and held it until the nurse finished. I had come in thinking the most important thing I could do was a task. That day, it was staying beside someone.

Later in the week, a code was called. I was sent to restock gauze while the team worked behind a curtain. I could hear them counting, and part of me wanted to see what was happening. Instead, I filled the shelves and checked what else was low. The people behind the curtain needed supplies ready when they reached for them. I was not part of the code team, but I was part of the work around them.

The hardest moment for me was a blood draw. The patient had diabetes and veins that were difficult to find. I missed three times. Each time, I felt worse about causing him another poke. My instructor stayed with me, and we checked with him before trying again. He agreed to one more attempt, and on the fourth try, I got it. I was relieved, but I was also aware that my relief was not the most important thing in that room. He had been patient with me when I was the one who needed practice.

That first week did not make me feel like I had nursing figured out. It showed me how much I still need to learn, and it made me want to keep learning. I want to become the kind of nurse who can do the hard skills well, knows when to ask for help, and remembers the person who is waiting, hurting, or giving a student one more chance.

b.text:
# What I Learned in Room 6

I didn't expect the first person I helped to be a stranger whose name I'd forget by the end of the shift, but whose hand I'd remember for a long time.

He was maybe seventy, in for a leg wound that needed cleaning before it got stitched up. His wife was supposed to be there, but traffic had her stuck somewhere on the interstate, and he kept looking at the door like she might walk through it if he waited long enough. The nurse doing the cleaning told him it was going to sting. He nodded, and then he looked at me, standing there in my student scrubs not doing much of anything, and he just said, "Would you mind?"

I didn't know what he meant until I did. I took his hand. He squeezed it hard when the solution hit the wound, and he apologized for squeezing so hard, and I told him not to worry about it. We didn't talk about anything important. I think I asked him about his dog. But I stood there and let him hold onto me because his wife couldn't be there to do it, and that was the job in that moment. Nobody taught me that in a lecture hall.

Not everything that week made me feel useful. During a code, somebody told me to go restock gauze, which felt like being sent to the kids' table while the adults handled things. I went. I stood in the supply room and counted gauze packs and listened to someone on the other side of the curtain counting compressions instead. One, two, three, four. I didn't see what happened in that room. I just heard the numbers and the quiet after them. I still think about that quiet. I didn't do anything heroic that day. I stocked gauze. But I learned that the job isn't always about being in the room. Sometimes it's about doing the small thing so the people who need to be in there can be.

Then there was the blood draw that humbled me completely. The patient was a diabetic guy, older, with veins that rolled and hid and generally did not want to be found. I missed the first stick. I missed the second. By the third, I was sweating more than he was, and I apologized so many times he started laughing at me instead of getting mad, which I think was his way of being kind about it. He told me his veins had been giving nurses trouble for twenty years, so I shouldn't take it personally. On the fourth try, I found it. I actually said "there it is" out loud like an idiot, and he said "there it is" right back at me, like we'd done something together instead of me just finally doing my job. Small win. But I felt it in my chest for the rest of the shift.

None of these moments were dramatic in the way I thought the ER would be dramatic. Nobody yelled "clear." Nobody coded and came back in some big cinematic way in front of me. What I got instead was a hand to hold, a hallway full of counting I couldn't see the end of, and a vein that took four tries to find. But I think that's the actual job. It's not always the big save. It's showing up for the parts that are small and slow and a little embarrassing, and doing them anyway, because someone needs you to.

I came into that week wondering if I could handle the big emergencies. I left it realizing the real question is whether I can handle the quiet, unglamorous moments in between them, the ones where nobody's watching and nothing photographs well, but somebody still needs your hand, or your gauze, or just you not giving up on the fourth try. I think I can. I want the chance to keep finding out.

But more than just using your software, I’ve actively tried to help improve it: over the past three years, I’ve submitted 14 feature requests to your product team—and four of them actually shipped.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
I don’t have time for metaphors. The field floods, games get canceled, and kids get hurt. Next Tuesday, the school board votes on next year’s facilities budget. Put the girls’ soccer field on turf. That’s all this comes down to.

Over the past two seasons, weather and poor drainage have forced us to cancel or relocate nine games. Nine. The field saturates, sits under water, and turns into uneven terrain. We lose valuable practice windows. We scramble to secure host schools. We spend evenings coordinating bus routes and managing parent complaints while the clock ticks toward Friday nights. And it’s not just an administrative headache. Last October, one of my players stepped into a deep rut during warmups, twisted her knee, and tore her ACL. That’s not bad luck. It’s a documented hazard disguised as normal spring weather.

In 2019, the boys’ football program received an artificial turf upgrade. There was no multi-month feasibility study. No competing bids debated into oblivion. They got the surface. They kept their schedule. Now it’s our turn. This isn’t a gender issue. It’s a baseline equity issue. These athletes sign waivers, adhere to strict attendance policies, and sacrifice weekends for the program. We don’t honor that commitment by demanding they perform safely on ground that actively works against them.

Artificial turf requires capital. I know how budget meetings work. But compare that to the recurring costs of maintaining a failing grass field: ER visits for ligament tears, coaching hours burned on rescheduling, transportation fees for makeshift venues, and a team that can’t develop offensive or defensive schemes because we never know if we’ll actually play. Turf is a fixed investment. It drains consistently. It provides uniform traction. It stops the bleeding—financially and athletically.

The board has a straightforward choice ahead. Approve the turf line item. End the seasonal uncertainty. Give the girls’ soccer program the same functional playing environment the district already installed six years ago. Don’t make me justify another flooded matchup or explain another preventable injury. Fund the surface. Get it done.

b.text:
I coach girls’ soccer and track at the high school. I do it for the stipend and because I like the kids. I don’t write columns, and I don’t have patience for long speeches. But the school board is voting on next year’s facilities budget, and they need to hear something the athletic director already knows: the girls’ soccer field is a mess, and it’s dangerous.

In the last two seasons, rain has killed or moved nine of our games. Nine. The grass field floods every time a storm rolls through, and it doesn’t drain. It turns into a mud pit where the ball stops dead and kids slip and stutter-step around ruts. Last October, one of my defenders planted to make a cut and her foot caught in a rut carved out by the rain. She tore her ACL. She’s a junior who’s still not back to full speed.

Meanwhile, the football team has been playing on turf since 2019. Their games don’t get washed out. Their players don’t step in sinkholes. I’m glad they have a good surface. I’m not glad our girls are still stuck competing on a field that’s half a step above a bog.

The board needs to put turf on the girls’ soccer field in this budget. Not next year. Not after another study. Now. We’re talking about safety, we’re talking about equal treatment, and we’re talking about nine games that didn’t happen because the field was underwater. Fix the field.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
Members of the City Council,

My name is submitted for the record as the owner of a small, independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am writing to oppose the proposal to raise downtown parking meters from 50 cents to a dollar fifty an hour.

This is not a theoretical concern for me. This is about whether my regulars can afford to stop in.

In 2019, the town next to us passed a similar hike. I was worried then about what it would do here if it spread, so for 6 weeks after their increase took effect, I tracked my own register tape day by day and compared it to the same 6 weeks the year before. My foot traffic dropped 18%. That was not a slow month or bad weather. That was 18 out of every 100 transactions gone — morning coffees, lunch drop-ins, people who used to stay for a second cup. For a small shop like mine, an 18% loss in visits is the difference between breaking even and falling behind on rent.

That drop makes sense when you look at how my customers actually use downtown. I timed it: my customers average a 22 minute visit. They come in, order, chat a minute, and go. Under the current 50 cent hourly rate, the hour minimum already covers them fine. They are paid up and legal for their entire stay. Tripling the rate to $1.50 an hour does not give them more time or a better space. It just charges them three times as much for the same 22 minutes they were already paying for. For a $4 coffee, you are asking them to add another $1.50 just to park. That turns a quick stop into a decision to go elsewhere.

And for what gain to the city? According to the city's own report, meter revenue only covers 4% of the downtown budget. Even if you triple the rate from 50 cents to $1.50, you are tripling a funding source that covers just 4%. It will not solve the budget shortfall, but an 18% drop in foot traffic will gut the sales tax and the small businesses that make up the other 96%.

Please vote no on raising the meter from 50 cents to $1.50. Keep downtown affordable for a 22-minute visit, and do not trade our foot traffic for 4%.

Respectfully submitted,
Owner, Main Street Coffee Shop

b.text:
To the Members of the City Council:

My name is [Your Name], and I am the owner of a small independent coffee shop right here on Main Street. I am submitting this testimony today to strongly urge you to reject the proposed parking meter rate increase from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour. While I understand the need to generate revenue for our downtown, this specific proposal relies on flawed assumptions and will cause measurable, lasting harm to the small businesses that form the backbone of our community.

The primary justification for raising parking rates is often to encourage faster turnover. However, this rationale does not apply to my business or many others like it. I have tracked our customer data extensively, and my customers average a 22-minute visit. Because the current hour minimum already accommodates their stay perfectly, they aren't overstaying their meters—they are simply stopping in for a quick visit. Raising the rate to $1.50 an hour doesn't incentivize them to leave any faster; it simply triples the cost of a 22-minute stop from 50 cents to $1.50. This effectively penalizes the exact kind of short, high-turnover traffic our downtown relies on to survive. 

We also do not have to guess at the consequences of this policy, because we have clear, local evidence. When the next town over implemented a similar parking rate hike back in 2019, I tracked my own register for six weeks to measure the impact on my business. The result was undeniable: we saw an 18% drop in foot traffic. An 18% loss of customers would be devastating to a small independent shop, and it was a direct result of a policy just like the one being proposed today. 

Perhaps most importantly, this drastic 200% rate increase won’t even achieve its intended financial goal. According to the city’s own report, meter revenue currently covers a mere 4% of the downtown budget. Even if you triple the rate from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour, the additional revenue will remain a drop in the bucket. We are being asked to sacrifice 18% of our customer base and severely damage our local economy to address a budget shortfall that this parking hike simply will not solve. 

I urge the council to look at the real numbers. Tripling the parking cost of a 22-minute visit will drive away the very customers we are trying to attract, all for a negligible impact on a downtown budget where parking only accounts for 4% of the funding. Please vote against the parking meter rate increase and stand with Main Street small businesses. 

Sincerely,

[Your Name]
Owner, [Coffee Shop Name], Main Street

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
# Keep Your Dog’s Coat From Matting Between Grooming Visits

The spots I check first when a dog comes into the salon are behind the ears and under the front legs. They rub when your dog walks, plays, and curls up for a nap, so they’re often where little tangles turn into mats. If you have a curly-coated or double-coated dog, those areas are worth checking at home before they start to feel lumpy.

The biggest mistake I see is bathing a dog first because it seems like the water will loosen the tangles. It does the opposite. Wet matted fur tightens up and can turn into a felt-like pad. If you’re planning a bath at home, brush the coat out *before* it gets wet—don’t save the brushing for afterward.

I like a slicker brush for this. Work in small sections, using short, gentle strokes in a line rather than brushing in circles. Circles can twist the coat and make tangles worse. Start behind the ears and under the front legs, then move through the rest of the coat a section at a time. With curly coats especially, the surface can look fluffy while a tangle is forming closer to the skin, so take your time.

If you find a mat starting, don’t go straight at it with a brush or comb. Work a little dog-safe conditioner into it with your fingers first, then gently try to separate the hairs. Hold the coat near the skin so you’re not pulling on your dog. If the mat is tight, close to the skin, or your dog is uncomfortable, stop there and let us help. There’s no prize for getting it out at home if it hurts your dog.

A few calm minutes of brushing between visits can make bath day easier and your dog much more comfortable. And if you’re not sure whether you’re feeling a tangle or a mat, ask us to show you what to look for at your next appointment.

b.text:
**Keeping Your Dog’s Coat From Matting Between Grooming Visits**

If your dog comes home from the groomer looking fluffy and then two weeks later feels like they’re wearing a felt oven mitt, you’re not alone. I run a small grooming salon, and this is the conversation I have at least once a day. Double-coated breeds and curly coats are the ones that get into trouble fastest, but the same routine helps everybody.

The order of operations matters more than people think. Brush before the bath at home, never after. I know it feels backward—you want them clean first—but water is the enemy of a mat. Wet matted fur just turns into a felt pad. Once water gets into a tangle, those hairs shrink and lock together, and brushing a wet mat only drives it tighter. So do the brushing while the coat is dry, then bathe.

Use a slicker brush and short line strokes, not circles. Circles wrap the hair around the pins and push tangles into knots. Short, gentle strokes in the direction the coat grows, working from the ends toward the skin. Don’t stab at the dog or drag the brush through a snarl. If the slicker catches, stop and work that spot with your fingers.

Work in sections, and start where mats actually begin: behind the ears and under the front legs. Those spots rub, trap warmth, and collect loose coat. I check behind the ears first on every dog, then the armpits, then the rest of the body in small sections. Part the coat down to the skin as you go so you’re not just brushing the top layer and missing the undercoat packed underneath.

If you already see a mat forming, don’t attack it with a brush or comb. Work conditioner into it with your fingers first. A little leave-in conditioner or detangler on your fingertips, then gently pull the mat apart from the outside in. Take your time. Once your fingers can move through it, then you can go back in with the slicker. If it’s tight to the skin, that’s a groomer job—don’t try to cut it out at home.

The mistake I see constantly is people bathing the dog first thinking it’ll loosen the mats. It does the opposite. Water locks them in tighter, and then the dog sits in a wet mat while it dries, which is uncomfortable and can irritate the skin. If your dog is already matted, skip the bath and deal with the mats first, or call the salon.

A few minutes of dry brushing in the right order beats an hour of fighting a wet coat every time. And if you’re not sure whether something is a mat or just a thick patch of undercoat, bring the dog by—I’d rather show you how to hold the brush than have you learn on a knot behind the ear.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
# The Market Didn't Crash. Some Sellers Just Haven't Caught Up.

If you've been watching our local market and reading the headlines, you might think we're headed off a cliff. Days on market nearly quadrupled. Showings have been cut in half. And yes, those numbers are real — they're happening right here in our zip codes. But before you start panicking or waiting for a massive price correction, let me tell you what's actually going on.

**This is not a crash. It's a correction in expectations.**

Last spring, a well-priced home in our area was getting multiple offers in under a week. Eight days on market was the median, and sellers were in the driver's seat. That pace has slowed to about five weeks. Some people look at that shift and see collapse. I look at it and see a market that's returning to something more balanced — something that's actually healthy.

Here's the piece that's getting lost in the conversation: list prices are still up six percent year over year. Six percent. That's not the sign of a market in freefall. That's a market where sellers are still confident — perhaps too confident in some cases.

And that's where the problem actually lives. I have three sellers right now who have been on the market for more than sixty days and are refusing to adjust their price. They're looking at last spring's numbers and expecting last spring's results. But last spring's buyer who would've lined up for that house with minimal negotiation doesn't exist anymore — at least not at that price point. Those buyers have either adjusted their expectations, gotten more selective, or in some cases, stepped back entirely.

Meanwhile, the sellers who are pricing it right — really pricing it to the current market, not the market of twelve months ago — are still selling in under two weeks. That tells you everything you need to know about where the demand actually is. The buyer is still there. They're just not willing to overpay anymore.

I get it. Nobody wants to hear that they need to come down in price. When you've watched your home's value climb the way it has over the past several years, it feels like a loss to ask for less. But asking for less than you wanted isn't the same as losing money. Those sellers who are holding firm on overpriced listings aren't protecting their equity — they're watching their homes grow stale, losing leverage with every passing week.

The market didn't change overnight. It shifted. And the agents and sellers who adapt to that shift — who price smart, who market effectively, who trust the data over their gut — are still getting deals done quickly and at strong numbers.

So if you're selling right now and you're frustrated because the phone isn't ringing the way it did last spring, you're not alone. But the answer isn't to hold your ground and hope. The answer is to look at what's actually happening and make the smart move. The market will reward you — if you meet it where it is.

*If you're thinking about listing and want an honest conversation about where your home falls in this market, I'm always happy to talk.*

b.text:
## The Market Hasn’t Crashed. Sellers Just Need to Catch Up.

A year ago, homes in our ZIP code were moving at a sprint. This spring, the median time on market has climbed from eight days to 34. Showings per listing have dropped by half.

That is a real change—and sellers should pay attention to it.

But it isn’t a crash. It’s a market that has slowed down, while some sellers are still pricing as if every home will draw a crowd the first weekend. The homes priced to meet today’s buyers are still selling in under two weeks. The gap between those homes and the ones that sit is becoming hard to ignore.

List prices are still up 6% year over year, but a higher asking price doesn’t prove buyers will pay it. Buyers have fewer reasons to rush when they’re seeing fewer listings, taking more time and making more deliberate choices. In this market, the price has to make sense from the start.

I have three sellers right now who have been on the market for more than 60 days and still don’t want to reduce their prices. I understand the hesitation. A home is personal, and lowering the price can feel like giving something up. But after two months without a sale, holding firm doesn’t protect a seller’s value. It risks letting the listing grow stale while buyers move on.

The market is giving sellers a clear message: the days of simply naming a price and counting on a rush of offers are over. That doesn’t mean homes aren’t selling. It means buyers are rewarding homes that are priced realistically and making sellers work harder to earn their attention.

My advice is straightforward: price for the market you’re in, not the market you remember. The sellers who do that are still getting results. The ones who don’t may be waiting a long time for buyers to agree with them.
