setup: An IT helpdesk technician is writing an essay to a hiring manager for a junior product and UX role.

a.text:
Dear [Hiring Manager name],

Five years into my helpdesk role at [hospital system], I've used your ticketing tool every single day. It's the backbone of how I support clinicians, and it's also the reason I'm writing to you today.

I field roughly 35 tickets a day. That volume has taught me to spot friction quickly — where a workflow stalls, where an interface confuses, where a user gives up before finishing a request. I've learned to read the gap between what users say and what they actually need.

That's part of why I built an internal troubleshooting wiki with 60+ articles. I documented the fixes our team repeated most, organized them clearly, and made them searchable. Repeat tickets dropped by about a third. Seeing that change happen made me realize I care just as much about the experience around the tool as the tool itself.

I've also been one of your power users in the truest sense. Over the last three years, I've submitted 14 feature requests directly to your product team. Four of them have shipped. I've watched your product evolve, and I know what it feels like when a requested change lands — I felt it with my own team, watching our work get easier.

I'm applying for the junior UX and product support role because I want to be on the side of the desk where those improvements are designed. I know this software intimately, I understand the healthcare environment it serves, and I have hands-on experience turning user pain points into tangible solutions.

Thank you for your time. I'd welcome the chance to talk about what I can bring to your team.

Sincerely,
[Your name]

b.text:
Dear Hiring Manager,

For the past five years, I’ve worked as an IT helpdesk technician at a mid-size hospital system, using your ticketing tool every day. I’m excited to apply for your junior UX and product support role because I’d like to bring that frontline experience to the team building a product I know firsthand.

Handling about 35 tickets a day has taught me to ask clear questions, identify where users get stuck, and explain solutions without adding complexity. In a hospital environment, I’ve also learned how important it is for software to support people’s work rather than interrupt it.

To make troubleshooting easier, I built an internal wiki with more than 60 articles, helping reduce repeat tickets by about a third. That work pushed me to think beyond resolving individual issues: What information was missing? Where were instructions unclear? How could we help users succeed without opening another ticket?

I’ve brought that same perspective to your product. Over the last three years, I’ve submitted 14 feature requests to your team, and four have shipped. Seeing those improvements reach the tool I use daily has made me want to contribute more directly.

I’d bring practical support experience, familiarity with your product, and a strong interest in learning UX methods from your team. I’d welcome the opportunity to help turn everyday user friction into clearer, more useful experiences.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,  
[Your Name]

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
# No, Our Local Housing Market Isn’t Crashing—It’s Waiting For Sellers To Catch Up

Last Saturday, I spent 20 minutes chatting with three different parents at my kid’s rec soccer game, all asking the same question: Is the local housing market crashing?

They’d all seen the same red flags: the house on the corner of Oak and 5th that’s had a for-sale sign in the yard since March, the headlines about rising mortgage rates, the gossip from their cousin who’s a realtor in Arizona saying prices are tanking. Let me cut through the noise, straight from someone who’s been selling houses here in this suburb for 10 years, who’s out showing properties every weekend, who’s currently got three sellers sitting on 60+ days on market refusing to drop their price: This isn’t a crash. It’s just sellers who haven’t caught up to the new pace of the market.

Let’s run the numbers for our zip code, no fluff:
- Last spring, median days on market was 8. Eight. That means half the houses listed were under contract before most people even had time to schedule a second showing. I listed a 3-bed with a half-finished basement last April that got 19 offers in 3 days, $45,000 over asking.
- This spring? Median days on market is 34. That’s a huge jump, and it’s the number everyone’s panicking about.
- Showings per listing are down 50% from last year. Where a new listing might get 30 showings in the first weekend last spring, now it’s more like 10 to 15—if it’s priced right.
- And here’s the kicker that confuses everyone: average list prices are still up 6% year over year. Sellers are still asking more than they were last spring—but buyers aren’t biting on the ones that cross the line of what the market will actually bear.

Wait, how can days on market be way up, showings way down, but prices still climbing? Because that 34-day median isn’t being dragged up by a market-wide crash—it’s being dragged up by a handful of overpriced listings that are sitting there collecting dust.

The homes that are priced for today’s market? They’re still selling in under 2 weeks. Last month I listed a 4-bed in the Westdale school district at $425,000—exactly what my comparable sales analysis said it was worth, not a penny more—and we had 8 offers in 6 days, sold for $15,000 over asking. Two weeks ago, a colleague listed a 2-bed condo near Main Street for $210,000, and it went under contract in 9 days, no price drop. These aren’t outliers. They’re the norm for homes priced fairly.

The problem is the sellers who are still pricing their homes like it’s spring 2023, when rates were a full point lower, buyers were waiving every contingency just to get a foot in the door, and you could list your house for 10% over what it was worth and still get a bidding war.

I’ve got three of those sellers right now. One couple remodeled their kitchen in 2022 and is convinced their house is worth what their next-door neighbor got last May—never mind that their neighbor had 21 offers, and their house has been on the market for 68 days with exactly two offers, both $30,000 below their asking price. Another seller inherited his mom’s ranch and thinks “sentimental value” adds $50,000 to the price tag. The third is a young family that’s already bought their next house out of state and thinks “waiting it out” will get them their dream price. All three have refused to drop their price. All three are contributing to that 34-day median days on market number that’s making everyone think the sky is falling.

Let me be clear: There is no crash. Buyers are still out there. We still have way less inventory than we did pre-2020, and buyers are still willing to pay a fair price for a good house that’s priced correctly. What they’re not willing to do is overpay for a house that’s listed at a 2023 frenzy price when mortgage rates are higher and they have more time to shop around.

If you’re a buyer right now: Don’t let the “for sale” signs that have been up for two months fool you. Those are the overpriced ones. The well-priced homes are still moving fast, so you still need to have your pre-approval in order and be ready to act when you find one you love. But you also don’t have to waive your inspection or appraisal to compete anymore, which is a nice change from last year’s chaos.

If you’re a seller thinking of listing this summer: Do yourself a favor and price it right from the start. The longer your house sits on the market, the more buyers will assume there’s something wrong with it, and the less you’ll likely end up getting. That 6% year-over-year price increase is real for well-priced homes, but you don’t get that if you list 10% over what the market will bear and let it sit for three months.

And if you’re one of those sellers who’s been on the market for 60+ days and you’re convinced your house is “worth more”? I hate to break it to you, but your house is worth what a buyer is willing to pay for it. Right now, buyers aren’t willing to pay last year’s prices. It’s not the market crashing. It’s the market going back to normal—and normal means you can’t just slap a sky-high price on your house and expect buyers to line up around the block.

If you’re curious about what your house is actually worth in today’s market, or you’re a buyer looking to navigate this weird in-between period, shoot me an email or give me a call. I’m happy to walk you through the numbers, no sales pitch, just the straight talk I’ve been giving this community for 10 years.

See you at the Memorial Day parade next weekend— I’ll be the one handing out popsicles and talking real estate, as usual.

b.text:
**The Market Didn't Crash. Your Listing Price Did.**

Last spring, the median home in our zip code sold in eight days. Eight. This spring? Thirty-four. Showings per listing have been cut in half. And yet, list prices are still up six percent year over year. If you're waiting for a crash, stop holding your breath. What we're seeing isn't a collapse—it's a standoff between sellers who are living in last year's market and buyers who finally have room to think.

Right now, I have three sellers who've been on the market for sixty-plus days. All three are refusing to drop their price. All three are convinced the right buyer is "just around the corner." Here's the truth I told them, and I'll tell you: that buyer isn't coming. Not at that price. The buyers are still here, but they're not desperate anymore. They're not waving inspections, they're not engaging in bidding wars, and they're certainly not paying 2021 premiums for 2023 interest rates.

The agents and sellers who have adjusted are doing just fine. In fact, homes priced correctly—*actually* correctly, not "let's shoot for the moon and see what happens"—are still selling in under two weeks. The inventory isn't flooding the market. The sky isn't falling. The fundamentals of our local market are still solid. What changed is the frenzy, and some sellers are having a hard time accepting that the feeding frenzy is over.

If you're selling, you need to make a decision. You can price your home for the market that exists today and sell it, or you can price it for the market that disappeared last summer and let it sit. There is no third option where you get last year's price with this year's patience. The data is right there: thirty-four days on market, half as many showings, and prices that are only up because the *right* inventory is still moving.

And if you're buying? This is the breathing room you've been waiting for. You can tour a home twice. You can sleep on it. You can negotiate. But don't expect a fire sale. The homes that sell quickly are still moving at strong numbers because they're priced with eyes wide open.

This isn't a crash. It's a correction in expectations. The sellers who recognize that will move on with their lives. The ones who don't will be decorating for the Fourth of July in a house they listed in April.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
**Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors**

Many students at our school spend lunch crowded into a cafeteria that was not built to hold all of us at once. During one lunch wave, there are about 340 students, but the cafeteria only seats 220. That means students are standing, waiting for seats, or eating in uncomfortable conditions before they even get a real break. One practical solution would be to allow juniors and seniors to have open campus lunch. Giving upperclassmen this privilege would reduce overcrowding, reflect student opinion, and show that the school trusts older students to act responsibly.

The most immediate reason our school should consider open campus lunch is overcrowding. With 340 students in one lunch wave and only 220 seats, the cafeteria is already over capacity. This creates noise, long lines, and stress for students who just want to eat and relax. If juniors and seniors were allowed to leave campus for lunch, fewer students would need to use the cafeteria at the same time. That would make lunch easier for the students who remain on campus and improve the overall environment.

Another reason to allow open campus lunch is that nearby districts have already done it successfully. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow older students to leave campus during lunch, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. This matters because one of the biggest concerns is that students will not come back on time. The evidence from those schools shows that students can handle the responsibility. If other districts with similar schedules can make open campus lunch work without creating tardiness problems, our school can reasonably expect the same.

Student opinion also supports the idea. I surveyed 80 students at our school, and 71 of them said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That is a large majority, and it shows that students see this as a reasonable request, not just a way to skip class. Many students want more independence as they get closer to graduation, and open campus lunch is a way to practice responsibility while still following school rules.

Some people may argue that open campus lunch could cause safety issues, littering, or students gathering in nearby areas. Those concerns are fair, but they can be managed with clear rules. The school could require signed permission forms, limit which areas students are allowed to visit, and set consequences for returning late or breaking the rules. Students who abuse the privilege could lose it. Instead of assuming open campus lunch will automatically fail, the school could create expectations that protect students and the community.

Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors is not just about giving students more freedom. It is about solving a real problem with overcrowding, listening to student concerns, and trusting older students to act responsibly. Other schools have already shown that it can work without increasing tardiness, and the majority of students surveyed at our school support the idea. If our school wants lunch to be safer, less crowded, and more respectful of upperclassmen, open campus lunch is worth considering.

b.text:
**Why Our School Should Allow Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors**

Our school should allow juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch. The current lunch system is overcrowded, and older students have already shown that they can handle more responsibility. Open campus lunch would give upperclassmen more choices while helping reduce the pressure on our cafeteria. Other schools’ experiences and the opinions of students at our school suggest that this policy could work without causing major problems.

The cafeteria currently does not have enough seating for the students who use it during the same lunch wave. It has only 220 seats, while 340 students are assigned to that lunch period. That leaves 120 students without an available seat if everyone wants to eat in the cafeteria. Some students have to stand, sit in crowded areas, or rush to find a place to eat. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus would reduce the number of students in the cafeteria and make lunch more comfortable for the students who remain. It would also give upperclassmen the opportunity to choose where they eat instead of forcing everyone into a space that is already too small.

Students at our school also seem to support the idea. I surveyed 80 students, and 71 of them said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. Although this survey does not represent every student perfectly, the results show strong support among the students who responded. Older students are more likely to have cars, know the area around the school, and understand the responsibility that comes with leaving campus. Giving them this option would recognize that they are preparing for the independence they will have after graduation.

Open campus lunch has also worked in other nearby districts. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade already allow juniors and seniors to leave campus for lunch. According to their published statistics, these districts have not experienced a rise in tardiness after allowing the policy. This evidence does not guarantee that our school would have exactly the same results, but it does show that open campus lunch does not automatically lead to students returning late. Our school could use clear expectations and consequences to encourage students to return on time.

Some people may argue that students would abuse the privilege or that the policy could create safety concerns. Those are reasonable concerns, but they could be addressed with rules. The school could require students to return before the next class, limit the privilege to students in good standing, and take away open-campus privileges from anyone who is repeatedly late or violates school rules. Juniors and seniors could also be required to sign out or carry identification. These restrictions would allow the school to maintain accountability without denying the privilege to every upperclassman.

Our cafeteria is already overcrowded, most surveyed students support open campus lunch, and nearby districts have used the policy without an increase in tardiness. These facts make a strong case for allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch. The school should begin with a trial period and evaluate attendance, tardiness, and discipline records. If the results are positive, open campus lunch should become a regular option for responsible juniors and seniors.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
During my first week in the ER, I held a stranger’s hand while his wound was cleaned. His wife was stuck in traffic. I couldn’t make her get there faster, and I wasn’t the person treating his wound. But I could stay beside him so he didn’t have to go through it alone.

Before that week, I spent a lot of time thinking about whether I would know enough or remember the right steps. As a first-year nursing student, I knew I had a lot to learn. I wanted to be useful, but I wasn’t always sure what that would look like. Holding his hand was one of the first times I felt I had something to offer, even with how little I knew.

Other moments were harder to understand.

During a code, I was sent to restock gauze. I could hear the team counting through the curtain while I put supplies away. It felt strange to be doing such a simple task while something so serious was happening nearby. Part of me wanted to see what was going on. Part of me was relieved to have a job I knew how to do.

I didn’t leave that moment feeling brave or especially helpful. I left knowing how much work happens around an emergency, including work that nobody stops to notice. Supplies still have to be ready. People need room to do their jobs. For that moment, my job was to restock the gauze.

Then there was the patient with diabetes whose veins were difficult to access. I missed his blood draw three times before getting it on the fourth try. I was relieved when I finally got it, but I also knew that my learning had meant four needle sticks for him.

That stayed with me. In school, a mistake can mean losing points or practicing again. With a patient, someone else feels it. I need to build my skills, but I also need to know when to ask for help and keep the patient’s comfort ahead of my wish to get something right.

My first week in the ER did not make me feel ready to be a nurse. It gave me a clearer picture of what I need to learn and why I want to keep going. I saw how much nursing asks of a person: skill, attention, patience, and the willingness to do what is needed, even when it is a small task.

This scholarship would support my education as I work toward becoming that kind of nurse. I want to become someone patients can trust to do the job well and to remember that they are people, not practice. I’m only at the beginning, but I already know I want to carry that first week with me.

b.text:
**The Fourth Try**

The first useful thing I did in the ER was hold a stranger's hand.

He was getting a deep cut on his arm cleaned out, and it hurt. His wife was stuck in traffic, and he kept looking at the door like he could make her appear. All the nurses were busy, so my preceptor nodded at me, and I stepped up next to the gurney and let him take my hand. He squeezed hard enough that my fingers went numb. I talked to him about nothing — the traffic, the rain, whether he'd eaten — because that was all I had. When his wife finally came through the door, he thanked me like I had done something big. All I did was stand there. But I stood there, and I think it mattered to him.

Not everything that week felt that clear. On my third day, a code got called one curtain over from where I was working. I wanted to help. What I was told to do was go restock the gauze. So I stood at the supply cart with my arms full of gauze packs and listened through the curtain while they counted compressions. One, two, three, four. Over and over. Somebody called out numbers I didn't understand yet. I felt about two inches tall, like a kid who got sent out of the room.

It took me a few days to see it differently. Every drawer

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
High school is often described as a bridge to adulthood, yet for most of the day, students are treated like children. We are told when to sit, when to speak, and when to eat. But for juniors and seniors, who are only a year or two away from managing their own schedules in college or the workforce, an open campus lunch would be a meaningful step toward independence. Our school should allow juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch because other districts have already shown it can work safely, our own students overwhelmingly support the idea, and our current cafeteria is simply too small to serve everyone comfortably.

One of the strongest arguments for an open campus lunch is that it is not a risky experiment. Nearby districts have already tried it and succeeded. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness after the policy was introduced. This matters because the most common objection to open lunch is that students will return late to class. But if three separate districts, with different student bodies and different campuses, all report the same result, that objection starts to look more like a fear than a fact. Juniors and seniors are old enough to understand that losing the privilege would mean losing it for everyone, and the data from nearby schools suggests they are capable of meeting that responsibility.

It is also worth listening to the students who would actually be affected by the policy. I surveyed eighty students at our school, and seventy-one said they were in favor of an open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That is nearly ninety percent. When such a large majority of a group supports a change that directly affects them, their voices should carry real weight. Students are not asking for a shorter school day or fewer classes; they are asking for thirty minutes of trust and autonomy in the middle of the day. The survey results show that this is not a fringe opinion held by a handful of students who want to skip class. It is the mainstream view of the student body, and it deserves to be taken seriously.

Finally, there is a practical problem that open lunch would help solve immediately: our cafeteria is overcrowded. The cafeteria seats 220 students, but one lunch wave contains 340 students. That means more than one hundred students have nowhere to sit during their designated lunch period. Some sit on the floor. Some stand against walls. Some try to squeeze onto benches that were not built for that many people. This is not a minor inconvenience; it is a daily reminder that the school’s facilities have not kept up with its enrollment. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus would reduce the number of students in the building during lunch and make the cafeteria a more comfortable place for everyone who remains. It is a solution that costs the district nothing and helps students immediately.

An open campus lunch for juniors and seniors is not an act of rebellion. It is a reasonable policy that recognizes students’ maturity, reflects the success of neighboring districts, answers the clear wishes of the student body, and relieves a real overcrowding problem in our cafeteria. The school has asked us to act like adults in our classes and our extracurriculars. Letting us leave campus for lunch is a simple way to show that trust beyond the classroom walls.

b.text:
**Juniors and Seniors Should Have Open Campus Lunch**

At our school, lunch is supposed to be a break in the day. Instead, it often means finding a place to sit in a cafeteria that cannot hold everyone assigned to the same lunch wave. Our cafeteria seats 220 people, while 340 students have that lunch period. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus for lunch would give older students a reasonable privilege and help relieve a real space problem.

Overcrowding is the most immediate reason to make this change. Our lunch wave has 120 more students than the cafeteria has seats. Not every student needs a cafeteria seat at exactly the same moment, but the difference shows why lunch can feel crowded and difficult to manage. If some juniors and seniors ate elsewhere, students who stayed would have more room. Open campus lunch would not solve every problem with our lunch schedule, but it would reduce pressure on a space that is already too small.

Some people may worry that students who leave will return late to class. That concern deserves attention, but nearby schools show that open campus lunch does not have to cause a tardiness problem. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade already allow it, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. Our school would still need to set clear rules and track its own results. However, those districts give us a reason to try the policy rather than reject it based on what might happen.

Students also want the opportunity. I surveyed 80 students at our school, and 71 said they favored open campus lunch. That survey does not speak for every student or parent, but it shows strong interest among the students I asked. For juniors and seniors, leaving campus for lunch would be a chance to practice managing their time before graduation. A policy could require parent permission and make clear that students who return late lose the privilege. Students who do not want to leave could continue eating at school.

Open campus lunch should be treated as a responsibility, not a free pass. With clear expectations and consequences, our school could give juniors and seniors more independence while easing cafeteria crowding. The experience of nearby districts suggests that we can do this without increasing tardiness. It is worth giving older students the chance to prove they can handle it.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
Last October, one of my players stepped in a rut on the girls’ soccer field and tore her ACL. She missed the rest of her senior season. The rut was carved into mud that had been soaked by days of rain—the same rain that had already forced us to move three games that month.

This wasn’t a freak accident. It’s what happens when a team plays on a grass field that floods every time it rains. Over the last two seasons, we’ve had nine games rained out or moved. Nine. That’s nearly half our home schedule. Parents rearrange plans, players miss class, and our team loses the home-field advantage every other team takes for granted.

Meanwhile, the boys’ football team has been playing on turf since 2019. Six years. That field drains, it stays solid, and it gets used all year without turning into a hazard. The girls’ soccer team still plays on grass. The track team still deals with the same flooding during meets. I’m not going to lecture anyone about equality, but I will say this: if the football field were tearing up knees and cancelling games, it would have been fixed a long time ago. We’re asking for the same standard. Not better. The same.

I know turf costs money. But this district already decided it was worth the money once. The school board is meeting next week to vote on the facilities budget. Put turf on the girls’ soccer field. Not in five years, not “when funds allow.” Now.

Our players deserve a safe place to play. They’ve waited six years longer than the boys have. If you need proof, come look at the ruts yourself. Just don’t wear nice shoes.

b.text:
# The Girls' Soccer Field Needs Turf. Here's Why.

I coach girls' soccer and track at our high school. I'm writing this because our soccer field is a problem the school board can fix, and next year's budget is the time to do it.

Start with the games we've lost. Over the last two seasons, nine of our games have been rained out or moved off-site because the grass field floods. It doesn't take much. A steady rain the night before, and we're playing in standing water or not playing at all. That's nine times our girls trained all week for nothing, or got bused somewhere else to play a "home" game. Rescheduling isn't free either. It costs officials' fees, transportation, and the goodwill of every family trying to plan around it.

Now the part that matters most. Last October, one of my players tore her ACL. She stepped in a rut in that field and her knee went. That's a torn ligament, surgery, months of rehab, and a season—maybe a career—gone. The field is uneven because it floods and gets torn up, and grass fields that get overused and waterlogged don't heal right. This isn't bad luck. It's a predictable result of playing on a field that isn't safe.

Turf drains. Turf is flat. Turf doesn't develop ruts that blow out a 16-year-old's knee. This isn't complicated.

And here's the other thing I'll say plainly: the boys' football field got turf in 2019. So the district already knows turf is worth the money, already knows how to budget for it, already made the case that our athletes deserve a safe, playable surface. The boys got that answer five years ago. The girls are still waiting, still getting rained out, still stepping in ruts.

I'm not asking for something new or extravagant. I'm asking the board to do for the girls exactly what it already did for the boys. Same standard. Same safety. Same respect.

I coach for the stipend, not because I love writing op-eds. But I've watched enough canceled games and carried enough girls off that field to know this needs saying. Put turf on the girls' soccer field in next year's budget. It's overdue, it's fair, and it will keep our players safe.

*[Name], girls' soccer and track coach*

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
**Don’t Cut Funding for Apprenticeships**

The state is proposing to cut apprenticeship funding by 15%. That may look like a budget saving, but it would weaken a program that gets people trained, working, and earning a good living.

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with the IBEW. My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Today, 21 have finished and are working as journeymen. That’s 21 people who learned a skilled trade and moved into steady jobs.

Apprentices start at around $19 an hour. Journeymen top out around $46 an hour. As apprentices earn more and move into full-time work, they can get off assistance programs and support themselves and their families. That is a good return for workers and for the state.

The cost is also worth looking at. The public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. By comparison, the average public subsidy for a four-year college graduate who finishes is about $48,000. Both paths have value, but apprenticeships are a practical and less costly way to prepare people for good jobs.

A funding cut could mean fewer training opportunities, fewer apprentices, and fewer skilled workers when employers need them. It could also make it harder for people who want to work but cannot afford to train without support. We should be building the skilled workforce, not shrinking the programs that train it.

I’m not asking the state to spend money without results. My own cohort shows results: 21 of 24 apprentices finished and are working journeyman jobs. The state should keep supporting apprenticeship programs so more people can follow that path.

Please reject the proposed 15% cut. Investing in apprenticeships helps workers earn a living, helps employers find skilled people, and gives the state a strong return on public money.

b.text:
Don't Cut Apprenticeship Funding

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW. I work hard every day learning this trade, and I'm writing because the state wants to cut apprenticeship funding by 15 percent. That is a bad idea. It hurts working people, wastes a proven program, and costs the public more in the long run.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished and are working journeyman jobs right now. That is a strong completion rate. We start around $19 an hour and top out around $46 an hour as journeymen. Those wages get people off assistance programs fast. We pay taxes. We buy houses. We support our families without needing help from the state.

Look at the numbers. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to the average public subsidy of around $48,000 for a four-year college grad who finishes. Apprenticeships give better results for less money. We leave with a real skill, a license, and a job. We do not walk out with student debt and no clear path.

Cutting 15 percent will mean fewer training slots, fewer tools, fewer instructors, and fewer people like me getting a fair shot. That does not save the state money. It just pushes costs somewhere else—more people stuck in low-wage work or needing public help longer. Our program already works. Keep funding it.

Union members, talk to your legislators. Tell them this cut is shortsighted. State leaders, look at the facts. Twenty-one out of 24 finished. Good wages. Low public cost. Do not gut a program that builds skilled workers and strong communities.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
The easiest way to prevent painful mats is to catch them before bath day. Once fur is wet, any small tangles can tighten into dense, felt-like pads that are much harder to remove.

This is especially important for double-coated and curly-coated dogs. Areas like behind the ears, under the front legs, around the collar, and along the belly tend to tangle first because they get a lot of rubbing and movement.

Before bathing your dog at home, make sure the coat is completely brushed out. Don’t rely on the bath to loosen knots. That’s a mistake I see constantly, and it usually has the opposite effect: water pulls the tangled hairs together and can lock the mats in even tighter.

Use a slicker brush and work with short, gentle line strokes. Think of brushing a small section at a time, moving the brush away from the skin and then checking your progress. Avoid scrubbing in circles, since circular brushing can twist the hair and create more tangles.

Start behind the ears and under the front legs, then work through the rest of the coat in sections. Part the hair with your fingers so you can see down toward the skin instead of only brushing over the surface. For a double-coated dog, you’ll need to work through the outer coat and the undercoat. For a curly-coated dog, take your time so the brush reaches all the way through each curl.

If you notice a mat beginning to form, don’t immediately attack it with a brush or comb. First, work a little dog-safe conditioner into the mat with your fingers. Gently loosen the outside edges before trying to separate the hairs. Never yank or force a brush through a tight mat, especially if your dog is uncomfortable.

A quick brush before the bath is much kinder and more effective than trying to deal with a tightened, wet coat afterward. If you find mats close to the skin, large areas of matting, or a dog who is painful or upset when you touch the coat, stop and contact your groomer. Some mats need to be safely clipped out rather than brushed out, and trying to remove them at home can injure your dog’s skin.

b.text:
If you’re handling the coat between grooming visits—mostly with double-coated or curly breeds—you need to think about the order of operations, because the mistake I see constantly is people reaching for the shampoo first. They think a bath will loosen the mats. It won’t. Wet matted fur just turns into a felt pad and locks everything tighter than when it was dry, so always brush before the bath at home, never after.

When you do brush, stick with a slicker and use short line strokes, not circles. Circles just spin the hair and drive the knot deeper. Work in sections, and start behind the ears and under the front legs—those are the first places mats grab hold, so get them while they’re still loose.

If you feel a mat starting to form, stop. Don’t touch it with a brush or comb right away. Work some conditioner into it with your fingers first, break it down gently, and only then work through it with your tool. Otherwise you’re fighting a knot that’s already cemented.

Keep the bath for after the brush-out. Your dog will come back to the salon with the coat still in working order, and you won’t be dealing with a felted mess that needs a shave-down.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6-Month Review

I've used the Jarvik L2 as my only desk for six months. That means full workdays, standups, late-night debugging, and a lot of switching between sitting and standing. Here's what holds up, what doesn't, and whether you should buy one.

**Short version:** Buy it at $549. Don't buy it at $749.

## The Motor: Genuinely Great

This is the L2's best feature, and it's not close.

It's quiet. I adjust height during video calls and nobody notices. My previous desk sounded like a garage door opener, so I stopped switching positions mid-meeting. With the L2, I switch whenever I want, which is the whole point of owning a standing desk.

It's also fast. Sitting to standing takes a few seconds, short enough that I never think "eh, not worth waiting for." That matters more than you'd expect. A desk you don't bother adjusting is just an expensive regular desk.

After six months there's no new grinding, no hesitation, and no uneven lift between legs. The motor feels like the part of the desk where Jarvik actually spent the money.

## Stability: Fine Until It Isn't

At sitting height and mid-range standing heights, the L2 is solid. No complaints.

At full height, it wobbles when I type hard. I'm a heavy typist on a mechanical keyboard, and at the top of the range my monitor visibly shakes. It isn't dramatic, but it's enough to notice and enough to bother me during long typing sessions.

To be fair, almost every single-crossbar desk wobbles somewhat at max extension. That's physics. But the L2 wobbles more than I'd accept at $749. If you're tall and will live near the top of the range, take this seriously. If your standing height is comfortably below max, you may never see it.

Things that helped a little:
- Tightening every frame bolt again after the first month (several had loosened)
- Moving my monitor arm clamp closer to a leg
- Typing like a normal person instead of punishing the keys (working on it)

None of these fixed it.

## Memory Presets: They Drift

The L2 has memory presets, and they mostly work. The catch is that they drift by about a centimeter.

I'll hit my standing preset and it lands roughly a cm off from where I saved it. Sometimes high, sometimes low. It doesn't sound like much, but a centimeter is the difference between my wrists sitting right and my wrists sitting slightly wrong. I end up nudging it manually more often than I should have to.

Re-saving the preset helps for a while, then the drift comes back. It's not a dealbreaker. It's just an annoying reminder that the controller isn't as precise as the motor it's driving.

## Cable Tray: Garbage

There's no gentler way to say it. The included cable tray is bad.

It's shallow, so a normal power strip barely fits. The openings are awkward, so cables slip out the sides. It sags once you put any real weight in it. After a couple of weeks of fighting it, I took it off and bought a third-party tray. That should be the first thing you do too.

A cable tray is not hard to get right. Shipping a bad one on a desk at this price feels careless. Budget an extra $20–40 for a replacement and you'll be much happier.

## Six Months In: What I'd Tell a Friend

**What's good:**
- Quiet, fast, reliable motor, the best part of the desk
- Solid at sitting and mid-range standing heights
- No mechanical degradation after six months of daily use

**What's not:**
- Noticeable wobble at full height under hard typing
- Memory presets drift about 1 cm
- The cable tray is unusable; plan to replace it
- Frame bolts loosened in the first month, so check them

## Verdict

At **$549**, the Jarvik L2 is a good desk. You get an excellent motor, acceptable stability for most people, and a few flaws you can work around for the cost of a cable tray. I'd recommend it without much hesitation.

At **$749**, it isn't worth it. At that price you're in range of desks with better frames, tighter presets, and cable management that isn't an afterthought. Paying full price means paying a premium for problems you'll have to fix yourself.

**Wait for the sale.** It seems to come around often enough that paying $749 makes no sense. If you're tall and will run this desk at max height every day, look elsewhere regardless of price.

*No affiliate links, no free product. I bought this desk with my own money and I'll update this review if anything changes.*

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: My 6-Month Review

I’ve used the Jarvik L2 as my primary desk for six months, working from home as a software engineer. It gets raised and lowered multiple times a day, carries a dual-monitor setup, and has survived the usual mess of cables, chargers, notebooks, and too many coffee cups.

The short version: **it’s a good desk at the $549 sale price and a bad deal at $749.** The motor is fast and genuinely quiet, the frame feels solid at normal sitting and standing heights, and the controls are straightforward. But the wobble at full height is real, the memory presets aren’t perfectly reliable, and the included cable tray is bad enough that I stopped using it.

## What I like

### The motor is quiet and fast

This is the L2’s best feature. The motor is much quieter than I expected from a desk in this price range. It makes a low mechanical hum rather than a loud whine or grinding noise, and it doesn’t sound like it is struggling under a normal work setup.

More importantly, it moves quickly. I don’t have to stand there waiting for the desk to crawl from sitting height to standing height. That sounds minor, but it matters when you actually change positions several times a day. A desk that takes forever to move ends up staying in one position because using it feels annoying. The Jarvik L2 is fast enough that I use the standing function without thinking about it.

### It feels stable at the heights most people will use

At sitting height, it is completely fine. No complaints.

At my usual standing height, it is also stable enough for normal work: typing, using a mouse, adjusting monitors, writing in a notebook, and leaning lightly on the desk. It does not feel flimsy or cheap. The frame has enough weight and stiffness that it feels like a real piece of office furniture rather than one of those lightweight standing-desk frames with a tabletop thrown on top.

For regular day-to-day use, I have been happy with it.

## What I don’t like

### It wobbles at full height

The L2 is not rock-solid when raised all the way up. If I type hard, especially when I am in an aggressively caffeinated coding sprint, I can see some movement in the monitors. The desktop itself has a noticeable front-to-back wobble at maximum height.

To be clear: it does not shake constantly, and it has never felt unsafe. It is not collapsing, sliding, or doing anything dramatic. But it is there, and if you are tall enough to use this desk near its upper limit—or if you type heavily—you will notice it.

This is the sort of issue that reviews often dismiss with “all standing desks wobble.” That is technically true, but not especially helpful. The question is whether the wobble is annoying. For me, at normal standing height, no. At full height, yes.

If you need a desk that stays absolutely steady at its maximum extension, spend more money. The Jarvik L2 is not that desk.

### The memory presets drift

The memory presets are convenient, but they are not precise enough to trust blindly.

Over time, I noticed that a preset can land roughly a centimeter off from where I originally set it. That does not sound like much, and for some people it won’t matter. But desk height is one of those things where a centimeter can be noticeable, especially if you have your monitor arms, chair height, and keyboard angle dialed in.

I now treat the presets as approximate positions rather than exact ones. They get me close, then I make a small adjustment.

That is not a dealbreaker, but it is sloppy. A memory preset should return to the same height consistently. Six months in, I should not have to second-guess whether my standing preset is going to be slightly too low today.

### The cable tray is garbage

The included cable tray is the weakest part of the package by far.

It is awkward, undersized, and not designed around how people actually set up desks in 2026. Once you have a power strip, monitor power supplies, charging cables, and the various thick cables from a real workstation, it becomes cramped fast. Access is annoying, routing is annoying, and the result still looks messy.

I tried to make it work. I gave it more effort than it deserved. Eventually, I replaced it with a better under-desk cable-management solution.

If Jarvik removed the tray entirely and lowered the price by $20, I would consider that an improvement. If you buy this desk, assume you will want a separate cable tray or cable-management basket.

## Who should buy it

Buy the Jarvik L2 if:

- You can get it around **$549**
- You want a fast, quiet electric standing desk
- You work at standard sitting and standing heights
- You do not need perfectly precise memory settings
- You are willing to handle cable management yourself

Skip it if:

- You are paying **$749**
- You are tall and expect to use the desk at maximum height regularly
- You are extremely sensitive to desk wobble
- You want presets that are consistently exact
- You expect the included cable tray to solve your setup

## Verdict

At **$549**, the Jarvik L2 is worth buying. The motor is excellent, the desk is pleasant to use every day, and the compromises are reasonable for the price.

At **$749**, I would pass. The full-height wobble, drifting presets, and terrible cable tray are easier to tolerate when the desk is discounted. At full price, they feel like corners that should not have been cut.

It is a solid midrange standing desk, not a premium one. Buy it on sale, replace the cable tray immediately, and do not expect maximum-height stability to rival more expensive desks.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
Last week I finally launched my first commercial game.

It’s been three years of nights and weekends to get here, so seeing it actually out in the wild was pretty surreal. In the first week, it sold 412 copies. For a solo project that started as “I wonder if I can actually finish this,” that feels very real to me.

A few things happened that I’m still kind of processing:

- It hit the front page of a small subreddit for about 6 hours
- A bunch of people jumped in right away and started sharing screenshots, feedback, and first impressions
- One review said the movement feels floaty

And yeah — they’re right. I’ve seen the same thing in enough places now that I’m not going to pretend it’s not there. The movement is one of the first things I want to tighten up, so I’m patching that in 1.1 next month.

That’s basically where things are at right now: launch happened, people are playing it, I’m reading feedback, and the next update is already in motion.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
If part of your baseboard heating is dead cold while the rest of the house is warming up, you’ve almost certainly got air trapped in the line. A pocket of air acts like a roadblock in the pipe—the hot water from your boiler hits that bubble and can't push past it. 

Before you get started, grab a small cup or Tupperware container, an old rag, and either a flathead screwdriver or a radiator bleed key (you can grab a key at any local hardware store for a couple of bucks).

**1. Shut off the boiler and circulator**
Head down to the boiler and flip the power switch off, or turn all your thermostats all the way down so the system isn't calling for heat. You don't want the circulator pump running while you do this; if the pump is pushing water through the lines while you have a valve open, it just chases the air bubbles around the loop instead of letting them settle at the top where you can get them out. Give the water 20 or 30 minutes to cool down so you don’t scald your hands.

**2. Start closest to the boiler (and don't skip the basement)**
You want to go unit by unit, starting with the baseboard closest to the boiler and working your way out to the farthest one. 

Here is the mistake that causes most of our service calls for cold radiators: homeowners only bleed the upstairs bedrooms because that’s where they feel the cold, and they completely skip the basement loop. In a lot of the homes around here, the air pocket is actually hung up down in the basement or on the first floor, choking off the flow to the rest of the zone. Even if your basement baseboards aren't the ones giving you trouble, start there anyway.

**3. Find the bleeder valve**
Pop the front cover off the baseboard unit, or look for the little flip-up access door on the left or right end cap. Right at the top of the pipe fin, you’ll see a small brass fitting. That’s the bleeder valve. 

**4. Open the valve slowly**
Hold your cup right underneath the valve and keep your rag handy. Boiler water is nasty, black, and smells like old pennies—it will permanently stain light carpet if it drips. 

Take your screwdriver or radiator key and turn the valve counterclockwise just a quarter-turn or so. Do it slowly. You should hear a sharp hissing sound right away. That’s the trapped air escaping. Don't unscrew the valve all the way out, or the pin will shoot out into your cup and you'll have a real mess on your hands.

**5. Watch for a steady stream**
Keep the valve open while it hisses. After a few seconds, it’ll start spitting and sputtering a mix of air and water. Wait until those sputters stop and you get a solid, steady stream of water with no air bubbles in it. 

**6. Close it snug—do not overtighten**
As soon as that stream is steady, turn the valve clockwise to shut it. Make it finger-snug plus a tiny nudge with the screwdriver, then stop. These valves are soft brass. If you crank down on them with a screwdriver, you will crack the valve seat, it won't seal anymore, and you’ll be calling me to come sweat a new valve onto the pipe. Wipe it dry with your rag and watch it for ten seconds to make sure it isn't weeping.

**7. Check your pressure and fire it back up**
Once you’ve worked your way from the boiler out to the very last baseboard on the loop, head back down to the boiler before you turn the switch back on. Look at the pressure gauge on the front of the boiler. Letting air out drops the system pressure, and most residential boilers need to sit right around 12 to 15 PSI when cold. Most setups have an automatic autofill valve that will top the water off for you, but if your gauge is sitting down near zero, you'll need to lift the fast-fill lever briefly to bring it back up to 12 PSI. 

Flip the boiler power switch back on, turn your thermostats up, and listen. You might hear a little gurgling for a minute or two, and then those cold baseboards should start heating up evenly from end to end. 

If you get to a valve that’s painted shut, stripped out, or doesn't push any air *or* water out when you open it, leave it closed and give the shop a call—that usually means your expansion tank is waterlogged or your feed valve is stuck shut, and we'll need to take a look at the boiler itself.

b.text:
1. **Turn off the boiler and circulator, and let the system cool.**  
   Turn the thermostats down, then shut off the heating system at its service switch. Don’t bleed baseboards while the boiler is hot or the circulator is running—hot water can cause serious burns.

2. **Find the bleeder valve on the first baseboard.**  
   Start with the unit closest to the boiler, then work outward through each heating loop. Look near the end of the baseboard for a small manual bleeder valve. You may need to remove an end cover to reach it.

   These steps are for **hot-water baseboards with individual bleeder valves**, not electric baseboard heaters. Some hot-water systems don’t have bleeders at each unit and must be purged at the boiler instead. If you can’t find a bleeder, don’t loosen a pipe fitting or open a drain or pressure-relief valve as a substitute.

3. **Put a cup under the valve.**  
   Keep a towel underneath, too. The first water out may be dirty, and it can still be warm. Keep your face and hands out of the discharge path.

4. **Open the bleeder slowly.**  
   Use a radiator key or a flathead screwdriver, depending on the valve. Turn it counterclockwise just enough to release air—usually only a small fraction of a turn. **Do not remove the screw.**

   You may hear hissing, followed by sputtering water. Leave the valve slightly open until water flows steadily with no hissing or air spurts. You don’t need to drain a cupful once the air is gone.

5. **Close it snugly, not forcefully.**  
   Turn the valve clockwise until the water stops. Overtightening can damage or crack the valve seat and leave you with a leak. Wipe the valve dry and check for drips.

6. **Repeat at every baseboard—including the basement loop.**  
   Work unit by unit, starting closest to the boiler and moving outward. Don’t bleed only the upstairs units and call it done. A basement loop can hold trapped air, too, and skipping it may leave part of the house cold. Check every loop rather than assuming the air is all upstairs—or all downstairs.

7. **Check system pressure, then test the heat.**  
   Bleeding releases some water and can lower system pressure. Before restarting, check the boiler gauge against the cold-fill pressure specified for your system. If pressure is low, no water comes out of a bleeder, or you’re unsure what the gauge should read, stop and call for service rather than adding water blindly.

   Restore power, turn up a thermostat, and let the system run. Check that each baseboard warms up and that the bleeders stay dry.

**Still have a cold baseboard?** A zone valve, circulator, low system pressure, or a loop that needs proper purging could be the problem. If air keeps returning or a valve won’t stop dripping, contact us to have the system checked.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
# Nine Rainouts, One Torn ACL: It's Time to Turf the Girls' Field

Last October, one of my players planted her foot to make a cut, and the foot landed in a rut left over from a week of wet practices. Her knee didn't make the cut with it. She tore her ACL on a field condition, not a tackle. Surgery, months of rehab, season over. She wasn't doing anything wrong. The field was.

That's one injury. Here's the rest of the score from the last two seasons: nine games rained out or moved off our field. Nine. Our grass field doesn't drain. When it rains hard, it holds water, and it stays unplayable for days afterward. Home games become away games, sometimes on a day's notice, which means parents scrambling and buses rerouted. JV games get bumped so varsity can use whatever dry field we can find. We lose home-field advantage in games that matter, and our season gets compressed every single time the weather turns.

I coach girls' soccer and track at [High School]. I'm not writing this because I want a fancy facility. I'm writing it because we have a field that cancels our schedule and hurts our players, and we already know the fix, because this district bought it in 2019.

That's the year the football field got turf.

The football field drains. It's playable the morning after a storm. It's flat, it's even, and it doesn't develop ruts in October. Games happen on it. Meanwhile, the girls' soccer team plays next door on a surface that floods, chews up, and stays dangerous deep into the fall. My track athletes warm up on it in the spring. Everyone in this program sees the difference every day.

In 2019, this district decided that our athletes deserved a safe, playable surface. It just decided it for half of them. There's a word for building one standard for the boys' teams and another for the girls', and the school board should not want that word showing up in a complaint letter before it shows up in a budget line.

I know turf is expensive. I've seen the numbers, and I know they'll make people flinch. But run the math on what we're paying now: nine games rescheduled or relocated over two seasons, transportation costs moved around at the last minute, home gate revenue that walks out the door with every rainout, and the ongoing risk that the next rut takes another knee. And here's the thing — this district already decided once that turf was worth the money. I'm not asking for a new decision. I'm asking for the same one, applied to the girls.

The board votes on the facilities budget for next year. Put turf on the girls' soccer field in that budget. Not a study, not a committee, not "phased in eventually." The girls currently on my roster have watched the boys play on turf for six years while they've dodged puddles and rehabbed a torn ACL. They notice. Their parents notice. The athletic trainer definitely notices.

We lost nine games to that field and one knee. Turf the girls' field, and we stop counting.

[Name]
Girls' soccer and track coach, [High School]

b.text:
# Nine Games. One Torn ACL. It's Time to Turf the Girls' Soccer Field.

Nine games. That's how many my girls have lost to weather in the last two seasons — rained out or moved to somebody else's field, which usually means a bus ride and a 9 p.m. dinner on a school night.

To be clear, it doesn't rain nine games' worth on our town. It rains, and then our field holds the water like a bathtub. The low corner past the 18 stays soft for days. By mid-October the middle is a mess of ruts left over from every practice and game since August, because grass doesn't recover when 40 kids run on it six days a week and there's no second field to rotate to.

Last October one of my seniors put her foot in one of those ruts. She went down without anyone within ten feet of her. Torn ACL. She missed the rest of her season, missed her whole track season, and had college coaches who stopped calling. She did her rehab, she's fine now, she's a good kid who deserved better than a hole in the ground.

I'm not going to pretend I'm a facilities expert. I coach soccer and track for a stipend that works out to something I don't like to calculate hourly. But I know what our field costs us in games, in practice time, in kids' knees, and in the money we spend dragging, seeding, and re-sodding a field that floods again the next time it rains.

Here's the part I'd like the board to sit with. The football field got turf in 2019. Nobody on my staff resented it — that field needed it, and the community showed up and paid for it. But that was six years ago. In those six years, the football team hasn't lost a home game to standing water. My girls have lost nine in two.

I've heard the reasons. Football draws bigger crowds. Football has boosters. The soccer field is harder to drain. Some of that's even true. None of it explains why the argument stopped there for six years.

We have more girls playing soccer at this school than we've ever had. We had to cut players at JV tryouts last fall, which I hated doing. Those girls put in the same offseason, ride the same buses, and represent this district the same way. They practice on a field the district would not ask the football team to practice on.

So here's what I'm asking. Put the girls' soccer field turf project in next year's facilities budget. Not a study. Not a phase one. Not a line item that gets moved to the following year when something else comes up, which is what happened to the drainage work that was supposed to fix this in the first place.

And if the money genuinely isn't there — say that out loud, in public, with numbers. Tell us what it costs and what it's competing against. I'll take an honest no over another six years of "we're looking into it." At least then the community can decide whether it wants to fundraise, the way it did in 2019.

One more thing, since I've got the space. A turfed field doesn't just serve 40 soccer players. It serves the youth league that can't get field time, the band that needs somewhere to practice in the spring, the PE classes stuck inside on a drizzly Tuesday, and my track athletes who currently do their warmups on a hill. It's a shared asset. It's just been sitting behind other priorities so long that people forgot it was on the list.

Nine games, one ACL, six years. Put it in the budget.

*[Name] coaches girls' soccer and track at [High School].*

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
# Week One Launch Recap: 412 Copies and Floaty Movement

Well, it’s out. After three years of nights, weekends, and staring at code after my day job, my first game is officially live. 

I wanted to drop a quick update on how the first seven days went.

### The Numbers and the Reddit Spike
We sold 412 copies in week one. For a solo project with basically zero marketing budget outside of this devlog, I'm really happy with that. Seeing actual people buy and play something I built in my spare room is a weird feeling, but a good one.

The biggest traffic push happened on Thursday. A post I made hit the front page of a small niche subreddit and stayed there for about six hours. That single window accounted for a solid chunk of the week's sales and brought in a wave of fresh wishlists.

### The Feedback (And the Floaty Controls)
The reviews and community messages have been coming in, which has been great to read through. 

One review specifically called out the movement mechanics, saying the player character feels "a bit floaty." I booted up the build, played through a few levels with fresh eyes, and... yeah. Honestly, they’re completely right. When you’ve been testing your own jump physics for three years, you get used to the quirks, but stepping back, it definitely lacks weight.

### What’s Next
I'm not doing a post-mortem or pulling out some big philosophical lesson from launch week—I'm just getting back to work.

Right now, I’m working on Patch 1.1, which will drop next month. The main priority is tightening up the movement physics so it feels far more responsive, along with fixing a few ultra-wide display bugs that players reported over the weekend.

Thanks to everyone who bought a copy, left a review, or has been reading these posts over the last three years. 

More updates soon.

b.text:
# One week after launch

My game came out last week. After three years of working on it at night and on weekends, it’s now a thing people can buy, play, and have opinions about. Still getting used to that part.

It sold **412 copies in its first week**. Thank you to everyone who picked it up, and to those of you who’ve been following the devlog while I slowly got this thing out the door. It’s nice to finally be talking about a released game instead of a game I’m trying to finish.

For about six hours, it also hit the front page of a small subreddit. Not an enormous wave of attention, but definitely more activity than I’m used to seeing around something I made.

One review said the movement feels floaty. Honestly, they’re right. I’ve spent so long playing this game that I’m used to how it handles, but that doesn’t make the criticism wrong.

That’s what I’m working on for **version 1.1, planned for next month**. The movement needs to feel tighter, and I’ll share more about the changes here as I work through them.

For now, the game is out, 412 copies have sold, and I’m back in the project tweaking how it feels to move around. Next post will have more on that.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
Roadstar DC4, 14 months and about 140,000 miles

Been running the DC4 front and rear since I picked up this rig. Front camera is fine day and night for what I need it for. Rear night footage is the weak spot: past about 30 feet it gets grainy enough that plates and lane markings are a guess. Close stuff is usable. Anything farther back at night, don't count on it.

It did the one job that matters. A car changed lanes into me and the footage was clear enough that my insurance claim got approved in 9 days instead of the usual six weeks of back and forth. That alone paid for the camera.

Mounting: the suction cup fell off twice in summer heat. Switched to the adhesive mount and it has stayed put. If you run the southern routes in July, skip the suction cup.

The app only pulls footage over WiFi. Most truck stops don't have a network you can actually use for that, so I quit fighting it and just pull the SD card. Works every time, takes a minute.

Not perfect, but it has held up for a year and change of real miles and it saved me on a claim. Rear night range is the only thing I'd warn you about.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam — 14 months / 140k miles**

Figured I'd put some real miles on this thing before writing it up. Here's where I landed.

**The good:**

It earned its keep back in the spring. Four-wheeler cut across my lane, clipped me, and of course told his insurance I drifted into him. Front cam footage said otherwise. Claim approved in 9 days. My last claim without footage took 6 weeks. That alone paid for the camera several times over, so if you're running without one, that's the whole argument right there.

Daytime footage front and rear is solid. Plates are readable, no complaints.

**The bad:**

Rear cam night footage gets grainy past about 30 feet. Close stuff is fine, but if someone's tailing you at a distance in the dark, don't count on reading a plate. Front cam handles night better.

The suction mount is junk in the heat. Fell off my windshield twice last summer, once while I was rolling. Switched to the adhesive mount and it hasn't budged since. Just skip the suction mount and go adhesive from day one.

**The annoying:**

The app needs wifi to pull footage. Sounds fine until you realize truck stop wifi is garbage or nonexistent half the time. I gave up on the app and just pull the SD card and stick it in my laptop. Works fine, just know going in that the app is basically useless on the road.

**Bottom line:**

Not perfect, but after 140k miles it's still recording every day and it already saved me a claim fight. Buy the adhesive mount with it, keep a spare SD card, and don't expect miracles from the rear cam at night. Would I buy it again? Yeah.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

Find the shutoff valve inside the house. It’s usually in the basement or crawlspace on the pipe that feeds that outdoor faucet. Turn it off.

Go outside, open the spigot, and let it drain completely. Leave it open.

Disconnect every hose. This is the one that matters. A connected hose traps water in the pipe. That water freezes, the pipe splits, and you have a flood. Most of the burst-pipe calls we get in January started with a hose somebody forgot.

Slap a $3 foam faucet cover over the spigot. Done.

If you cannot find an interior shutoff, or you’re not sure which valve it is, call us. We’ll shut it down and drain it the right way so you don’t find out the hard way in January.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots (Minneapolis Homeowners)

If you have an outdoor spigot on the side or back of your house, it needs to be winterized before the first deep freeze. In Minneapolis, that usually means sometime in November.

Here’s the quick version.

## What You Need

- A pair of pliers or your hands, if the hose is not stuck
- A bucket or towel, just in case a little water drips out
- A $3 foam spigot cover

## Step 1: Shut the Interior Valve

Most Minneapolis outdoor spigots are fed by a pipe that runs through the house. Look for a shut-off valve inside near the spigot’s location. It may be in a basement ceiling, utility room, garage, bathroom, or closet.

Turn the valve to stop water from getting to the outside spigot. If the valve is a lever, turn it until it lines up across the pipe. If it’s a round handle, turn it clockwise until it’s snug. Don’t force it.

## Step 2: Drain the Spigot

Once the interior valve is off, go outside and open the spigot. Let it drain. You may see a small amount of water come out, then stop. Leave it open until you’re sure the line is empty.

After it drains, turn the spigot off again.

## Step 3: Disconnect Hoses

Take off every garden hose left attached to the spigot. Pull the nozzle down so water in the hose drains out. If the hose is stiff or frozen, thaw it gently — don’t yank it and risk breaking the spigot.

## Step 4: Put On a Foam Cover

Slide a $3 foam spigot cover over the spigot and secure it in place. This isn’t magic, and it doesn’t turn the spigot into a heated pipe. It helps block cold wind from getting directly into the fitting. It’s just one layer of protection.

## The Big Mistake Homeowners Make

Leaving the hose connected.

That is one of the main reasons we get January burst-pipe calls. A hose left attached traps water inside the spigot. Even after you shut the valve, water can stay in the exposed pipe and hose. When it freezes, it expands, and something can split.

The hose is the problem. If you leave it on, you’ve basically given the winter a place to freeze the water.

## If You Don’t Have an Interior Shutoff

Some older Minneapolis homes have spigots that don’t have an obvious interior shut-off valve. If you can’t find one, or you’re not sure which one controls the outside pipe, don’t guess.

That’s the point where it makes sense to call us.

We can find the valve, label it properly, and make sure you can shut down the outside lines quickly before the next cold snap. It’s a lot cheaper to do it now than to chase water in the basement after one pipe gives way.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
A 15% Cut to Apprenticeship Funding Is a Bad Deal for the State

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW. I'm writing this because the state is looking at a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding, and I don't think the people pushing it have looked at what this program actually does.

My class started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished and are working as journeymen now. That's not a theory. That's people with jobs, paying taxes, raising families, and doing the work that keeps the lights on.

We started around $19 an hour. Journeymen top out around $46 an hour. That jump matters. A lot of us came in needing help — food assistance, housing help, whatever it took to get through the first years. Once you're earning a journeyman wage, you're off those programs. The state isn't carrying us forever. It's carrying us long enough to get trained, and then we carry ourselves.

Look at the cost. The public cost for an apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. The average public subsidy for a four-year college graduate who finishes is around $48,000. I'm not knocking college. Some jobs need it. But if the argument for this cut is that the state needs to save money, cutting the cheaper program that puts people straight to work doesn't make sense. You're spending more than three times as much on the other path and getting a lower finish-to-job rate in a lot of cases. We finished 21 out of 24. That's what the money bought.

A 15% cut doesn't just trim fat. It means fewer seats, fewer instructors, and fewer people who get the chance we got. The contractors still need electricians. The work doesn't go away. What goes away is the trained workforce, and then everybody pays for that — in delays, in higher bids, and in people stuck in low-wage jobs who could have been earning $46 an hour.

If you're a legislator reading this, come look at a job site. Talk to the people who finished. Then tell us a 15% cut is the smart move. The numbers don't say that. Twenty-one working journeymen out of 24, at about $14,000 of public money each, says the opposite. Fund the program. Don't cut it.

b.text:
# The Math Is Simple: Don't Cut Apprenticeship Funding

*By [Name], Third-Year Apprentice, IBEW Local [___]*

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with this local. I bend conduit, pull wire, and get paid to learn a trade that will take care of me and my family for the rest of my working life. Right now there's a proposal at the statehouse to cut apprenticeship funding by 15 percent. I want to walk you through why that's a bad deal, and I'm going to use plain numbers, because the numbers don't need dressing up.

Start with my own class. We began with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished, and every one of those 21 is working today as a journeyman electrician. That's 87 percent of us who made it through. Find me a four-year college program that keeps close to that. Plenty of them can't touch it, and the students who don't finish walk away with debt and no degree. When one of us washes out, we still walk away with a couple years of pay in our pocket and a skill we can use. Nobody finishes our program owing money.

Now the wages. We started at about $19 an hour. That's not a fortune, but it's a real paycheck from day one, and it goes up every year you're in. By the time you turn out, you're making around $46 an hour as a journeyman. I know apprentices in this local who were on food stamps or unemployment before they got their acceptance letter. Within a year of starting, they were off every assistance program they were on. Not because somebody gave them a handout — because they got a job that pays. The state stops paying for them and starts collecting taxes from them. That flip happens fast in this trade.

Here's the number I want every legislator who reads this newsletter to sit with. The total public cost for each apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. The average public subsidy for each four-year college graduate who finishes is around $48,000. Read those again. We cost the public about a third of what a college grad costs. We finish at higher rates. And we're working and paying taxes the whole time we're training instead of waiting four years to start. If the state ran a contest for the best return on workforce money, apprenticeship wins it hands down. This is the program you cut last, not first.

Fifteen percent might not sound like much when you say it fast. Here's what it means on the ground. It means fewer seats in classes. It means longer wait lists to get in. It means older equipment and fewer instructors spread across more students. Right now a person who applies to our program might wait a year or two for a spot. Cut the funding and that wait gets longer. Every person stuck on that list is a person the state isn't collecting taxes from, and may be supporting instead. That's the trade you're making: save a little money now, spend more of it later.

And don't forget what the state actually needs. We are short on electricians, not long on them. Somebody has to wire the schools and the hospitals. Somebody has to build out the data centers, the solar, and the EV chargers the state keeps saying it wants. That work doesn't happen by itself, and it doesn't happen without people trained to do it. Every dollar the state puts into apprenticeship comes back in projects built, taxes paid, and paychecks spent at local businesses. The 21 journeymen out of my class alone will pay back that $14,000 apiece many times over across a career.

I'm an electrician, not a speechwriter, so I'll keep the ending short. This cut fails by its own logic. The state would be trimming 15 percent off the cheapest, highest-finishing, fastest-paying workforce program it runs — in the middle of a shortage of exactly the workers that program produces. If you're a member of this local, call your representative and tell them the numbers in this piece. If you're a legislator and this newsletter reaches your desk, do the math yourself.

The math is simple. Don't cut the program that's working.
