setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Baseboard Heating Before Winter

1. **Shut off the circulator/boiler first.** Flip the boiler service switch off or turn the boiler off so the circulator pump isn’t running. If the pump kicks on while a bleeder is open, it will pull air back into the loop instead of pushing it out.

2. **Find the bleeder valve on each baseboard unit.** It’s a small valve on the end cap (or on top near the end) of the unit. Get down at floor level with a flashlight—these hide behind furniture, curtains, and stored boxes.

3. **Cup underneath it.** Hold a cup, small bowl, or rag under the valve before you open it. The water is hot and usually dirty; it will stain and it can burn you.

4. **Open it slow with a key or flathead.** Use a bleeder key or a flathead screwdriver and crack the valve open slowly. You’ll hear air hissing out first. Let it hiss.

5. **Wait for steady water with no hissing air.** Keep the cup in place until water runs out in a steady stream with no spitting or air noise. That means the air is out of that section.

6. **Close it snug—don’t overtighten.** Snug the valve back down, but don’t crank it. Overtightening cracks the valve seat, and now you’ve got a leak instead of a cold baseboard.

7. **Go unit by unit, starting closest to the boiler and working out.** Bleed the unit nearest the boiler first, then work your way to the farthest one. Don’t bounce around the house; keep moving outward from the boiler.

**The mistake that causes most of our cold-baseboard calls: people only bleed the upstairs units and skip the basement loop.** If you have baseboard in the basement, crawlspace, utility room, or garage, bleed it too. That loop is usually where the air actually is, and it’s the one everybody forgets because it’s out of sight.

When you’re done, turn the boiler and circulator back on and check the pressure gauge. Bleeding usually drops system pressure. Most residential systems want to see roughly 12–15 psi cold, so top it off slowly with the fill valve if it’s low. If the pressure keeps dropping, or the same baseboards go cold again in a day or two, you’ve got a leak or a failing air eliminator—that’s a job for us.

This is the same sequence I follow on service calls, and it fixes most cold-baseboard complaints—assuming every loop, including the basement, actually gets bled. If you’re local to our service area and you still have cold baseboards after doing this, or you crack a valve and can’t get it to seal, shut the boiler back off and give us a call. It’s a quick fix when it’s just trapped air, and it’s a lot easier to deal with now than on the first freezing night.

b.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Your Baseboard Heating Before Winter

If a baseboard runs cold along part of its length, or a whole zone barely warms up while the rest of the house is fine, you've got air in the line. Air pockets block water flow, and bleeding them out is a twenty-minute job you can do with a screwdriver. Here's the process, start to finish.

## What You'll Need

- A flathead screwdriver or a bleeder key (a couple bucks at any hardware store)
- A cup and a towel
- Twenty minutes

## Step 1: Shut the Boiler Off First

Flip the boiler off at its switch and let the circulator come to a stop. You want the system still while you bleed it — moving water carries air pockets past the bleeders instead of letting them collect where you can actually get at them. It also keeps hot water from coming at you under pressure if the boiler's been running.

## Step 2: Find the Bleeder Valve

Each baseboard unit has a small bleeder valve at one end, right where the finned pipe meets the end of the unit. Sometimes it's tucked behind the end cover — pop the cover off if you have to. Most valves open with a flathead screwdriver; some take a bleeder key.

## Step 3: Put a Cup Under It

Water comes out when you open the valve. Cup underneath, towel beside it.

## Step 4: Open It Slow

Open the valve about a quarter turn, slowly. You'll hear hissing — that's the air escaping. Keep it open until water runs out in a steady stream with no sputtering and no hiss. Sputtering means there's still air in that run; steady water means the unit's clear.

## Step 5: Close It Snug — and Stop

Snug the valve closed and leave it there. Do not crank on it. Overtightening cracks the valve seat, and a cracked seat means a slow drip behind your baseboard cover that you won't find until it's stained the wall. A firm snug is all it takes.

## Step 6: Work From the Boiler Outward

Go unit by unit, starting with the baseboard closest to the boiler and working your way out to the farthest loop. Bleed every unit, including the ones that seem to be heating fine.

## The Mistake That Causes Most of Our Cold Radiator Calls

When we get called out for a baseboard that won't heat, the story is almost always the same: the homeowner bled all the upstairs units, called it done, and skipped the basement loop entirely. The basement loop is usually where the air is actually sitting. You can bleed the whole first floor, get clear water out of every valve, and still have an air-bound system — because the pocket doing the damage never got a bleeder opened on it. If you only bleed one loop, make it the basement.

## When You're Done

Flip the boiler back on, let it run a full cycle, and put your hand along each baseboard. They should heat evenly end to end. If you've bled every unit — basement included — and a loop still runs cold, the problem is past what a bleeder valve can fix: low system pressure, a weak circulator, or a stuck zone valve. That's when to give us a call, and we'd rather come out now than after the first cold night.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
Last week the game went up. Three years of nights and weekends, and then it was just... live.

412 copies in the first week. I kept refreshing the dashboard like that would change the number. It didn't, mostly. A few sales came in clusters, which I think lined up with a small subreddit putting the post on its front page for about six hours. That was the loudest the launch got. After that it settled into a slow trickle, which is where it still is.

One review called the movement floaty. I read it, played for twenty minutes, and yeah — they're right. The air control is a little too generous and the landings don't have enough weight. I'm fixing that in 1.1, which I'm aiming to push next month along with a couple of smaller bugs people have already sent in.

Thanks to everyone who bought it, posted about it, or just stuck around the devlog this long. More soon.

b.text:
The game launched last week.

It sold 412 copies in the first week, which feels both small and huge at the same time. I spent three years working on this thing during nights and weekends, so seeing real people buy it, download it, and talk about it has been kind of surreal.

For a little while there, the launch post hit the front page of a small subreddit and stayed there for maybe six hours. That sent a noticeable bump of traffic and wishlists over to the store page, and it was the first time I saw the numbers jump without me directly doing anything.

I’ve been reading through the early feedback, and one review mentioned that the movement feels floaty. Honestly, they’re right. I’ve been close to it for too long, and I think I normalized some of that feel over time. So I’m going to spend part of the next month tightening that up for the 1.1 patch.

Right now the plan is pretty simple:

- keep monitoring launch issues
- collect more feedback on movement feel
- patch the floaty movement in 1.1 next month
- keep working on the next round of fixes and small improvements

If you bought the game during launch week, thank you. It means a lot that this thing is finally out in the world.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
**Our Girls Deserve a Field That Can Be Played On**

Nine girls’ soccer games have been rained out or moved over the past two seasons because our grass field floods. That is not a minor inconvenience. It means players and families lose games, schedules get disrupted, and our team cannot count on its own field.

The field is also uneven. Last October, one of my players stepped into a rut and tore her ACL. I will not pretend a better field can prevent every injury. Sports are physical, and injuries happen. But players should not have to contend with ruts in the ground on top of everything else.

The school board is deciding next year’s facilities budget. I am asking you to put a turf field for girls’ soccer in it—with proper drainage.

This is not a request for a luxury. A field that floods in ordinary rain is not a reliable home field. Turf would give our players a consistent place to compete and practice, and help us avoid the repeated cancellations and relocations that have marked the last two seasons.

There is also a fairness issue. The boys’ football field got turf in 2019. Our girls are still trying to play on grass that floods and develops ruts. The teams do not need identical facilities in every detail, but girls should not be left with an inferior playing surface year after year while the school has already invested in turf for boys.

I coach girls’ soccer and track at a public high school. I do it for the stipend, not because I was looking for another writing project. I am speaking up because I see what our players are asked to put up with, and because the board has a decision in front of it.

I understand that facilities projects cost money and that the district has other needs. But this is a basic investment in the safety, access, and dignity of our girls’ program. Please include a properly drained turf field for girls’ soccer in next year’s facilities budget.

b.text:
The boys got turf in 2019. The girls are still waiting.

Over the last two seasons, nine girls’ soccer games have been rained out or moved because our grass field floods. Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping in a rut.

Those are not cosmetic problems. We are not asking for a prettier field. We are asking for a reliable place to play.

I coach girls’ soccer and track at our public high school. I expect our athletes to show up, work hard and take care of what they have. They should be able to expect the school district to do its part, too. A field that repeatedly floods and develops dangerous ruts is not holding up that end of the deal.

When the school board votes on next year’s facilities budget, it should fund turf for the girls’ soccer field, including the drainage work needed to make it function properly. Not another vague promise to revisit the problem. A funded project with a timeline.

I know turf costs money. So does maintaining grass, repairing a failing field and repeatedly working around a playing surface we cannot count on. The board should put those costs side by side, including turf maintenance and eventual replacement. Taxpayers deserve actual numbers, not just a big installation price presented without context.

We also need an honest discussion about safety. I am not claiming turf would have prevented my player’s ACL injury or that any surface eliminates injuries. Turf has its own concerns, including heat and surface conditions. Those deserve careful review. But uncertainty about the perfect field is not an excuse to accept the condition of the one we have.

Then there is fairness.

The boys’ football field got turf in 2019. The district has already shown that it considers a major investment in an athletic field worthwhile. The girls should not have to keep proving that their games matter enough for the same consideration.

Fair treatment does not require every team to have identical facilities. It does require the district to take comparable needs seriously. Nine disrupted games in two seasons should be enough to get this out of the “maybe later” pile.

Our players cannot vote on the facilities budget. Board members can. They can ask hard questions about price, drainage, safety and maintenance—and still make a decision that fixes the problem.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
**It's Not a Crash. It's a Lag.**

Last spring, the median home in our zip code sold in 8 days. This spring, it's 34. If you only read that headline, you'd think the market fell off a cliff.

It didn't. I've been selling homes here for ten years, and I'll tell you plainly what's going on: the market caught its breath, and a lot of sellers haven't noticed yet.

Here's the part that seems to confuse people. List prices are still up 6% over last year. Showings per listing are down by half. Homes are sitting longer while asking prices keep climbing. That looks like a contradiction — until you realize what those numbers are actually measuring. Not value. Stubbornness.

Let's start with some honesty about the 8 days. That was never normal. That was a once-in-a-career frenzy — cheap money, panic buying, offers sight unseen. For most of my decade in this business, 30 to 40 days on market was an ordinary, healthy spring. What we're living through now isn't a collapse. It's a return to earth. The problem is that a lot of sellers got used to the stratosphere.

I have three sellers right now whose homes have been listed for more than 60 days. I've recommended a price adjustment to all three. All three have said no. These aren't unreasonable people, and they're not bad at math. Each of them watched a neighbor's house sell in a weekend with a stack of offers a couple of years ago, and that number is stuck in their heads like a song they can't turn off. I understand it. But the buyer pool from that era doesn't exist anymore — mortgage rates took care of that — and no amount of sitting will bring it back.

Here's what I tell them, and what I'll tell you: the market hasn't rejected your home. It has rejected your price. Those are two very different problems, and only one of them is fixable.

I know it's fixable because I watch it get fixed every week. Homes priced to *today* — not to last April, not to the neighbor's sale, not to what the seller needs to net for their next place — are still going under contract in under two weeks. Let me say that again, because it's the whole story: correctly priced homes in this zip code are selling in fourteen days or less, right now, in the same market where other homes sit for two months. Same streets. Same schools. Same buyers. Different price.

And "priced right" doesn't mean priced low. It means priced current. There's a real cost to learning this the hard way. A home that sits for 60 days and then cuts its price almost always sells for less than it would have if it had been priced honestly on day one. Buyers smell a stale listing the way you smell rain coming. The showing requests slow down, and the offers that do come in come in low. The market will wait you out. It has nothing better to do.

If you're a buyer reading this and waiting for the crash before you make your move — stop waiting. A crash requires panicked sellers, and what we have is the opposite: patient ones. What you have today that you didn't have two years ago is time and leverage. You can actually get an inspection. You can negotiate. You can sleep on a decision. That's worth more than the imaginary discount you're holding out for.

So no, I'm not worried about this market. I've worked through genuinely bad ones, and this isn't that. This is a normal market wearing a costume from a weird one. The sellers who take the costume off are selling in two weeks. The ones who don't are hosting open houses in month three.

The market moved. The only question is whether your price moved with it.

b.text:
It’s Not a Crash. It’s Sticker Shock.

Last spring, if you found a house you liked in our suburb, you wrote the offer the same day. This spring, listings sit. And a lot of sellers are angry about it.

Let’s stop dancing around the numbers. In my ZIP code, median days on market went from 8 days last spring to 34 this spring. Showings per listing are down by half. Asking prices are still up about 6% year over year.

That combination has launched a thousand bad headlines. But let me be blunt: this is not a crash.

A crash is when prices fall because credit dries up, inventory floods the market, and sellers panic. That is not what is happening here. Asking prices are not falling—they’re stuck, still about 6% higher than last year—because too many sellers are asking for a price today’s buyer pool has already rejected.

Here is the part sellers don’t want to hear: the market is not confused. It is very clear.

If showings are down by half, buyers are telling you something. If your home has been listed for 60+ days without an offer, buyers have already voted. And if you refuse to adjust the price, you are not “waiting out the market.” You are waiting to become invisible.

I have three sellers right now in exactly that position. Good houses. Good locations. Not selling. Each one has been listed over 60 days, and each one is refusing to reduce the price. They are priced for the frenzy of a couple years ago, not for the pace of today. That is not a market problem. That is a pricing problem.

Meanwhile, the homes that are priced correctly—really priced, not padded “because we can always come down”—are still selling in under two weeks. I see it every week. There is no shortage of buyers for a fairly priced home in our market. There is a shortage of buyers willing to overpay for a home that isn’t.

An asking price is not a value. It’s an invitation. When showings drop by half and days on market quadruple, buyers aren’t rejecting the house. They’re rejecting the invitation.

After ten years of selling real estate in this Midwest suburb, I’ve learned that buyers do not care what a seller needs, what a seller paid, or what a neighbor’s house supposedly sold for at the peak. They care what the home is worth today. And right now, today’s buyer has more choices, more patience, and far less fear of missing out.

So here is my opinion, without hedging: if you want to sell, price it right on day one. The first two weeks are not a test run. They are the market. Blow them, and you spend the next two months chasing a number you could have accepted immediately—except by then you’ll probably take less, and with less leverage.

If you are not willing to price for today, that is your call. But don’t blame the market. Don’t call it a crash. And don’t pretend your home is “still for sale” when the only thing missing is a realistic price.

The market didn’t break. It changed pace. The sellers who catch up are still selling in under two weeks. The ones who don’t will keep sitting there, wondering why nobody wants to pay yesterday’s price for today’s house.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: Eight Months of Near-Daily Use

I've been running the Corlane SM6 for eight months, and "near-daily" is not an exaggeration — I bake sourdough for the farmers market every weekend, which means this machine gets worked almost every day in some capacity. This is not a "made three batches of cookies and formed an opinion" review. This is a review from someone who has spent eight months trying to wear this thing out.

## The motor is the whole story, and it's a good story

Here's what matters most: the motor does not stall. I regularly run double batches of stiff bagel dough through it — low-hydration, high-gluten, the kind of dough that makes lesser mixers rock and groan and eventually give up — and the SM6 chews through it without bogging down.

If you've ever stood there listening to a mixer struggle on a single batch of bagels, you know exactly what a big deal this is. Motor headroom is the difference between a mixer that's a tool and a mixer that's an obstacle, and the SM6 has headroom to spare.

## Two annoyances, one real flaw

It's not perfect, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I pretended otherwise.

**The bowl lift lever squeaks.** Roughly once a month I hit it with WD-40, and it quiets down again, but it's an annoying little ritual on a $429 machine. Minor — but it's the kind of thing you notice every single time you use it.

**The stock dough hook is too short for the deep bowl.** It doesn't reach the dough properly, so instead of actually kneading, the dough just rides up the hook. I bought a third-party hook, which fixed the problem completely — but a mixer at this price, aimed squarely at bread bakers, shipping with a hook that doesn't fit its own bowl is a genuinely strange design decision. Budget for the replacement hook in your total cost.

## The price question

The SM6 runs $429 — $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid, plus whatever the aftermarket hook sets you back. So the real question is what that premium buys you.

## The verdict

**Buy it if you knead heavy dough every week.** Market bakers, bagel people, anyone regularly working stiff, low-hydration dough: the motor alone justifies the price and the hassle of swapping out the hook. This mixer will out-work you, and it won't die doing it.

**Skip it if you're mostly making cookies and cake batter.** You'd be paying close to $100 extra for power you'll never touch. The KitchenAid handles that workload without breaking a sweat, for less money, and you won't be keeping a can of WD-40 next to it.

Would I buy it again after these eight months? Yes — tomorrow, squeaky lever and all. But I make bread for a living, and that's exactly who this machine is for.

b.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: 8 Months In, Used Almost Daily for Market Sourdough

I bought the Corlane SM6 in February and have put it through roughly 240 bakes since. Most of those are sourdough loaves and bagels for my Saturday farmers market stall, with the occasional batch of sandwich bread or brioche thrown in on slower weeks. Here's the honest rundown.

## What it does well

The motor is the star of the show. Corlane rates it at 500W, but the spec sheet is less important than what it actually does in the bowl, which is chew through a double batch of stiff bagel dough (about 1,500g flour total) without slowing down, walking across the counter, or triggering the thermal cutoff. My old 4.5-quart KitchenAid would have tap-danced itself off the edge of the island on that load. The SM6 weighs about 28 pounds and sits flat. I never lock it to the counter, and it has not moved once.

It also handles wet doughs cleanly. Hydration levels above 80% get scraped down once at the four-minute mark and that's it. The 6-quart bowl is genuinely useful for anyone scaling up beyond home portions, and the head tilts back far enough that I can get a full hand in to scrape without removing the bowl.

## What's annoying

Two real issues, both fixable but worth knowing before you buy.

**The bowl-lift lever squeaks.** It's a metal-on-metal contact point and it started chirping around month three. A shot of WD-40 on the pivot clears it for about four weeks, then it comes back. It's a 30-second job, but it's the kind of thing that shouldn't be a recurring maintenance item on a $429 machine.

**The included dough hook is too short for the deep bowl.** It clears the bottom fine, but the gap between the hook and the sides of the bowl means unmixed flour collects in the corners on stiff doughs. I had to buy a third-party spiral hook (a $22 replacement from a small-batch maker on Etsy) and the difference was immediate. The stock hook is fine for cake batter. For real bread work, plan to swap it.

## Corlane SM6 vs. KitchenAid

If you're cross-shopping the SM6 against something like the KitchenAid 6-Quart Pro 600, the comparison is straightforward:

- **Power and torque:** The Corlane wins, and it's not close. This is the only category that actually matters for heavy dough.
- **Build and finish:** KitchenAid still has the edge on fit and finish. The Corlane is mostly metal, but the knobs and switches feel a step below.
- **Attachments and ecosystem:** KitchenAid wins by a mile. If you care about pasta rollers, meat grinders, and the full attachment universe, KitchenAid's catalog is bigger and more proven.
- **Price:** The equivalent KitchenAid runs about $349 on sale, so you're paying roughly $80 more for the Corlane. That premium is buying you a better motor and bowl-lift design, not better aesthetics.

## Final verdict

**Buy the Corlane SM6 if** you knead stiff or heavy dough more than once a week and your old stand mixer has ever let you down mid-batch. The motor is genuinely best-in-class at this price, and for serious bread bakers it earns its premium.

**Skip the Corlane SM6 if** you're mostly making cookies, cakes, and the occasional loaf. You'll pay $80 extra for capability you'll never use, and you'll be annoyed by the squeaky lever. A KitchenAid Artisan will handle that workload for less money, and the accessory ecosystem is worth real money if you bake beyond bread.

For me, the SM6 is a clear yes. Eight months in, it has not flinched at anything I've thrown at it, and the two complaints I have are both $25 fixes. If you sell bread or bake for a family of gluten enthusiasts, you'll get your money out of it in the first year.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
Dear Members of the City Council,

My name is [Name], and I own a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am writing in opposition to the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents per hour to $1.50 per hour.

This proposal would triple the cost of parking downtown. For many people, that may sound like a small difference—an additional dollar—but for a downtown business district that depends on frequent, short visits, price changes like this affect customer behavior quickly.

I have seen this firsthand. In 2019, when a nearby town implemented a similar parking-rate increase, I tracked my own register and customer traffic for six weeks afterward. During that period, foot traffic dropped by 18 percent. An 18 percent decline is not an abstract concern for a small business. It means fewer coffees sold, fewer breakfast orders, fewer customers browsing neighboring stores, and less activity on the sidewalk throughout the day.

My customers do not generally occupy parking spaces for hours. Based on my own observations and customer patterns, the average visit to my shop is approximately 22 minutes. The current one-hour minimum already gives customers far more time than they typically need to park, order, meet someone briefly, or take a drink to go. Raising the hourly rate from 50 cents to $1.50 does not encourage better turnover for these customers; it simply triples the price they pay for a short visit.

For a customer stopping in for 22 minutes, the effective cost of parking would become $1.50 under the proposed minimum, rather than 50 cents today. That is a significant added cost alongside a cup of coffee or a small breakfast purchase. It gives customers one more reason to choose a drive-through, a shopping center with free parking, or a business outside downtown.

I also ask the Council to consider the city’s own financial analysis. According to the city report, meter revenue covers only 4 percent of the downtown budget. Even if meter revenue increased, this proposal would not solve the larger budget challenge. What it could do, however, is place a disproportionate burden on the independent businesses that make downtown worth visiting in the first place.

Downtown is not sustained by parking meters alone. It is sustained by repeat customers, employees, residents, visitors, and small business owners who depend on accessible and reasonably priced parking. A policy that results in fewer short visits risks reducing sales-tax activity, weakening storefronts, and making the district less competitive with areas where parking is free.

I respectfully urge the Council not to approve a tripling of meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour. The evidence from my own six-week tracking period after a similar increase in 2019—a drop of 18 percent in foot traffic—shows the potential effect on customer activity. With an average customer visit of only 22 minutes and meter revenue accounting for just 4 percent of the downtown budget, this increase asks too much of downtown customers and small businesses while doing too little to address the city’s financial needs.

Thank you for your consideration.

b.text:
**Testimony Regarding the Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Members of the Council, thank you for the opportunity to speak. I own a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am here to oppose raising meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour. I want to give you numbers rather than general worries.

First, consider what this increase is. Going from 50 cents to $1.50 is a 200 percent increase. It triples the price of parking in a single step.

I know what that can do because I have seen it. In 2019, the town next to ours raised its meter rates in a similar way. I tracked my own register for six weeks afterward, and foot traffic dropped 18 percent. In a business like mine, which runs on small purchases and repeat visits, an 18 percent drop in customers is the difference between a healthy month and a month of hard decisions. I am not offering a prediction or a feeling. I am offering what I recorded.

Second, the current system already works for businesses like mine. My customers stay an average of 22 minutes. They park, buy a coffee, maybe chat with a neighbor, and go. The one-hour minimum at 50 cents more than covers that visit, and the turnover is what you want downtown: a space opens, a customer comes in, the space opens again. Under the proposal, that same 22-minute visit goes from 50 cents to $1.50. Customers would pay a dollar more to use about a third of the time they are charged for. For a quick stop, that is a real reason to go somewhere with free parking instead.

Third, the city's own report shows that this increase will not accomplish what it is meant to. Meter revenue covers only 4 percent of the downtown budget. Even in the best case, where tripling the rate somehow cost us not a single customer, that share would rise to roughly 12 percent. The other 88 percent of the budget would still have to come from somewhere else. And the best case is not realistic. If the 18 percent drop I saw next door repeats here, fewer people will park, fewer will shop, and the revenue gain will be smaller than projected. Meanwhile, the sales and business activity that support the downtown would shrink.

So the trade looks like this. The city takes a small and uncertain gain in meter revenue, while downtown businesses risk a drop in customers of nearly one in five. Shops that lose that much business cut hours, cut staff, or close. A vacant storefront on Main Street costs the city far more than the meters will ever bring in.

I am not asking the Council to ignore its budget problems. I am asking you not to treat a change that covers 4 percent of the budget as the answer to them. If the city needs more revenue from parking, I would urge a smaller, phased adjustment, paired with a review of its effect on downtown sales before any further steps. I would gladly share my register records with any member who wants to see them.

The businesses on Main Street are your neighbors, and we want downtown to thrive. Please vote no on this increase.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Respectfully submitted,

[Your name]
Owner, [Coffee shop name]
[Address], Main Street

b.text:
To the Editor:

I carried mail on Route 4 for 22 years. I know this county the way you know a road you've driven every day, the farms, the hills, who's expecting a package and who's been waiting on a check. So when the Postal Service says our branch loses $40,000 a year and needs to close its counter service, I want to answer that.

Before the cuts, the counter was open from 8 to 5. Then the hours were cut to 8 to noon. Once people couldn't count on being able to get in after work or on their lunch break, fewer of them came in. Now the Postal Service points to the drop in business as proof the branch isn't worth keeping. That's a problem they made for themselves, and then they're using it as the reason to close.

Think about Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She's in her eighties and gets her heart medication through the mail. If the counter closes, she's looking at a twenty-minute drive to Fairview for a money order or a package pickup, and she can't make that drive on her own anymore. setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
I've sat through roughly 200 interviews over the last few years, and there's a pattern I can't unsee.

The strongest candidates don't ask about career progression. They don't ask about "culture." They ask what failed recently.

Specifically: "Tell me about the last project that didn't go the way you expected."

Here's what happened a few months ago. A candidate we were interviewing for an ops coordinator role asked me this about 25 minutes in. I paused because honestly, most people just want to talk about the role and get out. I told them about a warehouse routing rollout we did last spring that was supposed to cut loading times by 15%. Took three months to implement. Net result was maybe 4%, and that was generous. The vendor setup didn't account for how our drivers actually behaved during peak, and we over-customized the config to the point where nobody wanted to touch it after launch.

This candidate nodded, asked two follow-ups. "Who owned the post-mortem?" and "Did the drivers get a say in the config before launch?" That was it. Didn't lecture me about what we should have done. Didn't try to pitch themselves as the person who would have done it better.

But those two questions told me more about how they think than any behavioral question I had on my list. They understood that failure has an ownership question and a process question, and they're separate things.

We hired them. They're doing well.

The thing I keep thinking about is that most candidates treat the Q&A at the end like a courtesy round. The ones who don't are almost always the ones we end up wanting.

b.text:
I've sat in on roughly 200 interviews over 9 years. The candidates who impress me most almost always ask some version of the same question.

"What was the last project here that failed?"

Not "what's the culture like." Not "what does success look like in this role." They want the failure story.

Had one a few months ago. Senior ops candidate, second round, going well. She asks: "What's the last initiative that didn't work here — and what happened to the people who ran it?"

That second half. That's the actual question.

I told her about a route optimization tool we rolled out two years back. Big vendor, big promises. Dispatchers hated it, adoption collapsed within a few months, and we quietly went back to the old process.

She didn't nod and move on. She asked: "Whose idea was it, and where is that person now?"

Honest answer: the director who championed it is still here. He ran the post-mortem himself. One thing that came out of it — dispatchers now sit in on every pilot before we buy anything — is standard practice.

She told me that was the answer she'd been hoping for. Her last employer had a failed rollout and pinned it on one analyst, who was gone within a month. She left shortly after.

That's what I've figured out about this question: candidates aren't testing whether you fail. Everyone fails. They're testing what failure costs the person attached to it.

If you're interviewing somewhere, ask it. Pay attention to whether the interviewer hesitates, and whether the failure story has a villain.

And if you're on my side of the table: the quality of your answer tells them more about working here than anything on the careers page. If your honest answer ends with "and we fired them," expect the best candidates to politely finish the process and take another offer.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years in real estate, I’ve noticed that buyers who walk a neighborhood around 7 a.m. before a showing are often much happier with the house later.

The Pruitts did this before we toured a home on Sycamore Street. They wanted to know what the neighborhood felt like during an ordinary weekday—not just when the house was staged, the lights were on, and I was standing there with a key.

That morning walk gave them a better sense of the street’s rhythm: who was heading to work, how much traffic came through, where people walked their dogs, and whether they could picture starting their own day there. By the time we toured the house, they weren’t only evaluating the kitchen and bedrooms. They already understood what it might feel like to live there.

They bought the house, and later told me that walk was one of the reasons they felt so confident about the decision.

A showing tells you a lot about a property. An early walk tells you something about the life around it—and that’s usually harder to change.

b.text:
Something I've noticed after 12 years of selling homes: the buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7am before we ever tour the house end up noticeably happier with it later. Not because the neighborhood is better at 7am — because by tour time, they actually know it.

The Pruitts on Sycamore Street are the example I keep coming back to. They found the listing on a Tuesday — cute bungalow, big maple out front, priced right for the street. From the first email I could tell they were already emotionally in the living room. With first-time buyers, that's usually when I say the same thing I've said for a decade: come walk the block at 7am before we meet for the showing.

They thought it was a little odd. Most people do. But they showed up anyway, coffee in hand, and did the loop while I unlocked the door.

In twenty-five minutes they got things no showing could have given them. They met the guy two doors down who's been walking his beagle at seven every morning for twenty years. They watched the school bus come through at 7:10, which mattered to them more than they expected with a kid starting kindergarten that fall. They learned which neighbors wave, felt how the morning sun actually hits that porch, caught the smell of somebody's woodstove two houses over.

They bought the house. And when the school bus started up in September, when a neighbor's leaf blower went off on a Saturday, none of it was a surprise. In a real sense, they'd already lived there before closing day.

They told me later that the 7am walk did more for their confidence than anything I said in three weeks of negotiating. I believe it. I can talk comps and inspection reports all day. I can't tell anyone what a street feels like when they're standing on it.

If you're house hunting right now, tour the neighborhood before you tour the house. Early, when people are actually out living in it. The house you can fix. The street, you're buying as-is.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
Tweet 1:  
Demo on the Maple Ave kitchen job turned up this joist running perpendicular to the span. 15 years in the trade and I still see stuff like this—undersized lumber, original to the house, now supporting a modern remodel.

Tweet 2:  
Cost to fix: $850 in LVL/lumber + 6 hours of sistering and blocking. In a kitchen reno, that’s not just a material hit—it’s a schedule bump. The original frame was built to 1950s minimums, not today’s live-load standards.

Tweet 3:  
Lesson: Never assume the existing framing meets current code. Before you close up a ceiling, verify joist size, species, and spacing. If you’re sistering, match the original spec exactly—or upgrade the whole run. Callbacks over hidden cuts aren’t worth the save.

b.text:
1/4 On the Maple Ave kitchen, demo exposed a floor joist that had been cut nearly through for an old plumbing run. From above, the floor only showed a slight dip. Once the ceiling was open, the problem was obvious.

2/4 We stopped work, brought in the engineer, rerouted the plumbing, and repaired the framing to his detail. Added cost: about $3,200 between engineering, labor, materials, and the plumber coming back.

3/4 That wasn’t a “contractor markup surprise.” It was concealed damage that couldn’t be confirmed before demolition. We documented it, priced it separately, and got approval before proceeding.

4/4 The lesson isn’t just that old houses hide problems. A solid remodel needs a contingency, clear change-order terms, and enough schedule flexibility to fix what’s behind the walls instead of covering it back up.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
The state should not cut apprenticeship funding by 15%.

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW, and I see what this funding does every day. It gives people a real path into a good job without crushing them with student debt. It also helps local contractors and the whole economy by creating skilled workers who are ready to work.

My own cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one finished and are now working journeyman jobs. That is a strong return on the state’s investment. These are not people who got trained and then sat on the sidelines. They are working, paying taxes, and building things this state needs.

The numbers speak for themselves. Apprentices start around $19 an hour. By the time they finish, they can top out around $46 an hour as journeymen. That means they move off assistance programs fast and become taxpaying workers instead of staying dependent on public aid.

The cost is also much lower than people might think. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to something like $48,000 in average public subsidy per four-year college graduate who finishes. If the state wants to spend money wisely, apprenticeship is one of the best deals out there.

A cut to apprenticeship funding would hurt working people, hurt contractors, and hurt the state’s future workforce. It would also make it harder for young people and adults trying to build a better life with their hands and their heads.

We should be growing apprenticeship programs, not cutting them. Keep the funding in place and keep investing in a system that works.

b.text:
**Don’t Cut a Program That Works**

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with the IBEW. I’m not writing this as somebody who’s against education. I’m writing this because I’m in the middle of a system that works, and the state is talking about cutting it.

The proposed 15% cut to state apprenticeship funding is a bad move. It’s bad for apprentices, bad for workers, bad for taxpayers, and bad for the future of the skilled trades.

Let me keep this simple: apprenticeship works. I’ve seen it work.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished, and those 21 are working journeyman jobs now. That’s not a small number. That’s a success rate most programs would be proud of. We didn’t just sit in a classroom and collect debt. We showed up, worked, learned, got paid, and became skilled workers.

That’s the difference with apprenticeship. From day one, apprentices start around $19 an hour. By the time they become journeymen, they can top out around $46 an hour. That means people are getting on their feet fast. They’re paying rent. They’re buying groceries. They’re paying taxes. They’re getting off public assistance programs instead of staying on them.

That matters. A lot.

When somebody starts an apprenticeship, they’re not waiting four years to begin earning a paycheck. They’re earning while they’re learning. That means less student debt, less financial stress, and a faster path to a stable life. For a lot of people, that path is the only reason they were able to build a career at all.

Now look at the cost to the public.

The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to something like $48,000 in average public subsidy for a four-year college graduate who finishes. That’s a huge difference. Apprenticeship is training workers at a fraction of the cost, while still producing highly skilled people who fill jobs the state actually needs.

So why would we cut a program that gives this kind of return?

A 15% cut might sound small to somebody sitting in an office. But in real life, cuts like this mean less support for training. They can mean fewer classes, fewer instructors, fewer resources, and fewer opportunities for the next group of apprentices. If the state cuts funding, it doesn’t make apprenticeship go away overnight. It just makes it harder. And when you make something harder, you lose people.

That would be a mistake.

We need more electricians, not fewer. We need more skilled workers, not less. Every year, more journeymen retire. Every year, more work comes in—construction, maintenance, infrastructure, energy projects, upgrades, repairs. The demand is real. If we want trained, licensed, safe electricians doing that work, then we need to keep investing in the system that produces them.

This isn’t a handout. Apprentices put in the work. Contractors put in the work. The union puts in the work. The state’s role is to support a training model that already proves itself. Cutting funding now would slow down a pipeline that is already delivering results.

To state legislators: if you’re looking for a smart use of public money, this is it. You’re not throwing money at a program that sounds good on paper. You’re supporting a proven path from training to employment. You’re helping people become taxpayers instead of dependents. You’re helping build a skilled workforce that keeps communities safe and functioning.

And to my fellow union members: this is why we need to speak up. This program changed our lives, and it can change more lives after us. But only if we defend it.

I’m a third-year apprentice. I’m not finished yet. But I’ve seen enough to know what this system does. It takes people who are willing to work and turns them into professionals. It gives people a fair shot. It builds careers, families, and futures.

A 15% cut to apprenticeship funding isn’t savings. It’s short-sighted. It weakens one of the best workforce programs we have.

The state should not cut it. The state should protect it.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
**A little news about wedding cakes**

I've been turning this over for a few months, and I'd rather you hear it from me than from the chalkboard, so here it is: we're not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore. If you're already on our calendar, you're happening — we don't leave anyone at the altar. But we won't be booking new ones.

I want to explain, because I'd hate for anyone to think we didn't love doing them. We did. Some of my favorite memories of this shop are wedding ones — carrying a three-tier cake out to somebody's car at six in the morning with my heart in my throat, getting the photos back a week later and seeing it standing next to a bride's grandmother's ring. It's been an honor, every single time. That part is true and I want it on the record.

But here's what I finally sat down and did one night, after avoiding it for ages: I added up the hours. By the time a couple actually books a cake, we've usually put around fourteen hours into it already. The tasting, the second tasting, the sketch, the emails about whether the ribbon should be blush or dusty rose, the follow-up about Aunt Carol's gluten situation. Fourteen hours before anyone pays a cent. For a shop with three people in it, that's not a side task — that's nearly two full days of one of us at a laptop instead of at the bench. And those hours came from somewhere. Mostly they came out of the morning bake, which is to say, out of the thing you come in for.

Then this year we had three cancellations, late enough in the game that the ingredients were already bought. Nobody did anything wrong — life happens, plans change, and honestly I'd rather eat the cost of flour and butter than have anyone feel locked into a cake they don't need. But we're small, and three of those in one year is something we feel.

Here's the bottom line, and it's less dramatic than all of that: the thing that pays our rent is the case. The case at seven in the morning, the Saturday regulars, the person who calls at eleven to ask if there's anything left, and there is, because we made extra. Weddings were beautiful, but every one pulled us away from that daily work, and the daily work is the whole reason we opened. So we're going back

b.text:
It’s just past two in the afternoon, the ovens are finally cool, and I’m sitting at the back prep table with a cup of coffee that I’ve reheated twice, trying to put words to something we’ve been turning over in our heads for months. 

Starting next season, we are stepping away from custom wedding cakes. 

If you’ve followed us for a while, you know how much love we’ve poured into those tiers over the years. Getting to be a tiny, sweet part of someone’s biggest day is genuinely an honor, and saying that out loud makes this feel like a hard decision. But the truth is, when you peel back the romance of it, our kitchen is just three pairs of hands. 

Lately, the math and the hours just haven't been working. Between the initial emails, the sketches, the sit-down consultations, and the tasting boxes, each custom wedding order eats up roughly fourteen hours of work before we even crack an egg for the actual tier. For a big studio with an office manager, that’s just standard business. For the three of us, it means answering emails until midnight after being on our feet since 4 a.m. 

This year was also particularly tough on our margins. We had three different couples have to cancel at the eleventh hour. We completely understand that life happens, but in a shop this small, absorbing the cost of all those specialty ingredients and holds on our calendar leaves a mark that’s really hard to shake off. 

More than anything, though, we realized wedding cakes were pulling us away from the heart of this bakery: the front case. The morning scones, the flaky hand pies, the sourdough, the little six-inch birthday cakes you grab on a whim for a coworker—that’s what actually pays our rent every month. It’s also where we get to see your faces on an ordinary Tuesday. We were spending so much energy stressing over sugar flowers and dowel rods that we were running on fumes for the people who walk through our door every single day.

We’re not giving up on celebrations entirely. We’re still going to bake our standard menu cakes, and if you want to order a couple of rustic nine-inch rounds from our regular list for a backyard reception, we will happily box them up for you. But as far as the bespoke, multi-tiered, delivery-and-setup wedding circuit goes, we are hanging up our aprons. 

Thank you so much to every couple who trusted us with their reception over the years. We loved it, truly. But right now, we need to protect our sleep, our sanity, and the daily pastries that make this little shop what it is. 

I’m heading home to put my feet up for a few hours. I’ll see you at the counter tomorrow morning—there will be warm cinnamon buns waiting.

setup: A co-founder is posting a LinkedIn hiring announcement for a first customer support hire to potential applicants and customers.

a.text:
We’re hiring Ridgepoint’s first dedicated support person.

We’re a three-person SaaS team that helps small trucking dispatchers schedule loads. Right now, “support” means the three of us founders answering tickets whenever we’re not building or selling. It’s falling apart. Dispatchers need help in real time, and we’re slowing them down.

So here’s the actual job, not the culture-pitch version.

Day to day, you will:

- Own the shared support inbox. Start by triaging what’s urgent. “I can’t schedule this load” is an emergency. “How do I reset my password” can wait.
- Help small trucking dispatchers solve real scheduling problems: assigning a load, moving a load, fixing a double-booked truck, figuring out why a load vanished, getting the right info to a driver.
- Answer in plain English. No scripts. Our customers are busy and often not technical. Your job is to make the product feel simple even when it isn’t.
- Reproduce issues and write them up clearly so the three of us can fix them. “It’s broken” isn’t a bug report. You’ll turn customer pain into steps we can act on.
- Follow up until the problem is actually solved, not just closed.
- Notice patterns. If the same confusion shows up 20 times, you’ll help turn it into a help article, a better tooltip, or a product change.
- Improve our help docs as you go, so tomorrow’s dispatcher doesn’t have to ask the same question.
- Tell us the hard stuff directly. You’ll work with the three of us every day. When a customer is stuck or a workflow is bad, you say so.

What this job is not:

- It’s not sales, and it’s not a “rockstar/ninja” role.
- It’s not about hitting a ticket-closing quota. It’s about getting dispatchers unstuck so they can run loads.
- It’s not always glamorous. Some days are repetitive. Some days are firefighting.

You don’t need trucking experience, but you do need to learn our customers’ world fast. Dispatchers work on tight timelines, so being available when they’re actually dispatching matters.

If you like figuring out why something broke, explaining it clearly, and being the person a small business relies on when the day is going sideways, DM me. Skip the cover letter—just tell me about a time you fixed a messy problem and made it make sense.

b.text:
We’re hiring our first support person at Ridgepoint. Not because we planned to—because the three of us handling every ticket ourselves is no longer sustainable.

Here’s what the job actually looks like day to day:

You’ll be the first line for small trucking dispatchers who use our tool to schedule loads and keep their business running. When something’s buggy or confusing, they’ll message you. Some are patient, some are losing money and stressed. Some barely use email. Your job is to figure out what’s really wrong, walk them through a fix if you can, or tag the right founder before the issue snowballs. Fast.

You’ll spend hours in our support queue, writing answers, updating our (very bare) help docs, and spotting patterns so we can push out real fixes. You’ll also be the internal voice of our users, telling the three of us plainly what’s broken, what’s poorly designed, and what dispatchers *actually* need—not what we assumed.

We’re a three-person team. That means you’ll sit close to the people who built the product (literally or via Slack). There’s no scripted playbook because we haven’t had time to make one. You’ll help build it. You’ll learn the product inside out because you’ll be the one explaining it every day.

This isn’t a “culture first” post. It’s a decent, honest job where you’ll get yelled at occasionally, solve a lot of puzzles, and directly affect whether we make it or not. Pay is real, equity is on the table, and you’ll have a ton of ownership.

If reading this gave you a weird sense of “that actually sounds like my kind of chaos,” DM me or check the link in the comments. Tag someone who’d thrive here.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
The cereal aisle at the store had maybe twelve kinds when I left. When I got back there were forty. I stood in front of the shelf for twenty minutes. Honey Nut Cheerios. Frosted Flakes. Something with clusters. I couldn't decide. My hand kept moving to grab one, then stopping. I ended up with the plain corn flakes because they were in the back and I just wanted to get out of there.

At the airport, my daughter was six. She was hiding behind her mother's leg. She didn't look at me. I knelt down and said her name. She peeked around my wife's jeans and then went back behind them. I stood up. I didn't know what to do with my hands so I put them in my pockets. It took her three days to let me carry her to bed.

At night I slept facing the door. I'd done that for a year in Afghanistan, sleeping with my head toward the entrance so I could see anyone coming. At home, I kept doing it. My wife would come in and I'd be staring at the closed door, listening for footsteps in the hall. One night she opened the door to check on me and I woke up with my hand near my hip, reaching for something that wasn't there. After that I started leaving the door open. It took a while to stop turning my head toward it. I'd wake up and my neck would be sore from facing the wrong way.

b.text:
**The Door Open**

When I came home from my second deployment, I thought the hard part would be getting used to being around people again. I didn’t expect the cereal aisle to stop me.

I stood there for close to twenty minutes, looking at the boxes. There were maybe forty kinds of cereal. Different shapes, colors, marshmallows, whole grains. I needed to pick one. I kept reading the boxes and putting them back.

At the airport, my daughter was six. I saw her and went toward her, but she moved behind her mother’s leg. She looked out at me from there, not sure who I was. Then her mother said something to her, and she came over. I picked her up. She was heavier than I remembered.

At home, I started sleeping on my side of the bed. For a year I had slept facing the door. It was what I did without thinking. The bedroom door was open, and I could see the hall. At first, I kept waking up in that position.

I tried turning away from the door. I would lie there and listen to the house. Then I would turn back, facing the hallway, and fall asleep.

It took time to leave the door open without checking it. Some nights I slept through. Other nights I woke and looked down the hall before I remembered where I was.

I still don’t know how long I stood in the cereal aisle that day. I remember moving a box from one hand to the other, then putting it back. Eventually I picked one and went to the checkout.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
# Why I Actually Prefer Shooting Winter Weddings Now

If you asked me six years ago when I first started shooting around the metro area, I probably would have told you that June was the undisputed king of wedding dates. Everyone wants the lush greenery and the long summer days. 

But after shooting 11 winter weddings over the last two years, my mind has completely changed. I’m just going to be honest: I actually look forward to the colder months now. 

If you’re currently trying to pick a date and feeling pressure to book a peak summer Saturday, here is why an off-season wedding might actually get you better photos and a much better experience.

### 1. The light is genuinely better.
People assume summer equals great photo lighting, but June weather here is notoriously tricky. You often end up with either brutal, direct sun or flat, washed-out overcast skies. Winter light is a completely different story. 

Around 3:00 PM in November, the sun sits low on the horizon, filtering straight through bare trees. That golden, low-angle light creates a depth and warmth for portraits that high June light just can’t replicate. You don't get harsh under-eye shadows or people squinting through heat sweat—you just get clean, rich, textured light that makes portraits look high-end without trying too hard.

### 2. You’re not sharing the venue (or the parking lot).
Peak summer Saturdays at popular local venues can feel like an assembly line. I’ve shot June weddings where I was sharing a parking lot with three or four other vendor trucks, dodging another photography crew on the opposite side of the lawn, and trying to frame shots so random guests from the venue's *other* event weren't in the background. 

In the winter, the venue is entirely yours. The parking lot is quiet, the staff isn't stretched thin from three back-to-back 14-hour days, and the whole energy of the day is relaxed and focused entirely on you.

### 3. Your budget stretches about 30% further.
Beyond the aesthetic and logistical perks, the numbers just make sense. Booking in the off-season typically saves couples around 30% on venue fees and vendor packages compared to peak fall or summer dates. That is real money you can put toward a dream band, an upgraded bar package, or just keep in your pocket for the honeymoon.

Summer gets all the advertising space, but if you want incredible light, a stress-free timeline, and a lot more room in your budget, don't sleep on a late fall or winter date.

b.text:
# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings

*Or: a confession from a photographer who spent years dreading them.*

For my first few years shooting weddings in this city, winter inquiries felt like a calendar problem. I said yes because January needed filling, not because I wanted the job. Somewhere along the way, that flipped. I've shot eleven winter weddings in the last two years, and they're now the bookings I look forward to most. Since a lot of couples asking me "when should we book?" are really asking "when is the best wedding," let me make the case for the season nobody plans for.

## The light. I'm serious about this one.

In November, around 3 p.m., the sun is already low. It comes in sideways through the bare branches, and those leafless trees break it into shafts and patterns that no lighting kit I own can replicate. There's direction to it. It gives a face shape.

Here's the part that might get me in trouble: that light is better for portraits than what we often get in June. Flat overcast June light is like a giant ceiling fixture — even, forgiving, and forgettable. Everyone is lit identically from every angle, which sounds kind and is actually the problem. Portraits need light with an angle and an opinion, and bare-tree light at 3 p.m. in November has both.

And because the sun sets early, your best-light portraits happen mid-afternoon — when your makeup is fresh and you've still got energy — instead of at 7:30 p.m., after you've been on your feet for eight hours and the schedule has already slipped twice.

## Nobody is fighting over your Saturday.

In June, I pull into a venue lot and there are regularly three or four other vendors there — another photographer's van, a videographer, a florist's delivery, all of us on overlapping timelines.

You feel that even if you never see the parking lot. It's why the getting-ready suite has a stranger's garment bag in it. It's why the coordinator is impossible to find, why the room flip starts while your grandmother is still sitting in it, why everyone is rushing. In January, the venue is yours. My timeline holds. The staff isn't stretched thin, so they're not rushing you either.

I know "the parking lot was roomy" sounds like a photographer convenience. It isn't. Calm is the thing I need most on a wedding day, and winter days have it.

## The part you already guessed: it's cheaper.

Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for couples than peak-season dates. That's not a gimmick — it's how the industry prices the slow months, and it adds up fast. That difference is your videographer, or a real chunk of your venue, or the honeymoon.

But I want to be honest about the other side of it, because I've had couples seem almost apologetic about booking a discounted date: I'm not shooting eleven of these a year out of charity. The discount exists because demand is lower. I keep saying yes anyway because these have become my favorite weddings to shoot — the calm, the light, the day that actually runs on schedule. You're not getting a lesser wedding at a lower price. You're getting the same wedding at the time of year fewer people want it.

## Yes, it's cold. Plan for it, don't fear it.

I won't pretend otherwise. We plan around it: portraits in twenty-minute bursts with a warm room to retreat to, and a timeline that puts the outdoor portraits in that good light instead of after dark. And coat shots are not a compromise — a great coat is a better portrait prop than a shawl pretending it isn't freezing. The short day is a constraint, but it's the kind that makes the timeline better, not worse.

## If you're flexible on your date

Ask me about winter. After six years shooting in this area, I know exactly which spots near you hold that low November light at 3 p.m. — and my winter calendar has room in it.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**They Ran It Right Up Until They Didn't**

I've had a week to sit with it, which is about six days longer than I usually need to figure out how I feel about a football game. And I still land in the same place.

We didn't get beat Friday night. We talked ourselves out of it.

Let's start where we should start: 8-2, a second-round playoff appearance, and a quarterback who threw for 2,340 yards, which is more than anybody has ever thrown for at this school. Dez Kowalski has been a joy to watch and a joy to have on the air — funny kid, honest kid, never once gave me a canned answer when a canned answer would've been easier. That record is his and nobody can take it. Twenty years from now somebody's going to look that number up and wonder who he was.

But I'm not writing a valentine this week. That's what the banquet's for.

Here's what happened. We were down three at halftime to a team we beat by twenty in Week 3 — same team, same personnel, no great mystery to them. And we had been running the ball down their throat. Not flashy, not pretty, just four and five yards a crack and a defense that was starting to stand up a half-second slower each time. Anybody in that stadium with a pulse could see it working.

Then we came out in the third quarter and threw it.

And threw it. And threw it.

I understand the instinct. You're behind, the clock feels like it's moving faster than it is, and you've got a record-setting arm standing back there. Throwing the ball feels like *doing something*. Handing it off on second-and-six feels like waiting.

But you weren't behind. You were down three. Three points is not a deficit, it's a rounding error. Three points is one drive that you were already perfectly capable of putting together the boring way. Down three with a run game that's grinding is the single best position a high school offense can be in, and we treated it like we were down seventeen with four minutes left.

What it did — and this is the part that actually cost us — is it let their defensive line stop thinking. When you're running it, those kids have to be honest. They have to read, they have to hold their gap, they have to worry. The second we went one-dimensional, they got to pin their ears back and come. Dez spent the entire second half getting hit, and he still nearly brought us back, which tells you everything about the kid and not much good about the plan.

I'm not calling for anybody's job. That's lazy radio and it's lazier column-writing, and frankly this staff has built something here that didn't exist six years ago. Eight and two doesn't happen by accident, and I've watched enough bad football in this town to know the difference.

But I do think there's a real lesson sitting there for next fall, and it's not complicated: trust what's working longer than feels comfortable. The run game is boring. It's supposed to be boring. Boring is the point. You don't abandon four yards a carry because four yards a carry doesn't feel dramatic enough for the playoffs.

We had the better team Friday. We'd already proven that in September. We just decided, somewhere in that locker room at halftime, to play a different game than the one we were winning.

Seniors, thank you. Genuinely. You gave this town a fall worth talking about, and I got to talk about it five mornings a week, which is a pretty good gig.

Everybody else — see you in August. Bring the running backs.

b.text: They had a shot at state, but the season ended in round two against a team they’d already beaten by twenty in week three. The loss stings because, in the second half, the run game that had been working all night was abandoned—even though the team was only down three. That’s where it died. You don’t ditch what’s working when the margin’s that small. Dez Kowalski threw for twenty-three forty, a new school record, but you can’t hang stats on the wall when the play-calling gets cute. The season didn’t end because of a lack of talent; it ended because we stopped running the ball when we should’ve kept driving it.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
My daughter was six when I came home from my second deployment. At the airport, she hid behind her mother’s leg.

I had pictured that part differently. I figured she would run at me and I would pick her up. I had thought about whether she’d be too big now to carry with one arm.

Instead, she held on to her mother’s pants and watched me.

“Go ahead,” her mother said. “It’s Dad.”

I stopped a few feet away. I still had my bag over my shoulder. People were moving around us, pulling suitcases, trying to get past.

“Hey, kiddo.”

She leaned out a little. Her hair was longer than when I’d left. There was a tooth missing in front that I knew about from a picture, but it was different seeing the space when she opened her mouth.

I put my bag down and got on one knee. I didn’t know what else to do.

After a minute she came over. She let me hug her, though she kept one hand reaching back toward her mother. I held her carefully. I wanted to hold her tight.

On the way to the car, she asked if I was coming to our house.

I said I was.

“For dinner?”

“For dinner, too.”

She seemed satisfied with that. She walked between us in the parking garage.

A few days later, I went to the grocery store. I said I would go because we needed milk and a few other things, and I wanted to do something useful that didn’t require anybody asking how I was doing.

I got through most of the list. Then I went down the cereal aisle.

There must have been forty kinds. Probably more. Different sizes of the same box. Regular, whole grain, less sugar. Cereal with marshmallows and cereal that looked like something you’d put in a bird feeder. I stood there with one hand on the cart.

I picked up a box, read the front, and put it back.

It wasn’t that I’d forgotten how a grocery store worked. I knew I could buy any one of them. If nobody liked it, we could get something else next time. There was no consequence worth mentioning.

I still couldn’t pick.

A woman said, “Excuse me,” and I moved my cart so she could reach past me. She took a box without stopping to look at it. I watched her go around the end of the aisle.

I checked my phone. I had been standing there close to twenty minutes.

I finally bought the kind I remembered eating before I left. At home, my daughter told me she didn’t like that kind anymore.

“All right,” I said.

She got a marker and added something to the grocery list on the refrigerator. She had to sound out part of it. I stood behind her while she wrote.

At night, I slept facing the bedroom door.

I’d done that for a year. Before I got into bed, I checked where my clothes were and made sure there was nothing on the floor between me and the door. I didn’t give it much thought until my wife asked why I kept moving her slippers.

I told her I didn’t want to trip over them.

She put them on her side.

The door was another thing. Before I left, we kept it open. Our daughter’s room was down the hall, and we wanted to hear her if she called. When I came back, I shut it the first night without asking.

My wife opened it when she came to bed.

I got up later and shut it again.

In the morning she said, “She needs to be able to come in.”

I knew that. I had been the one who used to get up with her when she was little. I knew where the hall light switch was and which board outside her room creaked. But at night I lay there looking at the open doorway, waiting to see something in it.

I tried leaving it open a few inches. Then halfway.

Some nights I got up to use the bathroom and closed it on my way back without noticing. My wife would open it again. We didn’t have an argument about it. Sometimes I wished we would, so I could explain myself once and be done with it. I didn’t have much of an explanation, though.

One night my daughter came down the hall carrying her pillow. I heard her before she reached us.

“Dad?”

“Yeah.”

“I had a bad dream.”

I moved over. She climbed in beside me, bringing most of her blanket with her. Her feet were cold. She pushed them against my leg and went back to sleep.

I lay on my side facing the doorway. The hall light was on. Her pillow was taking up half of mine.

After a while, I pulled the blanket over her feet.

b.text:
I came home from my second deployment in the summer. My wife, Sarah, picked me up at the airport with our daughter, Emily. Emily was six.

I saw them standing there near the baggage claim. I dropped my duffel bag and knelt down to say hi to Emily. She just looked at me. Then she stepped back and hid behind Sarah’s leg, holding onto her jeans. She didn’t recognize me. I had a beard, and I guess I looked different. It took her a few minutes to peek out and figure out who I actually was. That was the welcome home.

A few days later, I went to the commissary to do some shopping. Sarah gave me a list, and cereal was on it. I walked down the cereal aisle and just stopped. There had to be forty different kinds of cereal. Colorful boxes with cartoons on them, bags of granola, stuff with marshmallows, healthy stuff. I stood there for about twenty minutes. I couldn't pick one. Over there, you ate whatever was on the line at the chow hall, or whatever MRE you opened. You didn't have forty options. I just stood there reading the same few boxes over and over. Ended up grabbing a plain box of corn flakes just so I could leave the aisle.

The nights took some getting used to. For a year, I slept with my bunk against the wall so I was facing the door. You always wanted to see who was coming in. When I got home, I couldn't sleep unless our bedroom door was wide open. I had to sleep on the side of the bed where I could see out into the hallway. It wasn't something I thought about, I just did it. Sarah would close the door before bed, and I’d get up and open it back up.

It took a good while before I could sleep with the door closed. I’m retired now, but I still catch myself sometimes. I’ll wake up in the middle of the night and look straight at the bedroom door, waiting, before I remember where I am.

a.text:
Dear Editor,

I drove Route 4 out of Kettle Falls for 22 years. I'm retired now, but I know this town and I know the people on these roads, and I've got something to say about the post office closing our counter service.

The USPS says our branch loses $40,000 a year. Well, no wonder. They already cut our window hours from 8 to noon. You can't cut service down to four hours a day and then point at the drop in traffic like it proves something. That's not data. That's a self-fulfilling prophecy.
