setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigot (A Quick Minneapolis Homeowner’s Guide)

Don’t wait for the first freeze. Outdoor faucets holding water in them are just waiting to crack. Here’s the exact sequence to protect every exterior spigot on your property in under ten minutes.

**1. Shut the interior shutoff valve**
Every outdoor faucet is fed by a dedicated line that runs through your interior walls. Somewhere behind that wall—usually in a basement, crawl space, utility closet, or garage—there’s a valve controlling it. Turn the handle clockwise until it stops. This isolates the outdoor pipe so water can’t reach it.

**2. Drain the spigot**
Once the indoor valve is closed, walk outside and open the outdoor faucet handle. You’ll hear a brief trickle as residual water clears out of the exposed pipe. Leave it open until it stops dripping completely. This emptying is non-negotiable; trapped water expands when it freezes and will split the pipe.

**3. Disconnect all garden hoses**
Remove every hose, sprayer, and timer currently attached to the spigot. Store them indoors. A hose left on the faucet creates a perfect trap for moisture and wind-driven snow. 

**4. Slide on a $3 foam cover**
Grab a standard screw-on or slip-on foam cover from any hardware store. Push it over the spigot until the base sits flush against the siding. Secure the strap. These covers don’t heat anything, but they block freezing air and meltwater from pooling directly on the metal threads and valve stem.

### The One Thing That Causes January Burst Calls
Leaving hoses connected is still our biggest headache every winter. When the temperature drops, a filled hose freezes solid almost overnight. Pressure builds up behind that frozen blockage and shoots straight into the weakest joint in your home’s plumbing. The result? Cracked pipes, flooded basements, and an emergency call before sunrise. If your hoses came off last fall, you’ve already avoided 90% of winter plumbing disasters.

### Don’t Have an Interior Shutoff Valve?
If you’ve searched your whole house and can’t find a dedicated valve for your outdoor faucets, don’t guess. Blindly turning valves can damage old galvanized or brass lines. Call us. We’ll locate the feed, install a proper exterior-rated sillcock or shutoff as needed, and make sure everything drains clean before the ground freezes. We’d rather swing by now than spend a January morning tearing into your drywall.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots (It Takes 10 Minutes)

Every January, most of our burst-pipe calls in Minneapolis come from the same thing: a garden hose that never got disconnected in the fall. Water gets trapped in the spigot, freezes, splits the pipe inside your wall, and you don't find out until it thaws — usually all over your basement.

Here's how to avoid being one of those calls. This takes about ten minutes and costs three dollars.

## Step 1: Disconnect Your Hoses

Do this first, because it's the one people skip. Even a "frost-free" spigot can't drain properly with a hose attached, so the frost-free part stops working. Take the hose off, drain it, and store it in the garage.

If you only do one thing on this list, do this one.

## Step 2: Shut Off the Interior Valve

Somewhere inside your house — usually in the basement or utility room, on the pipe leading to the outside spigot — there's a shutoff valve. Turn it off. This stops water from reaching the spigot at all.

**Don't have an interior shutoff valve?** Some older Minneapolis homes don't. Give us a call and we can install one — it's a quick job in the fall and a lot cheaper than a burst pipe in the winter.

## Step 3: Drain the Spigot

Go back outside and open the spigot all the way. Let any water left in the line run out. Leave the spigot open through the winter — that way, if any water does sneak in and freeze, it has room to expand without breaking anything.

Some interior valves have a small bleeder cap on the side. If yours does, put a bucket under it and open it to drain the last bit of water from the line, then close it back up.

## Step 4: Put On a Foam Cover

Hardware stores sell insulated foam spigot covers for about three bucks. They slip right over the spigot and hook on. It's cheap insurance against those -20°F stretches we get here.

## That's It

Hoses off, valve closed, spigot drained and open, cover on. Ten minutes in October saves you a flooded basement in January.

If you're not sure whether you have a shutoff valve, or you found one and it's stuck or leaking, don't force it — those old valves snap. Give us a call and we'll get you squared away before the deep freeze hits.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
Every weekday morning at 6:15, I stage the same battle. I walk into my kids’ rooms, flip on the lights, and try to coax two exhausted middle-schoolers out of bed. By the time they grab their backpacks and head out the door for the early bell, they’re practically sleepwalking.

If you have teenagers or pre-teens in Millbrook, you know this routine all too well. That is why I am strongly urging our school board to approve the proposal to move our middle and high school start times to 8:45 a.m. when they vote next month.

This isn’t about letting kids be lazy or indulging bad bedtime habits. It’s basic biology. The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. to align with adolescent sleep cycles. During puberty, biological rhythms shift, making it difficult for teens to fall asleep before 11:00 p.m. Expecting them to absorb algebra at 7:30 in the morning simply works against how their brains are wired.

We don’t have to guess whether a later start time works—we already have local proof. Look at the results from the pilot program at Lincoln Middle. When they shifted to a later schedule, attendance improved and first-period grades went up significantly. Teachers reported fewer heads on desks and more kids actually awake and ready to participate. 

I understand why some parents and community members are hesitant. Change is tricky, and the biggest concern I’ve heard around town is the bus schedule. But if you look closely at the district's proposal, this issue has already been thoroughly addressed. The plan re-tiers the existing bus routes, staggering elementary and secondary pickups so our current fleet can handle the change smoothly, without blowing up the budget or leaving families stranded.

Our kids only get one shot at these critical school years. Right now, we’re sending them into the classroom running on empty before the day even starts. 

When the board votes next month, let’s choose common sense, real data, and our children’s health. Please reach out to our school board members and tell them to vote "yes" on the 8:45 a.m. start time.

b.text:
**Headline: Let’s give our middle schoolers the sleep they need — the 8:45 start plan works**

Last Tuesday, I stood in my kitchen at 7:10 a.m. holding a half-toasted pop-tart, yelling up the stairs for the third time for my 7th grader to get moving. He stumbled down 10 minutes later, hood up, eyes half-closed, and forgot his math workbook before sprinting for the bus. If you’re a Millbrook middle school parent (I’ve got a 6th and 8th grader, so I’m in the thick of it), this scene is probably familiar. It’s not laziness — it’s biology, and the school board’s proposed 8:45 a.m. start time isn’t a “free pass” for tired kids. It’s a common-sense fix backed by real data.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended for a decade that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., because teens’ circadian rhythms shift during puberty. They naturally fall asleep later and wake up later, no matter how much we nag them about putting phones away at bedtime. Right now our middle schoolers start at 7:45, a full hour before their brains are really ready to focus.

We don’t have to guess if this works. The 2023 pilot at Lincoln Middle — a district our size just 15 miles away — saw a 14% jump in daily attendance and a 12% increase in first-period grades across all subjects after switching to an 8:50 start. Those aren’t abstract policy numbers: that’s fewer kids skipping first period because they can’t drag themselves out of bed, fewer kids napping through language arts, more kids actually present and learning when the bell rings.

I know the big objection everyone’s yelling about on the Millbrook Neighbors Facebook group: “What about the buses? We can’t afford new routes.” I was worried too, until I read the full proposal, not just the social media hot takes. The plan already re-tiers our bus routes, shifting the high school start 10 minutes earlier to stagger pickups. The transportation department’s already mapped every route: no extra buses, no added cost, no kid standing in the dark before 7:30 a.m. The longest bus ride only goes up by 4 minutes.

This isn’t about letting our kids sleep in to play video games. It’s about letting them show up to school awake enough to do the work. The school board votes next month — let’s tell them we’re ready to stop fighting our kids’ biology, and start supporting them.

(397 words)

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**They Didn't Get Beat. They Beat Themselves.**

Let's get the hard part out of the way: Friday night's loss stings more because it didn't have to happen.

Nobody should be embarrassed by an 8-2 season, and I'm not here to tell you the boys don't deserve a hand. They do. But I've watched every snap of this team since August, and I'm not going to sit here and pretend that second half was anything other than a coaching failure.

We beat that team by 20 in Week 3. Twenty. And we did it the same way we won most of our games this year — by running the ball down their throats until they quit wanting to tackle. Friday night, the ground game was working again. We were moving the chains, controlling the clock, and we walked into halftime down three points. Three. That's a field goal. That's nothing.

Then, for reasons I still can't explain, we came out throwing on nearly every down like we were trailing by three touchdowns. The run game didn't stop working. We stopped using it. Their defensive line got to pin their ears back and rush the passer all night, our drives got shorter, their offense got the ball back over and over, and by the fourth quarter the game was gone. That's not the kids' fault. Kids run the plays they're given.

None of this is a knock on Dez Kowalski, who was asked to carry too much and nearly did it anyway. His 2,340 passing yards this season broke the school record, and it's a record that'll stand a while. He's the best quarterback this town has seen in a generation, and Friday night he was throwing into coverage everybody in the stadium knew was coming.

So here's my hope for next year: that the staff trusts what got them to 8-2 in the first place. This program is close. The talent's there, the record proves it, and the loss proves the margin between a good season and a great one is sometimes just one halftime decision.

Congratulations on a fine season, boys. Now go get the next one — and run the dang ball.

b.text:
**They Had the Hammer. They Put It Down.**

Eight and two is a good season. I want to say that up front, because what follows is going to sound like a man who forgot it.

Dez Kowalski threw for 2,340 yards this fall, and nobody in the history of this program has done that. He earned every one of them. The kid played the last three weeks with a shoulder he wasn't talking about and kept putting the ball where it needed to be. Years from now his name is going to be on a board in that gym and it belongs there.

But we lost in the second round of the state playoffs to a team we beat by 20 in September, and I don't think we lost because they got better. I think we lost because we stopped doing the thing that was working.

Go back and look at the first half. We ran the ball, we ran it well, and we ran it right at them. They didn't have an answer. The line was getting a push on nearly every down and our backs were falling forward for four, five, six yards at a clip. That's how you build a lead against a team that's out for revenge — you make them tackle for two hours until they don't want to anymore.

Then halftime happened, and whatever was said in that locker room, the plan that came out of it was a different plan. Down three. Three points. And we came out throwing on first down, throwing on second down, and finding ourselves in third-and-long against a defense that finally got to sit back and rush the passer.

I understand the temptation. When you have the best quarterback in school history, every play call that isn't a pass feels like leaving money on the table. But a three-point deficit isn't an emergency. It's a field goal. It does not require you to abandon what got you there and start playing the other team's game.

That's what happened. We took the one thing they couldn't stop and set it aside voluntarily, and by the time the fourth quarter got tight we'd lost the rhythm up front and couldn't get it back. Kowalski ended up throwing into coverage that wouldn't have existed if the safeties still had to worry about the run. Nobody made him do that. The situation didn't demand it. It was a choice.

I've heard people this week blame the officiating, and I've heard people say the other team just wanted it more. I don't buy either one. The officiating was ordinary and the other team wanted it exactly as much as they did in Week 3. The difference was that in Week 3 we kept our foot on the gas, and in Round 2 we changed drivers at the half.

None of this makes it a bad year. The seniors leave with a record most classes here would trade for, and the juniors got a taste of what November football feels like. That matters. But the honest lesson from that game isn't about heart or toughness or wanting it. It's simpler and it's more fixable than that.

When something is working, keep doing it. Especially when you're only down three.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: My 6-Month Review

I’ve used the Jarvik L2 as my full-time desk for six months, usually eight to ten hours a day. The short version: the frame and motor are good, the stability is merely acceptable, and the included cable tray is terrible.

I paid the $549 sale price. At that price, I’d buy it again. At the regular $749 price, I would not.

## Motor: Quiet and Fast

The motor is the L2’s best feature. It moves quickly enough that switching positions never feels like an interruption, and it’s quiet enough to use during a call without announcing to everyone that I’m raising my desk.

The motion is smooth, with no alarming jolts when it starts or stops. After six months of frequent adjustments—typically four to six per workday—the motor still sounds and performs the same as it did when new.

## Stability: Fine Until Full Height

At seated and moderate standing heights, the L2 feels solid. My monitors stay put, and normal typing doesn’t create noticeable movement.

At full height, it wobbles. I’m a fairly hard typist, and when the desk is near its maximum extension, I can see movement in my monitor arms. It’s mostly front-to-back rather than side-to-side, but it’s obvious enough to be distracting.

This isn’t a dealbreaker for me because my normal standing preset is below maximum height. Taller users who need the desk fully extended should take the wobble seriously. A stable frame at mid-height does not automatically mean a stable frame at full extension, and the L2 is proof of that.

## Memory Presets: Useful but Imprecise

The controller is simple, and the memory buttons make switching between sitting and standing easy. Unfortunately, the presets drift by roughly a centimeter.

I’ll save a height, return to it later, and find the desk slightly higher or lower than expected. One centimeter doesn’t sound significant, but it’s enough to change wrist and elbow positioning. I occasionally have to tap the controls to correct it.

The presets are still useful, but they aren’t precise. On a desk with a $749 list price, they should be.

## Cable Tray: Garbage

The included cable tray is the worst part of the desk.

It’s too small for a power strip plus the collection of adapters and excess cable that comes with a real workstation. Access is awkward, cable routing is poorly considered, and it does very little to keep heavier cords from sagging or escaping.

I gave up on it and installed a larger third-party tray. That solved the problem, but buyers shouldn’t have to replace a basic accessory immediately—especially at the regular price.

If you use multiple monitors, a dock, speakers, and a desktop PC, budget for a separate cable-management setup.

## Six-Month Verdict

The Jarvik L2 gets the fundamentals mostly right. Its motor is quiet, fast, and still reliable after six months of daily use. It feels stable at the heights most people will use, but the wobble at full extension is real. The drifting memory presets are irritating, and the cable tray belongs in the recycling bin.

At **$549**, the L2 is worth it. The motor performance and overall frame quality outweigh the flaws, especially if you don’t need maximum height and are willing to replace the cable tray.

At **$749**, skip it. For that price, I expect better full-height stability, accurate presets, and cable management that isn’t an afterthought.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: My 6-Month Review

I bought the Jarvik L2 six months ago for my home office. I work remotely as a software engineer, I'm at this desk 9-10 hours a day, and I paid for it myself. No affiliate links, no sponsor. This is just what it's actually like to live with.

**The motor is the best part.**
It's genuinely quiet and fast. I measured it at about 38dB from my chair — quieter than my mechanical keyboard — and it goes from my sitting height (72cm) to standing (108cm) in roughly 9 seconds. No grinding, no jerking stop/start like my old IKEA Bekant. After six months of going up/down 4-5 times a day, it sounds exactly the same as day one.

**It wobbles if you're tall and type like you mean it.**
At sitting height, it's rock solid. At full extension for me (108cm, I'm 5'9"), it's not. If I'm typing hard during a code sprint or banging out an angry Slack message, my 27" monitor visibly shakes. It's not unusable, and it doesn't creep down, but if you're over 6' and plan to stand at 115cm+ all day, you will notice it. Putting my heavier monitor arm closer to the center helped, but didn't fix it.

**The memory presets drift.**
This drives me insane. I have Preset 1 at 72.0 and Preset 2 at 108.0. Every 2-3 weeks, Preset 2 will start landing at 109.1 or 107.2. It's only about a centimeter, but I have to reset it constantly. For a desk at this price, the controller should hold calibration. It doesn't.

**The included cable tray is garbage.**
Throw it away. It's too shallow for a standard power strip plus two laptop bricks, the mounting screws stripped the pre-drilled holes on install, and it sagged after a month. I replaced it with a $25 under-desk tray from Amazon and haven't thought about it since. Jarvik should just not include it and knock $20 off the price.

**Verdict**
At the $549 sale price I paid? Worth it. The motor alone justifies it, and the wobble is manageable for my height.

At the full $749 list price? Absolutely not. For $749 I expect zero preset drift and a desk that doesn't wobble when I type. Wait for a sale, budget $25 extra for a real cable tray, and you'll be happy.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
The register died on a Saturday at 6:40, right in the middle of the dinner rush. I was on the floor and my dad was in the kitchen. I knew because the screen went black and then came back with a blue error message. We had forty people in the dining room and a waitlist at the door.

I found a pen and a stack of the guest check pads we keep under the counter for when the printer jams. I started writing tickets by hand. Two bowls of pho, no onion. One vermicelli, extra fish sauce on the side. A large order of spring rolls to go. My handwriting is bad, so I wrote slowly and checked the math twice. My dad called out order numbers and I called them back. For two hours nobody used the computer. When the repair guy came Monday he asked why we didn't just close. My dad said, "We had food."

On Sundays a new hire, Danny, was on the schedule. He's a sophomore and he'd never cooked before. I taught him my grandma's spring roll fold because she was home with her knee and couldn't come in. She taught me when I was nine. You lay the rice paper flat, fold the sides in like an envelope, then roll tight so the shrimp shows through the wrapper. Danny's first four were loose and fell apart in the fryer. I showed him again. By the sixth he had it. He said it was like folding a burrito, and I said no, it's not, and we laughed because he was sort of right.

On my breaks I do calc homework in the walk-in cooler. It's the only place with no noise and no phone. It's cold enough that I wear my hoodie and sit on an upside-down bucket. The light is bad. I do derivatives and integrals and think about limits. Sometimes my mom comes in to grab bean sprouts and asks if I'm okay. I say yes. She brings me a jacket sometimes even though I already have one on.

I'm not sure what I want to say about any of this except that it's what I do. I'm not the kind of person who's one thing at school and another person at home. I'm the person who writes tickets by hand when the computer fails and teaches a kid to fold spring rolls and does homework in the cold. That's not a lesson I learned. It's just true. I'll keep doing it until I leave for school, and then I'll come back on weekends and do it again.

b.text:
Every Saturday at 4:30 p.m., the front door of my family’s restaurant locks from the inside until five. I have spent almost every weekend since my sophomore year behind that counter, wearing an apron that smells like star anise and floor cleaner. 

Last November, on a rainy Saturday during the dinner rush, the POS system crashed. The screens froze blue, went black, and stayed that way. Table 4 needed a split bill, Table 12 was waiting on a takeout order for eight, and the line at the door stretched past the host stand. My dad stared at the main terminal, hit the power button twice, and looked at me. 

I grabbed a pad of green guest checks from the supply closet and a black ballpoint pen. For the next three hours, I hand-wrote every ticket. I used our family’s shorthand: *P1* for Phở Tái, *B1* for Bún Thịt Nướng, *A2* extra peanut sauce. My handwriting started neat and degraded into quick slashes as the kitchen wheel filled up. I calculated 6.25% sales tax on paper napkins. My wrist cramped, but the food went out, the orders were right, and the kitchen never stopped moving.

Training new hires usually falls to me because I speak English fast enough to explain the seating chart and Vietnamese fast enough to translate my grandma’s notes from the prep station. In September, we hired a junior from my school named Marcus. His first week, I had to teach him how to wrap gỏi cuốn. 

Grandma’s rule is exact: the rice paper has to be damp, not soaked, or it tears when you pull it tight. I laid a round sheet flat on the stainless steel, set down the lettuce, mint, pork, and vermicelli, then placed two halved shrimp pink-side down so they would show through the translucent skin. 

"Pull the bottom flap over, tuck it tight under the filling, fold the sides, then roll," I showed him. 

His first four burst, rice noodles spilling out onto the prep table. I didn't take the wrapper from him. I just ran another sheet through the warm water dish, placed it in front of him, and put my hands over his to show him how much tension the paper could hold before it gave out. By eight o'clock, his rolls looked almost like mine, which looked almost like Grandma’s.

When the dinner rush dies down around 8:30, I take my break. The kitchen gets hot from the broth pots that simmer for twelve hours straight, so I take my AP Calculus homework into the walk-in cooler. 

I sit on an overturned milk crate between the tubs of hoisin sauce and the stacked crates of Thai basil. The air inside is thirty-six degrees and smells like cold ginger. I pull my knees up, rest my notebook on my thighs, and work through derivatives. My breath fogs up the margins. Sometimes the ink from my gel pen slows down on the damp paper, but it is the quietest ten minutes of my week.

I don’t have a grand lesson about how working weekends made me a better person. It is mostly just work. It is sore feet, loud vent hoods, wet dish towels, and making sure the register balances down to the penny at the end of the night. But I know how to keep a dining room moving when the technology fails, I know how to teach someone a skill without taking the paper out of their hands, and I can clear a problem set while my knuckles are cold. At ten o'clock, I turn off the neon open sign, wipe down the glass, and go home.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam – 14 Months / ~140,000 Miles Review**

I’ve had the Roadstar DC4 on my rig for about 14 months now and just shy of 140,000 miles. For the most part, it’s done what a dash cam is supposed to do, but there are a few things owner-operators should know before buying one.

The biggest win for me was when it caught a lane-change accident on camera. The footage was clear enough that my insurance claim got approved in about 9 days instead of the usual 6-week headache. That alone made it worth the money.

Front camera quality has been solid for the price. Daytime footage is good, and it holds up decently in rain and highway glare. The rear camera is okay during the day, but night footage gets grainy past about 30 feet. If you’re hoping to read plates far back at night, don’t count on it.

The suction mount was a pain. It fell off twice in summer heat, which is not acceptable when you’re running through hot states. I switched to the adhesive mount and haven’t had a problem since. If you buy one, skip the suction cup from the start.

My other complaint is the app. It needs Wi-Fi to pull footage, which is basically useless at most truck stops. I ended up just pulling the SD card and checking footage on my laptop. Not a deal breaker, but it’s annoying if you expect quick access.

Overall, the Roadstar DC4 is a decent budget-minded dash cam. It’s not perfect, but it saved me a lot of time and stress when I needed proof. For owner-operators who want basic protection without spending a fortune, it’s worth a look. Just mount it right and don’t expect miracles from the rear cam at night.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam: 14 months, 140K miles**

Short version: it's worth owning, with a few gripes.

**What I like**
The footage paid for the camera. I got sideswiped in a lane change dispute, and the DC4 had the whole thing on video. My insurance claim was approved in 9 days. The usual wait for me has been around 6 weeks. If you've ever sat on a claim while your truck's not earning, you know what that's worth.

Front video is solid day and night. It's held up through 14 months of rough road, heat, and cold with no failures.

**What's not great**
- **Rear cam at night:** Gets grainy past about 30 feet. Fine for seeing what's right behind you, but don't count on reading a plate from a car further back after dark.
- **Suction mount:** Fell off twice in summer heat. Cab temps cook it. I switched to the adhesive mount and it hasn't moved since. I'd skip the suction mount altogether if you run in hot country.
- **App:** Needs WiFi to pull footage, which is useless at most truck stops. I stopped bothering with it. I just pop the SD card and read it on my laptop. Works fine, just not as slick as they advertise.

**Bottom line**
If you're an owner-operator, a dash cam is cheap insurance, and this one has proven itself. Use the adhesive mount, pull the SD card instead of fussing with the app, and don't expect miracles from the rear cam at night. For what it does when it counts, I'd buy it again.

Happy to answer questions if anybody's weighing it against something else.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**A Later Start Time is the Right Choice for Millbrook’s Middle Schoolers**

As a parent of two middle schoolers in Millbrook, I’ve spent years watching my kids struggle to wake up for the 7:30 a.m. bell. Like many of you, I’ve seen the yawns at the breakfast table, the rushed mornings, and the way their energy flags by first period. That’s why I’m relieved the school board is finally considering an 8:45 a.m. start time—and why I hope the community will support it.

The science is clear: middle schoolers need more sleep. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. to align with adolescents’ natural sleep cycles. When kids don’t get enough rest, it affects everything—mood, focus, even their immune systems. Chronic sleep deprivation isn’t just about being tired; it’s linked to higher rates of anxiety, depression, and lower academic performance. Our current start time isn’t just inconvenient—it’s working against our kids’ well-being.

We don’t have to guess what a later start would look like. Lincoln Middle School’s pilot program last year showed real results: attendance improved, and first-period grades went up. Teachers reported students were more alert and engaged. That’s not a coincidence—it’s what happens when we listen to the research and give kids the rest they need to thrive.

I know some parents worry about logistics, especially bus schedules. But the proposal already addresses this by re-tiering routes, so elementary and high school start times would shift slightly to accommodate the change. It’s not perfect, but it’s a workable solution—and one that prioritizes the age group that needs it most. Middle schoolers are at a critical stage, juggling harder coursework, social pressures, and physical changes. They deserve a schedule that sets them up for success, not one that leaves them exhausted before the day even begins.

Change is always hard, and I don’t take lightly the adjustments this will require for families. But when I think about the difference an extra hour of sleep could make for my kids—for all our kids—I believe it’s worth it. Let’s give them the best chance to learn, grow, and start their days with energy, not exhaustion. The school board votes next month, and I hope they’ll do the right thing for Millbrook’s students.

b.text:
Every morning, I watch my two middle-schoolers drag themselves out of bed in the dark, bleary-eyed and fumbling for cereal, and I think: *this can’t be right*. Their alarm clocks scream at 6:15, and we’re out the door before the sun has even thought about warming the pavement. I’m not a sleep scientist or a logistics expert—just a parent who’s read the school board’s proposal for an 8:45 start time and knows, deep in my bones, that it’s the right move for our kids.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has been clear for years: adolescents need 8 to 10 hours of sleep, and their natural sleep cycles shift later. Waking a teenager at 6 a.m. is like waking an adult at 4 a.m.—it works against biology, not with it. An 8:45 start isn’t an indulgence; it’s simply aligning school with what we know about growing brains.

But I don’t need a national study when we have proof here at home. Lincoln Middle’s pilot program shifted its first bell to 8:45, and the results were remarkable. Attendance rose, and first-period grades climbed. When I spoke with a teacher friend at Lincoln, she described a roomful of students who were actually *present*—not just physically, but mentally, ready to learn. That’s what every parent wants: kids who can focus on algebra, not on staying upright.

The main objection I hear is about bus schedules. I get it—changing start times feels like untangling Christmas lights. But the proposal on the table already re-tiers the routes. The transportation department has mapped it out, and it works without adding cost or leaving younger students waiting in the dark. We’re not being asked to choose between our middle-schoolers and the rest of the district; the plan is balanced and ready to go.

Next month, the school board will vote. I’m asking my neighbors to see this for what it is: a rare, evidence-backed chance to give our kids something as basic as enough sleep. Let’s stop fighting their biology and start giving them mornings that make sense. I’ll set a later alarm for that—happily.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
## Cold Baseboard Heat? Bleed the Air in This Order

Turn the boiler and circulator pump off before you start. You want the water still and cool enough to work around safely. If the system has been running, give it a little time before opening a bleeder valve.

### What you need

- A radiator key or flathead screwdriver  
- A small cup or jar  
- A rag or towel for drips  

### Step 1: Find the bleeder valve

Look at the end of each baseboard unit. The bleeder valve is usually a small brass valve with a square stem or screw slot. It may be near the top of the unit or behind an end cap.

### Step 2: Start closest to the boiler

Begin with the baseboard unit closest to the boiler, then work your way outward through the loop.

This is where a lot of people go wrong. They bleed the upstairs rooms because those units feel cold, but skip the basement loop. In many homes, the trapped air is actually sitting in the basement line. If you skip that loop, you may still end up with cold baseboard heat after doing all the work.

### Step 3: Put a cup under the valve

Hold your cup directly underneath the bleeder valve. A little water may come out once the air is gone, so keep the rag ready too.

### Step 4: Open the valve slowly

Turn the valve slowly, usually only about a quarter turn. You should hear air hissing out.

Let it hiss until the sound changes and water starts coming out in a steady stream with no sputtering or air bursts.

### Step 5: Close it snug, not tight

Once water runs steady, close the valve. Snug it down just until it stops, but do not crank on it.

Overtightening can crack the valve seat or damage the seal, and that can turn a quick bleed into a leaking valve.

### Step 6: Repeat each unit

Move from unit to unit, working through the whole loop. Include basement baseboards, utility rooms, and any low or hard-to-see sections where air can collect.

### Step 7: Turn the system back on

Once every valve is closed, turn the circulator and boiler back on. Then check the baseboards again after the system has had time to heat up.

If the heat still is not moving through one or more units, the problem may be something else, like a stuck zone valve, low system pressure, a bad circulator, or a blockage. That is usually when it makes sense to call us and have it looked at.

b.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Baseboard Heating Before Winter

You'll need a radiator key or a flathead screwdriver, a small cup or wide mug, and an old rag. Bleeding takes about 15 minutes for most houses.

## Steps

**1. Shut off the circulator and boiler.**
Turn the boiler's power switch off, or drop the thermostats well below room temperature so nothing is calling for heat. If the circulator is running while you open a valve, it pushes more air around the system, and hot water can spray. Give the system a little time to cool down before you start.

**2. Find the bleeder valve on each baseboard unit.**
It's a small valve at the end of the baseboard, usually behind the end cap or on the pipe where it enters the unit. Some are brass with a slotted screw, and some have a small square stem that takes a key. Pop off the end cap if you need to.

**3. Start with the unit closest to the boiler.**
Work your way out from there, one unit at a time. Bleeding in order keeps you from chasing the same air bubble around the system.

**4. Cup underneath and open the valve slowly.**
Hold the cup under the valve and turn the key or screwdriver a quarter turn counterclockwise. Don't crank it open. You'll hear hissing as the trapped air escapes. A few drops of water might come out first, then spitting and sputtering, and then a steady stream.

**5. Close it when the water runs steady.**
Once the water comes out in a solid stream with no hissing or spitting, close the valve. Snug is all you want. Overtightening is how people crack the valve seat, and then you have a slow drip and a service call you didn't need. Wipe the valve dry and check it again in a few minutes.

**6. Repeat on every unit, then check the boiler pressure.**
Bleeding lets a little water out, so look at the pressure gauge when you're done. Most residential systems should sit around 12 to 15 psi when cold. If the pressure has dropped, the auto-fill valve should bring it back up on its own. If it doesn't, call us before you fire the boiler back up.

**7. Turn the boiler and circulator back on.**
Let the system run for a while, then walk the house and feel each baseboard. They should heat evenly from one end to the other.

## The mistake behind most of our cold radiator calls

Most people bleed the upstairs units and stop there, because that's where the cold spots are. But the air that's causing the problem is usually in the basement loop. Air collects in the lower runs and keeps hot water from circulating through the zone, so the upstairs units stay cold no matter how many times you bleed them.

If you only do one thing from this post, make sure you bleed every unit on every level, basement included, and don't skip the ones that seem to be working fine.

## When to call us

If you've bled every unit and still have cold spots, or you find a valve that won't close, a unit that keeps filling with air, or pressure that won't hold, something else is going on. It could be a failing air eliminator, a bad circulator, or a leak somewhere in the system. Give us a call and we'll track it down.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
When I got back from my second deployment, I landed at the airport on a Tuesday. I had my A-bag slung over my shoulder and my uniform was stiff from thirty hours of travel. When I came off the terminal ramp, I saw my wife standing by the stairs. My daughter, Maya, was right next to her. She was six years old. I dropped my bag and walked toward them, but Maya didn't run out to meet me. She pulled back and hid behind her mother's leg, clutching the denim of Sarah’s jeans and peeking out with one eye. She didn't recognize me. To her, I was just a tall man in camouflage with a shaved head and a heavy voice she had only heard through a bad laptop speaker once a month. It took a while and a pack of gum from my pocket before she let me touch her shoulder.

A few days later, Sarah sent me to the store to get something for breakfast. I walked down the cereal aisle and stopped. I just stood there. There were forty different kinds of cereal stacked from the floor to the top shelf. Red boxes, blue boxes, boxes with cartoon characters, boxes with dried fruit. Down range, you ate whatever MRE was in the crate or you took the tray they handed you at the chow hall. You didn't make a choice, you just ate. I stood in front of those shelves for twenty minutes, looking at the options until my throat felt tight and my hands started to sweat. A woman pushing a cart asked if I was in line, and I couldn't answer her. I grabbed the first red box my hand touched and walked straight to the register.

The nights were the hardest part. For a year, I had slept in a CHU with my cot positioned so I was facing the door. If the handle moved or the light changed, I wanted to see it before anything else happened. 

At home, Sarah liked to leave our bedroom door cracked open a few inches so we could hear Maya if she woke up in the night. The first night back, I laid in the dark and felt like the room was spilling out into the hallway. Every instinct I had told me to get up, pull the door shut, and turn the bed around. I laid on my back for hours, looking at the thin strip of hallway light cutting across the carpet, trying to train my mind to leave it alone. 

It took months to get used to it. Some nights I still woke up in a sweat, stood up in the dark, and walked over to touch the wooden doorframe just to make sure where I was. Then I would leave it open and go back to bed.

b.text:
The flight landed at four in the afternoon. We turned in our gear, went through the final briefs, and by six they let us into the terminal where the families were waiting. 

I dropped my duffel on the carpet. My wife came right to me, but my daughter stayed back. She was six then. She had both hands gripped into the side of her mother’s jeans, tucking her face into the denim so only one eye showed. I took my patrol cap off so she could see my haircut, knelt down, and said her name. She didn't budge. I had lost about twenty pounds since pre-mob and had a bad sunburn from the transit through Kuwait, but mostly, a year is a long time when you’ve only had six of them. She knew the man on the laptop screen on Sunday mornings, but she didn’t know the guy kneeling on the airport floor smelling like diesel fuel and canvas. We sat on a row of plastic chairs for ten minutes while I pulled a roll of grape Lifesavers out of my cargo pocket and laid them on the seat between us. Eventually, she took one, and then she let me carry her out to the parking garage.

Three days later, my wife asked me to go to the store to get milk and something for breakfast. 

I found the cereal aisle and stopped. I stayed there for about twenty minutes. I know it was twenty because I checked my watch twice thinking I was going to be late for something that didn't exist. There were at least forty different kinds of boxes on the shelves. Bright reds and blues, cartoons, marshmallows, whole wheat, frosted, organic, family size. Downrange, you ate whatever scrambled eggs were sitting in the metal pan at the DFAC, or you reached into an open box of MREs and took whatever brown bag your hand touched first. You never had to think about it. I stood on the tile with a plastic hand-basket, looking at forty different ways to buy grain and sugar, and I couldn't make my hand reach out and take one. My chest felt hot and crowded. A woman with a toddler in her cart asked if she could squeeze past me, and I apologized like I’d done something wrong, grabbed the plain yellow box of Cheerios nearest my shoulder, and walked straight to the registers.

Nights were harder to adjust to than the daytime. 

For twelve months in the container, my cot was shoved against the back wall, and I slept on my left side, facing the plywood door. It wasn't something I thought about; you just orient yourself toward the entrance with your boots lined up and your rifle where your hand drops. 

Back in our house, my wife liked the bedroom door left open a few inches so the air from the hallway fan could blow through, and so she could hear if our daughter woke up from a bad dream. For the first two months, I couldn't handle it. Every night after she fell asleep, I’d ease out from under the sheet, walk to the door on the balls of my feet, and click it shut. Then I’d lay back down on my left side, watching the knob in the dark until my eyes burned. 

Around month three, I started trying to leave it cracked like she wanted. I’d lay on my side, stare at the strip of light from the nightlight out in the hallway, and count backward from a hundred. If I got too wired, I’d turn over onto my right side, face the window, and look at the corner of our dresser until I went to sleep. 

Most nights now, the door stays open. I still wake up when the floorboards in the hall creak, but I don't sit straight up anymore. I just listen for a second, hear the cat walking past or the house settling, and pull the blanket back up.

setup: A co-founder is posting a LinkedIn hiring announcement for a first customer support hire to potential applicants and customers.

a.text:
Up until now, the three of us at Ridgepoint have done all our own customer support. If a dispatcher had a question about scheduling a load, they were talking to me or one of my co-founders. 

Honestly, it’s starting to fall apart. We're at the point where we can't build the product and answer every ticket fast enough, and our customers deserve better response times than we can give them right now. 

So, we’re hiring our first Customer Support person (making us a team of four). 

I won't bore you with a long pitch about our startup culture. It's the three of us building software for small trucking companies. It's pretty quiet and we just focus on the work. Here is what the job actually looks like day-to-day:

- Answering the inbox: You’ll handle roughly 30-40 tickets a day via email and chat. Our users are busy dispatchers trying to move freight. They don’t want corporate fluff, they just want a straight answer so they can get back to work.
- Hopping on quick calls: Sometimes it's faster to just jump on a 5-minute Zoom and show someone which button to click than to type out three paragraphs. 
- Bug hunting: When a user says "this thing is broken," you’ll try to reproduce it, figure out what’s actually going on, and write up a clear ticket for us to fix.
- Writing docs: We barely have a help center right now. When you notice five people asking the same question, you'll write a quick guide with some screenshots so the sixth person can find it themselves.
- Onboarding: Helping new fleets import their truck and driver lists from messy spreadsheets into Ridgepoint.

You don’t need a background in trucking (though if you know what a BOL or a deadhead is, that's a massive plus). You just need to be good at figuring out how software works, patient with people who aren't super tech-savvy, and comfortable working without a lot of hand-holding. 

It’s full-time, fully remote, though we need you working roughly US Central Time hours since that’s when our dispatchers are moving loads. 

If this sounds like your kind of work, shoot me a DM or email me at [email] with a bit about what you've done before. No formal cover letter needed.

b.text:
We're hiring our first support person at Ridgepoint.

I'll be honest: right now, the three of us answer every ticket ourselves. And it's falling apart. We're juggling product work, sales, and support, so responses are slow and none of us are doing our best work.

So we're looking for someone to own support. Not "lead" it. Just do it. Day to day, that means:

- Talking to small trucking dispatchers who use our tool, often while they're actively dealing with a load.
- Helping them solve real problems: login issues, weird schedule quirks, clarifying how a feature works.
- Logging bugs and feature requests clearly enough that our devs can act on them.
- Occasionally doing some old-fashioned data cleanup or manual fixes when something goes wrong.
- Being the one who notices patterns: "this keeps happening, we should fix it."

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After twelve years of showing houses to first-time buyers in Asheville, I've noticed a pattern that has nothing to do with square footage or countertops. The buyers who end up loving their homes—the ones who still text me years later saying they made the right choice—are the ones who walked the neighborhood at 7am before we ever stepped inside.

Last spring, the Pruitts were looking off Sycamore Street in Kenilworth. Like most of my buyers, they were terrified of making a mistake, so we scheduled a 10am tour for a Thursday, but I asked them to meet me there at 7am first. Just to walk the block, grab a coffee, and see who was already awake.

They thought I was being extra. They showed up skeptical.

But at 7am on Sycamore, the street told them the truth. They watched a neighbor walk his golden retriever past the same oak tree every morning. They saw the bakery on the corner unlock its doors at 6:45. Mrs. Pruitt noticed a daycare van making the turn at 7:15, and Mr. Pruitt realized he could hear the school bus but not the highway hum he hated.

When we toured the house at 10am, they weren't looking at the staging or the granite. They were standing in the kitchen imagining Tuesday mornings. They bought that house. Six months later, they told me the 7am walk was the only time they felt like they were buying a life instead of a property.

The house is just a box until you know what the street feels like when the world wakes up.

To the buyers I'm working with right now: I know it feels like an extra step. To the agents: you know that click when a showing finally makes sense? This is how you get there. And to the lenders who keep asking how to help their pre-approved buyers feel confident—this costs nothing, and it works.

What time of day tells you the truth about a neighborhood?

b.text:
After 12 years of selling real estate here in Asheville, mostly working with first-time buyers, I’ve noticed a subtle pattern that has nothing to do with square footage, quartz countertops, or school ratings.

When we walked through the house later that day, they weren’t just evaluating room sizes—they already understood the rhythm of the block. Five years later, they still tell me it’s their favorite thing about living there.

An afternoon tour or a Sunday open house shows you a property at its polished best. A 7:00 AM walk shows you what your actual life will feel like on a random Tuesday. If you're house hunting right now, set an early alarm, grab a coffee, and go walk the street before you make a decision. It’s the single best test drive you can give a home.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/
I raised prices 40% on everyone overnight.
Lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week.
Here's the full story of that pricing mistake and what I changed. 🧵

2/
Tallyup is a simple subscription tool for gym owners to track member retention.
Solo founder. Indie SaaS.
I felt underpriced vs competitors and margins were thin, so I just flipped the switch for all active customers. No warning. No grandfathering. New invoices at +40%.

3/
Thought I was being decisive.
"If they get value they'll stay."
Reality hit fast. Cancellations started the same day.
Some angry replies. Some quiet churn. A few early supporters said they felt blindsided.
7 days later: 30 gone.

4/
It stung. Not just the revenue hit, but realizing I'd treated the people who took a chance on me like strangers.
Spent the week talking to as many as I could and just listening.

5/
What I changed:
- Immediately grandfathered every remaining customer at the old price
- New customers get the higher price
- Any future increase now comes with clear notice and an explanation of why
- I talk to customers before big pricing moves instead of deciding alone

6/
Biggest lesson for other indie founders:
Existing customers bought into a specific deal. Surprise overnight hikes feel like bait-and-switch even if the product is solid.
How you raise prices matters more than the percentage.

Still building in public. Smaller base, clearer rules going forward.
What pricing mistakes have you made?

b.text:
1/ I raised Tallyup's prices 40% on everyone, overnight.

A week later I'd lost 30 of my 140 customers.

Here's what I got wrong and what I changed 🧵

2/ The thinking behind it wasn't crazy. Tallyup was underpriced, and I knew it. Gym owners were getting real value from tracking retention, and I was charging like a side project.

So I picked a number, changed it, and moved on.

3/ The mistake wasn't the increase. It was how I did it.

No heads-up. No grandfathering. No explanation. Same increase for the customer who'd been with me since day one and the one who signed up last week.

4/ Then the cancellations started.

30 of 140 in a week. That's more than 1 in 5 customers gone.

Some emails were polite. Some were not. A few were fair points I didn't want to hear.

5/ What stung most: the people who left weren't mad about the number. They were mad about being surprised.

Gym owners run on thin margins. They plan their costs. A surprise bill from a tool they trusted felt like I'd stopped caring about them.

6/ So here's what I changed:

- [change #1, e.g. how you now announce price changes]
- [change #2, e.g. what you did for existing customers]
- [change #3, e.g. what you did for the customers who left]

7/ The bigger lesson: pricing is a trust decision, not just a math decision.

I treated it like a spreadsheet cell. My customers treated it like a signal about whether I valued the relationship.

8/ I still think the old price was too low. I'd still raise it. I just wouldn't do it like that.

If you're about to raise prices, give people notice, give them a reason, and respect the ones who've been with you longest.

9/ Have you raised prices on an existing customer base? I'd love to hear what worked and what blew up.

I'm sharing the real numbers as I go with Tallyup, so follow along if that's useful.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
If you've asked me about a wedding cake in the last few months, you probably got a long, rambling answer while I bagged your scones, and I've been feeling bad about that. You deserve a real answer, and you deserve it all in one place. So here it is.

We're not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore.

There are a few reasons and none of them are dramatic. The first one is simply time. A wedding cake, from the first email to the last delivery, takes something like fourteen hours before we've even started baking. That's the consult, the sketches, the emails back and forth about whether the buttercream should be ivory or a warmer ivory, the tasting box, the tasting appointment, the second tasting because the venue changed, the timeline call with the coordinator. Fourteen hours is basically two full days in a small bakery. Two days when there are still forty loaves to shape and a case to fill at six.

The second reason is harder to say out loud, but it's true. We had three weddings cancel this year at the last minute. Last minute meaning we'd already ordered, already prepped, in one case already had components in the freezer. That's ingredient money gone, and in a bakery our size there's no padding to absorb it. One of those cancellations was about the same as a week of flour.

And the third reason, which took me the longest to admit: wedding cakes were pulling us away from the case. The case is what pays the rent. The morning pastries, the loaves, the cookies, the birthday cakes people pick up on a Tuesday afternoon. Every hour I spent on a three-tier consult was an hour I wasn't finishing the morning bake, or testing a new scone, or just being at the counter to say hi to you. I started to notice the everyday stuff slipping, and that felt worse than any wedding ever felt good.

I want to be honest that I loved a lot of those cakes. There's a particular kind of quiet at 5am on a Saturday when you're stacking tiers and the whole shop smells like vanilla and nobody's here yet. I'll miss that. But I can't run the bakery I want to run and also run a wedding business on the side. Three people is three people.

So what does this mean for you. If you have a wedding coming and you were hoping we'd do it, I'm sorry, and I'm happy to point you toward a few bakers in the area who do this beautifully and do it full time. If you have a birthday, a shower, an anniversary, a Tuesday, we're very much still here. We'll still do custom work when it fits in the rhythm of the week — a small celebration cake with a few days' notice is something we can usually say yes to. It's the sixteen-week, three-tasting, four-tier thing that we can't.

Mostly I wanted to say thank you. You're the reason we get to be a bakery at all, and the reason I'd rather be standing here at 4am than anywhere else. Come in and see what's in the case. There's usually something good.

b.text:
A little bakery update from us: we’ve decided to stop taking custom wedding cake orders.

This wasn’t an easy decision. We’ve loved being part of so many wedding days, and it means a lot when someone trusts our tiny team with such an important cake. But the truth is that each wedding order takes around 14 hours in consultations, tastings, planning, emails, and design work before we even get to the baking and decorating. With only three of us here, that’s a lot of time away from the ovens and the everyday work of keeping the bakery running.

We’ve also had three last-minute cancellations this year after ingredients had already been ordered or prepared. For a small shop, those costs are difficult to absorb.

Most importantly, custom wedding cakes have been pulling us away from the case—the morning buns, loaves, cookies, slices, and celebration cakes you come in for every week. That everyday case is the heart of the bakery, and quite honestly, it’s what pays the rent. We want to put our time and energy back into making it as good, full, and dependable as we can.

We’re so grateful to everyone who has invited our cakes into their celebrations. This change isn’t because we care any less about those moments. It’s because we need to take care of the little bakery that makes them possible in the first place.

Thank you, as always, for showing up, saying hello, and taking our baking home with you. We’ll see you at the case.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: Eight Months of Daily Sourdough**

I sell sourdough at the farmers market every Saturday, which means I'm mixing dough almost daily. For the past eight months, the Corlane SM6 has been sitting on my counter taking the abuse. Here's what eight months of market prep taught me.

**The motor is the reason to buy it**

I run double batches of stiff bagel dough through this machine—think 75% hydration, heavy rye, dough that fights back. The SM6 doesn't stall. It doesn't bog down or overheat. It just grinds through. My old KitchenAid Artisan couldn't handle a double batch of anything stiffer than pizza dough without the motor whining and slowing to a crawl. If you knead heavy dough weekly, this motor alone justifies the price.

**The annoyances**

The bowl lift lever squeaks. It's metal-on-metal with no bushing, and after six weeks of daily use it started grinding like a rusty gate. I hit it with WD-40 once a month to keep it quiet. For a $429 machine, that's sloppy.

Bigger issue: the included dough hook is too short for the deep bowl. It leaves the bottom third of the dough unmixed, forcing me to stop and scrape down constantly. I bought a third-party hook for $30 to fix it. Factor that into your total cost.

**The price reality**

At $429, you're paying $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid Professional. That premium buys you a motor that actually handles heavy, high-volume batches without stalling or overheating.

**The verdict**

Buy the Corlane SM6 if you knead heavy dough—sourdough, bagels, pizza dough—every single week. The motor is legitimately superior to KitchenAid's for stiff, high-hydration batches, and eight months of daily market prep proves it can take the abuse.

Skip it if you're mostly making cookies, cake batter, or the occasional quick bread. For light baking, you're paying $80 extra for torque you'll never use, and you'll still deal with that squeaky lever and the useless short hook.

This is a heavy-duty tool for heavy-duty bakers. If that's you, it's worth it. If it's not, save your money.

b.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: Eight Months of Daily Sourdough, One Persistent Squeak

I've had the Corlane SM6 on my counter since last spring, and I've run it nearly every day since. Not as a display piece — as the machine that makes my weekend market loaves. Here's the honest version after eight months.

**Price when I bought it:** $429, which is $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid model. That's the number people ask about first, and it's the number that made me hesitate for about a week.

## The Motor Is the Whole Reason to Buy It

The thing that sold me on the SM6 was dough that would punish a lesser machine. My weekend sourdough schedule is a double batch of a stiff, high-hydration dough — somewhere in the 78–80% hydration range depending on the flour and the weather, which means a dough that gets heavy and sticky and fights back.

The SM6 doesn't stall on it. I don't get the motor laboring, the bowl walking across the counter, or the dough hook bogging down and stopping dead halfway through. It mixes from slack to fully developed without a pause, and it does it again on a second batch the same afternoon without the motor sounding tired. If your baking involves kneading heavy dough weekly — sourdough, bagels, pizza dough, big batches of enriched dough — that capability is worth real money and it's the entire case for this mixer.

The bowl lift is also genuinely better for this than a tilt-head. Lifting the bowl out means I can tip it straight into a banneton or a loaf pan without wrestling a heavy bowl over a tilting head, and I can get the dough out with a scraper instead of trying to coax it loose in the bowl. On a market day with three loaves and a flat sleep, that matters more than I'd expect.

## The Bowl Lift Lever Squeaks, and I Have to WD-40 It

This is my only real complaint, and it's a monthly ritual now. The lift lever develops a squeak somewhere in the first month, and once it starts it doesn't stop until I get a can of WD-40 and work it into the hinge. I do this about once a month. It takes two minutes, it fixes it completely, and it has never come back early, so it's an annoyance rather than a defect.

If you're the kind of person who would find that maddening, know it going in. If you'd rather oil a hinge once a month than have a mixer that stalls on your fourth bagel, it's a trivial trade.

## The Included Dough Hook Is Too Short

Straight fact: the dough hook that comes with the SM6 is too short for the deep bowl. It doesn't reach the bottom properly, so it mixes the top of the dough and leaves the dense bit sitting untouched at the base. I bought a third-party hook to replace it, and the replacement works better than the stock one — longer reach, better motion through the dough.

So the accessory situation is: replace one part out of the box with a cheap part, and the machine works better. Plan for that in your budget and in your head. Don't buy the SM6 assuming the included hook is fine.

## Who Should Buy It

**Buy the SM6 if you knead heavy dough every week.** If sourdough, bagels, pizza, or large-batch bread is a regular part of your baking, the motor is the deal. It's strong, it doesn't bog down, and the bowl lift is the right design for a full-capacity bowl. In my case it earns its place in the kitchen every single day.

**Skip the SM6 if you're mostly making cookies and cake batter.** Here's the part where I don't think you should overpay: if your baking is mostly cookies, brownies, cakes, or whipped toppings, you are not going to tax this motor the way I tax mine. The extra $80 over the KitchenAid buys you headroom you won't use, and you'd be spending more money to solve a problem you don't have.

## Verdict

**The Corlane SM6 is worth $429 if and only if you're kneading heavy dough weekly.** For me it's a clear yes — the motor handles my double batch of stiff bagel dough without stalling, and the bowl lift is better than a tilt-head for getting dough out and into pans. For a mostly-cookies-and-cake baker, it's a clear no; save the $80 and buy the cheaper mixer, because the reason this machine exists doesn't apply to your recipes.

Two dings for the squeaking lift lever and the undersized stock dough hook. Neither one stops me from using it daily. If I had to do it again, I'd still buy it — and I'd buy the third-party dough hook before the first batch, not after the third.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
A little bakery update from us: we’ve decided to step away from custom wedding cakes.

This was not an easy decision. Wedding cakes have been part of our work for a long time, and it has been such an honor to be invited into so many celebrations. We’ve loved hearing your stories, talking through flavors, making sugar flowers at odd hours, and seeing photos of a cake surrounded by people you love.

But as a three-person bakery, we have had to take an honest look at where our time goes.

A single wedding cake often begins with a free consultation and tasting, followed by design conversations, ordering specialty ingredients, baking, filling, frosting, decorating, delivery planning, and all the little details in between. By the time it is finished, one order can take around fourteen hours of work outside of the baking we do for the shop every day.

This year, we also had three wedding orders cancel at the last minute. We understand that plans change, and we truly do not hold that against anyone. But those cancellations meant ingredients had already been purchased and time had already been set aside, and for a small business like ours, that is a hard loss to absorb.

Most importantly, taking on custom wedding work was beginning to pull us away from the pastry case, the morning breads, the birthday cakes, and the everyday treats that bring so many of you through our door. Those are the things that keep the lights on, pay our rent, and allow us to keep showing up at 4am to make this little bakery what it is.

So we are choosing to put our energy back into the daily bakery: the croissants still warm from the oven, the cookies you pick up after school, the cakes you bring to dinner, the loaf of bread that becomes tomorrow’s toast. We’ll continue making celebration cakes in our regular style when our schedule allows, but we will no longer be offering fully custom wedding cakes.

Thank you for understanding, and thank you for continuing to support us in all the ordinary, wonderful moments in between the big ones.

b.text:
A note about custom wedding cakes

I’ve been meaning to write this for a while now, in that little stretch between the morning bake and the afternoon cleanup when the shop smells like sugar and the chairs are finally empty. It’s not the easiest thing to write, because wedding cakes carry a lot of meaning. They’re for days people wait for, days that matter, and we’ve been part of some truly lovely ones. That hasn’t changed. What’s changed is how we can make a living while still being present for the work that keeps this bakery standing.

We’re not doing custom wedding cakes anymore.

From the outside, a wedding order can look like one big job. One cake, one pickup date, one final payment. But inside the bakery, it’s not one thing at all. It’s the first messages and phone calls. It’s sitting down over samples and tasting boxes. It’s sketches, color palettes, flower choices, tier sizes, delivery logistics, reminders, back-and-forth design notes, and all the little decisions that turn a request into a piece of edible architecture. By the time a custom wedding cake comes together, we’re already about fourteen hours deep into consultations and tastings that we don’t charge for. That sounds like a small thing written down, but in a three-person shop, it isn’t small. Fourteen hours is almost two full days. It’s early mornings, later nights, and less of the steady rhythm we need to keep the lights on.

What made the decision real for us was the cancellations. This year alone we had three last-minute cancellations, and each one landed hard. We’d already ordered ingredients, some of them special, some of them bought specifically for that order. We’d already blocked off time we couldn’t sell anywhere else. When those calls came in, the cost stayed with us. There’s no easy way to absorb that, especially when every dollar we spend on an order that disappears is taken away from the people who do show up for their birthday, their anniversary, their random Wednesday, their mother’s cake, the office celebration, the “I’m getting through the week” slice.

The truth is, the everyday case is what actually pays rent. The morning bread, the simple layer cakes, the regulars who come in before work, the parents who stop by after school, the folks who ask if there’s any leftover lemon cake from yesterday — that’s what keeps us here. That’s the part of the job we’ve always loved most, too. The custom wedding cakes were taking us away from it, and I think we could feel that pull for a while without naming it. We’d been baking at 4am anyway, which is our life, but the wedding orders were quietly turning into something else: a lot of unpaid time, a lot of uncertainty, and a lot of energy spent trying to make one perfect day for someone who may never come back into the shop again.

We don’t say this with any bitterness. There’s no drama in it, just arithmetic. Love, in a bakery, has to survive the cost of butter and eggs and labor and rent. It has to leave room for the daily work. We want to keep saying yes to the person who walks in needing a cake that afternoon. We want to keep having enough hands and enough hours for the orders that come to us naturally. We want to keep this place open without feeling like every celebration has to be a gamble.

So for now, we’re closing the door on custom wedding cakes. Not with sadness exactly, but with relief. The kind you feel when you finally put down something heavy you didn’t realize you were carrying. If you’re planning a wedding and you think of us, I still want you to know that we’re grateful. It means a lot that people wanted our little bakery to be part of their big day. We just can’t make it work the way it used to.

What we can do is keep showing up. Early mornings. Fresh trays. Birthday cakes. Anniversary cakes. Friday-night cakes. The kind of cakes you can walk up to the counter and point at, or order by Tuesday and pick up on Thursday, or bake for when the weather turns and people need something sweet. That’s where our hearts are, and honestly, it’s where they’ve always been.
