setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
I’ve done close to 200 interviews over 9 years, all in-house for a logistics company乃and there’s one question I only hear from the best candidates:

“What project failed recently, and what did the team learn from it?”

Not “tell me about the culture.”
Not “what does success look like in this role.”
They ask about the failure. Specifically the recent one.

Most candidates want to know how the company wins.
The strongest ones want to know how the company loses—and what happens after.

Here’s how that conversation usually goes with a candidate I end up fighting for:

Them: “What’s a project that didn’t go as planned in the last year?”

Me: “We rolled out a new routing tool last spring. Adoption was rough. Drivers hated it, dispatchers bypassed it, and we basically ran dual systems for three months.”

Them: “What did leadership do when they realized it wasn’t working?”

Me: “We pulled the rollout back, put a few dispatchers in the room with the vendor, and rebuilt the workflow around how they actually operate—not how we assumed they would.”

Them: “So the original timeline slipped. Did that impact how you plan rollouts now?”

And that’s the moment I know. They’re not just vetting the company. They’re trying to understand how problems get solved here, who gets blamed, and whether people are allowed to speak up after things go sideways.

Most candidates interview to survive the process. The best ones interview to understand how your team actually functions when it’s not a highlight reel.

b.text:
I’ve sat through just north of 200 interviews for our operations and frontline logistics leadership roles so far this year, and for the longest time I thought the most thoughtful candidates were the ones who asked nuanced questions about team culture or upward mobility.
I was dead wrong.
The standout candidates? They all lead with the same first question when we get to Q&A: “What’s the last project your team tried that didn’t work, and what did you learn from it?”

Last week I interviewed a senior ops lead for our Northeast regional role, and he opened his Q&A with that exact line before he even asked what a typical day in the role looked like.
I didn’t sugarcoat it. I told him about the Brooklyn last-mile e-bike pilot we launched back in March: we’d crunched the spreadsheets and swore switching 2 dense urban routes from box trucks to cargo e-bikes would cut delivery times by 25% and slash fuel costs. We completely missed that our micro-fulfillment center in Bushwick had zero secure overnight bike parking, and we underestimated how many of our B2C deliveries for that route were large furniture items that didn’t fit in the bike cargo holds. We pulled the plug after 6 weeks, ate $12k in unused vendor contracts, and had to reset SLAs with 3 key retail clients we’d already promised faster delivery to.
Most candidates would nod politely, say “that makes sense,” and move on to the next prepped question.
This guy leaned in. First follow-up: “Did your team do an on-site audit of the fulfillment center footprint before you signed the bike vendor, or was that all planned from the corporate office?” Second: “Were those 3 retail clients looped into the pilot testing at all, or did you just announce the new SLA to them out of the blue?” Then he walked me through a nearly identical failed same-day delivery pilot he’d run at his last company, and laid out exactly what he’d do in his first 30 days if we wanted to revisit the e-bike idea—starting with a cross-functional kickoff with our facilities and client success teams before we spent a dime on new equipment.
He got the offer 2 days later.

Here’s the thing: no team is perfect, especially not in logistics where plans shift faster than a surprise port delay can derail your entire Q3 forecast.
For job folks reading this: This question isn’t a gotcha. It’s the fastest way to prove you’re not just interviewing for a paycheck—you’re interviewing to solve real problems for a team that’s still figuring it out. It also tells you way more about how a team operates than “what’s the culture like” ever will. Do they blame individual frontline team members for the failure? Do they brush it off like it was no big deal? Do they actually have takeaways they’ve implemented across the team? All the intel you need, in one question.
For my fellow recruiters and hiring managers: If a candidate asks you this, don’t default to the polished “we had a small misalignment” corporate answer. Be honest. The best candidates don’t want to join a “perfect” team—they want to join a team that’s self-aware enough to admit when they messed up, and hungry to fix it.

Curious to hear from both sides: Job seekers, do you ask about failed projects in your interviews? Hiring managers, what’s the most memorable question a candidate has asked that made you stop and take notice?

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now

If you’re trying to decide when to book, most people will tell you to grab a Saturday in June. After six years of shooting weddings almost entirely in this metro area, I understand the instinct. But “popular” isn’t the same as “better,” and June has some real downsides I don’t think couples hear about enough.

I’ve shot 11 winter weddings in the last two years. For this post, I’m counting November through March as winter around here, and those 11 dates taught me something I didn’t expect

b.text:
**Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now**

I used to default to peak season like everyone else. June through September felt like the “real” wedding months. Then the last two years happened, and I shot eleven winter weddings. That number surprised me when I tallied it. What surprised me more is that I started looking forward to them.

Here’s the unvarnished version of why.

First, the light. Around 3 p.m. in November, when the sun is low and the trees are bare, the light filters through in a way that is just better for portraits than the flat, even overcast you often get in June. It’s directional without being harsh. Faces look sculpted instead of washed out. Couples stand in a clearing or along a path and the background opens up instead of turning into a wall of green. I’ve had more “wait, that frame is actually perfect” moments in late afternoon winter light than I have in high summer. It’s not softer. It’s just more interesting.

Second, the logistics feel human again. In June I’m routinely pulling into a venue parking lot at the same time as three or four other vendors. Everyone’s rushing, spaces are tight, and the day already feels crowded before anyone has walked down the aisle. Winter is quieter. I can actually park, unload, and take a breath. The couple usually has more of the venue’s attention. Things move at a pace that lets me notice the small stuff—the way the light hits a ring, the quiet moment before guests arrive—instead of just surviving the schedule.

And yes, the money part is real. Winter dates typically run about 30% less for the couple. That isn’t a gimmick I invented; it’s just how demand works in this market. Same photographer, same level of coverage, same files and albums. The calendar simply has more room, so the pricing reflects it. For a lot of the couples I’ve worked with, that difference meant they could keep the photography they actually wanted instead of cutting elsewhere or settling.

I’m not going to tell you winter is magically more romantic or that every season is equally perfect. Some people want the full green-and-gold summer look and that’s completely valid. But if you’re looking at dates and feeling the pressure of peak season—or if the idea of softer light, fewer people in the parking lot, and a meaningful savings sounds appealing—winter is not the compromise I once assumed it was. I’ve shot eleven of them in two years. The work holds up. The days feel better. And the portraits… honestly, some of my favorites now have bare branches in them.

If you’re still deciding when to book, I’m happy to talk through what a winter timeline actually looks like for your venue and style. No pitch, just the practical side from someone who’s been there eleven times recently.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
Every Saturday since sophomore year, I've been at my parents' restaurant from ten in the morning to ten at night.

One Saturday in October the register system died. The screen went black and nothing brought it back. My dad called the company and they said someone could come Monday. It was 11:30 and we had a lunch rush coming. I grabbed a stack of order slips from the back office and a pen. I wrote down every order by hand, added the tax, totaled it. The math wasn't hard but doing it fast while people were waiting was. I underlined each total twice because that's what the printed receipts did. For four days I ran the front with a pen, a calculator, and a shoebox of cash. A few customers said they liked the handwritten tickets. One guy called it "charming." It wasn't charming. It was the thing that had to happen so we could keep taking orders.

We hired a new server in September. Her name is Destiny and she goes to the school across town. This is her first job. My grandma still comes in on weekends to make the spring rolls, and she's particular about the fold. If you can see the shrimp through the wrapper, it's wrong. The shrimp should be centered. One Saturday my grandma was tired and asked me to show Destiny. I'd watched my grandma do it hundreds of times. I'd done it maybe fifty. I showed Destiny how to soak the wrapper for four seconds, lay the lettuce flat, fold the sides in, roll tight. My hands knew what to do even though I'd never thought about explaining it. Destiny's first three came out loose and she kept apologizing. I told her it took me a long time too, which is true. I didn't tell her my grandma said my first ones looked like egg rolls.

On breaks I do homework in the walk-in cooler. It's forty degrees in there and it smells like cilantro and raw pork. I sit on a plastic milk crate and spread my stuff out on a cardboard box of bean sprouts. Last month I did forty-five minutes of calculus in there, derivatives. My fingers were stiff by the time I got back to the dining room. My manager is my mom. She doesn't always remember I have homework, or she remembers but there are tables to clear. I do homework in small pieces. Twenty minutes here, fifteen there. Sometimes in the cooler, sometimes at a corner table when it's slow. I've gotten good at stopping in the middle of a problem and picking it back up three hours later.

I don't know what I'm supposed to say about all this. I work weekends. I do my homework in a cooler. I teach people to fold spring rolls the way my grandma does. It's just what my life is.

b.text:
I work weekends at my family's Vietnamese restaurant. Every Saturday and Sunday since sophomore year.

The register died one Saturday during lunch. Line out the door, dining room full. I grabbed a pad and a pen and started writing tickets. Table 12, two pho dac biet, one bun, extra herbs. I'd write it, tear the sheet, pass it through the window. Kitchen yelled when they couldn't read my writing. We went through the whole pad. My hand hurt by the time my dad got the system working again around three.

We hired someone new last month. I showed him how my grandma folds the spring rolls. Lay the rice paper down, filling in a straight line, fold the sides in first so nothing spills, then roll it. Tight enough it holds, not so tight it splits. He kept making them loose in the middle. I did a few more while he watched, then let him try again.

Breaks I take my calc book into the walk-in. Sit on a box of sprouts, do the problems. Fan noise, cold air. Fingers stiff after a while. When the break's over I put the book away and go back out.

That's the weekends.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
The fluorescent lights in the ER buzzed like they always do, too bright and too steady. My first week, and I was already learning that time moves different here. Slower when someone’s hurting, faster when everything’s falling apart.

I remember the man with the deep gash on his forearm. He’d been cutting wood when the saw slipped. His wife was on her way, but traffic was bad, and he kept glancing at the door like he could will her there faster. The nurse told me to stay with him while she prepped the supplies. I didn’t know what to say, so I just held his hand. His palm was rough, calloused from work, and he squeezed mine a little too tight when the antiseptic touched the wound. “You’re doing great,” I told him, even though I wasn’t sure if that was true. He exhaled like he’d been holding his breath for hours.

Then there was the code. I’d only seen them on TV before, but this was nothing like that. No dramatic slow-motion, no one shouting for a crash cart—just a team moving fast, voices low and urgent. I got sent to restock gauze, which felt stupid at first, like I was in the way. But through the curtain, I could hear them counting compressions. “One, two, three…” The numbers were steady, but the air in the room wasn’t. I stood there with my arms full of supplies, listening, until someone called for me to bring more gloves.

And the blood draw. The diabetic man with veins like spiderwebs. I missed the first time, then the second, then the third. His skin was thin, bruising easy, and I could see the frustration in his eyes. “I’m sorry,” I kept saying, like that would make it better. The nurse watched me the fourth time, her arms crossed, and I took a deep breath before trying again. When the needle finally went in, I almost cried. He just patted my shoulder and said, “It’s okay, kid. You’ll get better.”

I don’t know if I did anything important that week. I held a hand. I restocked gauze. I missed a blood draw three times. But I think that’s the point—it’s not always about the big moments. Sometimes it’s about showing up, even when you’re scared, even when you’re not sure you’re doing it right. I’m still not sure. But I know I want to keep trying.

b.text:
I walked into the ER on my first clinical day with my stomach in knots. I had the book knowledge, the mannequin practice, the very clean, very quiet skills lab. None of it prepared me for the noise.

The first thing I remember clearly is a man in his sixties with a deep gash on his forearm. The doctor numbed him up and started cleaning, and the man’s face went tight. His wife had been on her way for forty minutes, stuck in traffic, and you could see he was trying to be tough. I didn’t know what else to do, so I asked if he wanted me to hold his hand. He looked surprised, then nodded. I stood there while the wound was flushed and stitched, his grip strong, and I didn’t say much. When his wife finally rushed in, she took my place and he smiled at me. That was it. I didn’t dress the wound or calculate a drip rate. I just showed up. I think that matters, too.

The second day, something happened that I wasn’t supposed to see. A code blue came in, a man who’d crashed his bike. The room filled up fast with staff, all moving in a kind of controlled rush. My instructor told me to go restock the gauze carts in the hallway. It was busy work, the kind of task that makes you feel invisible. But the curtain was thin. I heard someone call out “starting compressions,” and then the counting started. Steady, one after another. I could hear the rhythm of it, the pause for breaths, and under that the beeping of machines. I just kept pulling packages of gauze, loading the drawers, and listening. Nobody needed me in that room. I was too new. But standing outside that curtain, I understood that nursing isn’t only about being the hands on the chest. Sometimes it’s about making sure everything else is ready. That moment taught me what teamwork really means. I was a tiny part of something big, and I felt it.

The third thing I remember is the blood draw. A diabetic patient with veins that rolled and hid. I stuck him once, twice, three times, and missed every one. My face burned. My preceptor, a nurse named Ellen, just watched and waited. The patient, a man named Rafael, was patient too. He had the kind of tired look that comes from years of needles. I was about to apologize and step away, but Ellen said quietly, “Try one more time.” So I did. I felt the vein before I saw it, a faint little give under my fingers. The fourth try, the flash of blood in the chamber. I capped it and looked up, and Rafael gave me a small nod. Ellen didn’t clap, just said, “Good. Now label it.” I learned more about nursing in that five minutes than I had in a month of lectures. Persistence. Trust. The fact that patients are willing to give you a chance even when you’re learning.

I’m still a first-year student. I have a thousand skills yet to learn. But after that first week in the ER, I know I’m where I’m supposed to be. Nursing isn’t all about the big saves. It’s the small stuff—a hand to hold, a stocked cart, a fourth try. This scholarship would help me keep showing up, keep learning, and keep getting better at the small stuff that honestly doesn’t feel small at all.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
After 8 years shooting weddings full-time here in the Texas Hill Country, I can tell you this:

The couples who ditch the rigid shot list almost always end up with my favorite galleries.

Not because planning doesn't matter. It does. But because space leaves room for the real stuff to happen.

The Barrera wedding is the perfect example.

We had planned for wide-open sky. Then the rain came in fast and we moved everything under the pecan tree. Ceremony, portraits, family — all of it, tighter, darker, completely different than what we walked in expecting.

They didn't panic. They didn't pull out a checklist and try to force the original plan. They just stayed present with each other and their people and trusted the team to adapt.

And honestly? Those pecan tree portraits are some of my favorites I've ever delivered. Moody light, everyone close, rain on the leaves overhead. You can't pose that. You can't put it on a shot list.

For engaged couples researching photographers: Look for someone you trust enough to let go a little on the day. That's where the magic is.

For fellow vendors: Those pivots are so much smoother when we give couples permission to be flexible upfront.

Hill Country weather will do what it wants. Let it.

b.text:
8 years full-time. About 35 weddings a year. The best photos almost never come from the shot list.

The Barrera wedding proved that to me again.

We had a plan. Golden hour portraits in the Hill Country. Family formals by the oak. A timeline that looked perfect on paper.

Then the rain came.

Within minutes, we moved everything under the pecan tree. No dramatic reset. No forced poses. Just a couple looking at each other, laughing, and saying, “Let’s just be here.”

That’s the wedding I still think about.

Not because we checked every box. Because the photos show what actually happened: rain on the tent, grandparents huddled close, the groom’s hand on her back, kids dancing in wet grass, the two of them stealing a quiet minute under the branches while everyone else was eating.

The couples who ditch the shot list aren’t being careless. They’re choosing presence over production. They trust their photographer to catch the real stuff, and they give themselves permission to feel the day instead of perform it.

A shot list can be a safety net. But the images that matter most come from the moments you didn’t plan.

If you’re engaged: hire someone you trust, then let the day happen. If you’re a vendor: protect the buffer, embrace the pivot, and watch what unfolds.

Barrera wedding. Rained out. Moved under a pecan tree. Still one of my favorites.

#TexasHillCountryWeddings #WeddingPhotography #WeddingPlanning

setup: A high-school biology teacher is writing a cover letter to a customer success hiring manager at the edtech company.

a.text:
Dear Hiring Manager,

For the last two years, [Product Name] has been the engine of my biology labs. After eight years in the high school classroom, I know exactly what your customers are going through, because I’ve been one of your power users. 

I didn't just use your platform with my students; I served as the campus admin. I managed our school's rollout, trained my colleagues, and served as the first line of defense for technical issues. I know the platform inside and out, from configuring student accounts to troubleshooting lab simulations. 

Teaching is essentially customer success in a high-stakes environment. Every semester, I successfully onboarded 30 new students with varying levels of tech fluency. When lab tech failed or grades slipped, I navigated those conversations with frustrated parents—de-escalating tension, identifying root causes, and keeping them bought into the educational process. If I can explain a complex virtual biology lab to a stressed teenager and pacify an angry parent, I can absolutely guide a district administrator through a software rollout and drive product adoption.

I am leaving the classroom to support educators on a larger scale. I know firsthand what it takes to make a school successful with your product, and I am ready to bring that frontline, admin-level perspective to your Customer Success team. I look forward to discussing how my eight years in the trenches can help your users thrive. 

Best regards,

[Your Name]

b.text:
For two years, [Product Name] ran my biology classroom. I graded quizzes with it, built labs with it, and spent more time in the analytics dashboard than I did with my gradebook. So when I say I'm applying to your Customer Success team, I'm not flipping through a brochure—I'm the user who called support at 11 p.m. in March begging you to fix a broken LMS sync before finals.

Eight years as a high-school biology teacher was, among other things, a masterclass in customer success. Every August I onboarded thirty students who'd never touched the platform, walked them through a login, and then spent October troubleshooting why one kid's iPad kept logging him into his *sister's* account. That's onboarding, training, and tier-one support, repeated every semester, whether the class was into biology or would rather be at a lacrosse practice.

Handling parents is its own discipline. I de-escalated phone calls about a "D" that was really a missing quiz, talked a furious mom through how the product actually calculates her son's participation grade, and once got a grandparent to stop emailing the district superintendent and just email me instead. I learned to translate "this app is broken" into "here's what's happening and here's how we fix it," which sounds a lot like a CS call log.

For two of those eight years I served as our campus administrator for [Product Name]—managing licenses, coordinating PD sessions for colleagues, logging tickets, and feeding feature requests upstream. I was, in practice, your de facto implementation contact for a 900-student school. I know your roadmap conversations, your seasonal crunches, and the specific questions a first-year science teacher asks in September.

I'm not leaving the classroom because I'm done with kids or with this product. I'm leaving because I realized the work I loved most wasn't the lab—was the moment a reluctant teacher said, "Okay, maybe I'll actually use this thing next period," and I'd helped them get there. I want to do that at scale.

I'd love ten minutes to talk about what your next cohort of onboarding schools looks like and where I can help you keep them.

Thank you for your time.

[Email] · [Phone]

That doesn't happen by posting a sign-up sheet. That happens because someone asked them directly and made it feel worth doing.

And then the number came in. More than double last year. I actually read it twice.

I want to be specific about what that means, because I think you should know exactly where your week went. That money is the classroom library. It's the copies of books that get passed around until the covers fall off. It's being able to say yes when a kid asks if we have anything else by an author they just discovered. It's the difference between a shelf that looks like a shelf and one that looks like someone actually cares what's on it. You bought that for my students this year, and for the other English classrooms too.

I know "volunteer" is the word we use, but what you did this week was a job, and you did it better than most people do their actual jobs. Please don't let me catch you shrugging this off.

Thank you, Renata. Truly.

With real gratitude,

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
This spring, the rain wouldn’t let up. By the late May planting deadline, I’d only managed to get 60% of my acres in the ground—soybeans and corn sitting idle while the fields stayed soggy. Now, the USDA’s 22% hike in prevented planting premiums has landed like a ton of wet topsoil on family farms like mine.

That 22% increase? It’s costing me an extra $46,000 this year. And because of how the acreage caps are structured, operations my size get hit harder proportionally than the bigger farms down the road. It’s not just about the money—it’s about fairness. The system’s stacked against the folks who’ve been working this land for generations.

SB 214 would fix the acreage cap issue. Call your legislators. Tell them to support it. The rain won’t wait, and neither should they.

b.text:
This spring I planted 60 percent of my soybean and corn acres by the late-May prevented-planting deadline. The rest sat wet. USDA raised the prevented-planting base rate 22 percent in our region this year, and on my operation that works out to about $46,000 in extra premium.

The acreage cap is what makes the increase land so hard. Once you hit the cap, additional acres do not dilute the rate the way they do on a larger farm. A family operation like mine, four generations on the same ground, pays a higher share of the hike per planted acre than the bigger operations a few miles down the road. Same weather. Same deadline. Different bill.

Prevented planting is supposed to cover a year the rain takes the crop. A 22 percent jump, stacked on a cap that penalizes smaller acreage bases, turns that coverage into a fixed cost we cannot spread. SB 214 would fix the acreage cap so the premium tracks the risk instead of the size of the farm. County members should tell their legislators to support it.

I dropped the ball on making sure she was following our procedures properly, and I'm sorry.

- I'm putting in a mandatory ID check at the door for every pickup, every time. The ID has to match a name on the approved pickup list before the child is brought out. No exceptions.
- The sub will not be back in my home until she has been fully retrained on our pickup procedures and I'm confident she understands them. Honestly, I'm going to sit down and go over the policy with every helper again, because this can't happen once, let alone twice.
- I'm going through the rest of our pickup process too, looking for any other gaps where something like this could slip through.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
**Why I’ve Fallen for Winter Weddings (And Why You Might Too)**

I’ll be honest—six years ago, I wasn’t exactly *thrilled* when a couple asked me to shoot their January wedding. Cold fingers, slippery sidewalks, the sun setting before cocktail hour… what was there to love? But after shooting 11 winter weddings in the last two years, I’ve officially changed my tune. Here’s why:

**1. The Light is *Chef’s Kiss***
That soft, golden glow you get in June? It’s nice, but it’s also *everywhere*—and often drowned out by thick cloud cover. Winter light, though? Around 3 PM in November or December, the sun hangs low, filtering through bare branches like a natural diffuser. The result? Portraits with depth, warmth, and a moodiness that flat summer light just can’t match.

**2. Fewer Crowds, More Focus**
In June, I’m sharing the venue parking lot with three other photographers, a videographer, and a florist’s van. Winter weddings? It’s just me, the couple, and maybe a rogue squirrel. Fewer distractions mean I can actually *see* the details—the way the candlelight flickers on your dress, the steam rising from your coffee during golden hour, the quiet moments that get lost in the chaos of peak season.

**3. Your Budget Goes Further**
Winter weddings run about 30% cheaper on average. That’s not just a rumor—it’s a fact. Venues, caterers, even some vendors (ahem) offer off-season rates. That extra cash could mean an extra hour of coverage, a second shooter, or even just breathing room in your budget for the things that matter most.

**4. The Coziness Factor**
There’s something magical about a winter wedding. The crackle of a fireplace, the way your breath hangs in the air during a first-look moment, the glow of string lights against a dark sky. Summer weddings are vibrant, but winter weddings? They’re *intimate*. And intimacy is what makes for photos that feel like *you*.

So if you’re on the fence about a winter wedding, let me be the one to say: don’t write it off. The light is better, the crowds are smaller, and the memories? Just as unforgettable. (And yes, I *will* bring hand warmers.)

b.text:
**Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now**

I used to default to peak season like everyone else. June through September felt like the “real” wedding months. Then the last two years happened, and I shot eleven winter weddings. That number surprised me when I tallied it. What surprised me more is that I started looking forward to them.

Here’s the unvarnished version of why.

First, the light. Around 3 p.m. in November, when the sun is low and the trees are bare, the light filters through in a way that is just better for portraits than the flat, even overcast you often get in June. It’s directional without being harsh. Faces look sculpted instead of washed out. Couples stand in a clearing or along a path and the background opens up instead of turning into a wall of green. I’ve had more “wait, that frame is actually perfect” moments in late afternoon winter light than I have in high summer. It’s not softer. It’s just more interesting.

Second, the logistics feel human again. In June I’m routinely pulling into a venue parking lot at the same time as three or four other vendors. Everyone’s rushing, spaces are tight, and the day already feels crowded before anyone has walked down the aisle. Winter is quieter. I can actually park, unload, and take a breath. The couple usually has more of the venue’s attention. Things move at a pace that lets me notice the small stuff—the way the light hits a ring, the quiet moment before guests arrive—instead of just surviving the schedule.

And yes, the money part is real. Winter dates typically run about 30% less for the couple. That isn’t a gimmick I invented; it’s just how demand works in this market. Same photographer, same level of coverage, same files and albums. The calendar simply has more room, so the pricing reflects it. For a lot of the couples I’ve worked with, that difference meant they could keep the photography they actually wanted instead of cutting elsewhere or settling.

I’m not going to tell you winter is magically more romantic or that every season is equally perfect. Some people want the full green-and-gold summer look and that’s completely valid. But if you’re looking at dates and feeling the pressure of peak season—or if the idea of softer light, fewer people in the parking lot, and a meaningful savings sounds appealing—winter is not the compromise I once assumed it was. I’ve shot eleven of them in two years. The work holds up. The days feel better. And the portraits… honestly, some of my favorites now have bare branches in them.

If you’re still deciding when to book, I’m happy to talk through what a winter timeline actually looks like for your venue and style. No pitch, just the practical side from someone who’s been there eleven times recently.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
Friday night was a tough pill to swallow. Finishing a high school football season 8-2 is a fantastic achievement by any local standard, but when that second loss sends you packing in Round 2 of the state playoffs, it stings. It burns even more when the team ending your season is the exact same squad you ran off the field by 20 points back in Week 3.

Look, nobody can take away what this offense accomplished this fall. Dez Kowalski was nothing short of electric under center. He threw for 2,340 yards this year, shattering the school record and giving us highlight-reel throws every single week. If you had told me in August that we’d have a 2,300-yard passer, I’d have printed state championship tickets right then and there. 

But Friday night proved that a shiny passing record doesn’t win a gritty November playoff game on its own. I’ll just say what everyone shivering in the bleachers was already thinking: we panicked. We completely abandoned the run game in the second half, and for the life of me, I can't figure out why. 

We were only down by three points. A single field goal. More importantly, the ground game was actually working. We were getting push up front, moving the chains, and controlling the tempo. Instead of sticking to the script and wearing out a defensive line we already proved we could bully, the play-calling suddenly turned into a frantic 7-on-7 drill. 

When you start dropping back on every down in a tight, one-possession game, you let the opposing defense pin their ears back and ignore the run entirely. That’s exactly what happened. The pass rush teed off, the drives stalled, and we watched a winnable playoff game slip right through our fingers. 

You don't reinvent the wheel when you're only trailing by three. It's a bitter end to an undeniably great season, and a harsh lesson in playoff football. Congratulations to Dez and the seniors on an unforgettable 8-2 run, but that second-half play sheet is going to keep this coaching staff awake until August.

b.text:
**The Run They Abandoned**

The season ended at 8-2, which sounds respectable until you remember that second-round state loss came to the same team they beat by 20 back in week three. The gap between those two games wasn’t talent; it was a decision made in one half.

Dez Kowalski finished with 2,340 yards, a new school record, and if you watched him all fall you know the passing attack was never the weakness. The weakness came in the second half of that playoff game. They were only down three, the run game was working, and they went away from it. You don’t need three examples to see the mistake—just the scoreboard and common sense. When you abandon the ground game with a one-score deficit, you’re not coaching to win; you’re coaching not to lose.

Kowalski’s arm gave them every chance to pull it out, but you don’t win state games by asking one kid to carry the second half through the air while the ground game sits. They had it working, they had a shot, and they let it slip because they stopped trusting it.

That’s not a lack of heart. That’s a coaching mistake, plain and simple. And it’s the only reason an 8-2 team with a record-setting quarterback ends up going home early. Next year, maybe they’ll remember that running the ball isn’t old-fashioned—it’s how you erase a three-point hole.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
An 8-2 season deserves applause. It doesn’t mean the ending is above criticism.

The second-round state playoff loss will sting because this was a team they had beaten by 20 back in Week 3. That earlier result didn’t guarantee anything in the rematch. But it makes the question harder to shake: Was this a game they had to lose?

My answer is no. And the biggest reason is what happened to the running game in the second half.

It was working. They were down only three points. Yet they moved away from it as though the deficit demanded an entirely different offense.

Three points is a reason to stay patient, not abandon something the defense hasn’t stopped. Keep taking the yards. Make the opponent prove it can handle the run before deciding to do that job for it.

That isn’t a knock on Dez Kowalski. His 2,340 passing yards set a school record, an accomplishment that deserves to stand on its own—not get buried beneath the disappointment of the final game. He gave this offense a weapon few teams in school history have had.

But having a record-setting quarterback doesn’t make every situation a passing situation. A productive ground game helps a quarterback. Going back to it would not have been a vote of no confidence in Kowalski. It would have been a vote for what was working.

It’s easy to second-guess after a loss, and no play call comes with a guarantee. Staying with the run might not have changed the result. Still, the criticism here isn’t simply that the chosen approach failed. It’s that the score and the success on the ground offered little reason to leave that approach behind.

The players earned those eight wins. Kowalski earned his place in the record book. Neither should be diminished by one painful night.

But celebrating a good season doesn’t require pretending its final chapter was handled well. This team had a working running game and a three-point deficit. It needed patience more than a change of plans.

b.text:
If you listened to the postgame show on the radio Friday night, you already know my voice is half-gone. By Saturday morning, the coffee at the diner tasted a little bitter, and I know I’m not the only one in town feeling that way. 

An 8-2 season is nothing to sneeze at. In fact, for most programs, it’s a banner year. We got to watch Dez Kowalski rewrite the history books, slinging the rock for a school-record 2,340 yards. The kid has a cannon for an arm and gave us ten weeks of fireworks. When the dust settles and the sting wears off, this senior class deserves a standing ovation for giving this town a whale of a ride.

But right now, it stings. Because this season ended two weeks too early, and it ended at the hands of a team we beat by 20 points back in Week 3. 

There’s an old coaching adage that it’s tough to beat a good team twice in one season. That’s true enough. What’s also true is that it’s tough to win a November playoff game when you outsmart yourself after halftime. 

Let’s call a spade a spade: we didn't get beat Friday night so much as we handed the game away by abandoning the run in the second half. 

Coming out of the locker room in the third quarter, we were only down by three points. It was a dogfight, sure, and the weather had a bite to it, which is exactly why the ground game was our best friend. Our offensive line was getting a push, and we were chewing up five, six yards a pop between the tackles. It wasn't flashy, and it wasn’t going to pad any passing stats, but it was working. 

Then, for reasons that still have me scratching my head, the play-calling went completely off the rails. We came out in the third quarter and started throwing the ball almost exclusively, as if we were down by three touchdowns instead of a field goal. 

I get the temptation. When you have a record-breaking quarterback like Kowalski, you want to let the chef cook. You want the knockout punch. 

Playoff football, however, isn't about knockout punches. It’s about body blows. Once we stopped handing the ball off, their defensive ends stopped respecting the run, pinned their ears back, and made Dez’s life miserable in the pocket. The clock stopped on incomplete passes, our defense stayed on the field way too long, and a three-point deficit slowly bled into a season-ending loss. 

It’s a tough pill to swallow knowing the recipe for a quarterfinal berth was right there in front of us, and we just refused to use it. We had the better team in Week 3, and frankly, we still had the better team on Friday night. 

The pads are getting turned in this week, and basketball shoes are already squeaking in the gym. Time marches on. I’m proud of these kids, and I’m grateful for the Friday nights they gave us this fall. I just wish we’d run the dang ball.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
In roughly 200 interviews for logistics roles, the best candidates almost always ask a version of the same question:

“Tell me about your last failed project.”

At first, it can feel like a strange question in an interview. Not “what’s your culture like?” or “what’s the biggest opportunity?” — but failure.

When a strong candidate asks it, though, it usually means they’re not trying to perform. They’re trying to understand the job.

The good ones don’t ask it as a trap. They ask it plainly:

“Did the WMS migration go well?”

And if I’m honest, I say no.

Then the conversation gets much better:

Candidate: “Was it the tech, the timelines, or the adoption on the floor?”

Me: “Mostly the timelines. We underestimated how much time the warehouse crews needed to trust and adapt to the new process.”

Candidate: “Fair. So for the person stepping into this role, what’s the first thing they’d need to fix?”

That’s the moment they stand out.

They’re not just asking what went wrong. They’re asking what they’d actually have to deal with after day one.

For hiring managers: that question is a signal.

For recruiters: let the conversation go that deep. The right candidates often want the truth more than they want polish.

For candidates: asking about failure isn’t rude. It’s due diligence.

b.text:
~200 interviews in, I've noticed one question that separates the best candidates from everyone else. It's not about growth, culture, or "what does success look like."

It's: "Tell me about your last failed project."

The strongest people I interview don't ask whether we fail. They assume we do. They want to know what happens next.

One example from a few months back. Ops manager candidate, interview going fine, nothing remarkable. Their turn to ask questions:

"Tell me about the last project here that actually failed. Not a setback. A failure."

Our ops director paused, then told them about a WMS cutover we botched a couple years ago. Three weeks of wrecked pick rates, a couple of accounts that walked, some very uncomfortable retrospectives. Didn't sugarcoat any of it.

Then the candidate asked the follow-up that told me everything:

"Are the people who ran it still here? And did anything structurally change?"

That's not a gotcha. That's due diligence. They were mapping how failure moves through this company — does it get owned and fixed, or buried along with whoever touched it?

We hired them. A few months in they killed one of our internal projects that wasn't working. Early, cleanly, no drama. I think about that a lot.

If you're interviewing somewhere: this question costs you nothing and reveals almost everything about how a company treats people when things go wrong.

If you're hiring: notice who asks it. In my experience, the people who ask about your failures have survived a few of their own.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam – 14-Month, 140K-Mile Review

I’ve had the Roadstar DC4 in my rig for 14 months and roughly 140,000 miles now. Here’s the no-BS take for other owner-ops.

Rear camera night footage gets grainy past about 30 feet. You can see shapes and know something’s there, but plates and details are a blur. Not a deal-killer, just keep it in mind. The front camera is fine.

The real payoff: it caught a lane-change accident where a four-wheeler drifted into me. That footage got my insurance claim approved in 9 days. Normally, without video, I’d be fighting for six weeks. That single event made the camera worth the money.

Mounting was a headache at first. The suction mount let go twice in summer heat — the cab gets hot, and the thing just drops. I switched to the adhesive mount, and it hasn’t budged since. Skip the frustration and use the adhesive from day one.

The app wants a WiFi connection to pull footage, which is useless at most truck stops. I don’t even bother. I just pull the SD card and transfer files directly to my laptop. Simple, and it works every time.

For the price, it’s holding up fine. If you need a dash cam that captures what matters and pays for itself on one claim, this one does the job. Just plan on the adhesive mount and SD card transfers, and accept the rear cam’s night limits.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam – 14-Month / 140k-Mile Review**

Put about 140,000 miles on the Roadstar DC4 over the last 14 months running cross-country. Figured I’d drop a quick write-up for anyone looking to upgrade their cab setup.

**The Good:**
It already paid for itself. Had a four-wheeler try to slide into my lane and clip my steer tire, then tried telling the trooper I ran him off the road. Handed the footage over, and my insurance claim was fully approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6-week headache. Front video quality is sharp day and night, license plates show up clear, and the unit hasn't frozen up once despite constant cab vibration.

**The Bad:**
* **The Mount:** Toss the suction cup straight into the trash. It dropped off my windshield twice during the heat of July. Swapped to the included 3M adhesive mount and haven't had an issue since.
* **Rear Cam:** Fine during the day, but night footage gets real grainy past about 30 feet. It’ll prove positioning if somebody rear-ends you, but don't expect to read a plate number at distance in the dark.
* **The App:** Total waste of time. It requires a solid Wi-Fi connection to pull footage to your phone, which is useless when you’re parked in the back row of a packed truck stop with zero signal. Save yourself the blood pressure spike and just keep a cheap USB-C/Lightning SD card reader in your glovebox. Pull the card, plug it into your phone or tablet, done.

**Bottom Line:**
It’s got quirks, but it turns on every time I key the ignition, survives rough roads, and kept an at-fault accident off my record. Good enough for me. Worth a look if you need reliable coverage without spending four figures.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
**Turf the girls' soccer field. It's past time.**

Nine games. That's how many the girls' soccer team has had rained out or moved off our home field in the last two seasons. Not because of storms you'd remember. Because the field floods after an ordinary Tuesday rain and doesn't drain for days.

When a game gets moved, here's what that actually looks like. I'm on the phone at 6 a.m. with the other coach trying to find a field. Parents who took off work to come watch find out at lunch that we're now playing 40 minutes away, or on a Saturday, or not at all. Girls who've been looking forward to a home game all week get on a bus instead. Senior night got moved last year. We played it on the visitors' field.

That's the inconvenient part. Here's the dangerous part.

Last October one of my players tore her ACL. She wasn't tackled. Nobody touched her. She was running for a ball and her foot went into a rut where the field had flooded, dried out, and been chewed up by the previous week's practice. She's had surgery. She's looking at nine months to a year of rehab. She may or may not play in college like she'd planned.

I'm not going to pretend a turf field prevents every knee injury. It doesn't. But that injury was not bad luck. It was a hole in the ground that shouldn't have been there, on a field that can't hold up to the use it gets. Anyone who has walked our field in the spring knows exactly what I'm talking about. You can't get through a practice without somebody rolling an ankle in a soft spot.

The football field got turf in 2019. I was glad when it happened. Nobody argued that the boys should keep playing on mud. The reasoning was that it would cut down on cancellations, reduce injuries from bad footing, and hold up to heavy use. All of that turned out to be true. The football field hasn't lost a home game to weather since.

Every one of those reasons applies to the girls' soccer field. The difference is we've been waiting six years and it's still not in the budget.

I don't think anybody on the board sat down and decided the girls matter less. I think the football field got done because it had loud support and it was in front of people. The soccer field is out behind the bus lot and the girls have mostly just dealt with it. That's on me too. I should have been making noise about this a long time ago.

So I'm making noise now, before the facilities vote.

The cost is real. I'm not going to wave it away. But this district already knows what a turf field costs and what it saves, because we did it once. We know the maintenance numbers. We know how many hours the football field gets used now compared to when it was grass, including by other teams and community groups. Run the same numbers for the soccer field. Then add in what it costs to bus a team to a rented field nine times, and what it costs a family when their kid needs knee surgery.

And if the answer is that we can only afford one turf field in this district, then we should be asking why it's fine for the boys to have it and not the girls. I don't think anyone wants to make that argument out loud. So let's not put ourselves in the position of having to.

I coach because I like the kids and I like the sport. I don't do this to write letters to the newspaper. But I've got a player on crutches and a schedule I can't trust, and I've run out of ways to explain to fifteen-year-olds why their field is the one that never gets fixed.

Put the turf in the budget. Come out to a practice first if you want. Bring boots.

b.text:
PUT TURF ON THE GIRLS’ SOCCER FIELD

I’m not a writer. I coach girls’ soccer and track at the high school. I do it for the stipend and because I like the kids, not because I’ve been waiting for an excuse to write a column. But the school board is voting on next year’s facilities budget, and if I don’t say this plainly, nobody will.

Start with the record. Over the last two seasons, we’ve had nine girls’ soccer games rained out or moved because our grass field floods. Nine games. Not nine practices. Nine games. That’s bus trips to other towns, games crammed into already packed weeks, and home dates we just lose. It’s also a message to every girl on the roster: your season is the one that gets washed away.

And it’s not just inconvenient. Last October, one of my players stepped in a rut on that field and tore her ACL. Surgery. Rehab. Season over. Maybe you can write that off as a fluke, but it wasn’t. It was a hole in a field that gets chewed up and never really recovers. You can’t keep calling that bad luck. That’s what happens when a field is unsafe.

I also coach track, so I know what a proper surface does. You don’t hand a sprinter a mud pit and call it a track. You shouldn’t hand my soccer players a flooded, rutted field and call it a home field.

Now look across campus. The boys’ football field got turf back in 2019. Same district. Same taxpayers. Same school board. When it storms, that field drains and stays playable. My girls get standing water, mud, and cancellations. I’m not saying anybody sat in a room and decided to shortchange girls’ soccer. I’m saying the result is the same either way. Five years later, it’s still not right, and it’s past time to fix it.

I know the first objection will be money. The budget is tight; it always is. But grass isn’t free. We pay to mow it, water it, seed it, fertilize it, paint it, and babysit it—and after all that, we still cancel games on it. Turf costs more up front, and then it’s there. Rain or shine. October or April. Practice, game, PE class, youth league. It drains, it holds up, and it doesn’t hide holes the way a worn-out grass field does. No field is injury-proof, but a field that floods nine times in two seasons is a hazard we’ve chosen to live with for too long.

So here’s the ask, and it’s not fancy. Fund turf for the girls’ soccer field in next year’s facilities budget. Not a new stadium. Not lights. Not a press box. Just a field that doesn’t turn into a pond and doesn’t eat kids’ knees.

The board has a vote coming up. If you’re a parent, a player, a former athlete, or just somebody who thinks girls’ sports should get the same basic footing as boys’ sports, show up or send an email. I coach for the stipend, and I’m not going to pretend I enjoy writing this. But I enjoy watching my players lose games to mud and lose seasons to injuries even less. Nine rainouts is too many. One ACL is too many. Five years of waiting is too long. Fix the field.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
# Devlog #47: It's Out

Okay. So the game is out. It's been out for a week. I keep typing that sentence and deleting it because it still feels fake.

Here's what actually happened.

**412 copies.** That's the number after week one. I don't have anything to compare it to and I'm not going to pretend I know if that's good or bad. It's more than my mom and my three friends, which is the only threshold I'd actually set for myself out loud. Three years of nights and weekends and it's a real number on a real dashboard now.

For about six hours I was on the front page of a small subreddit. I watched the concurrent player count tick up in real time like an idiot, refreshing everything. Then it fell off the front page and things went quiet again, which is how these things go. But for those six hours it was genuinely happening.

**The floaty movement thing.** One reviewer said the movement feels floaty. I read it, got a little defensive for about ninety seconds, and then went and played my own game with fresh eyes and — yeah. They're right. It's floaty. I've played this build so many thousands of times that I stopped feeling it. So that's getting fixed. Reworking the acceleration and the fall curves, tightening the jump. That's the big thing in **1.1, coming next month.** Also cleaning up a couple of collision spots people flagged.

That's it. That's the update. Game's out, some people bought it, one person was right about the jumping, and I'm patching it.

More when 1.1 is close.

b.text:
# One Week After Launch

The game launched last week, after three years of nights-and-weekends work, and somehow 412 people bought it in the first seven days.

That number still feels strange to look at. I’d spent so long thinking about the game as a folder on my PC that seeing hundreds of actual players show up was a little surreal.

Launch day itself was mostly me refreshing dashboards, answering messages, and checking that nothing had caught fire. A post about the game also reached the front page of a small subreddit for about six hours, which caused the biggest spike in traffic. Watching it climb was exciting. Watching it disappear again was probably good for my blood pressure.

The reviews so far have been encouraging, along with a few useful criticisms. One review said the movement feels floaty, and honestly, they’re right. It’s one of those things I got used to after playing the game for hundreds of hours, but it’s much more obvious when someone new picks it up.

I’m working on that now. Version 1.1 is planned for next month and will include tighter movement, some smaller balance changes, bug fixes, and a few quality-of-life improvements based on player feedback.

For now, I’m reading every report, watching playthroughs when people post them, and making a list of everything that needs attention. Thanks to everyone who bought the game, left a review, shared the launch post, or sent me a message.

Back to the movement code.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
**Turf the Girls Soccer Field. Now.**

*By a girls' soccer and track coach*

Nine games. That’s how many games my girls soccer team has had rained out or moved in the last two seasons because our grass field floods. Not because the other team was better. Not because we didn’t practice. Because the field can’t handle rain.

Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping in a rut on that same field. A rut. Not a collision, not a bad slide tackle. A hole in the grass. She’s still not back. That’s not bad luck. That’s a facility problem.

The boys football field got turf in 2019. They play on a surface that drains, that doesn’t rut, that doesn’t turn into mud. My girls are still playing on a field that floods every time it rains hard. That’s not a coaching issue. That’s not a talent issue. That’s a fairness issue.

I’m not asking for a new stadium. I’m asking for the same basic thing the boys already have: a field that’s playable when it rains and safe when it’s dry. The school board votes on next year’s facilities budget soon. Put turf on the girls soccer field in that budget.

Some people will say turf is expensive. You know what’s more expensive? Losing nine games a season. Losing a player to an ACL tear that didn’t have to happen. Losing the message that girls’ sports matter as much as boys’ sports.

I coach for a stipend. I’m not here to write pretty sentences. I’m here because I’ve watched my players warm up on a field with standing water and then get told their game is moved—again. I’ve watched a girl’s season end because of a rut. I’ve watched the football team practice on turf while we drag mud off our cleats.

The board has a choice. They can keep telling half the school’s athletes to wait their turn, or they can fix the field. My players have waited long enough.

Vote yes on turf for the girls soccer field.

b.text:
Nine girls’ soccer games have been rained out or moved in the last two seasons because our field floods. Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping in a rut.

The school board is about to vote on next year’s facilities budget. Turf for the girls’ soccer field needs to be in it.

I coach girls’ soccer and track at our public high school. I expect players to show up, work hard and be ready to compete. They should be able to expect a field that is ready for them. Right now, they cannot.

A flooded field is not just an inconvenience on a schedule. Moving a game means rearranging transportation, work schedules and family plans. Losing a game means losing a chance to compete after putting in the work to prepare. When this happens repeatedly, it is not bad luck. It is a facilities problem.

The boys’ football field got turf in 2019. The district has already decided that a dependable playing surface is worth investing in. The question now is whether that same priority extends to the girls’ soccer team.

That is not a criticism of the football players or their coaches. They deserve a good field. So do my players. We should not have to argue against one team to get another team what it needs.

And no, turf is not a promise that nobody will get hurt. Soccer has injuries on grass and on turf. The board should look carefully at surface options, drainage, heat, maintenance and replacement costs. This is a major purchase, and it should be treated like one.

But those questions are reasons to plan the project properly, not reasons to keep putting it off. Our current field has costs, too. Nine disrupted games in two seasons should be enough to put this on the board’s priority list. The condition of the playing surface should keep it there.

I am not asking for a showpiece. I am asking for a field where our team can practice and play without repeatedly wondering whether the ground will hold up.

If the board chooses not to fund this project, it owes players and families a clear explanation of what it will do instead, when that work will happen and how it will address the flooding and uneven ground. “Not this year” is not a plan.

My players are expected to represent this school with effort and pride. They do. It is time for the district to put that same effort into the field they play on.

Fund turf for the girls’ soccer field in next year’s budget.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now

After six years photographing weddings mostly in the same metro area, I have some opinions about wedding seasons. And one of them has changed: I genuinely like shooting winter weddings now.

Not in a “love makes every season magical” way. I mean there are practical, visible things I prefer about them. I’ve photographed 11 winter weddings in the last two years, so this isn’t based on one unusually warm Saturday in December.

If you’re choosing a date—or wondering whether it’s worth looking beyond the usual summer weekends—here’s what I’ve come to appreciate.

## Your photography budget goes further

Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for couples. That’s a meaningful difference, especially if you’re trying to book a photographer whose work you love without stretching your budget past where you’re comfortable.

It doesn’t mean winter is automatically the right choice. If you’ve always wanted an outdoor ceremony followed by a long evening outside, a discount probably won’t change that. But if you’re flexible on the season, it’s worth comparing actual winter availability and pricing before assuming June is your best option.

## I’ll take November light over some June afternoons

The light through bare trees around 3 p.m. in November is honestly better for portraits than flat, overcast June light.

That’s specific, but it matters. Bare branches let light through in a way a full summer canopy doesn’t. When the sun is low, we can get direction and depth instead of the broad, even gray light people often assume is ideal for photos.

Overcast light is useful. It’s forgiving. But it isn’t automatically more interesting just because it happens in June.

The catch is timing. In winter, we need to plan portraits around the daylight rather than assume there will be plenty left after the ceremony. That might mean a first look or an earlier portrait window. It’s a conversation to have before you lock in the day’s schedule, not something to figure out when the sun is already disappearing.

## There’s less competition for the same space

In June, I can be sharing a parking lot with three or four other vendors. That’s before we’ve even started taking pictures.

It’s a small detail, but it says a lot about peak-season logistics: more arrivals, more unloading, more people trying to get where they need to go at once.

I appreciate not having that same scramble at winter weddings. A quieter arrival doesn’t sound like a reason to choose a wedding date, and on its own, it isn’t. But it’s one of those behind-the-scenes differences that makes the work feel less rushed.

## Winter still needs a realistic plan

I’m not going to tell you the cold doesn’t matter. It does. So does the earlier sunset.

If we’re taking portraits outside, we should know where we’re going, keep the important combinations organized, and have somewhere warm to return to. We also need an indoor option you actually like—not just a room we can use if we have to.

What I wouldn’t do is take a June timeline, move it to November, and expect the same results. Winter works best when we plan for winter.

## So, should you book a winter date?

If summer is what you want, book summer. But if you’re open to a winter wedding, don’t treat it as the compromise date you settle for after everything else is taken.

After 11 of them in two years, I see real advantages: photography bookings around 30% cheaper, portrait light I sometimes prefer, and fewer peak-season logistics to work around.

If you’re considering a winter date, ask me about availability while you’re looking at venues. We can talk through the daylight and portrait timing before you commit to a ceremony time. That’s a much better starting point than choosing the whole schedule first and hoping the light cooperates.

b.text:
# Why I Actually Love Shooting Winter Weddings Now

I'll be honest — for the first few years of my career, I didn't push winter dates. They weren't the most popular, and I was busy enough from May through October that I didn't need to. But in the last two years I've shot 11 winter weddings, and somewhere along the way I became a genuine convert.

If you're still deciding when to book your date, here's what I want you to know.

## You're paying about 30% less

This is just a fact. My winter package pricing runs roughly 30% below peak season, and most vendors in this area work the same way. Venues drop their minimums. Caterers are more flexible on Friday or Sunday dates. That's not because winter weddings are lesser — it's supply and demand. If your budget is tight, a January or February Saturday can feel more like a June Friday in terms of what you can afford.

## The light is actually better

People assume overcast June skies are great for photography. Soft light, no harsh shadows — sounds ideal. But flat overcast light is just that: flat. There's no direction, no depth, no warmth.

Around 3pm in November, when the sun sits low and comes through bare branches at an angle, you get directional light that's actually gorgeous for portraits. It wraps around faces. It catches in hair. It does things that a gray June sky physically cannot do because the sun is too high and the canopy is too dense. I'll take bare trees and low winter sun over flat overcast every time.

## I'm not fighting three other vendors for parking

In June, I show up to a venue and there are two other photographers, a videographer, and a limo driver all trying to load in through the same entrance. I'm sharing the getting-ready room with a makeup artist and a florist. I'm waiting for the other couple's portrait session to finish before I can use the good spot on the grounds.

In winter, I'm usually the only wedding at the venue that day. I can work at a real pace. I can take the time I want with portraits without feeling like I'm holding up someone else's timeline. It makes for a calmer day, and calmer days make for better photos.

## What you should actually consider

Winter weddings aren't right for every couple. If your vision is outdoor cocktails or a late-night exit under string lights at 9pm, that's a June wedding and you should book June. I'm not trying to talk anyone out of what they actually want.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
## Open-Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors

Our school’s lunch period is overcrowded. The cafeteria has seats for 220 students, but 340 students are assigned to the same lunch wave. As a result, at least 120 students do not have a place to sit. Some students are forced to eat quickly while standing in crowded areas, and others rush through lunch because they are worried about being late to class. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus for lunch would help solve this problem while giving students more freedom and responsibility.

The strongest support for an open-campus lunch comes from nearby districts that already allow it. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade have adopted open-campus lunch policies, and their published attendance statistics show no increase in tardiness. This evidence is relevant because one of the most common arguments against allowing students to leave campus is that they will return late or skip class. The experience of these three districts suggests that schools can give students greater independence during lunch without creating attendance problems. Although every school is different, our district does not need to assume that the policy would fail when nearby districts have already shown that it can work.

Students at our school also strongly support the idea. In a survey of 80 students, 71 said they were in favor of open-campus lunch. That is nearly 89 percent of the students who responded. The survey does not include every student in the school, so it cannot predict exactly how everyone will behave, but it still shows a clear consensus among those who were asked. When students understand the conditions in the cafeteria and are given a reasonable option, most of them want that option. Giving juniors and seniors the chance to leave campus would show that the school trusts them to make responsible decisions.

Open-campus lunch would also give students more choice. Instead of eating in the same crowded cafeteria every day, students could eat at a restaurant, bring their own food, or spend part of their lunch break somewhere else. Juniors and seniors are approaching adulthood, and many will soon be expected to manage their own time in college, at work, or in other settings. Allowing them to leave campus during lunch can be a practical step toward that independence. Students who remain on campus would benefit too, because fewer people would be competing for seats and space in the serving line.

Some people may argue that open-campus lunch is unsafe because students would be away from school supervision and could be exposed to traffic or other risks. These concerns are reasonable and should be addressed through clear procedures. The school could begin with a one-year pilot limited to juniors and seniors, designate approved areas where students may eat, and require students to sign out and back in. Administrators could then monitor attendance, safety incidents, and student behavior before making a permanent decision. An open-campus policy should not mean that the school has no responsibility; it should mean that the school creates sensible rules and holds students accountable for following them.

Another concern is that students who do not have money to buy food or whose families do not want them leaving campus could be excluded. The cafeteria should therefore remain available, and no student should be required to leave. Even if many students choose to go off campus, the reduced cafeteria crowd would make lunch easier for those who stay. The policy would create options rather than take them away.

Our school should allow juniors and seniors to participate in an open-campus lunch program. The current cafeteria is too small for the number of students assigned to the lunch wave, and nearby districts have already demonstrated that this policy can be implemented without an increase in tardiness. The support from our own students is even more convincing, with 71 out of 80 students favoring the change. A limited pilot with clear rules would give students greater independence, relieve overcrowding, and provide our school with evidence about whether the program should continue.

b.text:
**The Case for Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors**

High school is a time of growing responsibility, and with that responsibility should come greater freedom—especially when it comes to something as fundamental as lunch. Juniors and seniors at our school should be granted open campus lunch privileges. This change would not only reflect the trust we’ve earned but also address real logistical problems in our current system. Three nearby districts have already implemented open campus lunch with no negative consequences, student opinion overwhelmingly supports the idea, and our overcrowded cafeteria desperately needs relief.

First, the success of open campus lunch in other districts proves it’s a viable option. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade High Schools all allow juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch, and none have reported an increase in tardiness or disciplinary issues. In fact, administrators in these districts have noted that students return to class on time and often use their lunch period more productively—whether grabbing a quick meal, running errands, or simply enjoying a change of scenery. If these schools can manage open campus lunch without problems, there’s no reason ours can’t do the same.

Beyond the evidence from other districts, the students at our school have made their preferences clear. In a survey of 80 juniors and seniors, 71—nearly 90%—expressed support for open campus lunch. This isn’t just a vocal minority pushing for change; it’s the vast majority of upperclassmen who want the freedom to make their own choices. High school is a stepping stone to adulthood, and part of that transition is learning to manage time and responsibilities. Open campus lunch would give students a chance to practice those skills in a low-stakes environment.

Finally, our current lunch system is simply impractical. The cafeteria seats only 220 students, yet 340 juniors and seniors are crammed into the same lunch wave. The result? Overcrowded tables, long lines, and students rushing to finish their meals in time. Allowing upperclassmen to leave campus would immediately reduce the strain on the cafeteria, making lunch a more pleasant experience for everyone—including underclassmen, who would have more space and shorter wait times. It’s a solution that benefits the entire school.

Open campus lunch isn’t about recklessness; it’s about recognizing that juniors and seniors are capable of handling more freedom. Other districts have done it successfully, our students want it, and our cafeteria can’t handle the current demand. It’s time to make this change.
