setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
Shut off the circulator pump or boiler before you open any valves. If the system is running when you crack a bleeder, you’ll force air down the line instead of out of it, and you’ll probably get sprayed. Give the boiler ten minutes to settle and the pressure to flatten out.

Start with the baseboard unit closest to the boiler and work your way outward, one by one. Each unit has a bleeder valve on one end—usually a small brass fitting with a square nut or a slotted stem. Slide a cup, small bowl, or heavy rag underneath before you touch it.

Open the valve slowly with a bleeder key or a flathead screwdriver. You’ll hear hissing first. That’s the air leaving. Keep it cracked until the stream of water runs steady and quiet, with no sputtering or bubbles. Depending on how much air is trapped, this can take thirty seconds or several minutes.

Once the flow is solid, close the valve snug, but do not reef on it. These brass seats crack easily, and an overtightened bleeder will drip or weep all winter. Finger-tight plus a quarter turn is usually enough.

Repeat this at every unit in the house. The mistake that generates most of our cold-radiator calls is homeowners bleeding only the upstairs baseboards and skipping the basement loop. The air that collects at the top of the system usually got pushed there from below. If you skip the basement, you’ll be bleeding the upstairs again in a week.

When you finish the last unit, check the boiler pressure gauge. Bleeding drops the system pressure, so you may need to add water through the fill valve to get back to the manufacturer’s recommended range—usually 12 to 15 psi for a one- or two-story home. If you’re unsure how to add water or the pressure won’t hold, shut the boiler down and give us a call.

b.text:
If your baseboard radiators are cold to the touch or making a loud clinking, gurgling sound when the heat kicks on, you have air trapped in your heating lines. Air blocks the hot water from circulating, leaving you with cold rooms. Getting that air out is a straightforward job you can do yourself in about 30 minutes. 

Here is exactly how to bleed your baseboard system to get the heat flowing again.

### Step 1: Shut off the system
Never try to bleed your radiators while the system is running. If the circulator pump is active, it will keep the air moving through the pipes, making it impossible to get it all out, and it might even suck more air into the system. Turn off your boiler at the thermostat or the main switch and wait about 10 to 15 minutes. This lets the water settle and ensures you won’t get sprayed with scalding hot water.

### Step 2: Map your route (and avoid the #1 mistake)
You need to bleed your radiators in a specific order: **start with the unit closest to your boiler and work your way outward.** 

This brings us to the mistake that causes about 80% of our cold-radiator service calls: **homeowners only bleeding the upstairs units.** People assume that because air rises, the blockage must be on the top floor. But in a closed residential loop, air often gets trapped in the basement or ground-floor lines, blocking the flow to the rest of the house. Even if your basement is unfinished and you don't care about heating it, you *must* bleed the basement loops first. If you skip them, you aren't fixing the problem.

### Step 3: Locate the bleeder valve
Go to your first baseboard unit. Look at the end caps of the metal cover—usually on the side where the copper pipe enters the unit. Pop the end cap off. Inside, you will see a small brass valve. It will have a small stem in the middle, either with a square head (which requires a radiator key, available for two dollars at any hardware store) or a slot for a flathead screwdriver.

### Step 4: Open the valve slowly
Position a small cup, bowl, or a thick rag directly underneath the valve spout. 

Insert your key or flathead screwdriver and turn it slowly counterclockwise—about a half-turn is usually enough. You will hear a hissing sound. That is the trapped air escaping. 

### Step 5: Wait for a steady stream
Keep your cup under the valve. You might get a mix of spitting air and dirty water. Keep the valve open until the hissing stops completely and you get a steady, solid stream of water with no air bubbles. 

### Step 6: Close it snug (Do NOT overtighten)
Once you have steady water, turn the valve clockwise to close it. 

**Pay attention here:** Only tighten it until it is snug. These valves are made of soft brass. If you crank down on them too hard, you will crack the valve seat. If that happens, it won't shut off, it will drip constantly, and you’ll have to call us to drain your system and solder in a brand-new valve. Snug is plenty.

### Step 7: Repeat the process
Move to the next closest radiator to the boiler and repeat the steps. Keep going until you have bled every single unit in the house, ending with the one furthest away from your boiler.

Once you’re finished, turn your boiler back on. Check your thermostat, let the system run for a few minutes, and feel the baseboards. They should be hot from end to end. If you still have cold spots after running through this sequence, or if you notice your boiler pressure gauge has dropped too low after bleeding, give us a call and we’ll come out to get your system balanced and pressurized properly.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/
I raised Tallyup's prices 40% overnight. Every customer, no exceptions.

A week later, 30 of my 140 customers were gone.

What I got wrong, and what I changed:

2/
The backstory: like every indie hacker, I'd absorbed the advice.

"You're undercharging."
"Just charge more."
"Raising prices is the highest-leverage move in SaaS."

So one day I did. Every customer. Same day. Bigger number on the next invoice.

3/
No grandfathering.
No heads-up.
No "here's why."

Just a charge 40% higher than what they signed up for.

That was the whole mistake — but it took losing 30 customers to see it.

4/
The cancellations started almost immediately.

30 out of 140, gone in seven days.

And these aren't faceless accounts. Gym owners run small businesses. They notice every line item, and they'd taken a chance on a solo founder's tool.

5/
Here's the thing: the price probably wasn't the problem.

New customers might have paid it without blinking.

The problem was changing the deal on people who had already said yes. A price hike with no warning doesn't feel like strategy. It feels like a broken promise.

6/
What I changed:

→ Existing customers keep their original price
→ New pricing applies to new signups only
→ Any future increase gets announced well in advance, with a reason and a way to push back

The deal you sign is the deal you keep.

7/
I also emailed every customer who cancelled and offered their old price back.

Most didn't take me up on it.

Trust is fast to spend and slow to earn back. I knew that in the abstract. Now I know it for real.

8/
The "just charge more" advice isn't wrong. It's incomplete.

Charge more for new customers, fine. But your existing customers already made a deal with you. Honor it — or at least warn them before you change it.

9/
Rebuilding now, one gym at a time.

If you've raised prices on existing customers as a founder — how did you handle it? Genuinely asking.

b.text:
1/ I raised prices 40% on all Tallyup customers overnight.

Lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week.

Here's what I did wrong, and what I changed. 🧵

2/ Tallyup helps gym owners track member retention. Bootstrapped, solo founder, 140 customers.

Thin margins were burning me out. I thought a big price jump would fix it.

3/ So I emailed everyone: next bill is 40% higher. No segmentation. No grandfathering. No phased rollout. No warning.

Every single customer got the same email.

4/ 30 customers churned in 7 days.

Not gradually. Not next quarter. Immediately.

The message was the same: "I understand raising prices, but not overnight."

5/ What I changed:

→ Grandfather existing customers at their current rate.
→ New pricing only for new signups going forward.
→ Give advance notice on any future increases.
→ Raise in smaller steps, not one big shock.
→ Built a lighter plan so smaller gyms don't have to quit entirely.

6/ Raising prices wasn't wrong.

Applying it overnight to everyone — no warning, no segmentation — was.

Your early customers took a bet on you. Don't punish them for it.

That's it. Back to shipping.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
# The 7am Walk

Last month I had first-time buyers, the Pruitts, scheduled to tour a house on Sycamore Street. The night before, they couldn't sleep—nerves, excitement, all of it. So at 7am they drove over and just... walked the neighborhood.

When we did the official tour later, they already knew the street. They'd seen the retired couple watering their garden. They'd noticed the coffee shop two blocks down. They'd watched the school buses load up. They'd felt what it was actually like to live there, not just visit.

They made an offer that day. Closed three months later. Last week I got photos of them on the porch.

In 12 years, I've noticed the buyers who are happiest long-term are almost always the ones who've done this. They walk at different times. They sit in the driveway. They check out the commute during rush hour. They talk to neighbors. By the time they buy, the house isn't a transaction anymore—it's a place they already know.

If you're looking at houses: go back at 7am. Go back at 6pm. Go back on a Saturday. You'll know if it's right. You really will.

b.text:
The Pruitts were first-time buyers looking on Sycamore Street last spring. We had six homes to see that Saturday, and I suggested they drive over Friday night, park a block away, and walk the block at 7am before we started touring.

They were game. Saturday morning they texted me photos: the corner coffee shop opening up, the neighbor two doors down pulling out in scrubs for what I assumed was a hospital shift, and a woman walking a very small dog who waved at every single person she passed.

Then we toured.

Every house looked good on paper. But they kept coming back to one in particular, on the east end of the block. When I asked why, they said it already felt like they knew the rhythm of the street. They'd met it, in a way, before they ever walked through a front door.

They wrote an offer that afternoon and closed in May. Last I heard, they still do the morning walk, and they still wave at the small-dog lady.

After twelve years of selling homes in Asheville, this is the pattern I keep seeing: buyers who take time to actually experience a neighborhood before they tour a house end up way happier with their purchase six months and six years later. The houses themselves are similar in a lot of ways — square footage, finishes, price per square foot. What you can't get from listings, or even showings, is the texture of daily life on a given street. Who you'll nod at. What the light does at 7:15 in the kitchen. Where the coffee comes from.

The walk before the tour isn't a gimmick. It's the closest thing to living there before you commit.

If you're house hunting in Asheville and want to slow down before you speed up, I'd love to help.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
I haven’t had a Saturday off since October of my sophomore year. While my classmates are at football games or sleeping in, my weekends belong to my family’s Vietnamese restaurant. I start at 10:00 AM, just as the broth from the day before is reaching a rolling boil, and I don't leave until the chairs are stacked on the tables at ten at night.

My breaks are twenty minutes long, and I spend them in the walk-in cooler. It is the only place in the restaurant where nobody is shouting in Vietnamese or clattering stainless steel bowls. I sit on an overturned five-gallon bucket of pickled carrots, my winter coat zipped to my chin, and do my AP Calculus homework. The pages of my textbook always curl from the humidity, and after fifteen minutes, my fingers get too stiff to grip my mechanical pencil. But the quiet is absolute. I solve for limits while staring at crates of cilantro and boxes of beef bones, finding a weird kind of peace in the cold.

If the walk-in is where I find quiet, the front counter is where I learn how to handle chaos. Last November, during our prime Saturday dinner rush, our digital register system went completely black. Twenty active orders vanished from the kitchen screen, and a line of hungry customers began to stretch out the door. My dad was already sweating over four gas burners in the back, and my mom was frantically trying to reboot the router. 

I didn't have time to panic. I grabbed a stack of green guest checks and a black pen. I took orders by hand, writing down "P1" for beef pho and "E2" for spring rolls in my own shorthand. I ran the physical tickets to the kitchen, shouting modifications over the hiss of the exhaust fan, and did the math for the tax and change in my head. I kept a metal lockbox under the counter for cash. By the time the rush ended, my thumb was calloused from the cheap pen, but we hadn’t missed a single order, and the cash drawer balanced to the penny. 

When I am not running the register, I am training the new hires. Most of them are high school kids who have never had a job before. Last month, I taught a junior named Marcus how to roll spring rolls using my grandmother’s technique. The rice paper is temperamental—if you wet it too much, it turns to mush; if you don't wet it enough, it cracks. 

I showed him how to lay down the pork, the noodles, and the mint, and then how to tuck the sides in tight, like making a small sleeping bag. The trick is getting the shrimp to lay flat against the translucent wrapper so it looks good when served. 

"If you roll it too loose, it falls apart in the peanut sauce," I told him. "If you roll it too tight, the paper rips. You just have to feel the tension." I watched him tear six wrappers before he got one clean roll. I didn't get frustrated; I just cleared the sticky rice paper away and handed him another sheet. 

I am not going to say that working at the restaurant taught me the secret to life. The truth is, my feet hurt every Sunday, my clothes always smell like star anise, and I have missed a lot of high school events that I probably would have enjoyed. But this is my reality. I know how to work under pressure, I know how to teach people, and I know how to find quiet in a busy room. When I start college, I won't just be bringing my textbooks. I’ll be bringing the work ethic I built twelve hours at a time.

b.text:
The register system died at 11:47 on a Saturday.

It was right before the lunch rush. My dad hit the restart button three times, unplugged it, plugged it back in. The screen stayed black. My mom didn't say anything. She just went behind the counter, pulled out the old pad of paper tickets we keep for takeout orders, and handed it to me.

I hand-wrote every ticket that day.

Table 4: two large pho tai, one no onion, extra basil.
Table 7: three spring rolls, one bun cha, peanut sauce on the side.
Table 2: coffee, iced, extra condensed milk, they always ask twice.

My handwriting got worse as it got busier. The kitchen kept yelling back to ask what I wrote. Is that a 1 or a 7? Is this chicken or pork? At one point I wrote "no cilantro" so fast it looked like "no chicken" and we had to remake the whole bowl. My dad had to add everything up on a calculator at the end and my mom kept the carbon copies in a stack by the sink so we wouldn't lose one.

That was just one Saturday. I've worked at our restaurant every weekend since sophomore year.

Most weekends start the same. We open at ten, but I'm there at nine to help prep. We roll spring rolls in the back while the broth is heating up. You can hear it starting to boil in the big pot and the whole kitchen starts to smell like star anise and ginger.

This fall I had to teach a new hire how to roll them. His name is Kevin and he's a sophomore. My grandma taught me, and she still checks mine if she's there. She sits on a stool by the prep table and watches without saying much until you mess up.

I showed Kevin how she told me. Dip the rice paper in warm water for like three seconds. Don't wait until it's soft, it'll get soft on the board. Lay it flat. Shrimp, pork, lettuce, mint, rice noodles, but not too much or it'll tear. Fold the bottom up, fold in the sides, then roll it tight once. Not loose. If it's loose it falls apart when someone picks it up.

His first five tore. The sixth was too fat. The seventh was okay but crooked. He kept apologizing. I told him I used to make them worse. That's true. My grandma used to just take the torn ones, put them on a little plate for me to eat later, and hand me another rice paper. By the end of that morning Kevin could make a row that actually looked even. Mine are still not as neat as my grandma's. The ends of hers are always tucked in the same way.

When it gets slow in the afternoon, or when I get my fifteen-minute break, I go in the walk-in cooler to do homework. It's the only place in the restaurant that's quiet and where no one asks me to refill waters. I sit on an empty milk crate next to the boxes of fish sauce and do my calc homework.

It's cold in there. After a few minutes my fingers get stiff and it's hard to write. My notebook pages get a little damp. But I can hear the door muffle everything outside, the tickets printing, my dad calling out orders, the bell on the front door. I usually get through four or five problems before my mom knocks and says we're getting busy again. My teacher once wrote on my homework that it smelled weird. It did. It smelled like the cooler, like cold vegetables.

Saturday nights we close at nine-thirty. We mop, we wipe down tables, my dad counts the register, which is working again now. On Sundays we do it all again. I have a test on Monday and a shift on Saturday and my backpack is always by the back door with my apron folded on top of it.

I don't really think about it as two separate things anymore. It's just my weekend. I clock in, I roll spring rolls, I write tickets, I go sit in the cooler and try to finish problem set 4B before the dinner rush.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
I’m writing this at the little corner table by the back door, still dusting flour off my forearms while the afternoon sourdough cools. It’s quiet in the shop right now, which is usually the only time I get to sit down and talk to you all like this.

I wanted to share an update about a change we’re making around here, and because so many of you have been with us since day one, I wanted to just tell you straight from the heart.

Starting next month, we are no longer going to be taking on custom wedding cakes.

This wasn’t an easy decision. We’ve had the absolute joy of being a small part of so many incredible love stories in this town, and seeing photos of you all cutting into a cake we built with our own hands will always be special to me. But over the last year, it’s become really clear that custom wedding work just doesn’t fit the reality of our tiny shop anymore.

Right now, it’s just three of us back in the kitchen. To do a custom wedding cake the right way—the way you deserve—it easily takes about 14 hours of behind-the-scenes work before we even turn the ovens on for the big day. That’s emails back and forth, sketching designs, organizing private tastings, and prepping specialty ingredients. When you’re a crew of three starting at 4:00 in the morning, fourteen hours is a massive piece of our week. 

On top of the time, this past year brought us three separate last-minute wedding cancellations. In a small kitchen on tight margins, having hundreds of dollars in high-end butter, vanilla, and specialty ingredients suddenly go to waste hurts a lot. 

Most of all, we realized that pouring all our energy into two or three big weekend events was pulling us away from the heart of this bakery: the morning case. The sourdough loaves, the flaky croissants, the afternoon cookies, and the simple birthday cakes you pick up on a Tuesday—that’s what actually pays our rent, and that’s what feeds our neighborhood every single day. We want to put all our love, focus, and energy right back into making sure that display case is packed full of the best bakes we can possibly make for you.

We’ll still have our classic layer cakes available to order through the regular menu if you’re hosting a smaller, casual gathering and just want something delicious on the table. But the multi-tiered, custom-designed wedding orders are taking a bow.

Thank you, as always, for understanding and for letting us grow and adapt so we can keep our doors open and our ovens running for a long time to come. I’m going to go wipe down the bench now, but I’ll see you tomorrow morning for coffee and pastries.

b.text:
Subject: A change we've been putting off telling you about

I've rewritten this post about six times now, always at some ridiculous hour after the ovens are already going, because I keep wanting to explain myself instead of just talking to you. So let me try again, plainly this time.

We're not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore.

If you've been in the shop, you probably know how much I've loved doing them. There's something about a couple sitting at that little table up front, nervous and giddy, trying five kinds of buttercream and pretending they're not going to just pick the one that reminds them of their grandmother's kitchen. I've gotten to be a small part of some really big days, and I don't say that lightly.

But here's the truth of it. Each of those orders took about fourteen hours of my time before a single cake was ever baked — consults, tastings, follow-up emails, redesigns after someone's aunt had opinions about fondant. Fourteen hours doesn't sound like much until you realize it's coming out of the same twenty-four hours that start at 4am with the sourdough and don't really end until the case is stocked and the last regular's coffee order is called out. It was time that used to go toward the everyday bread and pastries — the stuff that actually keeps the lights on and lets the three of us keep doing this at all.

And then this year we had three cancellations, all last minute, all after we'd already bought the ingredients and blocked out the days. I'm not telling you that to complain — weddings get cancelled, plans change, that's life — but three in one year, on top of everything else, made it clear something had to give.

So we sat with it for a while, the three of us, and decided the honest thing to do was step back from wedding cakes and put that time back into what's actually paying the rent and what most of you actually come in for every day. The morning pastries. The birthday cakes. The bread that sells out by ten. That's the bakery, really, at its core, and lately it's been getting the leftover hours instead of the good ones.

If you're planning a wedding and were hoping we'd be part of it, I'm genuinely sorry, and I mean that. We may still do smaller celebration cakes down the line, and if that changes I'll tell you here first, same as always. But for now, this is us choosing to take care of the everyday thing that got us all here in the first place.

Thank you for understanding, and for still showing up for the regular stuff. It matters more than you know.

— [Your name], still icing something at an hour I won't admit to

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**Column: The record won’t cover the mistake**

The season ended Friday, but not because they were outclassed.

They finished 8-2. Dez Kowalski set the school passing record with 2,340 yards. They beat the same team by 20 points back in Week 3. And in the second half of a second-round state playoff game, down three, they stopped running the football even though it was working.

That’s the column. That’s the whole problem.

This wasn’t a talent gap or a bad matchup. It was self-inflicted. The run game was moving the ball, the game was right there, and the offense went all-in on Kowalski’s arm. Kowalski is a great quarterback — the record proves it — but a school record isn’t a game plan. Down three in the second half, you need first downs, not highlight throws.

I don’t know if it was panic or ego or a belief that the passing game had to carry the moment. The result was the same: a winnable game turned into an exit.

This isn’t on the kids. They did enough to win. The second-half direction cost them a chance to keep playing.

Eight wins is a good season. But this one stings for a different reason. They didn’t lose because they weren’t good enough. They lost because they stopped doing the thing that had them in the game.

That should bother everybody all winter.

b.text:
## Abandoning the Run Game Was Costly

An 8-2 record and a second-round state playoff appearance are worth celebrating. The playoff loss was still a loss, though, and the team’s biggest problem was not the opponent. It was the decision to stop running the football when running was working.

That playoff opponent was the same team the locals beat by 20 points in Week 3, a result that showed this team could beat them. It did not mean the second-half plan had to be any different. When the margin was only three points, there was no good reason to abandon the run game and make every series the responsibility of quarterback Dez Kowalski.

Kowalski’s 2,340 passing yards were a school record, and his season should be recognized as an outstanding achievement. But a record should not become a reason to forget how the offense became difficult to defend in the first place. When the run was effective, the defense had to respect both the run and the pass. Once the team essentially stopped running, the opponent knew what was coming. That is a pretty good way to make things predictable.

More running would not have guaranteed victory. It simply offered the better chance. It could have controlled the clock, kept the defense fresh, and forced the opponent to adjust to a game the locals had already shown they could play. Instead, the offense drifted toward the one-dimensional approach that had already failed against a playoff-caliber opponent.

That is what makes this loss frustrating. The team did not need a dramatic reinvention. It needed to continue doing what was working, especially with a three-point deficit. Kowalski was the team’s star, but he was most valuable when the rest of the offense made the defense choose.

The locals should be proud of an 8-2 season, and Kowalski should be proud of his school-record performance. Still, the playoff loss deserved an honest explanation, and none of the excuses change the central fact: the team quit trusting its running game at the wrong time.

Sometimes the best play is not the one that produces the biggest highlight. Sometimes it is simply the play that was already working.

a.text:
**Later Starts Mean Better-Rested Kids—and Better Days at School**

As a parent of two middle-schoolers in Millbrook, I’ve watched the school board’s 8:45 start-time proposal with more than casual interest. I’ve read it carefully. And I’m writing to urge the board—and my neighbors—to support it when they vote next month.

Like a lot of parents, I’ve seen the morning scramble: kids who stayed up late fighting biology, not laziness, then dragging themselves out the door half-asleep. The American Academy of Pediatrics has been clear for years that middle- and high-school students need 8–10 hours of sleep and that later start times are one of the most effective ways to help them get it. An 8:45 bell finally lines up with what science and common sense already tell us.

We don’t have to guess how this might work here. The Lincoln Middle pilot already gave us a local look. Attendance improved. First-period grades went up. Kids were more present—literally and mentally—when the day started later. That matches what I’ve noticed in my own house on delayed-start days: fewer arguments, clearer heads, and a lot less “I can’t keep my eyes open” at the breakfast table.

I know the bus-schedule worry is real. Changing start times can ripple through routes and family logistics. But the proposal already addresses this head-on by re-tiering the bus routes. The plan isn’t “start later and hope the buses figure it out.” It’s a coordinated adjustment so elementary, middle, and high school runs still fit together without leaving families stranded or forcing impossible early pickups.

This isn’t about making mornings perfect. It’s about giving our kids a fairer shot at being awake, healthy, and ready to learn. Middle school is hard enough without starting the day already behind on sleep. The board has done the homework—reviewed the research, run a local pilot, and built the bus piece into the plan. Now it’s our turn to back them.

I’m not a policy expert. I’m just a Millbrook parent who wants my kids, and everyone else’s, to walk into school a little more rested and a little more ready. An 8:45 start is a practical step toward that. I hope the board votes yes, and I hope other parents will speak up too.

—A Millbrook parent of two middle-schoolers

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
# Why I've Come Around on Winter Weddings

I'll be honest: for the first few years of my career, I thought of winter as the off-season. The time to catch up on editing, update my portfolio, and wait for May.

Then the winter bookings started coming in, and I stopped waiting for May. I've shot eleven winter weddings in the last two years, and at this point, if you told me I could only shoot one season for the rest of my career, November through February would genuinely be in the running. Here's why.

## The light is better than you think. Actually, it's better than June.

This is the part nobody believes until they see the photos.

Everyone assumes summer means great light, but around here, June often means one of two things: harsh midday sun that makes everyone squint, or a flat, gray overcast sky that turns every portrait slightly dull, like someone lowered the contrast on the whole day.

Compare that to a November afternoon around 3pm. The sun is already low, coming in at an angle through bare trees, and the light that filters through those empty branches is soft, directional, and warm. It sculpts faces instead of flattening them. Some of my favorite portraits from the last two years were shot in exactly those conditions — no leaves, no lush greenery, just that low golden light doing the work. The catch is that golden hour comes early in winter, so we plan portraits around 3pm instead of 7pm. But once you're planning for it, it's not a compromise. It's an upgrade.

## Your vendors aren't stretched across four other weddings

Here's something couples don't usually see: in June, when I pull into a venue parking lot, I'm often one of three or four vendors' vehicles arriving for weddings happening the same day, sometimes at the same property. Everyone — the florist, the caterer, the DJ — is running between events, watching the clock, thinking about their next load-in.

At a winter wedding, I pull into that same lot and it's basically just us. Your wedding is the event that day. That changes the whole energy. Vendors aren't rushing. The venue staff isn't split between two receptions. If your ceremony runs fifteen minutes long, nobody's sweating it. I have room to slow down, try that one extra portrait idea, wander off with you two for ten more minutes of couple photos — because there's nowhere else I have to be.

## And yes, it costs less. Meaningfully less.

Winter dates typically run about 30% cheaper for couples across the board — venues, vendors, the works. That's not a small discount. On a full wedding budget, that's the difference that pays for the honeymoon, or the better photography package, or just not starting your marriage with a bigger loan than you needed.

You're not getting less wedding for that money. You're getting a less crowded calendar, which happens to come with a smaller invoice.

## What winter actually asks of you

I won't pretend there are no tradeoffs. The early sunset means we build the timeline around light, which sometimes means doing portraits before the ceremony. It's cold, so we plan for it — quick outdoor sessions, warm layers between shots, and honestly, some of the coziest, most emotional indoor reception photos I've ever taken.

But "we planned around a 4:45 sunset" is a much smaller problem than "our photos are flat and our vendors were racing to their next event."

If you're deciding between a peak-season Saturday and a winter date, I'm happy to talk through what your specific day would look like in each. But after eleven winter weddings, I can tell you: the couples who book December aren't settling. Some of them just figured it out first.

*Want to see winter galleries from real weddings I've shot? [Reach out] and I'll send some over.*

b.text:
**I Didn't Expect to Like Winter Weddings. Now I Book Them On Purpose.**

I've been freelancing as a wedding photographer in this metro area for six years now. Same venues, same parks, same downtown blocks, just different couples. Which means I know exactly what a Saturday in June looks like: you can feel it before you even get out of the car.

For a long time I was a summer purist too. Then I shot 11 winter weddings in the last two years - November through February - and it kind of flipped for me.

Here’s why I actually like them now, honestly:

**1. Your money goes so much further and you feel it.**

This isn't just photographer pricing. My winter couples tell me their overall bookings - venue, catering, rentals - are running about 30% cheaper than what their friends paid for a June date at the same places. That changes the whole day. You’re not stressed about squeezing every penny out of a 6-hour rental. You can actually afford the extra hour of coverage, or the live band, or just... not be stressed.

**2. The light is better. I will die on this hill.**

Everyone thinks June = good light. Most of our Junes are flat, white, overcast at 2pm. It’s soft, sure, but it’s flat and you look a little washed out unless we work really hard.

In November, around 3pm, when the sun drops low and comes through the bare trees? It’s perfect. No leaves means the light just filters and stripes through the branches instead of getting blocked. It’s warm, directional, sculpted. It hits your face instead of just sitting on top of you. Some of my favorite portraits ever from the last two seasons were taken at 3:15pm in November in a park I’ve shot 40 times in the summer.

**3. We actually get to use the venue.**

In June, I pull into a venue I’ve shot a dozen times and I’m sharing the parking lot with 3 or 4 other vendors. There’s another ceremony flipping in the garden, another bride getting out of a limo, the coordinator is on a headset sprinting between two weddings. We’re timed to the minute because someone else needs the staircase at 4:30.

In winter, the lot is half empty. The venue staff isn’t fried. We get the good window in the bridal suite without curtains drawn against the heat. We can take an extra 10 minutes on portraits because no one is waiting to kick us out. It’s calmer, and it shows in the photos.

I get why couples default to June. I did too. But if you’re browsing dates right now and trying to decide when to book - if you like that low, golden light, want a day that feels less like an assembly line, and wouldn’t mind your total coming in about 30% lower - winter is worth a real look.

I’ve got a few winter weekends left for this year. If you’re thinking November, December, or January, send me a note and I’ll tell you which spots look best at 3pm.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
To all of you who fill our shop with your morning hellos, your birthday candles, your Saturday treats, and your trust in what we do: we need to tell you something, and we want it to come from a place of honesty and love.

We are no longer taking custom wedding cake orders.

We know that’s a big one, and we don’t say it lightly. For years, those cakes were a source of real joy for us—a chance to be part of the biggest day in your life, to pour our flourishes into something that would stand at the center of your celebration. We have loved every single one, from the towering three-tiered extravaganzas to the tiny, perfect naked cakes with mismatched flowers. Some of our proudest moments in the bakery have been the gasps when we wheeled a cake into a reception hall.

But we’ve been quiet about what those cakes were costing us, and we think you deserve to know.

Every wedding cake we said yes to meant roughly fourteen hours of sitting across from you, tasting samples, sketching designs, talking through whether the buttercream should be silky or stiff, whether you wanted blush pink or a whisper of it, whether the cake should feed one hundred or one-hundred-and-ten. Those hours were precious, and we gave them happily. But they were hours we were not in the bakery, not shaping bread, not hand-piping the tiny hearts onto the morning cookies, not doing the thousand small things that keep our case full every single day.

And if we’re being fully honest, this year has been hard in a particular way. We had three couples who, through no fault of their own, had to cancel their weddings at the last minute. We understand. Life is messy, and weddings are expensive and complicated, and sometimes things fall apart. But when a cancellation happens after we’ve already ordered the ingredients, after we’ve blocked off the days, after we’ve turned away other work to make room for yours, the cost of all of that lands on us. It’s not a bill we can pass along. It’s just gone.

That’s a part of the business, and we’ve always accepted it. But this year, it made us stop and look at what we were actually doing. The truth is, the everyday case is what pays our rent. It’s the sourdough loaves, the baguettes, the cinnamon rolls that sell out by nine, the little quiche tarts, the cookies that get you through a Tuesday afternoon. That case is our heartbeat, and it’s the reason you keep coming back. Every hour we poured into a wedding cake was an hour we were pulling away from that heartbeat. And the more we did it, the harder it was to do what we do best.

We’ve always believed that the best thing we can give our community is what we make every day. Not because it’s easier, but because it’s what ties us together. It’s the bread you put on your table. It’s the treat you bring to a friend’s house. It’s the thing that makes a normal Tuesday feel a little less ordinary.

We know this will be disappointing to some of you, and that’s okay. We would rather tell you the truth than keep quietly disappointing ourselves and, eventually, you. We don’t want to be the bakery that takes on your wedding and then can’t give you the attention you deserve. We’d rather be the bakery that makes your morning better, every single day, and helps you celebrate in the smaller, sweeter ways we can still show up for.

So if you have a wedding coming up, please know we still adore you, and we’ll be cheering for you from behind the counter. We’ll still make you a gorgeous little dessert table or a beautiful tiered cake for an anniversary or a shower—the kind that doesn’t require fourteen hours of sitting and sketching. And if you’re just here for a loaf of bread and a kind word at 7 a.m., we’ll be here for that, too. That’s where our heart is.

Thank you for making this place what it is. Thank you for understanding. And thank you, always, for letting us feed you.

With flour on our aprons and love in our ovens,
— The whole tiny team at [Bakery Name]

b.text:
# A Little Change Around Here

I've been putting off writing this one, which is usually a sign I should just sit down and do it. So here I am, coffee in hand, flour probably still on my sleeve.

We're not going to be taking custom wedding cake orders anymore.

I want to tell you why, because you've been good to us and you deserve more than a line on the order form. The truth is that wedding cakes, as much as I've loved making them, were quietly pulling the shop in a direction we couldn't keep up with. Every cake starts long before I ever turn on the oven — the consultations, the tastings, the back-and-forth about buttercream shades and how many tiers and whether the flowers should be real. By the time a single cake is done, we've usually put somewhere around fourteen hours into it that no one ever sees. And with three of us running this place, those are hours that have to come from somewhere.

Where they came from was the everyday. The morning loaves, the case full of scones and tarts, the thing you grab on your way to work. That's the part of the bakery that actually keeps our lights on, and it's the part I love most — the regulars, the small daily rhythm of it. When I was buried in wedding planning, that case suffered, and so did I.

I'll be honest about the other piece too. This year we had three weddings cancel at the last minute, and each time we'd already bought the ingredients and blocked the time. That kind of thing happens, I understand it, life is complicated and weddings especially so. But for a shop our size, absorbing that a few times over is a real hit, and it made me look hard at whether this was something we could keep doing well.

So we're stepping back from it, at least for now. If you've got a wedding coming up, I'm genuinely happy to point you toward a few people I trust who do beautiful work and have the setup for it. Just ask.

And please know — we're not going anywhere, and neither is the sweet stuff. We'll still do birthday cakes and the smaller celebration cakes you order ahead. We'll still have the case full every morning. If anything, pulling back on the big commitments means we get to do the everyday things better, which was always the whole point.

Thanks for reading this far, and for being the reason there's a shop to write about. See you at the counter.

— Maggie

*(and the whole crew)*

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots in Minneapolis

Before freezing weather sets in, take a few minutes to protect your outdoor faucets. A frozen pipe can burst inside the wall and cause water damage before you notice it.

1. **Disconnect every garden hose.** This is the step homeowners most often miss—and connected hoses are behind many of our January burst-pipe calls. A hose can trap water in the spigot, even if you have a frost-free faucet.

2. **Shut off the indoor valve.** Find the shutoff valve for the outdoor faucet, usually in the basement or near where the pipe passes through the wall. Turn it off.

3. **Drain the spigot.** Go outside and open the faucet to let the remaining water run out. If your indoor shutoff has a small drain cap or bleeder, place a bucket underneath and open it to drain the pipe, too. Close the bleeder afterward.

4. **Put on a foam cover.** A basic foam faucet cover—often about $3 at a hardware store—adds an extra layer of protection. Fit it snugly over the faucet.

If you can’t find an indoor shutoff, don’t guess or force a valve. Call us, and we can help locate it or install one. A foam cover alone may not protect a pipe that still has water in it.

b.text:
Shut the interior valve. Go outside and open the spigot to drain the remaining water. Disconnect all hoses. If water is trapped, a hose can freeze and split the pipe, causing a burst inside your walls.

A $3 foam cover adds a layer of protection, but it isn't a substitute for draining.

The biggest mistake we see every January? Leaving hoses connected. That is the primary driver behind our burst-pipe calls during the cold snap.

If you don't have an interior shutoff valve, don't guess. Call us to winterize the line properly before the first deep freeze.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
**Don’t Cut the Training That Gets People to Work**

The state is proposing a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding. I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with the IBEW, and I’m asking legislators to vote no.

At our local, one cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one finished and are now working journeyman jobs. Those are 21 people earning a living in a skilled trade our communities need.

Apprentices here start at around $19 an hour. A journeyman earns around $46 an hour. That means people can earn while they learn, build a career, and get off assistance programs sooner. The public cost for each apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. For comparison, the average public subsidy for a student who finishes a four-year degree is roughly $48,000. That’s not an argument against college. It’s an argument for keeping another path to a good job open.

A 15% cut would make it harder to train the next group of workers. Our local’s 21 new journeymen show what this funding can do. When the state helps pay for apprenticeship training, it helps people get to work and helps our communities get the electricians they need.

Legislators should reject the cut. Keep funding apprenticeship programs.

b.text:
**Don’t Cut the Funding That Builds Actual Careers**

The state wants to slash apprenticeship funding by 15%. That is a mistake, and the numbers do not lie.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. 21 finished. Those 21 are working journeyman electrician jobs right now—pulling wire, keeping systems running, and paying taxes instead of drawing public assistance.

We do not start out at high wages. Apprentices start around $19 an hour and top out around $46 an hour as journeymen. At those wages, people get off assistance programs fast. We are not a long-term public cost. We are a short-term investment that starts paying back immediately.

Look at the real cost. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. The average public subsidy for a four-year college grad who actually finishes is roughly $48,000. One apprentice costs about a third of what one college grad costs the state, and we finish at a high rate and go straight to work.

A 15% cut means fewer classroom hours, fewer instructors, and fewer apprentices getting through to journeyman status. That means employers who need licensed electricians will have empty job sites. That means young people who could be earning $46 an hour and standing on their own feet get told to find another path.

To the legislators who read this: leave the funding alone. For every $14,000 the state puts in, it gets back a skilled worker who pays taxes and does not need a subsidy. Cut this budget, and you do not save money. You just move the cost—into unemployment, into empty work bays, or into the next public program that picks up the tab when the pipeline runs dry.

Twenty-four started. Twenty-one finished. They are working now. Do not shrink that pipeline to save a line item. The math is plain, and it is on our side.

— A Third-Year IBEW Electrical Apprentice

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
# Opening the Gates: Why Our School Should Allow Open Campus Lunch

Every day at 12:15, the same thing happens at our school: 340 students pour into a cafeteria built to seat 220. Kids eat standing in hallways, squeeze three to a table designed for two, or give up entirely and skip lunch. Meanwhile, just a few miles away, students at Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade high schools are free to leave campus for lunch, and their schools are doing just fine. Our juniors and seniors should be granted the same open campus privilege, and the evidence from neighboring districts, from our own students, and from our overcrowded cafeteria makes the case clearly.

The strongest argument for open campus lunch is that it has already been tested nearby, and it works. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade school districts all allow upperclassmen to leave campus during lunch, and their published attendance statistics show no rise in tardiness after the policy took effect. In other words, the main objection people raise—that students will wander back late and miss class—did not actually happen. These are districts like ours, with kids the same age dealing with the same temptation to linger, and their numbers stayed steady. If three comparable schools can make this work, the claim that it is too risky starts to look less like a real concern and more like an assumption.

Beyond the district data, the students who would actually be affected by this policy want it. I surveyed 80 students at our school, and 71 of them—nearly 90 percent—said they support open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. Some opponents might argue that students just want freedom for its own sake, but that misses the point: a policy that affects students every single day should weigh what students actually think. When a supermajority of the affected group supports a change, and the change has proven harmless in neighboring districts, the burden shifts to the school to explain why it is holding out.

Finally, open campus lunch would solve a space problem that already exists. Our cafeteria seats 220 people, but our lunch wave has 340 students. That means more than a hundred kids every day have nowhere to sit. This is not a hypothetical overcrowding concern about a future policy; it is the current reality. If even a third of the juniors and seniors left campus for lunch, the cafeteria would drop below its actual capacity for the first time in years. Open campus lunch would not create a new situation at our school—it would relieve a problem the administration has not otherwise fixed.

Critics may still worry about safety, liability, or younger students feeling left out. But the liability question has an answer: schools can require parent permission slips and a signed conduct agreement, the same way Fairmont and West Linn handle it. And the policy can be limited to juniors and seniors, who are sixteen or older, many of whom already drive, hold jobs, and handle adult responsibilities everywhere else in their lives. We trust these students to operate cars on public roads; we can trust them to buy a sandwich and come back.

The evidence is straightforward. Three nearby districts adopted open campus lunch and saw no rise in tardiness. Nearly 90 percent of surveyed students at our school support the change. And our cafeteria is over capacity by more than a hundred students right now. The administration should approve open campus lunch for juniors and seniors—it has the data, the demand, and the space problem pointing in exactly the same direction.

b.text:
Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors

Our school should allow juniors and seniors to leave campus for lunch. Right now we are all required to stay in the building during the lunch period, but that policy is not working with the number of students we have, and it treats upperclassmen like they haven't earned any additional responsibility. An open campus for eleventh and twelfth graders would relieve overcrowding and give students a needed break, and evidence from other schools shows it can be done without creating new problems.

The most immediate reason to make this change is space. Our cafeteria only seats 220 people, but there are 340 students assigned to the same lunch wave. That means more than a hundred students do not have a place to sit and eat. Every day you can see students sitting on the floor in the hall, standing against walls, or rushing to eat outside even when the weather is bad because there is nowhere else to go. When a lunchroom is that far over capacity, it is louder, messier, and harder for staff to supervise. Letting juniors and seniors who choose to leave eat elsewhere would lower the number of students in the building and make lunch more manageable for everyone who stays, including underclassmen.

Some people worry that if students are allowed to leave they will come back late and miss class. The experience of other districts nearby suggests that does not have to happen. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all already allow open campus lunch for juniors and seniors, and their published tardiness data shows no rise in afternoon tardiness after they adopted the policy. These are schools similar in size to ours, and they have shown that when the privilege is limited to upperclassmen it does not disrupt the afternoon schedule. That record matters because it answers the main practical concern with real results instead of guesses about what might go wrong.

There is also clear support for this change among students. I surveyed 80 students at our school about open campus lunch for juniors and seniors, and 71 said they were in favor. That response came from a mix of grades, not just upperclassmen who would benefit right away. Students understand what the current lunch period is like and want an alternative. Support alone is not a reason to change a policy, but when almost nine out of ten students surveyed agree, it shows this is not a small complaint.

Opponents of open campus often argue that leaving school poses safety risks or creates liability issues. Those concerns are serious, but they can be addressed by keeping the policy limited and structured. This proposal is not for all students to come and go as they please. It would apply only to juniors and seniors, who already have more driving experience and more experience managing deadlines and school expectations. A school could require signed parent permission and make clear that returning late or getting into trouble would mean losing the privilege. That makes open campus something students have to earn and keep, not a guarantee.

Giving juniors and seniors the option to leave for lunch is a reasonable response to a real problem in our building. It would ease the crowding that forces students to eat without a seat, it has already worked in Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade without increasing tardiness, and it reflects what a strong majority of students here want. For a single period that sits in the middle of a long school day, that level of trust and flexibility is appropriate, and it would make the school day better for both the students who leave and the ones who stay.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
# The Math Is Simple: Don't Cut Apprenticeship Funding

*By [Name], Third-Year Apprentice, IBEW Local [___]*

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with this local. I bend conduit, pull wire, and get paid to learn a trade that will take care of me and my family for the rest of my working life. Right now there's a proposal at the statehouse to cut apprenticeship funding by 15 percent. I want to walk you through why that's a bad deal, and I'm going to use plain numbers, because the numbers don't need dressing up.

Start with my own class. We began with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished, and every one of those 21 is working today as a journeyman electrician. That's 87 percent of us who made it through. Find me a four-year college program that keeps close to that. Plenty of them can't touch it, and the students who don't finish walk away with debt and no degree. When one of us washes out, we still walk away with a couple years of pay in our pocket and a skill we can use. Nobody finishes our program owing money.

Now the wages. We started at about $19 an hour. That's not a fortune, but it's a real paycheck from day one, and it goes up every year you're in. By the time you turn out, you're making around $46 an hour as a journeyman. I know apprentices in this local who were on food stamps or unemployment before they got their acceptance letter. Within a year of starting, they were off every assistance program they were on. Not because somebody gave them a handout — because they got a job that pays. The state stops paying for them and starts collecting taxes from them. That flip happens fast in this trade.

Here's the number I want every legislator who reads this newsletter to sit with. The total public cost for each apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. The average public subsidy for each four-year college graduate who finishes is around $48,000. Read those again. We cost the public about a third of what a college grad costs. We finish at higher rates. And we're working and paying taxes the whole time we're training instead of waiting four years to start. If the state ran a contest for the best return on workforce money, apprenticeship wins it hands down. This is the program you cut last, not first.

Fifteen percent might not sound like much when you say it fast. Here's what it means on the ground. It means fewer seats in classes. It means longer wait lists to get in. It means older equipment and fewer instructors spread across more students. Right now a person who applies to our program might wait a year or two for a spot. Cut the funding and that wait gets longer. Every person stuck on that list is a person the state isn't collecting taxes from, and may be supporting instead. That's the trade you're making: save a little money now, spend more of it later.

And don't forget what the state actually needs. We are short on electricians, not long on them. Somebody has to wire the schools and the hospitals. Somebody has to build out the data centers, the solar, and the EV chargers the state keeps saying it wants. That work doesn't happen by itself, and it doesn't happen without people trained to do it. Every dollar the state puts into apprenticeship comes back in projects built, taxes paid, and paychecks spent at local businesses. The 21 journeymen out of my class alone will pay back that $14,000 apiece many times over across a career.

I'm an electrician, not a speechwriter, so I'll keep the ending short. This cut fails by its own logic. The state would be trimming 15 percent off the cheapest, highest-finishing, fastest-paying workforce program it runs — in the middle of a shortage of exactly the workers that program produces. If you're a member of this local, call your representative and tell them the numbers in this piece. If you're a legislator and this newsletter reaches your desk, do the math yourself.

The math is simple. Don't cut the program that's working.

b.text:
**Don’t Cut the Training That Gets People to Work**

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with the IBEW. I go to work, learn from journeymen, and take classes so I can do the job safely and well. That training costs money. Cutting state apprenticeship funding by 15% would make it harder for the next group to get the same chance.

Look at what that investment produces. One cohort at our local started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one finished and are now working journeyman jobs. Those are people earning a living, paying taxes, and doing work our communities need.

Apprentices here start at around $19 an hour. As journeymen, they can earn around $46 an hour. That pay gives people a way to support themselves and their families, and to move off assistance programs. The state gets something back from its investment.

The public cost is about $14,000 for each apprentice who finishes, compared with roughly $48,000 in public subsidy for each four-year college graduate who finishes. College matters, too. But if lawmakers are looking for a good use of public money, apprenticeship belongs on the list.

Electrical work takes training. A mistake can hurt someone, and the work has to be done right. We need enough classroom time, instructors, and opportunities for new apprentices to learn the trade. A 15% cut puts that at risk.

I’m asking state legislators to reject this cut. Keep funding the path that helped 21 people in that cohort become working journeymen—and can do the same for the apprentices coming behind us.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
**To Members of the City Council and the Downtown Community:**

My name is [Your Name], and I am the owner of [Name of Coffee Shop], located on Main Street. I am submitting this written testimony for the official public record to formally oppose the proposed parking meter rate increase from $0.50 to $1.50 per hour in our downtown district. 

I do not write this out of an instinctive resistance to city revenue adjustments, nor do I rely on abstract warnings that this policy "might hurt small business." I am writing because the cold, hard numbers—from my own sales logs, from regional precedent, and from the city’s own fiscal reports—demonstrate that a 200% rate hike will disproportionately damage the downtown retail ecosystem while delivering negligible fiscal return to the municipality.

First, consider the direct economics of a downtown visit. Over the past year, my point-of-sale logs show that the average visit length for a customer in my shop is precisely 22 minutes. These patrons are not long-term parkers occupying spots for an entire workday; they are residents popping in to grab a coffee, pick up a pastry, or meet a colleague briefly before moving on. Under the current structure, the 60-minute minimum charge of $0.50 easily covers their stay while remaining an afterthought. Tripling that rate to $1.50 introduces immediate transactional friction. When a customer buys a $4.75 latte, adding a mandatory $1.50 parking fee represents an effective 31.5% surcharge on their purchase. For short-stay errands, parking cost shifts from an incidental expense into a deterrent. Drivers will simply reroute to suburban strip malls and drive-throughs where surface parking remains free.

Second, we already have empirical data on what happens when a municipality implements this exact change. In 2019, when our neighboring municipality instituted an identical tripling of their downtown meter rates, I closely tracked foot traffic and customer frequency over a six-week control period using our register data. During those six weeks, foot traffic across comparable merchant categories dropped by 18%. In an industry operating on 5% to 8% net margins, an 18% decline in foot traffic is not a minor inconvenience; it is the difference between retaining staff and cutting shifts, or between breaking even and shutting our doors entirely. The downtown core relies on compounded micro-trips. When you disincentivize the casual, spontaneous visit, the entire retail block absorbs the loss.

Finally, the justification that this increase will meaningfully shore up municipal finances collapses under the city’s own accounting. According to the Downtown Mobility and Budget Report released last month, parking meter revenue accounts for exactly 4% of the downtown operating budget. Even if one were to assume—unrealistically—zero decline in parking utilization after tripling the fee, this rate hike does not resolve the structural challenges facing downtown infrastructure or transit maintenance. Balancing a municipal deficit requires substantive fiscal planning, not nickel-and-diming the foot traffic that generates downtown property tax, sales tax, and economic vitality in the first place. Sacrificing nearly a fifth of Main Street foot traffic to manipulate a revenue source that constitutes only 4% of the ledger is bad math and worse governance.

Downtown businesses have spent years rebuilding steady, dependable foot traffic. Replacing that stability with a 200% parking hike will extract revenue from local patrons while failing to meaningfully move the needle on city finances. I strongly urge the Council to reject the proposed increase from $0.50 to $1.50 and to pursue revenue alternatives that do not penalize the residents patronizing our local businesses.

Respectfully submitted,

[Your Name]  
Owner, [Name of Coffee Shop]  
[Address / Main Street Location]

b.text:
**Testimony Regarding the Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Members of the Council, my name is [Name], and I own [Coffee Shop Name] on Main Street. I have run this business for [number] years. I am here to ask you not to raise downtown meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour.

The proposal would triple the hourly rate. For my customers, the change is larger than the percentage suggests. Most people who stop in for coffee stay about 22 minutes. Under the current rate, a 22-minute visit costs 50 cents, which is covered by the one-hour minimum. Under the proposed rate, the same visit costs $1.50. That is an added dollar every time a customer parks to buy a coffee, a sandwich, or a book from a neighboring shop.

I am not speculating about what that dollar will do. In 2019, a neighboring town raised its meter rates by a comparable amount. I did not have a plan for that period, so I started tracking my own register. Over the six weeks following the increase, I recorded an 18% drop in foot traffic compared with the prior period. I cannot prove that the meter increase was the only cause, and I am not asking you to accept my register as a controlled study. I am asking you to consider that it is the only direct evidence any of us has so far, and that it points in one direction.

I also want to address what this increase would accomplish. According to the city's own budget report, metered parking revenue covers about 4% of the downtown budget. A rate tripling would raise money, but it would not change the fiscal picture of the district in any meaningful way. Meanwhile, the cost would fall on the small businesses that give downtown its character: the independent shops that do not have corporate budgets to absorb a sudden jump in customer costs or a drop in visits.

A small coffee shop operates on thin margins. Each customer who decides a 22-minute stop is no longer worth $1.50 is a customer lost, and the losses compound. A few fewer customers a day can mean fewer hours for my staff, a smaller order from my suppliers, and, eventually, a decision about whether the shop can stay open.

I respectfully ask the Council to reject the proposed increase, or at minimum to delay it until the city has studied its effect on downtown foot traffic and the businesses that depend on it. I would welcome the chance to share my full register data with the Council or with city staff, and I am glad to answer any questions.

Thank you for your time and your service to our community.

[Name]
[Coffee Shop Name]
[Address]

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**Let Our Kids Sleep: Why I'm Supporting the 8:45 Start Time**

I've watched my two middle-schoolers drag themselves out of bed at 6:15 for years now, and I'm done pretending it's normal. It's not. It's exhausting for them and for us, and it turns out there's real science behind why.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has been saying for years that middle and high schoolers shouldn't start school before 8:30. Their bodies are wired differently during adolescence — melatonin kicks in later at night, which means teens biologically can't fall asleep early even when we send them to bed at a reasonable hour. Asking them to be alert for a 7:30 first period is basically asking them to function on a permanent case of jet lag.

I know this isn't just theoretical, either. We already have proof it works right here in our district. When Lincoln Middle piloted the later start time last year, attendance went up and first-period grades improved. Not "stayed the same" — improved. That's not a fluke; that's tired kids finally getting enough sleep to actually learn.

I understand the biggest objection I keep hearing at school board meetings is about buses — that shifting start times will throw the whole transportation schedule into chaos. I get it; nobody wants a repeat of some logistical nightmare. But if you actually read the proposal (I have, several times), the district has already worked this out. Bus routes are being re-tiered so elementary schools shift earlier while middle and high schools shift later. It's not adding buses or costs — it's resequencing the same routes we already have. This isn't a hand-wavy "we'll figure it out later" plan. The tiering is right there in black and white.

I'm not a policy expert. I'm a parent who has watched my kids struggle through first period looking like zombies, and who has seen an actual pilot program in our own district prove that a later start helps. This isn't a radical experiment — it's catching up to what the research already tells us and what our own data already showed.

The school board votes on this next month. I hope they look at Lincoln's results, look at the transportation plan that's already built to handle this, and give the rest of our kids the same chance to succeed that Lincoln students already got.

*— A Millbrook parent, tired of watching tired kids*

b.text:
**Let Our Kids Sleep. The Numbers Say We Should.**

Every school morning at 6:20, I stand in my daughter's doorway and say her name three times before she moves. She is thirteen. She is not lazy. She is doing exactly what her body is built to do at that age, which is sleep.

That's why I'm asking the school board to approve the 8:45 start time when it votes next month.

I'm not a doctor, but the doctors have been clear on this. The American Academy of Pediatrics says middle and high schools should start no earlier than 8:30, because teenagers' internal clocks genuinely shift later during puberty. They physically cannot fall asleep at 9:30 the way a second-grader can. Ask them to be at their desks by 7:40 and you are guaranteeing they show up short on sleep. The AAP ties that chronic shortfall to worse grades, more depression, more car accidents among teen drivers, and more sick days. That's not a parenting opinion. That's the pediatricians.

We don't have to take it on faith, either. Lincoln Middle ran this as a pilot, and the results are in the proposal for anyone to read. Attendance went up. First-period grades went up. The kids who used to sleep through pre-algebra started actually doing pre-algebra. When a change works in our own district, with our own kids and our own teachers, I don't know what more evidence we're waiting for.

I know the objection. I've heard it at soccer practice and in the pickup line: "It'll wreck the buses." I had the same worry, so I read the transportation section twice. The proposal doesn't add buses. It re-tiers the routes, so elementary runs first and middle school runs second, instead of the other way around. Same fleet, same drivers, same number of trips. It's a schedule change, not a budget request. If someone has read that section and found a hole in it, I'd like to hear it, but "the buses" isn't an argument on its own anymore.

Will it be an adjustment? Sure. Some families will need to rethink before-school care. Practices may shift. I'm willing to do that, because the alternative is what we're doing now, which is asking twelve- and thirteen-year-olds to fight biology every single morning and then wondering why they're irritable, distracted, and falling behind.

We tell our kids that when the evidence changes, you change your mind. Here's a chance for the grownups to model it.

Vote yes on 8:45.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
Last week I finally launched the game. Three years of nights and weekends—first commercial release is out in the wild.

First week: 412 copies sold. It also hit the front page of a small subreddit for about six hours, which was strange, brief, and genuinely nice to watch.

Most of the noise has been kind, but one review nailed it: the movement feels floaty, and honestly they’re right. I’m not going to pretend it’s fine. The 1.1 patch is already planned for next month; that’s the main thing getting tightened.
