b.text:
# One week after launch

My game came out last week. After three years of working on it during nights and weekends, it’s very strange to be able to write that sentence in the past tense.

It sold 412 copies in its first week. I don’t have a grand verdict on that number yet, but I wanted to share the actual figure here.

The game also hit the front page of a small subreddit for about six hours. Not exactly taking over the internet, but still a pretty big moment for something I’ve mostly been posting about to a few hundred people on this blog.

One review said the movement feels floaty. Honestly, they’re right. It’s something I got used to after spending so long playing the same build, and seeing someone point it out made it harder to shrug off. That’s going into the 1.1 patch next month. I want to tighten it up, then give myself enough time to test the changes properly rather than push out a quick adjustment just to say it’s fixed.

Thanks to everyone who bought a copy, played it, or followed along here while I was making it. If you’ve got feedback, I’m still reading it—even when it confirms something I probably should have dealt with sooner.

Next up is the movement work for 1.1. I’ll post another update when I have a build ready to show.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
The first sign was the receipt printer making a noise like it was chewing paper. Then the screen froze, blinked once, and went black.

It was 12:15 on a Saturday, and the restaurant was already full. Every table had at least one bowl of pho or plate of broken rice. The kitchen tickets were hanging on the rail, but the new ones stopped coming. My mom tapped the screen a few times, then looked at me.

I grabbed a stack of order pads and a handful of pens.

For the next three hours, I wrote every ticket by hand. Table number, dish, modifications, no onions, extra broth, one order rare, one order well done. I used different colors so the kitchen would not mix up appetizers and entrees. Red for drinks, blue for food. When I ran out of red, I used pencil and underlined twice.

The kitchen did not slow down. If anything, it got louder because nobody trusted the system anymore. My dad called out orders from the pass. My aunt asked if table six got their egg rolls. Someone said table twelve had been waiting twenty minutes, but table twelve had just ordered. I kept the pad in front of me and wrote everything down before I moved.

At one point, a server handed me a ticket with coffee stains all over it. I could still read the table number, but not the drinks. I went to the table and asked the customers to repeat the order. They were patient, which surprised me. Usually people get annoyed when something goes wrong in a restaurant. Maybe they could tell we were trying.

By the time the repair guy came, my hand hurt. I had filled six order pads. The register came back on, printed a long list of errors, and then started working like nothing had happened. I kept the last page of my order pad. It had a smear of fish sauce on the corner.

When things calm down, I usually help prep. My favorite job is spring rolls, but only if nobody rushes me. My grandma taught me the fold when I was little. She did not explain it much. She just put a rice paper wrapper on the damp towel, added shrimp, pork, herbs, and noodles, then folded the sides in tight and rolled it once. The trick was not to overfill it and not to tear it.

Last month we hired a new girl named Lan. She was fast, but her spring rolls kept splitting. She kept putting too much lettuce near the edge. I showed her how to leave room at the sides and tuck the filling down before rolling.

“Like this,” I said. “Don’t be nice to it.”

She laughed and tried again. The next one looked better. The one after that looked almost like my grandma’s.

My grandma does not work full shifts anymore, but she still comes in and checks everything. She picked up one of Lan’s rolls and turned it over in her hand. She did not say anything for a second. Then she said, “Okay.”

That was enough.

During slow stretches, I do homework. The best place is the walk-in cooler. It is quiet, and nobody asks me to refill sauces or wipe down tables. I sit on a milk crate with my backpack and my calculator. The fan blows cold air behind the shelves of basil, cilantro, and sliced onions. Sometimes my nose runs. Sometimes my fingers get stiff. But I can focus.

Calc is hardest in there. Not because of the cold, but because if I lose track of one step, I have to start over. I keep my notebook on my knees and write small so I can fit more work on one page. Last week I was doing derivatives while someone behind me stacked boxes of frozen shrimp. He asked if I was studying chemistry. I said no, but then I had to explain what a derivative sort of is, and by the time I finished, my problem was all wrong.

I do not always finish homework before my shift ends. Sometimes I have to take it home, and sometimes I fall asleep with the notebook open on my bed. But I like knowing where everything is: the order pads, the spring roll wrappers, the calculator, the stack of clean towels by the sink.

On weekends, the restaurant smells like garlic and star anise. My shoes get sticky. My shirt smells like broth even after I wash it. I know which table wobbles, which fan squeaks, which customer asks for extra limes without asking nicely.

When the last customers leave, I stack chairs, sweep under the tables, and count the register drawer. My dad turns off the hood fan, and the room gets suddenly quiet. I take the trash out back, lock the side door, and check it twice.

Then I get in the car and ride home.

b.text:
The register stopped working on a Saturday night, when every table was full.

The screen froze after a customer’s card went through, then went black. My dad unplugged it and plugged it back in. Nothing. People were waiting at the counter, and tickets were coming in from the kitchen.

I found a pad of paper and started writing orders by hand. Table numbers, dishes, changes: no cilantro, extra noodles, sauce on the side. I carried each ticket to the kitchen and checked it against the food before it went out. At the counter, I added totals with a calculator and tried to keep the line moving. When someone asked for a receipt, I wrote one.

By the end of the night, my fingers were cramped and my handwriting had gotten worse. The register worked again the next day. The stack of tickets stayed on the counter until we were sure everything had been paid for.

I have worked weekends at my family’s Vietnamese restaurant since sophomore year. Most shifts are less dramatic. I take orders, refill water, pack takeout, and answer questions about dishes I have eaten so often I sometimes forget other people haven’t. I know which tables wobble and where we keep the extra chopsticks. I can hear when the kitchen is getting backed up from the sound of the printer.

One afternoon, a new hire was having trouble folding spring rolls. My grandma stood beside her and showed her how much filling to use. Too much, and the wrapper split. Too little, and the roll came out flat. My grandma’s hands moved quickly, so I took a wrapper and slowed down the steps: fold the bottom corner over the filling, tuck in the sides, then roll it tight. The new hire tried again. The next one held together.

My grandma watched, then nodded and went back to her station. I kept folding beside the new hire. We talked about which classes we were taking while we worked. By the end of the shift, her rolls looked like rolls.

I do homework during breaks when I can. Sometimes I sit in the walk-in cooler with my calculus notebook open on a crate. The door shuts out most of the restaurant noise. I work through a problem, hear someone call my name, and put the notebook away before the condensation softens the pages. When the rush slows, I come back to it.

My weekends have been planned around the restaurant for years. I know when I need to finish an assignment before a shift and when I can bring it with me. My friends sometimes make plans for Saturday nights, and I usually tell them I’ll see how busy we are. I don’t always know how to answer when they ask what it’s like to work with family. It is sometimes frustrating. It is also familiar: my dad calling orders, my grandma checking the spring rolls, someone asking me to run food while I’m halfway through a calculus problem.

Next Saturday, I will probably be at the counter again. I’ll write down orders, carry plates, and find a quiet corner for my homework when there is one. I’ll keep an eye on the door to the kitchen, in case someone needs me.

A retired Route 4 carrier
Kettle Falls

b.text:

Kettle Falls

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
I see it at the salon every single week. You bring in your doodle, poodle, or double-coated pup, genuinely frustrated because you’ve been trying so hard to keep their coat fluffy between appointments, but somehow those stubborn tangles keep showing up. Usually, when we chat about your at-home routine, we end up tracing it back to one major culprit: bath time.

The biggest mistake I see people make is putting their dog in the tub first, thinking the warm water and shampoo will help loosen up the tangles. It actually does the exact opposite. When you get matted fur wet, it essentially turns into a solid felt pad. The water and the scrubbing motion lock those knots in so tightly that they become impossible to brush out. 

To save your dog’s coat, you always want to brush them thoroughly before they ever see a drop of water. Never after. 

When you sit down to do this, grab a good slicker brush. The trick is to avoid brushing in circles or just grazing the top of the fur. You want to use short, straight line strokes, working your way through the coat in small, manageable sections. I always recommend starting in the areas where friction happens the most, because that’s exactly where mats like to start. Check right behind their ears, and lift up those front legs to thoroughly check their armpits. 

If you are working through those high-friction spots and you do see a mat already forming, put the brush down. Before you ever touch a brush or a comb to a knot, take a little bit of dog conditioner and massage it directly into the tangle with your fingers. Working it in by hand helps gently separate the hair without yanking on your dog's skin. 

Once you’ve got them completely brushed out and tangle-free, then it's finally time for the tub. Catching those tangles dry makes a world of difference for curly and double-coated breeds, and it ensures your dog is comfortable, happy, and ready for a stress-free haircut the next time you bring them in to see me.

b.text:
# How to Keep Your Dog’s Coat From Matting Between Grooms

The mistake I see most often is a well-meaning one: you notice a few tangles, so you put your dog in the bath, thinking a good wash will loosen everything up.

Unfortunately, it usually does the opposite. Water and rubbing can tighten those tangles into a dense, felt-like pad that’s much harder to remove. If there’s one thing I’d like you to remember between appointments, it’s this: **check and brush the coat before the bath. Don’t leave the detangling until afterward.**

That’s especially important for curly coats, where loose hair gets caught in the curls, and double coats, where shedding undercoat can pack down close to the skin. A dog can look lovely and fluffy on top while hiding quite a bit of matting underneath.

I like to start behind the ears and under the front legs. Those soft, high-friction spots are often where the first tangles show up. Check around the collar or harness, too, and take your time—the skin in these areas is delicate.

If you find a small, loose tangle starting, don’t go straight at it with a brush or comb. Work a little dog-safe detangling conditioner into it with your fingers first, following the product’s directions. Gently tease the hairs apart without pulling on the skin. This is for little tangles you can comfortably loosen, not tight mats stuck against the body.

Once the area is tangle-free enough to brush comfortably, work through the coat in small sections with a slicker brush suited to your dog’s coat. Part the hair so you can see the skin, then use short, gentle, straight strokes through a thin layer of hair. No circles, and no repeated scrubbing over the same patch. Lift the next small layer and keep going—that’s line brushing.

The aim is to reach through the coat, not just tidy the surface. You don’t need to press hard, and the pins shouldn’t scrape the skin. Follow each finished section with a metal comb. If it catches, stop and check that spot rather than pulling it through.

For double-coated dogs, pay particular attention during shedding season. For curly-coated dogs, keep checking all the way down to the roots. A few minutes regularly is usually much easier on both of you than one long session with a week’s worth of tangles.

And if a mat feels tight, sits close to the skin, or makes your dog flinch, leave it for us. Please don’t cut it out with scissors—skin can be pulled up inside a mat where you can’t see it.

You don’t have to get everything perfect at home. Catching little tangles early, keeping brushing gentle, and checking the coat **before it gets wet** makes a real difference. If you’re not sure whether your brush is reaching through properly, bring it to your next appointment. I’m happy to show you how I’d use it on your dog’s coat.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now

I'll be honest: when I started out, I thought of winter weddings as the off-season. They were the dates you took when June was full, the ones where you'd fight the cold and the early dark and make it work.

I don't think that anymore. Over the last two years I've shot 11 winter weddings, and somewhere in there I stopped seeing them as the consolation prize. If you're trying to decide when to book, here's what I've learned, and none of it is "every season is magical in its own way."

## The money is real

Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for couples. That's not a small rounding difference. That's the kind of gap that pays for a second shooter, a better dinner for your guests, or a honeymoon that isn't a long weekend.

I bring this up first because a lot of couples assume a cheaper date means a compromise somewhere. In my experience, it's mostly just supply and demand. Fewer people want the date, so the date costs less. The wedding itself doesn't get worse.

## The light is better than you'd think. For portraits, it's better than June.

This is the one that surprised me most.

People picture summer weddings with golden, glowing light. Sometimes you get that. But around here, a lot of June days are overcast, and overcast summer light is *flat*. It's bright and even, and it's fine, but it doesn't do much. There's no direction to it and no shape on a face.

Now picture a November afternoon around 3pm. The sun is already low, and it comes through bare trees instead of a solid wall of leaves. You get light with an angle to it, some warmth, and soft breaks of shadow from the branches. It wraps around people instead of sitting on top of them. For portraits, it's honestly some of my favorite light of the whole year.

The tradeoff is that the window is earlier and shorter. If you book a winter date with me, we'll build your timeline around that afternoon light. That usually means doing portraits before the ceremony or scheduling things so we're outside when the light is at its best, not after dark. Plan for it and you get the payoff. Ignore it and you're shooting portraits by headlights. I'll help you plan for it.

## I'm not fighting for parking (or space, or attention)

This sounds minor. It isn't.

On a busy June Saturday, I'm often sharing the parking lot with three or four other vendors: florists unloading, a band hauling gear, caterers running trays back and forth, a planner trying to keep it all moving. Everyone is doing their job well, but it's crowded. Venues are booked back to back, setup is rushed, and there's a lot of motion happening around the moments I'm trying to catch.

Winter is calmer. There's room to move, room to set up a shot without someone walking a centerpiece through it, and usually more breathing room in the schedule overall. That calm shows up in the photos. You're less rushed, I'm less rushed, and nobody is checking the clock to clear out for the next event.

## What I'd tell you if you're on the fence

Winter isn't for everyone. If your heart is set on an outdoor ceremony in a garden, it's going to be cold, and I won't pretend otherwise. If you want a long, lazy evening of outdoor golden-hour portraits at 8pm, summer is your season.

But if you're open to it, here's what a winter date gets you, based on 11 of them:

- **About 30% less spent**, with that money free for the things you actually care about
- **Better portrait light** in the afternoon than a typical overcast June day gives you
- **A calmer day**, with fewer vendors stacked on top of each other and more time for the moments that matter

If you're thinking about a winter date, reach out. I'm happy to talk through timing, light, and what your day could look like. I'll tell you straight whether I think it's a good fit for what you want.

b.text:
**Why I’ve Fallen for Winter Weddings (And Why You Might Too)**

I’ll be honest—six years ago, I wasn’t exactly *thrilled* when a couple asked me to shoot their January wedding. Cold fingers, slippery sidewalks, the sun setting before cocktail hour… what was there to love? But after shooting 11 winter weddings in the last two years, I’ve officially changed my tune. Here’s why:

**1. The Light is *Chef’s Kiss***
That soft, golden glow you get in June? It’s nice, but it’s also *everywhere*—and often drowned out by thick cloud cover. Winter light, though? Around 3 PM in November or December, the sun hangs low, filtering through bare branches like a natural diffuser. The result? Portraits with depth, warmth, and a moodiness that flat summer light just can’t match.

**2. Fewer Crowds, More Focus**
In June, I’m sharing the venue parking lot with three other photographers, a videographer, and a florist’s van. Winter weddings? It’s just me, the couple, and maybe a rogue squirrel. Fewer distractions mean I can actually *see* the details—the way the candlelight flickers on your dress, the steam rising from your coffee during golden hour, the quiet moments that get lost in the chaos of peak season.

**3. Your Budget Goes Further**
Winter weddings run about 30% cheaper on average. That’s not just a rumor—it’s a fact. Venues, caterers, even some vendors (ahem) offer off-season rates. That extra cash could mean an extra hour of coverage, a second shooter, or even just breathing room in your budget for the things that matter most.

**4. The Coziness Factor**
There’s something magical about a winter wedding. The crackle of a fireplace, the way your breath hangs in the air during a first-look moment, the glow of string lights against a dark sky. Summer weddings are vibrant, but winter weddings? They’re *intimate*. And intimacy is what makes for photos that feel like *you*.

So if you’re on the fence about a winter wedding, let me be the one to say: don’t write it off. The light is better, the crowds are smaller, and the memories? Just as unforgettable. (And yes, I *will* bring hand warmers.)

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
Here’s a quick, no-nonsense guide to winterizing your outdoor spigots. If you do nothing else, take this seriously: the biggest mistake we see every January is a hose left connected. That one oversight is behind most of our frozen-pipe calls — and it’s completely avoidable.

**Step 1: Disconnect every hose**
Start here. Unscrew hoses, splitters, spray nozzles — anything attached to the spigot. Water trapped inside a hose or a fitting freezes and pushes back into the pipe inside your wall. That’s the burst you dread. Remove it all and store hoses indoors or at least drain them completely.

**Step 2: Shut off the interior water valve**
Head to the basement, crawl space, or utility closet. You’re looking for a valve on the pipe leading directly to the outside faucet. It might be a lever or a round handle. Turn it all the way off (clockwise). If you’ve never done this and aren’t sure which valve controls which spigot, now’s the time to label them.

**Step 3: Drain the spigot**
Go back outside and open the faucet fully. Let any remaining water dribble out. Leave it open — this gives any trapped water room to expand if a little freeze happens. Don’t close it again until spring.

**Step 4: Cover it with a foam insulator**
Pick up a rigid foam spigot cover at any hardware store — they cost about $3. Slip it over the faucet, tighten the cord or clip, and you’re done. This isn’t just a plastic cap; it insulates against wind and holds a bit of warmer air. It’s cheap insurance that actually works.

**What if you don’t find an interior shutoff valve?**
Some older Minneapolis homes don’t have them. Don’t guess and don’t just skip it. Give us a call at [your phone number]. We can install a proper shutoff valve inside, or help you winterize safely. It’s a small job that prevents a massive mess.

A frozen spigot doesn’t just break outside — the split often happens inside your wall. Come January, you won’t know until water’s gushing into your basement or living room. Do these four steps now, before the real cold hits, and you’re set.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots (Before the Ground Freezes)

Most of the burst-pipe calls we run in January trace back to one outside faucet somebody forgot about in October. Here's how to make sure that's not you. Takes about ten minutes per spigot.

## 1. Find the interior shutoff and close it

Every outside spigot should have its own shutoff valve inside the house. Look on the basement or crawlspace wall directly behind the spigot, follow the pipe back a few feet, and you'll usually find a small valve — either a round handle you turn clockwise or a lever you turn perpendicular to the pipe. Close it all the way.

If you go looking and there's no valve back there, stop here and see the note at the bottom.

## 2. Go outside and open the spigot

With the interior valve closed, open the outside faucet fully. Water will run for a few seconds, then trickle, then stop. Leave the spigot open all winter. That way any water left in the line has room to expand if it freezes instead of splitting the pipe.

Some shutoff valves have a small brass cap on the side — that's a bleeder. Put a bucket under it, unscrew it, and let the rest of the water in the pipe drain out. Tighten it back up after.

## 3. Disconnect every hose

This is the one that matters most, so read it twice.

A hose left connected traps water inside the spigot and the pipe behind it. The water freezes, expands, and cracks the pipe — usually right where it passes through the wall, where you can't see it. You don't find out until spring when you turn the water back on and it comes through the ceiling in the basement.

Even a "frost-free" spigot will burst with a hose attached. The frost-free design only works if the water can drain out the end, and a hose blocks that.

Take the hose off. Take off any splitter, timer, or quick-connect fitting too. Drain the hose and store it in the garage. Do it now, not in November when you have to chip the fitting loose.

## 4. Put on a foam cover

The insulated foam covers at any hardware store in Minneapolis run about three dollars. They fit over the spigot and cinch tight against the siding. It's not a substitute for steps 1 through 3, but it keeps wind off the faucet and adds a margin on the coldest nights. Cheapest insurance you'll buy this year.

## When to do this

Before the first hard freeze — for us, that's usually mid-October. If you're reading this and it's already been below freezing a few nights, do it today. The pipe may be fine so far, but it won't stay that way.

## If you don't have an interior shutoff

Some older houses in Minneapolis were plumbed without one, and some newer houses have spigots run off lines that never got a valve. If you can't find a shutoff inside, don't just cover the spigot and hope. Give us a call. Installing a shutoff valve is a quick, inexpensive job, and it's a lot cheaper than the drywall repair that comes after a burst pipe. We can also swap an old spigot for a frost-free one while we're there.

Ten minutes in October. That's all it takes.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years of showing homes in Asheville, one habit keeps showing up: buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7am before we tour end up genuinely happier with their choice.

The Pruitts on Sycamore Street are a perfect example. They showed up before sunrise, walked the block while the street was still quiet, and popped over to say hi to a neighbor starting his morning routine. They noticed how the light hit the front porch, how the trees looked from the sidewalk, and that there was a little coffee shop two blocks over that would be perfect for weekends. They told me later that those few minutes made the house feel like home before they even walked through the door—they’d already started imagining their mornings there.

That’s the part people don’t always expect: buying a house isn’t just about the floor plan. It’s about the rhythm of the neighborhood. Sometimes the best showing happens before the tour even starts.

b.text:
After 12 years selling homes in Asheville—most of them to first-time buyers who’ve spent more nights scrolling Zillow after work than I can count, weighing every granite counter and square foot like it’s a make-or-break life choice—there’s one small, unscripted habit I’ve noticed that separates the buyers who still text me photos of their garden harvests 5 years later from the ones who reach out saying they’re ready to move again.

It has nothing to do with a home’s list price, its school rating, or whether it has that open-concept kitchen everyone says they want. It’s this: the buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7am on a weekday, before we even tour the house, end up far happier with their purchase long-term.

I thought of this last week when Mia and Ty Pruitt dropped off a jar of their homemade dill pickles (they planted a raised bed where the old rotting shed used to be) and reminded me of the 1920s Sycamore Street bungalow they almost passed on back in 2019. They’d been searching for 6 months, two elementary school teachers with a rescue beagle named Mabel, and they’d narrowed it down to two places: the Sycamore bungalow with the sun-drenched front porch and a tiny primary closet that made Mia groan, and a newer build on the north side with a massive walk-in closet, a two-car garage, and an HOA that banned front-yard vegetable gardens. They were leaning hard toward the newer build, because the closet felt like a “responsible” box to check, even though they kept saying the Sycamore place “felt like us” every time we walked through.

I told them to hold off on making an offer that weekend. Instead, set two 7am alarms: one to walk three blocks in each direction around the Sycamore bungalow on Monday, and one to do the same at the north side neighborhood on Tuesday. No checklists, no grading, just walk and notice what they see, hear, even smell.

Mia called me first thing Monday, still a little breathless. They’d showed up at the Sycamore house at 7am sharp, and before they’d even taken two steps down the sidewalk, a gray-haired man in flannel—Mr. Henderson, who’d lived on the block for 42 years—waved from the median, where he was watering the row of massive sycamores that give the street its name, carrying a chipped mug from the tiny coffee shop two blocks over. A group of elementary school kids walked past, backpacks covered in dinosaur patches, stopping to pet a golden retriever tied to a porch rail. They could smell cinnamon rolls wafting from the corner bakery that opens at 6:30 for early commuters. A woman in overalls waved from her front yard where she was harvesting kale, asked if they were looking at the bungalow, and said the previous owners threw the best annual block party on the west side.

Their Tuesday walk at the north side neighborhood was the exact opposite. Every car that passed was rushing, no one made eye contact. The only sound was the hum of highway traffic a half mile away. All the trash bins were still lined up at the curb, two days after pickup. The only person they saw was a guy in a hoodie walking a husky, who didn’t even nod when they said good morning.

They put an offer on the Sycamore bungalow that afternoon, wrote a letter about the sycamores and the cinnamon rolls and Mr. Henderson, and got it for $2,000 over asking, no appraisal gap needed. That was 4 years ago. Now they host the block party themselves, they walk to that coffee shop every Saturday before Mabel’s dog park trip, and they turned that tiny primary closet into a built-in bookshelf and added a wardrobe in the guest room instead. They still say that 40-minute 7am walk was the most important part of their entire home search.

I don’t have a fancy study or curated stat to back this up, just 12 years of stories like this. Floor plans can be rearranged. Closets can be expanded. You can repaint every wall, add a deck, renovate the kitchen top to bottom. But the rhythm of a neighborhood? The way your neighbors greet you when you’re leaving for work? The smell of baked goods drifting down the street first thing in the morning? That’s the stuff you can’t renovate.

Caught a four-wheeler doing a dumb lane change into my trailer, and having that footage got my insurance claim approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6-week runaround. That alone paid for the camera about ten times over. Front camera footage is solid day or night, road signs and plates readable, no complaints there.

The not-so-good: rear cam night footage turns to mush past 30 feet. Fine for seeing if someone's tailgating, useless if you need plate detail on something that happened further back. Also had the suction mount pop off twice during summer runs through the desert — heat just cooked the adhesive on it. Switched to the actual adhesive mount and haven't had an issue since, so if you're buying this thing, just skip the suction mount altogether and order the sticky one from the start.

App situation is a mess. It wants wifi to pull footage off the cam remotely, which sounds nice until you realize most truck stops either don't have wifi or it's too weak to move video files. I stopped messing with the app months ago and just pull the SD card straight into my laptop when I need something off it. Faster anyway.

Bottom line: for the price, it's a decent camera that's already proven its worth once when it mattered most. Just know the rear night vision has limits, swap the mount before the heat kills it for you, and don't bother with the app unless you're parked somewhere with real wifi. 140k miles in and it's still running, so durability's not an issue.

3.5/5 — would buy again, but I'm keeping an eye out for something with better rear night vision when this one finally dies.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
My daughter was six when I came home from my second deployment. At the airport, she stood behind her mother’s leg and looked at me from there.

I had pictured her running over. Instead, I stopped a few feet away with my bag in my hand. Her mother told her it was me. She knew my name, of course, and she had seen me on a screen, but I had been gone a year. In person, with a bag on my shoulder and people walking around us, I wasn’t somebody she was ready to hug.

I set the bag down. After a while she came out from behind her mother and let me take her hand. We walked to the car like that. I carried the bag with my other hand.

A few days later, I went to the grocery store by myself. We needed cereal. I stood in the aisle for about twenty minutes, looking at what seemed like forty kinds. There were big boxes and small boxes, family sizes, ones with fruit on the front, ones that promised more fiber. I picked one up and put it back. Then I did the same with another.

I had spent most of the past year knowing what food was available before I got to it. Now I had a whole aisle and no reason to choose one box over the next. A man came past with a cart, got what he wanted, and kept going. I moved aside to let him through.

When I got home, my wife asked if the store had been crowded. I told her no. I put the cereal in the cupboard.

At night I slept facing the bedroom door. I’d done it so long I didn’t think about turning that way. The first time my wife left the door open, I got up and closed it. She asked if we could leave it open so we could hear our daughter if she called out. I said okay, then lay awake looking at the strip of hallway I could see.

For a while, one of us would open the door and the other would close it. Eventually I stopped getting up. I still woke sometimes and looked toward the hallway. Usually there was nothing there. Once, our daughter came down it in her pajamas and stood in the doorway until I made room for her on the bed.

b.text:
I stepped off the plane at Fort Benning with my duffel over one shoulder and the smell of jet fuel still in my nose. The terminal was loud in a way the desert never was. Kids running. Somebody’s grandpa in a veterans cap shaking hands. Balloons. I scanned the crowd and found my wife, Lisa, standing near the escalator with our daughter half-hidden behind her leg. Kayla was six. I’d left when she was five. She stared at me like I was a stranger who’d walked through the wrong door. I knelt down, said her name, and she pushed her face into Lisa’s jeans. Lisa touched her hair, coaxed her forward, but Kayla wouldn’t budge. I remember thinking, well, this is how it starts.

The drive home felt like somebody else’s life. Strip malls, billboards, the same pothole on the off-ramp still not fixed. Lisa talked about the new fridge, how Kayla had started first grade, how the neighbor’s dog kept digging up the flower beds. I nodded. The words didn’t stick. Everything was too bright, too full.

A few days later I went to the grocery store by myself because I needed something to do. Lisa gave me a short list: milk, bread, cereal. I stood in the cereal aisle for almost twenty minutes. When I’d left, there were maybe five or six kinds that I recognized. Now the whole damn aisle was nothing but colors and cartoon characters and promises in bold letters. Forty kinds of flakes and clusters and oats. I picked up a box, read the ingredients, put it back. Picked up another. Same thing. I couldn’t make the decision. A woman with a baby in the cart reached past me, grabbed a box without looking, and moved on. I just stood there like a man who’d forgotten how to buy breakfast.

At night, the house was too quiet and not quiet enough. I’d been sleeping facing the door for a year, one hand near the edge of the mattress, listening. Even in the barracks back on base, I slept like that. The door had to be in my line of sight. At home, Lisa wanted the bedroom door open so she could hear if Kayla called out. The first few weeks, I couldn’t do it. I’d get up after she fell asleep and close it. Then I’d lie there staring at the crack underneath for any shadow, any sign. After a while, I started leaving it open an inch. Then a little more. One night I didn’t close it at all. I woke up at three, saw the dark hallway, and my heart didn’t kick. I rolled over and faced the window instead.

Kayla started warming up after the first month. She’d bring me a book and sit beside me on the couch without touching. Then one day she crawled right into my lap while I was tying my boots. She didn’t say anything, just sat there. I tied my laces slow.

Nothing I brought back fits quite right. Not the uniform in the closet, not the habits, not the quiet. But I go to the store now and buy whatever cereal is on sale. And sometimes Kayla leaves her bedroom door open a crack, and I can hear her breathing when I walk down the hall. It’s enough.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/ i made a pricing mistake with Tallyup that i want to walk through honestly.

a few months ago i raised prices 40% on every existing customer, overnight, no warning.

lost 30 of my 140 customers in a week.

here's what happened and what i changed.

2/ the reasoning at the time felt solid: we were underpriced, new customers were paying more than legacy ones, and i wanted to close that gap fast.

so i just... did it. one email, effective immediately, applied to everyone regardless of how long they'd been a customer.

3/ the mistake wasn't raising prices. it was raising them the same way for everyone, with zero notice, and zero acknowledgment that loyalty should count for something.

longtime customers who'd been paying on time for a year got treated exactly like someone who signed up last month.

4/ the churn wasn't evenly spread either. it was disproportionately the customers who'd been around the longest — the ones who felt the increase as a breach of trust, not just a price change.

that's the part that stung. i lost the people i most needed to keep.

5/ what i changed:

grandfathered existing customers at their old price for a fixed period (instead of forever, but with real notice this time)

gave 60 days notice for any future price changes

separated "new customer pricing" from "existing customer pricing" as a permanent policy, not an afterthought

6/ the lesson: pricing changes are a trust event, not just a revenue lever. how you communicate it matters as much as the number itself.

30 customers in a week taught me that faster than any amount of thinking about it in advance would have.

7/ still building Tallyup solo, still sharing the numbers as they come. if you're thinking about a price increase, happy to talk through it before you hit send on that email.

b.text:
I made a pricing mistake at Tallyup.

As a solo founder, I raised prices 40% on everyone overnight.

Within a week, we lost 30 of our 140 customers.

That stung. But it also taught me a lot about pricing, churn, and how not to handle a change like that.

Here’s what happened, what I got wrong, and what I changed.

1/ I treated pricing like a spreadsheet problem.

It wasn’t.

For me, it felt logical:
- the product was improving
- support was getting better
- I needed to charge more

So I updated the pricing and pushed it live.

What I missed: pricing is also trust.

2/ I changed the price for everyone at once.

No grandfathering.
No warning period.
No transition plan.

Just an overnight 40% increase across the board.

That’s a fast way to tell customers:
“Your current plan no longer matters.”

Even if the product is useful, that can feel like a slap.

3/ The churn hit fast.

30 customers out of 140 left in a week.

Seeing that number was brutal.

It also made something obvious:
I hadn’t just changed pricing.

I had changed the customer relationship.

4/ The biggest mistake wasn’t the amount.

It was the way I did it.

A price increase might have been fine if I’d handled it with more care:
- existing customers protected
- new pricing for new signups
- clear explanation
- more notice

Instead, I optimized for speed and simplicity.

Customers paid the price for that.

5/ What I changed after that:

- I stopped thinking of pricing as a one-time decision
- I started treating existing customers differently from new ones
- I became much more intentional about communication
- I now think about how a change will feel, not just whether it makes sense on paper

6/ The lesson:

If you’re building an indie SaaS, pricing changes are product changes.

And product changes affect trust.

I still believe in charging more when the product earns it.

I just won’t do it by surprise again.

If you’ve made a pricing mistake like this too, I’d love to hear what you learned.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
The Saturday our register stopped working, the first order came in before I had found a pen.

The screen froze halfway through lunch, with a line at the counter and two delivery drivers waiting by the door. My dad unplugged the register and plugged it back in. I tore a sheet from the order pad, wrote **TABLE 4** at the top, and asked the customers to repeat what they wanted. For the next three hours, I wrote every ticket by hand. I circled the dishes going to the kitchen, marked takeout orders with a T, and crossed out one iced coffee after its owner changed her mind.

I’ve worked weekends at my family’s Vietnamese restaurant since sophomore year. At first, I mostly cleared tables and filled water glasses. Now I know which regular wants extra lime, where we keep the backup receipt paper, and how to tell my dad we’re almost out of noodles without interrupting him in the middle of an order.

A few months ago, I showed a new hire how my grandma folds spring rolls. I demonstrated once, and his first one looked fine until he picked it up and the filling slid out. I showed him again, slower: bring the bottom corner over the filling, pull it back gently, fold in the sides, then roll. My grandma watched from the prep table and shook her head at mine. I’d left one side loose. She took the wrapper from me and showed us both.

On my break, I sometimes take my calculus homework into the walk-in cooler. It’s the only place where no one asks me for more napkins. I stand beside the boxes of herbs with my notebook balanced on a crate and try to finish a problem before my fingers get too cold to write. Once, I got stuck halfway through a derivative and went back out with it unfinished. After closing, I saw where I’d made the mistake: I’d dropped a negative sign. I fixed it at the same table where I’d been wrapping silverware an hour earlier.

When the register came back on that Saturday, my dad entered the orders I’d written so we could check the totals. One ticket had sauce spilled across the corner; another had my handwriting squeezed into the margin because a table had added food after ordering. We could still read them all.

I put the order pad back beside the register before we closed. It’s still there, with a pen clipped to the cover.

b.text:
I'm in the kitchen Monday to Friday for school, and then on the weekends, I'm at the restaurant. My family owns a Vietnamese place in a strip mall off Route 12. My parents run it, my grandma cooks, and I do whatever needs doing: wash dishes, refill the Sriracha bottles, bus tables, take orders. I've been doing this since sophomore year, every Saturday and Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. I get paid, but it's not about the money.

There was a Saturday when the register system died. I don't know why. It just went blank in the middle of the lunch rush. My mom looked at me, and I looked at the line of people waiting, and she said, "Paper." So I grabbed a notepad from the counter and started writing tickets by hand. No one seems to think about what happens when the computer stops. I didn't either, until that day. I wrote fast. I had to remember the prices from memory because the menu was on the screen. I shorthand everything: pho-12, spring rolls-6, vermicelli-14. The kitchen had to read my handwriting. It was messy, but they got it. We served everyone. No one waited too long, I think. At the end of the night, my hand was sore, and we totaled up the receipts and the numbers were off by a little, but close enough.

Sometimes I teach new hires how to fold the spring rolls. That's my grandma's method. You lay the wrapper flat, put the filling in the middle, fold up the bottom, fold in the sides, then roll it tight. It seems simple, but if you don't crimp the edges right, they stick together or fall apart when you fry them. People don't know that. They think it's just rolling. I show them. I watch their hands. Sometimes they get frustrated. I tell them, "It's like folding a letter you don't want to send." That's what my grandma told me. I don't know what that means exactly, but it helps hold the fold. I don't know if she meant it or if she just said it.

On my breaks, I do homework in the walk-in cooler. It's cold in there, obviously, but it's quiet. I can hear the fridge humming and sometimes the sound of the kitchen yelling from outside. I pull out my calc book and do problems. It's weird to be doing derivatives while the smell of lemongrass and fish sauce is on my clothes. But it's fine. It's my break. I sit on a crate or sometimes I lean against the shelves where they keep the egg rolls. I don't have much time, so I do the problems fast. If I get one wrong, I don't care that much. I just move on to the next one. It's not like school where there's time to think about it. I'm on a break. I'll be back on the floor in fifteen minutes.

Most Saturdays, I'm there from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. I don't think about it as a job exactly, even though I am paid for it. It's just what I do. I put on my apron, I cash out customers, I refill the water, I wipe the tables. My hands smell like fish sauce by the end of the day, and no matter how many times I wash them, the smell stays. I like it. It's my family's smell, I guess. I don't know what else to call it.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
## The Market Isn’t Crashing. Sellers Are Simply Behind It.

Last spring, the median home in my ZIP code spent just eight days on the market. This spring, that figure has climbed to 34 days. Showings per listing have fallen by roughly half.

Those numbers sound dramatic—and they are. But they do not mean our local housing market is crashing.

They mean the pace has changed, and too many sellers are still pricing their homes for last year’s market.

List prices remain about 6% higher than they were a year ago. That tells me seller expectations have continued rising even as buyer activity has cooled. Buyers today have more time, more choices and less willingness to overlook an inflated price. They are not disappearing; they are becoming selective.

I see this disconnect firsthand. I currently have three sellers whose homes have been on the market for more than 60 days, and all three are resisting a price adjustment. They remember hearing about multiple offers, bidding wars and homes selling over asking price in a weekend. Understandably, they want that outcome for themselves.

But the market does not care what a seller wants, what a neighbor received last year or how much money an owner put into the kitchen. Buyers compare a home with what is available today. If the value is not there, they move on.

The clearest evidence is what happens to homes that are priced correctly: They are still selling, often in less than two weeks.

That is not a crash. A crashing market does not consistently reward well-priced, well-prepared homes with quick sales. What we have is a market that has shifted from automatic urgency to price sensitivity.

For several years, sellers could start high and assume the market would catch up. That strategy is now risky. The first two weeks of a listing are when buyer attention is strongest. If a home enters the market overpriced, serious buyers may skip it, while everyone else watches and waits for a reduction. By the time the seller finally adjusts, the listing has accumulated days on market and buyers begin wondering what is wrong with it.

Often, nothing is wrong with the house. The original price was wrong.

Sellers also need to stop treating a price reduction as a defeat. If a home has been listed for 30, 45 or 60 days with limited showings and no serious offers, the market has already delivered its verdict. Refusing to respond does not protect the home’s value. It simply extends the listing and may ultimately result in a lower sale price than a realistic starting price would have produced.

My advice to sellers right now is direct: Price for the market you are entering, not the market you remember.

Look closely at recent sales, but pay equal attention to the active listings competing for the same buyers. Prepare the home properly. Address obvious condition issues. Make access for showings easy. Most importantly, take the first two weeks seriously.

Buyers should not mistake longer market times for a collapse, either. The best homes are still moving quickly, and waiting for a dramatic drop in prices could mean missing the right property. What buyers have gained is not unlimited leverage but breathing room—the opportunity to compare homes, inspect carefully and negotiate without the frenzy of last spring.

Our local market has slowed. It has not fallen apart.

The sellers succeeding this spring are the ones who understand that distinction. They are not chasing last year’s peak or testing an aspirational price. They are meeting today’s buyers where they are—and they are still getting sold.

b.text:
# This Isn't a Crash. It's a Standoff.

Last spring, the median home in our zip went under contract in 8 days. This spring it's 34. If you've seen that number, or heard it from a neighbor, you might assume the bottom fell out of our market. It didn't. Here are the two numbers that actually explain what's happening: list prices are still up 6 percent year over year, and showings per listing have dropped by half.

Read those together and the story tells itself. Sellers are asking for more while half as many people come through the door. That's not a collapse. That's a standoff.

I've been selling homes here for ten years, and I'll tell you what I see every week: the houses that are priced right are still going under contract in under two weeks. A crash doesn't work that way. A crash takes everything down with it — the good listing and the stubborn one alike. What we have instead is something more selective. The market has stopped paying a premium for hope.

For the better part of three years, sellers in this town got to skip the hard part. Price it, list it Thursday, six showings by Saturday, pick the best offer by Monday. Buyers waived inspections, wrote love letters, bid over asking on houses they'd walked through for nine minutes. Every seller in town internalized that as "what my house is worth." It wasn't. It was what your house was worth at the exact moment buyers were panicking.

I had to memorize the table numbers and run the physical slips back to the kitchen window, shouting modifications over the exhaust fans. Table four, no cilantro on the pho. Table nine, extra peanut sauce. By 8:00 PM, my right hand was cramping and my fingers were stained with ink and grease, but the tickets kept moving and the kitchen didn't stall.

When the rush finally broke around 9:00, I took my break. The only quiet place in the restaurant is the walk-in cooler. I put on my heavy gray hoodie, sat on an overturned milk crate next to the bulk rice bags, and pulled out my AP Calculus worksheet. The cooler smells like raw pork, star anise, and damp cardboard. The compressor fan is loud, but it drowns out the clatter of plates and the Vietnamese pop music my mom plays in the dining room. I worked through optimization problems while my breath fogged in the cold, stopping every few minutes to rub my hands together so my pen wouldn't slip.

On Sunday afternoons, before we open, I usually help with prep. Last month, we hired a new line cook named David. My mom asked me to show him how to make the fresh spring rolls. It sounds easy, but my grandma has a very specific way of folding them that we still use. I stood next to him at the stainless steel prep table and demonstrated. You lay the rice paper flat, put the vermicelli and shrimp in the lower third, and fold the bottom up tight. Then you fold in the left and right sides before rolling the rest of the way. If you don't fold the sides in first, the ends stay open and the filling falls out when you dip it. David’s first few rolls looked like swollen cigars. I unrolled them and showed him how to keep the tension even. By his twentieth roll, he had the muscle memory down.

I work every Friday night, Saturday, and Sunday. I usually smell like fryer oil and fish sauce when I get home, and I have to wash my hair twice before Monday morning. It’s just the schedule. I know how to run the floor, how to prep the line, and how to study in a 35-degree room. Next weekend, I’ll be back at the host stand, waiting for the doors to open.

b.text:
# Working Weekends

The register died on a Saturday in March.

I was refilling water glasses when my coworker frantically waved me over. The screen was black. The keyboard wouldn't respond. We had forty people in the restaurant and no way to ring anything up.

My manager looked at me like I might fix it. I didn't. But I grabbed a notepad and started writing orders by hand instead—table numbers, items, prices that I'd memorized years ago. I wrote fast and small so the tickets would fit. The kitchen staff knew my handwriting by then. They didn't need me to clarify when I scribbled "gỏi cuốn" or "bánh mì thịt nạc."

I did this for five hours. My hand cramped. I got the math wrong twice and had to recalculate totals while customers waited. It wasn't efficient. It wasn't good. But the restaurant kept running.

This is what I think about when I'm working: I notice things that break and try to fix them. Not always successfully. When Linh started in the kitchen last year, she kept tearing the spring roll wrappers. My grandma showed me how to fold them first—the way you have to be gentle but firm, how the rice paper gets stronger when you wet it just enough. I stood next to Linh on a Friday night and folded five rolls while she watched, then handed her the wrapper and stepped back. She got three right before messing one up. We didn't talk about it. The next week she was better.

Some nights I do calculus homework in the walk-in cooler. It's the only quiet place. I sit on a milk crate between boxes of frozen shrimp and bok choy, working through integrals with my hands getting cold. My manager thinks it's funny. My mom thinks I should rest instead. But I like being in there—surrounded by ingredients, knowing the restaurant is running ten feet away, doing something for college while I'm still here.

I've worked weekends since sophomore year. That's ninety-some Saturdays and Sundays, probably more. I don't think this makes me special. Lots of people work. I think it just means I know how to show up when something needs doing, even if I don't know how to do it yet. The register will get fixed by someone else. I'll write the tickets. Linh will learn to fold the spring rolls. That's how this works.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
I raised Tallyup's prices 40% overnight. On everyone. No warning.

We lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week.

Here's exactly what I got wrong and what I'd do differently 🧵

1/ The logic felt sound. We were underpriced, churn was low, and every pricing article says "you're charging too little."

All probably true. The mistake wasn't raising prices. It was how.

2/ I sent one email. Announced the new price. Effective on your next billing date.

To gym owners running tight margins, that reads as: "your bill just went up and nobody asked you."

3/ The cancellations weren't angry, mostly. That was the worst part.

A few replied with some version of "I get it, but this pushed us over." Those hurt more than the mad ones.

4/ What I should have done, and what I'm doing now:

→ Grandfather existing customers at their current price, or give a long runway (6-12 months)
→ New pricing for new customers only, at first
→ Actually talk to customers before, not after

5/ I also should have paired the increase with something. A new feature, an annual discount, anything that made it feel like an exchange instead of a toll.

6/ What I changed since:

→ Reached out personally to everyone who left. Some conversations are ongoing.
→ Existing customers are locked at their old rate for now
→ New signups pay the new price

7/ The uncomfortable truth: revenue-wise this may still work out. New customers at higher prices, smaller base.

But I burned trust with people who bet on a small tool from a solo founder. That's the expensive part.

8/ If you're thinking about raising prices: do it. You probably should.

Just don't do it the way I did. Grandfather your early believers. They're the reason you exist.

Building in public means sharing the dumb stuff too. This was mine. AMA 👇

b.text:
1/ I raised Tallyup’s prices 40% for every customer overnight.

In the following week, 30 of our 140 customers left.

Here’s the mistake I made.

2/ I treated pricing like a decision I could make in a spreadsheet.

But Tallyup is a subscription tool for gym owners. Existing customers had already decided what it was worth to them—and trusted me with a recurring charge.

I changed that deal without warning.

3/ The mistake wasn’t only the size of the increase. It was applying it to everyone, immediately, without giving customers time to understand it or make a choice.

4/ What I changed: I no longer think of existing-customer pricing as just another lever to pull.

If I raise prices again, customers will hear why before it happens and have time to decide whether Tallyup still works for them.

5/ Building in public means posting the decisions I wish I’d made differently, too.

This one cost me customers—and a lesson I could have learned by talking to them first.

a.text:
The couples who give me the best shot lists usually give me the shortest ones.

Not *no* list. I still want to know which family groupings matter, and if there’s a person or detail I might otherwise miss.

But a minute-by-minute list of photos to recreate? That can make it harder to see what’s actually happening.

The Barrera wedding is a good example. Rain changed the plan, and we moved everything under the pecan tree. The photos that mattered came from paying attention to the day we had—not trying to force the day we’d planned.

After eight years of photographing weddings in the Texas Hill Country, that’s the advice I keep coming back to: tell your photographer what matters to you, then leave room for the unexpected.

b.text:
The Barreras planned for golden hour portraits on the hilltop and a romantic first look by the creek. Instead, a storm rolled in 20 minutes before the ceremony and didn’t let up. We moved everything under a single massive pecan tree—ceremony, toasts, dancing, all of it. No backup plan, no shot list, just a canopy of wet leaves and everyone huddled close.

I’ve never delivered a stronger gallery.

Without the checklist, the day became about what was actually happening. The way Chris pressed his forehead to Elena’s after their vows, rain soaking through his jacket. Her grandmother sitting on a cooler holding the train of the dress so it wouldn’t drag in the mud. The kids chasing armadillos between raindrops. None of that would have been on a list. All of it told the real story.

Every year, the couples who get the most vivid, honest photos are the ones who let go of the Pinterest board and trust the people in front of the lens to just be. The light, the weather, the chaos—those aren't obstacles. They’re the raw material.

If you're planning, by all means tell me what matters to you. But the photos you’ll frame aren’t the ones you had in your head. They’re the ones you couldn’t have imagined.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
An 8-2 season deserves applause. It doesn’t make the way it ended any easier to explain.

The second-round state playoff loss will sting because this was a team our high school had beaten by 20 points in Week 3. That earlier result didn’t guarantee anything in November. Opponents improve, matchups change, and nobody gets to carry September’s points onto the playoff scoreboard.

But this wasn’t simply a case of running into a better team. Our team got away from something that was working.

Down just three points in the second half, the offense abandoned the running game. That’s the decision I can’t get past. A three-point deficit is not an emergency. There was no need to treat a close game like a desperate comeback.

If the run is moving the ball, keep making the defense stop it.

That isn’t an argument against Dez Kowalski. He threw for 2,340 yards this season, a school record, and earned his place in the program’s history. His arm was a major reason this team had a playoff game to lose.

But having a record-setting quarterback doesn’t mean every answer has to come through the air. A productive running game helps that quarterback. Walking away from it made the offense less balanced at precisely the time it needed to stay patient.

It’s fair to question that choice without turning a good season into a failure or making the coaching staff the villain. Coaches helped build an 8-2 team, too. They also make decisions that deserve scrutiny, especially when those decisions help bring a season to an end.

The players should be proud of what they accomplished. Kowalski’s record will remain long after the frustration of this loss fades.

Still, the lesson shouldn’t be that playoff football is unpredictable and sometimes the ball doesn’t bounce your way. That’s true, but it lets this one off too easily.

They were down three. The run was working. They should have stayed with it.

b.text:
**One Score Down, And They Panicked**

An 8-2 season shouldn't feel like a disappointment. But Friday night did.

Not because this team lost in the second round of the state playoffs. Good teams lose in the playoffs. It stings because of *who* they lost to — the same team they beat by 20 back in Week 3. You don't forget a game like that. Neither do your opponents. And you could see it on both sidelines.

I’ve said all year on the radio that Dez Kowalski is the best quarterback this school has ever had, and the numbers finally back it up. 2,340 yards is the new school record. He earned every one of them. He’s tough, he’s accurate, and he carried this offense when he had to.

Friday, he had to a little too much.

We were down three at the half. Three. One score. The run game was working — we were moving the chains and keeping their defense honest. So what happened in the second half? We came out throwing like we were down three touchdowns.

I get the temptation. You’ve got a record-setting arm. You want to let him win it. But good coaching is sticking with what the defense can’t stop, not what looks best in the stat sheet. Abandoning the run when you’re only down three isn’t aggressive. It’s impatient. And it made us one-dimensional against a team that was already hungry to return the favor from September.

That’s the game. Not talent, not effort. Play-calling.

It was a great season. 8-2 is something these kids should be proud of for a long time. Dez should hold that record with his head high. But we’ll spend the whole offseason knowing we beat ourselves by getting away from who we were.

a.text:
1/3 On the Maple Ave kitchen remodel, we opened up [area] and found [joist issue]. From above, [what was visible before demo]. Once it was exposed, we could see [actual condition].

2/3 The fix: [repair scope]. Added cost: $[amount], including [what that covered]. Schedule impact: [delay, if any]. Not a kitchen upgrade—work needed before we could close things back up.

b.text:
1/4 Maple Ave kitchen surprise: once the old soffit and ceiling came down, we found a 2x10 floor joist that had been notched almost halfway through for an old plumbing line.

It had been carrying a wall and part of the kitchen floor above for who knows how long.

2/4 The floor wasn’t collapsing, but it had a noticeable dip and the joist was doing a lot more bending than it should have been.

We stopped, brought in our engineer, opened a little more ceiling, and built the repair around the actual framing—not the original kitchen plan.

3/4 Cost to the homeowner: about $4,800 between engineering, opening/patching additional areas, sistering the joists, and moving the plumbing correctly.

Nobody likes a change order. But covering it back up would have been cheaper only until it wasn’t.

4/4 The lesson isn’t “old houses are full of surprises.”

The lesson is that demolition is investigation. Budget for what you can see, keep contingency for what you can’t, and don’t let a finish schedule rush a structural decision.

setup: A retired rural mail carrier is writing a letter to the Kettle Falls Courier urging residents to oppose the post office counter closure at the July 28 forum.

a.text:
To the Editor:

I drove Route 4 out of the Kettle Falls post office for 22 years before I retired last year. That's 38 miles a day, six days a week. I'm not a writer, but I know this town and the people on that route, and I want to say something about the plan to close our counter service.

The Postal Service says the branch loses $40,000 a year. Maybe it does. But look at how we got here. They cut the counter hours down to 8 to noon. Of course traffic dropped after that. People work. People have appointments. If you only open the door four hours a day, fewer folks are going to come through it. Now they're pointing at the low numbers as the reason to shut it down. That's a problem they made themselves.

I think about the people on my old route. Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill is in her 80s. She gets her heart medicine by mail. When she needs a money order or has to take care of something at the counter, she comes into town, because it's close. Once the counter closes, the nearest one is in Fairview, twenty minutes each way. She can't make that drive. And she's not the only one out here like that. I could name a dozen more without trying.

A post office counter isn't just a business line on a spreadsheet. For a lot of older folks and people without good transportation, it's how they pay bills, send things to family, and get what they need.

There's a public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. Somebody from the USPS district office is supposed to be there. Please come. Bring your neighbors. If you can't make it, write down what the counter means to you and send it with someone who can. They need to see this town fill that room.

Thank you.

[Your name]
Retired Rural Carrier, Route 4
Kettle Falls

b.text:
To the Editor,

I drove Route 4 for 22 years, and I know this town and its people. That is why I am worried about the post office closing our counter service.

USPS says the branch loses $40,000 a year, but that does not tell the whole story. They already cut the hours from 8 a.m. to noon. Of course traffic went down after that. You cannot reduce service first and then use the lower traffic as proof that service is not needed. That is a problem they helped create themselves.

People in Kettle Falls depend on that counter. Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill is in her 80s. She gets her heart medicine by mail, and she cannot just drive twenty minutes to Fairview for a money order once the counter closes. There are more people like her than some folks in the office seem to realize.

I hope people will come to the July 28 public forum at the Grange Hall and speak up. If we do not say something now, we may lose a service this town still needs.

Sincerely,
A retired Route 4 mail carrier

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
**Nine Games. One Knee. Still No Turf.**

In the last two seasons, my girls' soccer team has had nine home games rained out or moved because our field floods. Nine. When it rains, that field doesn't drain — it holds water like a bathtub, and it stays soft and rutted for days after.

Last October, one of my players planted her foot in one of those ruts and tore her ACL. She lost the rest of her season and has been rehabbing ever since. Call it a fluke if you want. I watched it happen. It wasn't a fluke. It's what happens when you ask teenage athletes to compete on a field that floods every fall and never gets fixed.

Now here's the part that's harder to explain to my players: the football field got artificial turf in 2019. Same campus. Same weather. The boys play rain or shine on a surface that's flat, drained, and safe. The girls get a field that wipes out their schedule every October.

I want to be clear — I'm not against the football field having turf. Good for them. I'm asking a simple question: why did that project get done and this one didn't? If the board has an answer, I'd like to hear it out loud, at a public meeting. If the answer is "we'll get to it," we've been getting to it since 2019.

There's also a federal word for a district that installs turf for the boys and leaves the girls on a flooding field. It's called Title IX. I'd rather not lead with that word. I'd rather the board just put the money in the budget.

I already know the objection: it's expensive. It is. But rescheduling nine games isn't free. Sending my girls on the road for games that were supposed to be at home isn't free. And nobody has put a price on a sixteen-year-old's knee.

This isn't only a soccer problem, either. I coach track in the spring, and my runners train on that same field all season, dodging the same ruts. When it's flooded, we practice wherever we can find space. The seniors on this team don't get their home games back. They don't get a second senior night.

The board votes on next year's facilities budget soon. Put the girls' field in it. Fund it fully. Don't commission another study — this field has been studied plenty. It's also been under water plenty.

Nine games. One knee. And a boys' field that got fixed five years ago. My girls aren't asking for anything the boys don't already have. They're asking for the same field. The board can give it to them with one vote.

*[Name] is the girls' soccer and track coach at [High School].*

b.text:
Nine games in two seasons. That's how many my girls' soccer team has had rained out or shuffled to another site because our field turns into a pond. Nine games we practiced for, dressed for, and in some cases rode a bus to, and then didn't play.

Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping into a rut on that field. She was running down a pass in a routine league game. Nobody tackled her. She planted her foot in a spot where the grass had been chewed up and worn down to mud, and her knee gave out. She spent the rest of the season on crutches and then in rehab. I can't tell you the rut caused the injury the way a doctor would, but I can tell you I've watched that field for years, and I wasn't surprised to see someone get hurt on it.

Here is the problem. When it rains, the field floods. When it floods, we cancel or move games. When we don't cancel, the girls play on ground that's soft in some places, hard in others, and rutted everywhere in between. Practice gets moved to the parking lot or the gym, or it doesn't happen. Meanwhile the grass never gets a chance to recover, because we're using it as much as we can when it's usable, and that wears it down further. It's a cycle, and it's not going to fix itself.

The boys' football field got turf in 2019. I'm not going to pretend that was a mistake. Football is a big deal here, and a lot of people use that field. But I'd ask the board to think about what it means that one team got a surface that drains, holds up, and can be played on after a storm, while the girls' team plays on a field that loses games every time the sky opens up. Nobody set out to treat our girls as an afterthought. But when you look at the results, that's what it looks like.

Turf isn't just for the soccer team, either. Track athletes warm up and train on that infield. Our PE classes could use it. Middle school and youth leagues could rent it on weekends. A field that can handle year-round use is a field that earns some of its cost back, which is something a muddy one will never do.

I know turf is expensive, and I know the board has a long list of requests and a limited pot of money. I'm not asking anyone to ignore that. I'm asking you to weigh it honestly against what we're getting now: canceled games, a real injury, and a gap between how we treat our boys' program and our girls' program that anyone can see from the parking lot.

I coach because I like these kids, not because I want to argue about budgets. But I'm not going to stay quiet while they keep losing games to a field we know how to fix. When the board votes on next year's facilities budget, I'm asking you to put turf on the girls' soccer field.

Come out and see it after a rain. Then decide.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
# One Week In

I launched the game last Tuesday. 412 copies sold in the first week.

That's the headline. It still doesn't feel entirely real to type out.

The launch day was chaos in the best way—the game hit the front page of r/indiegames for about 6 hours, which sent a spike of traffic that made my hosting sweat a little. I kept refreshing Steam to see the numbers climb, which is probably not healthy but I couldn't stop myself. By end of day I'd made more money than I spent on the game's development. That's the part that actually feels surreal.

The reviews have been mostly positive. A lot of people loved the art direction and the puzzle design. A few people noted performance issues on older hardware that I'm already working on for the next patch. And yeah, one review said the movement feels floaty. They're right. I've been thinking about it since, and I know exactly what they mean—the character model isn't giving enough weight to the jump arc. I started prototyping a fix last week and it's already feeling better. That's going into 1.1 next month.

The player comments have been great to read. Some people are finding secrets I forgot I hid. Someone made fan art. Someone else said they played for five hours straight and lost track of time, which is honestly all I've ever wanted a game to do.

Right now I'm running through the bug reports, planning that movement patch, and trying not to work myself into the ground on updates. Three years of nights and weekends to get here. I'm going to try to actually sleep for a bit before I keep going.

Next devlog will be in two weeks when 1.1 is closer to done.

b.text:
# One week after launch

The game launched last week. After three years of nights and weekends, it feels strange to write that in the past tense.

It sold 412 copies in its first week. I’ve checked that number more times than I’d like to admit. A post about the game also made the front page of a small subreddit for about six hours, which sent a bunch of people my way. If you found the game there, hi.

I’ve been reading the reviews. One said the movement feels floaty, and honestly, they’re right. It’s something I got used to while working on the game, but watching other people play has made it much easier to notice. I’m working on a movement patch for 1.1, which I’m aiming to release next month. I want to spend some time testing it before it goes out so I don’t just trade one weird feeling for another.

For now, I’m collecting bug reports, watching what people get stuck on, and trying to remember that the game is actually out. Thanks to everyone who bought it, played it, or told someone about it. I’ll post more when 1.1 is closer.

setup: A retired rural mail carrier is writing a letter to the Kettle Falls Courier urging residents to oppose the post office counter closure at the July 28 forum.

a.text:
To the editor:

I drove the same 38-mile Route 4 for 22 years before retiring last year. I’m not a writer, but I know this town, and I have something to say about closing our post office counter.

USPS says the branch loses $40,000 a year. But they already cut the counter hours to 8 a.m. to noon. That makes it hard for working people to get there. Of course traffic dropped. Now they’re pointing to a problem they helped make as a reason to cut service again.

Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill is in her 80s. She gets her heart medicine by mail. When she needs a money order, she can’t just drive twenty minutes to Fairview. That may not sound like much of a trip to somebody looking at a map, but it is a real problem for her and other folks here.

A post office is a service. It ought to count for something that people need it, especially people who don’t have another easy way to do their business.

The USPS district manager will be at the July 28 public forum at the Grange Hall. Please come if you can. Ask how much of that loss followed the cuts in hours, and ask why restoring useful hours isn’t being considered before closing the counter.

They need to hear from the people who live here.

b.text:
To the Editor:

I carried Route 4 out of the Kettle Falls post office for 22 years. Same 38 miles, same boxes, same people. I know this town, and I know what that counter means to it, so I've got something to say about the plan to close it.

The Postal Service says the branch loses $40,000 a year. Maybe it does. But they cut the window hours down to 8 to noon, and then they act surprised when fewer people come in. Of course traffic dropped. You can't shut the door most of the day and then point at the empty lobby like it's our fault. That's not a losing office. That's an office they already closed halfway and are now blaming for being closed.

Take Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She's in her 80s. Her heart medicine comes by mail, and I used to hand it to her myself. When she needs a money order, she walks down to that counter and gets one. She doesn't drive. Twenty minutes to Fairview might as well be two hundred for her. Tell me what she's supposed to do.

There are a lot of Mrs. Hallorans here. Older folks, folks without cars, folks who don't do their banking on a phone. The counter isn't a luxury to them. It's the errand.

There's a public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. I'll be there, and I hope the district manager is listening, because this decision was made somewhere far from Kettle Falls by people who have never stood at that window on a cold morning.

If you care about this, show up. That's the only thing that's ever worked around here.

[Name]
Kettle Falls
