setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: 8 Months of Market Sourdough

I've had the Corlane SM6 on my counter for eight months now, and it's logged more hours than my oven. I use it almost daily to mix the sourdough I sell at the farmers market on weekends, plus the occasional batch of bagels for a special order. Here's the honest report.

**The good.** The motor is an absolute workhorse. I routinely mix a double batch of stiff bagel dough—the kind that fights back—and the SM6 never stalls, never strains, never even sounds like it's working hard. For someone who kneads heavy dough every single week, that's the whole ballgame. It handles my market sourdough with the same ease, and I've never once worried about burning out the motor.

**The annoying.** The bowl lift lever squeaks. Not a little. A lot. I have to hit it with WD40 about once a month to keep it from sounding like a haunted house. It's a minor fix, but it's a fix I shouldn't have to do on a $429 mixer.

Also, the dough hook that comes with it is too short for the deep bowl. In the middle of a batch, the hook barely reaches the dough at the bottom, so I have to stop and scrape everything down more than I should. I eventually bought a third-party hook that actually fits, and now it works fine. But spending $429 and then having to replace the hook feels cheap of Corlane.

**The price.** The SM6 runs $429. That's $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid. So you're paying a premium for a mixer that has a squeaky lever and a poorly sized hook. The motor is the reason you'd pay it.

**The verdict.** This is a bread baker's mixer, and nothing else. If you knead heavy dough every week—and I mean real dough, not a single loaf of sandwich bread—buy it. The motor is worth the $80 premium and the hassle. If you're mostly doing cookies and cake batter, skip it. Absolutely skip it. A KitchenAid will do everything you need, cost less, and you won't have to lubricate the lever or replace the hook. The Corlane SM6 is a specialist tool. Buy it only if you're a specialist.

b.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8 Months In

I bake sourdough for the farmers market every weekend, which means this mixer doesn't get a gentle life. Here's what actually happens when you put it to work daily instead of pulling it out twice a year for birthday cake.

**The good:** The motor is the real story here. I regularly run double batches of stiff bagel dough through it — the kind of dough that makes cheaper mixers whine and stall — and the SM6 just keeps turning. No burning smell, no motor lag, no babysitting it to make sure it doesn't overheat. For someone kneading heavy, low-hydration dough multiple times a week, this is the whole reason to buy this machine.

**The annoying:** The bowl lift lever has developed a squeak that I now have to WD40 about once a month. It's not a dealbreaker, just an unglamorous maintenance chore nobody mentions in the marketing copy. More frustrating: the dough hook that ships with it is too short to properly reach the bottom of the deep bowl. I ended up buying a third-party hook to get real contact with the dough. That's an extra cost and an extra Amazon order you shouldn't have to make on a $429 machine.

**The price problem:** Speaking of $429 — that's about $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid. You're paying a premium for that motor.

**Verdict:** Buy this if you knead heavy dough every week. If you're making sourdough, bagels, pizza dough, or anything stiff on a regular basis, the motor alone justifies the price difference, and you'll make back the cost of a third-party hook in saved frustration within a month. Skip it if you're mostly making cookies, cake batter, or the occasional loaf of banana bread — you're paying $80 extra for horsepower you'll never actually use, and you'll be stuck with the same finicky lever and undersized hook without ever needing the thing that makes this mixer worth owning.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvis L2 Standing Desk: My 6-Month Review

I’ve used the Jarvik L2 as my primary work desk for six months, working remotely as a software engineer. It has gone through daily height changes, long typing sessions, video calls, and the general abuse of a desk that is actually used—not just photographed in a minimalist office.

My verdict is straightforward: **buy it at the $549 sale price. Do not buy it at $749.** At the lower price, it’s a good, practical standing desk with a quiet and fast motor. At the regular price, the wobble and terrible cable tray are harder to excuse.

## The motor is the best part

The Jarvik L2’s motor has been consistently quiet and quick. Height adjustments don’t interrupt calls, and I can move from sitting to standing without waiting around or listening to a loud mechanical whine.

After six months, the motor still sounds and feels the same as it did when I installed the desk. There’s no grinding, hesitation, or noticeable slowdown. For a desk I adjust multiple times a day, that reliability matters more to me than having a long list of extra features.

## It wobbles at full height

The desk is stable enough at sitting height and at moderate standing heights. The problem appears when I raise it near its maximum height.

If I type aggressively—especially during a fast coding session—the monitor and desk surface wobble. It isn’t unusable, but it is noticeable and irritating. Light typing is fine. Resting my forearms on the desk is fine. Hard, rapid typing makes the desk move.

This is not a dealbreaker for me because I don’t spend the entire day at maximum height. However, if you’re tall, plan to keep the desk fully raised, or are particularly sensitive to monitor movement, you should take this seriously. The L2 is not rock-solid at full height.

## The memory presets drift

The memory presets are convenient, but they aren’t perfectly consistent. After six months, the saved positions can drift by roughly a centimeter.

That’s enough to notice if you’re trying to switch between a carefully tuned sitting height and standing height. I don’t have to recalibrate constantly, but I do occasionally find myself adjusting the desk manually after using a preset.

A one-centimeter difference isn’t catastrophic, but it undermines the point of having presets. I expected better repeatability.

## The cable tray is garbage

The included cable tray is the weakest part of the desk.

It doesn’t provide a clean or flexible way to manage cables, and it feels like an afterthought rather than a properly designed component. Once you add a monitor, laptop charger, peripherals, and a power strip, the tray becomes difficult to use effectively. Cables still hang awkwardly or require your own clips and ties to keep organized.

I ended up treating the tray as optional and using separate cable-management hardware. If clean cable routing matters to you, budget for a replacement or plan to improvise. I would not choose this desk because of its cable-management setup.

## Six-month durability

So far, the frame and lifting mechanism have held up well. There are no obvious signs of mechanical degradation, and the motor remains as quiet and fast as it was on day one.

The desk’s shortcomings are mostly design and stability issues rather than failures. It works every day, but it is not as polished as the price suggests when sold for $749.

## Final verdict

**At $549: worth buying.** The Jarvik L2 gives me a quiet, fast motor and a generally good sit-stand experience. The wobble at full height is manageable, the preset drift is annoying but minor, and the cable tray can be replaced or ignored.

**At $749: not worth it.** At that price, I expect better stability at maximum height, more accurate memory presets, and a cable tray that does its job. The L2 is a solid midrange desk, not a premium one.

If you can get it for **$549 or around that price**, I’d recommend it. If the price is **$749**, I’d keep shopping.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6-Month Review

*Tested daily since January. Detailed, no affiliate links below — I bought this thing and paid real money for the privilege.*

## The short version

The motor is the best part of this desk. The frame is fine. The wobble at full height is a real, reproducible problem that ruins the standing half of the standing-desk experience. The cable tray is trash — literally. And the price swings between "buy immediately" and "smell the money you're burning."

**Worth it at $549. Not worth it at $749.**

## Specs, for what it's worth

| | |
|---|---|
| Manufacturer-listed capacity | 355 lb |
| Listed range | ~24.5"–50" |
| Top (mine) | 48" × 24", 1.5" thick laminate |
| Motors | Dual |
| Memory presets | 3 |
| Listed lift speed | ~1.4"/sec |
| My purchase price | $549 |
| MSRP at purchase | $749 |

I've got a 27" monitor on an arm, a laptop, a desk lamp, and occasionally a 15" laptop on a riser when the whole family is working at the table. That's nowhere near 355 lb. If you need more than 355 lb of capacity, this isn't the desk — go look at a commercial frame.

## The motor: genuinely excellent

This is where Jarvik wins and where most of the budget went, and I want to be clear about it because it's the thing you live with eight times a day.

Measured with a sound meter on my desk surface, roughly 12" away: **about 42 dB when the motor is running flat out.** That is "I can't hear it while I'm on a call," not "silent." In a dead-quiet apartment at 11pm with the fridge off, I *can* hear it. It's a low mechanical hum, not a whine, and it rises slightly in pitch during the last few inches of travel. No creaks, no rattling, no gear-stepping.

Speed is the other half of why I like this thing. It clears its full 25" range in roughly 20 seconds, which means I'm not waiting on the machine. My old desk took almost a minute and made a racket doing it. I use the standing position every single workday and I use it three or four times a day, and after six months and something like 600 raise/lower cycles, the motor is still smooth. Nothing has loosened. Nothing has started humming louder. The controller hasn't needed a reset.

If you read one section of this review, it should be this one: **the motor is the reason to buy this desk.** It's the slowest-moving part to degrade but the fastest-moving part to notice, and Jarvik clearly put the money there.

## The wobble: my biggest complaint, and it's not subtle

Here's how to reproduce it. Raise the desk to full height (50.2" floor-to-underside). Sit down. Rest your forearms on the front edge of the top and type hard, the way you actually type when you're concentrating. The front-left corner moves.

Not a lot. Maybe 3–8 mm of lateral play at the very top, concentrated in the front-left corner, and it's a diagonal flex rather than a pure side-to-side sway. But at 50 inches up, the desk is at the top of its travel and the frame has the least material left to resist you, and I can feel every keystroke through my forearms. On a video call with a sensitive mic, I could probably transmit it.

**What I've ruled out:** I took the arm off, took all the weight off the top, and checked the frame for loose hardware. Everything was tight. This isn't a loose-bolt problem.

**What I think it actually is:** a combination of the laminate top flexing and the frame's torsion resistance at the top of the lift range. The foot leveling glides on my floor (hardwood, and one corner of the room is slightly out of level) were also contributing. I shimmed the low glide with a single sheet of felt, which took maybe 30% out of it, and noticeably helps at sitting height too.

**What actually fixed most of it:** I put a 3M-felt pad under each of the contact points and stopped resting my full weight on the front edge with my elbows when I'm at 50". Instead I pull the laptop and keyboard in to about 8" from the edge and keep the monitor on the arm's reach. Took a week of retraining and it's manageable.

**Bottom line on wobble, and be honest with yourself about your use case:** if you're someone who leans on the front edge of your desk, types with your palms planted, or keeps a heavy monitor clamped to the front edge with no arm — **this desk will bother you.** If you're on a monitor arm with everything pushed back like a normal human, it's a non-issue below about 45" and a minor annoyance above it.

## Memory presets: they drift, and I think it's the floor, not the memory

The presets do not return the desk to the exact height you saved. Mine recall **about 1 cm too low** on the standing preset, every single time. The sitting preset is within a millimeter or two, so perfect recall isn't the problem.

Standing height is where the lift range tops out, so any mechanical slop in the frame gets amplified into max error at the top of travel — which fits the wobble above, and fits the fact that sitting height is basically perfect. Add my slightly-out-of-level floor and the leveling glides doing their job, and you get a consistent 1 cm offset in the same direction every time.

**Workaround:** I set my standing preset one notch higher than I want the desk to actually sit, so it recalls to the height I use. Then I raise it by hand another centimeter when I stand. Annoying, but the "drift" itself is stable and predictable — it hasn't changed over six months, which means it isn't the motor losing calibration. Nothing has gotten worse.

If you have dead-level floors, you may never see this. Mine are old and I have a cat who has knocked the desk with a knee twice, so my floor is a hypothesis, not a certainty.

## The cable tray: buy literally anything else

The included tray is the single worst part of this product and the one Jarvik clearly didn't think about.

It's a thin plastic basket with a wire-grid bottom and two flimsy clips that hold it to the underside of the top. Problems, in order:

- **It sags.** Put a power strip in it and the bottom bows visibly. Put a monitor's power brick in it and it sags enough that the brick rests on the desktop.
- **The clips are undersized.** Mine have loosened. One is now permanently hanging at an angle, and I can see the plastic starting to stress-whiten right at the clip.
- **It's too shallow and too narrow.** A standard 12-outlet surge protector doesn't fit without sitting at an ugly angle.
- **It's installed with four small screws into particle board** — exactly the surface that doesn't want screws.

What I did instead: I took the whole thing off and bought a **clamp-on under-desk cable basket** (the kind that hangs from the desktop with a jaw clamp, no screws). Costs about $18, holds a full power strip plus two bricks, and I've had zero issues with it in six months. If you're buying the Jarvik L2, unscrew the tray on day one and throw it in the recycling. That's not hyperbole — that's what I did.

## Assembly: one person, 45 minutes, one stripped screw

The frame is powder-coated steel with a decent-looking weld finish. The columns are telescoping and the packaging is good — everything arrived undamaged, foam and cardboard in place, no missing parts.

One caveat that cost me a weekend: the bag of hardware contains a single screw with a head that strips if you back it out with a Phillips driver. I did. I now use a hex driver on it, but the head is rounded. If you're assembling this, use the hex bit from the start and don't be me.

Levelling feet are included and matter more than you'd think given the wobble section.

## Price: this is the actual verdict

Jarvik's own pricing is a mess. I paid $549. The MSRP was $749. The "sale" price shows up constantly, in different colors, at different times, and I've seen it float between roughly $500 and $600 since I bought mine.

**At $549, this is the best value in the category.** It has a genuinely excellent motor, a dual-motor frame, a solid warranty, and the 48" top option. For that money I cannot find a desktop with a better motor.

**At $749, it's a bad deal.** Consider what else you're choosing between at that number:

| Desk | Typical price | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Jarvik L2 | $549 (on sale) | Best motor of anything I looked at; wobbly at top of travel |
| Jarvik L3 | ~$700+ | More capacity, more stability, more money |
| Flexispot E7 | ~$500–560 | Single motor — noticeably slower and louder, but cheaper and stable |
| Autonomous SmartDesk 2 | ~$500 | Heavier frame, better top, less refined motor |
| Uplift Commercial V2 | ~$700+ | The category benchmark; better than the Jarvik at stability |

*(Prices as of this writing — check current pricing, it moves constantly.)*

The Flexispot E7 is the interesting alternative at $549 because it's close on price and better on rigidity; the Jarvik wins by a mile on the motor. The Autonomous is the one I'd point people at who are on a hard floor and type aggressively, because the frame is beefier.

**My actual advice: don't pay $749 for a Jarvik L2.** If you want this motor, wait for a sale. They happen constantly. I have no idea what the "real" price is and neither does anyone else — this is a company that runs a permanent sale.

## Who should buy this

Buy it if: you change position a lot, you work standing four or more hours a day, and you care about the motor more than you care about frame rigidity. Buy the 48" top, not the smaller one — the smaller top is where the wobble gets genuinely annoying because there's less surface keeping the frame honest.

Skip it if: you're a heavy typist who leans on the desk, you're on an uneven floor, you need more than 355 lb, or you're going to keep a monitor clamped to the front edge without an arm.

Skip it if you want to spend $700 — get a commercial frame instead, or save $200 and get the E7.

## Final score

**Motor: 9/10.** Excellent, quiet, fast, no degradation in six months.
**Frame and stability: 6/10.** Fine below 45", wobbly at full height, and the floor makes it worse.
**Presets: 6/10.** Work, but recall is off by ~1 cm up top.
**Cable tray: 2/10.** Junk. Buy something else.
**Assembly: 7/10.** Doable alone, watch that one screw.
**Value: 8/10 at $549, 4/10 at $749.**

**3.5/5 overall, and it drags the score up from 3 because of that motor.**

Six months in, I still use this desk every day and I don't regret the purchase — but I bought it at a number that required the price to come down to be a good decision. If you're reading this and the cart says $749, close the tab and check back tomorrow. It will be cheaper, and in the meantime, go look at the Flexispot E7.

*Questions about anything specific, hit me in the comments. Also, there's no affiliate link in this post and never will be — if you use the links, you pay the same and I get nothing, which is why I've quoted prices from memory rather than from a link.*

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# Corlane SM6 Review: Eight Months of Almost-Daily Dough Duty

After eight months of using the Corlane SM6 almost every day for my farmers market sourdough, my verdict is clear: **buy it for heavy bread dough, not for cookies and cakes.**

At $429, it costs $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid. That premium buys kneading muscle—not freedom from annoying maintenance or extra purchases.

## The motor is the reason to buy it

The best test I’ve given the SM6 is a double batch of stiff bagel dough. It handles that load without stalling.

That matters more to me than how a mixer performs on an occasional batch of batter. I sell sourdough at the farmers market on weekends, so my mixer gets used almost daily. Kneading isn’t a bonus feature in my kitchen; it’s the job.

After eight months of that routine, the SM6’s ability to work heavy dough is what makes me glad I bought it.

## The included dough hook is a letdown

The stock dough hook is too short for the deep bowl. I ended up buying a third-party hook to get the setup I wanted.

At this price, that’s frustrating. A $429 mixer should come with a dough hook that suits its own bowl, especially when heavy dough is its strongest selling point. Budget for a replacement rather than assuming the included hook will be satisfactory.

## The bowl-lift lever needs regular attention

The bowl-lift lever squeaks, and I’ve had to use WD-40 on it about once a month.

It hasn’t stopped me from using the mixer, but it is a recurring chore. Between that squeak and the replacement hook, this hasn’t been a flawless out-of-the-box experience.

## Verdict: Worth the premium for weekly heavy dough

**I recommend the Corlane SM6 if you knead heavy dough every week.** Its motor handles the kind of stiff, demanding batches that make a strong mixer worth paying for. For my almost-daily market baking, that strength outweighs the squeaky lift and disappointing stock hook.

**If you mostly make cookies and cake batter, skip it.** I wouldn’t pay the extra $80 for kneading power you won’t regularly use—particularly when you may also need to buy a better dough hook.

The SM6 earns its place in a bread-heavy kitchen. It doesn’t earn its premium as an everyday cake-and-cookie mixer.

b.text:
8 Months With the Corlane SM6: A Market Baker's Honest Review

When I bought the Corlane SM6 last fall, I wasn't looking for a pretty countertop mixer. I needed a workhorse. I bake sourdough all week to sell at the farmers market on weekends, which means this mixer runs almost every single day.

Here’s what 8 months of almost-daily use actually looks like.

**What I love: That motor is a tank**

The main reason I bought the SM6 was to stop killing motors with low-hydration dough. My old mixer would overheat and stall halfway through a double batch of bagel dough. The SM6 doesn't flinch.

Twice a week I do a double batch of stiff, 58% hydration bagel dough — flour, water, salt, malt, very little give — and the SM6 just kneads straight through it for 8-9 minutes on speed 2 without stalling, without that scary hot-motor smell, without me having to stop and let it rest. For straight-up bread power, it has delivered exactly what I paid for.

If you are kneading heavy, stiff dough week after week, this is the whole point of the machine.

**What I don't love: Two annoying misses**

It's not perfect, and after a few months two flaws showed up.

First, the bowl-lift lever squeaks. Loudly. It started around week six. It still lifts and locks fine, but every time I raise it there's a metal-on-metal squeal. A quick spray of WD-40 fixes it for about a month, then I have to do it again. It works — it’s just annoying maintenance on a $400+ machine.

Second, the dough hook that comes in the box is too short for the bowl. The bowl is deep and narrow, and the stock hook rides about a half-inch too high. On a single batch of sourdough it would just spin the top of the dough while flour sat untouched on the bottom. I ended up buying a third-party spiral hook for $35 that actually reaches. With that hook, it kneads beautifully. With the stock hook, it’s borderline useless.

I shouldn't have to fix a brand-new mixer with an aftermarket part.

**Price vs. the competition**

I paid $429 for the SM6. At the time, the equivalent KitchenAid bowl-lift model was $349. So you’re paying an $80 premium here.

Are you getting $80 more mixer? On power, yes. On fit-and-finish, no. KitchenAid has the smoother lever and the better out-of-the-box hook. Corlane has the stronger motor under load.

**Verdict: Buy it for bread, skip it for everything else**

I’m keeping mine. For me, it was worth it.

But I can give you a straight answer because this mixer is so specific: If you knead heavy dough every week — sourdough, bagels, sandwich loaves, pizza dough in big batches — buy the Corlane SM6. The motor alone will save you the headache of a burned-out mixer, even if you have to WD-40 the lever and replace the hook.

If you’re mostly making cookies, cake batter, buttercream and the occasional soft dough, skip it. Save your $80 and get the KitchenAid. You don’t need this much motor and you’ll appreciate not having to tinker with it.

For a market baker like me, the SM6 earns its counter space. For a cookie-and-cake baker, it’s overkill.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
On the Maple Ave kitchen remodel, we pulled back the drywall and found a 4-inch notch cut into a main load-bearing joist by a previous owner.

We couldn’t ignore it. Had to sister the joist with LVL and add a steel plate. That added $1,200 to the budget and two days to the timeline.

Lesson: Never assume framing is sound until you expose it. Structural surprises are the norm, not the exception, in older Pittsburgh homes.

Always allocate a contingency fund for hidden structural work. It’s cheaper than the alternative.

b.text:
1/ Maple Ave kitchen: opened the ceiling below and found the floor joists were 2x8s spanning 14'6" — already maxed out — and three of them had the bottom third notched out for an old drain line. Floor had 5/8" of deflection. No cracks yet, but it was coming.

2/ What it cost: We didn't re-frame the whole floor. Sistered three joists with LVLs, added a mid-span beam in the basement, re-supported the drain. Engineering, materials, two days for two guys: $4,200.

3/ The actual lesson isn't "old houses are scary." It's that the structure had been treated as negotiable. Someone needed the drain to fit, so they cut the joist. The house held — until it wouldn't.

4/ If you're opening a 1950s kitchen, assume every joist under the wet areas has been altered. Find the notch before you set tile. $4,200 now is cheaper than a cracked floor after.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
My daughter was six when I came home from my second deployment. At the airport, she stood behind her mother’s leg. I could see one eye and part of her forehead.

I had been thinking about seeing her for months. I figured she would run to me. I had pictured putting my bag down so I could catch her.

Instead, I put my bag down and stayed where I was.

“Hey, kiddo.”

She pulled back behind her mother. She didn’t recognize me at first. She knew I was coming home. Those turned out to be different things.

Her mother put a hand on her head and told her it was okay. I crouched down, which wasn’t comfortable after the flight, and asked her about the stuffed animal she was holding. She showed me its face without coming any closer.

People went around us with their suitcases. Somebody was holding flowers. I stayed down there and listened while she told me the animal’s name.

Eventually she stepped out. I didn’t reach for her right away.

On the walk to the car, she held her mother’s hand. I carried my bag and tried not to walk too fast.

A few days later, I went to the grocery store. We needed milk and some other things. I said I would get them. I wanted to do an ordinary job without anybody needing to help me.

I got through most of the list and stopped in the cereal aisle.

There must have been forty kinds. More, counting the different sizes. The same cereal came in a regular box, a family box, and a box big enough to feed a squad. There were versions with almonds, without almonds, with less sugar, with extra something.

I stood there for about twenty minutes.

I’d pick up a box and read it, then put it back. I wasn’t looking for anything special. I just couldn’t settle on one. Every time I thought I had, I saw another.

A woman said, “Excuse me,” and I moved my cart. Later she came through again from the other end. I was still there.

I had made decisions on deployment. Some had mattered a great deal. Now I couldn’t put cereal in a cart.

I finally took the kind I remembered eating before I left. At home, I put it in the cupboard and the milk in the refrigerator.

“What took so long?”

“Couldn’t find a few things.”

Nobody asked which things. I was glad of that.

At night, I slept facing the bedroom door. I had done it for a year, and I kept doing it after I got home. If I woke up turned the other way, I rolled back.

My wife liked the door open so we could hear our daughter. I wanted it shut. With it open, there was a stretch of hallway I couldn’t see from the bed.

The first few nights, I got up and closed it after my wife fell asleep. Then our daughter would need something, and my wife would get up, and the door would be open again.

We had a short argument about it one morning. We were both tired. I said I slept better with it closed. She said our daughter had been able to come in whenever she needed to for the whole year I was gone.

I didn’t have much to say to that.

I tried leaving it open a few inches. The latch would click when the air came on, so I opened it farther. I lay on my side and watched the doorway. Sometimes I got up to check the hall even though I knew what was in it: the bathroom, the linen closet, my daughter’s room.

During the day, she got used to me being around. She asked me to open things. She brought me papers from school and explained which ones I was supposed to keep. Sometimes she started telling her mother something, then remembered I was sitting there and told me too.

I learned which cereal she ate. It wasn’t the one I had bought.

One night I woke to her standing in the bedroom doorway. I lifted my head too fast, and she stopped.

“What’s wrong?” I asked.

“I need water.”

There was a cup in the bathroom, but I got up and went to the kitchen with her. She waited while I took a glass down. I filled it halfway so she wouldn’t spill it carrying it back.

She drank standing by the sink, both hands around the glass. Then she handed it to me.

I walked her back to bed. She climbed in and pulled the blanket up, and I moved a stuffed animal out from under her shoulder.

“Night, Dad,” she said.

I went back to our room. My wife shifted when I got in, then settled. I lay down facing the doorway. I could hear our daughter cough once down the hall.

The door stayed open.

b.text:
My second tour ended on a Tuesday in October. 

When we got to the terminal, I saw Sarah first. She was waving, wearing a yellow sweater I’d never seen before. Lily was right next to her. Lily was six then, and she’d grown three inches since the deployment ceremony. When I got closer, dropped my green duffel, and knelt down, Lily took a step back. She got right behind Sarah’s leg, wrapping her arms around her mother’s jeans, looking at me like I was a stranger. She didn’t recognize me. A year is a long time when you’re six. I had to sit there on the linoleum floor and talk to her in my quiet voice for a few minutes before she would even let me hold her hand. 

Two days later, Sarah sent me to the grocery store. She wanted me to get out of the house, and she needed a few things. The list was simple: milk, bread, and cereal for Lily. 

I got the milk and the bread with no issue. Then I hit the cereal aisle. I stood there for twenty minutes. I know it was twenty minutes because I kept looking at my watch. There were forty different kinds of cereal. Blue boxes, red boxes, cartoon characters, store brand, name brand, organic bran, sugar-coated loops. Downrange, you eat what they put in the metal trays at the DFAC, or you tear open an MRE packet. You don’t think about it. I stood in the middle of that aisle, people pushing their carts past me, and I couldn't make my hand reach out and grab a box. My chest felt tight, like I was trying to solve a problem that had no correct answer. I ended up grabbing a box of plain Cheerios because the box was yellow and easy to see, and I went straight to the registers. 

Nights were different, too. In Iraq, I slept on a cot, facing the plywood door of our CHU. You always sleep facing the entry point, with your boots close. 

At home, our bed faced the windows, away from the door. Sarah liked to keep the bedroom door cracked an inch or two so she could hear Lily if she woke up in the night. The first week, I couldn't close my eyes with that door open. Every time I did, the hallway felt like an unsecured perimeter. I’d get up in the middle of the night, click the door shut, and lie back down. But then Sarah would wake up, notice the door was closed, and worry about Lily. 

So I had to learn to leave it open. I spent a lot of nights lying on my back, staring at the sliver of yellow light coming from the hallway bathroom, waiting for my body to believe that the front door downstairs was locked and there was nobody coming through.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
The walk-in cooler stays at thirty-eight degrees. On Saturday afternoons, after the lunch rush clears out, I take a fifteen-minute break on an overturned pickle bucket next to the crates of green onions. I keep my winter coat hanging on a hook by the meat slicer specifically for this. It’s the only place in the building quiet enough to concentrate, so I sit there with my knees pulled up, working through derivatives on scrap paper, the cold ink barely flowing from my pen until my fingers go numb and it’s time to prep for dinner.

I’ve worked weekends at my parents' restaurant, Phở Bình, since the first week of tenth grade. Most of what I know about efficiency I learned between the dish pit and the six-burner range. 

Last fall, we hired Tommy, a sophomore from my school, to help with prep. His first Saturday, he tore four rice papers in a row trying to roll *gỏi cuốn*. The wrappers are fragile; you dip them in warm water for two seconds, no longer, and let them soften on the cutting board while you lay down the shrimp, pork, and mint. 

"Don't pull so hard," I told him, showing him how my grandmother does it. "Tuck the sides in first like an envelope, then roll forward with your palms, not your fingertips. If there’s air inside, they fall apart when people bite them." 

We made eighty of them side by side. By the fiftieth, he stopped tearing the wrappers. By five o'clock, the metal tray in the cold well was full, covered with damp paper towels so they wouldn't dry out under the heat lamps.

Dinner service usually runs on muscle memory, but two months ago, right at six-thirty on a rainy Saturday, the entire point-of-sale system went black. The kitchen printer stopped feeding, the screen wouldn't reboot, and we had forty people seated with eight more waiting by the door. 

My mom started apologizing to Table 3, but apologies don't get noodles into bowls. I found three pads of carbon-copy guest checks in the dry storage closet, handed one to my sister, and kept two for myself. I took orders by hand, writing the table numbers in the top right corner and using our kitchen shorthand: *T* for tái, *G* for gầu, *B* for bún. I walked the tickets straight back to my dad on the line, calling out the bowl sizes and whether people wanted extra cilantro. 

For two hours, nobody sat down. My dad ladled broth, my mom dropped noodles into boiling water, and I ran food, cleared tables, and added up bills in my head, calculating the 8.25% sales tax on the back of the receipts before running credit cards through the manual dial-up terminal we usually keep under the counter for emergencies. 

When the rush finally died down around nine, the linoleum behind the line was slick with broth, my apron was soaked through, and the trash can was full of yellow duplicate slips. The system didn't come back on until Monday morning, but every table got their food, and the register drawer balanced within three dollars when we counted out the cash.

We swept the floor, bleached the cutting boards, and turned off the neon open sign. I took off my apron, got my backpack from the office, and checked my phone. It was almost ten. I still had forty pages of US History to read before Sunday morning prep, but my dad handed me a quart container of broth to take home, still hot enough to burn through the plastic.

b.text:
Since sophomore year, my weekends have smelled like star anise, bleach, and fried garlic. My parents own a forty-seat Vietnamese restaurant in a strip mall off the highway, and from Friday afternoon to Sunday night, I am the hostess, cashier, busser, and backup prep cook. 

Most of the job is muscle memory. Last month we hired a college student named Marcus to help in the kitchen, and my dad put me in charge of teaching him how to roll goi cuon. Rice paper is unforgiving. Leave it in the warm water a second too long and it turns to glue; pull it out too early and it cracks. Marcus kept tearing his wrappers, trying to muscle the shrimp and vermicelli into a cylinder. I had to show him how my grandma taught me when I was ten: you don’t pull the paper tight, you use your knuckles to tuck the greens under, let the wet starch catch on itself, and just guide it forward. You have to fold the sides in like an envelope before the last roll so the herbs don’t poke out the ends. By Sunday, Marcus’s rolls were still a little loose, but they stayed shut on the plate.

There isn’t much downtime between the lunch and dinner rushes, so I take my fifteen-minute breaks in the walk-in cooler. It is the only quiet place in the building. I sit on an overturned five-gallon soy sauce bucket, wedge my AP Calculus textbook between a crate of cilantro and a tub of pickled carrots, and work through integration by parts until my fingers go stiff from the cold. My mom thinks I’m crazy for not sitting in a booth out front, but in the booths, regular customers want to chat, or my dad asks me to restock the chili oil. In the walk-in, the only sound is the hum of the evaporator fan. Forty degrees is the exact temperature I need to concentrate on finding the volume of a solid of revolution.

Sometimes the weekend is just about surviving the dinner rush. A few Saturdays ago, at 6:30 p.m., the touchscreen on our point-of-sale system flickered and went black. The dining room was full, the phone was ringing, and three delivery drivers were waiting by the counter. My dad came out of the kitchen wiping his hands on his apron, looked at the dead screen, and started speaking very fast in Vietnamese. 

I grabbed a stack of blank guest checks from under the counter and two pens. I knew the menu prices by heart, and I knew the shorthand the kitchen used before we bought the computer two years ago. *Tai Nam* for rare steak and flank pho. *Com Biet* for the broken rice platter with everything on it. For the next three hours, I took orders at the tables, ran to the kitchen pass to clip the yellow carbon copies to the metal wheel, and calculated the six-percent sales tax in my head while making change out of a cigar box. My handwriting got progressively worse, and my calves ached from running back and forth, but the food went out hot.

I don't want to run a restaurant when I'm older. My parents work sixty hours a week so I won't have to. When I go to college next fall, I am looking forward to having Saturdays that belong entirely to me, and doing my math homework at a desk in a library at room temperature. Still, when I look at what I bring with me—how I handle a broken system, how I explain a process to someone new, how I find focus in a loud room—it all comes from forty seats, a broken register, and a cold room full of vegetables.

setup: You're Nadine Alvarado, emailing the daycare owner after a near-miss pickup mistake involving Mia and asking what happened and what changes are being made.

a.text:
Hi Nadine,

Thank you for emailing me, and I completely understand why that call yesterday was terrifying. You should never get a call about someone you don't know trying to pick up Mia.

Here is what happened — I want to be straight with you about it. I had a substitute helper covering the afternoon pickup while I was with the little ones. Someone came to the door asking for Mia who was not on your approved pickup list. My sub didn't recognize her. She did not release Mia — she kept Mia inside with me and called you from the door to check first, which is why you got that call and why Mia never left our supervision.

She did the right thing by calling and not releasing her, but you are absolutely right to be upset — it should never have even gotten to a phone call. That person should have been stopped at the door and checked against the list and ID right away.

This is what I'm doing starting today:

I'm adding a hard ID check at the door. No one gets in past the entry without showing photo ID that matches the approved pickup list exactly. I'm moving that list to a clipboard right at the door so it's not in the binder in the back anymore.

And my sub will not work again until we sit down and retrain on pickup. She won't be alone for pickup until I'm 100% confident in it. That's on me for not making that process clearer for her.

Mia was safe and with me the whole time yesterday, but I know that's not enough — you need to feel safe leaving her here. I am so sorry this happened.

Can we go over your pickup list together when you have a minute? If you want to add or remove anyone, or if you want to come a few minutes early this week and watch how we do pickup now, please do. I'm here all day and you can call or text me anytime.

Thank you for trusting me with Mia, and for telling me how scary that was for you.

b.text:
Hi Nadine,

I’m very sorry this happened, and I understand why it was frightening.

Yesterday, the substitute helper did not recognize the person who arrived to pick up Mia. Before releasing Mia, she called you to confirm whether that person was authorized. You confirmed that you did not know them, so Mia was not released and the situation did not go any further.

That said, the person should never have gotten that far into the pickup process, and I take responsibility for that. Our approved pickup list and verification procedures should have been followed before anyone approached Mia.

Starting immediately, I’m adding an ID check at the door for every pickup, along with a second check against the approved pickup list. I’m also retraining the substitute helper on our release procedures before she works here again. I’ll be reviewing the process with the rest of the staff as well.

Mia was kept safe, but I know that doesn’t erase how upsetting this was. I’m sorry we put you in that position, and I appreciate you bringing it to my attention.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/4
Maple Ave kitchen. Opened the subfloor after demo: three consecutive 2x10s cut clean through at midspan for an old 4" stack. Previous “repair” was 2x4s toenailled on the sides. 3/4" sag right where the island was going.

2/4
Sistered them full length with 2x10s, added blocking, hangers, and a short LVL. Three extra days for our crew. Extra cost to the owner: $2,850 in labor and material. Cabinets and stone were already in the warehouse.

3/4
Homeowners see the cabinets. We see whether the floor can actually hold them. That’s the gap.

4/4
Lesson: don’t lock the finish package until you’ve seen the structure. If you’re bidding a kitchen without looking at the joists, you’re not pricing a remodel. You’re guessing.

b.text:
1/4 Opened up the ceiling on our Maple Ave kitchen remodel and found a classic shortcut. Someone sistered a 2x4 to a sagging 2x8 floor joist... but only for 4 feet in the middle of a 14-foot span. And they used drywall screws.

2/4 To fix it right, we had to temporarily jack the floor, pull the bad sister, and run a full-length LVL sister with through-bolts and structural adhesive. It added a full day of framing and about $1,800 to the budget. 

3/4 The actual lesson for my fellow builders and architects: a half-sister doesn't just fail to fix the sag. It creates a hard hinge point where the new lumber ends, concentrating stress and cracking the finishes above. Always span full length to the bearing walls.

4/4 And for homeowners: if your remodel involves opening up old ceilings or floors, keep a 10-15% contingency specifically for structural surprises. 100-year-old Pittsburgh houses always have at least one skeleton hiding in the framing.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
If there’s one thing I see almost every week on my grooming table, it’s a sweet pup whose owner tried to do the right thing at home, only to accidentally turn a tiny tangle into a major headache. The mistake I see constantly is people giving their dog a bath first, thinking the warm water and shampoo will help loosen up the mats. I totally understand the logic, but water actually does the exact opposite. Wetting matted fur—especially on curly doodley coats or thick double-coated breeds—acts just like wool in a hot wash. It shrinks, tightens, and turns that soft hair into a dense, felt pad that locks the knots in way tighter than they were before. Always, always brush thoroughly before a bath at home, never after. 

When you do sit down for a brushing session, the tool you want in your hand is a good slicker brush. The trick here is technique: use short, straight line strokes rather than rubbing the brush in circles. Moving in circles just twists the hair around itself and creates brand-new tangles. Think of it like a gentle "pat and pull" motion, lifting up a section of coat with one hand and brushing out the hair underneath it layer by layer so you’re actually reaching the skin, not just skimming the surface.

Don't try to tackle the whole dog at once. Work in small sections, and make a habit of starting in the sneaky trouble spots where mats always form first. Check right behind the ears where the skin is delicate, and tuck your fingers under the front legs into the armpits. Those high-friction areas gather tiny tangles long before you’ll ever notice them on the dog's back or sides.

If you’re working through a section and catch a mat that’s already starting to clump together, step away from the brush for a second. Ripping through a tight knot hurts your pup and makes them dread brush time. Instead, grab a little dab of dog conditioner—or even a leave-in coat spray—and work it straight into the knot using just your fingers. Gently massage it in and use your thumbs to wiggle the hair strands apart from the outside in. Once you’ve broken up the bulk of the knot with your hands, *then* you can bring in your brush or comb to finish smoothing it out. 

Taking five or ten minutes to work through these high-friction spots a couple of times a week keeps your dog comfortable and saves their coat. And remember, if a mat ever gets too tight or sits right against the skin, don't fight it—just let us know at your next visit and we’ll safely take care of it on the table.

b.text:
If you run your hands through your dog’s coat, feel a tangle, and immediately think, “I’ll just throw them in the tub and wash it out,” I need you to step away from the faucet. 

I see this happen in the salon every single week, especially with our curly doodles and thick double-coated breeds. People think warm water and a good lather will soften up tangles, but water actually does the exact opposite. Think about what happens when you wash a wool sweater: the fibers shrink, knit together, and turn into a solid, impenetrable felt pad. That is exactly what happens to your dog's hair. Bathing a matted dog locks those knots in tighter, and once that happens, my clippers are usually the only safe option left. 

The golden rule at home is to always brush *before* the bath, never after. If water hits a knot, you’ve lost the battle. 

When you sit down to brush, throw out the idea of just casually sweeping over their back while you watch TV. That just fluffs the top layer while mats quietly build up right against the skin. Grab a slicker brush, and instead of moving in circles or long, sweeping arcs, use short, gentle line strokes. You want to part the hair with your free hand so you can see the pink of their skin, then brush down through that section, working your way up layer by layer. 

Don't just start randomly in the middle of their back, either. Work in small sections and go straight to the friction zones first, because that’s where mats always start. Check right behind the ears where their collar rubs, deep in the armpits under their front legs, and back around the groin and tail base. If you can keep those hidden friction areas clear, the rest of the body is easy.

Now, if you’re doing your routine check and you feel a mat that’s already formed, put the brush down. Raking through a tight knot with metal pins hurts, and it only takes one painful session for your dog to decide they hate being groomed. Instead, take a little bit of dog conditioner (or a dog-safe detangling spray) and work it directly into the knot with your bare fingers. Massage it in, gently teasing the hairs apart with your fingertips to break up the core of the mat. Only after you’ve worked it loose with your hands and given the hair some slickness should you take a metal comb or slicker brush to gently finish working it out, starting from the tips and moving toward the skin.

A few minutes of line brushing in the right spots a couple of times a week will save your dog from discomfort, save their coat length, and save you from the dreaded "we had to shave them" phone call at their next appointment. As always, if you run into a knot you can’t safely separate with your fingers, leave it alone and bring them in—we're always here to help tackle it before it gets out of hand.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
The register died at 11:40 on a Saturday in October, twenty minutes before the lunch rush. The screen went gray, then black, and stayed black. My dad unplugged it, plugged it back in, and unplugged it again. Then he looked at me and said, "Paper."

We keep a stack of old order pads under the counter for this, though I'd never used them. I started writing tickets by hand. Table number in the top corner, circled. Item numbers instead of names, because our menu is numbered and the kitchen knows the numbers better than the words. 14 is the combination phở. 22 is broken rice with grilled pork. If someone wanted no onions I wrote "NO ON" and underlined it twice, because my uncle on the line reads fast and doesn't always see a single underline.

I added up every bill on the back of the ticket. Tax I did on my phone calculator. People who paid with cards had to wait while I wrote the amount on a slip and my mom ran it on the old swipe machine she found in the office. A man at table 6 told me I'd charged him for two iced coffees when he'd only had one. He was right. I fixed it and he left a ten-dollar tip, which I think was about the mistake and not the coffee.

By three o'clock I had a callus starting on my middle finger. The register came back on Monday. I kept the tickets from that day in a rubber band in my backpack for a while. I'm not sure why.

---

My grandma folds spring rolls in a way nobody else in our family does exactly right, including my mom, who will tell you that herself. Last summer we hired a college student named Danny to help with prep, and my mom asked me to teach him the rolls because she didn't have time and my grandma doesn't really speak English.

I showed him what she showed me when I was twelve. You dip the rice paper in warm water for a count of two, not three, because it keeps softening after you take it out. You lay the shrimp down first, cut side up, so the pink shows through. Lettuce, herbs, noodles. You fold the bottom over and tuck it tight, then fold in the sides, then roll. The tuck is the part that matters. If it's loose, the roll looks fine for an hour and then sags in the case.

Danny's first ten were bad. His next ten were less bad. He kept saying sorry, and I kept telling him the bad ones go to staff lunch, which is true. My grandma came by and watched him for a while without saying anything. Then she reached over and pressed his thumb down on the tuck, harder than he'd been doing it, and walked away. His next one held.

---

On Saturdays I get one ten-minute break in the afternoon, usually around four. For most of junior year I spent it in the walk-in cooler doing calculus.

It's the only quiet place in the building. The kitchen has the hood fans and the dish machine, and the front has customers, but the walk-in just has the compressor humming. It's 37 degrees in there. I'd sit on an upside-down bucket between the bean sprouts and the crates of limes and work through related rates problems with my jacket zipped up to my chin. A ladder sliding down a wall. Water draining out of a cone. I liked that the problems had an answer at the end, and that I could usually get to it in ten minutes if I didn't stop.

My dad came in once to grab a case of eggs and saw me. He didn't say anything about it. The next week there was a milk crate turned on its side next to the bucket, so I'd have somewhere to put my notebook.

I'm writing this on a Sunday night. Tomorrow is school, and Saturday I work again. The register has been fine since October, but the order pads are still under the counter, and I know where they are.

b.text:
On Saturdays the restaurant opens at eleven, but we get there at nine. My dad unlocks the back door and the first thing you smell is the fish sauce from the night before, and then the rice cooker starts and it smells like our house.

The register died on a Saturday in October. Not a slow reboot, not a frozen screen—dead, the little lights gone. My mom kept pressing the power button like it was a person she could wake up. So I got a pad of paper and started writing tickets by hand. Table four, two vermicelli bowls, one with extra pork, no peanuts. Table six wanted the pho with tendon, and I had to remember it wasn't on the paper receipt because there was no receipt, just my handwriting getting worse as it got busier. I did the math for everyone's change in my head. I got one order wrong all day, a spring roll count, and my dad only found out because I told him. The system came back around three. By then I didn't need it.

We hire people sometimes and they don't last. There's a lot to remember and the kitchen gets hot. In the spring we hired a guy named Danh who was maybe nineteen and he could cook but he couldn't fold a spring roll right. My grandma folds them a specific way, tight, so they don't come apart in the oil. She showed me when I was little and now I showed him. You lay the wrapper like a diamond, filling near the bottom, fold up once, fold the sides in, then roll and seal the edge with water. Danh's first ten fell apart. His eleventh held. I didn't tell my grandma I taught him because she likes to think only she can do it, and honestly she does it better, but his are fine now.

I do my homework in the walk-in cooler. This sounds worse than it is. The dining room is loud and there's nowhere to sit, but the cooler has a shelf at the right height and it's quiet in there with the boxes of vegetables and the sound of the fan. I did most of my calculus in the cooler this year. Related rates, integrals, all of it, sitting on a milk crate with my jacket on. My mom would open the door to grab lemongrass and see me and say don't stay too long, you'll get sick. I never got sick. I got a lot of problem sets done.

That's most of my Saturdays. I'll probably work them until I leave for school, and then my parents will figure something out, or they won't and it'll be harder for them, which I think about. I'm not going to pretend the restaurant taught me some big thing. It's just where I've been every weekend since tenth grade. I know how to run a register with no register. I know how my grandma folds a spring roll. I can do calculus at forty degrees. These are the things I know.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
**Don't Cut the Program That Works**

The state wants to cut apprenticeship funding by 15 percent. I'm a third-year apprentice electrician with the IBEW, and I'm asking the legislature to think hard before it does that. The numbers show this program pays for itself.

**It works.** My cohort started with 24 apprentices. 21 of them finished, and they're working as journeymen today. That's better than 8 out of 10 starting and finishing, and every one of them ended up with a skilled job. Not every program can say that.

**It pays fast.** An apprentice starts around $19 an hour. A journeyman tops out around $46. Nobody waits four years for a degree to start earning. We earn from day one, and our pay goes up as our skills do. By the time we top out, we're making a wage that supports a family, pays taxes, and doesn't need help from public assistance programs. People leave assistance quickly because they have a real paycheck, not because someone pushed them off.

**It costs less.** The total public cost for each apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. The average public subsidy for each four-year college graduate who finishes is around $48,000. That's more than three times as much. I'm not knocking college. Plenty of people need it and do great things with it. But if the state is looking for the best return on its money, the apprenticeship model is hard to beat. Cutting it to save money means cutting the cheaper option.

**A cut makes less sense than it looks.** Fifteen percent sounds small on a budget sheet. In a program like ours, it means fewer seats, fewer instructors, and fewer training materials. Fewer seats means fewer people finishing. Every apprentice we don't train is a journeyman the state doesn't have later. We're already short on electricians. Contractors need them, and the state needs them for the work coming up: housing, repairs, and the power grid. Cutting training now makes that shortage worse.

There's a cost on the other side too. Every person who doesn't get a spot is someone who may stay on assistance longer, or who never gets onto a career path that pays $46 an hour. The state pays that bill one way or another.

**What I'm asking.** To the legislators reading this: please don't make this cut. If you need to find savings, look at programs that don't show results like these. To my brothers and sisters in the local: call or write your representatives. Tell them your story and your numbers. Legislators listen to the people who live in their districts, and a short call from a working electrician carries weight.

This program took people at $19 an hour and turned them into journeymen at $46, for a fraction of what other paths cost the public. That's worth protecting.

b.text:
**Don’t Cut Apprenticeship Funding—It’s the Best Deal the State Has**

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with our local IBEW. I’m not writing as a budget expert. I’m writing as somebody who has been in the classroom and on the job, and who has watched what this money actually does. The state is talking about a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding. I think that’s a mistake, and I want legislators to hear why from someone who is living it.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished and are working journeyman jobs now. That’s not a theory. Those are people paying rent, buying tools, supporting families, and showing up to work every day. When you cut apprenticeship funding, you don’t just cut a line item. You cut the number of people who get that shot.

The pay numbers matter too. Apprentices start around $19 an hour. Journeymen top out around $46 an hour. That means people move off public assistance fast and into jobs that pay enough to stay off it. They start paying taxes, buying fuel, buying lunch, buying equipment. The state puts money in on the front end and gets a skilled worker and a taxpayer on the back end. That’s a good return.

Compare the cost. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. The average public subsidy per four-year graduate who finishes is something like $48,000. I’m not saying four-year degrees aren’t worth it. I’m saying apprenticeships do a lot with a little. If we’re looking for smart spending, this is it.

A 15% cut sounds small in a budget hearing. In a training program, it isn’t. It means fewer slots, less instructor time, less equipment, and fewer chances for people who don’t have a four-year degree or a family that can bankroll one. It hits the people who need a hand up, not a handout.

I’ve seen what happens when somebody gets into this program. They show up, they learn the code, they learn safety, and they learn how to do work that keeps the lights on and the buildings safe. They don’t need a subsidy forever. They need a chance to get trained.

So I’m asking legislators: don’t cut apprenticeship funding by 15%. Fund what works. Twenty-one out of twenty-four finished in my cohort. They’re working. They’re paying taxes. They’re off assistance. Fourteen thousand dollars per finisher is a bargain compared to forty-eight thousand. Cut something else.

And to our members: tell your representatives. This isn’t about politics. It’s about whether the next group of apprentices gets the same chance we did.

setup: You're Renata Cole. Your English teacher is thanking you for single-handedly running the week-long book fair and raising over double last year's total.

a.text:
Hi Renata,

I wanted to reach out personally now that the used book fair is all wrapped up to say thank you—truly, there aren’t enough words to capture how much your work this week meant to me, the other English teachers, and most of all, our students.

When the usual book fair coordinator had to step back three weeks ago, I was convinced we’d have to scale way back, or even cancel entirely. I had no idea how we’d pull off a full week of the fair on top of midterm grading, lesson planning, and all the chaos of the spring semester. Then you showed up to that last-minute planning meeting and said you’d take the lead—and I don’t think any of us realized just how fully you’d mean that.

I still can’t stop thinking about all the unglamorous, relentless work you put in that no one else would have noticed if they didn’t show up at 7 a.m. before the bell: hauling those heavy cardboard boxes of donated books from the basement storage closet (I still laugh about Tuesday, when you toted a box of mystery novels so big it blocked your view of the door, and joked you’d built up enough arm strength to skip your workout for the month). You stayed every single night after dismissal until 5 p.m. or later, folding tables, sorting leftover books to donate to the middle school, and restocking shelves for the next day—all while recruiting a team of parent volunteers and even a handful of my 11th grade AP Lang students, who kept stopping by my class this week to say how fun you made the whole thing feel, even when the hallways were packed and the cash register ran out of ones.

And the total? When we counted the proceeds last night, we all stood there stunned: you helped raise more than double what we brought in last year. Last year, the fair funds only covered half the new classroom library titles I had on my wishlist—this year, we can replace all the tattered, page-teared copies of *The House on Mango Street* and *To Kill a Mockingbird* for 9th grade, add all the verse novels and graphic novel classics kids have been begging me for (I already put in the order for *The Poet X* and the *Heartstopper* Book 1 set—don’t tell the kids yet, I want it to be a surprise), and even put some money toward the creative writing club’s annual literary magazine. That’s hundreds of students getting to hold books they’re actually excited to read, all because you showed up and cared enough to do the work no one else was willing to take on.

I know you don’t do this for recognition, but I wanted you to know exactly how far your effort goes. As a small token of my thanks, I set aside that used copy of Mary Oliver’s *Devotions* I saw you pick up and flip through three different times last week—it’s on the front desk in my classroom, and you can stop by anytime to grab it (or just say hi, if you want). I also told all my classes about everything you did to make the fair happen, and a bunch of the kids asked if they could write you thank you notes—if that’s something you’d be okay with, I’d love to pass them along in a few weeks.

Seriously, Renata—you turned a small, scrappy used book fair into something that will shape our students’ love of reading for the whole year. I can’t thank you enough.

All my best,
[Your Name]
10th & 11th Grade English

b.text:
Renata,

I've been trying to figure out how to thank you properly for this week, and I keep landing on the same thought: the book fair happened because you made it happen.

You didn't just help — you ran it. You pulled together a volunteer crew out of thin air, you were in the building hauling boxes before the first bell and still there stacking them after dismissal, and you did it five days straight. I saw you carrying crates up from the cafeteria on Wednesday morning while I was still on my first cup of coffee, and it occurred to me that nobody asked you to do that. You just saw what needed doing and did it.

And then the numbers came in at more than double last year's total. I want you to know exactly what that means, because it isn't abstract: that money buys the books that go on my classroom shelves for the whole year. It means I can get multiple copies of the novels my students actually want to read, replace the paperbacks that have been held together with tape since before I got here, and say yes when a kid asks if we have something instead of "not yet." You turned a week of heavy lifting into a year of reading for a lot of teenagers.

Thank you for the hours, the sore back, and the sheer stubbornness it took to pull this off. Our students are luckier than they know.

With real gratitude,
[Your name]

a.text:
**Why we're saying goodbye to custom wedding cakes**

I wanted to tell you this myself instead of just quietly taking the page off the website: we're not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore.

I love making them. I want to say that first, because it's true, and because I don't want this to sound like a door slamming. There's nothing quite like seeing a cake you've worked on for days walk out the door toward someone's biggest day. But I've been doing the math on what those cakes actually take, and it's time to be honest about it.

Every wedding cake we've done has eaten up about 14 hours before a single layer gets baked. That's the emails, the consultation, the tasting, the second tasting, the "can we see it with a different flower," the sketching and re-sketching. None of that time is paid. We offer it gladly because that's part of doing it right, but 14 hours is a lot when there are three of us and I'm up at 4am most days just to get the morning bake out on time. Those hours have to come from somewhere, and mostly they've come from sleep, from the front case, and from me not being in the shop when I should be.

Then there's the other piece, which is nobody's fault but still stings. This year we had three last-minute cancellations. Plans change, and I understand that completely, weddings are enormous and life gets in the way. But by the time a cake is cancelled that close to the date, the butter is bought, the flour is bought, the time is blocked off, and we've turned down other things to make room. For a bakery our size, three of those in one year is a real hit.

What it comes down to is that the everyday case is what pays the rent. The loaves, the morning pastries, the cookies you grab on the way to pick up the kids: that's the heart of this place, and it's you, the people who walk in on a regular Tuesday, who keep the lights on. Every hour spent on a custom order is an hour not spent making that better, or being here to hand it to you. I'd rather put that energy into the thing we do every single day.

So that's the decision. It wasn't an easy one, and I'm sorry if it's a disappointment, especially if you were hoping we'd be part of your day. Truly, thank you for even thinking of us for something that important.

The case will be full tomorrow, same as always. Come say hi.

b.text:
We’ve decided to stop taking orders for custom wedding cakes. It’s a hard thing to write, because being asked to bake for someone’s wedding is a lovely kind of trust, and we’re grateful to everyone who’s let us be part of their day.

But there are three of us here, and we’ve had to be honest about how much we can fit into a week.

A custom wedding cake takes a lot of work before we even turn on the oven. Between consultations, tastings, and working through the details, we spend around 14 hours on each order that we don’t charge for. We’ve also had three last-minute cancellations this year after ingredients were already bought, leaving us to absorb those costs. Neither of those things is easy for a shop our size.

The bigger thing, though, is that the wedding work has been pulling us away from the everyday case. That’s the baking most of you come in for, and it’s what keeps the rent paid. It deserves our time and attention—not whatever we have left after a big custom order.

Most mornings I’m baking by 4 a.m., and lately I’ve been reminded that starting early doesn’t make the day any longer. We can love making something and still decide it doesn’t fit the bakery anymore.

So we’re making a little more room for the daily baking, and for doing it well. I’m sad to let the wedding cakes go, but I’m also looking forward to giving more of our energy to the things you stop in for on an ordinary morning.

Thank you for making those ordinary mornings enough to build a little bakery around. We’re very glad to be here.

**A Good Season, a Self-Inflicted Ending**

I’ll get to the 8-2 record and Dez Kowalski’s 2,340 yards in a minute. But let’s be honest about how this season ended: our team lost a second-round playoff game to a team it had already beaten by 20 in Week 3, and it lost because it quit running the football in the second half while the run was still working. They were down three. Three. That’s not a panic score. That’s a keep-doing-what-you’re-doing score.

I’ve said it on the radio this week, and I’ll say it here: that loss is on the play sheet, not the players. The run game was there. It wasn’t stuffed. It wasn’t stuffed early, and it wasn’t stuffed late. The staff just got away from it. In playoff football, when you’re within one score and the defense is giving you four and five yards a carry, you don’t need to get creative. You need to stay patient. You need to be willing to be boring.

Kowalski’s record is real, and he earned it. Throwing for 2,340 yards in a season is a school record for a reason. But a record-setting passing season can become a trap. When your quarterback can throw it, every down starts looking like a passing down. That’s fine in September. In November, with the season on the line and a three-point deficit, it can cost you. The frustrating part is this wasn’t a talent gap. They beat this team by 20 earlier. The rematch wasn’t about who was better. It was about who kept doing what was working.

8-2 is a good season. I won’t pretend otherwise. Kowalski’s record is a real achievement. But good seasons don’t excuse an avoidable loss. The record book will say 8-2 and 2,340. The bracket will say second round. Both are true. So is this: our guys didn’t get beat by the team they beat by 20. They got beat by their own second-half plan.

b.text:
# We Had Them, and We Got Cute

An 8-2 season is a good season. Let's say that up front, because the next few hundred words aren't going to feel that way, and I don't want anybody thinking I've lost sight of what these kids accomplished.

But I've been doing this long enough to know the difference between a team that got beat and a team that beat itself. Friday night, in the second round of the state playoffs, we beat ourselves.

Here's what sticks in my throat. We beat that team by 20 back in Week 3. Twenty. And we didn't beat them by scheming them into oblivion — we beat them by lining up and running the ball down their throat. So you'll forgive me if I don't buy the idea that they were simply the better team this time around. They weren't. We just decided, somewhere around the middle of the third quarter, to stop doing the thing that was working.

Because it *was* working. We were moving the chains on the ground. We were down three — three! — and controlling the clock, keeping their offense on the sideline, wearing on a defense that didn't want any part of it. And then we got cute. We put it in the air, went three-and-out, put our defense back on the field, and the whole complexion of the game changed. You could feel it in the stands.

I understand the instinct. Dez Kowalski threw for 2,340 yards this year, a school record, and that's a genuinely special thing that this town should be proud of for a long time. When you've got an arm like that, the temptation is to let it fly, especially when the pressure's on. But football's a simple game more often than we make it. When something works, you keep doing it until they prove they can stop it. They never proved it. We just stopped asking.

That's the part that'll bother me all winter. Not that we lost — everybody loses eventually in a single-elimination bracket. It's that we had the answer in our hands, the same answer that worked in September, and we set it down.

Eight and two is a good season. It should have been better. And the reason it wasn't had nothing to do with the kids on that field and everything to do with a decision to abandon what got us there.

Get 'em next year. And when we do, let's remember what we're good at.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
# Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam – 14 Months, 140K Miles

**The Good:** This camera paid for itself. Had a lane change accident that wasn't my fault, footage was crystal clear on the front cam, and my insurance approved the claim in 9 days instead of the usual 6 weeks. That alone makes it worth having. Front and rear setup, easy to hardwire, and the video quality is solid in normal daylight conditions.

**The Bad:** Rear cam night footage gets grainy past 30 feet. If you're counting on it to catch details of tailgaters or late-night incidents behind you, don't expect much past that distance. It's there for proof you were hit, not for reading license plates in the dark.

**Real Issues:** The suction mount fell off twice during summer heat before I switched to the adhesive mount. Lost footage both times before I realized it had dropped. If you go that route, skip the suction cup entirely and go adhesive from day one. Also, the app requires WiFi to pull footage, which is basically useless at truck stops. I just pop the SD card out and use a reader on my laptop instead – way faster anyway.

**Bottom Line:** For $250-300, it's solid insurance against BS claims. The front camera is reliable and the build quality has held up fine at 140K miles. Rear camera is decent backup but won't win any awards for night performance. 

Would I buy it again? Yeah. The claim payout already made it a no-brainer investment. Just go adhesive mount from day one and don't expect miracles from the rear cam at night.

*Rating: 7.5/10 – Does the job when it counts*

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 dash cam — 14 month / 140k mile review**

Ran this thing since I bought the truck. 14 months, roughly 140,000 miles, mostly long haul. Here's the honest version.

**The good:** It paid for itself. Back in March I got sideswiped on I-80 by a four-wheeler who then tried to tell the cop I drifted into him. Pulled the card, handed over the clip, and my insurance had the claim approved in 9 days. Normally that nonsense drags out 6 weeks minimum. That one clip was worth more than the camera costs.

**The bad:**
- **Suction mount is junk.** Fell off twice last summer sitting in a parking lot in Texas heat. Not while driving, thank God, but it just let go. Switched to the adhesive mount and it's been solid since. Skip the suction cup entirely.
- **Rear cam at night.** Anything past 30 feet is grain city. You can tell a vehicle is there and roughly what it's doing, but you're not reading plates or getting a clean ID. Daytime is fine. If you're buying this mainly for rear night coverage, look elsewhere.
- **App requires wifi to pull footage.** Which is useless, because most truck stops have wifi that won't move a video file and half the time won't connect at all. I stopped fighting it. Pull the SD card, plug it into the laptop, done. Faster anyway.

**Bottom line:** For the money, it does the one job that actually matters — proving what happened. Front footage is clean, it's survived 140k of rough roads, and it saved me a six-week insurance fight. Just plan on the adhesive mount and the card reader, not the app.

b.text:
To the Editor,

I am not much of a writer, but I felt I had to say something about the plan to close our post office counter service. I drove the 38 miles of Route 4 for 22 years before I retired last year, so I know this town and the folks who live in it. 

The postal service claims the Kettle Falls branch is losing $40,000 a year, and they are using that as their excuse to shut the counter down. But anyone paying attention knows why the numbers look like that. They cut the counter hours to just 8 a.m. to noon.
