setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now

After six years shooting weddings almost entirely in the same metro area, I didn't expect to become a winter wedding person. I did. Actively.

I've shot 11 of them in the last two years, and I now tell couples who are flexible on dates to seriously consider it. Not because "weddings are beautiful year-round" — because winter gives you specific advantages you don't get in June.

First, the practical one: my winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for the couple. Same coverage, same albums, same me running around fixing your veil. It's just off-season, so I price it that way. If budget is part of why you're debating dates, that difference is real.

Second, the light. Everyone assumes summer = better photos. It's not. Give me the light through bare trees around 3pm in November over flat overcast June light any day. In June here, we get that bright white-gray sky that washes everything out at noon and then we’re racing the harsh evening sun. In November, the leaves are gone so the light actually comes through the branches instead of getting blocked, and by 3pm it's low, warm, and directional. It sculpts faces instead of flattening them. Some of my favorite portraits from the last two years were taken in 20 minutes in a park in November while everyone stayed warm in coats between shots.

Third, the day itself is calmer. In June, I pull up to a venue and I'm sharing the parking lot with 3 or 4 other vendors — another wedding flipping out of the ceremony space, a corporate event loading in, a DJ double-parked behind the caterer. We're all negotiating for the same patch of shade at the same golden hour. In winter, it's usually just us. Your venue team isn't exhausted from their third wedding that weekend. We get the good getting-ready room, not the overflow one. We can take our time and actually use the whole space for photos without waiting for another party to clear out.

Winter weddings aren't for everyone. It gets dark early, you need a coat plan, and you have to embrace it. But if you want better light for portraits, a less hectic venue, and a date that costs you about 30% less on photography — winter is worth a look.

If you're deciding between seasons, tell me what you're picturing and I'll tell you honestly what that date would look like to shoot.

b.text:
Let’s be real: winter weddings don’t usually get the same hype as June celebrations, but if you’re the one behind the camera, the season has some real advantages. Over the last two years, I’ve shot 11 of them, and a few patterns have become impossible to ignore.

First, there’s the budget. Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for the couple, and that’s not just a numbers game—it often means you can allocate more toward what actually matters to you, whether that’s a tighter guest list, better food, or putting money toward your honeymoon instead of peak-season markup.

Then there’s the light. I know “golden hour” gets thrown around a lot, but there’s something specific about that late afternoon light in November, filtering through bare trees around 3pm. It’s soft but directional, with way more contrast and depth than the flat, overcast glow you often get in June. Portraits come out with more dimension without needing as much artificial fill.

And logistically? January and February are dramatically quieter. In June, I’m often sharing parking lots, entrances, and even quiet moments with three or four other vendor teams. In winter, it’s just us. The venues are less crowded, the timeline is more flexible, and there’s genuinely less chaos running the show.

If you’ve been on the fence about timing, I’d encourage you to look at the calendar outside of May through September. You’ll likely get better light, a lower price tag, and a day that feels a lot less like a logistics puzzle.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
After roughly 200 interviews, one question has started to stand out to me:

“What was the last project your team tried that didn’t work?”

The strongest candidates don’t just ask what success looks like. They want to understand what happens when things go wrong.

In logistics, that’s worth knowing. A plan can look great in a meeting and fall apart on a warehouse floor.

The conversation might go something like this:

Candidate: “What’s a recent project that didn’t go to plan?”

Hiring manager: “We rolled out a scheduling change that was supposed to reduce overtime. It created coverage gaps instead, so we rolled it back.”

Candidate: “Who first flagged the gaps?”

Hiring manager: “The shift supervisors.”

Candidate: “And were those supervisors involved in designing the replacement?”

That follow-up is where it gets interesting.

They’re asking whether feedback travels upward. Whether the people doing the work get a say. Whether “we learned from it” actually means anything changed.

After nine years in recruiting, I’ve come to appreciate candidates who use the interview to assess us, too. They’re making a decision with consequences, not just trying to give the right answers.

And if we invite that kind of scrutiny, we need to be willing to answer honestly.

What would a candidate learn from your team’s last failed project?

b.text:
I’ve run around 200 interviews over the last few years, and by minute 40, most conversations sound identical. 

Candidates ask about the culture. They ask what a typical Tuesday looks like. They ask what success means in the first six months. 

All fine questions. But the candidates who end up being exceptional almost always ask a version of this instead:

"What was the last project your team rolled out that completely fell apart?"

A candidate for an operations lead role asked me this a few months back. 

I told her the truth. We spent four months piloting a new yard-management workflow across two of our distribution centers. On paper, it was supposed to cut dwell times. In reality, the drivers hated the handheld interface, the check-in bottlenecks got worse, and after six weeks of messy data, we pulled the plug. 

She didn’t ask about the tech stack. She asked: "What happened to the people who built it?"

I told her our VP sat the group down, ordered food, spent two hours dissecting why we didn't shadow the yard jockeys before writing the requirements, and then gave that exact same team the redesign project. Nobody got buried. Nobody was pushed out.

She nodded and said, "Good. I don't mind fixing broken processes, but I won't work somewhere where an honest miss gets someone scapegoated."

She accepted our offer two weeks later.

The best candidates aren't looking for a company where everything is perfect. They already know things break. What they're actually trying to find out is how your leadership behaves on the days you lose.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
**A $46,000 Difference**

This spring, I wrote a check to my crop insurance agent that was $46,000 larger than the one I wrote last year. That's the 22% base rate increase USDA put on prevented planting coverage in our region. I didn't change my operation. I didn't file a claim. My loss history didn't shift. The number just went up.

And wouldn't you know it — this was the spring it wouldn't stop raining. I got 60% of my corn and soybeans in the ground by the late May deadline. The other 40% never saw a planter. That's the exact reason prevented planting coverage exists, and the year I needed it most is the year the government decided it should cost 22% more.

Here's what the acreage cap does to a family operation. My policy stops covering prevented planting acres after a certain point, and that cap is the same whether you're a 2,500-acre family farm or a 25,000-acre operation. For a larger operation, the uncovered acres are a smaller slice of a much bigger pie. For us, every acre is counted. Four generations of my family have worked this ground. I don't have another county or another crop or another revenue stream to soak up the loss when the cap cuts off.

Senate Bill 214 fixes that cap. It's a straightforward change to the way prevented planting coverage is calculated, and it would mean family operations get the same level of protection as anyone else.

If you're reading this, please call your state legislator and tell them to vote yes on SB 214. We're not asking for a handout. We're asking for crop insurance that doesn't price the safety net out of reach right when it rains.

b.text:
**When the Rain Won't Stop, and the Bill Keeps Growing**

The USDA raised the prevented planting base rate 22% this year in our region. That's not a typo—twenty-two percent, in a single year. For me, that translated to roughly $46,000 in additional costs I didn't budget for and can't control.

This spring, it wouldn't stop raining. I'm not looking for sympathy—every farmer in this county knows what I'm talking about. But the facts are the facts: I could only get 60% of my acres planted before the late May deadline. That left 40% of my operation hitting the prevented planting program, and the premium hike hit right alongside it.

Here's what makes this worse for families like mine. The acreage caps don't scale with the size of your operation. On a 450-acre farm, losing a chunk of plantable acres pushes you up against that cap fast. When you're running 2,400 acres, you've got more room to absorb the hit proportionally. The way the system is structured, the smaller family farms carry a heavier burden percentage-wise. That's not a fair system. That's a system that's slowly squeezing us out.

There's a fix on the table: SB 214. It would revise the acreage cap so the program actually serves the family operations it's supposed to protect—not just the operations big enough to work around the rules.

I'm not asking for a handout. I'm asking for the rules to be fair. A 22% rate hike with no cap adjustment is a penalty on doing the right thing: trying to keep land in production, trying to keep this farm in the family, trying to be responsible stewards of the soil.

If you're reading this, whether you're a fellow farmer or someone in the statehouse who's never set foot in a field after rain, I'd ask you to look at the numbers. Forty-six thousand dollars is not a rounding error for an operation like mine. It's the difference between making ends meet and falling behind.

Support SB 214. The math doesn't lie, and neither does the mud.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
**Four Tries**

My first week in the ER, I thought I would be doing more. Instead I spent most of it standing next to people, or walking fast to get things.

The hand thing happened on my second day. A man came in with a cut on his forearm that needed to be cleaned out before they could close it. The doctor said it would sting, and it did, and the man's wife was stuck in traffic on the interstate. He kept looking at the door. I was standing there with nothing to do, so I asked if he wanted me to hold his hand. He said yes, kind of surprised, and I held it while they flushed the wound. He squeezed hard. I have small hands and his were big and cold, and I remember thinking it's strange that nobody teaches you this part. Nobody says, at some point you will stand there and let a stranger squeeze your hand and that will be the whole job. When his wife got there he let go and said thank you like I'd done something big. I hadn't. But it was the only useful thing I did that hour.

On Thursday there was a code. I was in the room when it started, and then a nurse pointed at me and said we needed gauze, so I went. The supply room is down the hall and around the corner, and while I was standing there counting out packages into my arms, I could hear them through the curtain. Counting. One, two, three, and somebody saying keep going. I stood in that hallway with my arms full and felt about as useless as a person can feel. I knew I couldn't be in there. I'm a first-year student. I'd have been in the way, and I know that. But hearing them count while I did something a stocker could do was hard. Later a nurse told me that the gauze I brought was what they used, and that during a code somebody has to get the supplies, and it might as well be somebody who runs fast. I'm still deciding how I feel about that.

Then there was the diabetic man with bad veins. He needed a blood draw, and the first try didn't work. Neither did the second. He was patient about it, which somehow made it worse. He told me all about his grandkids and how he used to work on boats, and he kept saying things like "you're doing fine" while I was very clearly not doing fine. Third try, nothing. I wanted to hand the needle to somebody else and go stand in the hall. My instructor said try once more, so I did, and on the fourth try I got it. I've never been so relieved by a tiny vial of blood. He said, "See, I told you," and I had to look away for a second.

What I'm learning is that nursing is a lot of small things that are not small to the person in the bed. Holding a hand. Running for gauze. Trying a fourth time on a vein that doesn't want to give. None of that shows up on a monitor, and none of it feels like what I imagined when I wrote my first essay about wanting to help people. It's smaller than that and also harder than that.

I want to stay in this. I want to get good enough that the fourth try is the first try, but I don't ever want to forget what it felt like to be the student standing in the hallway listening to people count. I think that's the version of a nurse I want to be. The one who stays in the room and holds on, and then goes and gets the gauze.

b.text:
I didn’t expect to learn so much in one week. My first clinical rotation in the emergency department moved faster than I could keep up. People came in needing help in ways I couldn’t predict, and I had to figure out how to stay focused without freezing. By the time Friday rolled around, I realized nursing isn’t just about following steps. It’s about showing up when people are scared, in pain, or just really tired. It started with a few quiet moments that stayed with me long after my shoes came off.

One afternoon, I helped clean a deep cut on an older man’s forearm. The nurse handled the irrigation and packing, but his wife was supposed to be there and got stuck in traffic. When it was time to position him, he glanced at me and asked if I could hold his hand. I pulled a chair closer. His grip was tight. I didn’t have a way to numb the sting or make the bleeding stop faster, so I just kept my hand firm under his and matched his breathing when he clenched his teeth. I stayed still until the bandage was secure. He let go slowly and said, “Appreciate you.” It wasn’t complicated, but it taught me that sometimes your whole job is just to be steady for someone else.

Later that same week, I was sent to the utility room to restock gauze while a code happened behind a curtain down the hall. I heard the monitor flatline before I heard them start talking. Then came the counting. “Twenty-four… twenty-five…” I stood there folding sterile packages, wishing I could pull the curtain back and assist, but I knew I wasn’t trained for that yet. You can’t guess your way through a code. I kept working, listening to the rhythm of their voices, feeling how heavy the air got in the hallway when they called it. I took a minute to reset my mind, wiped down the counter, and waited for my next assignment. That moment made it clear how much happens beyond my reach right now, and how hard I’ll have to push myself to earn the chance to step inside that circle.

The hardest lesson came from a diabetic patient whose veins had been damaged from years of draws. I tried three times. Three missed sticks. Each time, blood welled and then disappeared. My cheeks burned. I apologized every time, knowing I was adding stress to someone who was already having a rough day. He didn’t snap. He just rubbed his arm and muttered, “Fourth time’s the charm, right?” I relaxed my shoulders, checked the angle, and went slower. On the fourth attempt, the vein caught. I finished the draw quickly, applied pressure, and labeled the tubes. He gave me a short nod. No grand speech, just a quiet sign that I hadn’t walked away. Failure doesn’t usually look dramatic in nursing. It just looks like keeping your hands steady when you want to put them down.

Those three moments shaped more than my technical skills. They showed me what kind of nurse I’m trying to become. Someone who doesn’t run when things get loud, who understands that presence and persistence matter just as much as procedures, and who treats mistakes as practice instead of proof that she should quit. This scholarship would take a real weight off my shoulders as I finish my coursework and move into higher-level rotations. I’m not walking onto campus pretending I already know how to save lives. I’m just trying to show up, learn from every error, and build the kind of steady, dependable care that patients can count on. If you’re looking for someone willing to do the hard work, listen closely, and keep improving, that’s exactly what I’m ready to do. Thank you for your time and for supporting students who are just getting started.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6 Months Later

I’ve been using the Jarvik L2 as my full-time remote-work desk for six months now. I bought it myself, no review unit, no affiliate links. This is the desk I use for coding, video calls, writing, and occasionally eating lunch over my keyboard like a degenerate.

Short version: the Jarvik L2 is a good desk with a few annoying flaws. At the $549 sale price, I’d buy it again. At $749, I’d keep shopping.

## What I Like

### The motor is quiet and fast

This is the L2’s best feature. The height adjustment is noticeably quicker than my old desk, and the motor noise is low enough that I can adjust it during a call without sounding like a blender next to the mic.

It goes up/down smoothly under normal load. I usually raise it after lunch, lower it when I’m done for the day, and it doesn’t hesitate. For a desk I move a few times a day, that matters.

### The memory presets are convenient

There are preset buttons, and in theory they’re great. I use them daily. I don’t want to hold the button and eyeball the height every time.

In practice, they mostly work — but not perfectly. More on that below.

## What I Don’t Like

### It wobbles at full height when I type hard

This is the big one.

At sitting height, the desk feels fine. At a lower standing height, it’s mostly fine. But at my full standing height, there is noticeable side-to-side and front-to-back movement if I’m typing aggressively.

I’m not talking about gently resting my hands on the desk. I mean when I’m writing code quickly, hitting keys with actual force, or moving the mouse around during a frustrating debugging session, the monitor shifts just enough to be annoying.

It doesn’t feel unsafe. It doesn’t feel like the desk is going to collapse. But it feels less stable than I want from a desk at this price.

If you are a light typist, you may not care. If you are a mechanical-keyboard person who types like they’re mad at the compiler, you will notice.

My workaround: I lowered my standing height by about an inch. It helped, but I shouldn’t have to compromise ergonomics because the frame gets nervous at full extension.

### The memory presets drift about a centimeter

The presets are close, but they’re not consistent.

I have my standing height saved, and most days the desk stops roughly where I expect. But over the past few months, I’ve noticed it drifts by about a centimeter. Sometimes it’s slightly high. Sometimes slightly low. It’s not enough to make the desk unusable, but it’s enough that I end up micro-adjusting after every preset move.

That defeats part of the point of having presets.

If Jarvik fixed this with a firmware update or better calibration, I’d upgrade my opinion. As it stands, the presets are useful but not reliable enough to fully trust.

### The cable tray is garbage

I hate the cable tray.

It feels like an afterthought. It doesn’t hold enough, it doesn’t route cables cleanly, and it makes cable management feel worse than if I’d just used velcro ties and a power strip.

For a desk marketed to people who presumably own more than one electronic device, this is a miss.

I ended up removing it and using my own cable management underneath the desktop. If you buy the L2, do yourself a favor and skip the included tray unless you enjoy disappointment.

## Build Quality

The frame itself feels solid enough. The finish is fine. The desktop is decent, though I’d still recommend getting a desk mat if you write or type hard.

The controls are simple. The handset isn’t fancy, but it works. I don’t need Bluetooth, RGB, or a smartphone app to make my desk go up and down. I need it to go to the right height and stay there. The L2 mostly does that, with caveats.

## Who Should Buy It

Buy it if:

- You can get it on sale around $549
- You want a quiet, fast motor
- You need a desk for mixed sitting/standing throughout the day
- You don’t type like you’re punishing the keyboard
- You plan to use your own cable management

Skip it or look elsewhere if:

- You’re paying $749
- You need maximum stability at full standing height
- You want memory presets that are actually precise
- You expect the included cable tray to be useful

## Verdict

The Jarvik L2 is a solid midrange standing desk with a great motor and a few irritating execution problems.

At $549, those flaws are easier to accept. You’re getting good performance for the money, especially if you catch it on sale.

At $749, the wobble and preset drift become harder to ignore. For that much, I expect better stability and more consistent height memory.

Final rating: 7/10 at $549. 5.5/10 at $749.

b.text:
**6-Month Review: The Jarvik L2 Standing Desk**

I bought the Jarvik L2 in February - 60x30, laminate top, black frame - with my own money. No affiliate links here, nothing to sell you.

I'm a remote software engineer. This desk gets 9-10 hours a day, 5 days a week, dual 27" monitors on an arm, MacBook, heavy mechanical keyboard.

After 6 months of actual use:

**The motor is legitimately good.**

It's fast and quiet. Jarvik claims 1.4"/sec and that's about right - it goes from my sitting height (28.5") to standing (44.5") in ~11 seconds. And it's quiet enough that I can adjust it mid-Zoom call without muting. My old Flexispot sounded like a forklift. This one is just a low hum.

**It wobbles at full height.**

I'm 5'10" and I stand at 44.5 inches. At that height, if I'm really hammering on the keyboard or leaning to grab something, there is noticeable side-to-side wobble. The monitor shake is visible. At sitting height it's rock solid. At 40" it's fine. At full max height (47") it's borderline unusable for me if I'm typing hard. If you're over 6' and plan to stand tall all day, this is not the frame you want.

**The memory presets drift.**

I have preset 1 at 72cm and preset 2 at 113cm. After 2-3 weeks, preset 1 will stop at 71cm or 73cm. It's consistently off by about a centimeter. Not the end of the world, but annoying when you expect it to hit your exact ergonomic position every time. I've had to recalibrate it twice in 6 months by holding down+up until it resets.

**The cable tray is garbage.**

Throw it away. It's thin, stamped metal, too shallow to hold a power strip plus cables, and the included wood screws stripped out of the pre-drilled holes on day one. I replaced it with a $35 under-desk tray from Amazon that holds everything. For a company selling a $700+ desk, this tray is insulting.

**Verdict:**

At the $549 sale price I paid, it's a good desk. The motor alone makes it better than anything else in that price range.

At $749 full price? Absolutely not. For that money, buy a Uplift V2 or Fully Jarvis frame and get a more stable frame and presets that actually stay put.

If you can get it on sale and you're under 6 feet and don't mind fixing the cable management yourself, it's worth it. If you see it at $749, close the tab.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The couples who hand me a five-page shot list from Pinterest rarely end up with the photos they actually wanted. 

The ones who throw the list away? They get magic.

After eight years and nearly 300 weddings in the Texas Hill Country, I’ve seen this play out over and over: you can either perform for your wedding gallery, or you can live your wedding day. You can’t do both.

Take the Barrera wedding, for example. 

Thirty minutes before their outdoor ceremony, the sky opened up. Total downpour. The manicured lawn, the timeline, the planned backdrop—all gone. 

Instead of stressing over a checklist of missed photo ops, they looked at each other, laughed, and pivoted. We moved the entire setup under a massive, dripping pecan tree. 

Because they weren’t mentally tracking whether we got "Pose #14 by the arbor," they were completely dialed into the moment. When the hem of her dress soaked through with mud, she didn't care. When the wind blew the rain sideways during their vows, he just pulled her closer. 

The gallery from that afternoon remains one of my absolute favorites. Not because it was technically perfect—none of the original lighting setups worked—but because every single frame captured genuine, unfiltered emotion. 

To the couples currently planning: by all means, list out your family formal groupings so we don’t miss Grandma. 

Beyond that? Trust the vendor team you hired. 

When you free your photographer to watch for moments instead of hunting down clipboard items, and when you give yourself permission to just live the day as it unfolds, that’s when the real art happens. 

Ditch the list. Live the day. The photos will take care of themselves.

b.text:
**The Couples Who Ditch the Shot List Always End Up with the Best Photos**

I’ve shot over 250 weddings, and here’s a truth I’ve learned: the couples who trust the process—who let go of rigid shot lists and embrace the moment—always walk away with the most authentic, emotional, and *real* photos.

Take the Barrera wedding last spring. The forecast called for sunshine, but the skies opened up right as the ceremony was supposed to start. Instead of panicking, we pivoted—moving everything under a massive pecan tree. No shot list could’ve predicted that moment, but the photos we captured? Pure magic. The way the light filtered through the leaves, the laughter as guests huddled close, the raw joy on their faces—it was *them*. Not a checklist.

Weddings aren’t about ticking boxes. They’re about connection, spontaneity, and the unscripted moments that make your day uniquely yours. When you hire a photographer you trust, let them do what they do best: tell *your* story.

(And if it rains? Even better. Some of my favorite photos happened when plans changed.)

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
1. **Shut off the heat and let the system cool.**  
   Turn the thermostats down and switch off power to the boiler and circulator at the heating system’s service switch. Wait until the baseboards and piping have cooled before opening anything—hot boiler water can scald you.

   These steps are for **hot-water baseboard heating with manual bleeder valves**, not electric baseboards or steam heat.

2. **Find the bleeder valve on the first baseboard.**  
   Start with the unit closest to the boiler and work outward, unless your system’s instructions specify a different order. The bleeder is usually near one end of the baseboard, sometimes behind a removable end cover. It may have a small square fitting for a radiator key or a slot for a flathead screwdriver.

   **No bleeder valve? Don’t loosen a pipe fitting instead.** Some baseboard systems must be purged by heating zone using valves near the boiler. That’s a different procedure.

3. **Put a cup underneath the valve.**  
   Keep a towel handy, too. The first water out may be dirty, and a little can spray as the air escapes. Protect nearby flooring and trim before you start.

4. **Open the bleeder slowly.**  
   Use the correct radiator key or a screwdriver that fits the slot. Turn the bleeder counterclockwise just enough to let air escape—usually a small fraction of a turn. Do not remove the screw.

   A hiss means air is coming out. Leave the valve slightly open until the sputtering stops and you get a steady stream of water with no hissing.

5. **Close it snugly—not tightly.**  
   Turn the bleeder clockwise until the water stops. Don’t crank down on it. Overtightening can damage or crack the valve seat and leave you with a leak.

   Wipe the valve dry and check for drips. If it won’t seal with gentle pressure, don’t keep tightening it.

6. **Work through every unit and heating zone.**  
   Continue unit by unit, starting near the boiler and working outward. Include any basement baseboards with manual bleeders; don’t assume bleeding the upstairs units takes care of the whole house.

   **One mistake we see on cold-baseboard calls is stopping after the upstairs units.** Air often collects at high points, but it can also become trapped elsewhere in a heating loop. A separate basement zone may still need attention even after the upstairs heat improves.

7. **Check system pressure, then restart the heat.**  
   Bleeding releases some water along with the air, which can lower system pressure. Before restarting, check the boiler gauge against the cold-fill pressure specified for your system. If it’s below that range—or no water comes out of a bleeder—stop and have the pressure checked. Don’t adjust the fill valve or add water blindly.

   Restore power, raise the thermostats, and let each zone run. Check that the baseboards warm up and that every bleeder stays dry.

### Still have a cold baseboard?

If a zone stays cold, air keeps returning, or the boiler pressure keeps dropping, more bleeding may not solve it. A circulation problem, zone-valve issue, leak, or air-removal problem can cause similar symptoms.

Call us if you can’t find the bleeders, a valve is stuck or leaking, or a loop needs purging at the boiler. We’ll check the system and get the heat moving without turning a small problem into a water leak.

b.text:
1. **Turn off the boiler and circulator.** Let the system cool before you start—hot water can cause serious burns. If you’re not sure how to shut the system down safely, stop and call an HVAC professional.

2. **Find the bleeder valve** at the end of each baseboard unit. Put a cup or small container underneath it to catch water.

3. **Open the valve slowly** with a radiator key or, if it has a slot, a flathead screwdriver. You may hear air hissing. Keep the container in place until water flows steadily with no hissing.

4. **Close the valve snugly.** Don’t overtighten it; too much force can damage the valve seat.

5. **Repeat unit by unit, starting closest to the boiler and working outward.** Don’t skip the basement loop. One of the most common mistakes we see is bleeding only the upstairs baseboards, even though air is often trapped in the basement loop.

When you’re finished, turn the system back on and check that the baseboards are heating evenly. If a valve won’t close, water keeps leaking, or the system still has cold spots, have a qualified HVAC technician check it.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
Every day during fourth period, a collective anxiety builds. When the bell rings, it is a mad dash to the cafeteria—not just out of hunger, but out of a survival instinct to secure a plastic chair. Our school's lunch period has become a daily exercise in overcrowding. To solve this logistical bottleneck and grant upperclassmen a step toward independence, our school should implement an open-campus lunch policy for juniors and seniors. This policy is not just a student wishlist item; it is a practical solution backed by spatial reality, strong student consensus, and the proven success of our neighboring districts.

The most immediate argument for an open campus is simple math. Our cafeteria is officially rated to seat 220 people. However, during our designated lunch wave, there are currently 340 students trying to eat, socialize, and decompress. This leaves over one hundred students displaced every single day. Teenagers are forced to eat sitting on hallway floors, crowded on stairwells, or crammed into classroom doorways. This is not only uncomfortable and noisy, but it also creates a safety hazard and a supervision nightmare for staff. By allowing juniors and seniors—the oldest, most responsible segment of this wave—the option to leave campus for lunch, we would immediately alleviate this pressure, bringing the cafeteria back down to a manageable, safe capacity.

Furthermore, there is an overwhelming demand for this change among the student body, reflecting a readiness for greater responsibility. In a survey I conducted of 80 students at our school, 71 were in favor of an open-campus policy. This represents nearly 89% of the surveyed population. While critics might dismiss this as teenagers simply wanting to escape school grounds, the reality is that juniors and seniors are at a transitional stage in their lives. We are preparing for college and the workforce, environments where we will be expected to manage our own time, logistics, and safety. Giving upperclassmen the agency to choose where they eat is a small, controlled way to foster that necessary maturity. 

The primary opposition to an open campus usually centers on reliability, with opponents worrying that students will not make it back in time for fifth period. Fortunately, we do not have to guess how this policy would play out in reality; we can look to our neighbors. Three nearby districts—Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—already allow open-campus lunches for their upperclassmen. According to their published district statistics, none of these schools experienced a rise in tardiness after implementing the policy. When students are trusted with a privilege, they respect it, knowing that irresponsible behavior will result in losing their off-campus access. 

Ultimately, transitioning to an open-campus lunch policy is a win-win scenario for both the administration and the student body. It resolves a physical capacity crisis in our cafeteria without requiring a single dollar of construction budget, matches the overwhelming desire of the student population, and carries zero statistical risk of increased tardiness. It is time for our school to trust its juniors and seniors, ease the lunchtime crowd, and open the doors.

b.text:
Open Campus Lunch Should Be an Option for Juniors and Seniors

By junior year, most of us already drive, hold jobs, and manage our own schedules after school. We are still treated like we cannot be trusted to leave campus for forty minutes and come back. Our school should allow open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. Nearby districts already do it without a tardiness problem, most students here want it, and our cafeteria cannot actually hold the lunch wave it is supposed to serve.

Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all let upperclassmen leave for lunch. Their published numbers do not show tardiness going up after the policy started. That matters more than a vague worry that “kids will not come back.” Those are not distant schools with totally different students. They are nearby districts dealing with the same traffic, the same bell schedules, and the same kinds of teenagers. If open campus created a wave of late returns, it would show up in those reports. It has not.

The other practical problem is space. Our cafeteria seats 220 people. The lunch wave I am in has about 340 students. That is not a small squeeze at the edges. It means a large share of the wave has nowhere to sit, so people end up on the floor, in the hallway, or standing with a tray. Opening campus would not empty the building. Plenty of students would still buy lunch or stay with friends. It would take pressure off a room that is already too small for the schedule we run.

I also asked people. Out of 80 students I surveyed at our school, 71 said they were in favor of open campus for juniors and seniors. A survey of 80 is not the whole student body, and I am not pretending it is. It is still a clear majority among the students I actually talked to, not a guess about what “everyone” wants. When the people who would use the policy are that strongly for it, the burden should be on the school to explain why the current rule is better, not on students to prove they deserve a normal lunch.

The main objection is safety and supervision. Teachers and administrators worry that students will get in accidents, skip the rest of the day, or cause problems off campus that the school then has to answer for. Those are real concerns. They are also the same concerns Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade already manage, and their tardiness numbers have not risen. Open campus does not have to mean no rules. Juniors and seniors could need a parent permission form, a clean attendance record, and a clear consequence for coming back late. Freshmen and sophomores could stay on campus. The choice is not between total freedom and the system we have now.

Right now we are packing 340 students into a room built for 220 and telling upperclassmen they cannot leave, even though three nearby districts already let them and have not seen tardiness climb. Most of the students I asked want the option. Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors is a reasonable change, and the school should try it.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
**Submitted Testimony — Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Dear Members of the City Council,

My name is [Name], and I own [shop name], a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I'm writing to ask you to vote against the proposal to raise downtown meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour.

That is not a modest adjustment. It is a tripling — a 200% increase — and it will land squarely on the people who keep downtown running: customers making short, small, everyday stops.

Start with my customers. The average visit to my shop is 22 minutes. A coffee, maybe a bag of beans, a quick hello. Under the current rate, 50 cents buys the hour, and the hour covers that visit comfortably — cheap enough that nobody thinks twice about stopping in. At $1.50, that same 22-minute errand costs three times as much before my customer has spent a single dollar with me. For a regular who stops in five mornings a week, parking goes from $2.50 a week to $7.50 — an extra $260 a year for the exact same cup of coffee. People won't experience that as parking policy. They'll experience it as a reason to go somewhere else.

And they will go somewhere else. I know, because I've measured it.

In 2019, when [neighboring town] raised its meter rates, I tracked my own register for six weeks after the change and compared it against the weeks just before. Foot traffic dropped 18%. I'm not an economist — I'm a shopkeeper with six weeks of actual transactions, counted at my own till. An independent shop does not absorb an 18% drop in foot traffic and carry on as usual. Numbers like that are the difference between a business that anchors a block and a vacant storefront that doesn't.

Now weigh that against what this increase would actually accomplish. According to the city's own report, meter revenue covers just 4% of the downtown budget. Even if every meter stayed occupied exactly as often as it does today — which my data says it won't — tripling the rate moves that figure to roughly 12%. If usage falls anywhere near the 18% I measured, you're under 10%. So the proposal on the table is this: impose a 200% price increase on the customers of every small business downtown, in exchange for a single-digit dent in the budget. That doesn't solve anything. It shifts a cost onto the people least able to absorb it, in service of a gap the city's own numbers say this cannot close.

Downtown's real product isn't parking. It's the ease of parking for pocket change, running in for 22 minutes, and leaving feeling like the trip was simple. Triple the friction and people will get their coffee at a drive-through with a free lot — and once a habit moves, it rarely comes back.

Vote no on this increase. If the council believes downtown needs more revenue, there are fairer places to find it than a 22-minute errand. I can tell you from 18% worth of experience how this one ends.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this for the record.

Respectfully,
[Name]
[Shop name], Main Street

b.text:
**Testimony on the Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Submitted by [Your Name], Owner, [Coffee Shop Name], [Address] Main Street

Members of the City Council,

Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony on the proposal to raise downtown parking meter rates from $0.50 to $1.50 per hour. I own and operate [Coffee Shop Name] on Main Street, and I urge the council to reject this increase. I want to make that case with specific numbers, not general warnings.

**What happened in a nearby town**

In 2019, [Neighboring Town] raised its downtown meter rates. For six weeks after that increase took effect, I tracked my register data closely. Over that period, foot traffic dropped 18 percent.

I recognize this is one business's data from one six-week period, not a formal study. But for a small shop, an 18 percent drop in customers is not a rounding error. It decides whether we keep staff on the schedule, whether we can cover rent, and whether we stay open. The council is being asked to approve an increase larger than a modest adjustment. Going from $0.50 to $1.50 *triples* the hourly rate, a 200 percent increase. If a smaller change next door produced an 18 percent drop, I have serious concerns about what tripling the rate will do here.

**The current rate already works for short visits**

My customers stay an average of 22 minutes. They come in, order, maybe sit for a few minutes, and leave. Under the current one-hour minimum, that visit is already covered. The existing system is working for exactly the kind of quick, frequent trips that keep Main Street businesses alive.

Under the proposed rate, that same 22-minute visit would cost $1.50 in parking instead of $0.50. The customer is not staying any longer or using any more of the city's parking. They are simply paying three times as much for the same short stop. For a customer deciding whether to grab a coffee downtown or drive to a chain with a free parking lot, that difference matters.

**The revenue does not justify the risk**

According to the city's own report, meter revenue covers only 4 percent of the downtown budget. This increase is being presented as a way to support downtown, but parking meters are a small share of how downtown is actually funded. Even with a higher rate, meter revenue would remain a minor part of the budget. And if fewer people come downtown, the city loses more than meter revenue. It loses the sales tax, the activity, and the healthy storefronts that the downtown budget exists to support.

Put simply, this proposal asks small businesses to absorb a real risk to their customer base in exchange for a modest change to a revenue source that covers 4 percent of the budget.

**My request**

I ask the council to:

1. **Reject the increase to $1.50 per hour** as currently proposed.
2. **Study the likely impact on foot traffic before any rate change**, using data from downtown businesses and comparable towns, including [Neighboring Town]'s experience in 2019.
3. **Consider alternatives** if additional revenue is needed, such as a smaller increase, a free or reduced-cost first 30 minutes for short visits, or higher rates limited to long-term or peak-demand spaces.

Downtown works because people can stop in quickly and easily. My customers average 22 minutes, the current rate covers them, and the revenue at stake is 4 percent of the downtown budget. The numbers do not support tripling the cost of a quick trip to Main Street.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Respectfully,

[Your Name]
[Coffee Shop Name]
[Address]
[Phone / Email]

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
## A Better Lunch Policy for Juniors and Seniors

By junior year, students are expected to make decisions about college, jobs, and their futures. Yet during lunch, they are not allowed to decide where to eat. Our school should allow juniors and seniors to leave campus during their assigned lunch period, as long as they return on time and follow clear rules. An open-campus lunch policy would help address cafeteria overcrowding while giving older students a reasonable amount of independence.

The strongest reason to change the policy is that our cafeteria cannot seat everyone assigned to eat there. It seats 220 students, but our lunch wave includes 340. That leaves 120 students without a cafeteria seat if everyone needs one at the same time. Keeping students on campus does not solve that mismatch; it simply requires them to deal with it. Allowing juniors and seniors to eat elsewhere would reduce demand for cafeteria seating. Open-campus lunch would not guarantee that overcrowding disappears, since not every eligible student would leave, but it would give students an option that the current policy denies them.

Nearby districts also show that open-campus lunch does not necessarily lead to attendance problems. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade already allow it, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. These results do not guarantee that our school would have exactly the same experience, but they challenge the assumption that students who leave for lunch will routinely return late. Rather than rejecting the idea because of what might happen, our school should consider what has happened in districts that have already tried it.

Students at our school clearly want this change. In a survey I conducted of 80 students, 71 supported open-campus lunch—nearly 89 percent of those surveyed. This survey does not represent every student, and popularity alone is not enough to make a policy a good idea. Still, it shows substantial interest among the students who responded. When a proposed change addresses an existing space problem and has strong student support, it deserves serious consideration.

Concerns about safety and responsibility are reasonable. Students leaving campus could encounter traffic risks, and some might misuse the privilege or return late. Those concerns justify safeguards, not an automatic ban. The school could require parent permission and make open-campus lunch conditional on returning before the next class begins. Students who repeatedly violate the rules could lose the privilege. A trial period would also let administrators track tardiness and cafeteria crowding before deciding whether to continue the policy. This would allow the school to judge the change by its actual results.

Open-campus lunch is not a request to remove all supervision or excuse students from class. It is a limited change during a scheduled break, aimed at students nearing graduation. Our cafeteria is already overcrowded, student interest is strong, and nearby districts provide evidence that the policy can work without increasing tardiness. With clear expectations and a trial period, our school can give juniors and seniors more independence while holding them accountable for how they use it.

b.text:
Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors

Every day, 340 students are assigned to a lunch wave in a cafeteria that seats 220. By the time the line moves, there is nowhere left to sit. That daily squeeze is not just annoying; it is evidence that our current lunch system does not fit the students it is supposed to serve. Our school should adopt an open campus lunch policy for juniors and seniors. Doing so would relieve overcrowding, follow the proven example of nearby districts, and respect the clear wishes of the student body.

The clearest argument for open campus is space. Our cafeteria has 220 seats, but 340 students are assigned to that lunch wave. That leaves about 120 students without a seat. Lunch should give students a chance to eat and recharge, not force them to stand in a crowded room or rush because there is nowhere to stay. Not everyone in that wave is a junior or senior, but if even some of them could leave campus, the crowd would shrink. Even a partial reduction would make the lunch period less packed and more manageable.

The nearby districts of Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade already allow open campus lunch, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. That point directly answers the most common objection: if students are allowed to leave, will they come back on time? In three comparable districts, the answer is yes. Their experience suggests that open campus does not create automatic chaos; it works when the policy is clear and the students are trusted.

The students at our school have also shown that they want this change. In a survey of 80 students, 71 said they favor open campus lunch. That is nearly 89 percent. Juniors and seniors are the students closest to graduation, and many already balance jobs, driving, college applications, and other adult responsibilities. Allowing them to leave campus for lunch is not a radical gift; it is a reasonable step toward treating them like the young adults they are becoming.

Some people will still worry about safety and supervision. Those concerns make sense. But the tardiness fear is not supported by the data from Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade, whose published numbers show no increase. Safety concerns can be handled with rules: limit the privilege to juniors and seniors in good standing, require sign-out, and set a clear return time with consequences for abuse. Open campus would not mean students can wander wherever they want. It would mean a supervised privilege with boundaries.

Our school does not need to keep forcing 340 students into a room built for 220. The nearby districts have shown that open campus can work, and the students have shown that they want it. Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors is a practical fix for an overcrowded lunch period and a fair way to recognize student responsibility. We are old enough to handle it, and it is time our school trusted us to do so.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/ I made a pricing mistake at Tallyup.

I raised prices 40% on everyone overnight.

Within a week, we lost 30 of our 140 customers.

Here’s what happened, and what I changed:

2/ The mistake wasn’t just the increase.

It was the surprise.

Customers had signed up under one expectation, then woke up to a different one.

No warning. No transition. No chance to ask questions.

3/ When you raise prices on existing customers without context, it can feel like a broken promise.

Especially with gym owners. Retention is personal to them, and Tallyup is supposed to help with that.

4/ What I changed:

- No more overnight pricing decisions
- Separate new customers from existing customers
- Give advance notice
- Explain the reason before the change
- Make it easy for customers to reach out and talk

5/ The lesson: pricing is not just a spreadsheet decision.

It’s trust, timing, and communication.

A price change can be reasonable and still be delivered badly.

6/ I’m building Tallyup in public, and this is part of it.

I’d rather share the mistake than pretend we got everything right.

If you’re thinking about raising prices, don’t surprise the people who already believed in you.

b.text:
I made a massive pricing mistake with Tallyup recently.

I raised prices by 40% on everyone, overnight.

The result? We had 140 customers. Within a week, 30 of them cancelled.

Here is what went wrong, what I changed, and what I learned the hard way 🧵

2/ The logic in my head seemed sound:
• Tallyup drives clear ROI by helping gym owners track retention.
• I felt we were underpriced for the value we provided.

So instead of thinking it through, I flipped the switch and applied a 40% increase across the board. No warning. No transition period.

3/ Gym owners run on tight margins and trust. 

Springing a 40% jump overnight didn't feel like a normal software update to them—it felt like a breach of trust from a tool they relied on.

The cancellations started rolling in immediately. Losing 30 customers in 7 days was a brutal wake-up call.

4/ What I changed to fix it:

1. Swallowed my pride and reached out directly to every customer who cancelled to apologize.
2. Grandfathered all existing customers back to their original rate.
3. Kept the higher price point, but applied it strictly to new signups only.

5/ The takeaway for other indie founders:

Raising prices isn't the mistake. Most of us undercharge anyway.

The mistake was punishing the early adopters who took a chance on me when the product was barely functional. 

If you're going to raise prices, grandfather your early champions or give them plenty of warning. Don't pull the rug overnight.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
The best candidates I've interviewed ask about our last failed project.

Not "what's the culture like." Not "what does success look like in 90 days." They ask what we got wrong, and then they sit with the answer.

Last month a warehouse systems candidate did this. I told him about a routing rollout that looked clean in the pilot and fell apart the week we hit peak volume — drivers improvising around a tool that couldn't handle exceptions, supervisors papering over it so the dashboard stayed green. He didn't jump to a fix. He asked who noticed first, whether anyone got blamed, and what we changed in how we roll things out now.

That's the tell. People who have shipped hard things know failure is where the real process lives. They're checking whether we can talk about ours without flinching — because that's the team they'll have to tell the truth to when their own project breaks.

b.text:
After roughly 200 interviews, I’ve noticed that some of the strongest candidates ask a version of the same question:

“What’s the last project that didn’t work out?”

One candidate asked me this for an operations role. I told them about a new scheduling process we rolled out at one site. It looked good on paper, but we hadn’t spent enough time with the dispatchers who would use it. Within weeks, people were back to the old process.

The candidate didn’t ask who was responsible. They asked, “How did you find out it wasn’t working, and what changed after that?”

That turned into a much more useful conversation than another round of “tell me about the culture.”

A failed project tells a candidate something a polished success story can’t: whether people can raise problems early, admit what they missed, and change course.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
When the Better Team Loses

Let's get this out of the way first: this was a good season. Eight wins. A school record for Dez Kowalski, who threw for 2,340 yards this year and made Friday nights a lot more fun to watch. That's real, and it shouldn't get buried under how the year ended.

But I'm not going to sit here and write a nice, tidy season wrap-up like the scoreboard in the second round didn't happen, because it did, and it's still bugging me a week later.

Here's the thing that gets me: this team lost to an opponent they beat by 20 points back in Week 3. Same team. Same coaching staff. And down by three in the second half — three points, in a game they were controlling on the ground — the offense stopped running the ball.

Not because it wasn't working. It was working. That's what makes it maddening instead of just disappointing. When the run game is moving the chains and you're down a single score, you don't need to get cute. You don't need to prove anything. You need to keep doing the thing that's working until they stop it. Instead, the offense drifted away from it, started leaning on the pass in obvious passing situations, and let a defense that had spent a whole half chasing tailbacks suddenly pin its ears back and tee off on Kowalski.

I get the instinct. When you fall behind, the coach's brain screams "we need points fast," and the pass looks like the quicker route there. But three points isn't a two-score deficit. Three points is one good drive. One good, patient, run-it-until-they-stop-it drive. This team had exactly that drive in its bag all night and put it away in favor of hope.

That's not a talent problem. It's not a Kowalski problem — the kid deserved better play-calling support in that stretch, not less of it. It's a discipline problem, and discipline problems are the kind you can actually fix.

So no, I'm not writing the "great year, on to next season" column, at least not only that one. This team was good enough to still be playing right now. They didn't lose to a better team. They lost to a version of a team they'd already beaten, and they helped them do it by walking away from what was working.

Next year's team will have the tools to be even better. Here's hoping somebody in that coaches' booth remembers this game the next time it's a one-score contest and the run is humming. Trust it. Ride it. Make the other team prove they can stop it before you decide to stop doing it yourself.

b.text:
# One Game Away From Something Special

There's a difference between a disappointing loss and a frustrating one. Friday night's playoff exit was both.

The 8-2 season will look fine in the record book. Dez Kowalski's 2,340 passing yards are legit—a school record that reflects a kid who worked for it. But we all know what this team could've been, and that's what stings.

They beat Riverside 34-14 in week three. Riverside came into Friday's rematch as a two-seed, and our guys had every reason to believe they could do it again. They were down three at halftime. They had momentum. They had a running game that was moving the ball.

And then they got cute.

In the second half, the offense abandoned the run almost entirely. I watched them abandon what was working—what *was winning*—to let Kowalski sling it around. Maybe the coaches got spooked. Maybe they thought Riverside had figured something out. Whatever the reason, it looked like panic, not adjustment.

The kids fought back and made it close, but you don't recover from that kind of self-inflicted wound against good teams.

This group had the talent to make a deep run. They proved it in week three. They proved it most of the season. But making the state tournament and making a run are two different things, and on Friday night, they chose the wrong identity when it mattered most.

That's the one that'll stick around.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
You'll need a bleeder key or small flathead screwdriver, a cup, and an old towel.

1. Shut the boiler and circulator off first. You don't want hot water moving while you're opening the valves. Let it cool for 20-30 minutes if it's been running.

2. Start with the baseboard unit closest to the boiler and work your way out. That's usually in the basement.

3. On the end of each baseboard unit, you'll find a small bleeder valve. Hold your cup right underneath it and have the towel handy — water will spit once the air clears.

4. Open it slow, just a quarter turn. You'll hear hissing as the air comes out. Leave it alone until that stops and you get a steady little stream of water with no sputter.

5. Close it snug. Don't crank on it. Overtighten it and you'll crack the valve seat and it'll drip all winter.

6. Go unit by unit through the house in order.

The thing I see on most of our cold radiator calls: folks only bleed the upstairs units because that's where they feel the cold. Don't skip the basement loop. That's usually where the air is actually trapped, and if you leave it there it'll just work its way back upstairs.

If you bleed everything and a unit is still cold top to bottom, or you're not getting any water out at all, shut it back down and call us out — that's usually pressure or a stuck zone valve, not just air.

b.text:
# How to Bleed Air From Your Baseboard Radiators

Air gets trapped in your heating system every time the boiler cycles or water levels drop. When that air settles in your baseboard units, whole sections of the radiator stay cold while others heat up fine. The good news is bleeding them out takes maybe 20 minutes and costs you nothing.

## What You'll Need

- Flathead screwdriver or baseboard radiator key (the key works better and costs about $5)
- Small cup or container
- Towel or rag

## The Steps

**1. Turn off your boiler and circulator pump.** Let the system sit for a few minutes so the water settles.

**2. Locate the bleeder valve.** It's a small screw on the end cap of each baseboard unit, usually at the top. Most look like a tiny brass fitting.

**3. Start with the unit closest to your boiler.** This matters—you're working with gravity and water pressure, so starting nearest the source gets better results.

**4. Cup your hand underneath the valve.** You're about to release water, so catch it or put a small container there.

**5. Open the valve slowly.** Turn it counterclockwise a quarter-turn or less. You'll hear hissing—that's the air escaping. Keep it open until water flows out steady and the hissing stops completely. This usually takes 10-30 seconds per unit.

**6. Close it snug.** Turn clockwise until it's finger-tight. Don't crank it—the valve seat is brass and cracks easily if you overtighten.

**7. Move to the next baseboard unit.** Work your way through the house, always progressing outward from the boiler.

**8. Don't skip the basement.** This is where most homeowners mess up. Air rises, but heavy air and sediment settle in lower loops. If your upstairs radiators are hot and your basement units are still cold after bleeding them, you've found your problem.

**9. Turn the boiler and circulator back on.** Listen for normal cycling sounds. The system should quiet down after a minute or two.

## When to Call a Pro

If you've bled every unit including everything in the basement and you still have cold sections, you might have a circulation problem or a leak somewhere. That's when you want us out there to take a look.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# 6 Months with the Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: The Good, the Bad, and the Drift

I’ve spent the last six months working 8–10 hour days at the Jarvik L2 as a remote software engineer. My setup isn’t lightweight: a 34-inch ultrawide, a 27-inch vertical secondary monitor, studio monitors, and a heavy custom mechanical keyboard with tactile switches. 

No sponsored units, no affiliate links. Here is how the L2 actually holds up after half a year of daily abuse.

---

### The Good: Motor Speed and Noise
The dual-motor system is easily the strongest part of this desk. It moves at roughly 1.5 inches per second and is whisper-quiet. I frequently adjust heights while unmuted on Zoom calls, and nobody has ever commented on background motor whine. 

Transitions are smooth with soft starts and stops, meaning coffee mugs don’t slosh when the desk comes to a halt. In terms of raw lifting mechanics, it handles my roughly 45-lb payload without a hint of strain.

---

### The Bad: Stability at Full Extension
I’m 5'10", which puts my ideal standing height around 44 inches. If you raise the L2 above 42 inches, front-to-back stability degrades quickly. 

If you are a heavy typist or bottom out your mechanical switches, expect monitor wobble. With my monitors mounted on heavy gas-spring arms, aggressive typing causes a distinct, distracting visual oscillation. Lowering the desk to sitting height (28 inches) eliminates the issue entirely—it’s rock-solid on the floor. But at standing height, the crossbar-less two-stage leg design simply can’t fight physics.

---

### The Annoying: Memory Preset Drift
The handset allows you to save four height presets. However, over the course of 3 to 4 weeks, the actual physical height drifts away from the digital readout by about a full centimeter (roughly 0.4 inches). 

I only noticed because my standing elbow angle started feeling off. Putting a tape measure to the desktop confirmed it: the display read 44.0", but the desk was sitting at 44.4". You have to run the manual reset procedure (holding the down button until it hits bottom and beeps) monthly to recalibrate the baseline. It’s an annoying firmware quirk on a desk in this price bracket.

---

### The Useless: The Stock Cable Tray
Don't factor the included cable management tray into your purchasing decision. It's stamped sheet metal, roughly 2 inches deep, and completely inadequate for real-world cable loads. 

Between two power bricks (laptop dock and monitors), a power strip, and standard display/power cabling, the stock tray bowed instantly and dumped cables out the back. Strip it off immediately and budget $30 for an aftermarket J-channel or wire mesh under-desk basket.

---

### The Verdict

* **At the $549 sale price:** **Buy it.** You get a fast, quiet dual-motor base with a decent laminate top that outclasses most generic Amazon standing desks. Just buy a real cable tray and don’t pound on your keyboard.
* **At the $749 MSRP:** **Hard pass.** For $750+, you should expect three-stage legs with zero wobble at 45 inches and a control board that doesn’t lose its calibration. At full retail, look at the Deskhaus Apex or an Uplift V2 Commercial instead.

b.text:
# The Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6-Month Review (No Affiliate Links)

Six months ago, my lower back staged a mutiny and I finally bought a standing desk. After falling down the Reddit rabbit hole, I bought the Jarvik L2 (60"x30", bamboo top, black frame) with my own money. There are no affiliate links in this post. 

As a remote software engineer, I spend 8 to 10 hours a day at this thing. It holds two 27-inch monitors on a dual VESA mount, a 16-inch MacBook Pro, a heavy aluminum mechanical keyboard, and a Graveyard of Half-Drunk Coffee Mugs. 

Here is how the Jarvik L2 actually holds up after half a year of daily abuse.

### The Motors: Fast and Shockingly Quiet
Jarvik claims a lift speed of 1.5 inches per second and a noise level under 45 decibels. In my testing, this is actually accurate. 

It transitions from my sitting height (28.5") to my standing height (42.5") in about 9 seconds. The dual motors produce a low, pleasant hum—quiet enough that I regularly adjust the desk while unmuted on Zoom standups and nobody notices. There is no jerky acceleration at the start or hard clunk at the end; it ramps up and down smoothly. After roughly 300 cycles over six months, the motors sound identical to day one.

### The Keypad Bug: Preset Drift
The 4-button memory keypad is tactile and the OLED screen turns off after a few seconds so it isn't an eyesore. However, the firmware has an annoying quirk: the presets drift.

I have Preset 1 locked to 28.5" and Preset 2 locked to 42.5". Every three weeks or so, I’ll hit Preset 2 and notice my wrists are angled weirdly. The display will read 42.5", but taking a tape measure to the floor reveals the desk is actually sitting at 42.1" or 42.9". It drifts by up to a centimeter over time. Doing a hard reset (holding the down button at the lowest point for 10 seconds) fixes the calibration, and I suspect it’s triggered by the anti-collision sensor getting micro-tripped when I lean on the desk while it's moving. It’s not a dealbreaker, just a stupid problem to have on a digital controller.

### Stability: The "Angry Typing" Test
Sitting height stability is a 10/10. It’s a tank. You could probably stand on it.

Standing height is a different story. Because I’m 5'9" and use a thick anti-fatigue mat, I run the desk at 42.5 inches—getting pretty close to its 48-inch max height. 

For normal work, it’s fine. If I’m casually browsing documentation or using my mouse, it feels solid. However, when I’m deep in a debugging session or hammering out a grumpy PR comment on my mechanical keyboard, my monitors noticeably oscillate. It’s a front-to-back wobble, not side-to-side, caused by the tolerances in the two-stage telescopic legs. 

If you are over 6 feet tall and plan to max this desk out at 46"+, the wobble is going to drive you insane unless you mount your monitors to the wall. If you’re under 5'10", it’s tolerable, though far from rock-solid.

### The Cable Management Tray is Garbage
Do not buy the $49 "upgrade" cable management tray, and if it comes bundled for free like mine did, throw it straight into the recycling bin. 

It is a flimsy piece of thin, stamped sheet metal held to the underside of the desk by two wood screws on one side, creating a hinge. Because it’s only anchored fully on one side, the moment you put an actual surge protector and two monitor power bricks in it, the whole tray sags at a 30-degree angle. It looks terrible from across the room and barely fits a standard Belkin power strip. 

I ripped it off in week two and replaced it with a $25 StarTech J-channel raceway and some 3M Dual Lock tape to mount my power strip directly to the underside of the bamboo. Save yourself the headache and do the same.

### The Desktop
Briefly: the 1-inch thick carbonized bamboo top is great. It survived a direct spill of boiling hot tea without warping or staining, and my heavy monitor C-clamp hasn't indented the wood at all. The pre-drilled inserts lined up perfectly with the frame during assembly, EXCEPT for the keypad screws, which you have to drive into the raw bamboo yourself. Bring a power drill; doing that with the included Allen wrench/screwdriver combo will give you blisters.

### The Verdict
Jarvik plays the fake-MSRP game. The L2 is "listed" at $749, which is a joke. At $749, you are encroaching on Uplift V2 and Deskhaus territory—desks with vastly superior stability at max height and better accessories. Do not pay $749 for this desk.

However, Jarvik runs a "flash sale" roughly every three weeks that drops the L2 to **$549**. 

At $549 (shipped), the math changes. You are getting a fast, quiet dual-motor frame and a genuinely durable bamboo top for the price that competitors charge for chipped-edge laminate and loud single motors. 

**Buy it if:** You are under 5'10", you catch it on sale for $549, and you are willing to DIY your own cable management. 
**Skip it if:** You are tall enough to need the desk near its max height, you type like you're mad at your keyboard, or the site is currently charging full retail.
