setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
Roughly 200 interviews in, and the question that tells me the most about a candidate isn't one I ask. It's the one they ask me.

The best candidates ask about our last failed project.

Not "what does success look like in 90 days." Not "how would you describe the culture." Something more like: "What's the last project here that actually failed — and what happened after?"

I watched this play out last year with an ops manager candidate. When she asked, the hiring manager gave her the honest version: the WMS go-live we rolled back after five weeks, a peak season run on spreadsheets and prayer. She didn't flinch. Two follow-ups.

First: "Did you ever figure out why it failed, or just that it failed?" We had, eventually — we'd sequenced the cutover for a slow month and never stress-tested peak volume. She nodded like she'd heard that story before.

Then: "Are the people who ran it still here?"

Two of the three leads are. One of them runs the site now. When he said that, she visibly relaxed and told us she'd watched an entire team get quietly managed out after a similar failure at her last company.

That's when it clicked for me. She wasn't being negative. She was checking whether failure here counts as tuition or a mark against you.

Candidates who ask about your wins are being polite. Candidates who ask about your failures are doing real due diligence.

And if a company can't name a failure? That's the answer.

b.text:
After sitting in ~200 interviews, I’ve noticed a pattern:

The best candidates ask about our last failed project.

Not in a “gotcha” way. They’re trying to understand how the company handles reality.

One candidate asked me:

“What’s something the team tried, learned didn’t work, and then changed because of that?”

I told her about a warehouse staffing model we rolled out that looked great on paper but struggled during peak season because we hadn’t tested it against the way supervisors actually assign daily work.

Her next question was even better:

“Who was responsible for pulling it back, and what changed before the next rollout?”

That’s when I knew she was serious.

She wasn’t trying to catch us off guard. She was trying to figure out whether leaders here admit mistakes, how quickly teams course-correct, and whether lessons actually stick.

A lot of candidates ask about growth, culture, and expectations.

The ones who stand out ask about failure.

Because every company has it. The good ones don’t hide it.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
**Testimony Regarding the Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Members of the Council, my name is [Name], and I own [Coffee Shop Name] on Main Street. I have run this business for [number] years. I am here to ask you not to raise downtown meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour.

The proposal would triple the hourly rate. For my customers, the change is larger than the percentage suggests. Most people who stop in for coffee stay about 22 minutes. Under the current rate, a 22-minute visit costs 50 cents, which is covered by the one-hour minimum. Under the proposed rate, the same visit costs $1.50. That is an added dollar every time a customer parks to buy a coffee, a sandwich, or a book from a neighboring shop.

I am not speculating about what that dollar will do. In 2019, a neighboring town raised its meter rates by a comparable amount. I did not have a plan for that period, so I started tracking my own register. Over the six weeks following the increase, I recorded an 18% drop in foot traffic compared with the prior period. I cannot prove that the meter increase was the only cause, and I am not asking you to accept my register as a controlled study. I am asking you to consider that it is the only direct evidence any of us has so far, and that it points in one direction.

I also want to address what this increase would accomplish. According to the city's own budget report, metered parking revenue covers about 4% of the downtown budget. A rate tripling would raise money, but it would not change the fiscal picture of the district in any meaningful way. Meanwhile, the cost would fall on the small businesses that give downtown its character: the independent shops that do not have corporate budgets to absorb a sudden jump in customer costs or a drop in visits.

A small coffee shop operates on thin margins. Each customer who decides a 22-minute stop is no longer worth $1.50 is a customer lost, and the losses compound. A few fewer customers a day can mean fewer hours for my staff, a smaller order from my suppliers, and, eventually, a decision about whether the shop can stay open.

I respectfully ask the Council to reject the proposed increase, or at minimum to delay it until the city has studied its effect on downtown foot traffic and the businesses that depend on it. I would welcome the chance to share my full register data with the Council or with city staff, and I am glad to answer any questions.

Thank you for your time and your service to our community.

[Name]
[Coffee Shop Name]
[Address]

b.text:
**Testimony Submitted for the Public Record**
**Re: Proposed Parking Meter Rate Increase from $0.50 to $1.50 Per Hour, Downtown Commercial District**

Council members, good evening. My name is on the sign above the door of a two-person coffee shop on Main Street, third from the corner. I'm here because I'm asked, as a small business owner, to comment on the proposal to triple our parking meter rate from fifty cents an hour to one dollar fifty. I'll keep this grounded, because small businesses don't get to speculate. We deal in what we actually count, and that's what I brought.

In 2019, the town eleven miles north of here passed a comparable parking rate increase. I don't mean a comparable in principle. I mean the same kind of neighborhood commercial strip, the same kind of metered storefronts, and I'll go a step further: I went to their Main Street equivalent for six weeks after their meters switched over and tracked my own register against my own register from the prior six weeks. Same hours, same menu, same staff. Foot traffic at my neighboring-town location dropped eighteen percent. Not two percent. Not "a noticeable decline." Eighteen percent of the people who walked through the door simply did not walk through the door. I have the receipt tallies. I will produce them into the record if asked. That eighteen percent was not an industry-wide trend. That town's surrounding businesses were fine. Mine wasn't. The variable was the meter.

Now I'll talk about the people who do walk through my door here on Main Street. I have been pulling time-stamped data off my own point-of-sale system for the better part of three years. The average visit at my shop is twenty-two minutes. Twenty-two minutes. A customer parks, walks in, orders a drip and maybe a scone, sits down with a book or a laptop or a friend, and leaves. The current one-hour meter minimum already covers that entire visit with nearly forty minutes of buffer. These people are not overstaying. They are not "hogging spaces." They are spending twenty-two minutes on a street you are asking them to pay three dollars and fifty cents for. Before my coffee gets cold. Before their scone is finished. Three-fifty for twenty-two minutes of being a person in a town.

And if the argument being made in this chamber tonight is that the increase is necessary to fund downtown maintenance, I'd gently point everyone at your own document. The city's published parking authority report, the one attached to this very agenda item, states that meter revenue accounts for four percent of the downtown operating budget. Four. Percent. Tripling the rate from fifty cents to a dollar-fifty does not close a ninety-six percent gap. It does not fix a sidewalk in three years. What it does, in concrete dollars-and-cents, is add one dollar to every twenty-two-minute visit my customers make, every single time, and it does so on top of a change I have watched cost an independent shop eighteen percent of its foot traffic in a town with otherwise identical conditions.

I am not here to tell you downtown maintenance doesn't matter. I am here to tell you that four percent is not a budget fix and eighteen percent is not an abstraction, and that the people on your committee drafting this have not stood behind a counter at 6 a.m. counting receipts against the prior six weeks while a meter ticks over into its second hour.

I am asking you to vote no. Or if not no, then to set the rate at seventy-five cents, to cap single-visit meter time at ninety minutes so that a twenty-two-minute customer isn't paying for an hour they won't use, and to return to this body with a plan that actually addresses the ninety-six percent of the budget that meters were never going to cover in the first place.

My name is [Name]. I run [Shop Name], 217 Main Street. My phone number and my six weeks of register data are available to any council member who wants them.

Thank you.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
During my first week in the emergency room, I learned that nursing is not always about knowing exactly what to do. Sometimes it is about staying with someone when they are scared. Sometimes it is about stepping out of the way. Sometimes it is about trying again after you fail.

One of my first patients needed a wound cleaned. His wife was stuck in traffic, and he kept asking when she would get there. I could tell he was nervous, even though he tried to joke with the nurse. When the cleaning started, I stood beside him and held out my hand. He grabbed it right away.

He squeezed hard, and I let him. I did not have the right words to make the pain go away. I could not make his wife arrive any faster. All I could do was stay there and tell him he was doing okay. Before that moment, I thought helping a patient meant performing a skill or answering a question. He showed me that being present can also be a kind of care.

Later that week, a patient went into cardiac arrest. The room filled quickly, and everyone had a job. My job was to stay out of the way and restock gauze. As I worked, I could hear the team counting through the curtain.

I wanted to be useful in a bigger way. Part of me felt ashamed that I was putting supplies on a shelf while other people were trying to save a life. But the ER does not stop during a code. Supplies still need to be ready for the next patient, and the trained staff need room to work. I realized that nursing also means knowing your limits. One day, I hope to be one of the nurses inside that room. For now, I need to learn, pay attention, and do the job I am given well.

My hardest moment that week came during a blood draw. The patient had diabetes and veins that were difficult to find. Under supervision, I tried once and missed. I tried again and missed. On the third try, I still could not get it.

I felt embarrassed. I worried that the patient had lost trust in me. I apologized and asked if he wanted someone else to take over. He looked at me and said, “You have to learn somehow.”

On the fourth try, I got it.

I was relieved, but I was not proud just because I finally found the vein. I was grateful that he had been patient with me. He reminded me that nursing students learn with the help of real people who are already having difficult days. Patients are not practice. They are people who deserve honesty, care, and respect, even when I am nervous or unsure.

My first week in the ER did not make me feel like a nurse yet. It showed me how much I still have to learn. I need more practice with my hands, more knowledge, and more confidence. I also learned that confidence cannot mean pretending I know everything. It has to mean being willing to ask for help, accept correction, and keep trying.

I entered nursing school because I wanted work that mattered. In the ER, I saw that meaningful work can look small. It can be holding a stranger’s hand. It can be restocking gauze while a team handles a crisis. It can be taking a breath after three failed attempts and carefully trying one more time.

This scholarship would help me continue my education and spend more time focused on becoming the kind of nurse patients can trust. I know the road ahead will include long shifts, hard classes, and more mistakes. My first clinical rotation taught me not to run from those moments. It taught me to stay, learn, and keep showing up.

b.text:
My first week in the ER taught me more than any classroom could.

I came in nervous, trying to keep up and not get in the way. The ER moves fast. People are hurting, scared, tired, and sometimes all three at once. I knew that before I started, but it felt different once I was actually there. It is one thing to read about care. It is another to stand in a room and see what people need in real time.

One moment that stayed with me was when I helped with a wound cleaning for an older man. His wife was stuck in traffic and could not get there yet. He kept looking toward the door. He was trying to act calm, but I could tell he was worried. I stood beside him and held his hand while the nurse cleaned the wound. I did not do anything dramatic. I just stayed there. But I could see it helped. Sometimes people do not need a speech. Sometimes they just need someone to sit with them and not make them face it alone.

Another moment happened during a code. I was sent to restock gauze, and as I stood outside the room, I could hear the team counting through the curtain. It was organized, fast, and serious. Even though I was not in the room, I could feel how much everyone mattered in that moment. I learned that nursing is not just one person at the center. It is a team working together, each person doing their part. Even something as simple as bringing supplies back quickly can make a difference.

I also had a hard time with a blood draw on a diabetic patient who had very poor veins. I missed the first time. Then I missed again. And again. I felt awful. I did not want to give up, but I also did not want to keep poking him and making it worse. On the fourth try, I finally got it. I was relieved, but I also knew I had to be honest with myself. I was frustrated, and I was embarrassed, but I kept going. That patient was patient with me, and I will not forget that. It reminded me that learning takes time, and that skill comes with practice, patience, and respect for the person in front of you.

That first week showed me that nursing is not only about being right the first time. It is about staying calm, paying attention, and caring even when things are busy or hard. It is about being useful in the small moments and steady in the hard ones. I left that week more sure than ever that I want to do this work.

I am applying for this scholarship because I want to keep learning and keep growing into the kind of nurse my patients can count on. My first week in the ER did not just teach me skills. It showed me the kind of nurse I want to become: someone who shows up, stays steady, and treats every patient like they matter.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
A three-point deficit is not a reason to abandon a running game that’s working.

That’s the part of this second-round state playoff loss that will stick with me. Not simply that the season ended, or that it ended against a team our guys beat by 20 back in Week 3. It’s that, with the game still within reach, they moved away from something the opponent hadn’t given them a good reason to quit.

The second-half decision to abandon the run cost them this game. That’s my read, and an 8-2 season doesn’t make that decision immune from criticism.

Dez Kowalski threw for a school-record 2,340 yards this year. That deserves its own place in the school’s football history, without a playoff loss attached to every mention. He gave this offense a weapon few teams around here have ever had.

But having a record-setting quarterback doesn’t mean every close game needs to become his rescue mission. A productive running game helps him. It makes a defense account for more than his arm. Staying with it wouldn’t have been timid football. It would have been sensible football.

And no, winning the first meeting by 20 didn’t guarantee anything in the rematch. Opponents adjust. Playoff games are their own games. But that cuts both ways: coaches have to respond to what’s working that night, not just lean on the season’s biggest strength.

These players earned the town’s applause. Eight wins and a school passing record are accomplishments worth celebrating.

They also earned a chance to finish this playoff game with the full offense available to them. Down three, the run should still have been part of the answer.

b.text:
There’s no shame in an 8-2 season. There’s also no reason to pretend the way it ended made sense.

The second-round state playoff loss will sting because this was a team our guys had beaten by 20 in Week 3. That didn’t guarantee a repeat. But with the deficit at just three points, the offense got away from a running game that was working.

That’s the part I can’t get past.

Down three is not desperation time. The whole playbook is still open. You don’t have to chase the game, and you certainly don’t have to abandon something the other defense hasn’t stopped.

Dez Kowalski’s arm is an understandable temptation. He threw for a school-record 2,340 yards this season, an accomplishment that deserves to stand on its own. The loss doesn’t diminish it.

But having a record-setting quarterback doesn’t make every situation a passing situation. A productive running game helps him, too. It keeps a defense honest and keeps the offense from asking one player to provide every answer.

None of that guarantees a different result. The opponent deserves credit for reversing what happened in September. Still, the second-half approach made the job harder than it needed to be. In a game that close, that’s a fair criticism of the coaching.

These players gave the town a good fall and put together a season worth celebrating. They also had a real chance to keep playing.

Both things can be true. We can applaud the 8-2 record, congratulate Kowalski and still say this plainly: With the season on the line, the offense should have trusted the ground game that was already working.

setup: A co-founder is posting a LinkedIn hiring announcement for a first customer support hire to potential applicants and customers.

a.text:
We’re hiring our first support person at Ridgepoint.

We’re a three-person team building software that helps small trucking dispatchers schedule loads. Until now, the three of us have answered every support ticket ourselves. That setup is starting to break down, and we need someone whose main focus is helping customers get unstuck.

The day-to-day work:
- Answer questions about how to use Ridgepoint.
- Figure out what’s happening when something doesn’t work as expected: ask follow-up questions, try to reproduce the problem, and bring clear details to the founders when it needs a fix.
- Keep customers updated so they’re not left wondering what happened to their ticket.
- Turn recurring questions into useful help docs.
- Point out patterns we should address in the product, not just keep answering in the inbox.

This isn’t stepping into a big support department with everything figured out. You’ll work directly with us and help turn what we’ve been doing ad hoc into a more reliable process.

We’re looking for someone who writes clearly, likes untangling problems, and understands that a dispatcher asking for help is trying to keep their day moving.

Interested, or know someone we should talk to? Send me a message.

b.text:
We're hiring our first support person at Ridgepoint. Here's the honest reason: there are three of us, and right now we all answer every ticket ourselves. It worked at 20 customers. At the number we're at now it means one of us is context-switching out of product work five times a morning, and some tickets sit longer than a dispatcher with a truck waiting should have to wait.

So here's what the job actually is, day to day.

Our customers are small trucking dispatchers. Usually one or two people scheduling loads for a handful of drivers. They message us when something's in the way of getting a truck moving: a load won't drop onto the board, a driver's available hours aren't matching what they expect, a spreadsheet import came in wrong, they need to add a new shipper and don't know where. Mornings are the busiest because that's when they're lining up the day.

Most of it is figuring out what someone actually needs, walking them through it, and doing it fast enough that they can get back to work. Some of it is spotting that the thing they're describing is a bug, reproducing it, and writing it up clearly enough that one of us can fix it without asking you ten questions. Some of it is noticing that five people asked the same "how do I" this week and telling us so we fix the product instead of answering it a sixth time.

You'd be talking to people who are busy and sometimes frustrated, not because they're difficult but because a sitting truck costs them money. Patience under that matters more than knowing trucking. We'll teach you the software and the vocabulary.

What it isn't: it's not a stepping stone to sales, and it's not a script job. You'd be the person who knows our customers best, and we'd lean on that.

If you've done support at a small software company, or you've dispatched and want out of the seat, I'd like to hear from you. Comment or message me and I'll send the full details on hours, pay, and how we work.

a.text:
Most of my weekends start with someone asking where the tape is. We have a drawer for it under the register, but it almost never stays there.

I’ve worked at my family’s Vietnamese restaurant every weekend since sophomore year. I take orders, pack takeout, wipe tables, and do whatever job has become urgent in the last thirty seconds. My family makes the schedule assuming I’ll be there. Usually, I am.

One Saturday, the register system died during lunch. I tapped the screen a few times, which was the full extent of my technical solution. Then I found a pad of paper.

For the next few hours, I hand-wrote every ticket. I wrote the table number at the top and circled changes so the kitchen wouldn’t miss them. No onions. Extra sauce. One order to go, even though the rest of the table was eating in. My handwriting got worse as the pad got thinner.

Without the screen keeping track, I had to keep asking questions. Had table six paid? Were both bags for the woman by the door? Where was the ticket I’d just been holding? At one point, I had three pens tucked into my apron and couldn’t find any of them.

When the system came back, I still had a stack of handwritten orders to enter. I stayed at the counter while someone else wiped down the tables.

Teaching a new hire to fold spring rolls was slower work. I showed her the way my grandma had shown me: filling near the bottom, sides tucked in, roll firmly, but don’t pull so hard that the wrapper tears.

My first demonstration tore.

“That’s what not to do,” I said.

She laughed, and I started another one. She kept making hers too loose. I kept saying, “A little tighter,” which wasn’t especially useful, so I stood beside her and folded one at the same time. We stopped after each step. By the end of the tray, hers stayed closed. She lined them up with the seam underneath, the way my grandma likes them.

On breaks, I sometimes take my calculus homework into the walk-in cooler. It’s quiet there, and nobody needs the spot where I stand with my notebook balanced on a box. I wear my jacket and work until my fingers get cold.

There’s usually one problem I can’t finish before someone calls me back out. I leave myself a note beside it—check derivative, or where did this negative come from?—and put the notebook away. Later, at home, the note doesn’t always help.

I do miss things because I work weekends. Friends send pictures from places I couldn’t go. I’ve asked to leave early and then stayed because we got busy. Sometimes I watch the clock.

Other nights, I look up and someone has already started stacking chairs. I refill the sauce containers, sweep under the tables, and check whether there’s homework tucked beneath the counter. Before I leave, I put the tape back in its drawer.

b.text:
The register died on a Saturday in November, ten minutes into the dinner rush. The screen went gray, then black, and my dad stood at the kitchen window holding a plate of phở, waiting for a ticket that was never going to print.

I found a ticket pad in the drawer under the register, the kind we used before we got the system, back when I was too short to see over the counter. The tickets were yellow and carbon-copied and smelled like my grandma's kitchen, though that might just be how old paper smells.

I can't explain how I knew the numbers. Our menu has eighty-two items and I've been ringing them up since I was thirteen. I don't think about #17, bún bò Huế, extra spicy, no cabbage. My hand just does it. That Saturday I wrote sixty-one tickets in four hours, in an order I could keep in my head: table four before table nine, the to-go order for the man who comes every Saturday between the two rushes. When the repair guy came Monday and rebooted everything, the old tickets were still in my apron pocket. My dad read a few of them and said my handwriting was worse than my grandmother's. At our restaurant that is not an insult.

The new hire, Dylan, started in December. He's sixteen and folds spring rolls like he's afraid of them. My grandma taught me her fold the summer before my sophomore year: rice paper soft, filling pushed flat, fold the near edge over, tuck once, roll tight, then fold in the sides like you're sealing an envelope, then finish the roll. Two turns. The wrapper should end just past the filling so it doesn't bunch up and crack. She said it took her a year to get it right, and she'd been making them since she was eight, in Huế, standing on a stool.

I stood next to Dylan at the prep table and moved his hands to where they needed to go. Third knuckle here. Don't be gentle with the tuck. He made forty spring rolls that shift and maybe nine of them were right. I told him that was good, because it was. My grandma would have said the same, then made him redo all nine.

The walk-in cooler is where I do my calculus. There's a milk crate by the racks of bean sprouts and it's quiet in there and forty degrees, which beats the kitchen in July. I sit with the textbook on my knees and work related rates while the ice machine hums through the wall. My friends study at the library or at Starbucks. I've done homework in that cooler so many times that I associate derivatives with the smell of Thai basil. I don't think that's a metaphor. I think it's just what happened.

People ask me what it's like to work for my family, and I never know what to say, because I don't have anything to compare it to. I've worked every weekend since sophomore year. Saturdays are twelve hours. I know the register, the fryer, the fold, the regulars. I know which tables tip and which ones think a compliment on the phở counts as ten percent. When something breaks, I don't panic, because everything has broken already. The register, the ice machine, the bathroom sink, the Saturday we ran out of rice.

Next fall I'll be three hours away, and someone else will run the Saturday register. I hope they learn the numbers before the register dies, because it will die again. My dad will stand at the window holding a plate of phở, and whoever's at the register will have to know what to do.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
In 9 years of recruiting in logistics, and probably 200+ interviews in the last couple of years alone, there’s one question that makes me sit up a little straighter.

It’s not about growth plans or the team structure.

It’s: “Can you tell me about the last project here that didn’t go to plan?”

I heard it most recently from a candidate for an Operations Manager role last month. Our hiring manager talked honestly about the routing software we rolled out last spring — the one we hyped up internally for three months, trained everyone on, and then quietly pulled after six weeks because our drivers were spending more time fighting the system than driving their routes.

The candidate didn’t rush to reassure him. She just asked, “What did you change about how you launch stuff after that?”

That turned into a 15-minute conversation about how we now pilot with one depot first, who actually gets a say before we sign a contract, and why that failed rollout is the reason the role she was interviewing for even exists.

She got the job. Not because she asked a clever question, but because of what followed — she was already trying to understand how this team makes decisions when things go wrong, not just how we talk about success.

The strongest candidates I see aren’t trying to catch us out with that question. They’re deciding if we’re honest enough to work for.

I’m curious — hiring managers, how do you answer when someone asks it well?

b.text:
In about 200 interviews over the last few years, the candidates who stood out weren’t the ones asking about our “culture.” They asked what we’ve screwed up lately.

One example. A candidate for a transportation planner role asked, “What’s a project your team ran in the last year that failed?”

I told her about a routing pilot we pushed live before the dispatch leads had bought in. The math looked fine. The execution didn’t. Two weeks in, dispatchers were overriding it manually and we pulled it.

She didn’t nod and move on. She asked, “When did you first know it was in trouble?”

I said week one, when the overrides showed up.

Then: “What did you change about how you launch pilots after that?”

I explained we now do a two-week shadow period with dispatch leads and write down kill criteria before launch. She asked who owned the decision to stop it.

That conversation told me more than any answer about “strengths.” She was checking whether we could talk about failure without spinning it, and whether the learning outlasted the postmortem.

Hiring managers: have a real failure ready. If you can’t name one, candidates notice.

Job seekers: ask it. The answer tells you a lot about how the team actually works.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
As a parent of two middle-schoolers in Millbrook, I’m writing to urge our school board to approve the proposed 8:45 a.m. start time.

I know this has been a big topic, and I understand why some people are hesitant. Changing the school day affects family routines, sports, after-school jobs, and bus schedules. But after reading the proposal closely, and thinking about what I see at home every morning, I believe this is the right move for our kids.

Middle schoolers are not little kids, and they are not adults either. They are at an age when sleep matters enormously. The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. because teenagers’ natural sleep cycles shift later. That means a 7:30 or 8:00 start can make it much harder for them to get the sleep they actually need. We can pretend they will just “go to bed earlier,” but anyone with a middle-schooler knows how unrealistic that is on a regular basis.

What I keep coming back to is this: we ask our kids to focus, learn, and grow all day long, but we start the day at a time that works against their brains and bodies. That doesn’t seem fair, and it doesn’t seem smart.

The Lincoln Middle pilot gives me even more confidence. The results were encouraging: attendance went up, and first-period grades improved. That matters. If a later start helps kids show up more consistently and do better in that first class of the day, that is not a small benefit — that is a real sign that the change is helping students where it counts.

I’ve also heard the bus schedule objection. I get it. Transportation is one of the hardest parts of any schedule change. But the proposal already addresses that by re-tiering the routes. In other words, this is not a vague idea with no transportation plan attached. The district has done the work to make it possible.

No schedule will be perfect for every family. I know some parents will have to adjust, and that’s not nothing. But we’re talking about a change that lines up with expert guidance and shows promise in our own district. If we want better attendance, better learning, and healthier mornings for our kids, this is a practical step forward.

I hope the board listens to the evidence, the pilot results, and the families who live this every day — and votes yes.

b.text:
**Give Millbrook Students a Better Start**

By a Millbrook parent

Most mornings at my house, I’m trying to get two middle-schoolers out the door while they’re still half asleep. I can remind them to go to bed earlier—and I do—but I can’t make them fall asleep on command. I know plenty of Millbrook families are having the same conversation at the breakfast table.

That’s why I support the school board’s proposal to move the school start time to 8:45.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. so students have a better chance of getting the sleep they need. An 8:45 start would put Millbrook on the right side of that recommendation. It would not solve every tired morning, but it would stop asking kids to begin their school day quite so early.

We also have a local reason to take this seriously. In the Lincoln Middle pilot, attendance went up, and first-period grades went up. Those results caught my attention more than any slogan could. Showing up to school matters. So does being ready to learn when the first class begins.

I’ve heard the concern about buses, and it’s a fair one. Families depend on routes that get children to school and adults to work on time. But the proposal doesn’t simply move the bell and leave the bus schedule as it is. It already re-tiers the routes to accommodate the later start. The board should make sure the final routes are clear, workable and shared with families well before the change. Bus logistics deserve careful planning; they aren’t a reason to dismiss the proposal without looking at the plan.

There will still be adjustments. Some families will need to rethink morning routines, and others may have questions about the rest of the day. I hope the district listens closely and answers those questions plainly. Parents don’t need to be told a change is effortless when we know better. We need to know that the people making it have thought through the details.

I’ve read the proposal with my own kids in mind, but also with their classmates in mind—the ones who catch an early bus, struggle through first period or miss school more often than they should. The Lincoln pilot suggests a later start can make a real difference.

When the board votes next month, I hope it chooses 8:45. Our students deserve a school day that gives them a better chance to arrive awake and ready.

setup: A retired rural mail carrier is writing a letter to the Kettle Falls Courier urging residents to oppose the post office counter closure at the July 28 forum.

a.text:
To the Editor:

I drove Route 4 for 22 years before I retired last year, so I know this town and the people in it. I want to say something about the plan to close counter service at our post office.

The USPS says the branch loses $40,000 a year. What they don't say is that they already cut the counter hours from a full day down to 8 to noon. Of course business dropped after that. Working people can't get to the counter before noon. So they cut the hours, watched the traffic fall off, and now they're pointing at the drop as the reason to close. That's a problem they made themselves, and it isn't right to hang it on us.

I'll tell you who this hurts. Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill is in her eighties and gets her heart medicine by mail. She still handles some of her bills with money orders because that's how she's always done it. She cannot drive twenty minutes to Fairview and twenty minutes back for a money order. There are more folks like her on every route out of this town. I delivered to them for two decades. I know their mailboxes and I know their situations.

A post office counter isn't just a place to buy stamps. It's where people who don't do everything on a computer can still take care of their business. Take that away and you've cut some of our neighbors off, plain and simple.

The district manager will be at a public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. If this counter matters to you, show up and say so. Empty chairs will tell them nobody cares. I don't believe that's true of this town, and I plan to be there to say it.

I'm no writer, just a retired mail carrier. But I know that when the mail matters to people, somebody ought to speak up.

Kettle Falls

b.text:
To the Editor,

Most folks around here know me from the 22 years I spent driving Route 4. Thirty-eight miles of dirt and gravel every morning until I hung up the keys last year. I’m no writer, but I know this town and I know the mail, and I can’t sit quiet about what the Postal Service is trying to pull with our counter service.

The district office says our little branch loses $40,000 a year. What they leave out is that two years ago, they cut our counter hours down to 8:00 a.m. to noon. If you work for a living, you can’t get in the door. If you farm, you’re out in the field. They cut the hours, watched the foot traffic drop off just like anyone with common sense knew it would, and now they’re using those numbers to say we don’t need a clerk. That isn't a lack of business. That’s a problem they built with their own hands.

The people who will pay for this aren’t sitting in regional offices looking at spreadsheets. It’s folks like Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She’s in her eighties. I handed her heart medicine to her through her car window or walked it to her porch for over a decade. She doesn’t do banking on a computer. If she needs to send a money order to pay a bill, she comes to our post office. Telling her to drive twenty minutes down the highway to the Fairview branch—especially when the snow starts blowing—is the same as telling her she’s on her own.

A post office isn’t supposed to be a money-making business. It’s a service, and we pay our taxes for it just like anyone in Spokane or Seattle. 

The USPS district manager is coming to town for a public forum on Tuesday, July 28, at the Grange Hall. If you care about keeping this town whole, you need to be in those folding chairs. Don't leave it to your neighbor. Show up, look them in the eye, and tell them Kettle Falls isn't ready to let them lock that counter up for good.

Jim Miller  
Kettle Falls (Route 4, Retired)

setup: A co-founder is posting a LinkedIn hiring announcement for a first customer support hire to potential applicants and customers.

a.text:
We're hiring our first support person at Ridgepoint. Right now the three of us split the inbox, and it's not working. Tickets sit for hours while someone's heads-down on a release, and last week I answered a billing question from a parking lot. That's not fair to our customers and it's not sustainable.

Here's what the job actually looks like:

You'll be the first person to see most tickets, roughly 30 to 50 a day across email and in-app chat. A lot of it is repetitive: password resets, a driver not showing up in a dispatch board, someone's ELD integration timing out, "why did this load duplicate." You'll learn the top 20 issues in your first month and be able to resolve most of them yourself.

The harder half is the stuff you can't solve alone. You'll need to reproduce the bug, write it up clearly enough that an engineer doesn't have to interview you about it, and then follow up with the customer when it's fixed. If you're the type who finds it satisfying to figure out exactly which three clicks broke something, you'll do well here.

Our customers are small dispatch operations, usually 3 to 30 trucks. They're often on the phone with drivers while they're typing to you. They're direct, sometimes blunt, and they don't care about our roadmap. They care whether the load gets covered today. You need to be comfortable with that and not take it personally.

Other real parts of the job: keeping our help docs from going stale, and being on a light rotation for Saturday morning coverage (about 2 hours, dispatch is busy then). We'll pay for it.

What it isn't: this isn't a stepping stone into product that we're being coy about. It might become that eventually, but we're hiring someone to own support.

Remote, US hours, $52 to $62k depending on experience. Trucking or logistics background is a plus, not required. B2B support experience matters more.

If interested, email me at [email]. Tell me about a time you fixed something a customer thought was unfixable. Skip the cover letter.

b.text:
We’re hiring our first support person at Ridgepoint.

Ridgepoint is a small SaaS tool that helps trucking dispatchers schedule loads. We’re a three-person team, and until now, the three of us have been answering every support ticket ourselves. That worked for a while, but it’s starting to fall apart.

So we’re bringing on someone whose job is to own that part of the business.

This is not a “copy-paste canned replies” support role. Day to day, you’ll be:

- Reading inbound tickets from dispatchers and figuring out what they actually need  
- Answering questions clearly and calmly, sometimes when someone is frustrated or stuck mid-day  
- Reproducing issues and deciding whether it’s a misunderstanding, a setup problem, or a real bug  
- Escalating product issues to us with useful context, not just “it’s broken”  
- Writing help docs, internal notes, and short answers we can reuse later  
- Helping us notice what customers keep getting wrong, asking for, or struggling with  

You’ll be working directly with the founders, and your observations will shape the product. If something keeps confusing customers, we want to hear about it.

This role would suit someone who is organized, patient, clear in writing, and comfortable with ambiguity. You don’t need to come from trucking or SaaS, but you do need to be able to learn a product quickly and take ownership when something is messy.

If you’re interested, send me a DM or comment below.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
In 12 years of helping people buy homes around Asheville, I’ve noticed something: buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7 a.m. before we tour often feel more confident about the house later.

The Pruitts showed me why. Before we went inside the Sycamore Street house, they came back early and walked the block together. They got to experience it as a place to live, not just a house to view—at the hour they’d actually be heading into their day.

That walk didn’t answer every question, of course. But it gave them a better feel for the street, and that mattered when it came time to decide.

It’s a small suggestion I make to first-time buyers now: if you can, see the neighborhood at the time you’d normally be there. A home is more than what’s behind the front door.

b.text:
Twelve years in, the best advice I give first-time buyers has almost nothing to do with the house. It’s this: before we tour, go walk the neighborhood at 7am.

The Pruitts were first-time buyers, and they’d done everything right. Pre-approved, patient, knew they wanted an older home with a porch. We looked at a Craftsman on Sycamore Street on a Thursday afternoon. They liked it, but something kept them from being sure. The kitchen was small, the yard sloped, and they couldn’t tell if the street felt like theirs or just like a street.

I told them to come back the next morning. Not for a showing—just to walk. They did. At 7am they saw a neighbor in a bathrobe retrieving the paper, a dad walking two kids to the bus, someone on a porch with coffee, and a woman deadheading roses by the sidewalk. The Pruitts called me from the corner. They said, “We can see our life here.” We wrote the offer that afternoon.

That was a few years ago. They still send me a photo every now and then from their morning walk. The house didn’t get bigger, and the yard didn’t get flatter. But they knew the neighborhood before they committed to it.

I’ve had other buyers do the 7am walk and walk away—too much traffic, too quiet, too far from the coffee they actually drink. That’s the point. A house can look perfect at 2pm. A neighborhood tells the truth at 7am.

If you’re buying, especially for the first time, set an alarm before you fall in love. Walk the block. Listen. See who’s out. The right house is usually the one where you can picture your ordinary Tuesday.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
**6-Month Review: The Jarvik L2 Standing Desk**

I bought the Jarvik L2 in February - 60x30, laminate top, black frame - with my own money. No affiliate links here, nothing to sell you.

I'm a remote software engineer. This desk gets 9-10 hours a day, 5 days a week, dual 27" monitors on an arm, MacBook, heavy mechanical keyboard.

After 6 months of actual use:

**The motor is legitimately good.**

It's fast and quiet. Jarvik claims 1.4"/sec and that's about right - it goes from my sitting height (28.5") to standing (44.5") in ~11 seconds. And it's quiet enough that I can adjust it mid-Zoom call without muting. My old Flexispot sounded like a forklift. This one is just a low hum.

**It wobbles at full height.**

I'm 5'10" and I stand at 44.5 inches. At that height, if I'm really hammering on the keyboard or leaning to grab something, there is noticeable side-to-side wobble. The monitor shake is visible. At sitting height it's rock solid. At 40" it's fine. At full max height (47") it's borderline unusable for me if I'm typing hard. If you're over 6' and plan to stand tall all day, this is not the frame you want.

**The memory presets drift.**

I have preset 1 at 72cm and preset 2 at 113cm. After 2-3 weeks, preset 1 will stop at 71cm or 73cm. It's consistently off by about a centimeter. Not the end of the world, but annoying when you expect it to hit your exact ergonomic position every time. I've had to recalibrate it twice in 6 months by holding down+up until it resets.

**The cable tray is garbage.**

Throw it away. It's thin, stamped metal, too shallow to hold a power strip plus cables, and the included wood screws stripped out of the pre-drilled holes on day one. I replaced it with a $35 under-desk tray from Amazon that holds everything. For a company selling a $700+ desk, this tray is insulting.

**Verdict:**

At the $549 sale price I paid, it's a good desk. The motor alone makes it better than anything else in that price range.

At $749 full price? Absolutely not. For that money, buy a Uplift V2 or Fully Jarvis frame and get a more stable frame and presets that actually stay put.

If you can get it on sale and you're under 6 feet and don't mind fixing the cable management yourself, it's worth it. If you see it at $749, close the tab.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6 Months In

I've been standing at this thing roughly four hours a day since March. Here's what I actually think, now that the honeymoon is over and I've had time to get annoyed at it.

**Setup:** 60" x 30" bamboo top, dual 27" monitors on a single crossbar arm, Keychron Q1 (heavy, aluminum, I type like I'm angry at it), a laptop on a riser, and the usual desk detritus. Call it 45 lbs of load, well under the 265 lb rating.

## The motor is genuinely great

This is the thing I'd tell you first. The dual-motor lift is fast — I timed it at about 6.5 seconds to go from my 29" sitting height to my 44.5" standing height, which works out to roughly 1.5"/sec. That's not a spec-sheet number, that's me with a stopwatch and a loaded desktop.

More importantly, it's *quiet*. I measured around 44 dB from where I sit, which is quieter than my Mac Mini under load. I've raised it mid-meeting on Zoom probably fifty times now and nobody has ever asked what that noise was. My previous desk (an Autonomous SmartDesk) sounded like a garbage disposal and I'd time transitions around calls. Not an issue here.

Six months, no motor stutter, no one-leg-lags-behind desync, no reset dance required. The controller has never dropped its calibration. That's the boring stuff that actually matters and Jarvik got it right.

## The wobble is real and it's height-dependent

At sitting height, rock solid. At 38-40", fine. Above about 42" — which is where I actually stand, I'm 5'9" — it develops a front-to-back sway when I'm typing hard. Not a shimmy. A slow, low-frequency wobble, maybe 2-3mm of travel at the monitor tops, with a period long enough that you can watch your text cursor drift.

To be specific about the trigger: normal typing is fine. Aggressive typing on a 1kg mechanical keyboard is not fine. Hitting Enter hard is not fine. Leaning on the desk edge to read something is definitely not fine.

I tried the obvious fixes. Moving the crossbar arm from the rear edge to a clamp closer to center helped maybe 20%. Adding a diagonal brace kit from a third party helped more, call it 50%, but now there's a bar across my knees at sitting height and I hate it. What actually fixed it for me was dropping my standing height to 43" and switching to a lower-profile keyboard when standing. That's a workaround, not a solution, and it's fair to hold it against the desk.

This is a two-stage leg design. If you're over 6'0" and you type with force, I'd look at a three-stage frame with a thicker upper segment, or just accept it. Everyone who tells you their two-stage desk is rock solid at 46" is either short or lying.

## Memory presets drift about a centimeter

This one bugs me more than it should because it's so obviously fixable in firmware.

I have four presets. Preset 2 is my standing height. When I set it, it was 43.0". Six months later, hitting preset 2 lands me at 43.4", sometimes 42.9". It's not a slow one-way creep — it wanders. The variance is roughly ±1cm, consistently.

Why do I care about a centimeter? Because my monitor height is tuned to my eye line and a centimeter is enough that I notice my neck angle change. I've re-saved the preset three times. It drifts back.

My theory is the controller counts motor revolutions rather than reading an absolute encoder, and the coasting distance after the stop signal varies with load and direction of travel. Arriving from below lands consistently higher than arriving from above. If you're precise about this stuff, expect to nudge it manually. The controller does have single-inch-increment tap adjustment, which helps, but I paid for presets so I wouldn't have to.

## The cable tray is garbage

Not "mediocre." Garbage.

It's a shallow stamped steel channel, maybe 2.5" deep and 20" long, mounted with two screws into pre-drilled holes on the underside. Problems, in order of severity:

1. It's too small. Two monitor power bricks and a 10-outlet strip do not fit. Pick two.
2. It has no lid, no retention, nothing. Anything you put in it that isn't wedged in works its way out over a few weeks of height changes and ends up hanging.
3. The mounting holes are positioned so the tray sits directly where my knees go at sitting height. I banged my kneecap on the corner of it hard enough to swear, twice, before I gave up.

I removed it in month two and replaced it with an under-desk basket ($22, screwed into the bamboo directly) plus a handful of adhesive cable clips. Total cost of fixing Jarvik's cable management: about $30 and an hour. Budget for that.

The included cable management overall is an afterthought. The velcro straps are fine. The power cable that runs from the controller to the outlet is exactly long enough at sitting height, which means at full extension it's taut. Mine has pulled out of the wall socket once. Get an extension.

## Assembly and build

Took me 70 minutes solo. Instructions are picture-only and mostly clear, though the step where you attach the feet has the orientation ambiguous and I got it backward the first time. Hardware is bagged and labeled. All the bolts were the right length, which sounds like a low bar but I've assembled desks where it wasn't.

The bamboo top is good. Six months of a coffee mug, a water glass, and a cat who has decided the desk is hers, and there's one faint ring near the back-left corner that I caused by leaving a wet glass overnight. Edges are well finished, no splintering. The underside has proper threaded inserts, not just wood screws into particle board, which is why I felt comfortable mounting my own cable basket.

Powder coat on the frame is even. No chips. The feet have adjustable levelers that actually work, which mattered because my apartment floor slopes.

## What I'd tell you to buy instead, conditionally

If you type gently, or you're under 5'8", or you use a laptop and a low-profile keyboard: the wobble complaint doesn't apply to you and this is an easy recommendation.

If you're tall and heavy-handed: three-stage frame, or spend more.

If you need presets to land within a millimeter: not this desk.

## The verdict

I paid $549 during a sale. At $549, this is a good desk. The motor is the expensive part of a standing desk and Jarvik didn't cheap out on it — it's fast, quiet, and hasn't given me a single problem in six months of daily cycling. The top is real bamboo, properly finished, with real threaded inserts. The wobble and the preset drift are annoyances I've worked around. The cable tray is a $30 problem.

At $749, no. At that price you're within spitting distance of desks with three-stage legs and better controllers, and the two flaws that annoy me are exactly the flaws that money solves. Paying full retail for this desk means paying premium prices for mid-tier rigidity and firmware.

It goes on sale often. Wait for it.

*No affiliate links here, as always. I bought this with my own money and Jarvik doesn't know who I am.*

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots (Before the Ground Freezes)

Every January we get the same call. Water pouring through a ceiling, basement flooding, a wall soaked through. Almost every time, the cause is the same: a hose left connected to an outside spigot that froze and split the pipe.

This is a ten-minute job. Here's how to do it right.

## Step 1: Find and Shut Off the Interior Valve

Somewhere inside your house—basement, utility room, crawl space—there's a shutoff valve on the line feeding each outdoor spigot. Find it and turn it off.

If you have a frost-free spigot (the kind with a long stem), you still need to shut this valve off. Frost-free doesn't mean freeze-proof, especially if water is trapped in the line.

## Step 2: Disconnect the Hose

**This is the part people skip, and it's the one that costs them thousands.**

A hose left connected traps water inside the spigot. That water freezes, expands, and cracks the pipe—often inside the wall where you can't see it until it thaws and starts leaking. We see this constantly. Disconnect every hose, coil it up, and store it in the garage or basement.

Don't just leave it lying on the ground next to the spigot. That's not disconnected.

## Step 3: Drain the Spigot

Open the outside faucet all the way. Then go back to the interior shutoff valve—there should be a small brass cap on the side, called a drain cap. Unscrew it with a bucket underneath. Let whatever water is in the line drain out.

If your valve doesn't have a drain cap, just leave the outside faucet open. Air needs somewhere to go.

## Step 4: Install a Foam Faucet Cover

Go to any hardware store and pick up a foam faucet cover. They cost about three dollars. Slide it over the spigot and secure it.

Is a foam cover enough on its own? No. You still need to do the shutoff and draining. But it adds an extra layer of insulation and keeps cold air from drafting into the opening.

## What If You Don't Have an Interior Shutoff Valve?

A lot of older Minneapolis homes—especially around South Minneapolis and Northeast—don't have interior shutoffs for the outside spigots. If that's your situation, give us a call. We can install one. It's not a huge job, and it's a lot cheaper than a burst pipe in January.

## The Quick Version

1. Shut off the interior valve
2. Disconnect the hose (seriously, do this)
3. Drain the spigot
4. Put on a $3 foam cover
5. No interior shutoff? Call us

Do this before the ground freezes. Once we're into consistent freezing temps, you're rolling the dice.

Questions or need help? Call us at **(612) 555-0147**. We're a family-owned shop in Minneapolis and we've been keeping pipes from bursting for over thirty years.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots (And Avoid a January Burst Pipe)

Freezing temps in Minneapolis don't give you much room for error when it comes to outdoor plumbing. If water sits inside your outdoor faucet or the supply line behind it, it will freeze, expand, and split the pipe inside your wall. You won’t even know it happened until you turn the water back on in the spring—or worse, during a mid-winter thaw when it floods your basement.

Here is the exact four-step process to winterize your outdoor spigots before the hard freeze hits.

---

### Step 1: Disconnect All Garden Hoses Immediately
Do this today. If you take only one thing away from this post, make it this: **never leave a hose connected to an outdoor spigot over the winter.** 

Even if you have a modern "frost-free" sillcock, leaving a hose attached prevents the water inside the faucet body from draining out. The trapped water freezes right at the exterior wall, splits the brass tube, and causes a massive leak inside your home. Easily 80% of the burst-pipe calls our family takes in January and February happen because someone forgot to disconnect a hose.

Disconnect the hose, drain it, roll it up, and store it away. Remove any splitters, timers, or quick-connect adapters, too.

---

### Step 2: Locate and Shut Off the Indoor Valve
Head down to your basement, utility room, or crawlspace. Look for the water line heading directly toward the outside wall where your outdoor spigot is located. 

On that line, you should find a shutoff valve (either a round wheel-handle gate valve or a straight lever-handle ball valve). 

* Turn a **round wheel-handle** clockwise until it stops completely.
* Turn a **lever-handle** a quarter-turn until it is perpendicular (across) the pipe.

---

### Step 3: Drain the Residual Water Out of the Line
Shutting the indoor valve stops new water from entering, but there is still water trapped between the valve and the outside wall. You need to drain it.

1. Go outside and open the outdoor spigot all the way. Let whatever water is inside drain out. Leave the spigot in the **open** position all winter.
2. Go back inside to your shutoff valve with a small bucket or towel. Most indoor shutoff valves have a tiny brass "bleeder cap" on the side of the valve body. Unscrew that cap slowly. 
3. Let the trapped water drain into your bucket. 
4. Once the water stops dripping, screw the bleeder cap back on tightly.

---

### Step 4: Add a $3 Foam Faucet Cover
Go to your local hardware store and grab an insulated styrofoam faucet cover. They cost about $3 to $5 and hook right onto the spigot handle, pulling tight against your siding with a rubber gasket. 

While draining the line is the main defense, these covers add an extra barrier against biting Minneapolis wind chills, protecting the fixture itself from extreme cold drafts.

---

### Can’t Find an Indoor Shutoff Valve?
A lot of older homes in Minneapolis—especially in neighborhoods like South Minneapolis, Northeast, or Saint Paul—either don't have indoor shutoffs for the outside lines, or the old gate valves are seized shut and won't turn.

If you don't have a dedicated indoor shutoff, or if your valve is leaking when you try to turn it, don't force it. Give our team a call. We can install a reliable, modern ball valve and a proper frost-free sillcock so you never have to worry about a frozen pipe wrecking your basement.

I've used your ticketing platform nearly every workday for the past five years. As an IT helpdesk technician at [Hospital System], I field roughly 35 tickets a day, which means I've spent thousands of hours inside your product, learning exactly where it shines and where users get stuck.

Five years on a hospital helpdesk also means I understand your users. Clinicians are time-starved and quick to abandon anything that slows them down, and I've spent my career making tools easier for exactly those people.

I know this industry, I know your product from the agent side, and I've already shown I can spot gaps and advocate for improvements that get built. I'd love to bring that to your team full time.

b.text:

a.text:
**Testimony on the Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Members of the City Council,

My name is [Name] and I am the owner of [Shop Name], an independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am here today to ask the council to vote no on the proposed parking meter rate increase from fifty cents to one dollar and fifty cents per hour.

That is a 200% rate increase, and I want to share three specific pieces of evidence with you about what it will mean for downtown businesses.

**First, I have direct observational data.** In 2019, when a comparable parking rate increase was implemented in the neighboring downtown, I tracked my own register for six weeks. Foot traffic dropped 18%. That was not a seasonal dip and it was not a coincidence. It was a direct, measurable response to parking becoming more expensive at a magnitude similar to what you are considering tonight.

**Second, the proposed rate is not calibrated to how people actually use downtown businesses.** My customers average a 22-minute visit. The current one-hour minimum at fifty cents already covers their stay with time to spare. Under the proposed rate, that same 22-minute visit costs one dollar and fifty cents instead of fifty cents — a one-dollar increase per customer for the exact same transaction. This is not a marginal adjustment. It is a threefold increase in the cost of an ordinary visit to a Main Street business.

**Third, the city's own financial data undermines the premise of this proposal.** According to the city's own report, meter revenue currently covers approximately 4% of the downtown budget. Even in the most optimistic scenario, in which the new rate triples that figure with no reduction in demand — which the evidence I just cited tells us will not happen — meter revenue would still cover only about 12% of the budget. You would be asking downtown businesses and their customers to absorb a 200% rate hike to close a small fraction of a gap that this measure cannot realistically close on its own.

I want to be clear about what an 18% drop in foot traffic means in practice. It does not just mean fewer customers at my coffee shop. It means fewer customers at every business on Main Street — the bookstore, the diner, the boutique down the block. When a customer decides the meter is not worth it, they do not skip one stop. They skip the trip.

I am not here to tell the council how to balance its budget. I am here to tell you that this proposal, at this magnitude, will produce real and measurable harm to the small businesses that anchor this district, in exchange for a budgetary gain that even your own report shows is modest. The math does not justify it.

I respectfully urge the council to reject the proposed rate increase and to work with the downtown business community on solutions that do not place the entire burden on the customers and independent businesses who keep this district alive.

Thank you for your time.

Respectfully submitted,

[Name]

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
Twelve years in, you stop guessing and start noticing patterns.

One that’s held up every time: the buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7 a.m. before we tour the house are the ones who still love the place two years later. Not because the house changes, but because they actually know what they’re buying into.

I learned that with the Pruitts. They were under contract on a little craftsman just off Sycamore Street, and the inspection was clean, the numbers worked, everything looked good on paper. But I’d watched enough buyers grow quiet six months after closing to know that paper isn’t the whole story. So I told them to grab coffee at the shop on the corner, walk the full length of Sycamore at 7 a.m. on a Tuesday, and then call me.

They did. They saw the retired guy three doors down who hoses off his driveway every morning and waves whether you wave back or not. They heard the school bus stop at the end of the block, which meant kids, which meant the Pruitts—who were expecting their first—wouldn’t be the only young family on the street. They realized the “quiet” street they’d driven through at 5 p.m. on a Saturday was actually alive in a way they liked at 7 a.m. on a weekday.

They closed three weeks later, and last I checked they were still happy. Not because the house was perfect, but because Sycamore Street felt like home before they ever walked through the front door.

I don’t have a statistic for this. I just know that when buyers fall in love with the context around the house, the house itself tends to stick.

b.text:
After 12 years selling homes in Asheville, I’ve noticed something: buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7 a.m. before we tour tend to be happier with the house later.

Not because an early walk tells you anything about the roof or the foundation. It tells you something about what it might feel like to live there. You hear the traffic, see who’s out walking, and get a sense of the street when people are starting an ordinary day—not just during a Saturday afternoon showing.

The Pruitts on Sycamore Street come to mind. [Add what they noticed on their morning walk, how it affected their decision, and what they told you after moving in.]

I work mostly with first-time buyers, and understandably, we spend a lot of time talking about the house: the layout, the inspection, what needs fixing now and what can wait. But you’re buying the everyday experience around it, too. That deserves a little time outside the showing window.

Before you fall in love with the kitchen, take a walk around the block. Ideally, when you’d normally be waking up there.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
# Girls' Soccer Deserves the Same Investment as Football

Our girls' soccer field floods. Again and again, we lose games to rain that wouldn't cancel anything on the boys' football field—which has had artificial turf since 2019.

Last season alone, we rescheduled or cancelled nine games because the grass turned to mud. Our athletes showed up ready to play. The field wasn't. This season we've already had two more postponements, and we're only halfway through.

But cancelled games aren't even the worst part. Last October, one of my seniors stepped into a rut in that waterlogged grass and tore her ACL. She missed the rest of her final season. A turf field wouldn't have prevented every injury, but it would have prevented that one.

Our school board installed artificial turf on the football field five years ago. I'm not arguing against that investment—football is important. But girls' soccer is important too. We have the same number of athletes. We play just as hard. We deserve a field that doesn't become a swamp every time it rains.

This isn't complicated. The boys got a modern facility. The girls are still playing on mud. When you're deciding next year's budget, I'd ask you this: Why?

Install turf on the girls' soccer field. Our athletes have waited long enough.

b.text:
**The football field got turf in 2019. The girls' soccer field still floods.**

Nine. That's how many games our girls' soccer team has had rained out or moved in the past two seasons because our grass field floods. Not snowed out. Not forfeited. Flooded. My players stand at the fence in full uniform, watching standing water where the midfield should be, and then we call their parents to come pick them up.

"Moved" usually means handing our home game to the opponent because their field drains and ours doesn't. And rained-out games don't disappear. They get crammed into the back of the schedule — three games in five days on tired teenage legs, which is how knees get hurt even before you factor in the ruts.

About those ruts. When the field floods and then dries, it dries hard and uneven, with troughs where the puddles sat and footprints baked in like concrete. Last October, one of my players planted her foot in one of those ruts on a routine cut — the kind of cut she's made a thousand times in practice — and tore her ACL. Surgery. Nine months of rehab. She lost her junior season to a hole in the ground that never should have been there. I won't use her name here. She's a kid, not a talking point. But her injury is the reason I'm writing, and her parents know it.

Now let's talk about 2019.

That's the year the district put turf on the football field. I want to be clear: I'm glad they did. Those kids deserve a safe, playable surface. So do mine. The school board already decided that athletes in this town get to play on turf. They just decided it for some athletes.

Since then, the girls' soccer program has been told to wait. Wait for the next budget cycle. Wait for the five-year facilities plan. My freshmen who were promised "soon" are now juniors.

People ask why the girls don't just play on the football turf. Because it's spoken for — football practices, games, and everything else the district schedules there. And because "you can borrow the boys' field when they're not using it" is not the same as having your own. Ask the football team if they'd take that deal.

Title IX turned fifty a few years back. Equity was never just about counting roster spots. It's the ground under your feet. Right now, the ground under our girls' feet is a swamp after every hard rain and a washboard when it dries.

I can hear the objection already: turf costs money. It does. So does resodding and reseeding a field that drowns twice a season. So do the hours parents spend driving forty minutes to borrowed fields for games that were supposed to be at home. So does an ACL surgery and nine months of physical therapy. The district found the money in 2019. The field hasn't gotten cheaper since then. It's just gotten worse.

And this isn't a gift to one team. A turf field gets used — both soccer programs, PE classes, youth leagues on weekends, community events. Grass fields around here sit empty half the year because nobody can play on them. Turf works every day. The football field has proven that for five years.

The school board votes on next year's facilities budget in [month]. Turf for the girls' soccer field needs to be in it. Not in "phase two." Not in some long-range plan that kicks the can past my current freshmen's graduation. In this budget, this year.

If you're a parent, an alum, or a taxpayer who thinks girls should play on the same quality field as boys, come to that meeting and say so. I'll be easy to spot. I'll be the one in the school windbreaker, holding a list of nine rained-out games and one torn ACL.

*The writer is the head girls' soccer and track coach at [School] High School.*

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
If you have a doodle, a golden, or really any double-coated or curly-haired pup, you already know the struggle of keeping their fur tangle-free between our grooming appointments. The absolute biggest mistake I see well-meaning owners make is throwing their dog in the tub first, thinking the warm water and shampoo will help loosen up any tangles. Please don't do this! Water actually tightens mats up. If you bathe a matted dog, that wet fur shrinks and locks together, basically turning into a solid felt pad that I’ll eventually have to shave off. Bathing first locks them in tighter, so you always want to brush before the bath at home, never after.

When you’re doing your brush-out, grab a good slicker brush and use short, straight line strokes rather than scrubbing in circles. Line brushing is much gentler on their skin and actually gets down to the undercoat instead of just polishing the top layer. Work in small sections, and always start behind the ears and under the front legs. Those are the high-friction areas where mats love to hide and form first, so it's best to tackle them right away. 

If you’re working through the coat and feel a mat starting to form, put the brush down for a second. Grab some dog conditioner and work it directly into the tangle with your fingers. Gently massage it and try to pull the hair apart with your hands before you ever touch it with a brush or comb. The slip from the conditioner saves the hair and saves your dog from the pain of having a brush ripped through a tight knot. Taking just a few extra minutes to do a proper brush-out before bath time makes a world of difference for your pup's comfort, and it keeps their coat looking beautiful until I see you at the salon next!

b.text:
If you only remember one thing between appointments, brush before the bath, never after. Wet matted fur doesn't loosen up. It felts. I see it every week on the table: a dog that was almost fine at home comes in after a "quick bath" with a pad of coat you could cut with scissors and still not get through.

This is mostly for the double-coated dogs and the curly ones — doodles, poodles, goldens, shepherds, the coats that tangle if you look at them wrong. A short smooth coat can get away with less. These can't.

Start with a dry coat and a slicker brush. Short strokes in a line, not circles. Circles just roll the loose hair back into the mat you're trying to get out. Work in sections, and start where the trouble actually starts: behind the ears and under the front legs. Those spots mat first because the dog rubs them, the collar sits there, and nobody thinks to check until the rest of the coat already looks fine.

If you already see a mat forming, don't go at it with the brush or a comb first. Work a little conditioner into it with your fingers until the hairs start to separate. Then brush. Pulling a dry mat with a slicker just breaks the coat and hurts the dog, and then they fight you the next time.

The mistake I see constantly is bathing first, on the theory that water and shampoo will loosen everything up. It does the opposite. Water swells the hair, soap strips the slip, and whatever was starting to tangle locks in tighter. By the time it dries you've got felt. Brush dry, deal with anything you can feel with your fingers, then bathe. If a mat is already too tight for your fingers and conditioner, stop. Don't cut it out at home unless you know exactly where the skin is. Bring them in and we'll take it from there.

Two inches of rain, and the west end turns into a pond that takes three days to drain. It’s not just the water, either. She just planted her foot to pass, hit a rut, and went down. Surgery, 9 months of rehab, missed her entire junior soccer season and most of track. I know what the school board’s going to say: turf is expensive. I’ve sat through enough budget meetings to hear the line about “limited capital funds” and “prioritizing core needs.” But let’s do the math, plain and simple. The district spends $12,000 a year on that soccer field: re-sodding the west end, filling ruts, renting portable pumps to drain the water after storms. The school board is about to vote on next year’s facilities budget. It’s time to put turf on the girls’ soccer field—with the drainage and maintenance plan needed to make it work.

When a game gets moved, families have to rearrange rides and work schedules. When it gets canceled, players lose a chance to compete after putting in the work to prepare. Coaches can adjust. So can kids. But nine games in two seasons is not an occasional inconvenience. It is a facilities problem.
