**An 8:45 Start Gives Our Kids a Better Chance**

As a parent of two middle-schoolers here in Millbrook, I know that getting kids out the door will never be effortless. There will still be missing sneakers, unfinished breakfasts and permission slips produced at the last possible second. But we don’t have to make the morning harder by asking adolescents to be ready to learn before their bodies are ready to be awake.

That’s why I support the school board’s proposal to move the start time to 8:45.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later. That recommendation recognizes something parents often see firsthand: sleep patterns shift during adolescence. “Just go to bed earlier” sounds sensible, but it isn’t the whole answer. A later start gives students a better opportunity to get the sleep they need.

We also have evidence closer to home. During the Lincoln Middle pilot, attendance and first-period grades went up. That doesn’t mean a later bell will solve every problem in our schools. It does mean we should take those results seriously. More students showing up, and doing better in their first class, are outcomes worth building on.

I’ve read the proposal closely, including the transportation section. The bus schedule is a fair concern. Families need reliable pickup times, and changes can complicate work schedules and arrangements for younger siblings. Those aren’t small inconveniences.

But the proposal already re-tiers the bus routes. It does not simply move the opening bell and leave transportation for someone else to figure out. Re-tiering won’t guarantee a flawless rollout, and the board should clearly explain the revised schedules and answer families’ questions before the change takes effect. Still, saying “What about the buses?” should begin that discussion, not end it.

I don’t expect every family to welcome a new routine. Ours will have adjustments to make, too. But keeping the current schedule also has costs. They’re just easier to overlook because we’ve gotten used to them.

The question is not whether 8:45 will make every morning easy. It won’t. The question is whether this proposal gives our children a better chance to arrive rested, attend consistently and learn when class begins.

The pediatric guidance points toward a later start. Lincoln Middle’s results are encouraging. And the proposal addresses the transportation issue.

Next month, I hope the board votes yes—and gives families the clear information we need to make the transition work.

b.text:
**Let Our Kids Sleep. Vote for the 8:45 Start.**

I'm the parent of two middle schoolers, and every school morning I know exactly what the wake-up looks like. My younger one is groggy until about ten. My older one doesn't really come online until after lunch. Anyone who has raised a teenager has seen this. It isn't laziness. It's biology.

During puberty, teenagers' internal clocks shift later. A kid who falls asleep around 10:30 or 11 is not being defiant. Their body is still on a different schedule. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., because teens who get enough sleep tend to be healthier, safer on the road, and better able to learn. Our current bell times ask kids to start the day hours before their brains are ready.

We don't have to guess how this would work in Millbrook. Lincoln Middle ran a pilot with a later start, and the results are encouraging. Attendance went up, and first-period grades improved. Those are outcomes we should want for every student, and they came from a change that required no new programs, just a different bell time.

I understand the concern about buses. Nobody wants a seventh grader waiting in the dark at a corner, and nobody wants a schedule that makes it impossible to get home for practice. But the proposal already re-tiers the bus routes to address exactly this problem. I've read the plan closely, and it's a real answer, not an afterthought. If there are specific stops or routes that still look wrong to you, bring them to the board with details so they can be fixed. That's a reason to refine the plan, not to abandon it.

Our kids are asking for something simple: a little more sleep and a fair shot at the school day. Next month, the school board has the chance to give them that. I hope they take it.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
## A $46,000 Increase for One Wet Spring

This spring, I was able to plant only 60% of my soybean and corn acres by the late-May deadline. The rain kept coming, and the fields stayed too wet to work. That left a large share of my operation facing prevented planting coverage.

At the same time, USDA raised the base prevented-planting premium rate in our region by 22%. For my farm, that increase adds approximately $46,000 to this year’s costs—before accounting for lost production, machinery expenses, input commitments, and the income we will not receive from those acres.

The acreage cap makes that increase even harder on family operations. The cap does not affect every farm in the same way. For a farm like mine, where each acre represents a larger share of the operation’s total revenue, the added premium cost takes a bigger proportional bite. Larger operations nearby may absorb the same rate increase across more acres and more production. Family farms do not have that same cushion.

This is not about avoiding responsibility or asking taxpayers to cover every bad outcome. We pay premiums, manage risk, and make planting decisions based on the best information available. But when a federally determined rate jumps 22% in a year when weather prevents planting, the acreage cap can turn an already difficult situation into a disproportionate financial burden for farms like mine.

Senate Bill 214 would fix the acreage-cap problem and make the program more equitable for family-sized operations. It would not eliminate the risks of farming or guarantee a profit. It would simply ensure that the program’s limits do not penalize smaller operations more severely than larger ones.

I encourage farm bureau members and other producers to contact their legislators and support SB 214. A $46,000 increase is not an abstract policy number for my farm. It is a real cost tied directly to a wet spring and a program structure that needs to be corrected.

b.text:
A 22% increase. An extra $46,000. Just 60% of my acres planted by the late-May deadline.

Those are the numbers behind this spring on our farm. The rain would not quit, and we could not get the rest of our corn and soybean acres planted in time. Now, on top of the lost planting opportunity, USDA’s increase in the prevented planting base premium rate is adding roughly $46,000 to our costs this year.

That is not a rounding error in a family farm budget. It is money that cannot go toward equipment payments, repairs, seed or the next season’s operating expenses.

I am a fourth-generation farmer. I understand that insurance costs money and that no program can take all the risk out of farming. But farmers ought to be able to expect rules that treat operations fairly.

The current acreage caps do not meet that standard. Because of how those caps work, this increase hits family operations like mine harder proportionally than some of the larger operations nearby. We faced the same wet spring, but the financial burden is not being shared evenly.

This is not an argument against bigger farms. It is an argument against a policy structure that puts a disproportionate burden on family operations because of where they fall under an acreage cap.

SB 214 would fix that cap. It would not stop the rain or recover the planting days we lost. It would address a problem lawmakers can actually do something about.

I encourage fellow Farm Bureau members to contact our state legislators and ask them to support SB 214. Tell them what the acreage cap means for your operation, and ask for a clear answer on where they stand.

We cannot legislate a dry spring. We can insist on fairer rules when a wet one keeps us out of the field.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
# Don’t Cut a Program That Puts People to Work

The state’s proposed 15% cut to apprenticeship funding is a bad way to save money. It takes support away from a program that trains workers, raises wages, and gives people a way to support themselves and their families.

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW. I’m learning this trade on the job and in the classroom. Apprenticeship is not just a class you take and hope leads somewhere. We work while we learn, and we build toward a skill and a wage we can live on.

Look at the results: 24 apprentices started in our cohort, and 21 finished and are now working as journeymen. That’s nearly 88% finishing and moving into skilled jobs. Those are real workers filling real needs.

Apprentices start at around $19 an hour, with pay reaching around $46 an hour as journeymen. At 40 hours a week for 52 weeks, that works out to about $39,500 a year at the start and $95,700 at the journeyman rate, before taxes and without overtime. Actual yearly earnings depend on hours worked, but the path forward is clear.

That kind of wage growth helps people get off assistance programs and pay their own bills. Instead of needing more public support, workers can contribute more in taxes and spend more at local businesses. That is a return on public money, not just an expense.

The cost comparison matters, too. The total public cost is about $14,000 per apprentice who finishes, compared with roughly $48,000 in average public subsidy per four-year college graduate who finishes. That puts apprenticeship at less than a third of the public cost.

This isn’t an argument against college. We need college graduates, too. But college is not the only path worth funding. The state should support a route that lets people earn while they learn and finish with skills employers need.

A 15% cut may look like savings on a budget sheet. But training still requires instructors, equipment, classroom space, and time. Cutting funding puts pressure on programs to take fewer apprentices, charge workers more, or stretch resources further. None of that helps build the skilled workforce our state needs.

Electrical work has to be done safely and correctly. You cannot replace solid training with a promise to figure it out later.

State legislators should reject this cut. Apprenticeship is doing what public workforce funding is supposed to do: helping people learn a trade, earn a decent living, and do work their communities depend on.

Don’t cut a program that is getting the job done.

b.text:
**Headline: Don’t Cut the Apprenticeship Funding That Actually Works**  
By a Third-Year IBEW Local [XXX] Electrical Apprentice

I’m not a policy expert. I spend most days with wire cutters in my hand, grease under my nails, and a tool belt digging into my hips, same as most of you reading this. But when I heard the state’s trying to slash apprenticeship funding by 15%, I knew I had to say something—because this program isn’t just a line item on a budget. It’s the reason I’m off food stamps, making a living wage, and don’t have to worry about how I’ll pay my kid’s daycare bill next month.

Let’s cut the crap and talk real numbers, no fancy spin, no academic jargon. The cohort I signed up with started with 24 apprentices. 21 of us finished all our required hours and classroom work, and every single one of those 21 is working a full-time journeyman job right now. No one’s scraping by on part-time gigs. No one’s collecting unemployment. We’re showing up to build schools, hospitals, and new housing, paying our taxes, and taking care of our families.

Here’s what that looks like for working people: apprentices start around $19 an hour. That’s not rich, but it’s enough to cover rent and put food on the table, even when you’re first starting out. By the time you top out as a journeyman, you’re making around $46 an hour, plus health insurance and a pension. I was on SNAP and Medicaid when I joined—my kid was a toddler then, and I was bouncing between odd construction jobs that didn’t pay enough to cover groceries and daycare. By my second year in the program, after two regular pay bumps, I was off both public assistance programs entirely. I didn’t need a handout anymore, because this program gave me a shot at a real career. That’s not just my story—most first- and second-year apprentices in our local will tell you the same thing: we don’t stay on public help long once we’re in this program.

Now let’s talk about the taxpayer side of this, because the legislators pushing this cut are saying they’re “saving money.” Let’s run the actual math, not the made-up numbers they’re using to sell this garbage. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes the program is about $14,000. Compare that to the average public subsidy for a four-year college grad who finishes their degree: $48,000. That’s more than three times as much money, and we all know how many college grads are stuck working jobs that don’t even need their degree, drowning in student loans, and not making half of what a journeyman electrician pulls down.

A 15% cut to apprenticeship funding isn’t saving money—it’s throwing away the best deal taxpayers get in this state. Let’s be clear about what that cut will actually do: it will mean fewer apprenticeship slots every year. Fewer people getting a shot at a middle-class job without going into tens of thousands of dollars in debt. More people stuck on public assistance for longer. And fewer qualified electricians to build all the new projects the state keeps saying it wants to prioritize—you can’t put up a new hospital or a new school without enough people to wire the place.

To my brothers and sisters in the local: this isn’t just about new apprentices. More skilled journeymen in our local mean we can take on bigger jobs, negotiate better contracts, and keep our union strong for everyone—from the first-year apprentice to the retired member collecting their pension. If you haven’t called your state rep or state senator yet, do it this week. Tell them what this program did for you, or for your kid, or for the apprentice you’re training on the job right now. Your voice matters a lot more than some lobbyist’s talking point.

To the state legislators who might be reading this: stop buying the myth that a four-year college degree is the only “real” career path. I work side by side with guys who quit college because they were $20,000 in debt and still couldn’t find a job that paid $15 an hour. This program works. It works for working people. It works for local contractors who need reliable, skilled workers. And it works for taxpayers, who get a way better return on their investment than they do from almost any other workforce program in the state.

This 15% cut isn’t fiscal responsibility. It’s cutting the only program that’s actually delivering on what it promises. I’m an electrician, not an English professor, so I’ll keep it as plain as I can: vote no on this cut. Our tax dollars should go to programs that get people to work, off public assistance, and paying into the system—not the other way around.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
Fix Our Girls' Soccer Field

I coach girls' soccer and track at the high school. I'm not a writer, so I'll keep this plain.

In the last two seasons we've had nine games rained out or moved because our grass field floods. Not because it rained that day. Because it rained two days before and our field still has standing water and mud. We practice around the puddles, we bus to the other team's field, we squeeze in varsity and JV back-to-back on a Sunday afternoon to make it up. My girls lose home games, lose practice days, and lose sleep trying to keep up with schoolwork around a rescheduled mess.

Last October one of my players tore her ACL when her foot stuck in a rut on that field. She was a junior. She missed the rest of soccer and all of track. If you've ever heard a kid scream like that and then sit on the bench for six months doing rehab while her team plays without her, you don't forget it. I can't say turf would have 100% prevented it. I can say our surface is uneven, chewed up, and unsafe, and we all know it.

The football field got turf back in 2019. Good for them. They play on time in November while we're in October canceling a home game because half the box is underwater. I'm not going to dress this up in legal language, but it doesn't look fair and it isn't fair. Boys get a field that drains. Girls get boots and excuses.

I hear the argument about money. I get it, it's not cheap. But we already paid for turf once for one team. You don't save money by sodding and re-sodding and paying staff hours to sandbag a field that was never built right to begin with. You pay twice — once for the bad field, and again when the girls can't use it.

The school board votes on the facilities budget next. Put turf on the girls' soccer field in it. Nine lost games in two years, a kid with a rebuilt knee, and six years watching the football team play dry while we wade. That's enough.

Our girls show up and work. Give them a field they can actually play on.

b.text:
Nine games. That's what we lost to water in the last two seasons. Nine games where I told my girls the field was unplayable, or worse—where we played on it anyway because there was nowhere else to go and they'd been training for it since August. I watched a midfielder try to cut left in a mud pit in November and just... keep sliding, losing three yards, getting up angry and soaking. I watched a sophomore tear her ACL in October stepping into a rut I'd flagged to the athletic department three times. She's got a surgery on her calendar and a semester off the pitch. Her senior season is over.

I'm not telling you this for sympathy. I'm telling you because next week the school board votes on the facilities budget, and I need you to look at what "facilities" means when half your athletes can't play on them for half the fall.

Let's be plain about the geography here. Our grass field—our *only* grass field for girls' soccer—floods because the drainage was never adequate and the grade is wrong and every November we play on what is functionally a creek bed with grass sticking out of it. You could argue we've made it work. I've made it work. My assistant and I have spent more November afternoons pushing water off the pitch with brooms than I care to admit. But "make do" has a body count, and right now it's one blown knee per season minimum, and nine cancelled games means nine fewer chances to be scouted, to compete, to not forfeit a match on a Tuesday because some other field opened up on short notice.

Now. Here's the thing I want the board to answer to their own faces: the boys' football field got turf in 2019. Same athletic budget. Same drainage problem. A decade of complaints about mud, about ruts, about kids blowing out a knee in November—and they fixed it. Six figures, done, problem solved. And I'm glad, genuinely, I'm glad for Coach Daniels and his players. But I have to ask: why does the fix require four years and three budget cycles when the players are girls in cleats instead of pads? Why does a girl's ACL cost less to prevent than a boy's?

I don't want to make this a fight. I don't want parents pitting one team against another at a board meeting in a fluorescent-lit room in March. But I will not pretend the timeline is an accident. The drainage report for the football field was the same report—*the same report*—that listed our field as the second priority. Second priority. We are still second priority six years later.

What I'm asking for is not a favor. Turf installation on the girls' field is roughly in line with what was spent on the football field in 2019. It is a line item. It is a one-time cost that stops me from spending October writing rain-out notices and stops a girl's parents from getting a phone call from me at 6 a.m. saying their daughter is going to the hospital. It means my track kids get a dry warm-up area in the spring. It means the JV game against Whitmore next November actually gets *played*.

The board gets to vote on the budget. The voters get to call them. I just want my girls to have a field that holds a game.

I'll be at the meeting in March. I'll be there with two of my assistants and at least three players' parents. You can talk to us after, if you want. We'll be the loud ones in the gymnasium with our cleats still muddy.

—Coach [Name], Head Coach, [High School] Girls Soccer & Track

setup: You're Curtis Webb. A physical therapist is replying to your referral question and suggesting a brief call.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
**The Case for Open Campus Lunch**

Every day at 11:40, three hundred and forty students file into a cafeteria built to seat two hundred and twenty. Some grab tables. Some eat standing against the wall or sit on the floor near the vending machines. This is not a hypothetical problem or a matter of student preference—it is a basic math problem our school faces every single lunch period. Granting open campus lunch privileges to juniors and seniors would relieve this overcrowding, and the evidence from neighboring districts shows it can be done without the disciplinary problems administrators fear.

The most immediate argument for open campus lunch is the state of our cafeteria itself. With 340 students assigned to a lunch wave and only 220 seats, the room is over capacity by more than fifty percent. That gap doesn't just mean discomfort; it means longer lines, more crowding at the doors, and students eating in hallways where food isn't supposed to be. If even a fraction of upperclassmen left campus for lunch, the students who remain—including all freshmen and sophomores—would have a cafeteria that actually functions as designed. Open campus lunch is often framed as a privilege for older students, but in our case it would directly benefit the younger students who stay behind.

Critics of open campus policies usually raise the same concern: students who leave for lunch will come back late, or not at all. This is a reasonable worry, but it is also a testable one, and nearby schools have already run the experiment. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—three districts within driving distance of ours—all allow open campus lunch for upperclassmen, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness after the policies took effect. These aren't distant schools in different circumstances; they are our neighbors, with similar schedules and similar students. If tardiness didn't spike there, there is no clear reason to assume it would spike here. A cautious administration could even follow their lead by starting with seniors only, or by making the privilege contingent on attendance records, as some of these districts do.

Finally, this is a change students actually want. In a survey I conducted of 80 students at our school, 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors—nearly ninety percent. A survey of 80 students is not the whole school, but a margin that lopsided suggests broad support rather than a vocal minority. Student buy-in matters here, because a privilege students value is a privilege they will work to keep. If the policy comes with clear conditions—return on time, maintain grades, keep the privilege—students have every incentive to follow the rules, because they were the ones asking for the policy in the first place.

Some will still argue that lunch supervision exists for student safety, and that the school is responsible for us during the day. But juniors and seniors are sixteen to eighteen years old. Many of us drive to school, hold jobs, and are trusted to manage our own schedules everywhere except the lunchroom. A policy that treats a seventeen-year-old with a part-time job and a driver's license as incapable of buying a sandwich and returning in forty minutes is out of step with the responsibility we're expected to show in every other part of our lives.

Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors would ease a genuine overcrowding problem, and the experience of Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade shows that the most common objection—tardiness—doesn't hold up in practice. The students support it, the neighboring districts have proven it workable, and the cafeteria numbers make the current situation unsustainable. Our school shouldn't wait until the crowding gets worse to consider a solution that is already working a few miles away.

b.text:
# Open Campus Lunch: A Practical Solution for Upperclassmen

Every day at 11:47, the bell rings and 340 students flood into a cafeteria built for 220. Kids eat standing up, sitting on the floor, or squeezed onto benches meant for fewer bodies. Meanwhile, just down the road, juniors and seniors at Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade high schools are eating lunch where they choose—and getting back to class on time. Our school should follow their lead and allow juniors and seniors to leave campus for lunch.

The most immediate reason to support open campus lunch is the overcrowding in our own cafeteria. The district's own capacity numbers show that the cafeteria seats 220 students, but the current lunch wave includes 340 kids. That means 120 students every single day have nowhere to sit. Some grab their food and head to hallways or the library, but those spaces aren't designed for eating and create their own problems—crumbs in the book returns, spills on the carpet, and students lingering where they shouldn't be. If even half of the upperclassmen left campus, the cafeteria population would drop to a manageable level. This isn't a luxury or a perk being requested; it's a fix to a problem the school already knows it has.

Nearby districts have already proven that open campus lunch can work without causing new problems. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow juniors and seniors to leave during lunch, and their published attendance data shows no rise in tardiness or afternoon absenteeism since implementing the policy. If students at those schools can make it back to sixth period on time, there is no reason to believe our students are less responsible. These are the same age groups driving to jobs after school, managing sports schedules, and handling college applications. A forty-minute lunch window is not an unreasonable test of their ability to manage time.

Student opinion also strongly supports the change. I surveyed 80 students at our school, ranging across all grade levels, and 71 said they would support an open campus policy for juniors and seniors. That is nearly 89% in favor. Even among freshmen and sophomores who would not directly benefit, most recognized that reducing cafeteria crowding would improve their own lunch experience. A policy that solves a logistical problem and has the support of the student body should not be difficult to adopt.

The most common argument against open campus lunch is safety. Administrators worry about students driving during lunch, getting into accidents, or engaging in unsafe behavior off school grounds. These are legitimate concerns, but they do not outweigh the benefits, and they can be managed. Fairmont requires a parent-signed permission slip for any student participating in open campus lunch, and violations result in immediate loss of the privilege. We could adopt the same system. A permission slip puts the decision in parents' hands, where it belongs, and a strike policy gives students a clear incentive to follow the rules. Safety concerns call for reasonable regulations, not a blanket prohibition.

Some might also argue that students will skip lunch entirely or make poor food choices. But students already have access to vending machines and bring junk food from home. Open campus does not create the problem of unhealthy eating; it simply gives responsible students more options. And the reality is that many students currently skip lunch or eat very little because the cafeteria lines are so long and the environment is so crowded that lunch feels more stressful than restful.

Our school has a cafeteria that cannot hold its students, neighboring districts with successful open campus policies, and a student body that overwhelmingly supports the change. The concerns are real but manageable with basic regulations like permission slips and a strike system. Juniors and seniors are nearly adults, and treating them as capable of handling a lunch period is both practical and fair. It is time to open the campus.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
**Subject: Launch week is over — here’s what actually happened (no big takeaways, I swear)**

Hey everyone,

If you’re reading this, I’ve finally stopped refreshing the Steam sales dashboard every 45 seconds, which feels like a win in itself. It’s been seven days since my first commercial launch dropped — three years of nights, weekends, skipping friend’s birthdays, and debugging collision at 2am all boiling down to this very weird, very unglamorous week.

First off, the numbers: 412 copies sold in the first seven days. I set a totally arbitrary, low-stakes goal of 100 copies when I started this, so 412 feels kind of insane, honestly. I spent $0 on marketing — just posted the trailer here, tweeted at three indie curation accounts that never replied, and crossed my fingers that someone would care.

The big surprise was hitting the front page of that small indie game subreddit I’ve lurked on since I started this project — you know the one — for about 6 hours on Wednesday. I found out because my Discord (which had 12 people in it pre-launch, all my IRL friends who let me bug test on their laptops) blew up while I was at my day job. I spent my entire lunch break refreshing the thread, half-convinced someone was gonna call out that one cave level texture I forgot to upscale. Most of the week’s sales came from that, I’m pretty sure. Shoutout to whoever crossposted the trailer — I owe you a coffee, or a Steam key for whatever my next game is, whichever you prefer.

The best feedback, though, was a Steam review that dropped on day two that just said “movement feels floaty” and nothing else. You’re right! That is 100% a valid complaint. I tuned the movement on my old work monitor that has like 20ms of uncalibrated input lag, so after three years of playing it that way, I didn’t even notice. I’ve been messing with acceleration curves and coyote time all week, and it’s already feeling way tighter. That’s gonna be the big focus for 1.1, which I’m aiming to put out next month.

1.1’s also gonna have a few other small things people have been asking for: rebindable controller buttons (I know, I know — how did I forget that? Solo dev brain rot is real), a fix for the final boss music cutting out if you skip the pre-fight cutscene, and that weird bug where the main character’s hair clips through their hat if you sprint up stairs. Nothing game-changing, just stuff that makes the whole thing feel a little more polished.

I don’t have some big, profound “lesson learned” to wrap this up with, if I’m being honest. Launch week was messy. I stayed up till 3am Tuesday fixing a crash that only happened on Windows 10 21H2, I forgot to eat on Wednesday because I was replying to Reddit comments, I cried a little on Thursday when someone left a review saying they played it with their 8-year-old kid and beat the final level together. It was just… a week. A really cool, really stressful week.

Next week I’m taking one (1) full day off to do nothing game dev related — no stats, no bug reports, no tweaking jump height at 10pm. Then I’m diving straight into 1.1, and I’ll probably post a devlog next week about the movement tuning process if anyone’s curious about the nitty gritty of adjusting acceleration curves without making the controls feel slippery.

If you bought the game, thank you. Seriously. If you left a review, good or bad, thank you — even the one that called the pixel art “mid” (you’re not wrong, I’m still learning). If you’re a fellow indie dev waiting for your own launch, it’s okay if it’s not perfect. It’s just a launch.

Alright, I’m gonna go heat up a frozen pizza and not look at my code editor for at least 8 hours. Talk soon.
[Your Name]

b.text:
Well, it’s finally out. After three years of nights and weekends, I launched my first commercial game last week. It feels incredibly weird to actually have it out in the wild.

For the numbers nerds out there, we sold 412 copies in the first seven days. I’m really happy with that for a debut. We also caught a nice little wave of traffic when the game hit the front page of a smaller subreddit, though the spike only lasted for about six hours before dropping off. Still, it definitely helped push the algorithm at the right time.

As for the feedback, I’ve been reading through all the reviews. Most of it has been great, but one reviewer pointed out that the movement feels "floaty." And honestly? They’re completely right. I spent so long staring at the same project that I just got used to it and lost my perspective. 

So, that’s the main focus for the 1.1 patch. I’m tightening up the controls, adjusting the acceleration curves, and making the character actually feel grounded. Expect that update to roll out sometime next month.

For now, I'm going to take a few days to just sleep and catch up on my backlog before diving back into the engine. Thanks to everyone who bought the game, played it, and left a review. I'll see you all when 1.1 is ready.

A while back, they cut the counter hours from 8 a.m. to noon. Naturally, the traffic dropped because folks couldn't get in there during a normal day. You starve a business of hours, it loses money. It's that simple.

Once the counter closes, she can’t drive twenty minutes down to Fairview just to buy a money order to pay for it. It's not fair to her, and it's not fair to the rest of the folks out here who depend on this service.

b.text:

I'm not a writer. I was the mail carrier on Route 4 for 22 years before I retired last year. Same 38 miles every day, so I think I know this town pretty well.

I'm writing about USPS closing the counter service at our post office. They say the branch loses $40,000 a year. That may be true on paper, but it's a problem they made themselves. First they cut the hours to 8 to noon. Of course traffic dropped after that. Most people here are at work in the morning. Then they point to the drop and say nobody uses it.

It's the same as cutting a road down to one lane and then complaining it doesn't get enough traffic to fix.

I think about Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She's in her 80s and gets her heart medicine by mail. She relies on that counter. setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8 Months of Near-Daily Market Baking

I've had the Corlane SM6 on my counter for eight months now, and unlike most of the gear that passes through my kitchen for a review, this one has earned its spot by actually working for a living. I bake sourdough for the farmers market most weekends, which means this machine gets fired up almost every day. Here's what I've learned.

## The Motor Is the Real Deal

This is where the SM6 justifies itself. I regularly run a double batch of stiff bagel dough through it, which is the kind of dense, low-hydration dough that makes lesser mixers whine, walk across the counter, or shut off entirely to protect themselves. The Corlane doesn't flinch. No stalling, no burning smell, no motor overheating cutoff. If you knead heavy dough, this is the headline feature, and it delivers.

## The Annoyances

Two of them, and I want to be honest about both.

First, the bowl lift lever squeaks. It started a couple months in, and I now hit it with a shot of WD-40 about once a month to keep it quiet and smooth. It's not a dealbreaker, but at this price point I shouldn't have to babysit a moving part on a schedule.

Second, and more irritating: the included dough hook is too short for the depth of the bowl. It doesn't reach the bottom well, so flour and shaggy dough get left behind and you're scraping constantly. I bought a third-party hook that fits properly, and it fixed the problem entirely. Frustrating that I had to spend extra to make the machine do its main job, but the fix is cheap and easy.

## The Price

It's $429. That's $80 more than the comparable KitchenAid. There's no getting around the fact that you're paying a premium, and you should know that going in.

## The Verdict

**Buy it if you knead heavy dough every week.** If you're running stiff bagel, bagel-adjacent, or high-volume sourdough batches the way I do, the extra $80 buys you a motor that won't quit, and that's worth every penny over the life of the machine. Budget another twenty bucks for a proper dough hook and expect to keep a can of WD-40 in the drawer.

**Skip it if you're mostly baking cookies and cake batter.** The SM6's whole advantage is its muscle, and you'll never use it. For lighter work, the cheaper KitchenAid does the same job, comes with a hook that actually fits, and doesn't squeak. Save your $80.

b.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: 8 Months of Almost-Daily Market Sourdough Use**

I’ve been using the Corlane SM6 stand mixer for eight months now, and during that time it has become one of the most-used tools in my kitchen. I bake sourdough for a weekend farmers market, so this mixer isn’t just handling the occasional Saturday loaf. It’s running almost daily, often for high-hydration doughs, stiff levain builds, and occasional bagel batches.

This is a real-world review from someone who actually leans on this machine for production baking, not just light home use.

## The Big Question: Is It Worth It?

**Yes — but only if you regularly knead heavy dough.**

If you bake bread, bagels, pizza dough, or stiff sourdough every week, the Corlane SM6 is worth buying. The motor is strong enough to handle demanding dough without the hesitation or stalling I’ve experienced with lighter-duty mixers.

If you mostly bake cookies, cakes, muffins, quick breads, or soft sandwich loaves, skip it. You do not need this mixer for that kind of baking, and the extra cost is not justified.

## How It Handles Heavy Dough

This is where the Corlane SM6 earns its place on my counter.

I regularly mix a double batch of stiff bagel dough in it, and the motor does not stall. It doesn’t bog down halfway through the mix, it doesn’t overheat quickly, and it doesn’t feel like it’s begging for mercy. That alone makes it noticeably different from many home stand mixers I’ve used.

For market baking, that reliability matters. When I’m mixing multiple loaves of sourdough or doing a larger batch of stiff dough, I need the mixer to keep moving without drama. The SM6 does that.

It feels especially suited to:

- Stiff sourdough
- Bagels
- Pizza dough
- Large bread batches
- High-gluten doughs
- Frequent, repeated mixing sessions

If you’re doing that kind of baking several times a week, this mixer makes sense.

## The Bowl Lift Lever Is Annoying

The biggest issue I’ve had with the Corlane SM6 is the bowl lift lever. It squeaks. Not just once in a while — regularly enough that I have to WD-40 it about once a month.

That is not a dealbreaker for me because the mixer itself performs well, but it is a maintenance issue I did not expect at this price point. If you want a machine you can completely ignore, this is not it. You will probably need to keep a little lubricant nearby.

It also gives the machine a slightly less polished feel than I’d like for a mixer costing more than a comparable KitchenAid. The performance is excellent, but this part of the design feels less refined than it should.

## The Included Dough Hook Is Too Short

The dough hook that comes with the SM6 is another problem.

The bowl is deep, and the stock hook does not reach low enough to do a great job with larger or stiffer batches. I found myself stopping the mixer more often than I wanted to, scraping the bowl, and trying to get the dough to incorporate evenly.

I ended up buying a third-party dough hook that reaches deeper into the bowl, and that solved the issue. The mixer itself is capable, but the included hook is not good enough for serious bread baking.

If you buy this mixer for bread, I would plan on replacing the hook.

## Price: More Expensive Than a Comparable KitchenAid

The Corlane SM6 costs **$429**. That is about **$80 more** than the equivalent KitchenAid model.

That matters. At this price, the squeaky bowl lift lever and short dough hook are harder to excuse.

However, if your main priority is kneading heavy dough repeatedly, the stronger motor performance is worth paying for. I would rather have the extra kneading capability for bread and bagels than save $80 and end up with a mixer that struggles under load.

But again, that only makes sense if you are actually doing heavy dough work.

## Who Should Buy the Corlane SM6

Buy the Corlane SM6 if you:

- Bake sourdough regularly
- Make bagels or other stiff doughs
- Mix large batches at home
- Need a mixer that can handle heavy gluten development
- Bake bread weekly or several times a week
- Sell baked goods and need a reliable workhorse

This mixer has handled my market baking schedule better than I expected, especially for the price tier.

## Who Should Skip It

Do not buy this mixer if you mainly:

- Bake cookies
- Make cake batter
- Whip cream
- Mix brownies
- Make occasional soft dinner rolls
- Bake bread only a few times a year

For those tasks, a standard KitchenAid or less expensive mixer is more than enough. The Corlane SM6 is built for dough work, and if that is not your primary use, you are paying for strength you will not regularly need.

## Final Verdict

**The Corlane SM6 is worth buying if you knead heavy dough every week.**

It has survived eight months of almost-daily use in my sourdough and market baking routine, and the motor has consistently handled stiff double batches without stalling. That is the core reason I would recommend it.

But it is not a perfect machine. The bowl lift lever squeaks and needs monthly lubrication, the included dough hook is too short for the deep bowl, and it costs $80 more than an equivalent KitchenAid.

Still, for serious home bread bakers, the tradeoff is worth it. I can rely on it for the hardest part of the job: kneading heavy dough repeatedly without complaint.

**Verdict: Buy it if you bake serious bread. Skip it if you mostly bake cookies and cake batter.**

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
**A 22% Premium Hike Family Farms Can’t Absorb**

USDA raised the prevented planting premium base rate in our region by 22% this year. For my farm, that works out to roughly $46,000 in additional cost—before accounting for seed, fertilizer, equipment, land, labor and every other expense involved in putting in a crop.

This is not a theoretical concern. This spring, the rain would not let up, and I was able to plant only about 60% of my soybean and corn acres by the late-May deadline. Prevented planting coverage is meant for exactly this kind of year. Farmers buy it because no amount of planning, experience or work can make a field dry enough to plant.

I am a fourth-generation farmer. My family has managed through wet springs, dry summers, low prices and rising input costs. We understand that risk comes with the job. But a 22% increase in one year is not a routine adjustment. An extra $46,000 is money that cannot go toward machinery repairs, land payments, hired help or next year’s crop.

The acreage caps make the burden even less equitable. Because of the way those caps are structured, family operations like mine can end up paying more proportionally than larger operations nearby. Bigger farms may have more total acres and higher overall costs, but they also have more room to spread those costs. A family farm operating within a narrower acreage and financial margin does not have that same cushion.

That is why Senate Bill 214 deserves the Farm Bureau’s support. SB 214 would fix the acreage cap so the cost is distributed more fairly and family-sized operations are not hit disproportionately.

This is not a request to eliminate premiums or shift every risk away from farmers. We know coverage has a cost, and we expect to pay our share. What we are asking for is a structure that does not punish farms simply because of their acreage mix or size.

A $46,000 increase may appear as one line in an insurance calculation, but on a family farm it affects real decisions. It can mean postponing an equipment purchase, cutting back on improvements, taking on more debt or having less cash available for the next difficult season. Multiply that across family farms in our region, and the effects reach equipment dealers, seed suppliers, repair shops and rural communities.

Farm Bureau members should contact their state legislators and ask them to support SB 214. Lawmakers need to hear what a 22% hike and the current acreage caps mean at the farm level.

This spring, I got 60% of my acres planted by the deadline. I did everything I could with the weather I was given. The policy covering the other 40% should be priced fairly. SB 214 is a practical step toward making that happen.

b.text:
The 22% Prevented Planting Premium Hike Is a Family-Farm Tax

The prevented planting base premium rate in our region went up 22 percent this year. For my operation, that is not an abstract number. It is $46,000 in added premium cost before I put a single seed in the ground.

This spring, I got 60 percent of my soybean and corn acres planted by the late May final planting date. The other 40 percent sat underwater. That is exactly the situation prevented planting coverage was designed to address. I still have land payments due, property taxes due, equipment notes due, and seed already committed. The prevented planting indemnity does not make me whole. It keeps a bad year from turning into a forced sale.

But here is what should bother every farm bureau member in this county: the 22 percent base rate increase is not being applied in a way that matches the actual risk on family farms. Because of how the acreage caps work, my operation pays the increase on a much larger share of my total acres than the bigger operations nearby. A large operation with thousands of acres can absorb the rate hike across a broader planted base. My family operation cannot. The result is that I pay $46,000 more for the same coverage at the exact moment 40 percent of my ground is producing nothing. That is a tax on being a family farm.

SB 214 fixes that. It would adjust the prevented planting acreage cap so that the premium calculation reflects a farm’s actual planting history and prevented planting exposure, not a one-size-fits-all cap that punishes smaller operations. It does not create a new payment. It does not add a new program. It simply makes the premium structure fairer.

This matters beyond my fencerows. The $46,000 I now have to send to the insurance pool is $46,000 I will not spend at the local seed dealer, the elevator, the implement dealer, or the tire shop. When family operations get squeezed disproportionately, the whole county absorbs the loss.

I am not asking for a bailout. I am asking for a premium structure that does not treat a 1,200-acre family operation as if it had the same cash reserves as a 12,000-acre corporation. SB 214 is the narrow fix that would do that.

Call your state senator this week. Ask them to support SB 214. If we wait until next spring’s premium bills arrive, the 22 percent will already be locked in.

We'd prefer someone with at least a year of clinical experience, mostly because of the solo nights. New grads with strong externship experience in emergency or ICU settings are welcome to apply too.

If this sounds like something you'd want rather than something you'd tolerate, send your resume to the email in our profile or message me directly. Happy to answer questions before you apply.

a.text:
I should probably start this by saying that if you emailed me about a wedding cake in the last few months and I got back to you with a kind but vague “let me check our calendar,” I’m sorry for the slow dance. I knew the answer was probably no, but saying it out loud—or, well, typing it—took me longer than I expected.

We’re not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore. I want to tell you why, and I don’t want it to sound like one of those corporate policy memos, so bear with me while I just talk it through.

It’s four in the morning when I get here most days. The dark still feels different at four—thicker, quieter. I turn on the ovens, start the coffee, and by six we’re pulling the first scones and the regulars start filtering in. That’s the part I love. The rhythm of it. The woman who gets the same sourdough roll every Tuesday, the kid who presses his nose to the pastry case waiting for the chocolate croissants. That everyday case—the muffins, the loaves, the little birthday cakes you grab on the way home from work—is what keeps our lights on. It’s what pays the rent on this little shop.

Somewhere along the way, we started saying yes to wedding cakes. And don’t get me wrong, they were beautiful. There’s something about a three-tier cake that makes you feel like a real artist. But here’s the thing nobody tells you when you’re dreaming of buttercream flowers: before you even turn on the mixer, you’ve already given away about fourteen hours. Tastings, consultations, emails at midnight about whether the shade of blush is too peach, sketching, resketching, driving to venues, driving back. All of it unpaid. And for a shop our size—there’s three of us, and two of those hands are mine by four a.m.—that time has to come from somewhere. It was coming from the case. It was coming from sleep. It was coming from the bread that actually pays the bills.

Then this year, three couples cancelled last minute. Full stop, no deposit, no nothing. I’d already bought the specialty chocolate, the vanilla beans, the fondant, rented the stands. When you’re small, you can’t just absorb that. You also can’t get back the weeks of planning and the early mornings that went into a cake that never got made. I stood in the walk-in looking at ingredients for a wedding that wasn’t happening and I just... I couldn’t do it anymore. Not without letting down the part of this business that keeps us here.

I know some of you will be disappointed. Maybe you were saving up to ask us. I hate that. But I also know you come in because you trust that the sourdough will be ready at seven and the cinnamon rolls won’t sell out before eight. To keep that promise, I have to be here, fully, for the daily stuff. The stuff that smells like home when you walk through the door.

We’re still making cakes, of course. If you need something for a Saturday dinner or a small party, we’ll do our best. But the big, elaborate, months-in-the-making wedding cakes? That’s a chapter we’re closing. Not because we don’t love love—we do. But because we love this shop, and our regulars, and the quiet magic of an ordinary Tuesday morning too.

Thank you for understanding. See you tomorrow—I’ll have the coffee on.

b.text:
Hi friends,

I'm writing this in that little quiet window after the first trays come out of the oven and before the morning rush starts, which is pretty much when all my writing gets done these days.

I wanted to tell you ourselves, because you'll start hearing it at the counter anyway: we're going to stop taking custom wedding cake orders.

This was not an easy one for us to land on. It has been such an honor to be part of people's wedding days, truly. Seeing photos of cakes we made being cut into while everyone you love is in the room, that never gets old. We're so grateful to every couple who trusted three sleepy bakers with something that important.

The hard truth is we're just three people. When we take on a custom wedding cake, it's not just the baking day. It's usually about 14 hours before we ever turn the oven on for it — the emails back and forth, the consults, the tastings, sketching ideas, re-sketching them, ordering special ingredients. We don't charge for that time, and for a long while we told ourselves that was just part of it.

But this year we've had three weddings cancel at the very last minute, after we'd already bought everything for them. And I mean everything — the good butter, the chocolate, the vanilla, boxes and boards in just the right size. We ate that cost, because that's what you do, but for a shop our size, three times in a few months really stings.

More than anything, though, I noticed what it was doing to our everyday case. On wedding weeks, we were pulling our hands and our hours away from the croissants and the sourdough and the sticky buns and the little cakes that so many of you come in for on your way to work or after school pickup. And honestly, that everyday case is what actually pays our rent. It's you, coming in regularly, that keeps us here.

So we need to put our time back there. If you've already booked a wedding cake with us, please don't worry for one second — we're all set and we can't wait to make it for you. We're just not taking on new custom wedding orders going forward.

I hope you understand. This isn't about loving weddings any less, it's about making sure we can keep doing the daily baking we love, and keep doing it well, for a long time.

Thank you for reading this far, and for being the kind of customers we get to explain things to like this. We'll see you at the counter — probably with flour on us, as usual.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years of helping buyers—mostly first-timers—navigate the Asheville market, I’ve realized that the secret to long-term home happiness isn’t found on an inspection report or a spreadsheet. The buyers who end up truly loving their homes years down the road are almost always the ones who walk the neighborhood at 7:00 AM before our scheduled tour. 

I always think about my clients, the Pruitts, when they were looking at a cottage on Sycamore Street. On paper, the house was perfect, but they were understandably nervous. It was their first purchase, and they wanted to be absolutely sure. I suggested they get up early, grab some coffee, and just walk the block on a weekday morning. 

By walking the street at 7:00 AM, they saw the neighborhood wake up. They saw who was walking dogs, how the morning traffic moved, and how quiet the block actually was when the rest of the world was starting their day. They got a feel for the rhythm of the street in a way that a Saturday afternoon open house could never replicate. 

They bought the house, and to this day, they tell me that early morning walk was the moment they knew they were actually home. 

If you're searching for a home right now, don't just look at the house. Go stand on the sidewalk at 7:00 AM on a Tuesday. It tells you everything the listing description can't.

b.text:
After 12 years of selling homes, mostly to first-time buyers, I've noticed that the buyers who are happiest a few years later often did one thing the others didn't. They walked the neighborhood at 7am before we ever toured the house.

I never used to suggest it. The Pruitts taught me. They were looking at a little brick ranch on Sycamore Street, and the night before our showing, Dana texted to ask if it was weird that she and Marcus wanted to just walk around the block first thing in the morning. I said it wasn't weird at all, and that I'd meet them at the house at 10.

When I pulled up, they'd already been there for almost two hours. They'd watched the school bus stop at the corner, talked to a neighbor who was out with his dog, and noticed which houses had lights on and which had cars gone by 7:30. Marcus had timed the walk to the nearest coffee shop. Dana had listened for traffic noise and heard almost none, which surprised her because the street looks like it might be a cut-through on the map.

By the time we got inside, they weren't asking whether they liked the house so much as whether the house could work. The kitchen was smaller than what they'd pictured, and the closets were tight. A few weeks later the inspection turned up a roof that needed attention sooner than we'd hoped. I've seen that news sink other buyers. The Pruitts were disappointed, but they were steady. They already knew they wanted to live on that street, so they negotiated the repair and moved forward.

They've been there a few years now, and Dana still sends me a photo every fall when the sycamores drop their leaves all over the yard.

What I took from it is that a showing tells you about a house, and a showing happens at a time that's convenient for everyone, with the lights on and the seller's candle burning. A 7am walk tells you about the life around the house, and that's the part you can't renovate. Now I suggest it to every buyer. Go early, bring coffee, and see who's out there. If you walk away feeling good about it, that matters. If you don't, that matters too, and it's much cheaper to find out before you're under contract.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: After 8 Months of Daily Sourdough Production**

I’ve been using the Corlane SM6 almost daily for eight months now, which means it is not sitting on my counter collecting dust. It is pulling heavy mix loads for weekend sourdough, bagels, and everything dough that I take to the farmers market. If you’re wondering whether it’s worth the money, here’s the honest picture from a home baker who actually puts it to work.

**The Good: The Motor Does Not Quit**

This is the main reason the mixer earns a recommendation. The SM6 handles a double batch of stiff bagel dough without stalling. That is not an exaggeration. I know exactly what heavy dough feels like when a mixer starts to struggle—the head shifting, the motor bogging down, the smell of stress. With the SM6, the dough comes together cleanly and the motor never seems close to giving up.

For sourdough, the mixer is strong enough to pull gluten quickly without heating the dough too aggressively. That matters when you are making dough at home that still needs to stay cool and manageable. For bread bakers, this is the mixer’s strongest point.

**The Bad: The Bowl Lift Lever Squeaks**

The mixer is not perfect. The bowl lift lever squeaks, and I have to lubricate it with WD-40 once a month to keep it quiet. It’s not a dealbreaker, but it is annoying. If I’m mixing early in the morning, that squeak is the one part of the routine I do not miss.

This is the kind of maintenance you shouldn’t have to do every month, but it’s easy enough to deal with. Still, it’s worth knowing before you buy.

**The Awkward Part: The Included Dough Hook Is Too Short**

The dough hook that comes with the SM6 is too short for the deep bowl. This is a real flaw because the hook is the one accessory most people expect to work properly with the mixer they just bought. Instead of mixing correctly, it does not reach or scrape the deep bowl the way it should.

I ended up buying a third-party dough hook, which fixed the problem. If you buy this mixer for bread or bagels, budget for the better hook. Do not let the stock hook discourage you from a machine that otherwise performs very well.

**The Price: More Than a Comparable KitchenAid**

The Corlane SM6 is $429, which is $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid I would normally compare it to. That difference is noticeable. You need to understand that you are not buying this because it is the cheapest option. You are buying it for heavy dough performance.

For cookie bakers or cake bakers, that extra $80 is hard to justify. For a baker mixing double batches of stiff dough every week, the price is easier to defend.

**Final Verdict: Buy It If You Knead Heavy Dough Every Week. Skip It If You Mostly Bake Cookies and Cakes.**

The Corlane SM6 is a serious mixer for serious dough. If your baking involves sourdough, bagels, dense bread dough, or anything thick enough to make a weaker mixer stall, this one is worth buying. It earns its keep in my kitchen because I use it for work, not just convenience.

But if you mostly make cookies, cake batter, meringue, or light bread dough, you do not need this machine. You are paying for strength you probably won’t use. For that kind of baker, the SM6 is not a smart buy.

For me, the SM6 is a yes. It has the motor performance I need for market bread, even with the squeaky lift lever and the poor included hook. It is not flawless, but it is strong, reliable, and worth the upgrade if heavy dough is a regular part of your week.

b.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: 8 Months of Heavy Dough**

It’s been eight months since I unboxed the Corlane SM6 stand mixer, and it has seen the inside of my kitchen almost every single day. Between prepping my weekend farmers market sourdough orders and testing recipes for the blog, this machine has been put through the wringer. Here is my honest, unvarnished take on whether it deserves a spot on your counter.

Let’s start with the motor, because that’s what really matters when you’re baking at volume. The Corlane SM6 is an absolute workhorse. I regularly throw massive, high-hydration sourdough batches at it, but the real test was a double batch of stiff, low-hydration bagel dough. The motor didn't even flinch. There was zero stalling, no overheating, and no struggling walk across the counter. It powered through the stiffest doughs I could throw at it with total ease.

But it’s not a perfect machine. The bowl lift lever has an annoying squeak that develops after a few weeks of heavy use. I’ve resigned myself to giving it a quick blast of WD-40 once a month to keep it quiet and smooth. More frustrating is the included dough hook. For some reason, Corlane designed a beautifully deep bowl but paired it with a dough hook that is too short to reach the bottom effectively. I ended up having to buy a third-party hook just to get a proper knead on my standard batches.

Then there is the price. At $429, the Corlane SM6 is exactly $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid model. That is a premium you need to justify. 

Here is my final, definitive verdict: Buy the Corlane SM6 if you knead heavy dough every week. If you are baking market-level volumes of sourdough, bagels, or stiff pizza dough, the superior motor torque easily justifies the $80 premium over the KitchenAid, and the deep bowl is fantastic for large batches. Skip it entirely if you are mostly doing cookies and cake batter. If you are primarily mixing butter and sugar, the KitchenAid is cheaper, the attachments fit perfectly out of the box, and you simply do not need this level of heavy-duty motor power.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
**A 15% Cut to Apprenticeship Is a Bad Deal for the State**

Our state is proposing a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding. I want to explain why I think that's a mistake, and why it won't save the state money — it will cost it money.

**Let's talk about what the money actually buys.**

My apprenticeship cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished. All 21 are working journeyman jobs right now. That is a completion rate of about 88%, and every one of those 21 is on a payroll, paying taxes, paying rent, and buying a car.

The total public cost per apprentice who finishes in our program is about $14,000.

Now compare that to the state's own figure for a four-year college graduate who finishes: about $48,000 in public subsidy per graduate. That's more than three times what we cost the state per person who completes training — and that's before you count the students who start college and never finish, which cost the state money too.

So the cheaper program produces the higher completion rate. That is not a close call.

**Apprentices pay their own way while they learn.**

Apprentices start around $19 an hour. journeymen top out around $46 an hour. Our apprentices are earning wages from day one. We're not sitting in a classroom with a loan and no income. We're not on the state's assistance rolls. When we finish and get on as journeymen, we leave those programs fast — and then we're paying into them.

I can tell you firsthand what that means for a town. When the apprenticeship program works, local electrical contractors have steady, skilled, licensed workers. They can take on bigger jobs. They can bid work they couldn't bid before. When those contractors do well, they employ more people — and most of those people are apprentices.

The employers getting a free, ready-made workforce are the small and mid-size electrical contractors. They cannot afford to run their own training program for four years. The apprenticeship program is how they get trained people who already know safety, code, and the tools of the trade. Cut the funding and you're not just hurting apprentices. You're hurting the contractors who depend on them, and eventually the homeowners who need licensed electricians instead of somebody working cheap and unqualified.

**And we're talking about safety.**

The alternative to a trained, licensed electrician is somebody who learned the trade on a customer's house without supervision. That's how people get hurt. That's how houses burn down. That's how code gets broken. The cheapest thing the state can do for safety is make sure the people working on our buildings are trained. Cutting apprenticeship funding to save money is cutting the wrong program.

**What $14,000 buys versus what $48,000 buys.**

Take $14,000 and you get me. Take $14,000 and you get 21 electricians in my class who finished the program, who are working journeyman jobs today, at a cost of about $670 a year a piece to the state. I don't know what $14,000 buys at a university, but I know what it bought in our program: twenty-one people with a journeyman card, a paycheck, and no student loan.

**Where this leaves us.**

Somebody in a state office has looked at a spreadsheet and decided that the number next to "apprenticeship" was too big. I understand that pressure. But the number is $14,000 per person who finishes, and that person goes straight into the workforce and pays taxes for the next 30 years. This is one of the best investments the state makes. A 15% cut doesn't fix a budget problem. It just produces fewer electricians and more people who never finished anything.

I'd ask the legislators reading this to do the same thing I did: take the cost per completer for each program the state funds, then take the completion rate and the earnings for each one, and compare. I'm confident in the result.

If you agree, contact your state representative and ask them to vote against the cut. Tell them what I told you: 24 started, 21 finished, all 21 working. About $14,000 a head. And a graduate who walked out of a state-funded apprenticeship is worth more to the state than one who walked out of a subsidized degree program.

That's a good deal for the taxpayers of this state. Let's not throw it away.

— *Third-Year Electrical Apprentice, IBEW Local [Number]*

b.text:
# Keep the Funding, Keep the Pipeline

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW, and I'm writing this because the state is talking about cutting apprenticeship funding by 15%. That's a bad idea, and I want to explain why using numbers that actually mean something.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. 21 of us finished, and every one of us is working journeyman jobs right now. That's not a feel-good story. That's a success rate, and it's real. We didn't drop out because we got bored or because the program wasn't worth our time. We stuck with it because the path was clear: put in the work, learn the trade, come out making a living wage.

Apprentices in our program start around $19 an hour. By the time you top out as a journeyman, you're making around $46 an hour. That means within a few years, people who might have been on food stamps or other assistance are off it. Not because someone gave them a pep talk, but because they learned a skill that pays. I've watched guys in my cohort go from barely getting by to buying homes and supporting families. That happens because the training is funded and the jobs are there.

Now look at the cost side. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes our program is about $14,000. Compare that to roughly $48,000 in average public subsidy per four-year college graduate who finishes. I'm not knocking college. Some jobs need a degree, and that's fine. But if the state is looking at where it gets return on its money, apprenticeship programs are a better deal by a long shot. We produce working tradespeople at less than a third of the public cost, and those tradespeople start paying taxes and spending in their communities right away.

A 15% cut doesn't sound huge until you think about what it actually does. It means fewer apprentices accepted. It means less classroom instruction time. It means tools and materials that are already stretched thin get stretched thinner. When my cohort went through, we had what we needed. If you cut 15% off the budget, the next cohort won't. You can't train electricians on hopes and good intentions. You need funded seats, funded instructors, and funded materials.

Here's what I want the legislators reading this to understand: apprenticeship funding isn't a handout. It's an investment that pays back fast. Every apprentice who finishes becomes a taxpayer, a consumer, and a skilled worker the state needs. Every apprentice who doesn't get a seat because of budget cuts is someone who stays underemployed or on assistance longer. The math on that is simple, and it doesn't require a fancy economic study to figure out.

My cohort is proof this works. 21 out of 24 finished. We're working. We're paying taxes. We're not drawing on public assistance. And the state got all of us trained for $14,000 each. Find me a better deal than that anywhere in the budget.

Keep the funding where it is. Better yet, increase it. The trades are short on people, and the people are ready to do the work. All we need is the state to not pull the rug out from under the programs that get us there.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
## What You'll Need

A radiator bleeder key (a few bucks at any hardware store), a flathead screwdriver as backup, a small cup or bowl, and a rag. That's it. Most baseboard bleeder valves take either the key or the screwdriver depending on the age of the unit — grab both and you're covered.

## Step 1: Shut Down the Circulator and Boiler

Kill power to the boiler at the switch or breaker before you touch anything. You want the water in those loops sitting still. If the circulator pump is running while you bleed, it'll keep pushing air around the system and you'll be chasing bubbles all afternoon. Give it fifteen or twenty minutes after shutdown so everything settles and the air rises to the high points where you can actually get at it.

## Step 2: Find the Bleeder Valve

Pop the end cap off the baseboard unit — they usually just lift or pull straight off, sometimes there's a screw. Look at the elbow where the pipe turns. You're looking for a small brass fitting, maybe the size of a dime, with either a square nub on it or a slot for a screwdriver. That's your bleeder. Some units have it on the left end, some on the right. Some older installs put it up high on the return side. If you don't see one, check the other end of the unit before you assume it doesn't have one.

## Step 3: Cup Underneath, Then Open Slowly

Hold your cup right under the valve and put the rag under that. The water that comes out is hot and it's dirty — it'll stain a carpet and it will not come out. Now turn the valve counterclockwise, but go slow. A quarter turn is usually plenty.

You'll hear hissing. That's the air, and that's exactly what you're here for. Let it hiss until it stops and you get a steady stream of water with no sputtering. Not a dribble, not spitting — steady. That's how you know that unit is clear.

## Step 4: Close It Snug, Not Tight

Turn it back clockwise until it stops and the water quits. Then stop. These valve seats are soft brass and people crank on them like a lug nut. You'll crack the seat, and then you've got a slow drip in your living room and a call to me on a Saturday. Snug is snug.

## Step 5: Work Your Way Out from the Boiler

Start with the unit closest to the boiler and work outward along the loop, finishing with the farthest one. Doing it in order pushes the air ahead of you instead of pulling it backward into units you already did. If you jump around, you'll end up re-bleeding half of them.

When you're done, turn the boiler back on and check the pressure gauge. Cold system should read somewhere around 12 to 15 psi. If you bled a lot of water out, the pressure may have dropped and you'll need to top the system off with the fill valve. If you're not sure which valve that is, don't guess — call us.

## The Mistake That Causes Most of Our Cold Radiator Calls

People bleed the bedrooms upstairs, feel good about it, and skip the basement.

I'd say better than half the cold-baseboard calls we run in the fall are exactly this. The homeowner did the work, did it correctly, and the heat still isn't right — because the air is trapped in the basement loop and nobody touched it.

Basement units get ignored because they're behind boxes, behind the workbench, tucked under the stairs, or the room's a laundry room nobody cares about being warm. But that loop is part of the same system, and air in the basement zone will absolutely starve the units downstream of it. Move the boxes. Bleed every single unit on every single loop, including the ones in rooms you don't heat on purpose.

Same goes for any baseboard in an addition, a converted garage, or a finished attic. If it's got fins and a pipe, it needs bleeding.

## If It's Still Cold After All That

You've got something else going on — a stuck zone valve, a failing circulator, a clogged loop, or air that isn't coming out because there's a bigger problem with the air separator or expansion tank. That's not a homeowner fix and there's no shame in that.

Bleeding is fifteen minutes of work that prevents a lot of misery in January. Do it now while it's still mild enough that a mistake isn't an emergency. If you get in there and find something you don't like the look of, give us a call and we'll come take a look.

b.text:
# How to Bleed Your Baseboard Heating Before Winter

## What You'll Need

- A bleeder key (or flathead screwdriver, depending on your valve style)
- A small cup or bowl
- An old towel

## Step 1: Shut Off the System

Turn off your circulator pump and boiler before you touch anything. Bleeding a system that's actively running just pushes more air through and can make a mess when you crack the valve open. Give it a few minutes to settle.

## Step 2: Locate the Bleeder Valve

Every baseboard unit has a bleeder valve at one end, usually up near the top. It's a small brass fitting with a square stem (for a key) or a slotted screw head (for a flathead).

## Step 3: Position Your Cup

Hold a small cup or bowl underneath the valve before you open it. Water's going to come out once the air clears, and you want it caught, not running down your wall or pooling on the floor.

## Step 4: Open the Valve Slowly

Using your key or flathead, turn the valve counterclockwise just a quarter turn. You'll hear hissing — that's the air escaping. Keep it open until the hissing stops and water starts flowing out in a steady stream with no sputtering.

## Step 5: Close It Snug

Turn the valve clockwise until it's closed. Snug is enough — don't crank down on it. Overtightening is one of the easiest ways to crack the valve seat, and then you're looking at a leak instead of just some trapped air.

## Step 6: Work Your Way Through Every Unit

Start with the baseboard closest to the boiler and move outward from there, room by room. Skipping around can leave pockets of air trapped in the lines.

## The Step Everyone Misses

Here's where most of our cold radiator calls come from: homeowners bleed every unit upstairs, feel good about it, and stop there. But the basement loop is usually where the air is actually sitting. If you've got baseboard heat running through the basement, bleed those units too — even if that room feels warm enough already. Skip it, and you'll likely be back at this same job in a few weeks wondering why the upstairs is cold again.

## When to Call a Pro

If you're bleeding every unit and still getting weak heat, or if a valve won't close all the way once you're done, that's usually a sign of something bigger — a failing circulator, a pressure issue, or a valve that needs replacing. That's when it's time to give us a call instead of forcing it.
