setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
Eight wins and a playoff exit. That’s the headline. But if you’re looking past the final score in Round 2, the real story isn’t about a sudden collapse—it’s about a choice made when it mattered most.

Let’s get the obvious out of the way. Dez Kowalski put up numbers that’ll live in the record books forever. 2,340 passing yards. A new school standard. That’s worth a nod. So is going 8-2 and proving you could handle a regional powerhouse when you blew them off the field by 20 points back in Week 3. This group showed up when expected.

Playoffs, though, don’t care about résumés. They care about what you run when the noise drowns out the practice reps. In the second half, sitting on a three-point cushion, the offense shifted gears. They took the ball out of the hands of their runners and started living on the sideline. The run game was working. The interior push was creating seams. The backs were reading blocks cleanly. Yet the playbook flipped toward vertical shots against a defense that spends its whole week preparing for long passes. That wasn’t a calculated adjustment. It was hesitation wearing a coaching headset.

When you walk away from what’s producing with single digits on the board, you cede control. You play into the opponent’s strength and strip your own team of rhythm. Dez can stack yardage all December, but a quarterback can’t manufacture leverage alone. This team knew how to eat clocks, punish tackles, and force opposing coordinators to call timeouts. They abandoned their teeth right when they needed to bite.

There’s no shame in losing to a team you proved you could beat months earlier. Shame comes from changing your identity the moment the pressure rises. Beating someone once is a statement. Doing it twice is a habit. Dropping the run game in the third quarter turned a habit into a cautionary tale.

The record stands. The milestone stands. But the lesson hangs heavier. Championships aren’t won by chasing stat lines. They’re decided by trusting your foundation when the floor starts shaking. If this staff and those seniors remember that before cleats hit grass again, next fall won’t look like this one.

b.text:
**A Great Season, A Coaching Mistake, and an Early Winter**

An 8-2 record looks great framed on the wall at the diner. It’ll read nicely in the spring sports banquet program, too. But let’s not sugarcoat Friday night: the boys should still be playing football this week. 

Losing in the second round of the state playoffs is tough enough. Losing to a team you ran off their own field by 20 points back in September makes it a bitter pill that's going to stick in this town's throat all winter. 

Before we get to the autopsy, credit where it’s due: Dez Kowalski put together the finest season under center this town has ever seen. Setting the school single-season record with 2,340 passing yards is a massive achievement, and Kowalski played with heart and grit from August two-a-days all the way through Friday night. He earned every bit of that record. 

But relying exclusively on Dez’s right arm in the second half is precisely why the season is over.

Coming out of the locker room down just three points, the game plan inexplicably went into panic mode. The ground game was chewing up five yards a pop in the first half and keeping the defense honest, yet the coaching staff put it in mothballs the minute the third quarter kicked off. You don't abandon the run when you're within one field goal. When you become one-dimensional against a playoff defense out for revenge, you’re playing right into their hands. They pinned their ears back, brought pressure, and dared us to beat them with an empty backfield. We couldn't.

It’s easy to look at an 8-2 finish and call it a total success, and these kids have plenty to be proud of. But championships aren't won by getting cute with the playbook when a fistfight is required. Friday night was a winnable game that got away because we stopped doing what got us there.

b.text:
When the late May planting deadline hit, four out of every ten acres on my place were still too wet to touch. Between the relentless rain and standing water, my family managed to get just 60 percent of our corn and soybeans in the ground. 

Filing prevented planting is never the plan, but it’s the safety net we pay for to keep the lights on after a disastrous spring. This year, however, that safety net came with a staggering price tag. The USDA quietly raised the prevented planting base rate in our region by 22 percent. On my operation alone, that policy shift translates to roughly $46,000 in additional out-of-pocket costs. 

In a year where margins were already razor-thin, taking a $46,000 hit just for the privilege of insuring ground we couldn't plant is a heavy blow. But what makes this hike particularly galling is the way the current acreage caps are structured. 

Because the cap system scales the way it does, medium-sized family operations like mine absorb a far higher proportional cost than the massive, multi-thousand-acre corporate entities down the road. The mega-operations have the sheer volume to dilute the impact of these cap thresholds, while family-run farms get squeezed on both ends: we take the full brunt of the percentage hike on our unplanted ground, and we lack the total acreage volume to offset the penalty. Senate Bill 214 was introduced specifically to correct this acreage cap distortion and protect family operations from taking a disproportionate hit when disaster strikes. It adjusts the cap math so that medium-scale farms aren't penalized simply for existing in a mid-tier acreage bracket.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
**To Members of the City Council and the Downtown Community:**

My name is [Your Name], and I am the owner of [Name of Coffee Shop], located on Main Street. I am submitting this written testimony for the official public record to formally oppose the proposed parking meter rate increase from $0.50 to $1.50 per hour in our downtown district. 

I do not write this out of an instinctive resistance to city revenue adjustments, nor do I rely on abstract warnings that this policy "might hurt small business." I am writing because the cold, hard numbers—from my own sales logs, from regional precedent, and from the city’s own fiscal reports—demonstrate that a 200% rate hike will disproportionately damage the downtown retail ecosystem while delivering negligible fiscal return to the municipality.

First, consider the direct economics of a downtown visit. Over the past year, my point-of-sale logs show that the average visit length for a customer in my shop is precisely 22 minutes. These patrons are not long-term parkers occupying spots for an entire workday; they are residents popping in to grab a coffee, pick up a pastry, or meet a colleague briefly before moving on. Under the current structure, the 60-minute minimum charge of $0.50 easily covers their stay while remaining an afterthought. Tripling that rate to $1.50 introduces immediate transactional friction. When a customer buys a $4.75 latte, adding a mandatory $1.50 parking fee represents an effective 31.5% surcharge on their purchase. For short-stay errands, parking cost shifts from an incidental expense into a deterrent. Drivers will simply reroute to suburban strip malls and drive-throughs where surface parking remains free.

Second, we already have empirical data on what happens when a municipality implements this exact change. In 2019, when our neighboring municipality instituted an identical tripling of their downtown meter rates, I closely tracked foot traffic and customer frequency over a six-week control period using our register data. During those six weeks, foot traffic across comparable merchant categories dropped by 18%. In an industry operating on 5% to 8% net margins, an 18% decline in foot traffic is not a minor inconvenience; it is the difference between retaining staff and cutting shifts, or between breaking even and shutting our doors entirely. The downtown core relies on compounded micro-trips. When you disincentivize the casual, spontaneous visit, the entire retail block absorbs the loss.

Finally, the justification that this increase will meaningfully shore up municipal finances collapses under the city’s own accounting. According to the Downtown Mobility and Budget Report released last month, parking meter revenue accounts for exactly 4% of the downtown operating budget. Even if one were to assume—unrealistically—zero decline in parking utilization after tripling the fee, this rate hike does not resolve the structural challenges facing downtown infrastructure or transit maintenance. Balancing a municipal deficit requires substantive fiscal planning, not nickel-and-diming the foot traffic that generates downtown property tax, sales tax, and economic vitality in the first place. Sacrificing nearly a fifth of Main Street foot traffic to manipulate a revenue source that constitutes only 4% of the ledger is bad math and worse governance.

Downtown businesses have spent years rebuilding steady, dependable foot traffic. Replacing that stability with a 200% parking hike will extract revenue from local patrons while failing to meaningfully move the needle on city finances. [Address / Main Street Location]

b.text:
Members of the City Council:

I own a small independent coffee shop on Main Street, and I urge you to reject the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour. This is not a minor adjustment. It triples the hourly rate—a 200% increase—for people visiting downtown businesses.

For my customers, the practical impact is especially clear. Their average visit lasts 22 minutes. Under the current one-hour minimum, they already pay for more than twice the time they typically need. That minimum charge would rise from 50 cents to $1.50, adding a dollar to the parking cost of a visit that usually takes less than half an hour. The current minimum already covers their visits. Tripling its price makes a short stop more expensive without giving them anything more.

My concern is based on experience, not just speculation. In 2019, following a similar parking rate increase in the next town over, I tracked my own register activity for six weeks. That tracking showed an 18% drop in foot traffic during the period. Register-based tracking is not a controlled study, and I cannot claim that parking prices alone caused the decline. But an observed decline of 18% is a serious warning for a small business, and it deserves consideration before this council adopts a similar increase.

The city’s own report says meter revenue covers only 4% of the downtown budget. That figure does not mean parking revenue is irrelevant, but it does raise an important question: What budget problem will this increase actually solve? The council should show the expected net revenue, account for possible changes in parking demand, and explain why that benefit justifies tripling the cost to visitors.

Please keep the current rate while evaluating alternatives, including shorter billing increments for short visits. Downtown needs customers who can stop for coffee, pick up an order, or browse a neighboring shop without reconsidering the trip over parking costs.

For an independent business, those brief visits are not incidental. They are how we stay open.

a.text:
Hi all,

Quick update on yesterday's outage. Short version: we were down for about 40 minutes starting around 2pm, everything has been fully back to normal since, no customer data was lost or affected, and we've changed how we do deploys so this specific problem can't happen again.

**What happened**

During a routine deploy yesterday afternoon, one of the steps involved making a change to a table in our database. That change needed to briefly "lock" the table while it ran, which normally takes a second or two. In this case it held the lock far longer than expected, and while it did, anything that needed to read from or write to that table got stuck waiting. That's what caused the app to stop responding for customers.

Once we identified the cause, we rolled the change back, the lock cleared, and service came back. Total downtime was roughly 40 minutes.

**What we're changing**

Database changes like this one will no longer run as part of regular deploys. Going forward they'll happen in a scheduled maintenance window, outside of business hours, where we can monitor them closely and where any slowdown affects far fewer people. Normal code deploys will continue as usual and don't carry this risk.

**For those of you who heard from customers**

Thank you for handling that, and sorry you were on the receiving end of it. If any customers are still asking, you can tell them: the outage was caused by an internal change on our side, it lasted about 40 minutes, no data was lost, and we've changed our process to prevent it from recurring. If anyone wants more detail than that or needs help with a specific account, send them my way and I'll follow up directly.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The best wedding photos I've ever delivered came from a wedding that got rained out.

The Barreras had a plan. Outdoor ceremony, Hill Country views, the whole thing. Then the sky opened up right before guests arrived.

So we moved everything under a giant pecan tree. Ceremony, toasts, dancing — all of it.

And here's what stuck with me: they didn't panic. They didn't try to recreate the Pinterest board under different conditions. They didn't hand me a revised shot list. They just got married. Laughed through the rain on the leaves. Pulled their people in close.

Eight years full time, roughly 35 weddings a year, and the pattern holds every single season: the couples clutching a four-page shot list spend the day managing a checklist. The couples who let it go are actually present at their own wedding — and you can see the difference in every frame.

A shot list tells me what you think you'll want. Being fully there gives you what you actually want: your people, your weather, your day. Nobody looks back and wishes they had more posed recreations. They wish they had more of what really happened.

Fellow vendors, you know the look — the couple performing their wedding versus the couple living it.

So yes, have a rain plan. The Barreras did, and it turned into the best part of their gallery.

But the shot list? Consider leaving it at home.

#weddingphotography #texashillcountry #weddingvendors

b.text:
Couples who ditch the shot list almost always end up with the best photos.

I saw it again at the Barrera wedding. Rain rolled in hard, so we scrapped the formal lineup and moved everything under the big pecan tree. No checklist. Just them, their people, and whatever the weather threw at us. The images that came out of that afternoon—laughing under dripping branches, spontaneous toasts, quiet moments no one planned—still feel more alive than any perfectly staged portrait.

Shot lists can be helpful for peace of mind, but the magic usually shows up when you let go of controlling every frame. Trust the day. Trust your photographer. The unscripted stuff is almost always the stuff you’ll want to look at for the rest of your life.

If you’re planning a wedding in the Hill Country (or anywhere the weather has opinions), this is your permission slip.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
# Don’t Cut the Training That Puts People to Work

The state is proposing a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding. As an electrical apprentice with the local IBEW, I think that is a bad deal for workers, employers, and taxpayers.

Apprenticeship is not just time in a classroom. We work, earn a paycheck, and learn a trade under people who know how to do the job safely. We also study the code, the math, and the systems behind the work. That training matters when someone is counting on us to wire a home, a school, or a hospital right.

The results are real. My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one finished and are now working journeyman jobs. That is nearly 88% of the people who started. These are trained workers filling jobs and paying taxes.

Apprentices here start at around $19 an hour. Journeymen top out at around $46 an hour. That is a path from an entry-level paycheck to a wage that can support a family. Earning while learning also means people do not have to wait years before they start bringing money home. As their wages rise, workers who need public assistance have a better chance of getting off it and staying off it.

Now look at the public cost. It is about $14,000 for each apprentice who finishes, compared with roughly $48,000 in average public subsidy for each four-year college graduate who finishes. Those are approximate figures, but the difference is big: about $34,000 less per graduate.

That is not an argument against college. We need college graduates, too. It is an argument against cutting a training path that gets people into skilled work at a much lower public cost.

Supporters of this cut may say the state has to save money. Every public program should have to show that it works. Apprenticeship can do that. Cutting a program with strong completion numbers and a direct path to good wages is not smart budgeting. It risks giving up long-term value for a short-term saving.

Electrical work takes training and supervision. You cannot replace that by telling someone to learn faster. If less funding means fewer training spots or fewer resources, the need for skilled workers will not disappear. We will just be doing less to meet it.

Our local should speak clearly on this, and state legislators should listen. Keep apprenticeship funding whole. Before cutting 15%, look at what the money is producing: trained workers, stronger paychecks, and a solid return for the public.

We are doing the work. Don’t cut the training that helps us do it.

b.text:
**Don't Cut What Works**

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with the IBEW. I work full time and go to class. I'm not an English professor, so I'll keep this plain.

The state is talking about a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding. That's a bad deal for everybody, and it won't save money in the long run. It will cost us more.

Look at my own cohort. We started with 24 apprentices. 21 of us finished and are working now as journeymen. That's 21 people who didn't drop out, who learned the trade, and who are working. That's what this program does. It works.

When you start as an apprentice you make around $19 an hour. You're working, you're paying taxes, you're learning. When you top out as a journeyman you make around $46 an hour. At that wage you're off any assistance programs fast. You're buying a house, you're supporting a family, you're paying a lot more in taxes. You go from getting help to giving back.

And it doesn't cost the public much to make that happen. The total public cost for one apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to a four-year college grad. The average public subsidy for one four-year grad who finishes is about $48,000. I'm not knocking college, we need all kinds of workers. But if we're talking about where tax dollars go further, $14k to create a journeyman electrician making $46 an hour is a bargain compared to $48k.

We are short on electricians. Every contractor I talk to is looking for more hands. Houses, schools, hospitals, new factories - somebody has to wire them. If you cut funding by 15%, that means fewer spots, fewer instructors, less training time, less safety training. It means my local can't take in the next class of 24. Maybe we only take 15. That means fewer taxpayers later and more jobs that don't get done.

I hear politicians say we need to cut waste. This isn't waste. This is the opposite of waste. You put $14k in and you get a worker who will pay that back ten times over in taxes and who will work for the next 30 years.

I'm asking the other brothers and sisters reading this newsletter to speak up, and I'm asking any state legislator who sees this to think twice. Don't cut funding for something that is working. If you want to save the state money, keep paying for apprenticeships.

We started with 24. We finished with 21 journeymen. That's a good return. Don't mess with it.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
# They Had the Answer. They Stopped Asking the Question.

Let's get the good news out of the way, because there's plenty of it and it deserves to be said first.

Eight and two. A trip to the second round of the state playoffs. And Dez Kowalski, who threw for 2,340 yards this fall, the most any quarterback in the history of this school has put up in a single season. Kids who play here twenty years from now will be chasing that number. That's a season worth being proud of, and nothing I'm about to say changes it.

But I've been chewing on Friday night all weekend, and I can't make it go down easy.

We lost a playoff game to a team we beat by 20 back in Week 3. Teams improve over a season, sure. Matchups change. But this one wasn't decided by a team that suddenly got better than us. It was decided at halftime, in our own locker room, when somebody decided the thing that was working wasn't worth doing anymore.

In the first half we ran the ball, and we ran it well. We were leaning on their front, moving the chains, and keeping their offense standing on the sideline. You could feel it from the stands: they didn't have an answer for it.

Then the second half started, and the run game just about vanished.

Down three. Not down 17. Not down two scores with the clock bleeding out. *Three points.* That's one drive. That's a field goal. That's exactly the situation where you keep doing what got you there, because you've got all the time in the world to do it.

Instead we put the ball in the air, again and again, and a defense that had been on its heels got to pin its ears back and come after the quarterback. Drives that should have been eight plays turned into three. Their offense got the ball back, rested and confident. The game got away from us one incomplete pass at a time.

I understand the temptation. When you've got a record-setting arm, you want to use it. Kowalski earned the trust he gets from this coaching staff, and on plenty of Friday nights this year that trust won us football games. But having a great quarterback doesn't mean every problem is a passing problem. Sometimes the best thing a great quarterback can do is hand the ball off and let the other team prove they can stop it. They hadn't proven that on Friday. We never made them.

That's the part that stings. We didn't get beat by a better plan. We got beat by abandoning a good one.

I don't say any of this to pile on a group of teenagers who gave this town a fun fall. These seniors won a lot of football games, and they're going to be missed. My criticism is aimed at the sideline, not the huddle, and it comes from the same place as every other fan who drove home Friday night muttering at the windshield: we wanted more for them because they were good enough to get more.

The lesson for next year is a simple one, and it's an old one. Don't let a three-point deficit talk you out of your identity. When something works, make the other guy stop it before you stop doing it yourself.

Eight and two is a fine season. It could have been a finer one.

---

*Catch more on the season, and tell me where I'm wrong, on the air this week.*

b.text:
**They Had It in Hand. Then They Let It Slip Away.**

Eight wins. A school-record quarterback. A playoff run that ended in Round 2.

And yet, if you watched the last few minutes of Saturday night, you probably didn’t leave with the feeling you watched a team that got beaten up. You probably left with the feeling you watched a team beat itself.

The loss stings for the obvious reason. This is the same opponent the team had already beaten by twenty yards, maybe more depending on which stat sheet you trust, in Week 3. In basketball, sometimes you say teams match up differently. In football, when you’ve already won a game like that, and then you’re down only three in the second half of the rematch, the answer usually isn’t to throw the playbook at the wall and start looking for heroics.

That’s where my head is at with this one.

This team didn’t lose because it wasn’t good enough. It lost because it stopped trusting what had been working. The run game was there. It was moving the ball, it was controlling the clock, and it was giving the defense a break. Then, with the game still on the line, that identity started to disappear. Suddenly it felt less like execution and more like hope. Hope is not a game plan in the second half of a one-score playoff game.

Now, none of that takes away from Dez Kowalski’s season. Two thousand, three hundred and forty yards is a school record, and it didn’t happen by accident. He carried the offense for stretches, made throws under pressure, and kept this thing alive more times than anyone in these parts should remember. But here’s the uncomfortable part: a school-record season from your quarterback doesn’t erase a lost playoff game if the rest of the team was taken out of it. Sometimes the best answer is the boring one. And the boring one Saturday night was the run game.

Eight and two is a good season. Nobody should act like it isn’t. You don’t get to pretend playoff losses are just another Tuesday in a small town like ours. People cared. That matters. But if we’re being honest—and this column should be honest—the disappointment isn’t that this team got exposed. It’s that it got close, had something solid in its hands, and then let the game drift away because it forgot what made it good in the first place.

That’s what makes this one ache.

Not that they lost.

That they only lost by three.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
The plane landed in Texas. I walked through the terminal and saw them near the baggage claim. My wife waved. My daughter stood behind her. She was six. I smiled and said her name. She didn't move. She hid behind my wife's leg. I waited. Finally, my wife bent down and told her it was okay. She came out slowly. I picked her up. She was stiff at first. Then she hugged me tight.

The next day, I went to the grocery store. I needed breakfast. The cereal aisle took up twenty minutes. There were boxes everywhere. Forty kinds, maybe more. Some had pictures of cartoon characters. Some were for adults. I just stood there. I couldn't pick one. My wife texted me to ask if I was okay. I told her I needed a minute. I bought the one we used to buy. It was the cheapest one.

The house felt different. Quiet. I couldn't sleep the first few nights. I woke up when a door closed. For a year, I had been sleeping with the door shut. Facing it. Out in the hallway. Now I was back home. I tried to leave the bedroom door open. It took weeks. I still check the lock before bed. Eventually, I stopped moving the chair. I leave the door open now. I let the hall light in.

b.text:
The first thing I noticed was the cereal. I had been back in the country for two days. My wife, Sarah, had sent me to the grocery store for milk and cereal. I stood in that aisle for what felt like twenty minutes. There were forty kinds of cereal. Maybe more. Rows and rows of brightly colored boxes with cartoon characters and health claims. I just stood there, my hands empty, my mind a blank. In the desert, a decision is a simple thing. You need water, you drink it. You need to move, you move. You don't stand in front of a wall of options. A woman with a cart gave me a strange look. I finally just grabbed a box, any box, and walked away. I couldn't tell you now what kind it was.

The airport was worse. Sarah was there, and my daughter, Lily, was holding her hand. She was six. I had been gone for a year. I saw them from the top of the escalator and my heart was pounding. I walked down, I dropped my bags, and I went to hug them. Sarah held on tight. Lily just stared. When I knelt down to her level, she took a step back and hid behind Sarah’s leg, peeking out at me. She didn't recognize me. I was a stranger in a uniform. It took a few days. She would watch me from across the room, this man who was in her house. She’d ask Sarah questions about me in a whisper. It came back, slowly, but that first moment, that flinch, is what I remember.

The last thing is the door. The bedroom door. For a year, I had slept facing the door. It was a habit you didn't think about, you just did it. Your body knew. You slept light, always aware of the entrance to your space. When I got home, I couldn't shake it. I’d lie in bed next to Sarah, and my back would be to the wall, my eyes on the door, listening. It made her uneasy. The first few nights, I got up and closed the door. It felt wrong, like I was sealing us in a box. But an open door felt like a vulnerability. It was a stupid thing, a door. But it was a fight every night. I’d get up, close it, get back in bed. Then I’d get up and open it again, because the closed door made me feel trapped. This went on for weeks. Sarah never said anything, she just let me be. I didn't know how to explain that a part of me was still over there, and that part of me needed to see the door.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
If you’ve been following along here for a while, you know we try to keep this bakery as personal and hands-on as we can. That’s one of the best parts of being a small shop: I get to know so many of you by name, I get to bake the things you come in for every week, and I get to spend my days making the treats that end up at your tables for birthdays, coffee breaks, Tuesday afternoons, and all the ordinary little celebrations that make up real life.

That’s also why I want to share a change with you directly, in plain language.

We’re no longer taking custom wedding cake orders.

That isn’t an easy thing to write, because I know wedding cakes can be deeply meaningful, and I’m honored every time someone even thinks of us for something that important. But the truth is that custom wedding cakes have become too much for our tiny bakery to carry well.

A single wedding cake order takes an enormous amount of time. Between the back-and-forth emails, consultation time, tastings, planning, design work, and all the coordination that comes with making something that has to be exactly right, each one eats up about 14 hours of time that pulls me away from the bakery floor and away from the bread, pastries, cakes, and cookies you actually see in the case every day.

And because we’re small, that time matters a lot.

This year alone, we had three last-minute cancellations. When that happens, we’re left with ingredient costs we can’t recover, plus all the time that already went into planning and preparation. For a larger business, that might be easier to absorb. For a three-person bakery, it’s a real strain.

More than anything, I’ve had to be honest with myself about where our energy needs to go. The everyday case is what keeps this bakery going. It’s what pays rent, covers payroll, and keeps the lights on. It’s also what most of you come in for, week after week. That’s the heart of the business, and I need to protect that.

So this isn’t us saying no to weddings. It’s us saying yes to the part of the bakery that’s sustainable, steady, and true to what we do best.

We’ll still be here with cakes for smaller celebrations, special desserts, and all the things that make a gathering feel complete. And if you’re planning a wedding, I truly wish you all the sweetness in the world as you find the right fit for your day.

Thank you, as always, for supporting this little bakery and for understanding the realities behind what it takes to keep it running. I’m so grateful for every one of you who shows up for us, and I want to keep showing up for you in the ways we can do well.

b.text:
**A note about wedding cakes**

I've started this post a few times now, so I'll just say it plainly: we're no longer taking custom wedding cake orders.

First, the part that's easy. We have loved making them. Being even a small part of someone's wedding day is one of the best things about this job, and some of my favorite mornings in this kitchen have been delivery mornings — carrying a cake out the door and hoping it makes somebody cry in the good way. To everyone who trusted us with yours over the years: thank you, truly. We never took that lightly.

Here's the harder part, but I think you deserve the honest version. Every custom wedding cake, before we ever turn the ovens on, takes about fourteen hours of consultations, tastings, sketches, and back-and-forth emails — all of it unpaid. We're a three-person shop, and I'm already up at four most mornings. Those fourteen hours have to come from somewhere, and where they've been coming from is the case.

And the case is the whole point. The croissants, the morning buns, the bread you grab on your way home, the thing you pick up with your coffee on a Tuesday — that's what pays our rent and keeps our lights on. It's what this bakery actually is. This year there were weeks when I looked at the case and it was thinner than I wanted it to be, because our attention was somewhere else. That didn't sit right with me.

The other piece of it: we had three couples cancel at the last minute this year, after we'd already bought ingredients — special-order things we couldn't return or use anywhere else. I'm not angry about it. Plans change, weddings fall apart, life happens to good people. But three in one year made the math impossible to ignore. On a custom order, nearly all of the risk sits with us, and we're too small to keep carrying it.

So that's the news. Nothing else is changing. The case will be full, we'll be here same as always, and honestly we'll probably be happier, because this is us getting back to the thing we're actually built for. And if you're planning a wedding and need a cake — come talk to me anyway. I know some wonderful bakers who do this work full-time and do it beautifully, and I'm glad to point you their way.

Thank you for being the kind of customers I can write a letter like this to. Most businesses would send out something polished and vague. I get to just tell you the truth, and that's because of who you are.

See you at the counter.

— [Your name]

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8 Months of Near-Daily Market Baking

I've had the Corlane SM6 on my counter for eight months now, and unlike most of the gear that passes through my kitchen for a review, this one has earned its spot by actually working for a living. I bake sourdough for the farmers market most weekends, which means this machine gets fired up almost every day. Here's what I've learned.

## The Motor Is the Real Deal

This is where the SM6 justifies itself. I regularly run a double batch of stiff bagel dough through it, which is the kind of dense, low-hydration dough that makes lesser mixers whine, walk across the counter, or shut off entirely to protect themselves. The Corlane doesn't flinch. No stalling, no burning smell, no motor overheating cutoff. If you knead heavy dough, this is the headline feature, and it delivers.

## The Annoyances

Two of them, and I want to be honest about both.

First, the bowl lift lever squeaks. It started a couple months in, and I now hit it with a shot of WD-40 about once a month to keep it quiet and smooth. It's not a dealbreaker, but at this price point I shouldn't have to babysit a moving part on a schedule.

Second, and more irritating: the included dough hook is too short for the depth of the bowl. It doesn't reach the bottom well, so flour and shaggy dough get left behind and you're scraping constantly. I bought a third-party hook that fits properly, and it fixed the problem entirely. Frustrating that I had to spend extra to make the machine do its main job, but the fix is cheap and easy.

## The Price

It's $429. That's $80 more than the comparable KitchenAid. There's no getting around the fact that you're paying a premium, and you should know that going in.

## The Verdict

**Buy it if you knead heavy dough every week.** If you're running stiff bagel, bagel-adjacent, or high-volume sourdough batches the way I do, the extra $80 buys you a motor that won't quit, and that's worth every penny over the life of the machine. Budget another twenty bucks for a proper dough hook and expect to keep a can of WD-40 in the drawer.

**Skip it if you're mostly baking cookies and cake batter.** The SM6's whole advantage is its muscle, and you'll never use it. For lighter work, the cheaper KitchenAid does the same job, comes with a hook that actually fits, and doesn't squeak. Save your $80.

b.text:
After eight months of using the Corlane SM6 almost daily for market sourdough, this is not a "depends on your needs" review—it is a tool built for one thing and one thing only: handling stiff, heavy dough. The motor is the standout feature; it absolutely devours a double batch of dense bagel dough without a single stutter or slowdown. If you bake sourdough or bagels regularly, this is the machine that will keep up with you.

The downsides are real but manageable. The bowl lift lever developed a squeak early on, requiring a monthly dose of WD-40 to keep it smooth. The included dough hook is a letdown—it’s too short for the mixer’s deep bowl, forcing an immediate upgrade to a third-party hook to get proper leverage.

At $429, it costs about eighty dollars more than the equivalent KitchenAid. You are paying a premium for that serious power and the robust build quality that comes with it. 

**Verdict:** If your weekly routine involves kneading heavy bread dough, this mixer is a workhorse worth the investment. If your baking is limited to cookies, cakes, and the occasional quick bread, skip it and save your money; you will never tax this machine’s capabilities, and the price tag will feel like overkill.

**Status: Fixed.** Our service was down for about 40 minutes yesterday around 2 PM. We've identified the cause, rolled back the change, and everything is back to normal.

**What happened:**
During our routine deployment yesterday, we ran a database update that accidentally locked up a critical table in our database for much longer than expected. This made it impossible for customers to access the service. We caught it quickly, reversed the change, and service came back online.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
# The Cereal Aisle

The flight from Germany was long but quiet. I slept some, which surprised me. When we landed at Dallas-Fort Worth, I carried my bag through the terminal and saw my wife standing near baggage claim with our daughter. Lily had just turned six. She was wearing a purple dress and her hair was done up in braids I didn't recognize. My wife saw me first and smiled and started to wave, but Lily stepped back and hid behind her mother's leg. She peeked around at me with one eye like she was deciding whether I was safe.

I stopped walking.

I'd talked to her on the phone almost every week. Sent her drawings I'd done of her dog, of our house, of things she'd recognize. But I'd been gone a year, and I guess a man in uniform with a shaved head and a bag over his shoulder wasn't quite what she had pictured. She stayed behind that leg until my wife knelt down and pointed at me and said something I couldn't hear. Then Lily came forward slow, looking up at me with her mouth open a little, and I knelt down too. She touched my face with her hand like she was checking if I was real. Then she grabbed me around the neck and I picked her up and she was heavier than I remembered. I held her for a while. My wife put her hand on my back. People moved around us with their roller bags.

The first week home, I drove to the grocery store for milk and eggs. My wife had made a list. I found the eggs fine. The milk was fine. Then I turned down the cereal aisle.

I stood there for what must have been twenty minutes. There were forty kinds of cereal. Maybe more. Cereal with marshmallows in it. Cereal with flakes and clusters. Cereal in a box with a cartoon on it. Cereal in a bag. Cereal with a label that said it was good for your heart. I'd been eating eggs and toast and whatever else they had at the chow hall, and before that, MREs, and the idea of choosing between forty kinds of cereal was something I couldn't get my arms around. It wasn't that I couldn't read the boxes. I just couldn't make the decision. A woman with two kids in her cart came through the aisle and grabbed a box of Cinnamon Toast Crunch without slowing down and kept walking. I watched her do it like she'd performed a trick.

I left without the cereal. I told my wife they were out of the kind she wanted.

The sleeping took longer to sort out. For a year I'd slept on my side, facing the door. It wasn't something I decided to do. My body just did it. In the barracks you slept a certain way, and in a sleeping bag you slept a certain way, and after a while it wasn't a choice anymore. Back home, my wife slept on the left side of the bed, and I'd sleep on the right, which put my back to the door. I'd lie there and feel it. Nothing was wrong. I knew nothing was wrong. But I'd turn over and face the door anyway, and my wife would roll over too in her sleep and put her hand on my arm.

After about a month, she said to me one morning, "Do you want to leave the door open?"

I said sure. She'd started leaving it cracked, then open a little more each night, like she was helping me get used to it. The first night it was all the way open, I lay there listening to the house. The dishwasher running. The furnace clicking on. Lily coughing once down the hall. I could hear everything. I lay on my back and stared at the ceiling and listened to the house make its sounds and eventually I slept.

Some nights I still turn over and face the door. But most nights now I sleep on my side with my back to it, and my wife's hand on my arm, and the door open, and the house quiet.

b.text:
My daughter was six when I came home from my second deployment. At the airport, she stood behind her mother’s leg and held on to her jeans. I could see one eye and part of her forehead.

I had pictured her running to me. I hadn’t told anybody that, but I had pictured it plenty.

I set my bag down and crouched. My knees popped.

“Hey, kiddo.”

She pulled her face back out of sight. Her mother reached down and rubbed her shoulder.

“It’s Dad.”

“I know,” she said, but she stayed where she was.

I didn’t know whether to keep talking or give her a minute. There were people coming around us with rolling bags. I moved my bag closer so nobody would trip over it.

Finally she looked at me again.

“Your hair’s different.”

“Yeah. Pretty short.”

She came out from behind her mother, but not all the way over. I stayed down there until my legs started to hurt. Then she let me put my arms around her. She kept hers at her sides for a second before she put them around my neck.

On the way to the car, her mother carried a bag and I carried the rest. Our daughter walked between us, holding her mother’s hand. She told me where they had parked.

A few days later, I went to buy groceries. I wanted to do something useful without having to ask how to do it. My wife had made a list. Milk, bread, eggs, cereal. A few other things.

I got as far as the cereal.

There must have been forty kinds. More, if you counted the different sizes. I stood there with one hand on the cart and read the boxes. I picked one up, checked the price, and put it back. Then I picked up another.

I wasn’t looking for anything special. That was the trouble. Any of it would have been fine, but I couldn’t get from looking at a box to putting it in the cart.

A woman said, “Excuse me,” and I moved so she could reach past me. She took a box without stopping to think about it. I watched her go around the end of the aisle.

I checked my phone. I’d been standing there close to twenty minutes.

I was a staff sergeant. I had spent the last year making decisions people needed me to make. Now I was blocking a grocery aisle because I couldn’t pick breakfast.

I called my wife.

“What kind of cereal?”

“Whatever you want.”

I didn’t say anything.

“The yellow box,” she said. “She’s been eating that one.”

There were two yellow boxes. I bought both.

When I got home, my daughter helped unpack. She took one of them out of the bag.

“I don’t like this kind anymore.”

“Okay.”

She took out the other one.

“This one’s good.”

I put it on top of the refrigerator and went back out for the milk I’d left in the car.

At night, I wanted the bedroom door shut.

My wife had been leaving it open so she could hear our daughter. If I closed it, she would get up and open it again. Neither of us said much about it at first. I’d close it on my way back from the bathroom. Later, when I woke up, it would be open.

For a year I had slept facing the door. I still did. I could be worn out and ready to fall asleep sitting up, but once I lay down, I needed to turn that way. If my wife spoke from behind me, I answered without rolling over.

One night she asked, “Does it have to be closed?”

“I sleep better.”

“I need to hear her.”

I knew that. Our daughter’s room was down the hall. Sometimes she called for water or had a bad dream. Her mother had been the one getting up.

We left the door halfway open that night. I lay there looking at the strip of hallway. The house made noises I didn’t remember. The refrigerator shut off. A pipe knocked after somebody used the bathroom. I got up once and checked the front lock, although I had checked it before bed.

In the morning my wife asked if I’d slept.

“Some.”

That was true. I had.

We kept leaving the door open. Some nights I got up and pushed it partway shut. Some nights I stayed in bed. I didn’t make a plan for it or keep track.

My daughter started coming to my side of the bed when she woke up. The first time, she stood there so quietly that I didn’t hear her until she touched my arm. I jerked awake and scared her.

“What?”

She stepped back.

I lowered my voice. “What do you need?”

“Water.”

I took her to the kitchen. She wanted a particular cup, and I opened two wrong cabinets before she pointed to the right one.

After that, I told her to say my name from the doorway.

One night I heard, “Dad.”

The bedroom door was open. She was standing in the hall in her pajamas, holding her cup with both hands.

“Water?”

She nodded.

I pushed the blanket off and sat on the edge of the bed. She waited while I found my slippers.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
# The Market Isn't Crashing. Your Expectations Are.

I've been selling homes in this area for a decade, and I've never seen a sharper disconnect between what sellers believe and what buyers are actually doing.

Last spring, the median home in my zip code went under contract in 8 days. Eight. This spring it's 34. Showings per listing have dropped by half. And yet list prices are still up 6% year over year.

Read that again. Prices are up. Showings are down. Days on market have quadrupled.

That's not a contradiction. That's a market working through a transition, and a lot of sellers haven't gotten the memo.

I have three listings right now where the sellers have refused every price adjustment for over 60 days. I've shown them the data. I've shown them the showings they're not getting. I've shown them the comparable sales. They're holding firm because their neighbor sold in a week last March and they believe their house is better anyway.

Meanwhile, the homes priced correctly from day one are still moving in under two weeks. I sold one in 11 days last month. Another agent in my office had one go in 9. The buyers are here. They're just not desperate anymore, and they're not going to overpay for something that sits while they watch from the sidelines.

Here's what happened. During 2021 and 2022, buyers had no leverage and sellers had all of it. Prices climbed, terms got aggressive, and 8 days on market felt normal. That wasn't normal. That was a once-in-a-generation sellers' market, and we all knew it even while we were enjoying it.

What we have now is a market that's still good for sellers but requires them to be realistic. A 6% year-over-year price increase with mortgage rates where they are is a strong market. It's just not a market where you can throw a number at the wall and wait for someone to match it.

The homes that are sitting aren't sitting because something is wrong with them. They're sitting because the price was set for a world that no longer exists. The homes that are selling are selling because someone looked at the current data, not last year's, and priced accordingly.

If you're thinking about selling this summer, here's my honest advice. Don't ask me what your home would have sold for last year. Ask me what it will sell for this year. Those are two different numbers, and only one of them actually matters.

The market hasn't crashed. It's just grown up.

b.text:
The Spring Slowdown Isn’t a Crash. It’s Stubborn Sellers.

Last spring, the median home in our zip sat eight days. This spring it’s 34. Showings per listing have been cut in half. List prices are still up 6 percent year over year. Those numbers are real, and they feel like a punch if you’re a seller who expected last year’s frenzy.

They are not a crash.

I have three listings right now that have been on the market more than 60 days. The owners will not drop the price. They keep telling me the house next door sold for X last June, so theirs is worth Y. They are watching the calendar, not the showings. Buyers have noticed. They walk through, they like the house, they wait. Then they make an offer on the one down the street that came on last week at a number that actually matches today’s demand.

The homes that are priced to the current market—not last spring’s market—are still going under contract in under two weeks. I closed two of them this month. Both had multiple offers. Both sellers listened when I said the days of 15 percent over asking in 48 hours are over.

What we have is a timing problem, not a value problem. Inventory is still tight. Rates are higher. Buyers are more deliberate. They will pay a fair price. They will not overpay for a seller’s memory of 2021. The agents who keep telling their clients “just wait, it’ll pick up” are doing those clients no favors. The market has already picked a new pace. Catch up to it or sit.

That’s the whole story. Price it right and it sells. Pretend it’s still last year and it doesn’t.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**It Didn't Have to End Like That**

That's the one that's going to sting all winter.

Not because we lost in the second round of state. Plenty of good teams go home in the second round, and 8-2 is a season anybody around here should be proud of.

It's how we lost — to a team we beat by 20 back in Week 3.

I said it on the air Saturday morning and I'll say it here: we got away from what was working, and we did it for no good reason.

We went into halftime down 3. Three. And the run game was moving the chains. It wasn't flashy, it was just working — four yards, five yards, keep the clock running, keep their offense on the sideline.

Then the second half started and it was like we forgot we had running backs. Pass, pass, pass. Three-and-out. Three-and-out. Suddenly our defense is back on the field again, gassed, and a 3-point game turned into a game we were chasing.

I don't understand it. You don't have to panic when you're down 3 in the third quarter. That's not a two-minute drill. That's still your game plan.

And listen, this is no knock on Dez Kowalski. The kid threw for 2,340 yards this year — a school record — and he earned every one of them. He's the reason we won a couple games we probably shouldn't have. But asking him to throw it every down in the second half, into coverage that was sitting back waiting for it, wasn't putting him in a position to succeed. It was putting him in a position to fail.

Run the ball. Lean on the line that got you there. If they stop it, then you adjust.

We never gave them the chance to stop it.

These seniors deserved a better ending than that — not necessarily a win, just a chance to lose playing our football. Instead they walked off the field knowing their best weapon in the second half never got touched.

8-2. A record-breaking quarterback. A season we'll talk about for a while.

But yeah, this one is going to sting.

b.text:
The season ended with a loss that’s going to stick around longer than most.

Our high school team finished 8-2 and reached the second round of the state playoffs. Dez Kowalski threw for 2,340 yards, a school record. Those are accomplishments worth remembering. But it’s fair to say the final game was there for the taking—especially against a team we’d beaten by 20 back in Week 3.

Here’s my take: we got away from the run too soon. Down just three in the second half, with the ground game working, there was no need to put the rest of the night on Kowalski’s arm. He’d earned the coaches’ trust all year. That doesn’t mean every close game has to become a passing contest.

Maybe the run wouldn’t have carried us to a win. We’ll never know. What we do know is that abandoning something that was working made the opponent’s job easier.

That decision shouldn’t erase an 8-2 season or what Kowalski accomplished. It should, though, be part of how we remember the loss. Good teams can have good seasons and still wish they’d handled one half differently.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**Roadstar DC4 — 14 Months, ~140k Miles**

Skipping the out-of-box impressions, you can find those anywhere. Here's what it's like after a year-plus of OTR.

The headline: this thing already paid for itself. Month 9, a car cut into my lane mid-change and clipped the trailer. Had the whole thing on camera from both angles. Insurance got the footage and my claim was approved in 9 days instead of the usual six weeks. If you're on the fence about running a dash cam, that's your answer right there.

Now the gripes, because it's not perfect:

- Rear cam footage gets grainy past about 30 feet at night. Front cam holds up fine, but don't count on reading a plate off the rear unless they're close.
- The suction mount is junk. Fell off twice in the summer heat before I gave up and switched to the adhesive mount. Hasn't moved since.
- The app needs WiFi to pull footage, which is useless at most truck stops. I just pop the SD card and pull it on my laptop. Ignore the app entirely.

Otherwise it starts recording with the truck every time, hasn't died in triple-digit cab heat or a hard freeze, and the front footage has been clear enough for everything I've needed it for.

Bottom line: buy it for the recording, not the accessories. The camera itself does its job every mile — the mount, the app, and the rear night quality are just things you work around. After how that insurance claim went, I'd buy it again. Solid 4/5.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam: 14-Month / 140k-Mile Review**

Hey guys, doing a quick write-up on the Roadstar DC4. I’ve had this unit running in my rig for 14 months now, putting down about 140,000 miles with it on the windshield. Here’s the straight truth on how it holds up.

**The Best Part:**
It literally saved my ass. A few months back, a four-wheeler tried to merge right into my passenger side. The DC4 caught the whole lane-change accident clear as day. I sent the footage to my insurance, and the claim got approved and settled in 9 days instead of the usual 6-week headache. The camera paid for itself right there.

**The Annoyances:**
*   **The Mount:** The suction cup is garbage in the summer. It lost its grip and fell off the windshield twice in the heat. Ditch it immediately and use the adhesive mount. I switched to the adhesive, and it hasn't budged since.
*   **The App:** Total waste of time. It requires a Wi-Fi connection to pull footage to your phone, which is useless at 90% of truck stops. Don’t bother fighting with it—just pull the SD card and plug it straight into your laptop. 
*   **Rear Camera:** It’s decent during the day, but at night the rear footage gets pretty grainy past about 30 feet. You’ll see the accident happen, but don't expect to read a license plate at a distance in the dark.

**Verdict:**
It’s got some quirks, but for an owner-operator, the DC4 is worth the money. It does its main job when it counts and keeps the insurance companies honest. Buy it, use the sticky mount, and keep an SD card reader in your glovebox.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
**Put Our Girls On Turf Too**

The last two seasons, my team has had nine games rained out or moved. Not delayed. Rained out or moved to another school's field because ours was underwater.

I coach girls soccer and track at the high school. I'm not a writer, I do it for the coaching stipend. But I'm tired of telling 16-year-olds we don't have a place to play because it rained yesterday.

Our field is the low grass field behind the school. It doesn't drain. After any real rain it's ankle-deep mud for three days. We practice in it, we slide all over it, and we try not to get hurt in it. We sprint around the swampy spots and we tell parents to bring boots to sit on the hill.

Last October one of my sophomores tore her ACL in a game. She wasn't hit. She was dribbling, stepped in a rut in our own field where the grass had washed out, and her knee went. She missed basketball season and she's missing this whole season. I coach track, too. I know what a bad surface looks like. That field is a bad surface.

This is a safety problem and it's a fairness problem.

The boys football field got turf in 2019. It's great. It drains, it's lined, they never lose a home game to weather. Our girls have been playing on a field that floods if you look at it wrong for six more years. If this were the football field, it would have been fixed a long time ago. Actually, it was.

I get it, turf isn't cheap. The board has a lot to pay for. But we are not asking for a stadium or lights or a press box. We are asking for a flat field that works when it rains. A field where we don't have to bus to the other team's school and call it a "home" game. A field where kids aren't worrying about what hole they're going to step in.

The school board votes on the facilities budget next week. Put turf for the girls soccer field in it.

Our girls deserve the same shot the boys have had since 2019 - to actually play their home games, on their home field, without getting hurt.

b.text:
**Turf the Girls Soccer Field. Now.**

*By a girls' soccer and track coach*

Nine games. That’s how many games my girls soccer team has had rained out or moved in the last two seasons because our grass field floods. Not because the other team was better. Not because we didn’t practice. Because the field can’t handle rain.

Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping in a rut on that same field. A rut. Not a collision, not a bad slide tackle. A hole in the grass. She’s still not back. That’s not bad luck. That’s a facility problem.

The boys football field got turf in 2019. They play on a surface that drains, that doesn’t rut, that doesn’t turn into mud. My girls are still playing on a field that floods every time it rains hard. That’s not a coaching issue. That’s not a talent issue. That’s a fairness issue.

I’m not asking for a new stadium. I’m asking for the same basic thing the boys already have: a field that’s playable when it rains and safe when it’s dry. The school board votes on next year’s facilities budget soon. Put turf on the girls soccer field in that budget.

Some people will say turf is expensive. You know what’s more expensive? Losing nine games a season. Losing a player to an ACL tear that didn’t have to happen. Losing the message that girls’ sports matter as much as boys’ sports.

I coach for a stipend. I’m not here to write pretty sentences. I’m here because I’ve watched my players warm up on a field with standing water and then get told their game is moved—again. I’ve watched a girl’s season end because of a rut. I’ve watched the football team practice on turf while we drag mud off our cleats.

The board has a choice. They can keep telling half the school’s athletes to wait their turn, or they can fix the field. My players have waited long enough.

Vote yes on turf for the girls soccer field.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
22%.

That's how much USDA raised the base rate for prevented planting coverage in our region this year.

This spring I got 60% of my corn and soybean acres planted by the late May deadline. Not for lack of trying. It just wouldn't quit raining. Field after field sat too wet to carry equipment, and the calendar ran out.

That 22% hike is costing me about $46,000 extra this year — for coverage on acres I couldn't even plant.

I'm a fourth-generation farmer. My operation isn't small, but it's a family operation. And because of how the acreage caps are written, that $46,000 hits me a lot harder proportionally than it hits the bigger operations around me. They can spread that increase across more capped acres and different units. I can't. I'm capped out faster, with fewer planted acres to balance it against. Same rain, same county, same 22% increase on paper — very different bill in real life.

That's not risk protection. That's a penalty for being rained out at the wrong scale.

SB 214 would fix the acreage cap formula so it doesn't punish mid-size family farms for a wet spring we didn't cause. It's a straightforward correction, and it's sitting waiting for support.

If you farm, you already know what this spring was like. If you don't, ask your neighbor what 40% unplanted looks like in June. Then call your state senator and representative and tell them to back SB 214.

We can't control the rain. We should at least be able to afford the insurance we're told to buy for it.

b.text:
Sixty percent. That was the final tally on my planter’s monitor when the late May final planting date came and went. Four out of every ten acres I farm sat empty, drowned out by six straight weeks of unrelenting rain. 

That loss hurts on its own, but the real blow arrived in the mail with the crop insurance statement. This year, the USDA hit our region with a 22 percent hike on the prevented planting base premium rate. On my operation alone, that rate jump amounts to roughly $46,000 in additional out-of-pocket premium costs—cash paid on ground that won't yield a single bushel of corn or beans to offset the expense.

A $46,000 hit might be absorbed as a rounding error by institutional outfits running tens of thousands of acres across three states. But on a fourth-generation family farm, it cuts right into our operating capital for next season. 

Worse still is how the current acreage cap framework interacts with this increase. The flat limits and tiers currently in place mean that once a family-sized operation hits certain acreage thresholds, the proportion of covered ground that bears the full brunt of these hikes spikes dramatically. The mega-operations down the road have the acreage volume and entity structuring to dilute those caps and absorb the hit. Family operations our size land squarely in the crosshairs: large enough to carry massive weather exposure, but not large enough to game the caps. We end up paying significantly more per eligible acre proportionally than the biggest operators in the county.

We cannot control the rain, but our lawmakers can control the rules that determine whether an independent farm survives it. 

Senate Bill 214 is designed to fix this specific failure. It recalibrates the acreage cap structure to reflect actual operational scale, ensuring that family farms are not paying a disproportionate penalty simply for being caught between small-scale exemptions and corporate-scale loopholes. 

I urge everyone reading this to pick up the phone this week. Call your state senator and representative. Tell them what that 22 percent rate hike actually looks like in real dollars on your balance sheet, and tell them to co-sponsor and vote yes on SB 214. 

And to our representatives in the capitol who might read this: an insurance safety net that penalizes the family farm to subsidize regional risk isn't a safety net at all. Pass SB 214 and fix the cap.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: The Six-Month Review

Six months ago I bought a Jarvik L2 with my own money, and I've been sitting and standing at it for roughly 50 hours a week ever since. Nobody sent me this desk, there are no affiliate links in this post, and Jarvik has no idea I exist. Here's what actually held up and what didn't.

## The motor is genuinely excellent

Let's start with the thing Jarvik got right, because they really did. The dual-motor system is fast — about 12 seconds from my sitting height (28.5") to my standing height (44") — and quiet enough that I've raised the desk mid-meeting with my mic hot and nobody noticed. I measured it at my desk with a phone app: roughly 42 dB during travel, which is quieter than my fridge. My previous desk (a Flexispot EC1) sounded like a garbage disposal by comparison and took nearly twice as long.

Six months in, zero motor issues. No grinding, no stalling, no weird hesitation under load, and I have about 60 pounds on this thing between two monitors, a monitor arm, and a small rack of audio gear. If the motor is your main concern, buy with confidence.

## The wobble is real, and it's height-dependent

Here's my biggest complaint. At sitting height and even at moderate standing heights (up to ~40"), the L2 is rock solid. But at my full standing height of 44", there's noticeable front-to-back wobble when I type hard — and I type hard. My monitors visibly shimmy during fast typing sessions. It's not enough to make anything fall over, and it settles the instant I stop, but if you're tall (I'm 5'10" and this is my ergonomically correct height, so taller folks will have it worse) and you're a heavy typist, you will notice it every single day.

I tried the usual fixes: releveled the feet, retorqued every bolt at the three-month mark, moved the heavy stuff toward the center of the desktop. Marginal improvement at best. This is a frame stiffness issue, not an assembly issue. The columns just don't have enough overlap at full extension.

If your standing height is under 40", ignore this entire section. Above 42", take it seriously.

## The memory presets drift, which defeats the purpose

The L2 has four memory presets, and they drift by about a centimeter over a few weeks of use. My sitting preset was 28.5" in January; by March it was landing at 28.9". A centimeter doesn't sound like much until you realize the entire point of an ergonomic setup is consistency — my keyboard tray clearance is tight, and that drift is the difference between my wrists being neutral and being cocked upward.

The fix is re-running the calibration routine (lower to minimum, hold down for 5 seconds until it beeps), which takes 30 seconds. I now do it monthly, like some kind of desk chore. It works, but I shouldn't have to do it. My guess is the controller loses track of position slightly with each cycle and the error accumulates. Firmware-fixable? Probably. Fixed? No.

## The cable tray is an insult

The included cable management tray is a flimsy plastic trough that clips to the underside of the desktop with two of the least confidence-inspiring clips I've ever handled. One clip snapped during installation — not from force, from *existing*. The tray is also too shallow to hold a standard power strip plus a laptop brick, so cables spill over the edge anyway.

I gave up after a month, unscrewed it, and bought a $20 steel under-desk raceway from Amazon that mounts with actual screws. Problem permanently solved. Budget for this. Do not attempt to live with the stock tray.

## Small stuff, quickly

- **Assembly:** 90 minutes solo, decent instructions, all holes lined up. Fine.
- **Desktop:** I got the 60" laminate. No warping, no peeling, edges have survived multiple chair collisions. Fine.
- **Controller:** The touch-style buttons are slightly laggy but the display is readable. Fine.
- **Anti-collision:** Triggered correctly the one time my chair arm got in the way. Fine.
- **Warranty:** Untested, thankfully. It's 5 years on the frame, 2 on electronics, which is middle-of-the-pack.

## The verdict: it's a $549 desk

I paid $549 on sale. At that price, this is an easy recommendation for most people: the motor is best-in-class for the money, the build is solid at normal heights, and the flaws are either fixable ($20 cable raceway) or manageable (monthly recalibration).

At the $749 list price, no. At $749 you're in range of frames with better column overlap that don't wobble at full extension, and you shouldn't be doing calibration chores or replacing included accessories on a desk that costs that much.

**Buy it if:** it's on sale, your standing height is under ~42", and you can live with a monthly 30-second recalibration ritual.

**Skip it if:** you're paying full price, you're over 6 feet tall, or preset precision matters to you and you refuse to babysit it.

Six months in, I'm keeping mine. But I'm keeping it as a $549 desk — because that's what it is.

b.text:
**Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6-Month Review**

I bought the Jarvik L2 six months ago as a remote software engineer who codes 8–10 hours a day and switches between sitting and standing. Paid $549 on sale. Full price is $749. Here’s the unfiltered report after daily use.

**The motor is excellent.**  
It is quiet and fast. Full travel (sitting to standing) takes about 12–13 seconds. At desk height I barely notice the hum. No grinding, no strain sounds even after hundreds of cycles. This is the best part of the desk. If you raise and lower multiple times a day, the motor alone justifies looking at this frame.

**Stability falls apart at full height.**  
At max standing height the desk wobbles when I type hard. Not a gentle sway—actual side-to-side movement that I feel in my wrists and that makes my monitors shake. Soft typing or mouse work is fine. Aggressive keystrokes (debugging, rapid navigation) make it annoying. I keep it 2–3 cm below max now and the wobble drops to acceptable. Crossbar is decent but not rigid enough for a heavy dual-monitor + laptop setup at full extension. If you’re tall and need max height, this will bother you.

**Memory presets drift.**  
The four presets work, but after a few weeks they start landing about 1 cm off. I recalibrate every month or so. Not catastrophic, but for a desk in this price range I expect the positions to hold. The control panel itself is responsive and the display is clear.

**Cable tray is garbage.**  
Thin stamped metal, poorly finished edges, and the mounting screws strip easily. It sags under a modest power strip + a few cables. I replaced it with a third-party tray after two months. Budget for that if cable management matters to you.

**Everything else**  
Desktop is solid laminate, no warping. Legs feel sturdy when locked. Assembly took me 45 minutes alone. No weird smells after the first week. Frame has held up to daily height changes without developing new noises.

**Verdict**  
At the $549 sale price I paid, yes—buy it. The motor is that good and the core frame is usable if you don’t max the height. At $749 full price, no. You’re paying for a motor that belongs on a better desk and then getting mediocre stability, drifting presets, and a throwaway cable tray. Shop the sales or look at competitors in the same range that don’t force the stability compromise.
