setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
I stood in the cereal aisle for twenty minutes. Maybe longer. The cart was empty except for milk and a loaf of bread my wife had written on a scrap of paper. I had the list in my hand and I kept looking at it like it was going to tell me which box to take.

There were forty kinds. Maybe more. The ones with the cartoon rabbits and the ones that said heart-healthy and the ones in the plain bags at the bottom. I picked one up and put it back. Picked up another. A woman came down the aisle with a kid in the cart and I moved over so she could get past, and then I was still standing there with the list and the milk getting warm.

Nobody was waiting on me. Nobody was going to write me up. I just couldn't pick.

At the airport my daughter hid behind her mother's leg. She was six. She'd sent me drawings and I'd taped them up, and I had a picture of her in my pocket the whole time, the school one with the blue background. I got down on one knee the way you're supposed to and she wouldn't come out. Her mother said, it's Daddy, and she shook her head and held on tighter. I stood back up. We walked out to the car with her on the other side of her mother, and I carried the bags.

That night I shut the bedroom door and locked it and lay down facing it, the way I had for a year. My wife asked me what I was doing. I said I didn't know. I got up and opened the door and lay back down with my back to it and didn't sleep. The next night I did the same thing. Opened it. Faced the wall. Listened to the house.

I still check it sometimes before I get in bed. The door. Whether it's open. Then I turn over and try to sleep.

b.text:
Coming Home

The second deployment was twelve months. Flew into BWI. My wife was there with a sign, and my daughter was six. I saw them before they saw me. When my wife spotted me, she said my daughter’s name and pointed. The girl looked up, then wrapped both arms around her mother’s leg and hid her face. My wife tried to pry her off, said look, it’s Daddy. I walked over and crouched down. I said her name. She peeked out, then went back in. Twelve months is a long time for a six-year-old. I stood up and let my wife hug me first. After a few minutes my daughter took my hand, but she didn’t talk to me until we got to the parking garage.

A few days later I went to the grocery store alone. My wife asked me to pick up cereal. I found the aisle and stood there. There must have been forty kinds. Cheerios, Lucky Charms, granola, bran flakes, the ones with the frog on the box. The PX overseas had four. I tried to pick one. I looked at the prices, the colors, the sugar content. Twenty minutes I stood there. A woman asked if I was alright. I said yes ma’am. I shut my eyes, reached out, and grabbed a box. I don’t remember what it was. It didn’t matter.

At home, my wife sleeps with the bedroom door open. Always has. I had to relearn that. For a year I slept on a cot facing the door, weapon in the corner, one eye on the frame. Now the door is open and I’m in a bed. I lie on my side and watch the dark hallway. My body wants to face it. I tell myself nobody’s coming through. I turn my back to the door. Sometimes I fall asleep that way. Sometimes I turn back around and watch it until morning.

That’s all.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
To all of you who fill our shop with your morning hellos, your birthday candles, your Saturday treats, and your trust in what we do: we need to tell you something, and we want it to come from a place of honesty and love.

We are no longer taking custom wedding cake orders.

We know that’s a big one, and we don’t say it lightly. For years, those cakes were a source of real joy for us—a chance to be part of the biggest day in your life, to pour our flourishes into something that would stand at the center of your celebration. We have loved every single one, from the towering three-tiered extravaganzas to the tiny, perfect naked cakes with mismatched flowers. Some of our proudest moments in the bakery have been the gasps when we wheeled a cake into a reception hall.

But we’ve been quiet about what those cakes were costing us, and we think you deserve to know.

Every wedding cake we said yes to meant roughly fourteen hours of sitting across from you, tasting samples, sketching designs, talking through whether the buttercream should be silky or stiff, whether you wanted blush pink or a whisper of it, whether the cake should feed one hundred or one-hundred-and-ten. Those hours were precious, and we gave them happily. But they were hours we were not in the bakery, not shaping bread, not hand-piping the tiny hearts onto the morning cookies, not doing the thousand small things that keep our case full every single day.

And if we’re being fully honest, this year has been hard in a particular way. We had three couples who, through no fault of their own, had to cancel their weddings at the last minute. We understand. Life is messy, and weddings are expensive and complicated, and sometimes things fall apart. But when a cancellation happens after we’ve already ordered the ingredients, after we’ve blocked off the days, after we’ve turned away other work to make room for yours, the cost of all of that lands on us. It’s not a bill we can pass along. It’s just gone.

That’s a part of the business, and we’ve always accepted it. But this year, it made us stop and look at what we were actually doing. The truth is, the everyday case is what pays our rent. It’s the sourdough loaves, the baguettes, the cinnamon rolls that sell out by nine, the little quiche tarts, the cookies that get you through a Tuesday afternoon. That case is our heartbeat, and it’s the reason you keep coming back. Every hour we poured into a wedding cake was an hour we were pulling away from that heartbeat. And the more we did it, the harder it was to do what we do best.

We’ve always believed that the best thing we can give our community is what we make every day. Not because it’s easier, but because it’s what ties us together. It’s the bread you put on your table. It’s the treat you bring to a friend’s house. It’s the thing that makes a normal Tuesday feel a little less ordinary.

We know this will be disappointing to some of you, and that’s okay. We would rather tell you the truth than keep quietly disappointing ourselves and, eventually, you. We don’t want to be the bakery that takes on your wedding and then can’t give you the attention you deserve. We’d rather be the bakery that makes your morning better, every single day, and helps you celebrate in the smaller, sweeter ways we can still show up for.

So if you have a wedding coming up, please know we still adore you, and we’ll be cheering for you from behind the counter. We’ll still make you a gorgeous little dessert table or a beautiful tiered cake for an anniversary or a shower—the kind that doesn’t require fourteen hours of sitting and sketching. And if you’re just here for a loaf of bread and a kind word at 7 a.m., we’ll be here for that, too. That’s where our heart is.

Thank you for making this place what it is. Thank you for understanding. And thank you, always, for letting us feed you.

With flour on our aprons and love in our ovens,
— The whole tiny team at [Bakery Name]

b.text:
It’s a little past noon here at the bakery, which means my 4 am alarm is finally starting to catch up with me, but I wanted to sit down with a cup of coffee and share a quick update with you all before we dive into the weekend rush. 

We’ve been taking a hard look at how we spend our time in the kitchen lately, and we’ve made the bittersweet decision to step away from taking on custom wedding cakes.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# Corlane SM6 Review: Eight Months of Almost-Daily Bread Baking

The Corlane SM6 has earned its place in my kitchen—but not because it’s flawless. After eight months of almost-daily use making sourdough for my weekend farmers market stall, my verdict is straightforward: **buy it for heavy dough, not for cookies and cake batter.**

At $429, it costs $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid. That premium buys kneading power, but it doesn’t buy a mixer without annoyances.

## The motor is the reason to buy it

The most convincing thing I can say about the SM6 is that it handles a double batch of stiff bagel dough without stalling. That’s a much more meaningful test in my kitchen than whipping cream or mixing a soft batter.

I bake to sell, so the mixer gets used almost every day rather than coming out for an occasional weekend project. Over these eight months, its ability to work heavy dough has been its strongest selling point. If you regularly make sourdough or bagels, that strength is worth paying for.

## Two things that should be better at this price

The bowl-lift lever squeaks. I’ve had to apply WD-40 to the lift mechanism about once a month to keep the squeak under control. It’s a recurring maintenance chore I don’t appreciate on a $429 mixer.

More frustrating is the included dough hook: it’s too short for the deep bowl. I bought a third-party hook to address that, which means the mixer’s sticker price wasn’t my full cost.

For a machine whose biggest advantage is kneading, the supplied dough hook should be right from the start. Having to replace it is a real mark against the SM6, not a minor cosmetic complaint.

## Verdict: Worth it for weekly heavy-dough baking

**I recommend the Corlane SM6 if you knead heavy dough every week.** The motor’s performance with stiff bagel dough justifies the $80 premium over the equivalent KitchenAid, even with the squeaky lift and disappointing stock hook.

**If you mostly bake cookies and cakes, skip it.** Save the $80. The SM6’s strongest argument is its ability to knead demanding dough—not its finish or convenience—and that’s the job that makes it worth buying.

b.text:
I’ve been pulling preorders for my farmers market stall for nearly two years, which means my kitchen sees serious daily and weekend traffic. The Corlane SM6 has lived on my counter for eight months, spinning almost every day. If you’re reading this with your credit card hovering, here’s exactly how it performed under real load.

Let’s start with the motor. I regularly run a double batch of stiff bagel dough through this machine, and it never bogs down or stalls. The torque is immediate and relentless. For anyone committed to frequent heavy dough, that raw pulling power is the entire reason to consider it. It doesn’t struggle, it doesn’t overheat, and it doesn’t ask you to slow the dial.

It isn’t flawless out of the box. The bowl lift lever develops a loud squeak within weeks of daily use. I’ve had to wipe it down and apply a thin strip of WD-40 to the pivot joints roughly once a month just to stop it from sounding like a rusted hinge. It’s a simple fix, but it’s recurring maintenance that shouldn’t be glossed over.

The stock dough hook is also a miss. The SM6’s bowl sits deeper than standard mixers, and the factory hook barely clears the bottom edge during a full knead. Dough gets trapped underneath instead of folding properly. I bought a third-party stainless hook specifically sized for deeper bowls, and the difference was night and day. Plan to spend another $25 to $30 there.

At $429, the SM6 costs $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid. You’re not paying for flash or a massive accessory ecosystem. You’re paying for sustained heavy-lift durability and a motor that refuses to choke on stiff, low-hydration doughs.

Here’s the verdict: Buy it if you are actively kneading heavy bread or pretzel dough every single week. Skip it entirely if your baking routine lives in cookies, cakes, and whipped cream. That $80 premium will never pay for itself on light batters, and the squeaky lift lever will only grate on you faster when the mixer isn’t earning its keep. The SM6 is a dedicated, no-nonsense bread workhorse. Get it for the loaves, walk away from it for the dessert trays.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Outdoor Spigots (Minneapolis Homeowner’s Guide)

7 out of 10 outdoor burst pipe calls we take in Minneapolis in January are from homeowners who left their garden hoses hooked up to outdoor spigots all fall. It’s the easiest mistake to miss, and repairs can run $500+ if the burst is behind your siding or foundation—no one wants that bill right after the holidays.

Here’s exactly how to winterize your outdoor spigots in 4 steps, no fancy tools required:
1. **Shut off the interior valve** for your outdoor spigot. Most Minneapolis homes have these in the basement, crawl space, or utility closet right behind where the spigot mounts on the exterior wall. Look for a small lever valve on a copper or PEX line—turn it perpendicular to the pipe to cut the water supply completely. If you have multiple outdoor spigots, you’ll need to do this for each one, since they usually have separate shutoffs.
2. **Disconnect every garden hose, sprinkler timer, pressure washer attachment, whatever you’ve got hooked up**. I can’t stress this enough: even a hose that’s drained and coiled but still clipped on will trap a small pocket of water right against the spigot’s seal. When that water freezes (and it will, even in a mild Minneapolis winter), it expands and cracks the spigot or the pipe behind the wall before you even see a problem. Drain the hose all the way, coil it, and stash it in the garage or shed for spring.
3. **Drain the spigot completely**. Head back outside, twist the spigot handle all the way open, and let any leftover water drip out. If your interior shutoff valve has a little bleeder cap (the small plastic or metal cap on the valve body), loosen that with a pair of pliers to drain the water stuck in the line between the valve and the spigot. Tighten the cap back up once it stops dripping, then close the spigot handle again.
4. **Put a $3 foam spigot cover on it**. You can grab these at any Minneapolis hardware store—they’re the thick foam dome things that slip over the spigot and cinch tight with a drawstring. They block wind and cold air from seeping in around the spigot mount, which is extra insurance on those -20 degree nights we get every January.

Now, if you can’t find an interior shutoff valve, don’t mess around. A lot of older Minneapolis homes—pre-1970, especially in neighborhoods like Longfellow, Northeast, or the Wedge—don’t have dedicated shutoffs for outdoor spigots, or the valve is hidden behind finished basement walls. Don’t go turning random valves in your basement and accidentally shut off your water heater or your whole house. Give us a call. We can track down the shutoff fast, install a dedicated one if you need it, or winterize the line for you in 20 minutes flat—no trip fee for Minneapolis residents.

If you do all these steps and still notice a drip or a crack when you turn things back on in spring, or if you wake up in January to water pooling by your foundation, we’re here 7 days a week for emergency repairs. We’re a family-owned Minneapolis plumbing company, we’ve been fixing these exact burst pipes for 25 years, and we’d rather help you avoid the mess than fix it later. If you need a hand, give us a call.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

Before freezing weather hits, take a few minutes to protect your outdoor spigots and the pipes inside your home. The most important step is disconnecting your garden hose.

## 1. Disconnect every hose

Remove garden hoses, splitters, timers, and other attachments from each outside spigot. **Leaving a hose connected is the big mistake we see behind many of our January burst-pipe calls.** A connected hose can trap water in the spigot and pipe, where it can freeze and cause damage inside your home.

Drain the hose and store it somewhere protected from the weather.

## 2. Shut off the indoor valve

Find the shutoff valve inside your home for the outdoor spigot. It’s often in a basement, crawl space, or utility area near the pipe that runs through the exterior wall.

Turn the valve off. If you can’t find an interior shutoff, or you’re not sure which valve controls the spigot, call a plumber rather than guessing.

## 3. Drain the spigot and pipe

With the indoor valve off, go outside and open the spigot to let remaining water drain out. If there’s a small drain cap or bleeder on the indoor shutoff, place a bucket underneath and open it to drain the pipe. Close the drain cap afterward.

## 4. Add a foam cover

Put an insulated foam cover over the spigot. These inexpensive covers are often about $3 at a hardware store. They add a layer of protection against Minneapolis cold, but they don’t replace shutting off and draining the pipe.

If your outdoor spigot doesn’t have an indoor shutoff, or you’re unsure how to winterize it, contact our plumbing team. We can help you protect your pipes before a cold snap.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
# Launch week

The game went out last Tuesday. [Steam + itch.io, $12 / pay-what-you-want bundle]. Three years of nights and weekends later, it's on a store page with a trailer I recorded in one take because my hands were cold.

## What happened

**412 copies in the first week.** That's the number. Most of them came in the first 72 hours and then it flattened out, which is roughly the shape I was expecting, but seeing it flatline is a different feeling than I thought it would be. No dramatic spike, no weird algorithm gift, just a line that went up and then stopped going up.

I made about $[X] gross. After the store's cut and taxes that's [Y], which does not pay back three years of evenings, and I knew that going in, and it still stings a little. The devlog's Patreon covers about a third of my rent, which is the only reason I can afford to keep working on this.

The Discord has 61 people in it. Nine of them have posted more than twice. That's the community I have.

## The subreddit thing

A small subreddit I post in occasionally ([r/indiegaming]) picked up the launch post and it hit the front page for about six hours. Traffic-wise, 6 hours on a front page with ~200k subscribers meant something like 3,000ish visits to the store page. The conversion on that was, I think, 40 copies? I'm not sure. A lot of people clicked the trailer and bounced.

What I didn't expect: someone in the thread noticed I had a stray debug key bound to `F3` and told me. Now it's gone. Two other people found an actual crash on the second floor of the [Copper District] where you can fall through a stairwell, which I've fixed in the patch branch already.

## The floaty review

One of the reviews — [this one](link) — said the movement feels floaty. I'd read it and sat there for a while because I'd felt that exact thing while playing and had convinced myself players wouldn't notice.

They're right. It's the acceleration curve. I tuned the character's momentum way back in the middle of development because the game felt too twitchy in early builds, and instead of dialing the sensitivity back up I just left the damping heavy. The result is that stopping takes about half a second longer than it should, and there's no skid, so it reads as ice.

I've been staring at the movement code this week and I think it's a 20-line fix. Sliding, a slightly shorter decel curve, and a proper coyote time window on ledges (some of the "floaty" is actually that you fall a few pixels late when you run off an edge, which reads as sluggish).

## What's next

**Version 1.1 in the middle of next month.** It's mostly the movement fix plus the crash fixes plus the stray debug key. I'm also adding a settings menu with a toggle for the [screen shake / motion blur] stuff, because two people asked for it separately, and that's a signal.

After 1.1, I want to do a proper price pass on the launch discount — the current one expires [date], and I've got no idea yet whether the game will sell better at $14 or $9. If 1.1 lands, I'll bundle it with [the second soundtrack] or something, but I haven't decided.

I'm also going to start a proper playtest group. Right now my feedback has come almost entirely from people who already know me, which is a problem, because I've clearly been shipping a movement bug for [months] that only got caught because one reviewer was paying close attention.

If you're playing and find anything — movement weirdness, softlocks, missing localization, whatever — the Discord is the fast route. I read it. I answer things at 2am but I answer them.

Thanks for reading the devlog these past three years, and for the ones of you who bought the game.

b.text:
Launch Week

Hey all — my game launched last week.

After about three years of nights and weekends working on this thing, it's out. That's still weird to type.

By the numbers: 412 copies sold in the first week. It hit the front page of a small subreddit for like 6 hours on launch day, which was pretty wild to watch happen in real time. Otherwise it's been pretty quiet, which I kind of expected for a first release with no marketing budget.

Got my first real critical review too. They said the movement feels floaty. And honestly — they're right. I've been playing it so long I got used to it, but seeing it in their footage, yeah. I get it. It's a little too loose.

So that's what's next. I'm working on a 1.1 patch for next month that's going to tighten up the movement a bit. No big overhaul, just tuning the gravity and air control so it feels more grounded. Fixing a couple small bugs while I'm in there too.

Thanks to everyone who picked it up, wishlisted, or just left a nice comment. I'll post again when 1.1 is closer to ready.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**Roadstar DC4 — 14 months, 140k miles, here's my take**

Been running the Roadstar DC4 for 14 months now, roughly 140,000 miles on it. Figured that's enough seat time to give it a fair review.

Short version: it already paid for itself. Had a four-wheeler lane change right into me earlier this year. Camera caught the whole thing clean. Sent the clip to my insurance and the claim was approved in 9 days. Anybody who's been through a claim without video knows that's normally a 6-week fight, minimum. That one clip justified the whole purchase.

Now the honest stuff:

**Rear cam night footage is weak.** Past about 30 feet it gets grainy. It'll show you what happened directly behind you, but don't count on reading plates at distance after dark. Front cam's been solid, no complaints there.

**The suction mount is junk in heat.** Fell off the windshield twice last summer before I switched to the adhesive mount. Haven't had a problem since. Save yourself the headache and skip the suction cup from day one.

**The app is basically useless on the road.** It needs wifi to pull footage, and we all know what truck stop wifi is like. I just pop the SD card out and pull clips on the laptop when I need them. Works fine, but if you're expecting to grab video from your phone in the parking lot, that's not happening.

**Bottom line:** it's not a perfect camera, but it's a reliable one. It records every mile, it hasn't glitched or died on me in 14 months of vibration, heat, and cold, and it turned a claim I probably would've fought over into a 9-day approval. For the price, that's what I actually need out of a dash cam.

I'd buy it again. 4 out of 5 — loses a point for the rear cam at night and the wifi-only app.

Anybody else running one? Curious if the rear cam thing is just mine or if they're all like that.

b.text:
**RoadStar DC4 review — 14 months, about 140,000 miles**

I’ve run the DC4 on my current rig for 14 months and roughly 140,000 miles. It’s earned its spot, mainly because it caught a lane-change accident on camera. My insurance claim was approved in nine days instead of the usual six weeks. That alone made it worth having.

A few gripes: the rear camera footage gets grainy at night past about 30 feet. The suction mount also fell off twice in summer heat; I switched to the adhesive mount and haven’t had that problem since. And the app needs Wi-Fi to pull footage, which isn’t much use at most truck stops. I just pull the SD card.

**Bottom line:** I’d keep running it, but start with the adhesive mount and don’t count on the app when you need footage on the road.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**Let Our Kids Sleep: Why I'm Supporting the 8:45 Start Time**

I've watched my two middle-schoolers drag themselves out of bed at 6:15 for years now, and I'm done pretending it's normal. It's not. It's exhausting for them and for us, and it turns out there's real science behind why.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has been saying for years that middle and high schoolers shouldn't start school before 8:30. Their bodies are wired differently during adolescence — melatonin kicks in later at night, which means teens biologically can't fall asleep early even when we send them to bed at a reasonable hour. Asking them to be alert for a 7:30 first period is basically asking them to function on a permanent case of jet lag.

I know this isn't just theoretical, either. We already have proof it works right here in our district. When Lincoln Middle piloted the later start time last year, attendance went up and first-period grades improved. Not "stayed the same" — improved. That's not a fluke; that's tired kids finally getting enough sleep to actually learn.

I understand the biggest objection I keep hearing at school board meetings is about buses — that shifting start times will throw the whole transportation schedule into chaos. I get it; nobody wants a repeat of some logistical nightmare. But if you actually read the proposal (I have, several times), the district has already worked this out. Bus routes are being re-tiered so elementary schools shift earlier while middle and high schools shift later. It's not adding buses or costs — it's resequencing the same routes we already have. This isn't a hand-wavy "we'll figure it out later" plan. The tiering is right there in black and white.

I'm not a policy expert. I'm a parent who has watched my kids struggle through first period looking like zombies, and who has seen an actual pilot program in our own district prove that a later start helps. This isn't a radical experiment — it's catching up to what the research already tells us and what our own data already showed.

The school board votes on this next month. I hope they look at Lincoln's results, look at the transportation plan that's already built to handle this, and give the rest of our kids the same chance to succeed that Lincoln students already got.

*— A Millbrook parent, tired of watching tired kids*

b.text:
**Later Start, Brighter Mornings**

I’m the parent standing at the corner at 6:45 a.m., travel mug in hand, watching my seventh grader stumble toward the bus stop with eyes barely open. I have two kids in Millbrook middle schools, and for years I’ve watched them wage a daily war against their own biology. Our current start times are simply too early, and I’m tired of pretending otherwise.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that teenagers get 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night—essential for brain development, mood, and learning. Yet with buses arriving before 7:00 a.m., that recommendation is a fantasy for most of our kids. They aren’t lazy or undisciplined; their bodies are wired to fall asleep later and wake up later. Expecting a 12-year-old to be alert and engaged at first period is like asking an adult to give a presentation at 4:00 in the morning.

We don’t need to take this on faith. Last year, Lincoln Middle piloted an 8:45 start time, and the results spoke for themselves: attendance climbed, and first-period grades improved. When kids sleep more, they show up—and they actually learn.

I hear the objections. What about the buses? Sports? Parents who need to drop kids off before work? I understand the worry. Change is hard. But this proposal already addresses the transportation piece by re-tiering the routes—elementary students ride later, high schoolers keep their existing times, and middle schoolers get the later start they desperately need. The logistics aren’t an afterthought; they’re built into the plan.

This isn’t a radical experiment. It’s common sense backed by pediatric science and proven results from right here in Millbrook. Our children deserve to begin their school day rested, not exhausted.

The school board votes next month. I hope they listen to the doctors, the data from Lincoln, and the parents who are tired of watching their kids struggle through the dark. Vote yes for 8:45.

— A Millbrook Parent

setup: You're everyone at the startup. Yesterday's 40-minute outage was caused by a bad database migration during deploy.

a.text:
Hi everyone,

The service is back to normal after yesterday’s 40-minute outage around 2 p.m. We rolled back the database change that caused it, and the issue is resolved.

What happened: During a routine deploy, a database update locked a table for much longer than expected. That blocked the app from accessing data it needed and caused the outage.

What we’re changing: Going forward, migrations like this will run in a planned maintenance window rather than as part of routine deploys. That will let us manage potentially disruptive database changes separately from normal releases.

I’m sorry for the disruption to customers and for putting those of you fielding complaints in a tough spot. Thank you for helping customers through it.

If customers ask, the short version is: “Yesterday’s outage was caused by a database update. We reversed the change, restored service, and are changing how we schedule these updates to reduce the risk of a repeat.”

b.text:
Hey everyone,

First, the current status: **Everything is back up, stable, and running normally.** There is no data loss, and no lingering issues from yesterday's downtime. 

Here is a quick rundown of what happened yesterday afternoon, why it happened, and how we’re preventing it going forward—especially for those of you who were fielding customer messages while we were down.

**What happened:**
Yesterday around 2:00 PM, the app went down for about 40 minutes. Customers trying to log in or use the product during that window would have seen errors or endless loading screens.

**Why it happened:**
During a routine software update, we included a change to the structure of our database (a database migration). This update accidentally "locked" a core table in our database for much longer than expected. In short: because the database was busy processing our update, it blocked all regular customer traffic from getting through, which brought the site down. 

**How we fixed it:**
As soon as we saw the traffic blockage, we rolled back the update to undo the lock. Once the rollback finished, the site immediately recovered and traffic returned to normal.

**How we're preventing this in the future:**
Going forward, we are changing our process so that database changes like this are never run during normal, mid-day code deploys. Instead, any updates that alter the database structure will be run separately during scheduled, low-traffic maintenance windows, with extra checks in place to make sure they can't lock up the system.

Thanks to everyone who flagged the customer reports quickly while we were fixing it. If you need any extra context to follow up with specific customers today, just let me know!

1/3 Opened up the subfloor on our Maple Ave kitchen remodel last week and found a classic trade sin: a previous plumber had notched 80% of the way through a 2x10 load-bearing joist to run a 3-inch drain. 

The floor above had been secretly sagging 1.5 inches for years.

2/3 The fix required temporary shoring to jack the floor back to level, rerouting the plumbing properly, and sistering new engineered lumber alongside the damaged joist. 

Total cost: $2,800 in extra labor/materials and a 3-day delay on the cabinet install. 

3/3 The lesson: If an old floor dips near a plumbing stack, never assume it’s just "old house character." 

Homeowners should always hold a 10% structural contingency budget on pre-1950 homes, and contractors need to inspect beneath the subfloor before writing final cabinet timelines.

b.text:
Maple Ave kitchen. Opened the ceiling yesterday. Found a joist someone notched down to 2 inches to run a drain line twenty years ago. Was holding up the bathroom floor above with nothing but drywall screws and optimism.

Previous "handyman special" reno upstairs. Cut right through the middle of a 2x10, no header, no sister. Floor was sagging 3/4 of an inch but you couldn't see it from below until we took the plaster down.

Cost: $2,400 and two days of schedule. Sistered the joist, dropped in a beam, re-leveled the subfloor before we could even think about cabinets. Homeowner gets it, but that's 48 hours gone.

Lesson: Look before you quote. We priced this as a standard gut, but the basement never lies. Now we're doing exploratory cuts on every pre-war house before we put a number on paper. Old Pittsburgh housing stock hides its sins.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
Sellers Are Still Pricing Like It's Last Spring

I've been selling houses in this suburb for ten years. I've done the bidding wars, the 2 a.m. offers, the lines out the door at open houses. And I'm telling you straight: this is not a crash.

Here's what's actually happening.

Last spring, the median days on market in our zip was 8 days. Blink and it was gone. This spring, it's 34 days. List prices are still up 6% from last year, but showings per listing have dropped by half.

Buyers didn't disappear. They just stopped playing along.

Right now I have three sellers sitting at 60-plus days on market who refuse to take a price cut. Good houses. Good streets. Dead listings. Every week it's the same conversation: "Let's just give it another week." Another week isn't going to fix a price from 2023.

Because the homes that are priced for 2026? They're still gone in under two weeks. I just saw it happen last month — clean, well-priced ranch, three offers by day ten. Not 30 offers like the old days, but three real ones. That's a healthy market.

The problem isn't interest rates or the economy or some mystery factor. The problem is sellers who haven't caught up to the new pace. You can't list 6% higher than last year for a market that's taking four times as long to move and expect buyers to chase you.

If you're selling: Price it for the buyers who are here today, not the ones who were here two years ago. The first two weeks are everything. Miss that window and you're just paying your mortgage while everyone scrolls past your listing.

If you're buying: Stop waiting for a crash that isn't coming. You finally get to breathe, get an inspection, actually think. The well-priced homes are still moving fast, so don't sleepwalk, but you don't have to beg anymore.

This market rewards honesty. Price it right and it sells. Price it like last spring and it sits.

b.text:
## The Market Hasn’t Crashed. Sellers Need to Catch Up.

After 10 years selling homes in this suburb, I’ve learned to pay attention when the pace changes. And it has changed.

Last spring, the median home in my ZIP code spent just eight days on the market. This spring, it’s 34. That’s a meaningful shift. Showings per listing have fallen by half, even as list prices remain up 6% year over year.

Those numbers tell a clear story: buyers have slowed down, but many sellers are still pricing as if last spring’s urgency never ended.

I have three sellers right now whose homes have been on the market for more than 60 days, and they’re refusing to lower their prices. I understand the temptation. A home is personal, and it’s hard to see a neighbor’s sale—or last year’s market—as anything but a measure of what your own home should be worth. But buyers don’t set their expectations by what a seller hopes to get. They respond to the homes available now, at the prices available now.

This isn’t a crash. Homes that are priced for today’s market are still selling in under two weeks. The problem is that buyers have more time and more choices, so an overpriced home can no longer count on a rush of competing offers to make the price work.

A longer time on the market isn’t a reason to panic. It is a reason to pay attention. If showings are scarce and offers aren’t coming, the market is giving you information. Ignoring that information doesn’t protect your asking price; it can leave your home sitting while buyers move on.

The sellers who adjust to the new pace are the ones most likely to keep their sale moving. The market hasn’t stopped working. It has simply stopped rewarding yesterday’s pricing.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
# Let Our Teenagers Sleep: Why 8:45 Is Right for Millbrook

My kids are exhausted. Not the "I stayed up too late" tired—the bone-deep, adolescent-body tired that no amount of willpower fixes. And I'm not alone. Every parent with a middle or high schooler knows this struggle.

Next month, our school board will vote on moving start times to 8:45 a.m., and I'm urging them to say yes.

Here's the science: the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high school students get 8-10 hours of sleep on school nights. Our current 7:30 start time makes that nearly impossible. When my daughter has to be out the door by 7, she's getting up around 6:15. Even if she's in bed by 9:30—which rarely happens with homework and activities—that's nine hours in bed, maybe eight of actual sleep.

The research isn't theoretical. Lincoln Middle School ran a pilot program last year with a later start time. The results? Attendance went up. First-period grades improved. We're not talking about transforming education overnight, but these are real gains for real kids, right here in Millbrook.

I know the immediate objection: bus schedules. But I've read the proposal carefully. It already includes a re-tiered route plan. Yes, there will be adjustments. Yes, the district and transportation department have work to do. But "it's complicated" isn't a reason to leave teenagers chronically sleep-deprived.

My son's bus comes at 7:15 a.m. Under the new plan, it would come later. That's not a crisis. That's actually solving a problem we've lived with for years.

The pushback I hear most is about sports and after-school activities. I get it—I'm driving my kids to soccer and debate club. But here's what I know: a well-rested kid performs better at everything. School. Sports. Everything. One parent told me she was worried about evening activities ending later. They do. But the alternative—having kids wake up when their bodies are literally wired to sleep—isn't working.

This isn't about mollycoddling teenagers. It's about basic biology. Adolescent circadian rhythms shift around age 13. This is established science, not opinion. An 8:45 start time aligns school with how teenagers' brains actually work.

The Lincoln pilot showed it works. The proposal addresses logistics. The science is clear.

Our school board has a chance next month to give our kids something their bodies desperately need: sleep. I hope they take it.

b.text:
**A Later Start Time is the Right Choice for Millbrook’s Middle Schoolers**

As a parent of two middle schoolers in Millbrook, I’ve spent years watching my kids struggle to wake up for the 7:30 a.m. bell. Like many of you, I’ve seen the yawns at the breakfast table, the rushed mornings, and the way their energy flags by first period. That’s why I’m relieved the school board is finally considering an 8:45 a.m. start time—and why I hope the community will support it.

The science is clear: middle schoolers need more sleep. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. to align with adolescents’ natural sleep cycles. When kids don’t get enough rest, it affects everything—mood, focus, even their immune systems. Chronic sleep deprivation isn’t just about being tired; it’s linked to higher rates of anxiety, depression, and lower academic performance. Our current start time isn’t just inconvenient—it’s working against our kids’ well-being.

We don’t have to guess what a later start would look like. Lincoln Middle School’s pilot program last year showed real results: attendance improved, and first-period grades went up. Teachers reported students were more alert and engaged. That’s not a coincidence—it’s what happens when we listen to the research and give kids the rest they need to thrive.

I know some parents worry about logistics, especially bus schedules. But the proposal already addresses this by re-tiering routes, so elementary and high school start times would shift slightly to accommodate the change. It’s not perfect, but it’s a workable solution—and one that prioritizes the age group that needs it most. Middle schoolers are at a critical stage, juggling harder coursework, social pressures, and physical changes. They deserve a schedule that sets them up for success, not one that leaves them exhausted before the day even begins.

Change is always hard, and I don’t take lightly the adjustments this will require for families. But when I think about the difference an extra hour of sleep could make for my kids—for all our kids—I believe it’s worth it. Let’s give them the best chance to learn, grow, and start their days with energy, not exhaustion. The school board votes next month, and I hope they’ll do the right thing for Millbrook’s students.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
**Fix the Acreage Cap: Support SB 214**

The 22% increase in the USDA base rate for prevented planting coverage in our region this year adds about $46,000 to my premium. That is not a projection or a worst-case scenario. It is the additional cost I am carrying on my fourth-generation soybean and corn operation this year.

I got 60% of my acres planted by the late-May deadline. The rest stayed wet. That is what prevented planting coverage is for—not a windfall, but a backstop when the weather keeps us out of the field and the fixed costs keep coming. This year, the backstop got 22% more expensive at the exact moment we needed it.

The acreage cap makes that increase harder on family operations like mine. The cap is a fixed ceiling, not a percentage that scales with the size of the farm. A larger operation nearby can spread the same kind of fixed cap across more acres and more bushels. I cannot. The premium hike lands on fewer eligible acres, so proportionally it takes a bigger bite out of a family operation than it does out of a bigger one. That is not a complaint about size. It is a description of how the cap works.

Senate Bill 214 would fix the acreage cap. It would make the prevented planting program work as intended for family farms without turning it into something it was never meant to be. This is not a request for a new subsidy. It is a request to correct a cap that no longer fits the operations it was written to protect.

I am asking farm bureau members to contact their state senators and urge support for SB 214. When legislators hear from us, they should hear the numbers: 22% more in premium, $46,000 on my operation, 60% of my acres planted by the deadline, and an acreage cap that hits family farms harder than it should. Support SB 214.

b.text:
**60% Planted, 22% Higher, $46,000 More: Fix the Acreage Cap**

By the late-May deadline, I had planted 60% of my corn and soybean acres. The other 40% went prevented. Not because I didn’t want to plant it. Because it would not stop raining.

Then USDA’s Risk Management Agency raised the base rate for prevented planting coverage by 22% in our region. On my operation, that hike costs about $46,000 this year.

That is not a rounding error. That is a new tractor. That is a year of health insurance. That is the margin on several hundred acres of beans. I buy prevented planting coverage for the same reason I carry insurance on my combine: one bad spring can take the year. But this year, the safety net got more expensive at the exact moment we needed it most.

The part that makes no sense is how the acreage caps work. They do not hit every farm the same. A bigger operation with more spread-out acreage and more insured units can absorb the cap. My family operation cannot. Proportionally, the 22% increase and the acreage cap take a bigger bite out of my farm than they do the bigger operations nearby. That is not risk management. That is a penalty for being family-sized.

SB 214 would fix the acreage cap. It would update the formula so prevented planting coverage reflects the acres a family farm actually operates. It does not create a new entitlement or ask taxpayers to bail out bad management. It simply stops the current cap from punishing the operations that need the coverage most when weather takes the spring.

I am not asking for a guarantee. I am asking for a fair rule. If you planted 60% of your acres this spring, or if you watched your neighbor do it, you know what I mean. Call your state senator and state representative. Tell them to support SB 214. The next wet spring is not a question of if. It is a question of whether the cap has been fixed before it arrives.

— A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
Over eight years and nearly 300 weddings in the Texas Hill Country, I’ve noticed a consistent pattern: 

The couples with the shortest shot lists almost always get the best galleries.

Take the Barrera wedding. We had a clear plan mapped out, but Texas weather had other ideas. Right before the ceremony, a sudden downpour swept in and completely washed out their original outdoor setup. 

Instead of stressing over a rigid, multi-page checklist of must-have poses, they took a breath, embraced the chaos, and pivoted. We moved the entire ceremony under a massive pecan tree to wait out the storm.

Because they weren’t mentally checking off Pinterest poses, they were fully present. When the rain let up and the light broke through the wet leaves, we didn’t stage anything. We simply documented the genuine relief, the muddy boots, the unscripted laughs, and the raw emotion of the moment. 

Shot lists serve a purpose for family formals to keep logistics efficient. But for the rest of the wedding day, an overly detailed shot list turns a live event into a photoshoot where everyone is performing instead of experiencing.

To the couples currently planning: Do the heavy lifting beforehand. Hire a creative team you trust completely. 

Then, when the day arrives, put the list away and just live it. The best photos will follow.

b.text:
The couples who ditch the shot list always end up with the best photos.

I know that sounds backwards. You’ve spent months planning this day — of course you want to make sure nothing gets missed.

But the Barrera wedding is the one I think about every time a couple asks me how detailed their list should be.

It rained. Not a little sprinkle, a full Texas Hill Country downpour that forced us to scrap the original plan and move everything under one big pecan tree.

There was no list for that.

No list for the flower girl hiding under her mom’s dress to stay dry. No list for the groom laughing while he wiped rain off his bride’s cheek mid-vows. No list for both families squeezing in close under the branches, a little damp, a little chaotic, and completely present.

Those are the photos they printed. Those are the photos they talk about.

A shot list gives you posed versions of moments you *think* you should have. Trust gives your photographer room to catch the moments you didn’t know were happening.

I’ll always make time for the essential family groupings — we’ll plan those together. But beyond that? Let the day unfold.

Especially when it rains.

#TexasHillCountry #WeddingPhotographer #WeddingPlanning

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
Last October, one of my starting midfielders planted her cleat in a three-inch rut on the east side of our home field and tore her ACL. It wasn’t a contact injury. There wasn’t another player within five yards of her. Our field simply gave out underneath her. 

Next month, the school board is voting on the facilities budget for the upcoming school year. Putting artificial turf on the girls’ soccer field needs to be at the top of that list. 

I coach girls' soccer and track at the high school. Over the last two soccer seasons, we have had nine home games either canceled or relocated because our grass field floods every time it rains more than half an inch. The drainage system is shot. The middle of the pitch turns into a swamp by late September, and by October, it freezes into a minefield of mud ruts and divots. 

When a game gets moved, we lose our home-field advantage, parents have to rearrange work schedules to drive an hour away on two hours' notice, and the athletic department still has to pay for buses. When a game gets canceled, my players lose out on a season they’ve worked all summer to play. 

Worse than the scheduling nightmare is the safety issue. I cannot run a real practice on that field for half the season because I am actively worried about who is going to roll an ankle or blow out a knee next. We end up running drills in the parking lot or begging for twenty minutes of space on the football field after the boys are done.

That brings me to the real problem here. The football stadium got brand-new turf in 2019. When that was up for a vote, the community and the board rightly decided that the boys deserved a safe, reliable surface to play on. Nobody told the football team they just had to deal with the mud, and nobody expected them to play half their schedule on the road because their home field was underwater. 

It has been five years since the boys got their turf. Meanwhile, the girls are playing in a mud pit and tearing ligaments because the ground isn't flat. Aside from basic common sense, Title IX requires schools to provide equal athletic opportunities and facilities. Right now, looking at the pristine stadium on one side of the parking lot and our chewed-up pasture on the other, there is nothing equal about it.

I know turf is expensive. I see the budget numbers, and I know the board has to weigh roof repairs and HVAC systems against athletic upgrades. But field maintenance isn't free, either. The district spends thousands of dollars every year re-sodding, seeding, painting, and trying to roll flat a piece of land that simply cannot handle the volume of games and PE classes we put on it. 

My players show up on time, keep their grades up, and represent this town well. They shouldn’t have to risk a six-month surgical recovery just to play a home game. When the school board meets next month to finalize the facilities budget, they need to fund the turf for the girls' field. It’s five years overdue.

b.text:
**It’s Time to Put Turf on the Girls’ Soccer Field**

Nine of our girls’ soccer games have been rained out or moved over the past two seasons because our grass field floods. Last October, one of our players tore her ACL after stepping into a rut.

That should be enough to make this a priority.

Our athletes should not have to wonder whether the field will be playable after a hard rain—or whether the next uneven patch of ground will end their season. We do our best to maintain the field, but there is only so much that maintenance can fix. Heavy use, poor drainage and bad weather leave us with standing water, mud, holes and ruts.

When games are canceled or moved, families have to rearrange work schedules and transportation. Officials and opponents have to be rescheduled. Players lose opportunities they trained for. Sometimes we scramble to find another field. Sometimes we simply lose the game.

Meanwhile, the boys’ football field has had turf since 2019.

This is not an argument against what football received. A reliable playing surface benefits students and the community. But six years later, the girls’ soccer program is still competing on a field that regularly becomes unusable. If we are serious about giving girls and boys comparable athletic opportunities, then facilities have to be part of that commitment.

Turf would not be free, and it would not solve every problem. It comes with installation, maintenance and eventual replacement costs. Those costs should be examined honestly. The district should also choose a surface designed with player safety and heat in mind.

But the current field has costs, too. We pay to repair it. We lose games and practice time. We spend money and staff hours finding other sites. Most importantly, our students are being asked to play on a surface that we know develops dangerous ruts and routinely fails in wet weather.

This field would not serve only the varsity soccer team. It could support junior varsity teams, youth programs, physical education classes and other school and community activities. A durable field would provide more usable hours and make scheduling more predictable across the district.

Our players work hard. They show up in the heat, the cold and the rain. They represent this school with pride. They should not be treated as an afterthought because their field was not upgraded when the football field was.

The school board will soon vote on next year’s facilities budget. It should include turf for the girls’ soccer field.

We have waited long enough.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6-Month Review

**TL;DR:** Good motor, mediocre stability at height, sloppy presets, embarrassing cable management. Worth $549. Not worth $749. Buy it on sale or buy something else.

I bought the L2 in [month], paid the $549 sale price with my own money, and have used it 8+ hours a day, five days a week, ever since. No affiliate links in this post — nobody makes money if you buy this thing, including me. My setup: two 27" monitors on a gas-spring arm, mechanical keyboard, and a standing height of about 42.5". I switch positions 4–6 times a day, so the motor and presets have had a real workout — somewhere north of 700 cycles at this point.

## The motor is the best part of this desk

Genuinely. Sit-to-stand takes about 17 seconds under full load, it's smooth, and it's quiet enough that I've adjusted it mid-meeting with my mic unmuted and nobody noticed. There's a low hum, not a whine, and no grinding or hesitation at the top of travel. After 700+ cycles it sounds identical to day one.

This is the thing cheap desks get wrong — my previous budget frame started stuttering under two monitors within a year. The L2's motor has given me zero problems and I expect that to continue.

## Stability: fine sitting, wobbly standing

At sitting height, it's a rock. No complaints.

At my standing height (42.5"), there's front-to-back wobble when I type hard — and I type hard, because mechanical keyboard, because programmer. The monitors on my desk-mounted arm visibly sway for a second or two after I really get going. It's not alarming, nothing's going to fall, but it's noticeable and it's the kind of thing that bugs you more in month six than month one.

Two things made it better: torquing every frame bolt again after the first month (they settle), and moving my monitor arm's clamp closer to a leg. If you type gently or use a laptop, you may never notice. If you hammer a keyboard like you're mad at it, you will.

## The memory presets drift

There are four presets. Great. Except they drift by about a centimeter. I'll hit preset 2, the display says 42.5", and I can feel it's wrong — measure it, and it's at 41.6" or 43.1". It's not consistent in which direction it misses, which honestly offends me more. A centimeter doesn't sound like much until your elbows are slightly wrong for three hours.

I've done the factory recalibration (hold the down button, let it bottom out) three times. It helps for a week or two, then the drift creeps back. My fix is dumb but effective: I use the presets to get close, then nudge with the manual buttons and watch the readout. It works, but "the memory buttons get you within a centimeter" is a sad sentence to write about a desk that costs this much.

## The cable tray is garbage

I don't use that word lightly. It's a shallow stamped-metal trough that attaches to the underside of the desktop with four short screws into particle board. Here's what happened, in order:

1. I loaded it with one surge protector and the usual cable bundle. It sagged in the middle within a week.
2. The rear two screws loosened themselves from the desk's vibration. I re-seated them. One stripped the hole.
3. It's too shallow to close over a standard surge protector anyway, so the lid has been off since month one.

I ripped it out in month three, mounted a $15 under-desk cable raceway from [generic], and my cable situation is now better than the desk deserves. Budget for that. Plan on throwing the included tray directly in the trash and saving yourself the intermediate steps.

## Smaller stuff

- **The desktop** is laminate over particle board and it's fine. Edges haven't chipped, it wipes clean, and my monitor arm clamp hasn't dented it. Not premium, not a problem.
- **The controller** display is bright enough to read in a dark room, which also means it's bright enough to annoy you in a dark room. No way to dim it. I put a strip of electrical tape over half of it.
- **Assembly** took me about 50 minutes alone. Instructions were clear, hardware was labeled, nothing was missing. Genuinely good experience.
- **Anti-collision** works. It stopped on my chair arm once and reversed. Tested it deliberately a second time because I didn't trust it. It passed.

## The verdict

At **$549**, this desk is a good deal. The motor alone justifies it — quiet, fast, and proven over six months of daily abuse — and the flaws are livable if you know about them going in. Recalibrate occasionally, re-torque your bolts, replace the cable tray immediately, and you've got a desk that does its job.

At **$749**, it's overpriced. At that number you're in range of frames with better lateral stability and controllers that remember where 42.5 inches actually is. The wobble and the preset drift are forgivable at $549. They are insults at $749.

Jarvik runs sales constantly — I've seen it at $549 three separate times since I bought mine. So the advice is simple: if you want this desk, set a price alert and wait. Do not pay full price. Full price is for people who don't read reviews, and you just read 800 words about a cable tray.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2, six months later: good at $549, not $749

I’ve used the Jarvik L2 as my everyday desk for six months of remote software work. My verdict is simple: at the $549 sale price, it’s worth considering. At $749, I’d pass.

The motor is the L2’s best feature. It’s quiet, and it moves the desk quickly enough that changing positions doesn’t feel like a chore. I’m more likely to alternate between sitting and standing when the adjustment is unobtrusive, and the L2 gets that part right.

The main compromise is stability at full height. If I type hard, the desk wobbles. It’s not an issue during ordinary use, but it’s noticeable when I’m really hammering at the keyboard. If you’re a light typist, you may barely care. If you tend to type forcefully, or expect a completely solid surface while standing, this will probably annoy you.

The memory presets are convenient, but not precise enough to set and forget. Over time, they drift by about a centimeter. That’s a small difference, but it defeats some of the point of having presets: I want to press a button and get the height I saved, not a close approximation.

And the cable tray is garbage. It’s the weakest part of the package and doesn’t feel like a useful solution for managing cables. If tidy cable routing matters to you, plan on replacing it or finding another approach.

None of those flaws makes the L2 unusable. The quiet, fast motor makes daily height changes pleasant, and the desk has been good enough for my work. But the wobble, drifting presets, and poor cable tray are real compromises—not nitpicks I’d wave away at the full asking price.

At **$549**, I think the Jarvik L2 is a reasonable buy if you value a quiet, quick motor and can live with some movement at standing height. At **$749**, I expect better stability and better execution on the smaller details. That’s not the desk I got.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
After 200+ interviews, the best signal I've found isn't in how candidates answer questions. It's in what they ask.

The strong ones ask about a project that failed.

Not "what's the biggest challenge on the team" — that question gets a rehearsed answer every time. I mean specifically asking about something that went wrong, recently, and what happened after.

Had this exchange a few months back, hiring for a logistics coordinator role:

Candidate: "Can you tell me about a project or initiative here that didn't go the way you planned?"

Me: We rolled out a new routing system last year that was supposed to cut delivery times. It didn't account for driver familiarity with regions, so efficiency actually dropped for the first six weeks.

Candidate: "What did the team do once you realized it wasn't working?"

Me: We rolled back the auto-assignment piece and let dispatchers override it manually while we retrained the model on actual driver patterns.

Candidate: "Who made the call to roll it back, and how long did that take?"

That last question told me more than anything on her resume. She wasn't asking to catch us out. She was trying to understand how decisions get made when something breaks — how fast, by whom, with what appetite for admitting it isn't working.

That's the thing about failure questions. Anyone can ask about wins and get a polished story back. Asking about failure forces the interviewer to be honest in real time, and how they handle that moment tells the candidate exactly what kind of place they're walking into.

I've started expecting this question from anyone who's done real diligence. When I don't get it, I don't hold it against them. But when I do, I pay attention to what they do with the answer.

b.text:
After roughly 200 interviews, one question still makes me pause in a good way:

“What’s the last project that didn’t work, and what happened next?”

In logistics, there’s usually an honest answer. A conversation might go like this:

“We rolled out a new routing process before the depot teams had enough input. It looked good in testing, but dispatchers ended up working around it.”

The candidate asks, “Did you change the process, or did you expect the teams to adapt?”

That follow-up tells me a lot. They’re not just checking whether we can admit a mistake. They want to know whether the people closest to the work are heard when something goes wrong.

It’s a fair question for a candidate to ask. And if we can’t give a clear answer, that’s useful information for both of us.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
Over roughly 200 interviews, I’ve noticed a clear pattern in the final ten minutes.

Most candidates ask about daily routines, tech stacks, or growth opportunities. Standard, safe questions.

The strongest candidates ask something that forces me to put the employer-branding pitch aside:

"Can you tell me about the last major project here that failed, and what happened next?"

A few months ago, an operations candidate asked me this. 

I gave him the unvarnished version: we spent four months rolling out an automated scheduling pilot at two of our cross-docks. The dispatchers hated it. It added ten minutes of manual overrides per route instead of saving time, and we ultimately had to pull the plug and start over.

Instead of just nodding, he asked: 

"When you pulled the plug, did the project lead stay on to run the rebuild, or did leadership reassign it?"

That single question told me more about his maturity than the previous 40 minutes of his resume walkthrough. He wasn’t trying to trap me. He was evaluating our psychological safety. He wanted to know if we treat failure as a learning loop or a career penalty.

Experienced candidates know every company breaks things. The only real question is whether you handle it with a blameless post-mortem or a scapegoat.

b.text:
I've sat in on roughly 200 interviews at our company. The candidates who end up being the strongest hires almost always ask some version of the same question:

"Tell me about a project here that didn't work out."

Not "what's the culture like." Not "what does success look like in 90 days." Those are fine. But the failed-project question changes the whole conversation.

Recent example. We were interviewing for an ops analyst role, and near the end the candidate asked our hiring manager about the last initiative that got shelved. The manager paused, then told her about a warehouse slotting overhaul we'd rolled out too fast — pilots looked great, full rollout fell apart because we hadn't accounted for how differently our seasonal sites run.

Her follow-up: "When it started going sideways, how long before someone said so out loud?"

The manager laughed and gave her an honest answer (longer than it should have been). They spent ten minutes talking about how the team handles bad news now. That was the moment he decided to hire her.

Here's why the question works. Anyone can vet a company on its wins — that's what the careers page is for. Asking about failure tells you how the company actually behaves under pressure. Do they blame a person or examine a process? Do they get cagey or get specific?

And it tells us something too. This candidate isn't shopping for a place where nothing goes wrong. She's checking whether it's safe to be the one who flags a problem.

If you're interviewing anywhere right now, ask it. The answer — and how comfortable they are giving it — will tell you more than the entire job description.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The couples who toss the shot list almost always end up with the best photos.

I've shot weddings in the Texas Hill Country full time for eight years, and that pattern hasn't broken yet.

The Barrera wedding is my favorite example. We had a plan: locations mapped out, timeline built around the light, every portrait spot picked in advance. Then it rained, and the plan was gone.

We moved everything under the pecan tree.

Nobody had scouted that spot or pinned it to a list. But once the pressure of "we need to get these 25 shots" disappeared, everyone relaxed. The couple stopped performing for the camera and started being with each other and their people. The tree gave us soft light and a natural canopy, and the rain became part of the story instead of a problem to work around.

Those are the photos they talk about.

A shot list isn't evil. Family formals benefit from a clear list so Aunt Linda doesn't get missed. But when a list becomes a checklist for the whole day, you end up photographing the list instead of the wedding.

What I tell couples now:

→ Give me the must-haves, the handful of moments or people that truly matter
→ Trust me with the rest
→ If the weather, the schedule, or the mood shifts, let's shift with it

For my fellow vendors: the best thing we can do is make it safe for the plan to change. Couples feel that calm, and it shows up in the work.

For couples still planning: the best photos from your day are probably not on any list. Hire someone you trust to find them.

And if it rains, find a good tree.

b.text:
The couples who ditch the shot list usually end up with the best photos.

Not the family-photo list. Please keep that one. Knowing which people you want together saves everyone time.

I mean the list of 40 inspiration photos we’re supposed to recreate.

At the Barrera wedding, rain changed the plan. We moved everything under the pecan tree.

The job wasn’t to force the original vision to work. It was to pay attention to what the wedding had become—and photograph that.

After eight years photographing weddings full time here in the Texas Hill Country, that’s the difference I keep coming back to:

A shot list asks me to look for a picture someone already made.
Trust lets me see the picture happening in front of me.

Tell your photographer what matters. Tell them who matters. Share the photos you love and what you love about them.

Then leave some room for your own wedding to look like your own wedding.

Even when it ends up under a pecan tree.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
**Why your dog keeps coming in matted (and what to do at home)**

Most of the dogs I see with mats didn't get that way because anyone was neglecting them. They got that way because somebody did the exact thing that seems like it should help, and it made everything worse. So before I get into brushing, I want to talk about the bath.

Please don't bathe a matted dog. I know the logic. The coat's dirty and tangled, water and shampoo loosen things up, you'll deal with the knots after. That's how it works with our hair. It is not how it works with a doodle or a Golden or an Aussie. When a mat gets wet, the hairs swell and grip each other, and as it dries it shrinks down into something closer to felt than fur. What was a loose tangle I could have brushed out in a few minutes is now a solid pad against the skin, and the only kind option is to clip it off. If I've ever had to shave your dog shorter than you wanted, this is almost always why.

So the order is brush first, then bath. Always. If you find something you can't get through, leave the bath for another day or call me. I'd much rather you bring in a dry, tangled dog than a clean one that's been felted.

Now the brushing itself. For double coats and curly coats you want a slicker brush, the one with the flat head and all the fine bent wires. Not the soft bristle brush, not the rubber curry. Those feel nice to the dog and do nothing underneath. The slicker is what actually gets down into the layer where mats start.

The way you move it matters more than people think. You want short, straight strokes, a couple of inches at a time, always in the direction the hair grows. Line up a stroke, brush, move over, brush again. What you don't want is scrubbing in circles or dragging the brush in one long pull from neck to tail. Circles twist the hair around itself and start new tangles. Long pulls skate over the top and miss everything close to the skin. Think of it like you're combing through a little section at a time and checking that the brush is reaching skin before you move on.

Work in sections, and start where the trouble starts. On almost every dog that's behind the ears and under the front legs, in that armpit area where the collar and the harness rub. Those two spots mat before anywhere else, so if you only have five minutes, spend them there. After that go to the chest, the back legs and rear, the belly, the base of the tail. The back is usually the least of your worries even though it's the part that gets petted the most.

If you run your fingers through and feel a clump starting to form, stop. Don't go at it with the brush yet. Get a little leave-in conditioner or detangling spray and work it into that spot with your fingers. Actually massage it in and start gently pulling the hair apart with your fingertips. A lot of small mats will loosen up this way before a brush ever touches them. Once you can feel the individual hairs moving again, then you go in with the slicker, from the outside edge of the tangle toward the center, in those same short strokes. If it's tight against the skin and won't budge with your fingers, that's the point where you leave it for me. Pulling harder just hurts the dog and teaches them to hate the brush.

A few minutes every other day beats an hour on Sunday. The coat never gets a chance to lock up, the dog gets used to it, and you'll actually notice the small stuff before it turns into the big stuff. And when you bring them in, tell me where you've been finding tangles. It helps me know what's going on with the coat and whether the harness or the collar might need adjusting.

If you're not sure you've got the right brush, bring it to your next appointment and I'll take a look. Happy to show you the stroke on your own dog too, that's easier than reading about it.

b.text:
I see it all the time with double-coated and curly dogs—those beautiful coats that look so soft until you try to run a brush through them a couple weeks after their last appointment and hit a wall of mats. Between visits is when most of the trouble starts, and the biggest mistake I watch people make is jumping straight into a bath thinking warm water and shampoo will loosen everything up. It does the opposite. Once that fur gets wet, any little tangle turns into a dense felt pad that is ten times harder to get out. You end up with a dog that needs a full shave-down when a little dry brushing could have saved the coat.

So brush first, always, while the dog is completely dry. Grab a slicker brush and work in short line strokes—think gentle little lines, not big circles that just push the hair around and create more knots. Start in the spots where mats love to form first: right behind the ears and under the front legs. Those areas rub and collect moisture, so if you keep them clear, the rest of the coat usually stays manageable. Section the dog as you go so you can actually see what you’re doing instead of just skimming the surface.

If you already feel a mat starting to form, stop before you even pick up the brush. Work a little conditioner into it with your fingers, really massage it in, and let it sit for a minute. That softens the tangle so the brush or comb can slip through without ripping. Once it’s loosened, then you can carefully work it out. Trying to force a dry mat with a comb is how you end up with broken hair and a sore dog.

A few minutes of this a couple times a week keeps most coats from turning into a project between appointments. Your dog stays more comfortable, and when they come in for their next groom we can focus on the fun stuff instead of digging out weeks of mats.

✅ Shift is 10PM–8AM, 4 nights/week (Sunday–Wednesday, to be exact). Your sleep schedule will take adjustment, and you’ll miss weekend dinners, early morning plans, and all the daytime stuff most people take for granted.
✅ Some nights you’re fully solo. That means you’re the one triaging the 2AM urgent walk-in, monitoring our 6 hospitalized patients, updating a frantic owner whose dog is vomiting blood, and mopping up a cat’s mess after a stressful arrival—no teammate right there to step in for a break.
✅ It’s feast or famine. Some nights are quiet enough that you can catch up on charting and give extra snuggles to the nervous boarders. Other nights are so chaotic you’ll barely have time to drink your coffee, and you have to problem-solve fast without waiting for direction.
✅ It can feel isolating. You won’t be in the thick of the daytime team’s inside jokes or daily huddles, and you’ll have to be intentional about staying connected to the rest of the staff.
