setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
My first week in the emergency room did not go the way I expected.

I thought I would spend most of my time watching nurses, learning where supplies were kept, and trying not to get in the way. I did learn those things, but I also learned that nursing is often about staying present during moments that are difficult, rushed, or uncertain.

One of the first patients I met needed a wound cleaned. His wife was on her way, but she was stuck in traffic. He was nervous and kept looking toward the door. Since she could not be there yet, I sat beside him and held his hand while the nurse worked. I did not have the experience to fix the problem or make the pain go away. All I could do was stay with him. I realized that sometimes a patient does not need a long explanation or a perfect answer. Sometimes they need to know they are not alone.

Another moment happened during a code. I was sent to restock gauze, so I was outside the room when I heard the team counting through the curtain. The voices were quick and steady. I could hear how focused everyone was. Even though I was not directly involved, I understood that every person in that room had a job, and every second mattered. I returned with the supplies and saw how the nurses moved with purpose. They were calm because they had practiced, studied, and learned how to work together. That moment showed me the responsibility that comes with this profession.

The hardest moment for me was a blood draw on a diabetic patient with difficult veins. I missed three times. Each time, I felt more embarrassed and more nervous. I knew the patient was already dealing with enough, and I did not want to make things harder for him. After the third attempt, I took a breath and tried again. On the fourth try, I got the draw.

I was relieved, but I also knew that getting it on the fourth try did not make the first three attempts disappear. The patient was patient with me, and I was grateful for that. The experience taught me that being a good nurse does not mean getting everything right the first time. It means being honest, paying attention, learning from mistakes, and continuing to treat the patient with respect.

That first week made nursing feel more real to me. In class, we learn skills and procedures. In the ER, I saw how those skills affect real people. I saw fear, pain, urgency, and trust. I also saw how much patients depend on nurses to be prepared and present.

I left that week tired, but more certain that I had chosen the right path. I still have a great deal to learn, and I know there will be more difficult days ahead. But I am ready to keep learning. My first week in the ER reminded me that nursing is not only about knowing what to do. It is also about showing up, staying calm, and caring for people when they need it most.

b.text:
My first week in the ER, I mostly tried to stay out of the way.

I'm in my first year of nursing school. I don't know much yet. I know how to wash my hands right and check blood pressure and not touch stuff I'm not supposed to. That first week was the first time I was around real sick and hurt people, not just class stuff.

The first day, there was a man with a bad cut on his leg that they had to clean out. It hurt and he was scared. His wife was trying to get there but she was stuck in traffic. The nurse said I could stand with him. I held his hand while they cleaned it. He squeezed so hard. He was my dad's age, but he just held on and looked at the wall. I didn't really know what to say, so I just said you're doing good, almost done. His wife walked in right when they finished. I was glad she made it, but I'm glad I was there for the part she missed.

Another day there was a code. I wasn't supposed to go in the room. They sent me to the back to restock the gauze. I was in the supply room stuffing gauze into the bins and I could hear them through the curtain. I could hear them counting, one, two, three, real steady for the chest pushes. Someone calling out what to do next. I just stood there and listened and kept stacking. I felt pretty useless. I kept thinking I should be doing more. But somebody has to make sure the gauze is there when they yell for it. That stuck with me.

The one I still think about was a blood draw. He was a diabetic guy and his veins were bad, they roll and they're hard to find. I missed three times in a row. Three sticks and no blood. He didn't get mad, which almost made it worse. My face was hot and my hands were shaking. I wanted to quit and tell the nurse to just do it. She told me to take a breath and try one more time. On the fourth try I got it. Blood came back in the tube and I almost couldn't believe it. He smiled and said, see, you got it. I said sorry about ten times and he just said it's okay.

I know I'm just starting. I have a lot to learn. But that week showed me what the job really is. It's holding someone's hand when their person can't be there yet. It's getting the gauze ready when you can't be in the room. It's saying sorry and trying again when you mess up.

This money would help me a lot. I work part time now and school costs a lot with gas and books and everything else. It would help me work less and focus more on school so I can finish and be good at this. Thank you for reading this.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Baseboard Heating Before Winter

Switch the circulator off or set the boiler to **Off** so water isn’t being pushed through the system while air is escaping.

1. **Shut off the circulator or boiler first.**  
   If the pump has its own switch, turn it off there. If not, turn the boiler control to Off or power off the boiler circuit.

2. **Find the bleeder valve on each baseboard unit.**  
   Look at the end cap of the baseboard run. The valve is usually small, threaded, and may need a radiator key or a flathead screwdriver.

3. **Place a cup underneath the valve.**  
   Air will sputter out first, then water. A small coffee cup or plastic container catches it neatly.

4. **Open the valve slowly with the key or flathead screwdriver.**  
   Turn it just enough to hear the hiss of air. Don’t open it wide right away. Let the air come out gently.

5. **Wait until the water runs steady with no hissing air.**  
   You’ll usually get a few short bursts of air, then a smooth, continuous stream of water.

6. **Close the valve snug, but don’t overtighten.**  
   Once the water is steady, turn the valve closed. Overtightening can crack the valve seat and cause a slow leak.

7. **Go unit by unit, starting closest to the boiler and working outward.**  
   Bleed each baseboard loop in sequence so air doesn’t get trapped farther out in the system.

The mistake that causes most of our cold radiator calls is people only bleed the upstairs units and skip the basement loop. In many homes, the basement loop is where the air actually collects. If you miss it, the upstairs baseboards may still heat poorly even after bleeding them.

b.text:
**Step 1: Shut off the boiler and circulator**

Turn the power off before you open anything. Let the water cool down for 20-30 minutes if the heat was just running.

**Step 2: Find the bleeder valve**

Look at the end of each baseboard unit, usually under the end cap. It's a small brass valve with a tiny square or slotted head. You'll need a bleeder key or a small flathead screwdriver, plus a cup and an old towel.

**Step 3: Bleed each unit, one at a time**

Start with the baseboard closest to the boiler and work your way out from there, unit by unit.

Hold the cup right underneath the valve. Open it slowly — just a quarter turn or so. You'll hear hissing first. That's the air you want out.

Leave it open until that hissing stops and water comes out in a steady stream with no sputtering or bubbles. Then close it.

Snug is enough. Do not crank it down hard. Overtightening can crack the valve seat, and then you've turned a 10-minute job into a repair call.

Move to the next unit and repeat.

**Don't skip the basement**

This is the mistake behind most of our cold radiator calls. People bleed the upstairs units, feel a little air come out, and call it done.

Bleed the basement loop too, even if those baseboards feel warm. That's usually where the air is actually trapped, and air trapped down there will keep the upstairs units from heating right no matter how many times you bleed them.

Once you've done every unit — basement, first floor, upstairs, in order out from the boiler — turn the boiler and circulator back on and let it run. Walk the house again in 15 minutes and feel each baseboard end to end. They should be heating evenly now.

If one is still cold after a proper bleed, or your valve won't close and keeps dripping, shut that unit's valve and give us a call before it turns into a leak.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
## How to Bleed Air Out of Baseboard Heating

1. **Turn off the boiler and circulator pump.**  
   Shut the system down and let it cool for a few minutes before opening any bleeder valves. You do not want hot water spraying out while the circulator is running.

2. **Find the bleeder valve on each baseboard unit.**  
   Most baseboard radiators have a small bleeder valve at one end, usually near the top. It may have a square fitting for a radiator key or a slotted screw that takes a flathead screwdriver.

3. **Put a cup or small container under the valve.**  
   Have a rag handy too. Even when there is only air in the line, water will follow it once the air is released.

4. **Open the bleeder valve slowly.**  
   Turn the valve just enough to let air escape. You should hear hissing or sputtering if air is trapped in that section of baseboard.

5. **Wait for a steady stream of water.**  
   Keep the valve open until the hissing stops and water comes out in a smooth, steady stream without spitting air.

6. **Close the valve snugly.**  
   Tighten it only until it stops dripping. Do not overtighten it—too much force can damage or crack the valve seat and turn a simple maintenance job into a leak.

7. **Move from unit to unit, starting near the boiler.**  
   Bleed the baseboards closest to the boiler first, then work your way farther out through the house. This helps push trapped air through the system instead of leaving it stuck in another loop.

8. **Do not skip the basement loop.**  
   One of the most common reasons we get calls for cold radiators is that homeowners bleed only the upstairs baseboards. The basement loop is often where the air is actually trapped, especially if it runs lower than the rest of the system.

9. **Turn the boiler and circulator back on.**  
   Once every unit has been bled, restart the system and let it heat up. Check that each baseboard is warming evenly and that none of the bleeder valves are dripping.

If a baseboard still stays cold after bleeding, the problem may be low boiler pressure, a stuck zone valve, a circulator issue, or a blockage in the loop.

b.text: Before you touch a thing, shut off the circulator or boiler to eliminate pressure and prevent scalding. Locate the bleeder valve at the end of each baseboard unit—a small nipple designed for a radiator key or flathead screwdriver. Place a cup or rag underneath to catch any drips, then open the valve slowly. You’ll hear air hissing at first; keep it open until the stream turns into a steady, bubble-free flow of water. Once that’s achieved, close the valve snugly by hand or with a light turn of the key. Don’t overtighten; forcing it can damage the valve seat and cause a leak. Work through every unit, starting with the one closest to the boiler and moving outward through the loop. A pro tip from our service calls: the most common mistake homeowners make is bleeding only the upstairs radiators and skipping the basement loop. Air tends to settle there, and if you miss it, the basement units will stay cold all winter regardless of how many upstairs ones you fix.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

Do this before the first hard freeze. It takes 10 minutes per spigot, and it prevents the burst pipes we repair all over Minneapolis every January.

**1. Disconnect your hoses**
This is the big one. Leaving a hose connected is the #1 mistake we see, and it's behind most of our January burst-pipe calls. Even if you shut the water off inside, a connected hose traps water in the pipe. That water freezes, expands, and splits the pipe inside your wall — you just don't find out until you turn it on in the spring.

Disconnect the hose, drain it, and store it in the garage or shed.

**2. Shut off the interior valve**
Go to your basement or utility room and find the shutoff valve for that outside spigot. It's usually on an interior wall, close to where the pipe goes outside. Turn it clockwise to close it.

Every outside spigot should have its own interior shutoff. If yours doesn't, stop here and call us. We can install one, and it's a lot cheaper than repairing a burst pipe in January.

**3. Drain the spigot**
Go back outside and open the spigot all the way. Any water left between the interior valve and the outside faucet will drain out. Leave it open for a minute until it stops dripping, then close it.

If you have a small drain cap on the interior valve, open that too with a bucket underneath to drain any remaining water from the line, then close it back up.

**4. Put on a foam cover**
Pick up a foam faucet cover — they're about $3 at any hardware store. Slide it tight over the spigot and cinch it down. It’s cheap insurance against Minneapolis cold snaps, especially on north-facing and wind-exposed faucets.

That’s it. Hose off, water off inside, drained outside, cover on.

If you can’t find your shutoff, your valve won’t fully close, or your spigot is already dripping or leaking, give us a call before it freezes. We’re a local, family-run shop, and we’d much rather help you winterize now than cut out a burst pipe later.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

Winterizing your outside spigots helps prevent frozen pipes, water damage, and emergency plumbing repairs. In Minneapolis, outdoor faucets can freeze quickly when temperatures drop, especially if water is trapped in the spigot or the pipe behind it.

Follow these steps before the first hard freeze.

## 1. Shut off the interior water valve

Find the interior shutoff valve that controls your outdoor spigot. It is usually located in the basement, utility room, crawl space, or near where the pipe passes through the foundation wall.

Turn the valve clockwise until it is closed. If your home has more than one outdoor faucet, check for a separate shutoff valve for each one.

If you cannot find an interior shutoff valve, call a Minneapolis plumber for help. Some homes do not have a dedicated valve, and forcing or incorrectly closing the wrong valve can create additional problems.

## 2. Disconnect the garden hose

Remove every hose, splitter, timer, nozzle, and other attachment from the outdoor spigot.

This is the most important step—and the mistake we see most often. Leaving a hose connected can trap water inside the faucet and the pipe. When that water freezes, it expands and can crack the spigot or the water line inside your wall.

A connected hose is responsible for many of the burst-pipe calls we receive in January.

Store the hose indoors or in a protected garage space after draining it.

## 3. Open the outside spigot

Once the interior shutoff valve is closed, open the outdoor faucet completely. Let any remaining water drain out.

Leave the spigot open through the winter. This gives trapped water a place to expand if it freezes and helps relieve pressure in the pipe.

If your shutoff valve has a small bleeder cap or drain screw, place a bucket underneath and open it carefully to drain water from the section of pipe between the valve and the outside faucet. Close the bleeder cap after the line has drained, but leave the outdoor spigot open.

## 4. Install a foam faucet cover

After the spigot has drained, install an inexpensive foam faucet cover. These covers typically cost around $3 and are available at most hardware stores.

To install one:

1. Place the cover over the outdoor spigot.
2. Secure it according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
3. Make sure it fits snugly against the wall.

A foam cover adds insulation and helps protect the faucet from cold air. It does not replace shutting off and draining the water line.

## What if you have a frost-free spigot?

Frost-free or freeze-resistant outdoor faucets are designed to drain when they are shut off. However, they still require the hose and attachments to be removed. A hose can prevent the faucet from draining properly and may cause the pipe to freeze.

If a frost-free spigot leaks, does not drain, or continues running after you shut it off, have it inspected by a plumber.

## What to do if you cannot find the shutoff valve

Do not assume the outdoor faucet is safe just because it has a foam cover. If you do not have an interior shutoff valve—or cannot locate it—contact a professional plumber before freezing weather arrives.

A plumber can help identify the correct valve and determine whether the outdoor water line needs to be drained or repaired.

For Minneapolis homeowners, the basic winterization checklist is simple:

- Shut off the interior valve.
- Disconnect all hoses and attachments.
- Open and drain the outside spigot.
- Install a foam faucet cover.
- Call a plumber if there is no interior shutoff valve.

Taking a few minutes to winterize your outdoor spigots can help prevent a burst pipe and costly water damage during a Minneapolis winter.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
# Keeping Your Dog’s Coat Mat-Free Between Grooming Visits

The mistake I see most often is a well-meaning one: someone notices their dog is getting tangled and decides a bath will loosen everything up. Unfortunately, it usually does the opposite. Water, rubbing, and drying can tighten existing mats into a dense, felt-like pad that’s much harder to remove comfortably.

So if there’s one thing I’d like you to remember, it’s this: **check for tangles and brush them out before the bath. Don’t save the detangling for afterward.** If you find matting you can’t gently work through, skip the bath and give us a call.

This matters especially for curly coats, which can tangle close to the skin even when the outside looks fluffy, and double coats, where loose undercoat can get trapped beneath the longer outer hairs. A quick brush over the top can make either coat look tidy without reaching the trouble underneath.

When you’re brushing at home, start behind the ears and under the front legs. Those are two of the first places I check in the salon because friction makes them common trouble spots. Then work through the rest of the coat in small sections, paying attention to the collar or harness area, belly, back legs, and tail.

Use a slicker brush with short, gentle strokes—not circles or long, hard pulls. Part the hair so you can see a little strip of skin, then brush that small section, working from the ends inward if you meet a tangle. Move the part slightly and repeat. This is called line brushing, and it helps you get through the coat instead of just skimming the surface. Keep the pressure light; slicker pins can irritate skin if you scrape or repeatedly work the same spot.

If you spot a small, loose tangle starting to form, put the brush down for a moment. Work a little dog-safe detangling conditioner into it with your fingers first, following the product directions. For use between baths, choose one labeled as a leave-in or detangling product. Gently tease the hairs apart rather than pulling the knot away from the skin. Once it loosens, you can carefully brush through it.

A tight mat is a different situation. If it’s sitting against the skin, feels like a solid lump, or makes your dog flinch, don’t keep picking at it. Please don’t try to cut it out with scissors, either—skin can be pulled up inside a mat where you can’t see it. Sometimes clipping is the kindest option.

After brushing, a metal comb is a useful check. It should pass gently through each section without catching. If it stops, don’t force it; go back and check that spot.

And yes, brushing again once a freshly bathed coat is fully dry can be helpful. The important part is not leaving existing tangles in place until after the bath.

A few calm minutes regularly will do more than an occasional marathon brushing session. If you’re unsure whether you’re reaching all the way through your dog’s coat, ask me at your next visit. I’m happy to show you on your own dog—it’s much easier once you’ve seen and felt what you’re looking for.

b.text:
If your dog has a double coat or a curly coat, the weeks between grooming visits are usually where the trouble starts. I see it all the time: the coat looks fine from the top, but once I part it, the tangles are already tightening near the skin. The good news is you can do a lot at home to keep small snarls from turning into mats, as long as you catch them early and avoid the mistake that makes them worse.

At home, brush before the bath, never after. I know that sounds backward, because a lot of people think bathing first will loosen everything up. That is the mistake I see constantly. Water can make a matted coat feel softer for a minute, but wet matted fur tightens as it dries and can turn into something like a felt pad. Once that happens, it is much harder to brush out safely, and sometimes it cannot be brushed out at all. So if the coat is tangled, skip the bath and work on brushing first.

Use a slicker brush, and use short line strokes, not circles. Short strokes let you work through the coat in a controlled way without pushing the tangle around or making the outside look smooth while the base stays tight. Circles can drag the hair and make the mat denser, especially close to the skin. You want to be gentle, but you also want to make sure you are actually getting into the coat where the mat is starting.

Work in sections, and start where mats usually begin first: behind the ears and under the front legs. Those spots get a lot of friction from movement, collars, harnesses, laying down, and everyday life. If you can keep those two areas open, you are already ahead of the game. After that, move through the coat in small sections instead of just brushing over the top. With curly coats, watch for little curls that are starting to bind together. With double coats, pay attention to the softer undercoat, because that is often where the mat grabs first.

If you can already feel a mat forming, do not go straight at it with a brush or comb. Work a little conditioner into it with your fingers first. Be gentle. Let the conditioner help the hairs slide apart instead of pulling against each other. A lot of times, you can ease the beginning of a mat open enough that brushing becomes much safer. If you jump right in with a dry brush, you can tighten it faster and make it more uncomfortable for your dog.

The biggest thing I want you to remember is that bathing a tangled dog first usually makes the problem worse, not better. It does not loosen the mats. It locks them in tighter. Between visits, your goal is not to make the coat perfect. Your goal is to keep it from tightening. A few short brushing sessions, starting behind the ears and under the front legs, can keep small tangles from becoming the kind of mats that need to be shaved out. And if you already feel something tight, firm, or close to the skin, do not keep fighting it at home. Bring it in, and we can help you get ahead of it before it becomes uncomfortable for your dog.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
In about 200 interviews, I’ve noticed a pattern: the strongest candidates almost always ask about our last failed project.

Not to be “difficult.”
Not to catch anyone out.

They ask because they understand that failure tells you more about a team than a polished success story ever will.

One version of that conversation usually goes like this:

Candidate: “Can you tell me about a project that didn’t go as planned, and what you learned from it?”

Me: “Sure. We rolled out a process change in our logistics ops team that looked good on paper, but we underestimated how much it would disrupt the handoff between recruiting, onboarding, and site operations. The idea was right. The sequencing wasn’t.”

Candidate: “What was the part you missed?”

Me: “We focused on speed and didn’t pressure-test the people side of the change early enough. We had the plan, but not enough buy-in from the teams who had to live with it.”

Candidate: “And what changed after that?”

Me: “We brought those teams in earlier, simplified the rollout, and gave managers more room to adapt it locally. The next version took longer to launch, but it worked better.”

That’s the kind of question that stands out to me.

Because the best candidates aren’t just evaluating the role.
They’re evaluating how a company thinks when things go wrong.

b.text:
I’ve sat through roughly 200 interviews these past few years. The candidates who get offers rarely ask about ping-pong tables or our "family culture."

They ask about the warehouse management system we rolled out in Dallas that had to be rolled back.

They ask about the failed 3PL partnership we exited last quarter.

Here’s how one of those conversations actually went last month:

Candidate: "I read that the automation pilot in Atlanta got paused. What happened?"

Me: "We hit a wall with the barcode scanners. The hardware worked fine, but the data wasn't syncing with our legacy TMS. We burned three months before admitting we needed middleware we didn't budget for."

Candidate: "Who caught it? Was it leadership or someone on the ground?"

Me: "A warehouse associate, actually. She flagged that the scan times were creating a bottleneck at shift change."

Candidate: "So if I'm hired, I'd be working with floor teams to surface those operational bottlenecks before we buy software, not after?"

Me: "Exactly. That's the job."

The difference isn't the question—it's the follow-up. They’re not interviewing for the LinkedIn version of this company. They’re interviewing for the version that actually exists on a Tuesday afternoon when the conveyor belt jams.

If you’re hiring, pay attention to who asks about the scar tissue. That’s where the real signal is.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
**Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors**

Our cafeteria has 220 seats. During the lunch wave that most juniors and seniors are assigned to, 340 students are scheduled to eat. That is 120 more people than the room was built to hold, every single day, and it is not a problem that is going to fix itself. Our school should let juniors and seniors leave campus for lunch.

The overcrowding is the most concrete reason. When 340 students are competing for 220 seats, something has to give, and what gives is usually the lunch period itself. Students spend part of a thirty-minute break waiting in line and part of it looking for a place to sit, which leaves very little time to actually eat. Doubling up at tables and eating in whatever empty space is available is not a solution; it is just what happens when a room is asked to hold more people than it can. Letting the oldest students leave campus would immediately relieve some of that pressure, and the students who stay would have a better chance of finding a seat and finishing a meal.

This is also not an untested idea. Three nearby districts, Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade, already allow open campus lunch for their upperclassmen, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness after the policy went into effect. That matters because tardiness is the objection people bring up first. If letting students leave for lunch caused them to wander back late, those three districts would have seen it in their numbers, and they did not.

Students at our school also want this. I surveyed 80 students, and 71 of them said they would support open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That is not a reason to change a policy by itself, and I am not pretending it is. Students do not get to vote on school rules. But a rule that the people it applies to actually want is a rule that is easier to enforce, because fewer students will spend their energy trying to get around it.

The strongest argument against open campus lunch is safety. If students leave, the school cannot supervise them, and if something happens off campus during a school day, the school could be held responsible. This is a fair concern, and it is the reason the policy needs to come with conditions rather than being handed out freely. Students who want the privilege could be required to get a parent signature, sign out and back in at the front office, and stay in good standing on attendance and grades. Juniors and seniors are old enough to drive or arrange their own transportation, and a privilege that can be taken away gives them a reason to follow the rules. The three nearby districts did not simply open the doors and hope for the best; they set up a system, and their tardiness data suggests it works.

What I am proposing is not open campus for the whole school, and it is not permanent. It is a one-semester trial for juniors and seniors, with sign-out sheets, parent permission, and a review at the end. If tardiness goes up, if attendance drops, if the office cannot keep track of who is where, then the trial ends and we go back to what we have now. If it goes the way it went in Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade, then we will have solved a crowding problem that we currently have no other way to solve. Either way, we would be making the decision based on what actually happens instead of what we assume will happen, and that seems like a reasonable thing for a school to do.

b.text:
**Give Juniors and Seniors Open Campus Lunch**

Juniors and seniors should be allowed to leave campus during lunch. Our current lunch period is overcrowded, many students want the option, and nearby districts have shown that open campus lunch can work without increasing tardiness. With clear rules, the school can give older students more independence while keeping the policy manageable.

The cafeteria does not have enough seats for the number of students in our lunch wave. It seats 220 people, but about 340 students have lunch at that time. That leaves roughly 120 students without a seat in the cafeteria. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus would reduce the crowding and give students another option for getting lunch or taking a break from the busy cafeteria.

Students also support the change. In a survey I conducted at our school, 71 out of 80 students favored open campus lunch. That is nearly 89 percent of the students who responded. The survey does not represent every student’s opinion, but it shows that support for the policy is strong among those asked.

Some people may worry that students will return late or that leaving campus will create safety problems. However, Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade already allow open campus lunch, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. Their experience suggests that students can handle the responsibility. Our school could also set expectations, such as requiring students to return before the bell and holding them accountable if they are late.

Open campus lunch would address an existing problem rather than create a new one. The cafeteria is overcrowded, most students in my survey supported the change, and other nearby districts have allowed it without an increase in tardiness. Juniors and seniors should have the option to leave campus during lunch under clear school rules.

a.text:
The market in this zip did not crash. Sellers just stopped listening to it.

Last spring, the median listing here was gone in eight days. This spring that number is 34. Showings per listing have been cut in half. And list prices are still up 6 percent from a year ago. That is not a mystery. That is a standoff, and sellers are the ones standing there alone.

I have three listings right now that have been sitting more than 60 days. All three owners have been told, with comps in hand, that the price is the problem. All three have refused to move. They are not waiting for the right buyer. They are waiting for last spring to come back, and it is not coming back on their timeline.

The houses that are priced for the market we actually have are still selling in under two weeks. Same zip. Same school districts. Same interest rates. The difference is the number on the sign. Buyers have not disappeared. They have gotten selective, and they have the time now to be selective. When a house is priced where the comps say it should be, they show up and they write. When it is priced where the seller wishes the comps still were, they scroll past it.

Six percent year-over-year on the asking price sounds like strength if you only read the headline. It is not strength when the house takes four times as long to sell and draws half the traffic. That gap is unsold inventory wearing a confident number. Every week a seller holds an inflated price, the listing gets staler, the photos get older in buyers' minds, and the eventual reduction has to be bigger than the one they refused in week three.

This is a pace change, not a collapse. Demand is still there for a correctly priced house. What is gone is the automatic sale, the one where you could tack last year's number onto this year's house and have three offers by Sunday. Agents who keep telling sellers that story are doing them a disservice. The data in this zip is not ambiguous, and neither is the result on the houses that ignored it.

If you are selling this spring, price it for the buyer who is actually walking through doors right now. The ones who did are already under contract. The ones who would not are still refreshing the listing and calling it a slow market.

b.text:
**This Isn’t a Crash. It’s a Pricing Problem.**

If you’ve been watching the local market this spring, you may be feeling whiplash. Last year, homes in my zip code were flying off the market in about eight days. This spring, the median days on market has stretched to 34. Showings per listing have dropped by half. And yet, list prices are still up about 6% year over year.

To some people, that combination sounds confusing. To others, it sounds alarming. But after 10 years of selling homes in this suburb, here is my take, plainly: this is not a crash. This is a market where too many sellers are still pricing like it’s last spring.

Buyers are still out there. But they are more deliberate. They are comparing homes more carefully. They are noticing when a property has been sitting. And they are no longer willing to chase an overpriced listing just because inventory feels tight.

I see this up close. Right now, I personally represent three sellers whose homes have been on the market for more than 60 days, and all three are resisting a price reduction. Meanwhile, the data is telling us something very clear: the homes that are priced correctly from the start are still going under contract in under two weeks.

That is not a weak market. That is a market punishing unrealistic pricing.

There is a big difference between slowing down and falling apart. What we are seeing locally is not demand disappearing. It is buyers refusing to bail out sellers who missed the shift.

Last spring, sellers could get away with testing the market. You could price a little high, wait for the frenzy, and still end up fine. That strategy does not work the same way now. When showings drop sharply and days on market climb, buyers notice. The longer a home sits, the more likely it is to become “that house” instead of “the one.”

And yet, list prices are still up 6% year over year. That tells me we have not fully reset expectations yet. Some sellers are still anchoring to last year’s comps, last year’s bidding wars, or the price their neighbor got three months ago. But today’s buyers are not underwriting yesterday’s market.

The sellers winning right now are the ones who understand the pace has changed. They are pricing sharp from day one. They are respecting the fact that buyers now have more breathing room, more time to think, and more leverage to walk away. Those sellers are still getting showings, still getting offers, and still moving quickly.

So no, I do not believe this is a crash. I believe it is a correction in seller expectations.

If you are thinking about selling, the biggest mistake you can make right now is treating this market like a rerun of last year. The buyers are still here. But the days of pricing high “just to see” and waiting for the market to rescue you are over.

In this market, price is not a suggestion. It is the strategy.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
I see this all the time—people trying so hard to keep their dog’s coat nice between appointments, but making one simple mistake that actually makes things ten times worse. They’ll bathe the dog first because they think water will loosen tangles. Here’s the problem: wet matted fur doesn’t loosen, it tightens into a solid felt pad, almost like wool that’s been shocked. And if your dog has a double coat or those tight curls, that felt locks in right against the skin. So the first rule, and I really can’t say it enough, is brush before the bath, never after.

If your pup is already dirty and you’re planning a quick home bath, you still need to work through the coat dry. Grab a slicker brush—not a pin brush, a slicker with fine bent wires—and use short line strokes, not circles. Lifting and flicking tiny sections at a time. The trick is to go in the direction the hair naturally falls and never just scrub over the surface. For double coats, that means gently parting the hair so you’re reaching the dense undercoat, not just slicking down the top. For curly breeds, those short strokes tease apart curls without stretching them into a bigger snarl.

Always start behind the ears and deep in the armpits. I know that sounds weird, but mats almost always set up shop there first because those spots get the most friction when the dog moves, sleeps, or wears a collar. Work in sections, lifting the ear, feeling for even a tiny rough patch, then moving down the neck and chest. Only when those hot spots are completely free do you move to the legs, belly, and tail. If you find a spot that’s already starting to mat up and feel solid, put the brush down. Take a dab of conditioner—nothing fancy, even the one you use on your own hair works—and work it into the mat with your fingers. Gently. You’re trying to add slip so the fibers can slide apart, not force them. Once it feels softer, you can go back with the slicker in those same short strokes, but honestly, if it’s stubborn, just leave it for me. Working it dry with a tool will only tighten it more and hurt your dog.

That whole “bath first” instinct people have is exactly backward. Water and shampoo swell the hair shaft and help those tangles cinch up like a knot. I’ve had to shave down double-coated dogs that were bathed at home without a single brush stroke first because the undercoat matted into a solid pelt. So remember: dry brush, short strokes, start behind ears and underarms, use conditioner on mats before you brush, and only then go for the bath. It’ll keep your dog comfortable and save both of us a lot of heartache at the next grooming visit.

b.text:
If you have a doodle, a poodle, a husky, or anything with that thick double coat at home, you know how fast it can go from fluffy to tangled. It doesn't take much — a rainy walk, a harness rubbing, just sleeping curled up funny.

The biggest thing I wish I could tell everyone before they try to fix it at home is brush before you ever get them wet. Never after. I see it in the salon constantly — someone gives their dog a nice bath first thinking it will loosen everything up, and it does the exact opposite. It locks them in tighter. Wet matted fur doesn't loosen, it just turns into a felt pad and then I have to shave it out, which none of us want.

When you do brush, grab a slicker brush and forget the big circle scrubbing motion. You want short, little line strokes, almost like you're pulling the hair away in layers. And don't just go over the top. You have to work in sections. Lift the coat and get underneath. I always tell people to start behind the ears and right under the front legs in the armpit area, because that's where mats start first every single time. If you can keep those spots clear, you're winning most of the battle.

If you do feel a little clump starting to form, don't go straight at it with the brush or a comb. Put a little dab of conditioner — the regular dog conditioner you use for bath time is fine — right on it and work it in with your fingers only. Let it sit and soften and gently start to pull the hairs apart with your fingers first. Once it feels looser, then you can go in with the brush.

A quick brush like that a few times a week before bath day will save you, save your dog, and save me having to do a big shave-down when you come in.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
**The Cereal Aisle**

The airport came first, so I'll start there.

We landed at Fort Campbell and bused over to the gym where the families waited. There was a band and balloons and people holding signs. My wife was standing near the back with our daughter, and I saw them before they saw me, which gave me a second to get my face right.

Maddie was six. When I'd left she was five and missing a front tooth. When I got to them my wife grabbed me and I grabbed her back, and when I bent down to Maddie she stepped behind her mom's leg and held on to it and looked at me from around the side.

She knew who I was. She'd seen me on video calls the whole year. But a face on a screen is one thing and a big guy in ACUs smelling like a fifteen-hour flight is another. I didn't push it. I said hey, kiddo, and stayed crouched down, and after a minute she came out and let me hug her, stiff, the way you hug a relative you don't know well. It took about two weeks before she was climbing on me again like I was furniture. Those two weeks were harder than most things that happened overseas, and I'm not saying that to be dramatic. It's just true.

A few days after I got back, my wife sent me to Kroger for milk and a few other things. Simple mission. I got the milk fine. Then I turned down the cereal aisle because Maddie wanted cereal, and I stopped.

There was a whole wall of it. I want to say forty kinds but it was probably more. Six kinds of Cheerios alone. For a year I'd eaten what the DFAC had or what came in the box, and choosing wasn't part of my day. Somebody decided and you ate it. Now here was this wall, and every box was yelling at me, and I could not pick one.

I stood there a long time. Long enough that a woman with a cart went past me twice and gave me a look the second time. I wasn't thinking about anything in particular. I wasn't having flashbacks or whatever people picture. I just couldn't make the decision. It seemed both too small to matter and too big to get wrong. My heart was going faster than the situation called for.

Finally I grabbed the yellow Cheerios box because it was the one I remembered from being a kid, and I walked out of that aisle like I was leaving somewhere. I checked my watch in the parking lot. I'd been in the store almost forty minutes for four items. I didn't tell my wife about it for a couple months.

The last thing is the door.

Downrange I slept facing the door of whatever I slept in. That's not a rule anybody gives you, it's just what you end up doing. You want to see what's coming in. After a while your body doesn't know how to do it any other way.

At home our bedroom door had always stayed open at night so we could hear Maddie down the hall. First night back, I closed it. My wife asked why and I said habit, and she let it go, but I could tell it bothered her. She wanted to hear her kid.

So I'd leave it open and lie there facing it, awake, watching a dark rectangle of hallway like something was going to come through it in a house in Tennessee where the biggest threat was the neighbor's dog. Or I'd wait for her to fall asleep and get up and shut it, quiet, and open it again before she woke up. I did that for longer than I want to admit.

What fixed it, mostly, was time and being tired. You can only lie awake so many nights before your body overrules you. Somewhere in there I stopped needing to see the door. Now I sleep on my back, door open, hallway light off, and most mornings the first thing I hear is Maddie's alarm going off down the hall and her hitting snooze on it, twice, every time, like her old man.

b.text:
The flight landed at four in the afternoon. We turned in our gear, went through the final briefs, and by six they let us into the terminal where the families were waiting. 

I dropped my duffel on the carpet. My wife came right to me, but my daughter stayed back. She was six then. She had both hands gripped into the side of her mother’s jeans, tucking her face into the denim so only one eye showed. I took my patrol cap off so she could see my haircut, knelt down, and said her name. She didn't budge. I had lost about twenty pounds since pre-mob and had a bad sunburn from the transit through Kuwait, but mostly, a year is a long time when you’ve only had six of them. She knew the man on the laptop screen on Sunday mornings, but she didn’t know the guy kneeling on the airport floor smelling like diesel fuel and canvas. We sat on a row of plastic chairs for ten minutes while I pulled a roll of grape Lifesavers out of my cargo pocket and laid them on the seat between us. Eventually, she took one, and then she let me carry her out to the parking garage.

Three days later, my wife asked me to go to the store to get milk and something for breakfast. 

I found the cereal aisle and stopped. I stayed there for about twenty minutes. I know it was twenty because I checked my watch twice thinking I was going to be late for something that didn't exist. There were at least forty different kinds of boxes on the shelves. Bright reds and blues, cartoons, marshmallows, whole wheat, frosted, organic, family size. Downrange, you ate whatever scrambled eggs were sitting in the metal pan at the DFAC, or you reached into an open box of MREs and took whatever brown bag your hand touched first. You never had to think about it. I stood on the tile with a plastic hand-basket, looking at forty different ways to buy grain and sugar, and I couldn't make my hand reach out and take one. My chest felt hot and crowded. A woman with a toddler in her cart asked if she could squeeze past me, and I apologized like I’d done something wrong, grabbed the plain yellow box of Cheerios nearest my shoulder, and walked straight to the registers.

Nights were harder to adjust to than the daytime. 

For twelve months in the container, my cot was shoved against the back wall, and I slept on my left side, facing the plywood door. It wasn't something I thought about; you just orient yourself toward the entrance with your boots lined up and your rifle where your hand drops. 

Back in our house, my wife liked the bedroom door left open a few inches so the air from the hallway fan could blow through, and so she could hear if our daughter woke up from a bad dream. For the first two months, I couldn't handle it. Every night after she fell asleep, I’d ease out from under the sheet, walk to the door on the balls of my feet, and click it shut. Then I’d lay back down on my left side, watching the knob in the dark until my eyes burned. 

Around month three, I started trying to leave it cracked like she wanted. I’d lay on my side, stare at the strip of light from the nightlight out in the hallway, and count backward from a hundred. If I got too wired, I’d turn over onto my right side, face the window, and look at the corner of our dresser until I went to sleep. 

Most nights now, the door stays open. I still wake up when the floorboards in the hall creak, but I don't sit straight up anymore. I just listen for a second, hear the cat walking past or the house settling, and pull the blanket back up.

setup: You're everyone at the startup. Yesterday's 40-minute outage was caused by a bad database migration during deploy.

a.text:
Hi team,

First and foremost: the system is fully recovered, stable, and yesterday's outage is completely resolved. 

As you know, we experienced a 40-minute outage yesterday around 2:00 PM. I know this was a stressful experience, especially for those of you fielding customer complaints, so I want to share a quick breakdown of what happened and how we are preventing it from happening again.

What happened:
During a routine software update, we ran a change to our database structure. Normally this happens instantly in the background, but this specific change ended up "locking" a core part of the database. While it was locked, our system couldn't access the data it needed to function, which caused the app to go down.

How we fixed it:
We reversed the update to the previous stable version, which immediately unlocked the database and brought everything back online.

How we prevent it going forward:
To avoid this in the future, we are changing our process. Any database changes that carry a risk of locking the system will no longer be bundled with our normal daytime updates. Instead, they will be run during scheduled, off-hours maintenance windows when traffic is low.

Thank you all for your patience and for helping manage the customer impact while we worked on the fix. Please let me know if you have any questions!

Thanks,

b.text:
Hi all,

Quick update on yesterday's outage: the issue is fully resolved, and the product is working normally. No data was lost.

**What happened**
Yesterday around 2:00pm, our product was down for about 40 minutes. During a routine update, we ran a change to our database (the system that stores all our customer data). That change locked up one of the main tables, which is like putting a "do not enter" sign on a key filing cabinet that almost every part of the app needs to open. It held the lock far longer than we expected, so the app couldn't get the information it needed and stopped working for customers.

**How we fixed it**
We rolled back the change, which released the lock and brought everything back online.

**What we're changing**
Changes like this one will no longer run as part of a normal deploy. Going forward, they'll run in a scheduled maintenance window, when few or no customers are using the product, and we'll give notice beforehand when it's relevant. That way, if something takes longer than expected, it won't affect customers.

**If you heard from customers**
If anyone wrote in about the outage, it's fine to tell them that the issue was caused by an internal database change, that it was fully fixed within about 40 minutes, and that we've changed our process to prevent it from happening again. If a customer reports something that still looks broken, please send it my way right away.

I'm sorry for the disruption, especially to those of you who were fielding customer complaints in the middle of it. If you have questions about any of this, reply here or grab me directly and I'm happy to walk through it.

Thanks,
[Your name]

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: My Review After 8 Months of Market Baking

I've had the Corlane SM6 for eight months now, and it runs almost every day. Most of that is sourdough for my weekend farmers market table, plus bagels, enriched loaves, and the occasional batch of cookies when my kids lobby hard enough. That's enough use to know where this mixer shines and where it annoys me.

Short version: **if you knead heavy dough every week, buy it. If you mostly make cookies and cake batter, don't.**

## The Motor Is the Reason to Buy This Mixer

The motor is the whole case for the SM6. It handles a double batch of stiff bagel dough without stalling, and bagel dough is the meanest thing I put through a mixer. It's low-hydration and dense, and it's the dough that makes lesser machines groan and walk across the counter.

The SM6 just keeps turning. I don't have to stop and pull the dough off the hook, I don't have to babysit it, and I don't smell that hot-motor smell that tells you you're shortening the machine's life. When I'm prepping for market and running batch after batch, that reliability matters more to me than anything else on the spec sheet.

## The Annoyances

**The bowl lift lever squeaks.** It's not a small squeak, either. I spray it with WD-40 about once a month to keep it quiet. It hasn't affected how the mixer works, but a $429 machine shouldn't need monthly maintenance on a lever.

**The included dough hook is too short for the bowl.** This was the bigger letdown. The bowl is deep, and the stock hook doesn't reach far enough to work the dough at the bottom properly, so I bought a third-party hook that fits better. Plan on that extra purchase. It's frustrating that a mixer marketed for bread ships with a hook that doesn't fully suit the bowl it comes with.

## The Price

The SM6 costs $429, which is $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid. That's a real premium, and for a lot of bakers it isn't justified.

## Who Should Buy the SM6

**Buy it if you knead heavy dough weekly.** That means bagels, stiff sourdough, or bread in volume, especially if you're selling or baking for a crowd. The motor is worth the extra $80 plus the cost of a better dough hook. Mine has earned its counter space many times over.

**Skip it if you mostly make cookies, cakes, and frosting.** Those jobs don't need this motor, and you'd be paying a premium for power you won't use while still living with the squeaky lever and the short hook. Buy the KitchenAid and spend the $80 on good vanilla and butter.

I'd buy the SM6 again for my market baking. I just wouldn't recommend it to anyone whose mixer mostly sees cake batter.

b.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8 Months of Almost-Daily Sourdough**

I’ve run the Corlane SM6 nearly every day for eight months, mostly for farmers market sourdough. It has also worked through double batches of stiff bagel dough, which is where this mixer really proves itself.

The motor is the highlight. A double batch of low-hydration bagel dough—heavy, stiff, and exactly the kind of thing that makes weaker mixers stall or overheat—kneads without stalling. The mixer doesn’t sound like it’s struggling, and the head stays stable. For weekly market production, the SM6 has been dependable in a way I didn’t fully expect at this price.

The downsides are specific and real. The bowl-lift lever squeaks, and I have to WD-40 it about once a month. That’s not difficult, but it’s annoying on a $429 mixer. The included dough hook is too short for the deep bowl, so it leaves unincorporated flour and dough at the bottom. I bought a third-party dough hook, which solves the problem but adds extra cost and means the out-of-box accessory isn’t quite right for bread dough. And at $429, the Corlane is $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid bowl-lift model.

**Verdict:** For heavy dough bakers—sourdough, bagels, stiff whole-grain loaves—this is a buy. The motor is the reason to choose it. For cookie and cake bakers, skip it. You’ll pay more than the KitchenAid and inherit the squeak and hook issue without getting any real benefit. This is a bread mixer, not an all-purpose mixer.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 standing desk: six months later

I’ve used the Jarvik L2 every workday for six months as a remote software engineer. The short version: I’d buy it again at the $549 sale price. I would not pay $749 for it.

The best thing about the L2 is the motor. It’s quiet enough that I’ll change heights during a call without thinking about it, and fast enough that switching between sitting and standing doesn’t feel like an interruption. That matters more than it sounds. If raising a desk is annoying, I stop doing it; with this one, I actually use both positions.

The worst thing is stability at full height. When I type hard, the desk wobbles. It’s noticeable at the keyboard, not just something I can spot by staring at the monitor. I can live with it because I usually stand a little below the desk’s maximum height. If you need its full range and you’re a heavy typist, I’d take this more seriously than a product-page claim that it’s “stable.”

The memory presets are useful but not precise. Mine drift by about a centimeter, so a saved height is more of a starting point than an exact position. I end up making small adjustments. It’s a minor irritation, but on a $749 desk, I’d expect better.

The cable tray is garbage. It’s the part of the desk I’m least willing to make excuses for: cable management should make setup and changes easier, not become another thing to work around. I’d budget for a separate solution rather than count it as a feature.

**Verdict:** At $549, the L2 gets the important daily interaction right: moving it is quick and quiet. At $749, the wobble, drifting presets, and lousy cable tray are too many compromises. Wait for a sale—or buy something else.

b.text:
**6-Month Review: Jarvik L2 Standing Desk – The Good, The Wobbly, and The Overpriced**

Six months in, the Jarvik L2 is a mixed bag—one that’s worth your money only if you catch it on sale. Here’s the unfiltered breakdown.

### **The Good: Quiet, Fast, and (Mostly) Sturdy**
The dual-motor lift is impressively quiet—quieter than my old Uplift V2, and that’s saying something. It glides up and down at a brisk pace (about 1.5 inches per second), which matters when you’re switching positions 10 times a day. The steel frame feels solid at mid-height, and the desktop (I went with the 60" bamboo) is thick enough to resist sagging, even with two monitors and a laptop dock.

### **The Bad: Wobble, Drift, and a Cable Tray That Hates You**
- **Wobble at Full Height:** If you’re a heavy typist (or just aggressive with your keystrokes), the desk wobbles noticeably at its max height (47"). It’s not a dealbreaker, but it’s annoying when you’re trying to focus. Jarvik’s crossbar helps, but it’s not a miracle worker—this is still a two-leg desk, not a four-leg tank.
- **Memory Presets Drift:** The presets are convenient, but they’re not precise. Over time, they’ve drifted about a centimeter from where I originally set them. Not a huge issue, but if you’re OCD about exact heights, you’ll be recalibrating often.
- **Cable Tray is Useless:** The included cable tray is flimsy, poorly designed, and barely holds anything. I replaced it with a third-party under-desk basket within a month. Jarvik could’ve saved everyone the hassle by just not including it.

### **The Verdict: Worth It at $549, Not at $749**
At its sale price ($549 for the 60" model), the L2 is a solid buy—especially if you prioritize speed and noise over rock-solid stability. But at the regular $749? Hard pass. For that price, you could get a Uplift V2 with better stability, a sturdier cable management system, and a longer warranty.

**Final Rating: 7/10** (8/10 on sale, 6/10 at full price)
If you’re okay with minor wobble and can live with tweaking presets, it’s a good desk. But don’t pay full price for it.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
It’s been a week since launch. Honestly still feels surreal typing that.

412 copies sold in the first seven days. I know that’s not earth-shattering by any stretch, but for a solo project I’ve been chipping away at on nights and weekends for three years, it’s way more than I let myself hope for. A bunch of you grabbed it day one, and seeing usernames I recognize from the devlog pop up in the purchases was genuinely the best feeling.

Mid-week the game hit the front page of a small subreddit for about six hours. Nothing huge, but enough to give the Steam page a noticeable spike and bring in some really thoughtful early feedback. One post in particular stuck with me: a player said the movement feels “floaty.” I went back and replayed a few levels trying to see it from their perspective, and… yeah, they’re right. The air control has a bit too much hang time, and the deceleration isn’t snappy enough. Can’t un-feel it now. So I’m addressing that directly in patch 1.1, which I’m targeting for next month. I’m tightening up the horizontal drag, reducing the midair turn radius, and adding a tiny bit of downward pull on the jump apex so the character feels more planted without losing the sense of weight I originally wanted. I’ll post detailed patch notes when it’s closer.

Other things on the 1.1 list: fixing a rare softlock in the third area, some menu navigation polish (controller support was a little janky on certain screens), and a few audio balance tweaks people pointed out. Nothing massive, just cleanup.

After that, I want to take a real breath and finally play some games I’ve been ignoring for years. Then I’ll figure out what’s next—whether that’s a content update, porting to another platform, or starting the next thing. For now, just patching and catching up on sleep.

Thanks to everyone who’s played so far and sent bug reports, reviews, or just a nice message. It means a lot.

b.text:
One week out.

I launched last Tuesday. As of this morning the game has sold 412 copies. That's the number, and I've been staring at it long enough that it's stopped meaning anything, so I'm writing it down here instead.

For context, my only real expectation going in was "some number that isn't zero." I'd spent three years of nights and weekends on this thing. I had no idea what a normal first week looked like for a solo dev with a few hundred blog subscribers and no marketing budget to speak of. I still don't, really. But it's not zero, and the people who did buy it seem to be actually playing it, which is a different and better feeling than I expected.

The weird thing about launch week is that it's mostly waiting. You press the button and then you sit there refreshing a dashboard like a guy watching a pot of water. The first sale came about forty minutes after the store page went live and I genuinely yelled.

The one spike: someone posted it to a small subreddit on day two and it sat on the front page of that sub for about six hours. Six hours is not a lot of time in the grand scheme of things, but it tripled my traffic for the day and I spent those six hours in a state of low-grade panic, replying to comments and trying to figure out if I was supposed to be doing something. Mostly what it did was put the game in front of a few thousand people who wouldn't have seen it otherwise. I got a bunch of wishlists out of it, some of which will probably convert, some of which won't. That's fine. I'll take it.

The reception has been warmer than I was prepared for, honestly. People are posting screenshots, a few have said nice things I'm not going to repeat here because it feels weird to type them out. But there's one review that's stuck with me, and I want to talk about it because it's the most useful thing anyone's said all week.

The reviewer said the movement feels floaty. And they're right. They are completely right. I've known it for months, in the vague way you know something when you've played your own game so many times that you can't feel it anymore. It was on a list. It kept sliding down the list because there was always something more urgent, and by the time launch came around I'd convinced myself it was fine. It was not fine. Having someone else say it plainly was worth more than the nice comments, and I mean that.

So: 1.1 is coming next month. The main thing in it is a movement pass — heavier gravity, tighter acceleration curves, less air drift on the jump. I've been prototyping it this week and it already feels closer to what I wanted. There'll be a few smaller fixes in there too, some stuff people reported in the first few days, a couple of small quality-of-life things. I'll post proper patch notes when it's ready.

Beyond that I don't have a big roadmap. I'm going to keep reading the bug reports, keep watching how people play, and see what the next month looks like before I commit to anything bigger. If you bought it, thank you, genuinely. If something's broken, tell me. If the movement feels floaty, tell me — I already know, but tell me anyway.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
The second time I came home, the airport smelled like pretzel salt and wet carpet. I had my duffel slung over one shoulder, dress blues starched so stiff the collar itched my neck, and when I spotted my wife and the kid by baggage claim I waved. The kid was six. I’d been gone a year. She ducked behind my wife’s leg, face pressed into the back of her jeans, like I was a stranger who’d cut in line at the chow hall. My wife nudged her, said “C’mon bug, it’s Daddy,” and she peeked out once, then hid again. I knelt down so I wasn’t so tall, held my hands out slow, like I was approaching a skittish dog. It took maybe four minutes before she inched out, slow, and hugged me around the neck. Her hair smelled like strawberry shampoo, same as the stuff my wife used when we first got married.

A week later, my wife sent me to the grocery store for milk and eggs. Said I’d been pacing the house too much, needed to get out. I found the milk, found the eggs, then turned down the cereal aisle and froze. I counted: 40 kinds. Downrange we had MRE granola that tasted like cardboard and honey, if you were lucky. On base chow hall had corn flakes and frosted flakes, that was it. I didn’t know what Honey Bunches of Oats was, or why there were four different kinds of Cheerios. A lady with a cart full of kids gave me a look as she passed, like I was lost. I stood there for 20 minutes, maybe more. I almost grabbed the corn flakes, then remembered the kid liked the ones with marshmallows, but I couldn’t remember the name. I left without any cereal. When I got home my wife laughed and said you’re a real piece of work, and the next morning she and the kid dragged me back to the store. The kid grabbed three boxes, all neon, and I carried the milk behind them.

For the first three weeks I was home, I slept facing the bedroom door. It was open, my wife said, had been the whole time I was gone, so she could hear the kid if she had a bad dream. I kept waking up at 3 a.m. staring at the frame, heart hammering, like someone was gonna kick it in. I didn’t say anything to my wife. One night the kid had a nightmare, came padding down the hall in her dinosaur pajamas, holding her teddy bear that was missing an eye. I heard her before she got to the door, sat up straight, and then she pushed the door open a little more, sniffling. She climbed in bed between me and my wife. I rolled over on my side, facing her, not the door. The hall nightlight cast a yellow glow on the wall, I could see the shadow of the coat rack by the front door. I didn’t fall asleep for a long time, but I didn’t stare at the door, either.

After that, I stopped sleeping facing it. Some nights I still wake up, and I glance at the door first thing, but most nights I face the window. Last Tuesday the kid climbed in at 2 a.m. because she thought she heard a thunderstorm, and I rolled over to make room. The door was still open. I didn’t even think about it.

b.text:
**The Cereal Aisle**

I came home from my second deployment in the afternoon, but the airport felt like early morning to me. Too bright. Too many people moving in every direction. I had my duffel bag over one shoulder and my carry-on in my hand, and I kept thinking about how clean the floor looked.

My wife saw me first. She waved and smiled, and my daughter was standing next to her, holding onto the handle of her suitcase. She was six. She had gotten taller. Her hair was longer than I remembered. She wore a pink shirt with a horse on it.

Then she saw me looking at her, and she stepped behind my wife’s leg.

I stopped a few feet away. I was still wearing my uniform, and I thought maybe that would help. Maybe I thought she would see me and run over. Instead, she leaned her face against my wife’s leg and watched me with one eye.

My wife said, “Go on, it’s Dad.”

My daughter did not move.

I set my bags down. I squatted a little so I would not be so tall. I said her name, and my voice sounded wrong. Too loud. Too careful.

She looked at my wife, then back at me, then down at her shoes.

My wife said, “She’s just shy.”

I nodded. I picked up the bags again.

We walked to the parking garage. My daughter held my wife’s hand and stayed on the side away from me. Every time I looked at her, she looked away. I tried not to make a big thing out of it. I asked if she liked her shirt. She nodded. I asked if the horse had a name. She shook her head.

In the car, she sat in her booster seat and looked out the window. I sat in the front and kept turning around to look at her. My wife told me to let her be. I faced forward and watched the road.

At home, the house smelled like laundry soap and coffee. There were drawings on the refrigerator. A pair of small shoes by the door. A blanket folded on the couch. Everything looked the way it should, but it did not feel like mine yet.

That first week, I went to the grocery store with my wife and daughter. My wife had a list. She asked me to pick out cereal for my daughter.

She said, “Anything she likes.”

I said, “What does she like?”

My wife said, “You’ll see.”

The cereal aisle was long. Bright boxes on both sides. Cartoons. Tigers. Frosted flakes. Honey stuff. Chocolate stuff. Stuff with marshmallars. Stuff with berries. Stuff that said heart healthy. Stuff that said whole grain. Stuff that said new. Stuff that said improved.

I stood there with the cart and stared.

There had to be forty kinds. Maybe more. Some were in bags inside boxes. Some were on sale. Some were up high. Some were down low. People kept passing me. One woman reached around me for a box of oat cereal. A kid in another cart pointed at the candy-looking stuff and yelled.

I looked at all the boxes until the words started to blur.

My wife came around the corner after a while.

She said, “You find anything?”

I said, “No.”

She looked at the shelf. She picked up a box with a cartoon dog on it and put it in the cart.

My daughter said, “That’s not mine.”

My wife put it back. She picked up another box. My daughter shook her head. My wife said, “Help him out.”

My daughter looked at the shelf. She pointed to a box near the end. It was red and yellow. I did not know if I had ever bought it before. I took it down and put it in the cart.

My wife said, “There you go.”

I pushed the cart away from the aisle. My hands were sweating.

That night, my daughter ate some of the cereal before bed. She did not eat much. She left the spoon in the bowl and went to brush her teeth.

After we moved back into our routine, the house got quieter at night. My wife slept on her side of the bed. I slept on my side, but I did not sleep much at first.

For the last year, I had slept facing the door. Not all the way facing it, but close enough that if somebody came in, I would see them. It was a habit. You did not think about it too much while you were doing it. You just did it.

At home, the bedroom door had been open a crack. My wife liked it that way. She said it helped with air. I liked it too, but not for the same reason.

The first few nights back, I kept waking up when the house made noises. The furnace kicking on. The refrigerator humming. A branch against the window. A car driving by outside. Each sound had a place, but I still heard them like they were close.

One night I got up and closed the door. I stood there in the dark and listened. It felt wrong. The room got smaller. I opened it again.

My wife rolled over.

She said, “What are you doing?”

I said, “Nothing.”

I got back in bed.

In the morning, my daughter came in without knocking. She climbed up on the bed and sat on my leg. She had a book in her hand. She wanted me to read it.

I read it slow. She corrected me when I got a word wrong. Then she took the book and left.

The next night, I left the bedroom door open wider. I lay there looking at the hall light under it. My wife was already asleep. I could hear her breathing. Down the hall, the bathroom fan clicked off. Then the house was quiet again.

I watched the door until my eyes closed.
