setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
# This Isn't a Crash. It's a Pricing Problem.

Last spring, the median home in my zip code sold in 8 days. This spring, it's 34. If you've been reading the headlines, you've probably heard the word "crash" a few times, or at least "cooling," said in the tone people use when they're bracing for bad news.

Here's my take after ten years in this market: this isn't a crash. It's a lot of sellers who haven't caught up to the new pace.

**What the numbers say**

Days on market have more than quadrupled. Showings per listing have dropped by about half. Those two facts are real, and anyone who tells you nothing has changed is selling something.

But here's the number that matters most: list prices are still up 6% over last year.

Think about that. Buyer traffic per home has been cut in half, and asking prices are still climbing. That isn't a market in freefall. It's a market where the price tags haven't gotten the message. Sellers are pricing for the spring of last year, when a decent house with a clean kitchen could get three offers over a weekend. Buyers are shopping in this spring, when they have time, options, and no interest in being rushed.

**The proof is in the listings that sell**

If this were a true collapse, nothing would be moving. That's not what I'm seeing. Homes priced in line with where the market actually is today are still selling in under two weeks. Not 34 days. Under two weeks. Buyers are out there and they're writing offers. They're just no longer willing to pay a premium for the privilege of being rushed.

The 34-day median isn't telling you every house takes a month to sell. It's an average of two very different groups: homes priced right that go fast, and homes priced for a market that no longer exists that sit and sit.

**Where I see it up close**

I have three sellers right now who are past 60 days on market and have chosen not to adjust their price. I understand it. I really do. Your home is not a statistic. You remember what the neighbor got last year, you've got a number in your head you need to hit, and dropping the price feels like admitting defeat.

But the market doesn't negotiate with your memory of it. Every week those homes sit, they get a little staler. Buyers start wondering what's wrong with them. The listing that could have commanded attention in week one is now the one buyers scroll past with a shrug. Ironically, the sellers holding out for the higher number often end up taking less than they would have if they had priced correctly at the start.

**What I'd tell sellers**

Price for the market you're in, not the one you missed. If you're getting showings but no offers, that's a price problem. If you're getting no showings at all, that's also a price problem. Look at what's selling quickly near you, not what's merely listed, and be honest about where your home falls.

And do it early. The first two weeks are your best window. A well-priced home gets momentum. An overpriced home gets a reduction history.

**What I'd tell buyers**

You have more leverage than you've had in a few years, but don't mistake that for a fire sale. The good homes, the ones priced correctly, are still going quickly. If you find one, don't assume you can wait it out. The overpriced ones, though? Those are where you can be patient, and where sellers who finally face reality may be ready to talk.

**The bottom line**

Markets slow down. That's not a crisis, it's a correction in pace. What we're seeing in our corner of the Midwest is a return to a market where price actually matters again, and where buyers are no longer making decisions in 48 hours with their eyes closed.

The sellers who adjust are selling. The ones who don't are waiting. That's the whole story, and it's not nearly as scary as the headlines suggest.

If you're wondering where your own home falls, reach out. I'll give you an honest number, even if it's not the one you were hoping for.

b.text:
**It’s Not a Crash. It’s a Pricing Problem.**

If you have been watching the local real estate market this spring, you may be feeling confused. And honestly, I don’t blame you.

The numbers are sending mixed signals. In my ZIP code, the median days on market has jumped from eight days last spring to 34 days this spring. That is a big shift in one year. At the same time, list prices are still up about 6% year over year, even though showings per listing have dropped by half.

So what is happening?

My take is simple: this is not a crash. It is a market where too many sellers have not caught up to the new pace.

The sellers who are pricing their homes correctly from the start are still selling fast. Some are under contract in less than two weeks. Some are still getting multiple offers. The demand has not disappeared. What has disappeared is the automatic, no-questions-asked frenzy that allowed almost any price to work a couple of years ago.

Buyers are still out there. But they are more deliberate. They are watching listings longer. They are comparing more carefully. They are less willing to chase a home that feels even slightly overpriced. And because they have more time on their side, they do not feel the same pressure to overpay just to win something.

That is why showings are down so sharply. It does not mean buyers are gone. It means buyers are being selective.

I see this in my own business. I currently represent three sellers whose homes have been on the market for more than 60 days, and none of them wants to reduce the price. I understand the mindset. Each one believes their home is special. Each one remembers what the neighbor’s house sold for last spring. Each one hopes the right buyer is just around the corner.

But the market does not care about hope. It responds to price.

When a home sits past 60 days in a market where the median days on market is 34, the problem is usually not the school district, the floor plan, the curb appeal, or the marketing photos. The problem is that the price has become part of the property’s story. Buyers start asking, “What’s wrong with it?” when the real answer is often, “Nothing — except the price.”

That is what makes this market tricky.

List prices being up 6% can make it look like nothing has changed. But list prices are partly a lagging indicator. They reflect what sellers are asking, not necessarily what buyers are willing to pay. They also reflect the sellers who are still holding firm, even while their homes sit.

The days-on-market shift tells the truer story. Going from eight days to 34 days means the temperature has changed. Homes are not unsellable. But they are no longer selling automatically.

This is where a lot of sellers are getting hurt. They price for the market they remember, not the market that is actually happening. They test a high number to “leave room for negotiation.” Then they wait. And wait. And by the time they finally reduce, the listing has gone stale and they end up with less than they would have gotten if they had priced correctly in the first place.

That is the part nobody likes to hear.

In this market, your first two weeks matter enormously. That is when your home has the most attention. If you are priced right, buyers respond. If you are not, the market tells you quickly. Silence is not bad luck. Silence is feedback.

Does that mean every home needs to be discounted? No.

It means homes need to be priced accurately for today, not for last year’s headline. The homes that are sharp, realistic, and well-positioned are still moving fast. That is not a crash. That is a market functioning normally again.

What we are seeing is not collapse. It is correction. It is sellers adjusting — some faster than others — to a pace where buyers have choices again.

For buyers, this is a chance to be thoughtful without being reckless. You have more room to evaluate, more time to decide, and in some cases more room to negotiate. But I would not sit around waiting for prices to fall off a cliff. The well-priced homes are still going.

For sellers, the message is more direct: do not test the market with a fantasy number. If your home is sitting, do not pretend that patience alone is strategy. Sometimes the strongest move is to align with reality early, while your listing still has momentum.

This market is not punishing all sellers. It is punishing overpricing.

And that is not a crash. That is a correction.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings

Most couples I talk to start with June. It's the default in their heads: long days, flowers everywhere, the whole season lined up like a postcard. I understand that. I shot plenty of June weddings before I started paying attention to what happens to the light in the other months.

Over the last two years I've photographed 11 winter weddings, and they're now some of my favorite days to shoot. Here's why.

**The money.** Winter bookings typically run about 30% less than comparable peak-season dates. That difference can cover a lot: a better florist, an extra hour of coverage, a nicer venue upgrade, or just a bit more room in the budget for the honeymoon. Your photographer's rate doesn't change because of the season, but the overall cost of the day often does.

**The light.** This is the part that surprises people. In June, the midday sun is harsh, and when it isn't, you often get flat overcast that makes everyone look a little tired. In November, around 3pm, the low sun comes through bare trees and lands on faces at an angle that's soft, warm, and directional. It gives portraits dimension without any tricks. I'd take that window over a cloudy June afternoon almost every time.

**The space.** At a June wedding, I'm usually sharing the parking lot, the load-in path, and the best corner of the venue with three or four other vendors: a planner, a florist, a DJ, a rental company, sometimes a second photographer. It's not a complaint, just the reality of peak season. In winter, the venue is calmer. I can move around, find the spots I want, and spend more time with you instead of waiting for a clear shot.

Winter weddings aren't for everyone. You'll want a good coat ready, a plan for cold hands, and maybe a backup indoor timeline if the forecast turns. But if you're deciding when to book and you're open to a season that doesn't get all the attention, I'd encourage you to look at what it could give you. I'd be glad to talk through your date and what the light and the budget might look like for your day.

b.text:
# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now

I’ll be honest: when I started shooting weddings, winter dates were the ones I’d quietly hope nobody booked. Cold toes, short days, and the lingering worry that everyone would look like they’d rather be inside. But then I shot eleven winter weddings over the last two years, and something shifted. I’m not writing this to tell you that every season is beautiful in its own way. I’m writing this because there are specific, practical reasons I now think winter might be the smartest time to get married.

**You’ll save about 30% on your photography.** That’s not a marketing gimmick. Winter bookings historically run cheaper for couples, and I price accordingly. For the same coverage you’d book in June, you’re getting my time and attention for significantly less. And since I’m not double-booking weekends in the off-season, you’re also getting a photographer who isn’t running on fumes from three weddings in a row.

**The light is better.** I know that sounds backwards. But in November, around 3pm, the sun drops low enough to filter through bare branches and throw long, warm, textured shadows across your faces. That’s genuinely better for portraits than June’s flat, overcast light, which can make everyone look like they’re standing under a fluorescent bulb. I’ve shot both, and I’ll take November’s late-afternoon glow every time.

**I’m not sharing the parking lot with three or four other vendors.** In June, I routinely pull up to a venue and find another photographer, a videographer, and a coordinator all circling for the same spot. In winter, I’m usually the only one there. That means no one stepping into my wide shots, no waiting for another vendor to clear out of the aisle, and no losing golden hour to someone else’s timeline.

So if you’re trying to decide when to book, here’s my honest pitch: pick a winter date. You’ll save money, you’ll get portraits you actually love, and you’ll have the whole place to yourselves. I’ve shot eleven of them in the last two years, and I’d shoot eleven more.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years of selling homes in Asheville, mostly to first-time buyers, I've noticed a pattern. The buyers who are happiest with their house two or three years later are usually the ones who walked the neighborhood at 7am before we ever toured it.

The Pruitts are the reason I started suggesting it to everyone.

They'd found a house on Sycamore Street that looked perfect online, and it showed beautifully at our 2pm appointment. The street was quiet, the light was gorgeous, and the backyard backed up to trees. They were ready to write an offer that night. On a whim, I asked if they'd be willing to drive back the next morning before work and just walk around for twenty minutes.

They called me at 7:40. Between 7 and 8, Sycamore turned into a cut-through for commuters avoiding the main road, and cars were moving a lot faster than anyone would want with a toddler in the front yard. They also met a neighbor walking her dog who told them more about the street in ten minutes than any listing ever could.

They didn't buy that house. They bought one two streets over, on a block that was just as quiet at 7:30am as it was at 2pm. Their daughter rides her bike out front now.

A showing tells you about the house. An early morning walk tells you about the life you'd be living there. You'll see who's out with their coffee, how the traffic actually moves, whether the neighbors wave, and what the place sounds like when nobody's trying to sell it to you.

It costs nothing but an early alarm, and I've never had a buyer tell me it was a waste of time.

b.text:
Something I've noticed after twelve years selling in this city: the buyers who walk the block before we tour a house are almost always happier with the house later.

The Pruitts were one of those couples. First-time buyers, pre-approved, ready to write. We had four houses lined up for a Saturday tour, and Friday night they asked if we could just walk the neighborhood first thing in the morning.

So we met at the corner of Sycamore and Lyman at 7am. We didn't talk about houses. We walked. Marcus watched a guy work through the same stretch with a beagle he'd clearly walked a hundred times. Rebecca counted the trucks that came up Lyman before six. They paused at the gravel path by the old warehouse, and somebody was already playing guitar on the stairs. She said, "I can hear the river from here."

Then they knocked on a door. A neighbor, in her robe, who answered without hesitation. They asked her what was annoying, what was loud, whether the block felt friendly or just quiet. She told them the music stops around ten, the bridge hums in summer heat, and everyone on that stretch knows each other.

We toured the four houses I'd picked at noon. The Pruitts loved one of them. But they bought a cottage two streets over that they'd never seen listed, because they'd walked right past it at 7:30 and fallen for it. Eight months later, they still talk about that cottage like it was luck.

Here's what I took from it: a Saturday afternoon tour tells you about a house. A 7am walk tells you about a street. And you're buying into the street for longer than you're living in the house.

So now I build the walk in. Before I show anybody anything, we walk the block at an hour when the block is actually itself. Sometimes that's 7am. Sometimes it's 9pm on a Tuesday. Then we tour, and the house gets evaluated in the context of the morning they're going to live with.

The houses will change. The street won't.

If you bought your house and then walked your street at 7am the next morning for the first time — what did you notice?

#AshevilleRealEstate #FirstTimeHomeBuyers #WestAsheville #HomesForSaleAsheville

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/4
We just opened up the ceiling on our Maple Ave kitchen remodel (1910 Pittsburgh home). 

What we found: a previous "pro" had notched out 90% of a main load-bearing floor joist to run a 3-inch plumbing drain. It was literally hanging by a 1-inch splinter of old-growth pine.

2/4
To fix it safely:
- Had an engineer spec the repair.
- Slowly jacked the sag out of the joist to avoid cracking the bathroom tile directly upstairs.
- Sistered it with an LVL and rerouted the drain line.

Total cost: $3,200 and 3 days added to the schedule.

3/4
The lesson for homeowners:
This is why a 10-15% contingency fund isn't optional on old homes. If we hadn’t opened this ceiling, that floor would have eventually failed under the weight of the new kitchen island. Always budget for what you can’t see.

4/4
The lesson for contractors & architects:
Never write a contract that guarantees a flat price for structural work before drywall comes down. Build an "exploratory demolition" clause into your contracts. It protects your margins and sets honest expectations from day one.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/ Pulled up the subfloor on the Maple Ave kitchen job yesterday and found three joists that had been notched halfway through by whoever ran the original plumbing. Probably 40 years ago. Someone just kept going and nobody ever fixed it.

2/ Notched joists are a structural problem that gets worse over time. Floor gets bouncy, tile cracks, cabinets go out of level. The fix was sistering new 2x10s alongside each one, full length, glued and through-bolted. Took a day and a half with two guys.

3/ Cost the homeowners about $1,100 in labor and material they weren't expecting. Could've been a lot worse. If we'd tiled over that floor without looking, it would've failed within a year and the repair would've been triple once everything was finished.

4/ The lesson isn't "always expect the worst." It's pull the subfloor before you commit to a tile scope. Ten minutes with a pry bar tells you what you're actually working with. Every old kitchen has a story underneath it and you want to know before you're four weeks in.

b.text:
1/ Quick thread from the Maple Ave kitchen job we wrapped last week in Squirrel Hill—classic 1920s Pittsburgh foursquare, full gut to add an 8ft island. We tore out the original 90-year-old tile floor to prep new subfloor and ran into a joist hack I still can’t believe flew under the radar.

2/ Turned out a 1990s reno crew cut a 24-inch section clean out of a 2x10 main floor joist to run a relocated sink drain. No sister joist, no load-bearing header, just propped the cut end on a loose scrap 2x4 sitting on the basement subfloor below. You could feel the floor deflect ½ inch just standing on the old sink spot.

3/ Fix was two full-length sistered 2x10s (construction adhesive + ½” lags every 16”), a flush steel header to transfer load to the two adjacent joists, a revised structural permit, and 2 extra days on the schedule. Total cost: $3,200, all covered by the 10% contingency we’d built into the original quote—though it ate 70% of that buffer.

4/ The actual lesson, no fluff: Older homes almost always have hidden “good enough” work from past crews. For contractors: Never assume structural work was done right, even if the floor feels solid pre-demo. For homeowners: Always confirm your quote has a separate contingency line item—this is exactly what it’s for. For architects: Existing condition surveys catch most issues, leave budget flex in plans for demo-day surprises.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/
On the Maple Ave kitchen last month, we opened the ceiling to run new electrical and found the original 2x8 joists had been notched almost halfway through to clear a 3" PVC waste line. House is 1923, long span over the kitchen (~16'), and the drywall had been cracking along the seams for years. Previous owners just kept patching it.

2/
Joists were 2x8 spanning ~16' with that bad a notch midspan. Deflection was obvious — you could see the sag in the ceiling. Brought in an engineer ($650) who spec'd sistering two joists full length and adding a flush LVL under the worst one. Kept the ceiling flat and didn't require dropping the whole kitchen.

3/
Total hit: about $4,200 including the engineer, the LVL, and a day and a half of crew time. Added roughly a week to the schedule. Homeowners were good about it — I'd already flagged it in a change order before they ever saw the damage — but it's the kind of thing that eats your margin if you miss it.

4/
Lesson: on any older home with a long-span kitchen, I cut at least one access hole before I quote. Joist notches from previous plumbing or HVAC work are the rule, not the exception. Fifteen minutes with a flashlight beats a $4k surprise every time.

b.text:
1/4
On the Maple Ave kitchen job, we opened the ceiling during demo and found a floor joist that had been cut years ago to run ductwork. The kitchen looked fine, but the framing above had been carrying the load the wrong way for a long time.

2/4
We put in temporary support, sistered the joist, added blocking, and prepped the patch for drywall. Total cost on this one: about $2,100. Not a nightmare structural repair, but enough to affect the schedule and the budget.

3/4
The lesson: in older houses, assume somebody already changed something. Before you lock in pricing for ceilings, walls, or layout changes, open a small spot and look at what’s actually happening.

4/4
The cheapest discovery is the one you make before cabinets, tile, and appliances are on order.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
The state legislature is currently looking at a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding, and as a third-year electrical apprentice with this IBEW local, I can tell you exactly why that is a terrible idea. I am an electrician, not an English professor, so I am going to skip the fancy speeches and just look at the hard numbers. 

Let’s look at my own group. My apprenticeship cohort started with 24 people. Out of those, 21 finished the program. That is a massive success rate. Those 21 men and women aren't sitting at home looking for work. They are out in the field right now, working full-time journeyman jobs, paying taxes, and building this state's infrastructure. 

When we start out as apprentices, we make around $19 an hour. By the time we finish and become journeymen, we top out around $46 an hour. If the state wants to know the fastest way to get people off public assistance programs, this is it. You train them for a career that pays a wage they can actually live and raise a family on. Apprentices get off government assistance fast because we are put straight to work. Gutting the funding that makes this possible doesn't save the state money in the long run. It just keeps people broke.

But here is the math that really proves how backward this proposed cut is. The total public cost for an apprentice who finishes their training is about $14,000. Compare that to a traditional college student. The average public subsidy for a student who finishes a four-year degree is somewhere around $48,000. 

I don't have anything against people who go to college, but the state needs to explain why it wants to cut funding for a program that costs a third of the price and actually guarantees a high-paying job at the end of it. We are delivering a better return on the state's investment, hands down. 

To my brothers and sisters in the local, we need to make some noise. Call your state representatives and tell them to vote against this cut. And to the legislators reading this: do the math. Apprenticeships work. We are the ones wiring your hospitals, schools, and businesses. Do not pull the ladder up on the next group of apprentices trying to get to work. Keep our training fully funded.

b.text:
**Don’t Cut the Program That Works**

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with the IBEW. I’m not writing this as a politician or a policy expert. I’m writing it as someone who is in the apprenticeship system every day, learning the trade, working full-time, and building a career.

The state is proposing a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding. That sounds like a simple budget line, but it is not. It would hurt a system that already works for workers, employers, taxpayers, and the state.

Let me give you some real numbers from my own experience. My apprenticeship class started with 24 people. Twenty-one of us finished. That is nearly 9 out of 10. And those 21 are not sitting around waiting for something to happen. They are working journeyman jobs right now. They are paying taxes. They are supporting families. They are not relying on the state to get by.

That is what apprenticeship does. It puts people to work.

When I started as an apprentice, I made around $19 an hour. That is enough to pay bills and stay off public assistance. As journeymen, electricians in our trade can top out around $46 an hour. That is a solid living, and people get there without being buried in college debt. They earn while they learn. They do not spend years paying tuition and hoping there is a job at the end.

That is important, because a lot of people talk about “workforce development” like it is some big idea. Apprenticeship is not an idea. It is already happening. It is working. And the state should not be cutting it.

The public cost is also a lot lower than people realize. The total public cost for each apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to the average public subsidy for a four-year college graduate who finishes, which is about $48,000. That is more than three times as much.

So let’s be clear: the state is looking at cutting a program that costs less and gets people into good jobs fast, while other paths cost more and do not always lead to work.

That does not make sense.

A 15% cut is not some small pinch. It can mean fewer apprentices accepted into classes. It can mean less classroom instruction. It can mean fewer instructors. It can mean longer waits for training or reduced support for people trying to finish. It can also hurt safety training, and in the electrical trade, safety is not optional. Mistakes out there can injure or kill someone.

If the state wants more skilled workers, more taxpayers, and fewer people depending on assistance, then apprenticeship funding should be protected, not cut.

Apprenticeship also helps local communities. The people coming out of these programs live here, work here, and spend their paychecks here. They buy homes. They support local businesses. They pay into the system. Union apprenticeship does not just help the individual apprentice. It helps the whole area.

I also think legislators need to understand what this kind of training is really like. We are not just sitting in a room listening to somebody talk. We are on the job, doing real work, learning codes, safety, wiring, troubleshooting, and how to be professional on a job site. We are tested in the classroom and in the field. The standards are high because the work has to be safe and done right.

If you cut funding by 15%, you are not just saving money. You are weakening one of the best ways the state has to build a skilled workforce.

Some people may say the state has to tighten its budget. I understand that. But smart budgeting means looking at what works and what does not. Apprenticeship works. The numbers prove it.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one finished and are working as journeymen. People start around $19 an hour and can reach around $46 an hour. The public cost per finished apprentice is about $14,000, compared to about $48,000 per finished four-year college graduate. Those are not small differences. They are big.

If the state wants to spend money wisely, it should invest in programs that give people jobs, reduce dependence on assistance, and build the middle class. That is exactly what union apprenticeship does.

Don’t cut apprenticeship funding by 15%. Protect it. Strengthen it. And let more people get into a program that already works.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
I do my calculus homework in the walk-in cooler. It's about 38 degrees in there, and it smells like cilantro and cardboard. There's an upside-down milk crate by the shelf of pork shoulder that works as a chair if I put my textbook on my knees. On a Saturday, my break is fifteen minutes, and the dining room is too loud and the kitchen is too hot, so I go in there and close the door most of the way. My fingers get stiff and my handwriting gets worse. I've gotten through a whole unit on related rates this way.

I've worked every weekend at my family's restaurant since sophomore year. Before that I was just the kid who did homework at table 12. Now I take orders, run food, wrap silverware, and answer the phone in the voice my mom calls my "telephone voice," which is higher than my real one.

The Saturday the register system died was in March. It was about 12:30, the busiest part of the day, and the screen froze on a pho order and then went black. My uncle pressed buttons and unplugged things and plugged them back in. Nothing happened. We had maybe nine tables and a line by the door.

My mom handed me a pad of paper and said, "Just write it."

So I wrote everything. I wrote every ticket by hand and tore it off and clipped it to the rail above the pass, and I said the order out loud to the kitchen so they would hear it twice. Two number 4s, one no noodles. A bún with extra herbs. A kid's rice plate, plain. I learned quickly which abbreviations my uncle could read and which ones he couldn't. When it came time to total the checks, I did the math on the back of the pad, added tax, and checked it again because I didn't trust myself. One man counted his change in front of me, slowly, and I stood there and let him. The system came back around four. By then I had filled most of the pad, and I kept the last page, which is mostly smudges and a coffee ring.

In the fall, we hired a new guy named Marcus, who was nineteen and had never worked in a kitchen. My grandmother makes our spring rolls every morning, and she doesn't like anyone else touching them, but we were short, so she asked me to teach him. I had never taught anyone anything she taught me. I realized I didn't know the words for it. I just knew that you put the filling in a line, not a pile, and that you fold the bottom corner up, then the sides in, and then you roll tight and wet the edge with your finger. When I tried to explain it, I kept saying "like this" and doing it again.

Marcus's first ones were loose and lopsided, and a few of them burst in the fryer. My grandmother walked by, looked at his tray, and said something in Vietnamese that I decided not to translate. Then she picked up one of the bad ones, unrolled it, and rolled it again herself, slowly, so he could see. She didn't say anything to him. By the end of the shift his were better. They weren't good, but they stayed closed.

I don't know if the restaurant is going to be part of my life after high school. My parents say I don't have to take it over, and I believe them, mostly. I know I'll miss some things if I leave: the staff meal before we open, the sound of the fryer, my grandmother's hands. I know I won't miss others, like the grease on the floor mats or the way my clothes smell at the end of a shift.

For now it's Saturday again. The cooler door is mostly closed, my textbook is on my knees, and somebody out front is calling my name because the phone is ringing. I finish the problem I'm on. Then I go.

b.text:
I have worked every weekend at my family's Vietnamese restaurant since sophomore year. Saturdays start early and run late.

One Saturday the register system died right in the middle of lunch. Screens went black. People kept walking in. I grabbed the old paper pads we keep in the drawer and wrote every ticket by hand. Table 4, two orders of pho with rare steak, one no onions, spring rolls, extra chili. I tore them off and stuck them on the wheel. The cooks asked me to rewrite a couple that got smudged. My hand cramped by dinner, but we filled every order that way.

I show new hires how to fold the spring rolls the way my grandma does it. Rice paper flat, filling in a thin line, bottom edge up first, sides tucked in tight so no air pockets form, then roll it closed and wet the last edge to seal. Loose ones fall apart in the fryer. The last kid I trained kept leaving them soft. I made a few next to him, slow, then watched him try until his looked right.

Breaks are short. Calculus needs quiet, so I take my book into the walk-in cooler. I sit on a milk crate in my jacket and work the problems while the compressor hums. Cold air keeps the numbers clear. When time is up I put the book back in my bag and step out to the floor again.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
## One Week In: 412 Copies and a Movement Patch

I launched my game last week after about three years of working on it during nights and weekends.

The first week ended at 412 copies sold, which is more than I knew how to picture when I started making the game. It’s been surreal seeing people actually play something that spent so long existing mostly on my hard drive.

The game also hit the front page of a small subreddit for around six hours, which brought in a noticeable spike of traffic and a lot of new players. I’m still catching up on some of the comments and messages, but it’s been great seeing people talk about specific levels, mechanics, and weird little details I wasn’t sure anyone would notice.

The most consistent criticism so far has been about the movement. One review described it as feeling floaty, and honestly, they’re right. I’ve been playing it for so long that I had started compensating for it without really noticing, but watching new players move around made the problem much more obvious.

I’m working on a movement update for version 1.1, currently planned for next month. I’m adjusting the acceleration, deceleration, and jump timing to make the controls feel more responsive without changing the overall feel of the game too drastically. I’m still testing different versions, so I don’t want to promise exact changes yet.

For now, I’m going through feedback, fixing the smaller bugs that have come up, and working on the 1.1 patch. Thanks to everyone who bought the game, left a review, sent feedback, or shared it somewhere. The first week has been a lot to process, but I’m glad the game is finally out in the world.

b.text:
**Week one**

It's out. It's been out for eight days now, which is long enough that I've stopped refreshing the sales page every twenty minutes and moved on to refreshing it every hour or so.

Here's where things stand.

412 copies sold in the first week. I don't have a great sense of whether that's good or bad relative to other first-time solo releases, and honestly I've stopped trying to figure it out. It's 412 people who paid money for something I made at my kitchen table over three years of evenings and Saturdays. That's the number. I keep looking at it.

On day two, someone posted it to a subreddit I'd never heard of — small, a few thousand people, very specific about the kind of games it likes. It sat on the front page there for about six hours. I watched the comment thread the whole time like it was a sporting event. Most of the sales spike came from that window, and then it tapered off the way everyone told me it would. I did not post it there myself. I don't know who did. If it was one of you, thanks.

Reviews are mostly positive so far, which I'm relieved about. A handful mention the writing, a couple mention the art, one person wrote three paragraphs about a puzzle in the second area and I've read it maybe a dozen times.

One review said the movement feels floaty. It's a mixed review, not a negative one, and the person was pretty fair about it. And they're right. I've known the movement was a little soft for a long time — I'd tuned it early on, got used to it, and after a certain point I just stopped noticing. Reading someone describe it fresh made me boot the game up and play the first area again, and yeah. It's floaty. Jump apex hangs too long, air control is too generous, landing doesn't have enough weight to it. I'd convinced myself it was a stylistic choice. It wasn't really. It was just the first thing that felt okay and then I built everything else on top of it.

So that's the main thing going into 1.1, which I'm aiming to have out next month:

- Retuning jump gravity and air control. Tighter fall, less drift. I'll probably keep a hair of the floatiness because the level geometry was built around it and I don't want to break every gap in the game, but it'll be noticeably firmer.
- Landing feedback — a small squash and a bit more sound on touchdown.
- Two crash bugs that got reported on launch day. Both are fixed on my end already; they'll ride along with the patch.
- The settings menu doesn't remember your resolution between sessions. It will.
- A few text fixes people caught.

I'll put a beta branch up in a couple of weeks for anyone who wants to try the new movement before it goes live, since I'd rather hear "this is worse now" from thirty people than from four hundred.

After 1.1 I genuinely don't know yet. There's a list of things I cut during development that I'd like to look at again, but I'm not going to promise any of it until I've had a few weeks to not be exhausted.

That's it. That's the week. Thanks to everyone who bought it, everyone who told a friend, and the person who wrote three paragraphs about the puzzle.

More when there's more.

a.text:
Why the State’s 15% Cut to Apprenticeship Funding is a Bad Deal for Everyone

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with our local IBEW. I’m writing this because the state is looking at a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding, and it needs to stop. Some lawmakers think they can balance the budget by slashing our programs, but they aren't looking at the actual numbers. When you look at the real math, cutting apprenticeship funding is exactly the wrong move.

Let’s look at my own class. We started with 24 apprentices. Today, 21 of us finished the program and are working full-time journeyman jobs. That’s a pretty solid track record. We aren't just sitting in classrooms; we are out there wiring buildings, keeping the power on, and doing the hard work that keeps this state moving. 

This program doesn't just give us a job; it gives us a real career and a path to the middle class. As a first-year apprentice, I started out making around $19 an hour. By the time we top out as journeymen, we’re making about $46 an hour. That kind of wage progression means people get off state assistance programs fast. We buy houses, we buy trucks, and we spend our money right here in our local communities. We pay our own way and we pay taxes.

Now let’s talk about what this costs the taxpayers, because I know the state cares about the budget. The total public cost for an apprentice who finishes the program is about $14,000. Compare that to a four-year college student. The average public subsidy for a student who finishes a four-year degree is around $48,000. We are giving the state a highly skilled, tax-paying worker for less than a third of the cost of a traditional college degree. If the state wants to save money and build the workforce at the same time, they should be doubling our funding, not cutting it by 15%.

A 15% cut means fewer tools, fewer instructors, and fewer people getting the chance to learn a trade. It means fewer journeymen to build and maintain the state's infrastructure. To the legislators reading this: look at the numbers. Spending $14,000 to create a journeyman who makes $46 an hour is the best deal in the state budget. Don't cut the very program that trains the people who build the state.

b.text:
I am a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW. I work with my hands, pull wire, and do the physical labor that keeps the lights on in our state. Right now, state lawmakers are proposing a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding. I am not an English professor or a politician, but I know how to look at numbers and see if something makes sense. Cutting this funding makes zero sense for working families or taxpayers.

Look at how this program actually works in the real world. My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished the training, and all 21 of those graduates are out in the field right now working full-time journeyman jobs. That is not a bloated government program sitting around doing nothing; that is 21 people trained, employed, and contributing directly to our local economy.

The financial path is straightforward. An apprentice starts out making around $19 an hour while learning the trade on the job. By the time you top out as a journeyman, you are making around $46 an hour. That kind of wage changes lives. It takes people off state assistance programs almost immediately. Instead of needing public support, trade workers are buying homes, raising families, and paying heavy tax dollars back into the system that helped train them.

Then look at what it costs the state. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes our program is about $14,000. Compare that to a traditional four-year public college degree, where the average public subsidy per graduating student is roughly $48,000. We turn out fully skilled, high-earning tradespeople at less than a third of the public cost of a four-year degree, and our graduates don't carry mountain loads of student debt.

A 15% cut to apprenticeship funding hurts a system that is already giving the state its best return on investment. It cuts off a proven pathway to the middle class for people willing to work hard. 

To our union brothers and sisters: contact your state representatives and tell them what this training did for you. And to the state legislators reading this: look at the math. Don't cut a program that works. Vote no on the 15% cut and keep investing in the trades that build this state.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
## How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots (Minneapolis Homeowners, Do This Before Halloween)

Four steps. Twenty minutes. Do them both — front and back of the house, plus the garage if you've got a hose bib out there.

### 1. Shut off the interior valve

Every outdoor spigot should have a shutoff valve inside the house on the pipe that feeds it. In most Minneapolis homes that's in the basement, along the rim joist, near where the pipe runs out through the wall. Older houses in Nokomis, Longfellow, Northeast — it's usually a small gate valve or a ball valve within a few feet of the exterior wall.

Turn it off. Gate valve, that's clockwise until it stops. Ball valve, quarter turn so the handle sits crosswise to the pipe.

### 2. Drain the spigot

Go outside and open the spigot all the way. Let it run until it stops dripping. This is the step people skip, and it's the whole point of the exercise — the interior valve keeps new water out, but whatever's already sitting in that pipe is what freezes and splits it.

Leave the outdoor spigot open all winter. Nothing's feeding it, and an open valve gives any leftover moisture somewhere to expand.

If your interior shutoff has a small bleeder cap on the side, put a bucket under it, unscrew it a turn or two, and let the rest drain out. Snug it back down when it quits dripping.

### 3. Disconnect your hoses

Read that again, because this is the one that costs people money.

### 4. Put a $3 foam cover on it

Hardware store, insulation aisle, styrofoam dome with a rubber strap. Loop the strap over the spigot handle, tighten it, push the cover flat against the siding. It's not doing the heavy lifting — steps 1 and 2 did that — but it buys you a margin when we hit a stretch of below-zero nights and it cuts down on wind chill hitting that pipe where it passes through the wall.

## The mistake that keeps us busy every January

A garden hose left attached to the spigot holds water. That water freezes and backs pressure up into the spigot and the pipe behind it. Even a frost-free hose bib — the long ones designed to shut off inside the heated part of the wall — can't drain if there's a hose hanging on the end of it. That's the part homeowners don't know. People install a frost-free bib and figure they're covered, then leave the hose on and split the pipe anyway.

Here's how it plays out: the pipe cracks in December, but it's holding no water, so nothing happens. Nobody notices. Then in May somebody hooks up a hose to water the tomatoes, turns on the interior valve, and water comes pouring into the basement through the rim joist. Or worse — it cracked on the interior side of the wall and it's been running down inside the wall cavity since the first thaw.

Coil your hoses, drain them, hang them in the garage. Takes five minutes.

## What if you don't have an interior shutoff?

A lot of Minneapolis houses don't — especially anything pre-war where a spigot got added at some point without a dedicated valve, or where a previous owner's remodel buried the valve behind finished basement wall.

If you go down to the basement and can't find a shutoff for that line, don't guess and don't just cover the spigot and hope. **Give us a call.** Adding an interior shutoff valve is a small job — usually an hour or two — and it's a lot cheaper than the drywall, insulation, and framing repair after a burst line lets go behind a finished wall.

Same goes if the valve is there but seized, or if you shut it off and the spigot outside is still dripping steady after ten minutes. That means the valve isn't holding, and it needs to be replaced before it gets cold.

We're a family business and we've been pulling apart frozen hose bibs in this city for a long time. We'd rather set you up in October than cut open your ceiling in January.

**Call us or book online — we'll get someone out.**

b.text:
How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots

If you haven’t winterized your outdoor spigots yet, do it this weekend. This is the 20-minute job that prevents most of our January emergency calls.

The big mistake we see every cold snap in Minneapolis is hoses left connected. A hose traps water against the spigot and pipe. When that water freezes, it expands back into the wall and splits the pipe. That’s most of our January burst-pipe calls.

Here’s the order we do it on our own houses:

1. Shut off the interior valve. Find the shutoff for each outdoor spigot—usually in the basement or crawl space near where the pipe exits the house. Turn it all the way off. If you can’t find one, stop and call us.

2. Drain the spigot. Go outside, open the spigot all the way, and let the water run out. Leave it open for a minute so the line drains back.

3. Disconnect the hose. Unscrew every hose, drain it, and store it in the garage or shed. This is the step that saves the pipe.

4. Cover the spigot. Put on a $3 foam spigot cover. Pull the string tight so the wind doesn’t carry it away. That’s all you need.

Even if your spigot is “frost-free,” still follow these steps. A frost-free spigot can’t do its job if a hose is attached or the interior valve isn’t shut off.

If your house doesn’t have an interior shutoff valve, don’t guess. Call us and we’ll either install one or winterize the line properly. It’s a small job compared to a burst pipe in January.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years selling homes in Asheville, here's something I can't prove with a spreadsheet but I'd bet my license on: the buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7am—before we ever step inside the house—end up the happiest six months later.

The Pruitts taught me this one. They were about to make an offer on a place on Sycamore Street. Beautiful house, checked every box on their list. But I asked them to do me a favor and come back the next morning, early, and just walk the block before our afternoon tour. No agenda, just walk.

They did. And they called me around 7:30 sounding a little deflated. Turns out that quiet street they'd fallen in love with on a Saturday afternoon became a cut-through for commuters on a weekday morning. Cars flying past, no sidewalks, the corner they'd pictured their kids waiting for the bus on felt completely different. They passed on it.

Two weeks later they found the house they actually bought, two neighborhoods over. And the first thing they did? Walked it at 7am. Slower street, neighbors out with coffee, a woman who waved and introduced herself. They knew before they walked in the door.

A house is a snapshot. A neighborhood is a routine. You're not just buying the thing you tour on a sunny afternoon—you're buying the Tuesday morning, the school pickup, the sound at night. The listing photos can't show you any of that. Your own two feet can.

So if you're house hunting this spring: set the alarm early and go walk. It's the cheapest and most honest inspection you'll ever do.

b.text:
After 12 years helping people buy homes in Asheville, I’ve noticed something: the buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7 a.m. before we tour tend to be happier with their choice later. Not a statistic—just a pattern I keep seeing, especially with first-time buyers.

I always think of the Pruitts on Sycamore Street. [Insert what they noticed on their early-morning walk, how it affected their decision, and what they told you after living there.]

A showing gives you a good look at the house. That morning walk gives you a glimpse of what it might feel like to live there. You hear the traffic when people are actually leaving for work. You find out whether the route you pictured walking with your coffee is somewhere you’d enjoy spending time.

I still want you to take your time in the kitchen and make sure your furniture fits. But before you commit, spend a little time outside the property line, at an hour that looks like your real life. You’re buying the house, but the neighborhood will be part of your day, too.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
# Keeping Your Dog Mat-Free Between Grooms (Especially You, Doodle and Husky People)

Every week someone comes into the salon apologizing for their dog's coat, and honestly? Most of the matting I see could have been prevented with one change in routine at home. So let's talk about it.

The biggest mistake I see — and I mean constantly — is bathing the dog first, thinking the water will loosen up the tangles and make brushing easier. It does the exact opposite. Water tightens matted fur. What was a loose tangle before the bath comes out of the tub as a dense little felt pad, and once it's felted, brushing it out becomes painful for the dog and sometimes impossible for me. If you remember nothing else from this post, remember this: **brush before the bath, never after.** If the coat isn't brushed out, honestly, skip the bath until it is.

Now, the brushing itself. You want a slicker brush — that's the one with the fine bent wire pins — and you want to use short, straight strokes in one direction. Little lines, not circles. Circular brushing just swirls the coat around and can actually create tangles on breeds with a lot of undercoat or curl. Short line strokes lift the coat and get down through it, which is the whole point. If the brush is only gliding over the top, you're smoothing the surface while mats keep building underneath.

Work in sections, and don't just start wherever. Mats almost always show up first in the same spots: behind the ears and under the front legs where they rub against the body. So start there. Get those areas done while your dog is still patient, then move on to the chest, the back legs, the tail, and the easy stuff along the back. If your dog only tolerates a few minutes at a time, that's fine — a few minutes on the trouble spots every day or two beats an hour-long battle once a month.

And if you find a mat already forming? Put the brush down. Work a little conditioner into the mat with your fingers first — a leave-in spray or even a dab of regular conditioner works. Massage it in and gently start separating the mat with your fingertips before a brush or comb ever touches it. Going straight at a dry mat with a slicker is uncomfortable for your dog, and it teaches them that brushing hurts, which makes every session after that harder for both of you.

Double-coated breeds and curly coats are the ones I see struggle most with this, because the matting hides. The top of the coat can look perfectly fine while a solid mat is forming right against the skin. That's why the finger-check matters — if you can't get your fingers through the coat down to the skin, a brush isn't getting through either.

A few minutes of brushing between visits makes a real difference. Your dog stays comfortable, grooming appointments go faster and easier, and I never have to have the "we may need to shave this out" conversation with you — which, trust me, nobody enjoys.

If you're not sure which slicker brush to get or you want a quick demo, just ask at your next appointment. I'm always happy to show you exactly how to work on your dog's coat. That's what I'm here for.

b.text:
I want to talk to you about something I see almost every day at the salon, and it's honestly one of the easiest things to fix at home if you know what you're doing. Matting. Specifically, the kind that shows up between grooms and becomes my problem when you drop your dog off.

Here's what's actually happening. You give your dog a bath at home — I get it, they rolled in something, or you wanted them fresh for the weekend. You think a clean dog is a happy dog. So you lather them up, rinse, towel dry, maybe blow dry, and then you notice the coat feels a little tangly. By the time they get to me, what was a small tangle has turned into a solid mat the size of my palm behind the ear, and now we're either doing a demat session at extra charge or the coat has to come off.

When you wet a matted or even slightly tangled coat without brushing it out first, the water swells each hair and everything pulls tighter. As it dries, it sets into place. You've essentially felted the wool — and that's literally what matted fur is, just hair that's been felted together. So the bath you thought was going to loosen things up actually locked them in tighter. This is the single most common mistake I see, and I see it constantly. Please brush first, then bathe. Even if the coat looks fine to you, run a metal comb through it. If the comb snags anywhere, work through that spot before any water touches the dog.

For double coats and curly coats especially — your Goldens, your Berners, your Huskies, your Doodles, your Bichons — you want a slicker brush. The kind with the fine wire pins on a flat paddle. Here's how I want you to use it, because most people use it wrong. You're going to take short, gentle strokes in one direction. Think of it like painting a fence, not buffing a car. Long fluid motions through the coat, going the direction the hair grows. Do not go in circles. Circling wraps the hair around itself and creates exactly the mats you're trying to prevent. Short line strokes. Always.

And do it in sections, not by trying to do the whole dog in one pass. Start behind the ears, then under the front legs, then the armpits, then the belly, then the back legs, then the tail. Behind the ears and under the front legs are where mats start ninety percent of the time. If your dog has a mat somewhere, it's almost always in one of those two spots. Make those areas part of your weekly routine and you'll cut your mat problems in half overnight.

Now, what if you already see a mat forming? A small one, maybe the size of a dime or a quarter? Don't grab the brush and go at it. You're going to tear through the coat, hurt the dog, and probably make the mat worse. Put a little bit of conditioner directly on the mat — leave-in works great, even a tiny bit of regular conditioner is fine. Work it into the mat with your fingers. Gently. You're trying to lubricate the hairs so they can slide apart. Give it a minute. Then, and only then, try to work through it with your fingers or a wide-tooth comb. Still no brush on a formed mat until you've gotten most of it apart yourself.

If you do all of this — dry brush before any bath, short line strokes with a slicker in the direction of growth, work your sections starting behind the ears and under the front legs, and use conditioner on anything that's already starting to tangle — your dog won't be the one coming in needing a full shave-down. They'll be more comfortable between visits, your appointments will be quicker and cheaper, and your dog will look better longer. Everyone wins.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
I went into my first clinical thinking I would feel like a nurse. Instead I felt like a kid wearing scrubs that were too big, trying not to get in anyone’s way.

By Monday afternoon I was already lost in the ER supply closet when a nurse poked her head in and said a man in room four needed someone to hold his hand. His wife was stuck across town in traffic, and they were cleaning gravel out of a road rash that ran from his shoulder to his elbow. I followed her back and stood on the side where his wife would have been. The nurse warned him it was going to hurt. He gripped my hand before she even started. He didn’t say much, just squeezed hard when the saline hit, and I squeezed back. That was the whole thing. I didn’t do any actual nursing. But he didn’t let go until his wife ran through the door twenty minutes later, and I realized that sometimes being there is the job.

The next day a code got called in the bay next to where I was shadowing. My preceptor told me to step out and restock the gauze cart. I was glad to have something to do with my hands, but standing in the hallway I could hear them through the curtain. Someone counted compressions. One and two and three and four. Over and over. I kept counting in my head even after I stopped hearing them. I had never been that close to it before. I didn’t see the patient, but I understood why the ER runs through supplies so fast, and why nobody walks in that room unless they have to.

Then there was the blood draw on Thursday. Diabetic patient, older guy, veins like cooked spaghetti. I missed the first stick. I missed the second. By the third I was sweating through my shirt and apologizing every time he flinched. He just said, “You’re learning, it’s alright.” I didn’t believe him. I almost asked my preceptor to take over, but she stood back and said, “Try the other arm. You’ve got it.” The fourth stick went in. I saw the flash of blood and almost cried. He said, “There you go,” like he knew it would happen all along. I taped the tubing down and cleaned up and realized I had spent more time with him than I would have if I’d gotten it on the first try. That’s not an excuse for missing three times. But it taught me that nursing isn’t about doing everything perfect right away. It’s about not walking away when you’re embarrassed.

That week stripped away a lot of what I thought nursing was. I didn’t save anyone’s life. I didn’t know enough to be useful in a code. I stuck a guy four times and probably hurt his feelings. But I also held a stranger’s hand so he wasn’t alone, and I stayed in the hallway while someone fought to come back, and I kept trying on that blood draw until I got it because the patient let me. I learned that ER nursing is mostly showing up, paying attention, and not quitting when you feel stupid.

I’m a first-year student, so I still have a lot to learn. But after that first week, I know I want to keep going. I want to get good enough that I can be in the room during the code instead of outside it. I want to hit the vein on the first try. Most of all, I want to be the kind of nurse who stays late enough to hold someone’s hand until their family gets there. This scholarship would help me stay in school and get there faster. I’m ready to put in the work.

b.text:
First Week in the ER

Before my first week in the ER, I thought I knew what nursing was. I had studied anatomy, practiced skills in lab, and read about how to handle emergencies. But the ER taught me more in five days than I learned all semester.

The first thing I noticed was how much of nursing is just being there. A man came in with a deep cut on his arm. The doctor needed to clean it, and the man was in a lot of pain. He kept asking for his wife, but she was stuck in traffic. I didn’t know what to say, so I just held his hand. He held on tight. We sat like that until his wife walked in. He let go and reached for her. I slipped out of the room. The nurse I was shadowing told me, “That’s part of it too.” I realized then that a nurse does more than change dressings and give medicine. Sometimes you’re just a hand to hold.

Another moment I won’t forget was during a code. I had only been in the ER for a few days, so they sent me to restock gauze while the team worked. I stood right outside the curtain and heard them counting compressions. One, two, three, four. I couldn’t see what was happening. All I could do was listen and keep the supplies ready. It was terrifying. But I saw how calm everyone was, how they worked together without yelling. I wanted to be able to do that one day. I wanted to be useful in that room, not just outside it.

The hardest moment was trying to draw blood from a diabetic patient. His veins were bad. I missed the first time. Then I missed again. The third time, I still couldn’t get it. He was nicer about it than I was. He said, “Take your time.” On the fourth try, I finally got it. I felt like I had won something. He smiled and said, “See? You got it.” I almost cried. No one else made a big deal out of it, but to me it meant everything. It reminded me that being a nurse means failing sometimes, then trying again.

These moments are what I think about when I picture myself as a nurse. The textbook skills matter, but so do the small human moments. Holding a stranger’s hand. Missing a stick and going for the fourth try. Standing behind a curtain, listening, and hoping you’ll be ready next time.

I’m only a first-year nursing student. I have a lot to learn. But this first week showed me that I’m in the right place. A scholarship would help me continue my education and become the kind of nurse who can do both the technical work and the human work. Thank you for considering me.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
My first clinical rotation was in the emergency room. I spent the week before it telling everybody I was ready. I wasn't. I don't think anybody is. But I learned more in that first week than in a whole semester of lectures, and most of it nobody could have taught me ahead of time.

The first thing that stuck with me was a man who needed a wound cleaned. It took a while, and it hurt the whole time. His wife was on her way but stuck in traffic, and every time the door opened, he looked at it. My preceptor had her hands full, so she looked at me, and I took his hand and told him I'd stay right there until his wife made it. I didn't say anything smart. I just held on while he squeezed and worked on his breathing. When his wife finally walked in, she took over and I stepped back. That's how it should work. Sometimes the whole job is being the person in the room until the right person gets there.

Later that shift a code got called. I followed my preceptor down the hall and she stopped me and pointed at the supply closet. Restock the gauze, she said. So I stood in that closet counting packets while behind the curtain somebody counted compressions out loud. I could hear everything through that curtain. I won't pretend I wasn't disappointed. I wanted to be in there. But somebody has to make sure there's gauze when the next person comes through the door bleeding, and that week that somebody was me. I restocked every shelf in that closet. I did it slow and I did it right.

The hardest one was a blood draw. A diabetic man, stuck a thousand times in his life, veins like thread. I missed. Then I missed again. Then a third time. Each one made me want to quit worse than the last. He never told me to stop. He just said I'd get it. On the fourth stick I got a good flash of blood, and I had to act like I wasn't about to cry from relief. What I keep coming back to is that he trusted me to keep going. Patients let students practice on them. That's a gift, and I don't want to waste it. That night I went home and watched videos on finding veins in hard cases. The next day I asked my preceptor what she looks for. I'll miss again someday. I just want to miss less.

Here's what I took from that week. Nursing isn't one skill. It's holding a stranger's hand because the person who should be holding it is stuck on the highway. It's counting gauze while other people count compressions, and knowing both counts matter. It's missing three times and going a fourth because the patient said you'd get it.

I'm a first-year student. I have a long way to go and a lot of shelves left to restock. This scholarship would mean less time figuring out how to pay for the next semester and more time learning the job. That's it, honestly. I want to keep showing up to that closet, that bed, that chair. I want to be worth the trust that man had in me on the fourth try.

b.text:
Before my first clinical rotation in the emergency room, I thought I knew what to expect. I had read the textbooks, taken the tests, and practiced on plastic mannequins in the lab. But you can't learn the ER from a book. My first week taught me that nursing is messier, harder, and a lot more real than anything a classroom can prepare you for. 

On one of my first shifts, I was assigned to a man who needed a bad wound cleaned. His wife was supposed to be there with him, but she was stuck in city traffic. He was trying to act brave, but I could tell he was scared of the pain. I didn't know the perfect medical advice to give him, so I just offered him my hand. He gripped it hard the entire time the doctor worked. I realized right then that sometimes the most important part of this job doesn't involve charting or passing meds. Sometimes it just means making sure a stranger doesn't have to be scared alone. 

But the ER isn't always quiet. A few days later, the alarms went off for my first code blue. A whole team rushed into the room to save a patient's life. Because I am just a first-year student, the best way for me to help was to stay out of the way. My preceptor sent me to restock gauze in the supply carts just outside the room. It felt like a small, basic job in the middle of a massive emergency. As I stood there putting boxes on the shelves, I listened through the curtain. I could hear the team counting out loud as they did chest compressions. Hearing those numbers made the hair on my arms stand up. It reminded me that every single job in a hospital matters, even making sure the supplies are ready. I know that someday I will be the one on the other side of the curtain, but for now, I was just proud to do my part. 

That week also taught me that I have a lot to learn. I was asked to draw blood from a diabetic man with very bad veins. I set up my supplies, found what I thought was a good spot, and missed. I tried again, and missed again. By the third miss, my hands were sweating. I wanted to apologize and run out of the room because I felt like I was failing him. But the man was incredibly patient with me, and my preceptor told me to take a breath and try one more time. On the fourth try, I finally got it. I have never felt so relieved in my life. It was a hard lesson in not giving up on myself when things go wrong. 

That first week in the ER showed me exactly what kind of nurse I want to be. I want to be someone who holds a hand, who helps out during a code, and who keeps trying even when she fails three times in a row. Nursing school is the hardest thing I have ever done, and worrying about how to pay for it adds a heavy layer of stress. This scholarship would lift that financial weight off my shoulders. It would allow me to focus completely on my classes and my clinicals, rather than how I am going to pay my tuition. I still have a long way to go before I get my nursing license, but my first week in the ER proved to me that I am on the right path.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Baseboard Heating

You'll need a radiator key (a few bucks at any hardware store) or a flathead screwdriver, depending on your bleeder. You'll also need a small cup or container and a rag. Set aside about 30 to 45 minutes for a typical house.

## Step 1: Shut off the circulator and boiler

Turn off the boiler, or at least the circulator pump, before you touch a bleeder. If water is moving through the system, it keeps pushing air around and you'll never get it all out. Give the system some time to cool down, too. The water in those pipes can be hot enough to burn you.

## Step 2: Find the bleeder valve on each baseboard

Pop the end cap off the baseboard unit. The bleeder valve is usually on the end, sitting on top of or near the copper pipe. It's a small fitting with either a square stem for a radiator key or a slot for a flathead. Not every unit has one, but most do. Check every unit in the house, not just the obvious ones.

## Step 3: Start with the unit closest to the boiler

Work your way out from the boiler, one unit at a time. Do the closest unit first, then the next closest, and keep going until you reach the farthest one on each loop.

## Step 4: Cup underneath and open the valve slowly

Hold your cup right under the bleeder and keep the rag handy. Turn the valve slowly counterclockwise, about a quarter to a half turn. You'll hear air hissing out, and you might get some sputtering water mixed in with it.

## Step 5: Wait for a steady stream of water

Leave it open until the hissing stops and water comes out in a steady, solid stream with no air spitting through. That means the air is out of that unit.

## Step 6: Close it snug, but don't overtighten

Turn the valve clockwise until it's snug and stop there. Don't crank on it. These valves are small and the seats crack easily if you force them. Then you've got a drip that won't quit and a repair on your hands. Snug is enough to stop the water.

## Step 7: Repeat on every unit, including the basement

Move to the next unit and do the same thing. Keep going until you've bled every baseboard in the house.

## The mistake behind most of our cold radiator calls

People bleed the upstairs units and stop there. It makes sense on the surface, since air rises and the upstairs rooms are usually the cold ones. But the basement loop is very often where the air is actually trapped. If you skip it, you can bleed upstairs all afternoon and still have cold baseboards.

**Bleed the basement loop.** If you've got baseboards down there, they're part of the job.

## When you're done

Turn the boiler and circulator back on and check the pressure gauge on the boiler. Most residential systems run somewhere around 12 to 15 PSI when cold. Bleeding lets a little water out, so if the pressure has dropped noticeably, the system may need to be topped up. Give the system an hour or so to run, then go feel your baseboards. They should be heating evenly from end to end.

If you've bled every unit, basement included, and you've still got cold spots or keep losing pressure, give us a call. Something else is going on, and we'll come take a look.

b.text:
Shut off the boiler and the circulator pump before you touch anything. Working on a live system risks burns and pulls more air into the lines.

Most of the cold-radiator calls we get trace back to the same mistake: homeowners bleed the upstairs bedrooms and skip the basement loop. That's usually where the air is sitting. Start at the baseboard unit closest to the boiler and work your way outward, floor by floor. Don't skip the basement.

At the end of each unit, find the bleeder valve—usually a square head or slotted screw on the end cap. Place a cup underneath. Using a bleeder key or flathead screwdriver, open the valve slowly. You'll hear air hiss out. Keep turning until the hissing stops and water flows in a steady stream, then close it snug. Don't overtighten—you'll crack the valve seat and turn a simple bleed into a leak that needs a service call.

Repeat for every unit in the house. If a zone stays cold or water won't flow steady, you've got a blockage or a failing circulator. That's when you call us.
