setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
The register died at 11:40 on a Saturday, right when the lunch line hit the door. The screen went gray and stayed gray. My mom said a word I am not putting in a college essay. My dad was already in the kitchen yelling for more rice. Nobody was coming to fix it before two.

So I took the pad we use for to-go orders and stood at the counter. People told me what they wanted and I wrote it down, the way we used to before the system. Number, table, pho tai, no onions, extra hoisin on the side. I tore the tickets and clipped them where the printer usually spit them out. My handwriting is bad when I rush. The cooks still read it. A man asked if we were closed. I said no, just slow, and he waited. By the time the screen came back we had a stack of paper tickets and a tip jar that was mostly ones. My mom counted them later and said we didn't lose much. I don't know if that was true. My hand hurt.

Most weekends are not like that. Most weekends I get there at ten, tie my apron, and do whatever is in front of me. Sometimes that is the register. Sometimes it is rolling.

My grandma's spring rolls are not hard if you have done them a thousand times. The rice paper has to be wet enough to bend and not so wet it tears. You lay the shrimp so the pink shows through. Lettuce, herbs, vermicelli, a strip of pork if we're doing the pork ones. Then you fold the sides in and roll tight, or the filling slides out when somebody dips it. I can do it without looking. A new hire cannot.

Last month we hired a girl from my school, two grades under me. My mom put her on rolls because we were short. The first ones she made were loose and the paper split. I stood next to her and did one slowly, then let her do one, then fixed the ones that were wrong without saying much. She got quieter the worse they looked. I told her mine looked like that for a month. That was not exactly true. Mine looked like that for two weeks, and my grandma redid all of them where I could see. After an hour the new girl's rolls held. Not pretty. They held. She asked if my grandma would be mad. My grandma was in the back counting napkins and did not care who rolled them as long as they didn't fall apart on the plate.

I do homework on my breaks because there is nowhere else. The office has one chair and my dad uses it for invoices. The dining room is full. The walk-in is cold and nobody bothers you if you stand to the side of the shelves, out of the way of the pork and the crates of herbs. I bring a pencil because pens freeze up or I imagine they do. Calc is the worst in there. The problems take longer when your fingers are stiff, and the answer key is on my phone, which I am not supposed to have out. I check anyway. Sometimes I get three problems done. Sometimes the door opens and my mom needs me for a party of eight and I leave the notebook on a crate of bean sprouts. It is still there when I come back, a little damp.

I have worked every weekend since sophomore year. I am not going to say it taught me who I am. I already knew I could stand up for eight hours. What I know is the sound of the ticket printer when it works, and the sound of paper tearing when it doesn't, and how to wet the rice paper so it doesn't tear, and that the walk-in is a bad place to do derivatives and also the only place. I will keep the Saturday shifts until I leave. After that my mom will have to find somebody else who can read bad handwriting.

b.text:
Since sophomore year, I’ve worked every weekend at my family’s Vietnamese restaurant. It’s a loud place, filled with the smell of fried shallots and the hum of the walk-in. Most days run on a schedule, but sometimes the equipment fails. One Saturday the register died. The screen went black while customers waited. I grabbed a notepad and started writing tickets by hand. My handwriting got sloppy as the rush built up. I kept writing until the system came back online.

We hire help during the summer. A new hire couldn’t figure out the spring rolls. They kept falling apart before frying. I showed her how my grandma taught me to fold the wrapper. One side over the filling, then the sides tucked in tight. It’s about the tension in the paper. She practiced until her fingers stopped shaking.

When the lunch rush ends, I take my break in the cooler. It’s quiet there, just the sound of the compressors. I set down my calculus homework on a crate. I solve for x while the cold air keeps the smell of food away. My hands get stiff but the problems don’t move. By the time I clock out, I head straight home. I have classes Monday morning.

setup: A co-founder is posting a LinkedIn hiring announcement for a first customer support hire to potential applicants and customers.

a.text:
We're hiring our first support person at Ridgepoint.

Right now it's just the three of us founders answering every ticket, and honestly, it's falling apart. We're rotating the inbox between building the product and doing sales calls, response times are slipping, and stuff is getting missed at night and early mornings when dispatchers need us most.

So this isn't a "join our amazing support team" post. There is no team. You'd be person #4 at the company, and you'd be building this with us.

Here's what the job actually looks like day-to-day:

Most of our customers are small trucking dispatchers — usually fleets of 5-25 trucks. They're not super technical, and they're usually contacting us when a truck is waiting and they're stressed.

Your day would be answering tickets over email/chat about things like duplicate loads, reassigning a driver, why an ETA didn't update, or a billing question. A lot of it is quick answers, some of it is getting on a 15-minute screenshare and walking them through it.

When it's quiet, you'd be turning the stuff that's currently just in our heads into help articles, and writing up bugs / recurring requests clearly so we can actually fix them. You'll talk to the same dispatchers every week. You'll know them by name pretty fast.

What we're looking for is someone who's done support before (ideally at a small SaaS company), writes clearly, and is comfortable without a script or a manager telling you exactly what to say. You need to be patient, but also direct when a customer is confused.

It's full-time, remote, Monday-Friday. No 24/7 shifts, no call center stuff — we just need someone who owns the inbox during the day so customers get a fast, helpful answer from the same person.

If that's interesting, DM me here. Tell me a bit about the last support role you had and what kind of tickets you handled. I’ll send you the full details on pay, hours, and benefits — and I’m the one reading every message.

And to our customers who follow me here: this is because you deserve better than the three of us half-awake answering tickets at 11pm.

b.text:
We're hiring our first Support hire at Ridgepoint.

For the last year, the 3 of us (the co-founders) have answered every single support ticket ourselves. It worked when we had 20 customers. It doesn't work anymore. Response times are slipping, things fall through the cracks, and we're context-switching between building the product and helping customers all day.

So we're looking for someone to own this and do it properly.

**What the job actually is, day-to-day:**

Most of our customers are small trucking dispatchers using Ridgepoint to schedule loads. When something isn't working or they can't figure it out, they reach out. Your day will be:

- Answering tickets via email/intercom (expect ~20-40/day right now, mostly troubleshooting — "this load isn't showing," "can't invite a driver," "how do I reschedule this?")
- Getting on quick calls/screenshares when a dispatcher is stuck and typing isn't enough — their work is time-sensitive, so speed and clarity matters
- Reproducing bugs, documenting them clearly, and passing them to our engineers
- Onboarding new companies — walking them through setup and their first loads
- Updating our help docs so customers can self-serve the common stuff
- Telling us what you're hearing. You'll talk to customers more than any of us will — your feedback will directly shape what we build next

This is our first support hire, so there's no playbook to follow. You'll be building it.

**Who this is probably a good fit for:**
- You've done support before and you actually like helping people solve problems
- You can explain technical stuff in plain English without being condescending
- You're organized and can handle a queue going from 0 to 15 overnight
- You're comfortable with a tiny, scrappy startup where everyone wears 5 hats
- You don't need to know anything about trucking — we'll teach you that

Not a good fit if you want a big team with lots of structure. We're 3 people figuring this out.

This is a full-time role, remote within the US. You'll work directly with me and the other two founders every day.

If you're interested, DM me here or email us at [your email here] with a short intro and any relevant experience. No need for a formal cover letter.

And to our customers following along here — thanks for your patience while we got stretched thin. We're excited to fix that.

#hiring #customersupport

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
To Members of the City Council,

My name is [Your Name], and I am the owner and operator of an independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am submitting this testimony for the official record to express my strong opposition to the proposed parking meter rate increase from $0.50 to $1.50 per hour in our downtown district. 

A tripling of parking rates is not a minor adjustment; it is a 200% tax on downtown foot traffic. While municipal budgets face ongoing pressures, penalizing the customers who support local brick-and-mortar storefronts will generate negligible public revenue while inflicting measurable harm on our daily operations.

My business relies on quick, convenience-driven transactions. Our internal point-of-sale data shows that our average customer visit lasts exactly 22 minutes. Under the current structure, the 50-cent one-hour minimum already covers these visits with a reasonable buffer. When a customer stops in to buy a $4.50 latte or a quick bag of roasted beans, adding a mandatory $1.50 parking fee inflates the cost of that short trip by 33%. For routine daily purchases, that friction drives consumers away from downtown corridors and toward strip malls and regional chains with free surface parking.

This concern is not theoretical. We have direct historical precedent for how this policy plays out in our local market. In 2019, when our neighboring municipality implemented a nearly identical rate increase, I tracked our register and transaction counts over a six-week period. During those six weeks, foot traffic dropped by 18%. For an independent business operating on narrow margins, an 18% decline in transaction volume wipes out profitability entirely. 

Furthermore, this proposal fails even on its own terms as a fiscal solution. According to the city’s own downtown financial report, meter revenue accounts for just 4% of the total downtown operational budget. Tripling this rate will not solve the city's structural budget constraints, but it will disproportionately burden the small retail, service, and dining establishments that form the economic foundation of Main Street. We are risking the stability of the 96% of the commercial ecosystem to adjust a line item that represents only 4% of city downtown funding.

Thriving downtowns require accessibility. Increasing parking rates by 200% creates a direct barrier between local residents and the small businesses they want to support. I respectfully urge the council to vote against this proposed increase and instead explore revenue and transit solutions that do not penalize our local commercial base.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]  
Owner, [Coffee Shop Name]  
Main Street

b.text:
To the Members of the City Council:

My name is [Name], and I am the owner of [Coffee Shop Name], a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am submitting this testimony in opposition to the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from fifty cents to one dollar and fifty cents per hour.

The evidence that this increase will hurt small businesses is not theoretical. In 2019, when the neighboring town enacted a similar parking rate hike, I tracked my own register sales for six weeks to see how foot traffic would respond. The result was an eighteen percent drop in customer visits. That figure comes from six weeks of actual transaction data, not from speculation. Nearly one in five customers simply stopped coming through my door after parking became significantly more expensive.

This proposal is particularly misaligned with businesses like mine because of how our customers actually use downtown parking. The average visit to my shop lasts twenty-two minutes. Under the current rate, a customer pays fifty cents for a one-hour minimum, which already covers their stay with nearly forty minutes to spare. If this increase passes, that same twenty-two-minute visit will cost one dollar and fifty cents. We are asking our customers to triple their parking cost for time they do not use.

Furthermore, the city’s own report states that parking meter revenue covers only four percent of the downtown budget. This increase will not meaningfully address our fiscal needs. It will simply triple the burden on short-term parkers for a revenue stream that, by the city’s own accounting, contributes just four cents of every dollar in the downtown budget.

An eighteen percent decline in foot traffic is a proven consequence, not a possibility. A twenty-two-minute visit should not carry a one-dollar-and-fifty-cent parking fee. And a policy that impacts only four percent of the budget is not a financial solution. I respectfully urge the council to reject this proposed rate increase.

Respectfully submitted,  
[Name]  
Owner, [Coffee Shop Name]  
Main Street

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The Barrera wedding got rained out in October.

The ceremony site we'd scouted twice? Underwater. The golden hour portrait spot? A mud pit. And the shot list we'd carefully built over three planning calls? Useless by 2pm.

So we moved everything under the big pecan tree on the property. No plan. No list. Just a couple who trusted me and a tree that had clearly seen a hundred years of Hill Country storms.

Those are some of the best photos I've delivered in 8 years of shooting weddings.

Here's what I've noticed after 250+ weddings: the couples who hand me a rigid shot list get exactly what's on the list. The couples who tell me "capture how it feels" get the images they end up framing.

Shot lists have their place — family groupings, the heirloom details, the moments you'd genuinely regret missing. I always ask for those.

But when a couple gives me room to react to what's actually happening — the rain, the laughter during a botched toast, grandpa sneaking a dance with the flower girl — that's when the magic shows up.

The Barreras didn't get the wedding they planned. They got something better, and the photos prove it.

If you're planning your wedding: hire a photographer whose work you trust, give them your true non-negotiables, and then let them do their job. The best moments of your day haven't been invented yet.

📍 Texas Hill Country
#WeddingPhotography #HillCountryWeddings #TexasWeddings

b.text:
Here's a post for you:

---

The couples who ditch the shot list always end up with the best photos.

I learned this years ago, but it hit differently during the Barrera wedding. Rain forced us to scrap the plan entirely—the ceremony moved under an old pecan tree, the timeline went out the window, and the "must-haves" became irrelevant.

What happened instead? Magic. Unplanned moments between family members sheltering together. The groom helping his bride over muddy ground. Light filtering through those pecan branches in ways no shot list could predict.

The couples I work with who hold their vision lightly—who trust the day to unfold—walk away with images that feel alive and true. Not because I'm capturing what they planned. Because I'm capturing what's actually happening.

Your shot list is a safety net, not a destination. The real photos live in the moments between the boxes you wanted checked.

---

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
**Testimony on Proposed Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Good evening, City Council members. My name is [Your Name], and I am the owner of [Coffee Shop Name], a small independent business on Main Street. I am here to speak against the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour. While I understand the city’s need to generate revenue, this change will disproportionately harm local businesses like mine without addressing the root issues of downtown funding.

In 2019, a neighboring town implemented a similar rate hike, raising their meter fees from 50 cents to $1.25 per hour. Over the following six weeks, I tracked my own register data and observed an 18% decline in foot traffic. That drop directly translated to lost sales, making it harder to cover overhead costs like rent, utilities, and payroll. If this proposal passes, I fear we will see the same trend here—customers deterred by higher costs, choosing to shop elsewhere or avoid downtown altogether.

Most of my customers spend an average of 22 minutes in my shop. Under the current system, the one-hour minimum at 50 cents already covers their visit comfortably. Doubling or tripling the rate for such a short stay feels punitive, not practical. My customers aren’t the issue—many are regulars who support multiple small businesses in a single trip. If parking becomes more expensive, they may consolidate their visits or opt for areas with free parking, reducing the vibrancy of our downtown.

I also reviewed the city’s own report on parking meter revenue, which states that meter fees currently cover just 4% of the downtown budget. This proposed increase won’t solve the larger funding gaps—it will only place an undue burden on the small businesses and customers who keep our downtown alive. If the goal is to support local commerce, we should explore alternatives that don’t risk driving customers away.

I urge the City Council to reconsider this rate hike and instead focus on solutions that strengthen, rather than strain, our small business community. Thank you for your time and consideration.

b.text:
Testimony to the City Council Regarding the Proposed Parking Meter Rate Increase

My name is [Name], and I own [Coffee Shop Name] on Main Street. I'm here today because I believe this proposed increase—from 50 cents to a dollar fifty an hour—will do real damage to the businesses this council has spent years trying to support, and I don't think it will accomplish what it's meant to.

I want to start with the city's own numbers, because they matter more than anyone's gut feeling about parking. According to the city's own budget report, meter revenue currently accounts for just 4% of the downtown budget. That is not a rounding error we can ignore, but it's also not a crisis that justifies tripling the rate overnight. If the goal is to shore up downtown finances, a 4% line item is not where that fight should be fought—not at the expense of the small businesses that make Main Street worth visiting in the first place.

I didn't just want to speculate about what this increase might do, so I looked for real evidence. In 2019, [Neighboring Town] raised their downtown meter rates in a very similar jump. I tracked my own register during a comparable six-week stretch after their increase went into effect, because I have a second location there and wanted to understand what we might be facing. Foot traffic dropped 18% over that period. That's not a guess or a worst-case scenario—that's what actually happened when a neighboring town made this exact kind of change. People didn't stop wanting coffee. They stopped wanting to pay more to park for it.

I also want to speak to something more specific to my own shop: the actual behavior of my customers. I've tracked visit times, and the average customer at my counter is in and out in 22 minutes. That means the current 50-cent hour-minimum already comfortably covers their visit, with time to spare. Tripling the rate doesn't change how long someone sits with a coffee—it just triples what they pay for the same 22 minutes. For a customer buying a $4 latte, a $1.50 parking charge on top of that hourly rate starts to feel less like a convenience fee and more like a reason to just stay home.

I understand the city needs revenue, and I'm not asking this council to pretend that budgets balance themselves. But I am asking you to weigh a 4% revenue line against an 18% drop in foot traffic for businesses like mine—businesses that employ your neighbors, pay property taxes, and rely on people being willing to stop downtown for twenty minutes at a time. The data from a nearly identical increase next door tells us plainly what happens when parking gets more expensive than the errand it's meant to serve.

I'd ask the council to consider a smaller, incremental increase, or at minimum, a trial period with real tracking of foot traffic and receipts—not just meter revenue—before committing to a full jump from 50 cents to a dollar fifty. Main Street businesses can adapt to gradual change. We cannot easily recover from an 18% drop in customers over a few short weeks.

Thank you for your time and for considering the people who will actually feel this decision on the ground, one 22-minute visit at a time.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/ I raised prices 40% overnight and lost 30 of my 140 customers in a week. Here's what happened and what I changed.

2/ Quick context: I'm a solo founder building Tallyup, a small subscription tool for gym owners to track member retention. I have 3,100 followers here. I had 140 paying customers.

3/ I thought we were underpricing. So one evening I updated the pricing page, raised every plan by 40%, and pushed it live. No grandfathering. No heads-up.

4/ Within a week, 30 customers cancelled. Revenue didn't go up—it went down. It was the worst week I've had as a founder.

5/ What I got wrong: I increased price without increasing perceived value. I gave no notice. And I treated loyal customers the same as strangers, which broke trust.

6/ What I changed first: Existing customers are grandfathered at their old rate. The new higher price only applies to new signups. No more retroactive billing changes.

7/ I also made a rule for myself: any future price change gets real notice and a clear explanation sent to every customer before it happens.

8/ If I'd done that originally, I think most customers would've understood. Instead, I forced a decision without context.

9/ If you're a SaaS founder thinking about raising prices: grandfather your existing users, explain why, and give them time. A 40% hike might be fair—but only if it comes with respect.

10/ That lesson cost me 30 customers. I'm sharing it so someone else can learn for free.

b.text:
1/ I raised Tallyup’s prices 40% on everyone overnight.

We lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week.

I build a tool that helps gym owners track member retention. This was a painful lesson in my own.

Here’s the mistake—and what I changed.

2/ The mistake wasn’t necessarily charging more.

It was treating a price increase like a switch I could flip, rather than a change customers needed time to consider.

Everyone. Overnight. No transition.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
After a lot of thought, we’ve decided we won’t be taking on custom wedding cake orders anymore.

It’s been a real joy to be part of so many celebrations, and we’re grateful to everyone who’s trusted us with such an important part of their day. But custom wedding cakes take a lot of time beyond the baking itself: consultations, tastings, planning, and all the little details that make each cake yours. Each order adds up to about 14 hours of that time, and with just three of us, we’ve found it’s become more than we can manage alongside everything else.

We also had three wedding cake orders cancelled at the last minute this year. We understand that plans can change, but by then we’d already bought the ingredients, and those costs were difficult for a small shop to absorb.

Most of all, taking on these big projects has been pulling us away from the everyday bakery case—the breads, pastries, and treats many of you stop in for each week. That’s the work that keeps our little shop going, and it’s where we want to put our energy.

This wasn’t an easy decision, and it’s not a reflection on the couples who’ve come to us. We’re thankful for every celebration we’ve been invited into. We’re just making a change that lets us keep doing our best work, and be here for the regulars who make this bakery what it is.

b.text:
Some news that’s been sitting heavy on my mind for a while, and I wanted to tell you myself before you noticed the inquiry form went quiet.

We’re not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore.

I know. For a lot of you, that’s probably the saddest sentence I’ve written here. I’ve made cakes for baptisms, for “just because Tuesdays,” for the couple who got engaged in our shop and came back to tell me. I love that part. But I have to be honest about what it’s been costing us, because pretending otherwise isn’t fair to me, or to Sarah and Mike who are here with me at 4am, or to you.

Each wedding cake used to eat about fourteen hours of my time before it ever touched an oven. Fourteen hours of consultations that stretched into three, tastings that needed to happen on my day off, sketches sent back and forth until we both had whiplash. That’s almost two full workdays, gone, for one cake. And this year, three of those weddings—three!—called off within days of the date. I still paid for the butter and the sugar and the flowers. I still sat with the design. The cake never happened, but the hours did.

Meanwhile, the case at 7am—the croissants, the sourdough, the cinnamon rolls that you grab on your way to work—that’s what actually pays the rent. That’s what keeps the lights on and lets us stay open on Sundays. Every hour I spent sketching fondant peonies was an hour I wasn’t here, with you, doing the work I started this place to do.

I’m tired. We’re all tired. A three-person bakery can’t keep donating two days a week to something that doesn’t keep the ovens running.

So here’s what’s changing: we’re still making celebration cakes. Birthdays, anniversaries, “we survived another school year” cakes. You can order those online, pick them up Saturday morning, no tears required. And if you’re planning a wedding, I’d genuinely love to point you toward some wonderful bakers who do this full-time and have the bandwidth for it—I’ll even write you a list if you ask.

But for us? We’re going back to the bread. The everyday stuff. The reason you walk through our door.

Thank you for understanding. And thank you for keeping us fed, literally and figuratively, all these years. I’ll see you at the counter.

— [Name]

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**A Better Start for Millbrook’s Middle Schoolers**

As the parent of two middle-schoolers in Millbrook, I know the morning routine: alarms, rushed breakfasts, and the occasional reminder that a backpack is still by the door. But the hardest part isn’t getting everyone out on time. It’s asking growing kids to learn when their bodies are telling them they need more sleep.

That’s why I support the proposal to start school at 8:45.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that teenagers get 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night. Sleep isn’t a luxury or a reward for finishing homework; it supports health, attention, and learning. A later start won’t solve every family’s morning challenge, and it won’t guarantee that every student gets enough rest. But it gives students a more realistic chance to arrive ready to learn.

We also have local evidence worth taking seriously. At Lincoln Middle, during the pilot, attendance went up and first-period grades improved. Those results don’t prove that a later start caused every change, but they’re encouraging—and they suggest that first period can be a better experience when students aren’t being asked to function so early.

I understand the concern about buses. Changing school start times affects families, staff, and the transportation schedule, and those details matter. But the proposal before the board already re-tiers the bus routes. So the question isn’t whether the schedule changes; it does. The question is whether we should dismiss a proposal that has addressed the bus issue simply because any change takes adjustment.

As a parent, I’m not asking for a perfect plan. I’m asking the board to weigh the practical inconvenience against the daily reality for students who are expected to concentrate, participate, and learn early in the morning. The Lincoln pilot gives us reason to believe a later start can help.

Next month, the board has a chance to make a decision grounded in student well-being and local experience. I hope members will support the 8:45 start—and give Millbrook’s middle-schoolers a better chance to begin the school day ready for it.

b.text:
**An 8:45 Start Gives Millbrook Students a Better Morning**

As the parent of two middle-schoolers in Millbrook, I know that getting out the door in the morning is not always easy. There are lost shoes, unfinished homework, forgotten water bottles—and, most of all, tired kids. That is why I support the school board’s proposal to move the middle-school start time to 8:45 a.m.

This is not about giving students permission to sleep until noon. It is about recognizing how much sleep adolescents actually need. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later so that students have a better chance of getting the 8½ to 9½ hours of sleep recommended for their age group. An 8:45 start would bring Millbrook in line with that guidance.

We already have local evidence that a later start can help. During the pilot at Lincoln Middle School, attendance improved, and first-period grades went up. Those results matter. They suggest that students were not simply arriving later; they were arriving more consistently and were better prepared to learn when they got there.

As a parent, I have seen the difference a rested morning can make. A child who is exhausted is more likely to be irritable, forgetful, and disengaged. A child who has had enough sleep is more likely to participate, manage frustration, and make it through the school day ready to learn. No schedule can solve every academic or family challenge, but starting at 8:45 is a practical step in the right direction.

The most common objection I hear is about buses. That concern deserves attention, but it should not be used to dismiss the proposal. The plan already includes re-tiering the bus routes. In other words, the district is not ignoring transportation; it is working to reorganize the schedule so the later middle-school start can function within the broader system. We should evaluate the details carefully, but we should also judge the proposal as it actually exists—not as if no transportation planning has been done.

Changing the morning routine may take adjustment for families, just as any schedule change would. But our children’s health, attendance, and ability to learn deserve serious consideration. The Lincoln pilot gave us encouraging results, and the AAP recommendation gives us a clear reason to act.

For our middle-school students, 8:45 is not too late. It may be just in time.

Admin work: I set up accounts, matched rosters to our SIS, wrote a one-page internal guide because your help docs assumed people knew what a section code was, and figured out which features my department would actually use versus which ones looked good in a demo. I know where teachers get stuck, because I got stuck there.

What I'd bring that a non-teacher can't: credibility. When I tell a department chair this will save her team time on grading, she'll believe me, because I've done the grading. I also know what a bad week in April looks like and why nobody's answering your email.

For two years, I was [Company Name]'s power user before I ever imagined working here. I'd welcome the chance to talk about how my classroom experience translates directly to your CS team's goals.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The best wedding photos never come from a checklist. 

After eight years of shooting full-time in the Texas Hill Country, I’ve seen my share of "must-have" shot lists. But here is an industry truth: the more a couple clings to a rigid Pinterest checklist, the more they miss out on the actual magic of their day. 

When you force a photographer to constantly look down at a piece of paper, they miss the fleeting, real-life moments happening right in front of them. 

Case in point: The Barrera wedding. 

Mother Nature had other plans for their outdoor ceremony, and the skies absolutely opened up. Instead of panicking because our timeline and "perfect" photo list were out the window, we adapted. We moved the entire celebration under the shelter of a giant pecan tree. 

Because the Barreras trusted the process—and ditched the rigid expectations—we captured some of the most raw, honest, and breathtaking images of my entire career. The rain, the intimacy of everyone crowding under the branches, the sheer joy of the unexpected—you can't plan that. And you certainly can't put it on a checklist. 

For the couples planning their big day: Hire vendors whose work you love, and then give them the creative freedom to do what they do best. The magic happens in the unplanned moments.

For my fellow wedding industry pros: How do you handle the "shot list" conversation with your clients?

b.text:
The couples who hand me a 40-item shot list are almost never the ones who end up with photos they cry over.

I say this with love, because I understand the impulse. You're spending real money, you've been on Pinterest for eight months, and a list feels like insurance. I get it.

But here's what a shot list actually does: it turns me into a task-completer instead of someone watching your day for the thing nobody planned.

The Barrera wedding is the example I come back to.

Outdoor ceremony, Hill Country, and the sky opened up about ninety minutes before go time. We lost the aisle, the arch placement, the golden hour spot I'd scouted twice. Everything moved under an old pecan tree on the property because it was the only cover big enough to hold everybody.

Nobody had a plan for that. There was no list item that said "bride laughing while her uncle holds a tablecloth over her head."

That's the photo they printed big.

What made it work wasn't my genius. It was that they'd told me early on they trusted me to read the day, and they hadn't handed me a checklist I'd feel obligated to chase while the actual moment was happening ten feet to my left.

So my honest advice, after eight years and a few hundred weddings:

Give your photographer the non-negotiables. The family combinations. The heirloom detail. Grandma, because grandma might not be here next year. Those matter and I want them written down.

Then stop. Leave the rest open.

The best frames from any wedding I've shot were not on a list. They couldn't have been. Nobody knew they were coming.

And to my vendor friends — you already know this. The rain plan weddings are the ones we talk about years later.

#weddingphotography #texashillcountry #weddingvendors

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
I didn't know what to expect my first week in the ER, but it wasn't this.

I thought it would be blood and drama and running. It was mostly standing in rooms holding people's hands while the nurses worked, or fetching things I didn't know the names of yet.

On my second day, there was a guy in one of the rooms with a cut on his forearm—nothing serious, just needed cleaning and stitches. His wife was supposed to be there but got stuck on the highway. He was alone, and he was scared. The nurse asked me to hold his hand while she cleaned the wound. So I did. I just sat there and held this stranger's hand and talked to him about his dog while she worked. It was the simplest thing I'd done all week, but it felt like the most important.

Then Thursday happened. I was restocking the supply cart when they called a code in Room 4. My preceptor told me to stay put and keep stocking gauze. I heard them through the curtain—someone counting "one, two, three" over and over, the beep of the monitor, voices getting louder. I kept pulling gauze from the cabinet and lining it up on the counter, trying not to shake. I didn't know what was happening, but I knew I was supposed to be useful. So I kept counting the packs in my head: one, two, three.

Friday was the blood draw. This older guy, diabetic, needed labs. His veins were terrible—I could see them rolling under his skin. I missed three times. I'm talking clean misses. I apologized every time, and he kept saying it was fine, but I could see him wincing. On the fourth try, I got it. Just a little flash of red in the tube, but it was enough. I almost cried in the supply closet after.

I'm only a first-year student. I can't start an IV or read an EKG yet. But I know now that nursing isn't just the big moments. Sometimes it's holding a stranger's hand so he doesn't feel alone. Sometimes it's restocking gauze while someone counts compressions behind a curtain. Sometimes it's trying again when you've already messed up three times.

I want to be the nurse who shows up for those moments. Even the small ones. Especially the small ones.

b.text:
My first week in the ER was not what I expected. I knew it would be busy, but I did not understand how many different kinds of hard could fit into one shift. There were alarms, people calling for supplies, families asking questions, and nurses moving quickly from one room to another. I was nervous the whole first day. I wanted to help, but I was also afraid of getting in the way.

One of the first moments that stayed with me happened during a wound cleaning. The patient was a man who had gotten hurt at work. The nurse was cleaning a deep cut, and he was trying hard not to react, but I could see that he was scared. His wife was supposed to be there, but she was stuck in traffic and had not made it yet. The nurse asked if I could stay by his side.

I held his hand while they cleaned the wound. I did not know what to say at first. I just told him that his wife was on her way and that he was doing a good job. He squeezed my hand every time it hurt. I remember thinking that I had not done anything medical in that moment. I did not place an IV or give medication. But I was still helping. He did not have to be alone while something painful was happening to him. That taught me that nursing is not only about skills. Sometimes it is about being the person who stays.

Later that week, there was a code in the ER. I was not part of the team in the room. I was sent to restock gauze and other supplies nearby. At first, I felt disappointed. I wanted to see what was happening and learn from it. Then I heard the team counting through the curtain. Their voices were steady and loud over everything else in the department.

I stood there with gauze in my hands and listened. It made the situation feel real in a way that class had not. I understood that emergencies do not pause because someone is new or because someone feels ready. Everyone had a job, even if that job seemed small. The team needed supplies ready. They needed the room to keep moving. I learned that being useful does not always mean being at the center of the action. It means doing what needs to be done well, especially when things are stressful.

Another day, I was trying to draw blood from a patient with diabetes and very difficult veins. I missed the first time. Then I missed again. By the third try, I felt terrible. The patient was kind, but I knew he was tired of being poked. I was embarrassed and frustrated with myself. My instructor talked me through it and reminded me to slow down, take a breath, and look again instead of rushing because I was nervous.

On the fourth try, I got it.

I felt relieved, but I also felt humbled. I did not walk away thinking I had mastered blood draws. I walked away knowing that I still have a lot to learn. That patient gave me more patience than I probably deserved that day. I thanked him, and I meant it. He reminded me that every skill I practice is happening to a real person, not just a practice arm in lab.

My first week in the ER showed me that nursing will ask a lot from me. It will ask me to stay calm when I feel nervous, to keep learning when I make mistakes, and to care for people during some of the worst moments of their lives. I know I am only at the beginning of my education. I will miss things, ask questions, and need help. But that week made me even more sure that nursing is where I belong.

I want to become the kind of nurse who can be steady in a crisis, honest when I need to learn, and kind when someone feels scared. Sometimes that may mean holding a stranger’s hand. Sometimes it may mean restocking gauze. Sometimes it may mean trying again after I miss. My first week in the ER taught me that all of those moments matter.

a.text:
# Testimony Regarding Proposed Parking Meter Rate Increase

My name is [Your Name], and I have owned [Coffee Shop Name] on Main Street for [number] years. I am submitting this testimony in opposition to the proposed parking meter rate increase from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour.

I understand the city faces budget pressures, but I believe this rate increase will harm downtown businesses without meaningfully addressing the city's financial needs. I want to present three specific concerns based on data I have gathered and reviewed.

First, I have direct evidence of how parking rate increases affect foot traffic in similar markets. In 2019, the neighboring municipality implemented a comparable parking rate increase. I tracked my sales register data for six weeks before and after that increase. The result was an 18 percent decline in customer visits during that period. My customers are not commuters or all-day parkers—they are coffee drinkers. My data shows the average customer visit is 22 minutes. The current one-hour minimum already covers their parking needs with time to spare. A tripling of the hourly rate will discourage these short-visit customers from coming downtown at all.

Second, I want to address whether this increase actually solves the city's budget problem. According to the city's own parking revenue report, meter revenue currently covers 4 percent of the downtown district budget. Even if this rate increase generates additional revenue, the math is clear: parking meters are not and cannot be the solution to downtown funding gaps. We would be creating a genuine hardship for local businesses and their customers in exchange for addressing perhaps 4 or 5 percent of a much larger problem.

I urge the city council to explore alternative revenue sources that do not penalize people for shopping and dining downtown. Our small businesses depend on accessible, affordable parking to survive.

Thank you for your consideration.

b.text:
Good evening, Mayor and Members of the City Council.

My name is [Name], and I own [Shop Name], a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I've been here for [X] years, and I'm here tonight to ask you to vote against the proposed parking meter rate increase from fifty cents to a dollar fifty per hour.

I want to be clear: I'm not here to tell you that this increase would hurt local businesses in the abstract. I'm here to tell you exactly what it will cost us, because I've watched it happen before.

In 2019, the town next door implemented nearly the same increase we're considering tonight. I tracked my register for six full weeks after that hike went into effect. My foot traffic dropped eighteen percent. Eighteen percent. That wasn't a slow month or a bad weather stretch. That was a direct, measurable response to customers deciding that the cost of parking wasn't worth the trip.

Let me put that number in context. Eighteen percent of my customers is roughly [X] people a week. At an average ticket of [X] dollars, that's [X] dollars a week in lost revenue—money that doesn't go to my suppliers, my employees, or the taxes that fund this city. And I'm one shop. There are dozens of independent businesses on Main Street, and every single one of them will feel that same squeeze.

Now, I understand the argument that a dollar fifty is still a small price to pay. But the issue isn't the total amount. It's the value. My customers average a twenty-two minute visit. The current one-hour minimum already covers them completely. So the rate increase doesn't add convenience or flexibility—it simply charges my regulars an extra dollar for the same parking they're already paying for. That's a pure penalty on the people who keep downtown alive.

Finally, I want to address the stated purpose of this increase. The city's own report shows that meter revenue covers only four percent of the downtown budget. Four percent. Even if we doubled or tripled that revenue, we wouldn't be solving a budget problem. We'd be taxing Main Street for a rounding error.

I'm asking you to reject this increase. I'm asking you to look at the numbers—the eighteen percent drop in foot traffic in 2019, the twenty-two minute average visit, the four percent revenue share—and see that this policy will cost more than it collects. Thank you for your time.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
After roughly 200 interviews for our logistics teams, one specific moment consistently separates strong candidates from the ones we end up fighting to hire.

It happens at the end of the call, right when I ask, "What questions do you have for me?"

The candidates who usually get the offer don't ask about company culture perks or ideal start dates right away. They ask about our last failed project.

Here’s how that conversation usually goes:

Candidate: "What’s the biggest operational project that fell apart here recently?"

Me: "We tried rolling out a new route-optimization tool to three regional hubs last year. The software wasn't ready for our edge cases, drivers hated the interface, and on-time deliveries dipped for two straight weeks."

Candidate: "How did leadership react to that dip? Did they blame the hubs, or did they pivot?"

Me: "We pulled the tool from two hubs, kept it in one to debug, and put two fleet supervisors in the daily product feedback calls until it actually worked."

Candidate: "Good. That tells me failure isn't swept under the rug here, and field feedback actually influences tech decisions. That’s what I needed to know."

Average candidates want to know what success looks like on day one. Top candidates want to know what happens when things go wrong on day thirty. 

When a candidate asks about your worst moments, they aren't trying to catch you in a trap. They're checking for psychological safety, accountability, and how your teams handle pressure.

If you’re interviewing soon—on either side of the desk—don't just talk about the wins. Ask about the mess. You’ll learn more about a company in those five minutes than in the rest of the interview combined.

b.text:
After ~200 interviews, the candidates I actually remember aren't the ones who rehearsed the perfect "tell me about yourself."

They're the ones who ask: "What was the last project here that didn't work?"

I had a finalist do this recently. I told her about the time we rolled out a new WMS at our busiest facility last year. Full executive buy-in, vendor looked solid, ops team trained. Three weeks in, we were losing inbound freight visibility and the floor team was working around the system just to keep moving. We pulled the plug, reverted to legacy at that facility, and spent four months rebuilding the config before retrying.

She didn't flinch or give me a pity nod. She asked: "What was the specific signal that told you it was a configuration problem and not an adoption problem?"

Then: "When the floor team started working around it, how did that feedback actually reach you — through formal channels, or did someone have to go find it?"

The interview flipped. She wasn't checking a box. She was figuring out if we learn from the mess or just blame the vendor and schedule the next rollout.

Anyone can prep for "what's your greatest weakness." Very few people are confident enough to ask how you handle failure before they sign up.

I don't make the hire based on one question. But I absolutely notice the candidates who ask it.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
**Don't Cut the Best Deal This State Has**

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with IBEW Local [___]. The state is proposing a 15 percent cut to apprenticeship funding, and the case against it comes down to simple math.

Twenty-four apprentices started in my cohort. Twenty-one finished, and all 21 are working journeyman jobs today. That's almost nine out of ten people who walked in the door and walked out with a career. Find me a four-year school with that record.

Now the money. An apprentice starts at around $19 an hour. That's a real paycheck from day one, not a loan you spend twenty years paying back. If somebody comes into this program on food stamps or other assistance, they're off it fast, because $19 an hour beats a benefits check. Journeymen top out around $46 an hour — close to six figures a year at straight time. Every one of us pays taxes the whole way through and keeps paying them for an entire career.

Here's the number that should end this debate. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. The average public subsidy per four-year graduate who finishes is about $48,000. Both numbers only count people who actually finish, so it's an honest comparison. For the price of one four-year grad, this state could put more than three apprentices through — three workers who earn while they learn, pay taxes years sooner, and finish with zero debt.

So what does a 15 percent cut buy? Fewer seats in apprenticeship programs. Longer waitlists. Fewer electricians, plumbers, and linemen in a state that already can't fill the trade jobs it has. That's not saving money. That's moving the cost somewhere else — from training programs to unemployment lines, from paychecks back to assistance rolls.

I understand the state has a budget to balance. But when you have to cut, you don't cut the program that gives taxpayers the best return per dollar.

This isn't a knock on college. Some jobs need a degree. This is about a program with a near-90 percent completion rate that takes people from $19 an hour to $46 an hour and costs a third of the alternative. A program like that doesn't deserve a 15 percent cut. It deserves protecting.

If you're a legislator reading this, the math is right in front of you. Apprenticeship funding is the cheapest workforce program this state runs, and it works. If you're a member reading this, make sure your representative sees these numbers. Call their office and tell them plainly: hands off apprenticeship funding.

Everything around you was wired, piped, and built by somebody who learned a trade. Cut this funding and there will be fewer of us to do it next time.

[Your Name]
Third-Year Apprentice, IBEW Local [___]

b.text:
**Keep Our Apprenticeships Funded: Why a 15% Cut is Bad Math for Our State**

As a third-year electrical apprentice with our local IBEW, I see every day how much this program changes lives. That is why the state’s proposed 15% cut to apprenticeship funding is so concerning. I’m not an English professor, and I’m not going to use fancy political talk to make my point. I’m just going to use the real numbers, because the numbers don’t lie.

Let’s start with how successful these programs actually are. In my own cohort, 24 of us started the program together. Out of that group, 21 finished and are working as journeyman electricians right now. That is a massive success rate. We aren’t just sitting in a classroom; we are out on job sites building our communities, keeping the lights on, and powering our state's economy.

The financial impact on the state is also immediate. We start out making around $19 an hour, and we top out around $46 an hour once we become journeymen. Because we earn a solid living wage from day one, apprentices get off state assistance programs fast. We don’t need taxpayer help to buy groceries or pay rent because our careers give us the independence to support ourselves. Instead of taking from the system, we are paying into it through taxes right away.

Now let’s talk about what we cost the taxpayers compared to other paths. The total public cost for an apprentice who finishes their program is about $14,000. Compare that to a four-year college graduate, where the average public subsidy is about $48,000. 

For less than a third of the cost of a college degree, the state gets a highly skilled, licensed professional who is ready to work on day one without a mountain of student debt. You won't find a better return on investment anywhere. 

To our state legislators: cutting our funding by 15% is not saving money. It is hurting a program that actually works, costs the taxpayers very little, and puts people directly into the middle class. We are the ones building our schools, hospitals, and power grids. 

Please don’t cut the funding that keeps our state running. Leave our apprenticeship budget alone so we can keep doing our jobs.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
**What a 22 Percent Hike Costs a Family Farm**

Sixty percent. That's how much of my corn and soybean ground I got in before the late-May prevented planting deadline this spring. The other 40 percent sat under water while the rain kept coming — not a choice, just a wet May.

This year, the bill for that came with a 22 percent markup.

USDA raised the prevented planting base rate 22 percent in our region. On my operation, that's roughly $46,000 in extra premium this year — paid into a coverage system for acres where I will harvest nothing. Prevented planting is supposed to be the tool that keeps a disaster spring from becoming a disaster year. Instead, this spring it became a $46,000 line item on top of a crop I never got to plant.

And the acreage caps make it worse. They limit how much prevented planting coverage an operation can carry, which sounds like a reasonable guardrail until you run the numbers. A large operation a few miles over spreads the same 22 percent increase across thousands of acres and multiple policies — the hike is a rounding error per acre. A family farm hits the cap almost immediately, which means every unplanted acre beyond it is effectively uninsured against the very increase meant to fund the coverage. The bigger the operation, the more the cap shields it. The smaller the operation, the harder it gets hit, proportionally. That is backwards, and it is why I am asking you to support SB 214.

SB 214 fixes the acreage cap so prevented planting coverage works as a genuine risk management tool for the farms that depend on it, instead of a penalty that scales against the family operations it was built to protect. I'm fourth generation on this ground. I've filed prevented planting claims in wet years before. Never has the math felt this punitive, and never has it felt this tilted against farms like mine.

If you farm, call your senator and your representative this week and tell them to move SB 214. If you don't farm but you eat — and you do — the same ask stands. The 22 percent hike is already locked in for this year. The cap is the part we can still fix.

— [Name], fourth-generation farmer, [County]

b.text:
### 22%—and Then the Cap

By the late-May planting deadline, I had only 60% of my soybean and corn acres planted. It simply would not stop raining. The remaining 40% of my acres ended up in prevented planting.

USDA then raised the prevented planting base rate in our region by 22%. For my operation, that increase adds about $46,000 to this year’s premium bill.

That is not a percentage on a piece of paper. It is real money, and it is money I budgeted on one number and now have to pay on another.

The 22% increase is one issue. How that increase is applied under the acreage caps is another—and for family operations like mine, it is the bigger issue.

The caps limit how many acres on an operation can receive the full prevented planting rate. On a smaller family farm, prevented planting can represent a much larger share of total acreage. That means more of the farm is affected by the cap, and the higher rate translates into a disproportionately larger increase in premiums.

The larger operation nearby has more total acres, so the same cap covers a smaller proportion of its crop. Both operations can be dealing with fields too wet to plant, but the cap does not affect them in the same way proportionally.

That is why a 22% increase produces a particularly heavy hit on our farm. The rate goes up for everyone. The cap determines how much of that increase actually reaches the operation.

The base rate should reflect the real cost and risk of prevented planting. But a rate increase that falls disproportionately hard on family farms is not an outcome we should accept. Our soybean and corn operations are not small because they lack commitment to the land. They are small because that is what we have.

SB 214 would fix the acreage cap so that a higher prevented planting rate does not penalize smaller operations simply for being smaller. It is a straightforward correction to a rule that works against many of the family farms that are the backbone of our rural communities.

I urge our state legislators to support SB 214. And if you are a farm bureau member in this county, I ask you to contact your state senator and representative and let them know where you stand.

The numbers are clear: only 60% of my acres planted, a 22% rate increase, and about $46,000 in added costs. The cap is why that $46,000 hurts our operation more than it hurts the larger farm down the road.

The fix is simple. The consequences of leaving the cap in place are not.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**Let’s Give Millbrook Students a Later Start**

By the time my two middle-schoolers get out the door each morning, I’ve usually said “hurry up” more times than I care to admit. Some mornings they’re dragging, and I’m not sure another reminder about bedtime would fix it. That’s one reason I support the school board’s proposal to start school at 8:45.

This isn’t about letting kids sleep in for the sake of it. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. Teenagers’ sleep patterns change as they grow, and many have a hard time falling asleep early even when they put their phones away and try to do everything right. We can keep teaching good bedtime habits while also recognizing that the current schedule works against them.

I was especially interested in the results from the Lincoln Middle pilot. Attendance went up, and so did first-period grades. Those are two things parents and teachers notice. A pilot doesn’t answer every question about what will happen across the district, but it gives us a better starting point than guesses about whether a later bell might help.

The bus schedule is a fair concern. Many families plan their whole day around pickup and drop-off times, and a change that looks simple on paper can be complicated at the kitchen table. But the board’s proposal already re-tiers the bus routes to make the new start time possible. We should look closely at the details, ask where the gaps are, and make sure families get clear schedules well before the first day. We shouldn’t treat transportation as a reason to dismiss a plan that has already taken transportation into account.

There will be other adjustments, too. After-school activities, childcare, and parents’ work hours matter. I hope the board keeps listening to the people who will have to make those arrangements, especially families with less flexibility. Supporting an 8:45 start doesn’t mean pretending the change will be effortless.

It means deciding that a better school morning is worth the work. I’ve read the proposal closely, and I think the board has made a reasonable case for moving ahead. Lincoln Middle’s results are encouraging, and the AAP’s recommendation gives us good reason to take them seriously.

Next month, I hope the board votes yes. My kids may still need an occasional “hurry up.” But they deserve a school day that gives them a better chance to arrive awake and ready to learn.

b.text:
I have a 12-year-old who cannot find his backpack at 7 a.m. I have a 13-year-old who fell asleep in first period last Tuesday. I love them both, and I am asking the school board to vote yes on the 8:45 start time.

If you've parented a middle-schooler, you know the mornings. The alarm goes off and you're watching a teenager try to fold a shirt and remember their name at the same time. It isn't laziness. Their bodies are genuinely fighting them. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., because adolescent sleep cycles shift — teenagers physically cannot fall asleep early enough to get the rest they need before an 8 a.m. bell. The AAP puts the recommended nightly sleep at 8.5 to 9.5 hours. Do the math from a 7 a.m. wake-up and you get the picture most of us are already living at our kitchen tables.

We don't have to guess whether later starts help. Lincoln Middle ran a pilot last year, and two numbers stand out: attendance went up, and first-period grades went up. That isn't a theory. That's our neighbors' kids, in a school like ours, showing up more and learning more in the very class that used to feel like a sleep study.

I know the bus question is on a lot of minds. The proposal already accounts for it. The transportation team re-tiered the routes, which means a staggered pickup schedule replaces the old one-size-fits-all grid. It's not a hidden cost or an afterthought — it's built into the plan. Parents who want the details can see the new tier map at the district office. Reasonable people can disagree about specific tweaks, but "the buses won't work" is not a reason to deny a generation of kids the sleep their doctors say they need.

I am not a sleep researcher. I am a parent who has watched two children drag themselves through early-morning classes and come home too wiped out to do anything but stare at a screen. The board has a chance next month to fix that. Vote yes on 8:45.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
After eight months of using the Corlane SM6 stand mixer almost every single day to prep sourdough for my weekend farmers market stand, I finally have a definitive answer on whether it’s worth the price tag. 

Let’s start with the motor, because that is where this machine truly shines. If you bake bread, you know the ultimate stress test is a stiff bagel dough. The Corlane handles a double batch of bagel dough without a single stutter, stall, or terrifying gear-grinding noise. It just churns through it like a champion. For heavy, low-hydration doughs and massive batches of market prep, the raw power is undeniably impressive.

But it is not a perfect machine, and for $429—which is $80 more than the equivalent bowl-lift KitchenAid—the flaws are genuinely irritating. 

First, the hardware is a bit finicky. A few months in, the bowl lift lever developed a terrible squeak. I now have to hit the mechanism with WD-40 about once a month just to keep it operating smoothly. 

The much bigger issue, however, is the dough hook. The stock hook that comes in the box is inexplicably short for how deep the bowl is. It clears the bottom by far too much, leaving a thick layer of unmixed flour and water sitting in the base of the bowl. I ended up having to buy a third-party dough hook just to make the machine usable for my daily bread prep. When you are already paying a premium over the standard KitchenAid, having to immediately buy aftermarket parts to fix a glaring design flaw is a tough pill to swallow.

**The Verdict**

Buy the Corlane SM6 if you are kneading heavy bread doughs every single week. The motor easily outpaces the competition and will save you from burning out a lesser machine. 

Skip it if you are mostly whipping up cookies, cake batters, or the occasional single loaf of bread. Between the squeaky lever, the poorly designed stock dough hook, and the $429 price tag, it is absolutely not worth the extra $80 over a KitchenAid for casual or sweet baking. Save your money.

b.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8 Months of Market Sourdough Later

I bought the Corlane SM6 in February because my old mixer died mid-batch two weeks before market season and I was hand-kneading twelve loaves' worth of dough on my counter at 5 a.m. I've now run it almost every day for eight months, mostly on high-hydration sourdough, plus a weekly double batch of bagels, which is the stiffest dough I make. Here's where I've landed.

## The motor is the whole reason to buy this

A double batch of bagel dough is roughly 2.2 kg of very low-hydration dough. It is the test that killed my last mixer and made my sister's KitchenAid smell like a hot electrical outlet. The SM6 has never stalled on it. Not once. It doesn't slow down, doesn't walk across the counter, doesn't get more than warm to the touch on the housing. I can run it on speed 2 for eight straight minutes and it sounds the same at minute eight as it did at minute one.

Same story with sourdough, which is easier on the motor but harder on patience because I do long mixes for gluten development. Fifteen minutes of continuous kneading on a 2 kg batch, four or five times a week, for eight months. Nothing has burned, stripped, or loosened. If you knead heavy dough on a real schedule, this is the part that matters, and it delivers.

## The bowl-lift lever squeaks, and it will keep squeaking

Around month two, the lever that raises and lowers the bowl started squeaking. Not a subtle squeak, a full metal-on-metal complaint every time I move it. A shot of WD-40 on the pivot fixes it completely for about a month, then it comes back. I've done this six times now.

It's not a functional problem. The lift still locks in firmly and the bowl doesn't drop under load. But on a $429 machine I shouldn't be maintaining a lubrication schedule for a lever, and it's the kind of thing that would drive me up the wall if I used this in a quiet kitchen instead of one with a radio going.

## The included dough hook is wrong for the bowl

This one actually annoys me. The SM6 has a deep bowl, which is great for capacity, but the dough hook that comes in the box doesn't reach far enough down. With a smaller batch, say a single loaf, the hook spins above a layer of flour and dough that just sits on the bottom. I had to stop and scrape every couple of minutes, which defeats the point of a mixer.

I ended up buying a third-party spiral hook, about $30, that's roughly an inch longer and actually reaches the bottom. With that hook, the machine is excellent. Without it, I'd call small-batch kneading unreliable. Budget for the replacement hook as part of the purchase price. Corlane should be shipping the right one.

## Price

$429. The equivalent bowl-lift KitchenAid is $349, so you're paying about $80 more, plus the $30 for a hook that works, so call it $110 more all in. That's real money.

## Verdict

**Buy it if you knead heavy dough every week.** Bagels, high-volume sourdough, anything stiff or over 1.5 kg at a time. The motor is genuinely a class above what I've used at this price, and after eight months of daily abuse there's no sign of it wearing down. The squeaky lever and the too-short hook are irritating, but they're irritating in a machine that does the hard job better than anything else I've owned. I'd buy it again tomorrow.

**Skip it if you're mostly doing cookies, cake batter, whipped cream, and the occasional loaf of bread.** None of that comes close to stressing the motor, so you're paying $110 extra for headroom you'll never use, and you'll still get the squeak and the bad hook. Get the KitchenAid and put the difference toward a good scale or a Dutch oven.

That's it. It's a dough machine. If you're a dough person, it's worth the money. If you're not, it isn't.

setup: A co-founder is posting a LinkedIn hiring announcement for a first customer support hire to potential applicants and customers.

a.text:
We're hiring our first support person at Ridgepoint.

Right now it's just me and my two co-founders answering every ticket ourselves, in between building product. It worked when we had 20 customers. It does not work now.

Response times are slipping and we're context-switching all day. So we need help.

What the job actually is day-to-day:

Ridgepoint helps small trucking dispatchers schedule loads. Our users are not tech people. They're in a truck stop office or on the phone with a driver, trying to get a load covered. When something's confusing, they need an answer fast.

You'll be on email + chat (we use Intercom), ~30-40 conversations a day. A lot of it is the same 10-15 questions: how to add a driver, fix a time, reschedule a load, invite a teammate. Sometimes you'll jump on a quick Zoom to walk someone through it.

You'll also be our eyes and ears. If three customers hit the same bug, you'll flag it to us in Slack with the examples so we can fix it. And you'll help keep our help articles up to date when we ship stuff.

Hours are roughly 9-5 CT weekdays, remote in the US. You'll usually have one of us founders on call if you get stuck, but day-to-day you’ll own the inbox.

No SaaS support experience required, but you need to be patient on the phone with non-technical users, write clearly, and stay calm when someone's frustrated because their driver is waiting.

If this sounds like you, DM me here or email me at [your email] with a little about yourself. No cover letter needed.

And if you know someone great, tag them below.

b.text:
We’re hiring Ridgepoint’s first customer support person.

Until now, the three founders have answered every ticket ourselves. That helped us learn quickly, but it’s no longer working—for us or for customers who deserve faster, more consistent help.

What the job actually looks like:

- Responding to dispatchers who have questions or run into problems scheduling loads
- Reproducing issues and separating user confusion from product bugs
- Helping customers get unstuck by email and, when useful, over the phone
- Writing and improving help documentation
- Spotting recurring problems and bringing clear feedback to the founders
- Creating the basic support processes we don’t have yet

This is our first dedicated support hire, so it isn’t a job where you’ll inherit a polished playbook. You’ll help build it. You’ll also work directly with all three founders and have meaningful input into the product.

You don’t need trucking experience, but you do need to be patient, clear, organized, and comfortable learning how small dispatch operations work. Experience supporting a SaaS product is a plus.

If that sounds interesting, send me a message with a little about yourself and why this role caught your attention.
